en: Chapter 1:
Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma. (MS 1.1.1)
Those words which are well-known in the world for particular meanings, these [should be used] as far as possible.

It should be understood that these [words] have precisely those meanings as found in the Sūtras; their meaning is not to be imagined through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and the like, nor is it to be defined by technical convention (*paribhāṣā*).

For in this way, the Vedic sentences themselves are explained by them. Otherwise, both the Vedic sentences would have to be explained and their own constituent word-meanings would also have to be explained—this would result in an excessive burden of effort.

[Otherwise] it would follow [that the word is meaningless]. In common usage, this word *atha* is observed to signify the commencement of what follows immediately after what has preceded. However, nothing preceding is perceived here. Yet there must be something [preceding], upon whose existence the desire to know Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) appropriately follows immediately. For it is thus conceived as having a well-known meaning.

[It] exists; that [is] indeed the study of the Veda, for when that exists, it (the desire to know dharma) is possible. This is not so. It is appropriate to desire to know dharma after other actions as well, even before the study of the Veda.
It is said: the Teacher employed the word "atha" with reference to that desire to know dharma which is not possible without the prior study of the Veda. How so?
A manifold investigation of Vedic statements will be undertaken here. Furthermore, we do not at all receive an injunction here prohibiting the inquiry into *dharma* prior to the study of the Vedas;
for this single sentence does not prohibit the inquiry into *dharma* before the study of the Vedas.

Furthermore, [the author] will later explain the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*). For in that case, the sentence would be split; for the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*) of this [passage], which prohibits the desire to know dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) prior to the study of the Vedas, is one thing, while the mode of expression of the same passage, which teaches immediate succession after [the study], is another.
[The phrase is: "Having studied the Vedas... (*vedān adhītya*).

In one [text], immediate sequence is prescribed while being restated, whereas in the other, it is the reverse. Furthermore, because the meaning is one, he will state that there is a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*).
However—
When one has studied the Veda, two things present themselves:

one must either return from the teacher's house or investigate the statements of the Veda. In this regard, this instruction is for the purpose of thinking: "May he not return from the teacher's house;
rather, how might he investigate the statements of the Veda?"
If this is so, then the study of the Veda cannot indeed precede the inquiry into Dharma.
For they hand down this traditional injunction: "Having studied the Veda, one should perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*).

And here, one who, having studied the Veda and being about to bathe, desires to inquire into Dharma would transgress this sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). Now, the sacred tradition is certainly not to be transgressed.

To this it is said: We shall transcend this tradition. By not transcending it, we would render the Veda—which is actually meaningful—meaningless. For its purpose is clearly seen to be the instruction of ritual action (*karman*). And the venerable ritualists do not declare that a fruit [accrues] from the mere recitation of it. Even as for that which they seem to declare, [it is merely figurative].

In that regard as well, [the author] will state that it is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) according to the principle: "In the case of substances, preparatory rites, and actions, because they exist for the sake of another, the mention of a fruit should be considered an *arthavāda*" (*JS* 4.3.1). Nor is this immediate succession after bathing prescribed for one who has studied the Veda; for there is no word here that expresses immediate succession. The suffix *-ktvā* is traditionally taught to denote anteriority in time.

It does not [mean] "immediately after" (*ānantarya*). For if it meant "immediately after," the visible purpose of Vedic study would be contradicted. However, this meaning could be obtained through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Moreover, this bathing is not enjoined for an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*); rather, by secondary indication, it signifies the conclusion of the restrictive observances such as bathing at the same time as the completion of Vedic study.
They say, "Having studied the Veda, one should bathe;
do not return from the teacher's house"—this is solely to avoid the contingency that [the study] has no unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
Therefore, having first completed the study of the Veda, dharma should subsequently be investigated.
Such is the force of the word *atha*. We do not say that the inquiry into dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) should not be undertaken immediately after any other action;

rather, the meaning of the word *atha* is that having studied the Veda, one should not perform the ritual bath (*snāna*) in haste, but rather the dharma should be inquired into immediately thereafter.
The word "ataḥ" (therefore) indicates what has preceded for the purpose of stating a reason, just as one might say: "This country is secure and well-supplied with food;
therefore, I dwell in this country. In the same way, it is understood that the Veda having been studied is the reason for the desire to investigate Dharma.

Immediately after this, one should desire to know Dharma; such is the force of the word *ataḥ* (therefore). For indeed, one who has not studied the Veda would be unable to investigate the Vedic sentences for the sake of Dharma.
Therefore, for this reason, one should desire to know Dharma immediately after [the study of the Veda]; such is the meaning of the word *ataḥ*.
The desire to know dharma is *dharmajijñāsā*; for that is indeed the wish to know it. Furthermore, how is it to be investigated?
What is dharma, and what are its characteristics?
What are its means of accomplishment,
what are the fallacious means of accomplishment,
and what is its purpose? In that regard, what is dharma?
"How is it characterized?"—this has been explained by a single aphorism: "Dharma is a matter characterized by an injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo ’rtho dharmaḥ*).
What are its means of proof, and what are the fallacious means of proof?
"And for what purpose [is it]?"—this is addressed by the definition of the remainder (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).

Wherein lies the supremacy of the Person (*puruṣa-paratva*), or where is the Person subordinate? This aphorism, "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*), is the summary of these propositions.
Is Dharma well-known or not well-known? If it is well-known, [then...]
It is not an object of inquiry;
moreover, if it were unestablished, it would be even less so. This is that very point.

The inquiry into Dharma would be purposeless; or rather, it is purposeful. For there are many learned people who hold conflicting views regarding Dharma; some declare one thing to be Dharma, while others declare another.
One who acts without such inquiry, adopting just any [view], might suffer failure and encounter misfortune. Therefore, Dharma ought to be investigated.
25*. For we maintain the thesis that it indeed unites the person with the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
This is now explained: [NOTES]

Dharma is a beneficial purpose characterized by Vedic injunction.

They say that *codanā* is a statement that impels one toward action; for it is observed [in common usage] that "I am doing this because I was urged by my teacher. That by which something is characterized is a *lakṣaṇa*; for they say, "Smoke is the *lakṣaṇa* of fire. That which is characterized by such [a statement]—

We maintain that this [Vedic] meaning connects a person with the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). For it is *codanā* alone that is capable of making known such matters as what has been, what is, what will be, the subtle, the hidden, and the remote;
no other sense organ whatsoever can do so.
But surely, an injunction might state even an object that is not so [as it is],
just as any common worldly statement such as "there are fruits on the riverbank" may be true,
and it may also be false.
It is said: this which is stated—that it both speaks and is false—is a contradiction. "It speaks" means it causes one to understand;
that is, it becomes the cause for one who is understanding. And when that which has become the cause exists, one understands.

He explains: If it is understood from the injunction that heaven results from the *agnihotra*, how can it be said that it is not so? Or, if it is not so, how is it understood? To say that one understands an object that does not exist is a contradiction.

Furthermore, from this statement, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," it is not understood with doubt as to whether heaven exists or does not exist. Nor could that which is understood with certainty be false; for that which, having arisen, perishes [and one realizes] "this is not so" [is false].
That is a false cognition. Yet it does not undergo subversion at another time, in another person, in another state, or in another place; therefore, it is not false. Therefore, it is not false.
As for worldly speech, if it comes from a trustworthy person or concerns an object within the range of the senses, [it is likewise not false].

That is indeed not false. However, that which comes from an untrustworthy person, or that which concerns a matter beyond the reach of the senses, originates from human intellect and is not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*). For it is impossible for a person to know such a thing except through verbal testimony. If it is argued that it was understood from another human statement, that too is equal to the first. In matters of this kind, the word of a human being does not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge.
It is like the speech of those blind from birth regarding the distinctions of form.
But surely, instruction is not possible for those who lack knowledge. Yet Manu and others have indeed provided instruction. Therefore, [it follows that] persons...
The wise and the learned [know this].
Just as it is understood from the very act of seeing that form is perceived by the eye, so it is said:
[this is] instruction.

For [cognition] arises even from delusion; when there is no delusion, it arises even from the Veda. Furthermore, from a human utterance, there arises the cognition: "This person knows thus," but not necessarily, "The object is thus. Indeed, the cognition arising from a human-made statement can even be erroneous. However, there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for the falsity of the Vedic word.
[Objection: But will there not be an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*)?
Having observed that human speech is false, one might infer that Vedic speech is likewise false because it shares the common nature of being speech.
This is not so, because they are different; for when one thing is false, [it does not follow that] another is [false].

The falsity of another [statement] must also follow, precisely because it is different [from the true one]. For when Devadatta is dark-complexioned, it does not necessarily follow that Yajñadatta is also dark-complexioned. Furthermore, there is an inference that the Vedic statement is false because it shares the same nature as human speech.

However, the conviction regarding the words of the Veda is based on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). And inference that contradicts direct perception does not constitute a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, that which is characterized by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is the object that brings about the highest good (*śreyaskara*). If this is so, then it is that which brings about the highest good which ought to be investigated; what is the use of an inquiry into *dharma*?
It is replied: That which indeed brings about the highest good—
That very thing is expressed by the word *dharma*. How is this understood?
For when someone performs a sacrifice (*yāga*), people call him "righteous" (*dhārmika*). And whoever is the agent of something, [that thing is named after him].

He is designated by that [action], just as one is called a "cook" or a "reaper. Therefore, that which unites a person with the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is alone expressed by the word *dharma*. This is true not only in common worldly usage, but also in the Veda:
By means of sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice;
those were the first established laws.
Thus they teach the Dharma. Here, both are indicated by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*):
the beneficial and the non-beneficial. What is the beneficial?

That which leads to the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) is the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and so forth. What is "harm" (*anartha*)? That which leads to transgression (*pratyavāya*), such as the *śyena*, the *vajra*, the *iṣu*, and so on. Since harm might otherwise be considered *dharma* in that context, the term "beneficial" (*artha*) is included [in the definition] to prevent this. But how, then, is this [the *śyena* sacrifice, etc. harmful?
For that [act] is indeed violence, and it is [prohibited].
But how is it that this harmful thing is taught as something to be performed? It is said: the Śyena and other such rites are not understood as things to be performed. For one who desires to kill—
"For this is the means to that," such indeed is their instruction. For they prescribe, "One practicing sorcery should sacrifice with the Śyena," but not, "One should practice sorcery."

But surely this sūtra is incapable of expressing these two meanings: that dharma is characterized by injunction (*codanā*) and not by the senses and so forth, and that dharma is a beneficial purpose (*artha*) and not a harmful one (*anartha*). For this is a single sentence; if it were so, it would be split.
It is said: this is the case where the meaning is understood from the sentence alone;
that, however, applies to Vedic [passages], not to the Sūtras. When the meaning has been understood from another source, the Sūtra serves this purpose.
Thus it is understood; and because a single part [of that] is formulated as a rule (*sūtra*), it is called a *sūtra*.

In this regard, it should be understood that these two are parts of two distinct sentences. Alternatively, it is stated that what exists as an object characterized by an injunction (*codanā*) possesses the nature of *dharma*.
62. Thus, [the two] have indeed the same meaning.

The investigation of its cause [is required] because of its unity of purpose. (MS 1.1.3)
We have stated that the knowledge of Dharma has its source in *codanā* (Vedic injunction). That was stated merely as a proposition. Now we shall examine its source:
whether it is *codanā* alone or something else as well. Therefore, it is not yet determined that Dharma is an object characterized by *codanā*.
That is said:

When there is contact of a person’s sense organs with existing objects, the arising of cognition is perception; it is not a means [for knowing dharma], because it is the apprehension of what is already present. (MS 1.1.4)

This is now examined: perception (*pratyakṣa*), for its part, is not a cause [for the knowledge of dharma]. Why? Because it has such a definition: "Perception is the arising of cognition in a person when there is contact of the sense organs with what exists. That cognition which arises in a person when there is a connection between the sense organ and an object is perception. And this object, being something yet to come into being, does not exist at the time of the cognition.
65*. This apprehension occurs of that which exists, not of that which does not exist. Therefore, perception is not the means [of knowing dharma].

This sūtra is not intended to determine any one among these—whether it be the intellect (*buddhi*), the birth [of cognition] (*janma*), or the contact (*saṃnikarṣa*)—as the sole cause. [Rather, it means: when there is a contact between the sense organ and its object...

It is determined simply that "it is not non-existent. If more than one [negation] were determined, the sentence would be split. Furthermore, because inference, comparison, and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) are preceded by perception, they too lack causal authority [in this matter].
Even non-existence (*abhāva*) does not exist, because—
"It exists" (astīti). "The state of being without cause" (akāraṇatvam iti).
But the relationship between a word and its meaning is innate; the knowledge thereof is instruction, which is non-deviant regarding an unperceived object.
That is the means of valid cognition for Bādarāyaṇa, because it is independent. (MS 1.1.5)
By "autpattika" (inborn), we mean "eternal. For "utpatti" (origination) is used figuratively to denote "existence" (*bhāva*). The existence of word and meaning is inseparable from their relation;

it is not a relation that occurs subsequently after both have already come into being. This inborn relation of the word with its meaning is the means of knowing *dharma*—characterized by the *agnihotra* sacrifice and so forth—which is not apprehended through perception or other [ordinary means of knowledge].

How so? For there is an instruction (*upadeśa*). An "instruction" is the utterance of a specific word. And there is no deviation from that knowledge; for that knowledge which has arisen does not become erroneous. And as for that knowledge which has indeed arisen—
It does not contradict [the truth], nor can it be said that "this is not so," just as it is understood.
It does not happen in such a way that it is not understood as "this is thus"; rather,
something else is in his heart.
Otherwise, it would be something else in speech. For one who speaks thus, this contradiction is understood—that it both exists and does not exist.
Therefore, that is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Because it is independent. For this being the case, no other condition (*pratyaya*) or another person need be depended upon; for this is a self-evident realization (*svayaṃpratyaya*). This view of Bādarāyaṇa is set forth in order to honor Bādarāyaṇa, not to exclude his own opinion.
The author of the *Vṛtti*, however, explained this passage beginning with "the investigation of its cause" (*tasya nimittaparīṣṭiḥ*) in a different manner:

"The means of valid cognition (*nimitta*) need not be examined. For perception and the others are well-known means of valid cognition, and the treatise (*śāstra*) is included within them; therefore, that too need not be examined."
But surely, because of deviation, the cause must be examined;
for since mother-of-pearl appears as silver, perception deviates from its object.

And because they are rooted in that [perception], inference and the other means of knowledge are also [included]. One who proceeds without having examined them therein might, as a consequence, be frustrated in his purpose and sometimes encounter misfortune.
This is not so; for that which is perception does not err. That which does err—
That is not perception. What, then, is perception?
When there is contact with that [object], the arising of cognition in a person through the sense-faculties is true perception.
It is the cognition whose object is that [thing].

The arising of cognition in a person when the sense organs are in conjunction with that very [object] is valid perception (*pratyakṣa*). That cognition which has one object but occurs when there is conjunction with another is not perception. But how is it understood that "this [cognition] is in conjunction with that" and "this is in conjunction with another"?
83*. Thus, that which does not involve association with another is association with that [very object]. The opposite of this is association with another. How is this known?

For when one perceives even a mother-of-pearl shell as silver, one thinks, "My eye is in contact with silver. 84*. How is this known? For when one perceives even a mother-of-pearl shell as silver, one thinks, "My eye is in contact with silver."
For where a subverting cognition arises— such as "this is not so;
this is a false cognition"—
that occurs upon contact with something else.

"Its conjunction is the opposite. How is this understood prior to the arising of the subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*), when at that time there is no distinction whatsoever between correct cognition and false cognition? When the mind (*manas*) is impaired, [it is understood].
Either the sense faculty [is impaired] by conditions such as cataracts,
or the external object [is obscured] by its subtlety and so forth; from that arises false cognition.
Correct knowledge occurs when [the causes] are unimpaired. For the contact between the sense organ, the mind, and the object is the cause of knowledge; for when that is absent, there is no knowledge.
A defect inherent within that [contact] is the cause of false knowledge. For when [the causes] are defective, knowledge becomes false. How is this understood?

Because we observe correct cognition once defects have been removed. If it is asked, "How is it known whether [a means of knowledge] is defective or non-defective?"—if, while searching with effort, we do not perceive a defect, we shall consider it non-defective due to the absence of evidence [to the contrary]. Therefore, that whose instrument is defective and that in which there is a cognition of falsity [is invalid].
"That very [cognition] is the incorrect cognition, and not any other.

But surely, every cognition is without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), like a dream. For it is observed that the nature of cognition is to be without an objective basis in a dream; and even for one who is awake, when there is a cognition such as "this is a pillar" or "this is a wall"...
Or rather, it is simply a cognition. Therefore, that too is without an objective basis (*nirālambana*).
It is said in reply: The cognition of a pillar for one who is awake is thoroughly ascertained;
how could it be erroneous?
If it is argued that [the cognition] was previously determined with such certainty even in a dream that there is no difference between the two cases,
we say no; for in a dream, one perceives what is erroneous (*viparyaya*).

If it is argued that because [the falsity] exists in one case, it will also exist in the other due to their similarity— if the dream-cognition is false because it is a cognition, then the waking-cognition ought to be false as well. Or, if [you claim] that the very perception [of falsity] is the cause for such a state [of being false], then...
It cannot be said that this [self] is other than the causal conditions; yet, it is from something else...

The falsity of the cognition of a dream is understood from its contrary [the waking state]. If one asks why, it is because for one who possesses sleep, the weakness of the mind makes sleep the cause of falsity, both at the beginning and at the end of a dream. For one who is in deep sleep (*suṣupta*), there is simply an absence of cognition;
indeed, one is called "deeply asleep" precisely because one is not cognizing. Therefore, the cognition of one who is awake is not... [like that of a dream].
"It is false. But surely there may be a defect in the instruments even for one who is awake?
If there were such a defect, it would be perceived. If you say that it is not perceived even at the time of seeing a dream, that is not so;
for upon waking, one perceives: "My mind was overcome by sleep."
But it is empty. How so?

We do not perceive any difference in form between the object and the cognition; moreover, our cognition is directly perceived. Therefore, we see that there is nothing whatsoever called the "form of the object" distinct from that [cognition].
This might be so.
If cognition were to possess the form of the object, then our cognition would be formless, whereas the external object would possess form;

for that [object] is perceived directly as connected with external space. For a perceptual cognition has the object as its domain, not another cognition as its domain; for it is momentary and does not endure until the time of another cognition.
Regarding the statement "it will remain [in its state]":
if it is argued that this [cognition], while itself arising, is known and makes another object known—just like a lamp—that is not so. For no one perceives a cognition when the object is unknown.

But when [the object] is known, one understands it through inference. In that case, simultaneity is untenable. [Objection: It is only when cognition has already arisen that the object is said to be "known," not when it has not yet arisen; therefore, cognition arises first.

The object is known afterwards. But surely, it is said that an object is known only when cognition has already arisen, not when it has not yet arisen. Therefore, cognition arises first, and the object is known afterwards. True; cognition arises first, but it is not known first. For there is indeed such a case as this: that [an object] is known...
That object is said to be "unknown" [only] when it is not being designated. Furthermore, there is no apprehension of the form of cognition apart from the designation of the object.
Therefore, cognition is not indescribable; and for us, that which is indescribable is perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Therefore, cognition is not perceived.
Furthermore, even if one were to grant that cognition has a single form, it would simply be non-existent;
however, the object, being present and perceptible, would not [be non-existent].

Nor is there identity [of form]. For we infer cognition (*buddhi*) as being indeed devoid of form (*nirākārā*), whereas we perceive the object (*artha*) itself as possessing form (*sākāra*) through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, cognition has the object as its objective support (*ālambana*).

Moreover, the cognition of a cloth occurs only when threads, which are its specific causes, are being employed. Otherwise, even when threads are being employed, a person with unimpaired sense faculties might occasionally have the cognition of a jar; however, this is not the case. Therefore, cognition is not without an objective basis (*anālambana*). Consequently, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not subject to deviation.

Inference (*anumāna*) is the cognition of an object not present to the senses (*asaṃnikṛṣṭe 'rthe*), based on the observation of one part [of a known relationship] by one who has already known the relationship. It is of two kinds: that in which the relationship has been perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣatodṛṣṭasaṃbandha*) and that in which the relationship has been observed through generalization (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭasaṃbandha*).

Among these, inference in which the relationship has been perceived through direct observation is, for example, the cognition of the form of fire from seeing the form of smoke. And inference in which the relationship has been observed through generalization is, for example, [inferring] Devadatta’s arrival at another location as being preceded by his movement.
Even with respect to the sun, there is the recollection of its motion.
Scripture (*śāstra*) is the cognition of an object not present [to the senses] arising from the cognition of words.
Comparison (*upamāna*) also produces a cognition regarding an object not present [to the senses] through similarity,
such as the sight of a *gavaya* producing the recollection of a cow. Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is the postulation of a fact because a seen or heard fact cannot otherwise be accounted for.
Just as, when Devadatta is alive, the perception of his absence from the house leads to the postulation of his unperceived presence outside;

so too, non-existence—which is the absence of a means of valid cognition—is the [means of knowing] the object "it does not exist," which is not in contact with the senses. Therefore, because it is well-established, its defining characteristic need not be further examined.
Now, let it be granted that perception and the other means of valid cognition exist;
however, verbal testimony is not a means of valid cognition. Why?
Because it is not a cause [of knowledge], since it apprehends only what is already present.
Sound is signless and immeasurable. For that which is an object of perception but is not perceived does not exist.

Just as, for example, the horn of a hare [does not exist]. Furthermore, the sense organs of cattle and other animals are perceived; yet, cattle are not perceived immediately after the sacrifice intended for those desiring cattle. Therefore, the sacrifice does not have cattle as its fruit. Moreover, the fruit of an action must exist at the time of the action; for at whatever time...
There is the crushing, and at that time there is the pleasure of crushing.
If it is argued that it will yield fruit at a later time, we say no;
for we understand that the desired fruit does not occur at a later time. Why?
When that [cause] was present, it did not give its fruit; when the fruit arises, that [cause] no longer exists. And being non-existent, how could it give?

Moreover, the fruit is heard to be [attained] at the very time of the action; this is understood from the statement that "the sacrifice is the instrument" (*karaṇa*), and if the instrument has already come into being, [it cannot produce a result at a later time].
"There must be an effect.
Yet we perceive another cause for the fruit that is directly evident.
And when a visible cause exists, it is not possible to postulate an invisible one.
Because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, we maintain that for the Veda, whose transgressions have been observed, even results such as heaven do not exist.
Furthermore, some Vedic statement contradicts what is perceived;
having prescribed the "piling of vessels" (*pātracayana*), it says: "This sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, goes straight to the heavenly world."

[The opponent] points to the visible body [as the self], yet that does not go to the heavenly world; for it is visibly seen to be burned. Nor is there any scriptural injunction stating "this goes. And a statement of this kind, which contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is not authoritative—such as the claim that "gourds sink in water."
Just as in the case of [the statement] "the pressing-stones float," there is a lack of confidence even in injunctions such as the Agnihotra due to that similarity;
therefore, dharma is not an object characterized by injunction.
"But the relationship between a word and its meaning is innate; from that comes the knowledge [of the meaning].

The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the previous position. The relationship between a word and its meaning is not of human origin; from that [relationship] comes the knowledge of the meaning characterized by the *agnihotra* sacrifice and so forth, [which is not attainable] through perception and the other [means of valid cognition].
[This applies] to that which is not being understood. And thus, it is said:
"The correct cognition is characterized by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*).
For if the relationship [between word and meaning] were of human origin, [it would not be authoritative].
If it were a cognition,
its falsity might be suspected; for then it would be a cognition dependent on another.
It might be so. But when the word itself speaks, how can it be false?
For at that time, no understanding is said to come from another person;
rather, [the word] is said to cause comprehension.
It becomes the cause for one who is awakening.
If, moreover, one awakens to the sound by oneself...

How could one say that he has been deceived by saying, "This is not so"? Nor would there be for him a doubt-producing cognition such as, "Is this an injunction or not? Nor is it a false cognition that, at another time, in another place, in another state, or in relation to another person, cannot be subsequently designated [as otherwise].
It occurs as follows: even for one who, having observed the error of another's cognition,
gives rise to an inferential cognition thinking, "He too will err here," that [inferential] cognition is also [sublated] by this direct perception.
That which is contradicted is sublated. Therefore, dharma is characterized solely by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*).
This might be so;
however, there is no [inherent] relation between the word and its object.
There is no connection;
how then could it have human authorship? Why?
Because if there were a connection with the meaning, [it would follow that it is not eternal].

If it were spoken with reference to a relationship characterized by conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*), then upon the utterance of the words "razor" and "sweetmeat," there would be the splitting and the filling of the mouth.
[This is not the case for] the causal and effectual, the instrumental and the consequential, the substratum and the dependent, the sexual union, and so forth.
"But the relations of a word are simply untenable.
It is replied: "The relation that ought to be designated here, that one you do not designate."
[He says: "That relationship between the signified and the signifier which is characterized by the nature of the name and the named.
He asks: "If the word is the signifier, why does it not signify when heard for the first time?"

It is said: In all cases, our own observation is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For we understand something to be a "cognizer" (*pratyāyaka*) upon seeing it produce a cognition (*pratyaya*), not when it is heard for the first time, because at the first hearing one has not yet seen it produce a cognition. The comprehension of meaning occurs only after [the word] has been heard a certain number of times. Just as the eye is not a non-seer simply because it does not illuminate without external light, so too [the word is not a non-cognizer].
If, when first heard, it does not cause comprehension, then the relationship between the word and its meaning must be something produced. Why?
Because by their very nature, these two—the word and the meaning—are unrelated. For we perceive the word in the mouth, [while the meaning is elsewhere].

They designate [them] on the ground that "this is the word, not the object" and "this is the object, not the word. There is also a difference in form: they utter this word "cow," while they comprehend the object possessing a dewlap and so forth.
Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, a relationship between two distinct entities is observed to be produced, as in the case of a rope and a jar. Now, in the word "cow" (*gauh*), what is the word?

"The [phonemes] *ga*, *au*, and the *visarjanīya*," says the venerable Upavarṣa. For in common worldly usage, the word "word" (*śabda*) is well-known to refer to an object perceived by the sense of hearing, and these [phonemes] are indeed perceived by the sense of hearing.
If this is so, then the cognition of meaning is not possible. How so?
Because in the cognition of each individual phoneme...

The meaning is not apprehended. Furthermore, there exists no other entity called a "collection" distinct from the syllables from which the comprehension of meaning could arise. For when the sound *ga* is present, the sounds *au* and the visarga are not; and when the sounds *au* and the visarga are present, [the sound *ga* is not].
At that time, there is no *ga*-sound. Therefore, there exists another word "go" distinct from the *ga*-sound and the other [phonemes], by means of which the comprehension of the object would occur.
If it is argued that the cognition of the object occurs through memory even when the word has disappeared:

No; for since memory (*smṛti*) is also momentary, it is equal [in this regard] to the syllables. There is no fault, because the final syllable, accompanied by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding syllables, is what conveys the meaning. But even so...
The common worldly statement, "We understand the meaning from the word," would be untenable.

It is replied: If it is not tenable, then let it be called untenable. For it does not follow that, merely because a worldly statement is untenable, [the object] is not apprehended through perception and the other means of valid cognition.
The meaning [of such statements] can be accepted;
for worldly utterances are seen to have both coherent meanings and incoherent meanings,
as in the case of "Devadatta," [and so forth].
"Bring the cow," and so forth—these and others such as "ten pomegranates, six cakes," and so forth.
Now, even the authors of the treatises have said this: "One expresses a process consisting of a sequence of prior and posterior stages by means of a verb, as in 'he goes' (*vrajati*)."
Just as the term "he cooks" refers to the period from the commencement until the completion [of the action],
even the words of a treatise author are not sufficient to establish this matter as being without authority.
Moreover, this is certainly not the case.
This is untenable in meaning. [For you claim that] from the syllables (*akṣara*) comes the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), and from the mental impression comes the comprehension of the meaning;
thus, the syllables would be the cause (*nimitta*) for the comprehension of the meaning. This [position of yours] is merely figurative.

If it is argued that this is merely a matter of terminology, we say no: the status of being a cause for the phonemes is not figurative, because [the effect] exists when they exist and does not exist when they do not. Even if it were figurative, [it would still be a cause].

One cannot postulate an object that is not apprehended by perception and the other means of knowledge merely on the grounds that a word might not be secondary (*gauṇa*). For when it is said, "The boy is fire," one does not conclude that the boy is actually a flame simply because the word "fire" must not be secondary. Nor...

The word "cow" (*gośabda*) is not perceived as something distinct from the phonemes *ga*, and so forth, because no perception of difference occurs and there is rather a perception of non-difference. For the phonemes *ga* and the others are indeed directly perceived. Therefore, the word "cow"—the word-unit (*pada*) beginning with *ga* and ending with the visarga—is nothing but the syllables themselves. There is no other entity called a "word" that exists apart from them. [Objection: But even in the hypothesis of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), there is the postulation of something unperceived. [Reply: It is said: in the hypothesis of a [distinct] word, there would be both that [mental impression] and the postulation of a word. Therefore, [it is better to accept that] it is the syllables themselves...
Such is the position. Now, what is the meaning of this word "cow" (*gauh*)?
We say it is the form (*ākṛti*) characterized by the dewlap and so forth. But is it not the case that the existence of such a form is itself yet to be proven?

Being perceptible, it cannot be something to be proven. For indeed, the *rucaka*, the *svastika*, and the *vardhamānaka* are seen through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If you say this is a delusion (*vyāmoha*), [we reply: no.
No. It cannot be said that there is no delusion when there is a perversion of conditions (*pratyaya-viparyāsa*).
Even in the absence of any such external object (*arthāntara*), a cognition (*pratyaya*) arises as a mental construction (*praṅkti*).

If it is argued that [the cognition] "herd" or "forest" occurs just like [the cognition of a person], we say no. This statement you have presented is incoherent. Are you thereby directly contradicting perception by asserting that the cognition of a "forest" occurs even when no forest exists, and that even the trees do not exist?

If this is so, that position has been refuted. Now, is the proponent of the existence of the universal (*ākṛti*) being censured because another tenet of yours is flawed? Even in the case of a forest, for you, it does not exist...

"Thus, the condition of being a forest [example] would follow. Even so, being unable to refute the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), they fall into a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) by refuting another established doctrine (*siddhāntāntara*), because that [refutation] is not a proof.
For he will say: "Let it be flawed..."

If it is faulty, what does it matter whether that which is faulty or not faulty establishes the subject under discussion, or whether my own position is refuted? Furthermore, since a forest is not perceived as something distinct from the trees,
it is understood that the forest does not exist.

If, in the case of a forest, a cognition contrary to its actual existence were to arise due to some other cause, we would understand that this cognition of a "forest" is false, and thereby conclude that the forest does not exist. However, the cognition regarding cows and such things does not undergo such subversion. Therefore, there is a disparity between the two cases. Furthermore, in the case of forests and the like, there is no subversion of cognition at all.

"It is not the case that they do not exist. Therefore, the comparison to a row of trees is irrelevant, for it is not the case that they do not exist. Consequently, the comparison to a row of trees is incoherent.
Thus, Jaimini’s statement that "the word-meaning is the form (*ākṛti*)" is established.
And just as the form (*ākṛti*) is the meaning of a word,
we shall demonstrate this more precisely below.
Now, what is the relationship (*saṃbandha*)?
When a word is understood, its meaning is understood;

however, it has already been established previously that this [word] is produced. Therefore, we consider that some person, having established the relationship between words and their meanings, [instituted them] for the sake of practical communication.
"The Vedas have been composed"—this is what is now being addressed: "Because the relationship [between word and meaning] is established as being non-human (apauruṣeya).
But how is it understood that this relationship is non-human?
Because of the absence of a person who could be a witness to the connection. How is it that there is no connection?
Because of the absence of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because the other [means of knowledge] are preceded by it. [Objection:

But surely, because it occurred long ago, it would not be an object for people of the present time through direct perception. [Response: It is not the case that something which occurred long ago would not be remembered. Nor is there a lack of memory regarding the Himalayas and so forth, as there might be regarding wells or groves.
This must be so. For among them, there may indeed be a separation from persons due to the destruction of a region or the destruction of a lineage;

however, there is no separation for persons from the linguistic usage of words and their meanings. It might be argued that persons who deal with the mere relationship [of word and meaning], disregarding the remembrance of an author as being useless, might forget it.
This is not so. For if a person were to establish a relationship and then employ it in linguistic usage,
he would necessarily have to remember it at the time of that usage.

For it is through agreement that the purpose of both the author and the user is accomplished, not through disagreement. For those who do not follow Pāṇini, or for one who does not accept Pāṇini’s work, the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* would not be understood by the term "vṛddhi" through usage. Likewise, for one who does not follow Piṅgala, or for one who does not accept Piṅgala’s work, a triplet consisting entirely of heavy syllables would not be understood by the letter *m*. Therefore, the author and the user must agree. Thus, by means of the Vedas...

Those who engage in linguistic usage must necessarily remember the author of the relationship between words and their meanings, as well as the author of the rules of usage. For if the author of the rule "vṛddhir ādaic" were forgotten,
one could not understand that "vṛddha" refers to a word whose first vowel among its vowels is a *vṛddhi* sound.
Something might be perceived [as such].

Therefore, because there is no recollection [of such an author], we understand that the Vedas were not composed by anyone for the sake of worldly usage after establishing a connection [between words and their meanings].
Even if forgetfulness were possible, we would still not establish the existence of a creator of the relationship without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
for just as there may be a non-perception of something that exists, we do not on that account alone establish the existence of a hare's horn without a means of valid cognition.
Therefore, the relationship between a word and its meaning is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). [Objection:

But surely we may understand the creator of this relationship through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). For we do not observe anyone understanding a meaning from a word for which no relationship has been established. If they were able to understand it, they would understand it even upon hearing it for the first time. Since such understanding is not observed, we consider that there must necessarily be a creator of the relationship.

If it is argued that [the relationship between word and meaning] is not established because there is no creator of the relationship (*saṃbandhṛ*), we say: no. Because the instruction [of the Veda] is given as an established fact (*siddhavat*).

For if meanings were not necessarily perceived due to the absence of a creator of the relationship, then [the existence of such a creator] would be inferred through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). However, [this is not the case].
We understand that there is an author of the connection [between word and meaning]. However, there is another way [of understanding it]:

children are seen perceiving a perceptible object while listening to elders engaged in communication for their own purposes. Those elders, when they were children, likewise [perceived it] from other elders.

Or it might be that they [the older speakers] learned it from others, and thus there is no beginning; or else, not even a single word was ever connected with its meaning, and subsequently the connections were established by someone. In this case, since the usage of elders exists, one cannot logically infer an author of the connection. Furthermore, while those who maintain the theory of usage among elders perceive [the relationship directly], others postulate an author of the connection.
But when perception is opposed, such a postulation is not valid. Therefore, there is no creator of the connection. And there is no deviation [of the word from its object].

Just as the word "cow" applies to that which possesses a dewlap and so forth in this region, so it is in all remote places as well. How could many establishers of the relationship ever come together? Even a single person would not be able [to do so].
Therefore, there is no relation.
Another says: "And there is no distinction [in time]. For there is no time whatsoever that exists apart from a relation.
In which [time] not even a single word was connected with any meaning. How so?
For the very act of establishing a connection is not possible. By one who is establishing this connection, it must necessarily be done by means of some word.
By whom was that which performs [the action] itself made? Or, if it were made by someone else, [then who made that other?]

Regarding the question "by what [is it established] for that?", [the inquiry] does not come to rest with "by what for that?". Therefore, one who necessarily establishes this connection must admit that there are certain words whose connections have not been [explicitly] formed, which are established through the usage of elders (*vṛddha*). And if [they exist],...

Nor is there even the presumption (*arthāpatti*) that a relationship must necessarily exist; for one might object: "How can children, whose relationship [to words] is not yet established, understand from the elders?
But this is not untenable when it is observed, for we do indeed observe children learning from the elders.
They are those who are currently practicing [the connection],
but not those who have not yet established the connection with its creator; therefore, there is a disparity.
When an object is not perceived—
such as a deity or the like— and the object is unperceived, [the statement] is meaningless.

Furthermore, it is impossible to apply a name [to things]. For names are established in order to comprehend specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*), having those specific distinctions as their objective referents. Since those specific distinctions are not known [in the case of the Veda], both [the application of names and the comprehension of distinctions] are untenable. Therefore, the relationship between a word and its meaning is non-human (*apauruṣeya*).
And for this reason—that [Vedic injunction] is the means of valid cognition;
for when this is the case, there is no dependence on another person or another source of cognition.
Therefore, dharma is characterized solely by the Vedic injunction (codanā), and not by any other characteristic.
The mention of Bādarāyaṇa has been stated.

Now, as for what was said—that the word [of the Veda] is not a valid means of knowledge because no fruit is seen at the time of the ritual action, and because the action is absent at a later time, and thus there is no proof—this is replied:
it would not be a valid means of knowledge [if that were the case].

If there were only five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then whatever by which something is cognized would be a means of valid cognition. Since something is also cognized by means of verbal testimony (*śabda*), therefore verbal testimony too is a means of valid cognition.

Just as with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). It is not the case that something is unperceived merely because it is not perceived by one means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) while being perceived by another. Nor is it heard in scripture that once an action has been performed, the fruit arises at that very moment.

However, it is by means of karma that the fruit is obtained. As for the objection that there exists another perceptible cause for the fruit at a later time, this is not a fault; for that [karma] itself is indeed [the cause].
In this regard, sound is also a cause.

As for the statement presented that contradicts perception—namely, "this sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, goes directly to the heavenly world," which is said to designate the perceptible body—it is replied:
because of its connection with the body.
He whose body that is, he too is called "the one equipped with sacrificial implements" (yajñāyudhin) because of those sacrificial implements.
He asks: who is this other?
"We do not perceive him.

"But surely we perceive him by means of the vital breaths and so forth; he who breathes out, breathes in, exhales, blinks, and performs such activities—he is the one here in this body who possesses the sacrificial implements. "But is it not the body itself that breathes out and breathes in?"

Vitality (*prāṇa*) and the other [breaths] are not qualities of the body. For they possess characteristics contrary to those of bodily qualities, because they do not persist as long as the body exists. The qualities of this [body], such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, exist for as long as the body exists; however, vitality and the others do not exist even when the body is present. Therefore, vitality and the others are not qualities of the body.

Furthermore, pleasure and the like are apprehended by oneself, and not like form and the other qualities of the body, which are perceived by others as well. Therefore, because of this difference from the qualities of the body, that which possesses the sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudhin*) is distinct from the body.

[The opponent] asks: "On what basis is there this conviction that there exists a possessor of pleasure and the like who is distinct from them? For we do not perceive its essential nature apart from pleasure and the like. Therefore, it is like the horn of a hare."
That [self] does not exist.
Now, if it is asked: "In the absence of that, to whom do pleasure and the rest belong?
we shall reply: "To no one at all."

For it is not the case that whatever is perceived must necessarily have a correlate. Only when both a relation and its correlate are perceived can it be understood that "this is the correlate of that. Indeed, having perceived the moon or the sun, one does not search for another correlate.

The thought arises: "To whom does this belong? It is determined that it belongs to no one at all. Therefore, there is no possessor of pleasure and so forth other than those very states themselves. Now, if it must necessarily be postulated for that which is perceived, then having perceived even the self (*ātman*) in this manner, we would have to search for yet another related entity to the question, "To whom does this [self] belong? Having postulated that as well, and then postulating yet another, and then yet another, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
It would be so. Now, if you posit some [relation] but do not posit another related entity as well,
you will stop at that very point and be satisfied with that much alone.
Therefore, being fully satisfied with consciousness alone, you ought to rest with just that.
To this it is replied: If there is no knower other than consciousness, then who is said to know? [Of what] is this knowledge?
By this [statement], there is a mention of the author:
"We shall postulate a self distinct from the cognition that 'this word must be meaningful'.
He says: "The gods will make this word meaningful."
If they think it should be conceptualized:
indeed, many people here are proponents of the existence of a self who directly assert the very words "there is a self," "there is a self."

Even though they exist, they are not capable of postulating the existence of a self (*ātman*), much less [claiming] that it "knows," given the observation of words such as "imperceptible" (*parokṣa*). Therefore, this is incorrect.
It is said in reply: by means of desire, the self...
We perceive [them]. How so?
For desire arises toward an intended object that has been perceived previously;
for example, those sweet fruits of trees which have never before been perceived by those of our own kind to the north of Mount Meru.
We have no desire for those [objects] themselves. Indeed, even when an object has been perceived by one person, there is no desire for it in another who has not perceived it.
Furthermore, there is desire for an object on one day that was perceived on a previous day. Therefore...

From that perception, we understand that it has the same agent. If this mere consciousness alone were the perceiver, then on the following day, whose desire would there be for it? Now, [if one asks...]
The knower is distinct from consciousness and is eternal;
therefore, he who was the perceiver on one day will be the very same person who seeks [the object] on the following day. Otherwise, desire would be impossible.
Here [the opponent] says: "In what respect do we have the conviction that [something] is untenable?
For we do not perceive anything other than consciousness (*vijñāna*) that has been apprehended by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And as for that which..."
We do not perceive it;
therefore, we understand that it simply does not exist, just like the horn of a hare. And even in its absence, the existence of consciousness is not untenable.

Precisely because it is apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). And its momentariness is likewise preceded by direct perception. Furthermore, if there were no knower distinct from consciousness, and if consciousness were not impermanent, then desire on a subsequent day would be untenable;

this too is [known] precisely because it is apprehended through direct perception. Indeed, it has never been observed that the very same person who was perceived on one day [is the same as the one perceived on another].
"He himself will be sought on the following day. But this is observed: in some cases one person desires what was seen by another, while in other cases he does not;
even within the same continuum, one person desires it [while another does not].
[The opponent claims: "One does not desire [it] in another continuum; therefore, there is no other [self] distinct from pleasure and so forth.

To this it is replied: It is not tenable to say that those who do not remember [anything] desire [this]. Furthermore, memory does not arise regarding what was never previously perceived. Therefore, [if everything were] momentary...
"Memory is untenable within the mere aggregate of consciousness.
To this, he replies: "Memory is also like desire. A cognition similar to a previous cognition, or a cognition whose object is the same as that of a previous cognition, is called memory. And that..."
Even when the observer has perished,
the arising [of cognition] on the following day is not untenable,
precisely because it is apprehended through direct perception. As for the cognition that occurs by means of one aggregate of constituents (skandha) regarding another aggregate of constituents:

That [consciousness] is perceived by another born from that same continuum, not by one born from a different continuum. Therefore, the aggregates (*skandha*) are empty of a solid mass. Now, regarding this point, there is a *brāhmaṇa* passage: "A mere mass of consciousness (*vijñānaghana*), having arisen from these elements..."
"Those very things perish along with it;
there is no consciousness after death.

To this it is replied: This is not so. Regarding something seen on one day, on the following day there arises the cognition: "I saw this. And this occurs in relation to the inner self (*pratyagātman*).
Not in another [life],
for that which was seen on another day is this very person; therefore, there exists another distinct from him.
Where this word "I" occurs.
It is said: the word "I" is also seen used figuratively for another, as for example: "I... (*aham*).
"Such-and-such is my son; I myself am Devadatta;
I myself am going.
To this, it is said: We do not [deny] this word "I," but...
We designate that which is applied to another object as the cause;
rather, it is the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that is distinct from the word.
For we recognize this object, thinking, "We ourselves perceived it on another day;
we ourselves remember it today. Therefore, we understand this object as being ours from yesterday.
"We ourselves are indeed here today.

Those who were both yesterday and today have not perished. Furthermore, regarding this matter, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "This very Self," having introduced it thus, they declare, "It is indestructible, for it is not destroyed. Thus, it is imperishable.
"Or rather, this self is of a nature that is not subject to annihilation,
whereas consciousness is perishable; therefore, it is other than that which is perishable."
Thus we understand. And it is not possible to understand it in such a way that objects exist exactly as they are perceived.
Just as they are not indeed perceived, so do they exist. For if that were the case— there would be no rabbit.

It might be understood that "the horn of a hare exists," yet it cannot be said that the notion of "I" is an illusion, because there is no subverting cognition to the contrary. Therefore, [the self] exists as distinct from pleasure and the other [mental states]. If this is so, then:
That very [Self] is designated as "the possessor of sacrificial implements.

He says: "If there is a knower other than consciousness, let that be pointed out apart from consciousness—'this is it,' or 'it is like this. But it is not pointed out. Therefore, there is nothing other than that."
To this it is replied: It is self-cognizable; it cannot be seen by another. How could it be demonstrated?
Just as a certain person with sight sees a form himself, yet is unable to demonstrate it to another who is blind from birth.
Nor is it understood that something does not exist merely because it cannot be demonstrated;

likewise, this person perceives himself, yet he is unable to show himself to another, because another perceiver lacks the capacity for vision directed toward that person. That other person, too, perceives himself.
Nor [is it] another's self.
Therefore, all [beings], perceiving themselves by their own respective selves, certainly exist,
even if they are not perceived by other persons.

297. Thus it is said. Now, regarding this matter, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "When speech has become silent, what light does this person have? 'He has the light of the Self (ātman),' O Saṃrāj," he replied.
Regarding the statement "it is not perceived by another," there is also a Brāhmaṇa passage: "It is ungraspable, for it cannot be grasped.
This has the intended meaning that it is not grasped by another. Why?
Because of the teaching of its self-luminosity (*svayaṃjyotiṣṭva*). Here too...
There is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "In this state, this person becomes self-luminous.
But by what means is this [self] described to another? To this as well—
Regarding the means (*upāya*), there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "He said, 'This Self is "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).
This is that very one.

It is impossible to point out [the self] as being of such a form. Whatever another perceives, the negation of that is the means for teaching it. Another perceives the body; by means of that, the self is taught. "The body is not the self. There exists something other than the body, and that is the self; thus, by the negation of the body, the self is taught.

Likewise, since the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are not the self, by the negation of them, that which is other than them is taught. Similarly, since pleasures (*sukha*) and so forth residing in another are perceived by another through their signs, they too are not the self; by the negation of them, that which is other than them is taught.
That he who perceives [an object] is none other than the person himself— this too is inferred from the activity of the person; namely,
that when this person exerts effort on the previous day toward the completion of tasks half-finished and the performance of remaining duties, therefore—
From his activity it is certainly understood that he perceives the eternal within the impermanent.
And it is taught through analogy: "In whatever way you yourself perceive your own self, understand it by this analogy—I too perceive it in exactly that same way."

Just as someone might describe their own sensation to another, saying, "It is as if I am being burned," "It is as if I am being struck," or "It is as if it happens to me"— therefore, because it is experienced by oneself, there exists a person distinct from that [sensation].

As for what is said—"Setting aside consciousness, let that [object] be demonstrated"—if you are indeed negating the means itself, it is impossible to attain the goal without the means. This very thing is the means for objects to be known: namely, that by which and in whatever manner they are known.
He said, "So be it. It is as follows: What is that which is called "white"?
That in which whiteness exists. What is that which is called "whiteness"? That in which the application of the word "white" occurs. Where does its application occur?

That which is understood when the word "white" is uttered—therefore, it is impossible to demonstrate the form of anything while setting aside consciousness. Furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that when a cognition is apprehended, the object of that cognition is thereby apprehended; for even when the cognition is not apprehended, the object is indeed apprehended. Indeed, it has already been stated previously that consciousness is not directly perceived, whereas the object to be known is directly perceived. Therefore, this must necessarily be done... [24] {1}

Furthermore, regarding the denial [of the object], it has already been stated that while one might indeed deny the cognition (*vijñāna*), one cannot deny the object (*artha*). Therefore, there exists a permanent person (*puruṣa*) distinct from pleasure and the other [sensations].
Now, as for what was said: "Having arisen from these very elements as a mass of cognition alone, it perishes after them."

Regarding the statement, "There is no perception after death," it is said here: "In this very matter, the Blessed One has led us into the depths of confusion. This is stated after raising an objection; subsequently, [the Buddha] denies that he intended to lead them into the depths of confusion.
Regarding this statement,
he described it thus: "Indeed, I do not speak of delusion."
"Verily, this Self, my dear, is indestructible and of a nature that does not perish; however, it comes into contact with the elements.
Therefore, it is not mere consciousness. Thus, there is a disparity [between the two views].

As for what was said—that this [statement] "he does not go" is not an injunctive word—let it not be an injunctive word. It will be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already understood from another scriptural injunction, namely, "one desiring heaven should sacrifice. Therefore, there is no contradiction.

*{1/139: TB, TC, M.pari., Tātp. om. pratyakṣādibhir}* *{1/140: E1,2,5, 6, TA, TB} [The text continues: ...by means of perception and the other [means of valid cognition]. The word "etc. (*ādi*) includes inference (*anumāna*), verbal testimony (*śabda*), comparison (*upamāna*), and presumption (*arthāpatti*). Among these, perception is that which is produced by the contact of the sense organs with their objects; it is of two kinds: external and internal. External perception arises from the contact of the five external sense organs—namely, the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body—with their respective objects, such as color-form and so forth. Internal perception, on the other hand, arises from the contact of the internal organ (*manas*) with the self (*ātman*) and the qualities of the self, such as pleasure and pain. Inference is the knowledge of an object not present to the senses, derived from a previously perceived mark (*liṅga*) that is invariably concomitant with it. Verbal testimony is the knowledge arising from words that are trustworthy and free from contradiction. Comparison is the knowledge of similarity based on the recollection of what has been previously perceived. Presumption is the postulation of something unperceived in order to account for a perceived fact. These are the four means of valid cognition other than perception. Negation (*abhāva*) is not considered a separate means of valid cognition, as its object is merely the absence of the other five. Thus, through these means of valid cognition, the existence of the self and the objects of experience is established. However, the existence of the Lord (*īśvara*) cannot be established by these means, because He is beyond the reach of the senses and lacks any perceptible marks. Therefore, His existence must be accepted on the basis of scripture alone. Furthermore, since the world is an effect, it must have an intelligent cause, and this cause is none other than the Lord. Thus, the existence of the Lord is proven through the method of presumptive necessity (*arthāpatti*). This concludes the discussion on the means of valid cognition. Now, we shall proceed to the examination of the categories of reality. First among these is the self (*ātman*). The self is defined as that which is the substratum of cognition, desire, and aversion. It is eternal, omnipresent, and distinct from the body, the senses, and the mind. Its existence is inferred from the presence of qualities such as cognition, which require a substrate. The self is of two types: the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*). The individual self is the agent of actions and the enjoyer of their fruits, while the supreme self is the Lord, the creator and sustainer of the universe. Through the practice of yoga and the cultivation of knowledge, the individual self may attain liberation (*mokṣa*) and become one with the supreme self. This is the goal of all spiritual endeavor. Some [maintain that] it is action (karma), because it is observed there.

It has been stated that the relationship between word and meaning is eternal. That is untenable, because the word is non-eternal. Once a word has perished, it is not possible for an uncreated relationship to exist again between this newly produced word and its meaning. For [the relationship] is not [perceived] from a word heard for the first time.

Someone understands a certain meaning from a word. But how, then, is sound impermanent? Because it is perceived at a time subsequent to effort; therefore, due to its immediate succession to effort, it is understood that it is produced by it. [Objection: But might it not manifest it? [Reply: We say no. For there is no means of valid cognition for its existence prior to manifestation. And what exists is manifested, not what does not exist.
Because it is impossible. (MS 1.1.7)
Furthermore, we do not perceive [the sound] even for a moment after it has been uttered; therefore, we understand that it has perished.
Nor is it the case that what exists is not perceived, because even when the causes of non-perception—such as obstruction and so forth—are absent, it is still not perceived.
And this [sound] has not failed to reach its object.
Because space is not an object [of auditory perception],
and because it is not perceived even within the cavity of the ear.
[The word *karoti*] follows from the word "karoti" [in the sūtra]; for there is a variant reading (*v.l.*): "And one does not utter this [word]. (MS 1.1.8)
Moreover, speakers employ such expressions as "make a sound" and "do not make a sound," yet they certainly do not fail to recognize that it is this very same sound.
And because [cognition] occurs simultaneously in different sentient beings. (MS 1.1.9)
Furthermore, we perceive sound simultaneously in various locations;

this would be impossible for a single, eternal entity. Since there is no distinction [in its nature], an eternal thing cannot possess multiplicity. However, in the case of many effects produced in various locations, a connection with multiple places is possible.
For this reason also, sound is non-eternal.
And [the same applies] to the relationship between the original material (prakṛti) and its modification (vikṛti).

Moreover, they explain that in the word *dadhyatra*, the vowel *i* is the original form (*prakṛti*) and the letter *y* is the modification (*vikṛti*). That which undergoes modification is impermanent; furthermore, a similarity to the vowel *i* is perceived in the letter *y*.
By that as well, the relationship of material cause and modification between those two is indicated;
and its increase occurs through the abundance of agents.

Moreover, when it is uttered by many people, a great sound is heard. If that sound were merely manifested, then whether it were being uttered by many or by few, it would be perceived as being of the same magnitude. Therefore, we consider that surely some part of it is produced by each individual, such that through this accumulation, it is perceived as great.
NOTES:
But in that case, the perception is equal. (MS 1.1.12)
By the word "but" (tu), the position is reversed. As for what was stated— that "this [sound] is produced because it is perceived at a time subsequent to an effort"—
if we are able to state the permanence of sound by means of a clear reason, [then our position holds].
Therefore, by the power of its eternal cognition, it will be manifested through effort. If it is unmanifest prior to pronunciation and is manifested through effort,
then this is equal for both positions.
The non-perception of an existing thing [occurs] because of the non-arrival of the object [to the senses]. (MS 1.1.13)
Furthermore, regarding the reason stated— that [the word] "perishes as soon as it is uttered"— if we are able here to clearly demonstrate its permanence,
then, by the power of that cognition of permanence, having observed that it is sometimes perceived and sometimes not perceived, one might [conclude something].

We shall postulate that the cause of perception is [the conjunction and disjunction]. Since that [perception] occurs only when conjunction and disjunction exist, we shall state that conjunction and disjunction themselves are the manifesters. If it is argued that [the sound] is heard even when conjunction and disjunction have ceased, this is not so; for conjunction and disjunction do not truly cease.
Because sound is perceived [there]. For those [conjunctions and disjunctions] are not perceptible.

If conjunctions and disjunctions alone manifest sound and do not produce it, then—since sound has space (*ākāśa*) as its object and space is unitary—whatever this space of the auditory organ (*śrotrākāśa*) is here, [that same space exists everywhere].

That very same [sound] would also be perceived in other locations; thus, being manifested by conjunctions and disjunctions produced by those residing in Śrughna, it would be perceived even in Pāṭaliputra.
But for one who holds that [the organs] produce [it]:

Its aerial conjunctions and disjunctions, because they reside in the air, will produce [the sound] only in the airs, just as threads produce a cloth only in the threads. It is logical that it is not perceived in Pāṭaliputra, because those [airs] are located in Śrughna. This is also the case for one who holds that [the sounds] manifest [the word].
This is not a fault even for that [theory]:
the conjunctions and disjunctions do not assist the ear-cavity when it is at a distance;
therefore, what is heard by the auditory organ located at a distance is not perceived. This is not so, because [if they were] unattained...

If conjunctions and disjunctions were to assist the auditory organ, then two people situated in near and distant locations would perceive the sound simultaneously; yet they do not perceive it simultaneously. Therefore, they do not assist by reaching [the object]. And if they do not assist, then conjunctions and disjunctions are not the cause for the perception of sound.

This is not so. For air-molecules impelled by a blow, striking against other stationary air-molecules, produce conjunctions and disjunctions in all directions; they continue to do so as long as their momentum lasts. And because air is imperceptible, these conjunctions and disjunctions are not perceived.

Sound is perceived only while those [causes] have not ceased, and not when they have ceased. Therefore, there is no fault. For this very reason, sound is perceived from a distance when carried by a following wind.

Furthermore, another reason has been stated: users of language employ such expressions as "make a sound" or "do not make [a sound].
If sound were undoubtedly eternal, the expression would have to be "make the use of sound."
Just as from cow dung [the word] "kurv" [is produced] in the process of withdrawal.

Simultaneity is like that of the sun.
As for the claim that it is impossible for that which exists as a single entity to be perceived simultaneously in multiple locations:
look at the sun, O beloved of the gods! Though it is one, it appears as if situated in many places. How so?

Furthermore, it is understood that the sun is one. It is said: Devadatta, facing east in the forenoon, sees the sun directly in front of him at present. Standing to his right, he does not see two [suns], nor does he see the sun as being transverse to himself at this moment.
[In the case of] Devadatta’s straightness, [it is said]:

"Therefore, there is only one sun. Because of its distance, its location is not determined; hence, there is delusion. Likewise, in the case of sound as well, there is no determination of its location due to delusion. If the auditory organ were to grasp the sound by coming to the place of the conjunction and disjunction, [then it would be perceived].

Nevertheless, it might still be perceived as having multiple locations at some point; yet it does not come to the location of its conjunctions. For the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*) is directly perceived and is apprehended as being in that specific location. However, the conjunctions and disjunctions of the aerial elements (*vāyavīya*), belonging to the imperceptible air, are not perceived even when they manifest in the region of the ear-cavity; thus, this is not untenable. It is for this very reason that there is the delusion that sound exists in various locations, and that sound is a location of space (*ākāśadeśa*). [Sound is] one.
Furthermore, it is like space; for this reason as well, [the sound] does not exist in various locations.

Moreover, since there is a single form [of the sound], even if there is a difference in location, let it be that the locations themselves are distinct, but the sound is not. Therefore, this too is not a fault.
