When [a sound] is currently produced transversely, it is another phoneme (*varṇāntara*), not a modification (*avikāra*). MS 1.1.16.

Furthermore, in the case of "na ca dadhyatra" (*na ca dadhy atra*), there is no relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*). The letter *y* is a different sound from the letter *i*; for those employing the letter *y* do not take up the letter *i*, just as those desiring to weave a mat do not take up *vīraṇa* grass. Nor is something called a "material cause" or a "modification" merely by observing a similarity.

For indeed, upon seeing a basket of curd and a basket of jasmine flowers, the relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) is not understood. Therefore, this too is not a fault.
It culminates in the increase of the resonance.
And since a great sound is perceived when many people are beating drums and uttering it,
it is understood from this that there is an accumulation of sound-parts for each individual person.

It is not so. For sound is partless, since no distinction of parts is perceived; and because it is partless, magnitude is impossible. Therefore, sound does not increase. When a soft sound is uttered by one person or by many, those very same syllables are perceived as if large or as if possessing parts, because they are grasped repeatedly and in immediate succession by conjunctions and disjunctions that pervade the entire circumference of the ear-cavity.
Conjunctions and disjunctions produced in uninterrupted succession, manifesting sound, are what is designated by the term "nāda" (articulate sound). Therefore, this increase belongs to the *nāda*,
not to the [eternal] *śabda* (word/sound).
The increase of sound is supreme;
[it is attained] by those who strike down [the obstacles].
But [the word] must be eternal, because its manifestation is for the sake of another. (MS 1.1.18)
Sound ought to be eternal. Why?
Because its manifestation is for the sake of another. "Manifestation" means utterance;

that is for the sake of another, in order to convey meaning to another. For if sound were destroyed as soon as it was uttered, one person would not be able to convey meaning to others. Therefore, it would not be uttered for the sake of another.

If, on the other hand, it has not perished, then it is logical that the comprehension of meaning arises from its being perceived many times. If you argue that the comprehension of meaning arises from similarity to a word that possesses meaning, we say no; for nothing possesses meaning, since all [words] are new. For some prior [word], the connection would have to be artificial.

If it is argued that [the cognition] will arise [later], it has already been stated that once the similarity is understood, the cognition would be diverted due to delusion, just as the cognition of a "garland" is diverted from the word "mālā.

If it is further argued that—just as there is no cessation of the cognition of "having a dewlap and so forth" from the word *gāvī*—the same will happen here, we reply: it is not the case that one intends to utter the word *go* (cow) there; nor is there a desire to utter another word here. Furthermore, this cannot occur through a single effort of articulation.
Furthermore, linguistic usage and the connection with meaning can be established. Therefore, because perception exists for the sake of another,
sound is eternal.

Because [the cognition] occurs simultaneously with respect to everything. (MS 1.1.19)

When the word "cow" (go) is uttered, a cognition arises simultaneously with respect to all cows; therefore, this word denotes the *ākṛti* (form). Furthermore, it is not possible to establish a relationship between the word and the *ākṛti*. For a creator could only establish such a relationship after having pointed out the *ākṛti*. And since many *ākṛtis* exist within a single individual cow (*gopiṇḍa*), by what means could one [distinguish] the specific *ākṛti* denoted by the word "cow" from among them without the word itself?
How will he teach it by means of this method?

However, if the word "cow" (go) were eternal, having been uttered many times and previously heard in connection with other individual cows, one would understand through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that it denotes the generic form (*ākṛti*). Therefore, for this reason as well, it is eternal.
NOTES:
Because of the absence of number. (MS 1.1.20)
People say, "The word 'cow' has been uttered eight times," not "eight words 'cow' have been uttered. What follows from this?
If it is so, it is understood from this statement that:

We ourselves recognize [it]; it is not due to any deficiency in our cognitive faculties. Likewise, others also recognize it, saying, "This is that very same thing. Just as we recognize it, others likewise ought to say that it is not something else.
Now, if it is thought that they say "that" because they are deluded by similarity despite there being difference, that is not so; for they do not perceive it as being "similar."

Rather, it is this very same thing. And when a difference is clearly known, it is understood that [the cognition] is a delusion. Yet there is neither perception nor any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish that "this is not another. It might be argued: "Cognition and action are also recognized through such re-cognition (*pratyabhijñā*); therefore, they too would have to be eternal. This is not a fault, for those two are not perceived by the senses. Or, if they were perceived, they would indeed be eternal.
If it is argued that the sound of today is different from the sound of yesterday because the former has perished, we reply: it has not perished.

For we perceive him again. Indeed, those who recognize through direct perception someone seen for a moment and then perceived again do not imagine that he has perished. If they were so to imagine, they would have no confidence upon seeing their mother, wife, or father for a second time. For one does not conclude "he is destroyed" merely because of non-perception, thinking "he does not exist."

Thus they imagine. When non-authoritativeness is understood, we conclude that [the object] does not exist. For when there is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there can be no non-authoritativeness. Furthermore, when it is understood through non-delusion (*avyāmoha*) that [the object] exists, there is no absence whatsoever. Nor is there delusion when the absence is unestablished.
Nor is non-existence established [as a positive entity]. Therefore, in the absence of delusion, there is no such thing as non-existence.
This has been proven through the aforementioned sequence. Consequently, even though they do not perceive what was previously uttered, they ought to understand that it has not perished. Just as...

Just as those who have gone out from their houses do not realize that someone has perished before their re-entry, even though they see all the household members upon entering again; in the same way, they cannot claim that this [person] is anyone other than that [same person]. This holds true even for those who maintain that all entities perish at every moment.

They too are unable to provide a verbal definition of sound. For they believe that because an end is observed, [sound must perish]; yet neither an end nor a destruction of sound is perceived. The cognition "that" is perceptual (*pratyakṣa*), while the cognition "similar" is inferential (*ānumānika*). And an inference does not arise in contradiction to perception, nor does it establish its own effect. Therefore, sound is eternal.

rather, upon seeing the form itself, one understands its impermanence, realizing that "this [form], produced by the conjunction of threads, perishes either through the destruction of the conjunction of threads or through the destruction of the threads. However, no such cause for sound is ever apprehended.
Because it is understood that [the object] will perish upon the destruction of that [connection], and because of the absence of any manifestation of the connection. (MS 1.1.22)

This is a sūtra following certain words. [The objection: "Could it not be that air is the cause? For air, having risen up, becomes sound through conjunctions and disjunctions. And thus the authors of the Śikṣā say:
"Air attains the state of sound. This is not so. If sound were composed of air (vāyavīya),...

It might be a particular configuration of air. However, we do not recognize the existence of aerial parts within sound, as we do recognize the threads that constitute a cloth; yet such is not the case. If it were so, we would perceive them. Furthermore, we do not touch any aerial parts residing in sound. Therefore, sound does not have air as its cause. Consequently, it is eternal.

[The word] would [not denote] the object, because the object is not the cause of that [word]. (MS 1.1.24)

Even if the word and its connection with the meaning are innate and eternal, nevertheless, Dharma is not characterized by *codanā*. For *codanā* is a sentence (*vākya*). Indeed, from the sentence "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra," one does not understand that heaven results from the Agnihotra based on any single word. Rather, it is understood when the three words are uttered. And there is no fourth word here other than this collection of three words.

Furthermore, this collection [of words] does not exist in the world such that meaning could be understood from its conventional usage. These individual words have been employed, and their meanings are eternal; however, the collection is not employed [as a single unit]. Therefore, the meaning of the collection is either artificial or a mere delusion. Nor is the sentence-meaning simply the word-meanings themselves, for a word operates in reference to a universal (*sāmānya*).

The sentence pertains to the particular. Furthermore, the universal is one thing and the particular is another. Moreover, there is no comprehension of the meaning of a sentence from the meanings of individual words, because there is no connection between them. If there were no such connection, then upon the comprehension of some word-meaning, another distinct meaning would necessarily be comprehended.
If one thing were understood, everything would be understood; yet this is not the case. Therefore, the meaning of a sentence is something other [than the sum of its parts].

It might be argued: "Even from a sentence that has never been used before, there is an understanding of the meaning through its inherent nature (*svabhāva*), even in the absence of a prior connection. If such a thing were imagined, it would mean that the word would overstep its own inherent property (*dharma*); and it is not a property of words that [meaning should arise] from what has never been used.
The meaning of the word "api" (even/also) is understood. For indeed, no one understands a meaning from some word heard for the first time. To this it is replied:

this is a property of the *pada* (word), not a property of the *vākya* (sentence). For even when understanding the meaning from a sentence that is perceived for the first time, [the meaning is grasped].

[They] are seen [to understand]. This is not so. If they were to understand from the first hearing, then everyone—both those who know the word-meanings and others—would understand; however, those who do not know the word-meanings do not understand.
Therefore, this is not so. But surely, even for those who understand while knowing the word-meanings, the connection with the sentence-meaning has not been previously established?

It will be so. For by means of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the [preceding] words, they will understand the meaning, just as one understands that very same word upon hearing it for a second time or thereafter. We say: no. If the final phoneme in a sentence, accompanied by the impressions generated by the preceding phonemes, [conveys] a meaning distinct from the meanings of the individual words, then at that time—*upakāras tu tadānīm*—[there would be a problem].

[The cognition of the sentence-meaning] is possible from the knowledge of word-meanings. Therefore, the cognition of the sentence-meaning is either artificial or a delusion; it is not possible for the knowledge of the sentence-meaning to arise by way of the word-meanings. [Objection: But surely this will be the case: from a word denoting a universal, such as "cow" or "horse,"...
When a qualifying term—such as "white" or "black"—falls upon [the object] from nearby, then the meaning of the sentence is understood. That is not so;
for how could the cognition produced by hearing a word expressing a universal, such as "cow" or "horse," which extends toward all cows and all horses, [be understood otherwise]?

It might deviate from a certain specific [meaning] in accordance with a sentence; however, the exclusion of "black" and so forth is not the word-meaning of a specific term such as "white. Nor can one postulate a meaning simply to avoid it being meaningless. Therefore, the sentence-meaning is not produced by the word-meanings. Consequently, it is artificial. Indeed, these are collections of words, and collections are seen to be created by persons, as for example—
"Today, as they roam through the groves of blue lotuses, making beautiful sounds and clothed in dark-blue silk, they seem as if they are perishing;
therefore, even the Vedic texts are man-made. [34]
the words "or" (vā)}* *{1/359:

From one or another [of these].
That [Veda] is a traditional instruction for the sake of action by living beings, because its purpose is based upon that [action]. (MS 1.1.25)

It is the utterance of words (*pada*) belonging to beings that exist within those very word-meanings (*padārtha*). A sentence is not established as having a distinct meaning independently of, or apart from, the word-meanings.

Why? Because there is a lack of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). There is no means of valid cognition whatsoever by which we might measure [such a thing]. For [a sentence] does not [function] when its word-meanings are disregarded.

The final phoneme of a sentence, when devoid of the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding phonemes, possesses the capacity to function toward an object distinct from the meanings of the individual words. But surely, there is presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) [to support this]?

As for the claim that we perceive an object distinct from the word-meanings (*padārtha*), and that this cannot be accounted for without postulating a *śakti* (potency), that is not correct. Because the [sentence] meaning has those [word-meanings] as its cause. There would indeed be an instance of *arthāpatti* (presumption) if, even in the absence of *śakti*, no other cause could be conceived. But another cause is indeed perceived. What is it? The word-meanings. For words, having denoted their respective word-meanings, cease their operation; it is now the word-meanings [that convey the sentence meaning].

Once they are understood, they cause the meaning of the sentence to be grasped. How so? For when a quality such as "white" or "black" is perceived, it is indeed capable of producing a cognition directed toward that which possesses the quality. Therefore, desiring to produce a cognition regarding the possessor of the quality, they utter the word expressing the quality alone. Thus, their intended purpose will be accomplished.
This is the intended meaning: there will be a comprehension of a specific meaning, and the comprehension of a specific meaning is the sentence-meaning.

If this is understood from something else alone, who would ever say that the power of a collection of words, never before seen, is understood from the meaning? Moreover, this is understood through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
For this state sometimes occurs even from mental affliction (*mānasa-āghāta*),
namely, when [words] have been uttered.
Word-meanings are not apprehended from words alone. In that case, they would necessarily fail to comprehend the sentence-meaning, if such a [causal relation] existed.
Yet, they do not necessarily comprehend it. Furthermore, even without the utterance of words, one who perceives whiteness...
He understands;

indeed, he understands that very thing which possesses the quality of whiteness. Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is simply the cognition of the word-meanings. It has no connection with a collection of words.
As for the claim that a word-meaning derived from direct audition (*śrauta*) ought not to be set aside due to some particularity in accordance with the sentence—
377*. True, this is so.

Where it is understood that a word-meaning (*padārtha*) employed in isolation becomes purposeless due to a lack of utility, there one might think, "Let there be at least the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*)," but this is not the case everywhere. And such being the situation, [the following applies].

The claim that the negation of other qualities is not the meaning of the word is also thereby refuted. Furthermore, the second case-ending and so forth, which are uttered following the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), state that the meaning of the nominal stem is a qualifier (*viśeṣaka*). And that specific mention (*viśeṣa-śruti*) would sublate the general mention (*sāmānya-śruti*). As for these...
It is observed that collections of words are composed by persons;
this has already been refuted by arguments such as the impossibility of recollection [of the original author].
Furthermore, there is no basis whatsoever for persons to compose sentences regarding matters of this kind.

It has been stated: "Dharma is a matter characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*)," because the relationship between a word and its meaning is not created by a person. In that regard, the objection based on words and sentences has been refuted. Now we shall raise an objection in another way: Vedic injunctions are of human origin; the Vedas were composed in recent times and are thus products of human effort.
And those are collections of injunctions (*codanā*);

if the Vedas are of human origin there, then the injunctions are undoubtedly of human origin. But how do some consider the Vedas to be created? Because they have names derived from persons; for the Vedas are designated by means of persons—such as the *Kāṭhaka* and the *Kālāpaka*.
"The Paippalādaka" and "the Mauhula"— for there is no designation without a relationship,
and there is no [relationship] of a person with a word.
[The opponent argues: There is a connection [between the Veda and its author]:

the agent is a person, and the word is the product. [Objection: But surely the designation [of the Veda] is characterized by its oral transmission (*pravacana*). [Reply: We say no. If this is so, then prior to the birth of Auddālaki, this text did not previously exist; thus, there is impermanence. [37] {1/390}

But there is merely a commonality of sound. (MS 1.1.31)
And as for the claim that [the word] *prāvāhaṇiḥ* [is derived from *pravāhaṇa*], that is not so;

since a person named *Pravāhaṇa* is unestablished, there can be no descendant of *Pravāhaṇa* called *Prāvāhaṇi*. The prefix *pra-* is established in the sense of "intensity," and the root *vah-* in the sense of "carrying" or "conveying. However, the combination of these two as a whole is nowhere established.

The suffix *ika*, however, is established not only in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) but likewise in the sense of the agent of an action (*kartṛ*). Therefore, one who causes to flow is a *prāvāhaṇi*. *Babara* is an imitation of sound. Thus, these two words will denote that very eternal entity. Hence it was said: "But there is merely a commonality of phonetic form."
Or rather, there may be an application [of a mantra] when something has been performed, because of its connection with the ritual action. (MS 1.1.32)

Now, how is it understood that this is not like the speech of a madman or a child? For we observe such [statements] as: "The trees performed a sacrificial session (*satra*)," and "The serpents performed a sacrificial session. Just as: "An old bull sings drunken songs."

"How indeed could an old bull sing? Or how could trees or serpents perform a sacrificial session (*satra*)? "By this procedure.

how could we say that the meaning of the sentence— which is refined and synthesized by these word-meanings— is like the speech of a madman or a child?
But surely this is seen to be untenable: "The trees performed a sacrificial session," and so forth. It is not untenable;

otherwise, [injunctions] such as "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra" would also be untenable. Moreover, even expressions such as "The trees performed a sacrificial session" are not untenable, for these are indeed praises of the sacrificial session (*satra*).

Even insentient trees by name have attended this sacrificial session, how much more so then learned Brahmins? Just as in the world one says, "At twilight even the deer do not roam about, how much less so learned Brahmins? Furthermore, since the instruction of a friend is unobjectionable and well-established, how could it be suspected of being like the words of a madman or a child? Therefore, [dharma] is characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*).
It is established that the object is the phenomenon (*dharma*). [39] {1/396} NOTES:

Since the Veda has action as its purpose, those parts that do not have that as their purpose are useless; therefore, it is said that [the Veda] is non-eternal. (MS 1.2.1)
He wept; because he wept, that is the origin of Rudra’s name, Rudratva.
Prajāpati cut out his own omentum.

Those who transmit the sacred texts recite sentences. Among those sentences, which do not convey an action or anything connected with an action,
they merely describe an existing fact— such as "Rudra wept" or "Prajāpati cut out his own omentum."
Passages such as "The gods, indeed, did not discern the directions" (devā vai diśo na prajajñire)—

of this kind— what dharma could they possibly measure? Now, if it be argued that some meaning will be inferred through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), or through modification (*vipariṇāma*), or by assuming a connection between remote elements (*vyavahitakalpanā*),
or by assuming a restriction (*vyavacchedakalpanā*), or by assuming a secondary quality (*guṇakalpanā*), then that which is being so inferred—
Who could possibly imagine this— that Rudra wept,

Therefore, anyone else might as well tear out his own omentum. At the time of preparing the sacrificial ground for the gods, the gods themselves did not know the directions;
thus, anyone else would likewise fail to discern the directions—and that is impossible.
The shedding of tears resulting from separation from what is beloved or from physical injury is called weeping,
and yet—

That occurs according to one's desire. Furthermore, no one would be able to sacrifice by cutting out their own omentum, casting it into the fire, and then sacrificing with a hornless animal that has arisen from it.

Nor, at the time of determining the site for the sacrifice to the gods, would anyone become confused regarding the directions. Therefore, these [other texts] are purposeless. Consequently, statements of this kind are said to be non-eternal (anitya).
"Even though they are eternal, nevertheless they do not perform their function eternally.
This is an objection directed at a portion of the statement.

Not of the entire sentence. [Response: It is not so, for there exists indeed a certain collection of words [which is complete even without being explicitly stated].
That which prescribes some matter even without explanatory passages (*arthavāda*),
whereas those others which function with reference to a different matter by being conjoined with them, are sublated by the sublation of a single part.

And because it would contradict what is seen in the treatises. (MS 1.2.2)

"The mind is a thief; speech is a liar"—statements of this kind lack authority with respect to *dharma*, because they are merely descriptive restatements of existing facts (*bhūtānuvāda*). Even if one were to interpret them through the theory of transformation (*vipariṇāma*) and other such means, it would follow that theft and lying must be performed; yet these cannot be carried out without violating the prohibitions against theft and false speech.
Nor can there be an option (*vikalpa*) between the two.
Because of this inconsistency: one [rule] would have to be a mere postulation, while the other would be directly perceived.

Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with what is observed. Therefore, it is only the smoke of fire that was seen by day, not the flame; and therefore, it is only the flame of fire that was seen at night, not the smoke.
Having departed from this world, fire has gone to the sun;
at night, the sun sets—this is what is intended to be established by this [statement].

However, both of these are stated in contradiction to what is observed. Therefore, this restriction is not proven. There is another contradiction with observation: "And we do not know this... [41] {1/}
Whether we are Brahmins or non-Brahmins,

Because it does not have action as its purpose, it is meaningless. Or, if there is an impossibility [of its being meaningful], there is a contradiction with what is seen in the scriptures. Therefore, that which contradicts direct perception is not a valid means of knowledge.

With reference to the *Gargatrirātra-brāhmaṇa*, it is said: "The face of one who knows this shines.

Just as one does not postulate that an experience is invalid simply because it is logically inconsistent, so too is the Vedic statement. How, then, is the traditional recollection (*smṛti*) regarding the "covering of all [the sacrificial post]" to be understood? It is an error. Why is it postulated to be an error? Because it contradicts the knowledge derived from the Śruti. Well then, why are these two injunctions not to be treated as optional alternatives (*vikalpa*)?

These two [alternatives] are like rice and barley, or like the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans]. An option does not arise when there is no cognition of confusion. If the cognition of covering the entire [post] is authoritative, then touching it is a delusion; if touching it is authoritative, then the Smṛti rule is a delusion. But by asserting an option, one at least admits the authority of touching it on its own side. And the source of that is the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). If that [Veda] is admitted as authoritative, [then the Smṛti must also be authoritative].

It is not optional. And since the traditional rule regarding the covering of everything is optional, it cannot, even in that alternative case, postulate a Vedic text [as its source], because it is sublated by the cognition of touch. Furthermore, as long as that cognition is free from delusion, a Vedic text cannot be postulated; nor is that cognition subject to delusion in the alternative case.

"There will be delusion regarding one alternative. For that which is the very basis for him in one alternative is the same in the other as well. If there is no delusion regarding one alternative because the authority of the Veda is equal [in both cases], then there is likewise no delusion regarding the other. And yet, that [basis] is not the Veda in one alternative.

For since that [text] has its syllables fixed, it cannot be said that it is a reading resulting from negligence. Therefore, it is understood that in this case, the cognition has not shifted to another position due to delusion. In that regard, the fact that the total veiling (*sarvaveṣṭana*) is rooted in cognition arising from misheard [texts], dreams, and so forth, is postulated because of contradiction. Indeed, when there is a contradiction, its authority (*prāmāṇya*) must not be accepted.
Thus, there is some means of valid cognition [for this]. Therefore, just as it is not possible to postulate a scriptural text in one position,
so it is in the other position as well, because the reasons are equal.

Moreover, in the case of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), there must be a determination from another source. What is this mutual dependence? If the memory is authoritative, then the tactile perception is an error;
if the tactile perception is authoritative, then the memory is an error.
Thus, this becomes a case of mutual dependence. In that situation, while the basis for the tactile perception is already established, the basis for the memory remains to be inferred.

Thus, this is a determination based on something else. Since its root is merely a conceptual construction (*kalpyamūla*), the authority of the Smṛti is untenable. Because of that lack of authority, the perception [of the *yava*] is not a delusion. Due to the absence of such delusion, the postulation of a Vedic text (*śruti*) for the sake of the Smṛti is impossible, as there is a lack of evidence. [Objection:

But if this were the case, then because the cognition of rice (*vrīhi*) as the means [to the sacrifice] is also free from delusion, the Vedic text regarding *yava* would likewise be untenable. [Reply: True, it would be untenable.

If it were not perceptible, it would be so; however, this is indeed perceptible, for there is no such thing as a perception that is logically untenable. This is because two scriptural statements exist; for these are two distinct sentences. Of these, by one the fact that barley alone is the means is understood, and by the other the fact that rice alone is the means is understood. And a meaning apprehended through a sentence cannot be denied. Therefore, regarding rice and barley...

And the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* [sāmans] has already been established. Therefore, it has been stated that a Smṛti which contradicts Śruti is not authoritative.
Consequently, practices such as the total wrapping of the sacrificial post (*sarvaveṣṭana*) and so forth are not to be respected.
And because the cause is observed. (MS 1.3.4)
Out of greed, some, desiring to obtain a dwelling, wrapped the entire *audumbarī* pillar; this is the seed of that Smṛti rule.

Desiring food, some practiced eating at the king’s meal after he had been purchased [as a slave]. And concealing their impotence, they practiced Vedic studentship for forty-eight years. From this, it is understood that this Smṛti originated from such motives.

Or it is another legal topic (*adhikaraṇāntara*). Here, there is another basis: some practiced out of greed.
Therefore, this is the traditional teaching (*smṛti*). And this is more reasonable than the hypothesis that it is a Vedic statement.
If it is argued that "it is not contradicted because it does not conflict with the teachings of the learned. (MS 1.3.5)
"One should perform [the rite] having sipped water;

This is not so; for it would contradict the sequence determined by the scripture. How? It will bring about the primary time;
or rather, when the cause is not apprehended, those [words] employed [in the Veda] should be understood [as authoritative].

The phrase "or rather" (*api vā*) serves to set aside the previous position. Such things as these are valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) precisely when their cause is not perceived. [Objection: But do they not contradict the sequence and the time? [Response: This is not a fault. Rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*) is a primary ritual act (*padārtha*), whereas sequence is a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) of those acts. A primary act does not become something that need not be performed merely for the sake of following a subordinate quality. When the object is attained, then there is no sequence at all;
with what, then, could there be contradiction? Likewise, if it is not performed by the right [hand], [there is no contradiction].

Thinking, "May time not cause opposition," one should not allow the ritual substance (*padārtha*) to undergo alteration by conforming to the requirements of time. Furthermore, there is purity and conduct characterized by dexterity.

Furthermore, such matters as the state of wearing the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavītitva*) do not constitute an interruption, because all these items are subordinate (*śeṣa*) to the ritual acts. Therefore, the validity of the sipping of water (*ācamana*) and other such rites is established.
If they were to oppose [the Veda],
since no opposition is observed among them, there would be an equal degree of disagreement. (MS 1.3.8)
"A sacrificial oblation (*caru*) made of barley;
boar-skin sandals;
on a mat of rattan he collects the *prājāpatya* offerings"—thus they recite the words "barley," "boar," and "rattan. In this regard, some apply the word "barley" (*yava*) to long-awned grains.

Some [use] the word *priyaṅgu* for the *varāha* plant; some use the word *varāha* for a boar, and some for a black bird. Some use the word *vetasa* for the *vañjulaka* tree, and some for the *jambu* tree. In that case, because the meaning of the object is understood in both ways, there is an option (*vikalpa*).

Or rather, [the Vedic words] are based on the treatises (śāstra), because they have those [treatises] as their cause.

The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the previous position. If the word *yava* [barley] should apply to long-awned grains by way of similarity to *priyaṅgu* [panic seeds], and if it applies to *priyaṅgu*, then it would apply to barley by way of similarity. What is the similarity? When the previous crop has been exhausted, both the long-awned grains and the *priyaṅgu* appear; this is the similarity between the two. But what, then, is the case here?

This is the certainty: that which belongs to those established in the *śāstra* is the meaning of the word. Who are those established in the *śāstra*? They are the *śiṣṭas*. Their tradition (*smṛti*) regarding words and the Vedas is uninterrupted. Therefore, the *śiṣṭas* are the authority for determining the *śruti* and the *smṛti*. For they record the following supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) when the *karambha* vessels made of barley are prescribed: "When other plants wither..."

Now, the Veda indicates that long-bearded barley (*dīrghaśūka*) is to be used, stating: "Then these [grains] rise up as if rejoicing. Since the word *yava* (barley) is seen applied to long-bearded grains in the Veda, it is understood that the term has an unbroken traditional usage (*avicchinnapāramparya*) for them. Therefore, its application to *priyaṅgu* (panic seed) is figurative. Consequently, the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) must be made from long-bearded barley.
Therefore, by saying "the cows run after the boar," he demonstrates the word *varāha*; and by saying "the cane grows in water," he demonstrates the word *vetasa* for the *vañjula* plant.
For cows indeed run after [their calves]; the *vañjula* tree grows in water; the *jambū* tree grows on dry land or in mountain rivers.

But that which is enjoined should be understood as authoritative, because it is not contradicted by a means of valid cognition.
Now, there are certain words that the noble ones (*ārya*) do not employ in any sense, whereas the barbarians (*mleccha*) do employ them in some sense;
such are the words *pika*, *nema*, *sata*, *tāmara*, and so forth.

Regarding these, there is a doubt: should the meaning be inferred from the verbal root by means of *nigama*, *nirukta*, and *vyākaraṇa*, or is that which the Mlecchas practice the meaning of the word? It has been stated that the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) is authoritative, not the tradition of the unlearned (*aśiṣṭa*). Therefore, the determination of meaning is based on *nigama* and the other authorities; in this way, *nigama* and the rest will possess their purposeful utility. Furthermore, the unlearned lack application (*anabhiyoga*) regarding the meanings of words, whereas the learned possess such application.

As for the others: since the meaning must therefore be inferred from the verbal root, this being the position reached, we reply: even that which is enjoined by those who are not learned (aśiṣṭas) should be understood [as authoritative] if it is not contradicted by the learned (śiṣṭas) and is not inconsistent with valid means of knowledge.

That which is being understood must not be abandoned as unreasonable. As for the claim that the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that applies to matters not apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Regarding the statement that those who are proficient in the meanings of words are the learned, to this it is replied:

The Mlecchas are more highly skilled than others in the rearing and binding of birds. As for the claim that [words] possess meaning through the Nigama, Nirukta, and Vyākaraṇa, their meaningfulness will apply only in those cases;

it does not apply where the word-meaning is understood even by Mlecchas. Moreover, if the meaning were to be determined solely through the Nigamas and other such sources, the meaning of words would become unstable.
In that case, there would be uncertainty. Therefore, "pika" should be understood as the cuckoo;
"nema" means half; and "tāmarasa" means a lotus.
"Sata" refers to a wooden bowl that is circular and has one hundred holes.
If it is argued that it is a treatise on ritual practice (prayogaśāstra), [then the answer is as follows].
In this regard, the *Kalpasūtras* serve as an illustration—such as those characterized as the *Māśaka*, the *Hāstika*, the *Kauṇḍinyaka*, and so forth.
Are these authoritative or not? Thus they are doubted. What is the prima facie position?

We say that for the ritual application (*prayoga*), a treatise (*śāstra*) of this kind is indeed the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). These are the words of those whose speech is truth. How is this understood? Because there is a correspondence between these [treatises] and the Veda. For the very same *grahas* that are in the Veda are here as well.

Those very same bricks that are [prescribed] in the Veda are the ones used here. Therefore, the teachers are speakers of truth; and there is a Vedic revelation stating, "The word of the teacher is authoritative. If it should be argued that their authority is not established through direct perception, we reply that there is no fault, as it is established by another means of knowledge—namely, by verbal testimony. Furthermore, they are accorded the same degree of respect as the Vedic sentences themselves. Therefore, they are authoritative.
iṣṭayaḥ}* Because there is no restriction regarding non-existence. (MS 1.3.12)
This is not so,
because there is no restrictive rule. This is not a correct connection,
because of the absence of a vowel.
And because there is no supplementary statement [to complete it]. (MS 1.3.13)
He chooses the officiating priests;
having been chosen, they perform the sacrifice;
they settle upon the sacrificial ground.

An injunction is not understood here, because of the indication of a present-tense suffix. Nor is there any supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) here that serves as a praise. Therefore, it is not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*). As for the "respect" (*ādara*) that was mentioned, that is due to its inseparability from the fact that it is recited in a collection mixed with Vedic sentences. As for the claim that it is "direct revelation" (*śruti*), that is not the case.

How is it an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*)? For there is another injunction: "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni. Here, the Teacher intends the Veda by the term "Teacher," in the sense that it accumulates knowledge in one's mind. Or rather, whatever is the word of the Teacher is authoritative; it depends upon that. Which is that? That which is accessible through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
As for what was said— that these are the words of those who speak the truth— that is not so; [because they are] supplementary [to other statements].

The authority of inference, memory, and customs is accepted. By the very same reason that these are authoritative, they deserve to be established as authoritative. Therefore, [customs such as] the *holākā* and so forth—

Or rather, the Āhnīnaibuka rite should be [performed] by the southerners; or else, it should be a universal duty (*sarvadharma*),

The phrase "or rather" (*api vā*) serves to set aside the previous position. Every dharma would be of such a nature. Why? Because that is the principle of its injunction (*vidhāna*).

An injunction is that by which something is enjoined; it is the word (*śabda*). That [word] is inferred from the Smṛti. And it is not logical for it to denote a class (*ākṛti*), nor is it logical for it to denote an individual (*vyakti*).

There is no single word that expresses the commonality shared by all performers [of a rite], which could be inferred. Therefore, it is logical that the injunction applies to all dharmas. Why? Because there is authoritative evidence stating that "the ritual items (padārthas) are to be performed."
But regarding the establishment [of such a rule], there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever.
As for what was said— that the ritual of the topknot is established— [that too is untenable].

and because there is no mark (*liṅga*) of something eternal. (MS 1.3.18)

This is a sūtra following upon certain words. Which are those words? Now, for what reason is there no fixed rule based on indicative marks (*liṅga*), as in the case of "the Hotṛ priest is white"? Even those who are dark-complexioned, tall, and red-eyed do not all perform the Ārhnīnaibuka and other rites. Furthermore, even those who do not possess such indicative marks perform them. Therefore, there is no fixed rule. "The Hotṛ is white" is a directly perceived scriptural statement (*pratyakṣā śrutiḥ*).
For a name [is applied] due to connection with a place. (MS 1.3.19)

Now, why is there no restriction based on designation? Those who are designated as "southerners" will perform the Āhnīnaibuka and other such rites; those designated as "northerners" will perform the Udṛṣabhayajña and others; and those [designated as] "easterners," [will perform their own].

[The opponent says: "They [perform] the *holākā* and so forth—for instance, 'the king [performs] the *rājasūya*. [The author replies: This is not so. The designation arises from connection with a region. And [the practices] such as the *holākā* and others belong to the easterners. Furthermore, one who has gone to another country does not necessarily perform the ritual acts of that other land. Therefore, there is no fixed restriction [in this case]. However, in the statement "The king [should sacrifice] with the *rājasūya*," the caste (*jāti*) is indeed restricted.
And [the customs] of the northerners, such as the bull-sacrifice (*vṛṣabha-yajña*) and others.} *{1/604: E4 (Fn.):

If it is argued that, for this reason, there would be no lack of restriction regarding other locations, [the response is: MS 1.3.20.

If you think this: "If the designation were due to conjunction with a location, it would not apply to one situated in another location; yet it does apply to one situated in another location, such as 'a person from Mathurā' (māthura), even though he is not connected with Mathurā. Therefore, the designation is not due to conjunction with a location. For the designation would indeed be like that of Mathurā [only if there were actual contact]. MS 1.3.21.

Even when a name is caused by connection with a place, it is not contradictory for one who has departed from that place to retain that name. For this designation based on connection (*yogākhyā*) depends merely upon the connection itself, and not upon a past, present, or future relationship. Indeed, it is observed that one setting out toward Mathurā is called "Māthura," as is one dwelling in Mathurā or one who has departed from Mathurā. However, for one who lacks any such connection whatsoever, [the name does not apply].
He is not a Māthura. Therefore, the determination [of ritual duties] is not by way of designation (*samākhyā*). Or rather, it is a property of the action, like the inclination of a slope. (MS 1.3.22)

Now, why is it that location (*deśa*) is not an auxiliary factor (*aṅga*) of the ritual action? That which consists mostly of black clay is [the location] for the *āhnīnaibuka* sacrifice and others. As it is said: "One should sacrifice with the *vaiśvadeva* on ground sloping toward the east."
But it is equal [to the case] with a property of the agent. (MS 1.3.23)
Just as a characteristic such as "darkness" that is not fixed in its locus does not accord with the actual state of things,
so too a characteristic of a place that is not fixed [does not accord].
Even in a place consisting mostly of black clay, others do not perform it;

likewise, they perform it even on another kind of ground. Therefore, there is no restriction based on locality. However, the rule that the site for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice must slope toward the east is fixed by the Vedic scripture.
Because there is no scriptural injunction regarding the production of usage, there would be no fixed rule for words, such as those established by region or gender. (MS 1.3.24)

Words such as *gaur*, *gāvī*, *goṇī*, and *gopotalikā* serve as examples. There arises a doubt: just as the word *go* is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for [the object] characterized by the dewlap and so forth, are words like *gāvī* and others likewise [means of valid cognition], or not? In this regard, is there one single word, with an uninterrupted tradition, that denotes the meaning?

Are the others corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśas*), or are they all beginningless? We say: "All. Why? Because of comprehension. For the object possessing a dewlap and so forth is indeed comprehended from words such as *gāvī*. Therefore, even a hundred years ago, the relationship between this word and its meaning certainly existed.

Beyond that, and further beyond that—thus there is beginninglessness. And it is already established that there is no creator of this relationship. Therefore, all [words] are correct, and one may speak using all of them; for all of them establish the meaning. For example: *hastaḥ* (hand),...

"Hand," "pāṇi"—these are uttered for the sake of meaning, not for the sake of some unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). For there is no scriptural injunction regarding their mere utterance. Therefore, one cannot maintain that only one among them is correct while the others are incorrect.

But how, then, can reality (*tattva*) be known in that case? He says: "It is possible. For those who have a purpose become diligent. And it is observed that for those who are diligent and practice [repetition], non-forgetfulness is logical. Moreover, this is directly perceived: that which is being practiced does not perish.
Thus, it should be understood that whatever those who are proficient teach is indeed correct.
Furthermore, in this regard, [the term] should be understood as "correct" (*sādhu*); and there is an incapacity [to produce it] because of its conformity [to the cause]. (MS 1.3.28)

Now, as for what was said—that meaning is understood from words such as *gāvī*, and therefore these too have an eternal connection with their referent—that is understood to be due to their incapacity. Someone desiring to utter the word *go* uttered *gāvī* due to an inability; another person understood that what he intended to express was the animal possessing a dewlap and other such features.

For that purpose, one who wishes to utter the word *go* (cow) utters *gāvī*. Having learned from this, others also utter *gāvī* when they intend to express "that which possesses a dewlap and so forth. Consequently, the possessor of a dewlap and so forth is understood from words such as *gāvī*, for *gāvī* is a form corresponding to the word *go*.
And because it is a part [of the whole], there would be a change of case-ending. (MS 1.3.29)

For this very reason, even when there is a displacement of case endings, comprehension still occurs. When a portion of the word "Aśmaka" is perceived—as in the expression "I am coming from the Aśmakas"—the complete form "from the Aśmakas" (aśmakebhyaḥ) is remembered. From that, the meaning "from the Aśmakas" is apprehended. In the same way, upon seeing words such as *gāvī* and so forth, the word *go* is remembered; from that, an object possessing a dewlap and other characteristics is understood.
Because there is no injunction for performance, there is unity of purpose due to the lack of division.

Now, a doubt arises: do words such as "cow" (gauh) and so forth serve as the means of valid cognition for the generic form (ākṛti) or for the individual (vyakti)? It is said in reply: first, let this be examined—whether those very words that are used in common worldly usage are the same as those in the Veda, or whether they are different. If they are the same, then too, are their meanings the same?

There is a doubt as to whether those [words] in the world are the same as others. To this we reply: that there are some words in common usage (*laukika*), others that are Vedic (*vaidika*), and their meanings are likewise distinct. Why? Because of the difference in designation and the difference in form. These are the worldly ones...

The distinction [in usage] is that these are designated as "Vedic. The form of the word *agniḥ* in the phrase "May Agni strike down the Vṛtras" is different from the worldly word *agni*. And because the words are different, their referents are not the same. Furthermore, they recite: "The oxen of the gods indeed carry [the burden] while lying on their backs.
Those who are the oxen of the gods—
When it is stated, "They carry on their backs," it is understood that those which carry on their backs are denoted by the word *go*.
Therefore, the meaning of the Vedic word *go* is different [from its common usage]. Likewise: "O Vanaspati, golden-leaved, bring the oblations to the gods; from of old, this is your purpose."
"The divine tree has golden leaves in the Veda; indeed, this is the divine honey, namely,
the clarified butter."

In the Veda, there is the word *madhu* [used] for clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Therefore, since these [Vedic words] have different meanings [than their worldly counterparts], this being the position reached, we reply: those very words that are worldly are the same as those that are Vedic, and those very meanings belong to them. Why? Because of the existence of injunctions for usage. In this way, the injunction for usage becomes possible.

If those very words are [the same as] those very meanings, then otherwise, if there were a difference in the words, the meaning would not be cognized; therefore, there is the identity of the word. It is replied: this is the purpose, but let the reason be stated. Then the reason is stated: "because of non-differentiation. There is no differentiation between those [words] and these [meanings].
We perceive them. For this very reason, they possess the same word-form. We understand those various meanings, and therefore we do not claim that they are different.
As for what was said—that those who speak with their mouths upward are "divine cows," and that which is clarified butter—

That is honey. That which has golden leaves is the tree. There is no statement that would declare that those which are lying on their backs while carrying [the load] possess the nature of cows. Rather, it is simply this: "Those which are cows carry [the load] while lying on their backs. And if the nature of being a cow were enjoined by this statement, [it would be redundant].

The statement "flowing face upwards" would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). Furthermore, no such things as "flowing face upwards" are well-known (*prasiddha*). Therefore, they would necessarily have to be enjoined;

and while they are being enjoined, it is not possible to enjoin the nature of being a cow (*gotva*), for in that case the sentence would be split. Moreover, if these other words were Vedic, then the meaning of "flowing face upwards" and so forth would not be understood; in that situation, it would be even more impossible to understand the nature of being a cow, whose characteristics are unknown. Nor is the mention of "flowing face upwards" purposeless.

"It will be meaningful by way of praise. In this manner, there is the "honey-nature" of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and the "golden-leaved-ness" of the tree (*vanaspati*). Therefore, those very same words and those very same meanings [apply].
If they are worldly, then they are indeed those same meanings.

Then there arises a doubt: is the meaning of a word the form (*ākṛti*) or the individual (*vyakti*)? But what, then, is the form, and what is the individual? The form is the mere universal (*sāmānyamātra*) of substances, qualities, and actions;
whereas the individual consists of the uncommon particulars (*asādhāraṇaviśeṣa*).
[The word denotes] the individual. Why is there doubt?
Because when "cow" is uttered, there arises a cognition of the universal, yet [the word] is connected with action only in the case of the individual.
This is stated: the individual (vyakti) is the meaning of the word. Why?

Because of the absence of injunctions for ritual application (*prayoga-codanā*). Injunctions for ritual applications—such as seizing (*ālambhana*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and immolating (*viśasana*)—would not be possible if the referent were the generic form (*ākṛti*). Where the utterance [of a word] would otherwise be purposeless, there the meaning is the individual. If it is argued that, therefore, elsewhere the word denotes the generic form, it has already been said: *Note: The text fragment ends with "uktam" followed by a marker, indicating the conclusion of a section.*

"And it is illogical for a single word to have multiple meanings. If it is asked, "How then is there a cognition of the universal? [the answer is: For the individual (vyakti), which is the referent of the word, the form (ākṛti) will serve as its mark;
that which possesses such a form is a "cow. It is just as in the case of one who has a staff.
"He is 'staff-bearer' (daṇḍin)," yet the word "staff-bearer" does not denote the staff itself. It is the same here as well.
The golden-leaved one is indeed the divine;
the golden-leaved one is indeed the divine tree; the golden-leaved one is the divine tree.
The golden-leaved god.
Because it is a word denoting a substance (dravya). (MS 1.3.31)
A word denoting that which has substance as its substratum is a "substance-word" (*dravyaśabda*);

in that case, there could not be a word expressing that which has substance as its substratum if the generic form (*ākṛti*) were the meaning of the word. [For example, in the injunctions] "six are to be given," "twelve are to be given."
"Twenty-four [cows] are to be given. For a generic form (*ākṛti*) is not connected with numbers such as six and so forth. Therefore, it does not denote a generic form.
And because of the observation of others. (MS 1.3.32)
"If the animal that has been dedicated should escape, one should sacrifice another of the same color and the same age"—
if this [scriptural statement] were a word denoting form (*ākṛti*), [then it would apply].
The grasping of anything else is not tenable; for even in the case of another substance that is an animal, it is that very same form [of the universal]. Therefore, [the word] denotes the individual.
But the generic form [is denoted by the word], because it serves the purpose of action. (MS 1.3.33)
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position. The meaning of the word is the *ākṛti* (form). Why?
Because it serves the purpose of action. The injunction, "One should pile the *śyenacit* (falcon-shaped altar)," is possible only with reference to the form.

If the word *śyena* denotes the class-form (*ākṛti*), then, since a specific individual (*vyakti*) cannot be produced by the act of piling (*cayana*) when the word is intended to denote an individual, the word would be meaningless because it would express an impossible object. Therefore, it denotes the class-form. [Objection: But the piling will be performed using individual *śyena* birds. [Reply: No; the meaning of the word *śyena* is not that which is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*).
For that which is most desired to be obtained is indicated by the word *śyena*. Therefore, the hawk (*śyena*) must be brought about through the act of piling (*cayana*);
this is possible only if the word denotes the form (*ākṛti*).

But is it not the case that in both instances the impossibility of the action itself is pointed out? [We reply: Form is not the meaning of the word. Why? Because the action would be impossible if form were the meaning of the word.
"One sprinkles the rice grains.
Likewise, the individual instance (*vyakti*) is not the meaning of the word;
for if the individual instance were the meaning of the word, action itself would not be possible.

"One should pile the *śyenacit* (falcon-shaped altar). As for what is said—that in the statement "one sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), the generic form (*ākṛti*) has the individual instance (*vyakti*) as its signified meaning—it can likewise be asserted in another case, namely "one should pile the *śyenacit*," that the individual instance has the generic form as its signified meaning. Which of these two is superior?
That the generic form is the word-meaning. If the individual instance were the word-meaning, [the following would occur].

It would not be applied to another individual. If, however, it is applied to another individual, then the individual is not the meaning of the word, for an individual is indeed devoid of all generalities and particularities. It is replied: this is not a fault. [For] in another individual, [the word applies to that which is] devoid of all generalities and particularities.

It will function in this way. If it were to function in another individual that is devoid of all generalities (sāmānya) and particularities (viśeṣa), then that would indeed be a generality itself. This is not so, for it is said: that object which is the substratum (āśraya) of both generalities and particularities is the individual (vyakti). And a word denoting an individual does not [denote] a generality.
It does not reside in the particular; rather, it denotes only their substratum. Therefore, its occurrence in another individual is not a fault. For that is not a universal.
If it also exists in other individuals, [then it is indeed a universal].

Why does the word "cow" not apply to an individual horse, which is likewise devoid of all general and particular properties? He replies: It will apply only to those things in which its usage has been observed, not everywhere. And the usage of the word "cow" has not been observed in the case of an individual horse; therefore, it will not apply there. If, wherever... [82] {1/}
The usage [of the word] has been observed; its application (*v�r̥tti*) occurs there.

However, in the case of a cow born today, the first usage would not be possible because it has not been observed there previously. Furthermore, the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyapratyaya*) would not be possible.
"This too is a cow," "this too is a cow";
or, "this is a cow."

Or it might be that [the cognition] is "this is a cow. However, a cognition of the universal (*sāmānya*) occurs even with respect to an individual cow (*govyakti*) never before seen. Therefore, one cannot maintain that the word "cow" denotes the individual by depending on its usage.
If that is so, then this is simply the inherent nature of the capacity [of the word], namely, that it applies to some particular individual.
It does not exist in any [particular] instance. For example, one might say: "Fire is hot, water is cold;
so too will this be. This is not established. For it is not understood that it exists in any particular individual instance.
"Not in any [particular] one"—this is true;

it will be that "cowness" (*gotva*) is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), [meaning] "in that individual (*vyakti*) wherein cowness resides. If that is so, then the individual would be perceived as qualified (*viśiṣṭā*).

And if it is qualified, the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) must be understood prior [to the qualified]. For no one is able to perceive something as qualified when its qualifier has not been perceived. Let it be so.

He will describe the configuration (*ākṛti*) as the qualifier and the individual (*vyakti*) as the qualified. For it is not the case that for one for whom the configuration is the word-meaning the individual is not the word-meaning, nor for one for whom the individual is the word-meaning is the configuration not so; both are the word-meaning of both. For someone, one or the other is intended to be expressed with predominance.
"Therefore, in this case, the form (ākṛti) is intended to be subordinate, while the individual (vyakti) is intended to be primary.
This is not so; for if both were being expressed, there would be a relationship of subordinate and primary between them. Furthermore, if the form is perceived here through the word...
In that case, it cannot be said that the individual (vyakti) is also the word-meaning. Why? Because the form (ākṛti) is eternally connected with the individual;

and when that related [form] is understood, the other related [individual] is understood. This is directly perceived by oneself: namely, that when a word is uttered, the individual is cognized. The distinction as to whether [the cognition of the individual] arises from the word or from the form is not perceptible. That [distinction] is understood through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). Even in the absence of the word, [the individual is understood when the form is understood].

One who understands the form (*ākṛti*) would [also understand] the individual (*vyakti*). However, if someone—due to some mental lapse—should fail to perceive the form even when the word has been uttered, he would never comprehend this individual. But surely the word applies to the form as qualified by the individual. If it were to apply to the form as qualified by the individual, [then...]

It would not be perceived as qualified by another individual. Therefore, the word is the cause for the cognition of the form (*ākṛti*), and the cognition of the form is the cause for the cognition of the individual (*vyakti*). But was it not said that [the individual] is perceived as subordinate? No; being subordinate does not contradict our position. In any case, it is indeed perceived. Whether it is subordinate or primary depends on the context. If it is uttered for its own sake, [it is primary].

If it is primary, then it is for its own sake; if, however, it is not for its own sake but only for the sake of another, then it is subordinate. In that case, there is no operation of the word itself.
Now, in the case of "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*),
the word *daṇḍin* does not denote the staff itself, and yet the person qualified by the staff is understood. Likewise here as well, the generic form (*ākṛti*) is not what is denoted.
Now, as for the claim that "the individual is understood as qualified by the form," this is not well said. It is true that the staff is not denoted by the word *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer);

however, there is no cognition of the staff-bearer when the staff has not been cognized. But the word *daṇḍa* exists as a constituent part of the word *daṇḍin*, by which the staff is made known. Therefore, this [position] is correct.
Namely: "When the qualifier is perceived, the qualified is perceived.
But surely, some part of the word *go* conveys the generic form (*ākṛti*), while another conveys the individual (*vyakti*).

Since it is said that the form (ākṛti) is understood from that [word], it does not follow that the word "cow" (go-śabda) is not expressive of the form. Nor is it the case that, just as the word "staff-bearer" (daṇḍin) is not applied to the staff itself, so too the word "cow" is not applied to the form. It is for this very purpose that the example was shown: that the word "hawk" (śyena) denotes the form alone.

Thus, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), since the word "hawk" is uttered even when there is no connection with an individual hawk, it is understood that the word denotes the form (*ākṛti*). However, the use of a word for an individual grain of rice is never observed without a connection to the form of rice.
Therefore, the view that the word denotes the form is superior.

E1,6; E2,4,5 (better): but not [so]}*
If it is argued that there would be no action, or if it is argued that there is an injunction regarding a different object rather than a substance; [this is not so]. (MS 1.3.34)
Now, as for what was said— that the action "he sprinkles the rice-grains" would not be possible,
that there would be no word for a substance,
and that the statement seen elsewhere, "six [cows] are to be given," would not exist— [this is addressed by the following: another...
"That which has that form" means it must be avoided.
NOTES:
{1/634: E4 (Fn.): if [it refers] to another}
Because the performance has that as its purpose, there is no division [of the ritual]. (MS 1.3.35)
Since the word has the generic form (ākṛti) as its meaning, it is employed in reference to that individual (vyakti) with which the generic form is connected.

For sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is indeed heard in the scripture as something to be performed upon a substance. Upon which substance? Upon that which is the means of sacrifice (*yajati-sādhana*). Because it is prompted by the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), it applies to the individual instance (*vyakti*) and not to the class-form (*ākṛti*), since [performing it on the class] would be impossible. In this context, the word "rice" (*vrīhi*) is employed as denoting the class-form (*ākṛtivacana*) for the purpose of qualifying the substratum of the sprinkling. For that word will cause the class-form to be understood, and once the class-form is understood, it will specify the substratum of the sprinkling. Therefore, there is no contradiction in its being a term denoting the class-form.

Thus, in the injunction "six cows are to be given as the sacrificial fee" (*dakṣiṇā*), when the number is to be applied to the substance of the fee, the word "cows" (*gāvaḥ*) serves as a qualifier denoting the generic form (*ākṛti*). Likewise, in the expression "another" (*anyam*), there is a connection with "otherness" (*anyatva*) regarding the substitute for what has been lost. In that case, the word "animal" (*paśu*) denotes the generic form and will be qualified by that form. Therefore, it is established that words such as "cow" (*gauḥ*) and "horse" (*aśvaḥ*) are denoters of the generic form.
NOTES:
It has been stated [in the preceding sūtra]: "This [Veda] is meaningful because it is handed down by tradition; therefore, everything [in it] must have that [dharma] as its purpose. (MS 1.4.1)
One should sacrifice with the Udbhid;
one should sacrifice with the Balabhid; one should sacrifice with the Abhijit.
"One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit.
In this regard, there is a doubt: are terms such as *udbhid* injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*), or are they names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*)? Why is there this doubt?

In both ways, this word *udbhidā* appears to be connected with the word *yajeta*. Does it enter into a relationship through grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*)—meaning "one should accomplish the sacrifice by means of the substance *udbhid*"—or through grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—meaning "one should sacrifice by means of the sacrifice *udbhid*"? In either case, this appears as a possibility within the sentence.
A doubt arises. What, then, is the prima facie position? We have already stated that the Veda has this purpose: that some portion of it is injunctive (vidhi).
That which makes known an unknown meaning,
such as "one should sacrifice with Soma"; and certain explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), which praise an injunction by inciting one toward it.
For example, there is a certain mantra such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity," which illuminates at the time of performance the meaning that has been prescribed.
For example: "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods," and so forth.

Therefore, these [names] such as *udbhid* must serve one of these purposes. Among them, it cannot first be an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), for that is a supplement to the sentence belonging to what is to be enjoined. Nor can it be a mantra, [as it lacks the characteristics of one].

Because there is no [other] thing of such a kind to be manifested, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*): the quality of being "udbhid" is enjoined as belonging to the sacrifice. Why? Because it favors what is already well-known (*prasiddhi*), because an injunction of a quality serves a purpose, and because it produces a specific engagement in action. Furthermore, these [terms] are not understood in common worldly usage to have the meaning of "sacrifice," nor are they defined as such by the Veda; therefore, they are injunctions of qualities.
If, then, no ritual act (*karman*) is enjoined, and since no ritual act has been enjoined, how can there be an injunction of a quality therein?

[The opponent claims: "It is meaningless. [We reply: No, we say. In the archetype, the Jyotiṣṭoma, the injunction of a quality will be meaningful. If it were a name, then "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*" would mean exactly the same thing as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*).

There would be no specific excellence in the performance [of the rite] itself. Furthermore, in the case of an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*), words such as *udbhid* and so forth will be meaningful by enjoining an additional purpose through their connection with that accessory. Therefore, the conclusion reached is that these are indeed injunctions of accessories.
This being the position, we reply:
recited}*
Or rather, it may be a name, because that which is new at its origin is not injunctive.

Or rather, the alternative position is reversed. We maintain that this must be a name; thus, it will enjoin a matter not previously enjoined—a sacrifice distinct from the Jyotiṣṭoma. And in this way, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) will denote the sacrifice. Otherwise, the direct statement, while intending to speak of "Udbhid" and so forth, would have to indicate by implication (*lakṣaṇā*) one who possesses the Udbhid and so forth—meaning, "one should perform [the rite] with a sacrifice characterized by the Udbhid. [This is because] by means of the sacrifice...

"One should do" (*kuryāt*) is the meaning of "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*). For sacrifice (*yāga*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*); and since *udbhid* and so forth are also designated by the instrumental case, they too are instruments.

In that context, the coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is consistent when *udbhidā yāgena* ("by means of the sacrifice called *udbhid*") is understood as a name of the ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*). If, however, it were denoting a substance (*dravyavacanatve*), [coordination would not be possible].

There would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) through an indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). And when there is a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the direct statement is superior. Therefore, it is the name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*). [Objection: But would not the well-known denotation as a substance (*dravyavacanatva*) be rejected, and an unknown denotation as a ritual action (*karmavacanatva*) be asserted? [Reply: It is said: its status as a denotation of a ritual action follows from the employment of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyānirdeśāt*). Why?

For the third case ending occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that denotes an instrument (*karaṇa*), and the sacrifice (*yāga*) is indeed the instrument. Therefore, we shall infer this [sacrifice] from this [word].

This is not correct. If, upon the mention of the third case, the cognition of a sacrifice were to arise from words such as *udbhid* and so forth, then this would be so. But for us, no such cognition arises.

Therefore, it is incorrect. If you argue that the statement of the instrumental case would otherwise be untenable, let it be untenable; however, it will never come to be a word denoting a sacrifice when its meaning is not understood.

Therefore, they are injunctions of qualities. If it is argued that this involves figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), we reply: it is better to assume figurative indication than to assume the naming of a sacrifice. For figurative indication is common in the world, whereas assuming what is not established is a forced construction. Moreover, if the name were being enjoined—

"It is not a sacrifice; or else, if it were a sacrifice, it would not be a name. Or, if both were enjoined, there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda). To this it is replied: "It will not be enjoined as a name, for *udbhid* and the others are merely restatements (anuvāda). If it is asked, 'From what [source] is their prior establishment?'—it is said in response: from the force of the word *ut*."

By the force of the word *udbhid*, the term *udbhid* denotes an action: the sacrifice is called *udbhid* because by means of it, the "breaking open" (*udbheda*)—that is, the manifestation—of cattle is accomplished. Similarly, it is *abhijit* because of conquering in a directed manner (*ābhimukhyena jayāt*), and *viśvajit* because of the conquest of all (*viśvajayāt*). This applies everywhere in such cases. Therefore, it is a name of the ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*). As for the objection that [a name] which does not produce a specific activity is useless—that is not so.
Even the name is meaningful through its connection with qualities and results. Therefore, it is established that names of this kind are indeed names of rituals.

In which [the mention of] qualities occurs primarily through connection with the principal [subject]. (MS 1.4.3)
One who desires cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā; the Bahiṣpavamāna stotra is threefold;

651*} Example: There is a doubt as to whether the words *citriyā*, *pavamāna*, *ājya*, and *pṛṣṭha* are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) or names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*). [The prima facie view is] on account of their well-known meanings.

Because they possess purposefulness and because they bring about a specific mode of activity, these are injunctions of accessories (*guṇavidhi*). Furthermore, these are not well-known rituals; nor are they derivative (*yaugika*) terms. For these are class-names (*jātiśabda*), and *citrayā* is an adjective denoting a quality (*guṇaśabda*). In the phrase "one should sacrifice with the *citrayā*," there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the sacrifice, since it is already known, and thus it is not an injunction of the sacrifice itself. If one were to assume a result for the accessory, there would be no intention to express the root *yajati* (to sacrifice). Likewise, [in the case of] "the *ājya*s are used..."

And they become the "back" (pṛṣṭha) [stotras]. Even when assuming them to be injunctions of qualities (guṇavidhi), there is no figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). Therefore, the initial position is that these are indeed injunctions of qualities.

This being the position reached, we reply: when there is doubt as to whether something is an injunction of a quality or a name, and another quality is taught therein, its connection is with the primary ritual action.

The meaning is that this is the name of the ritual action (*karman*). For if it were an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Since a male animal is already established [by another rule], a female animal [is enjoined here]; furthermore, "animals" is the result.
It is not possible to enjoin "the variegated quality" by means of a single sentence. If the variegated quality were being enjoined, it would be enjoined with respect to the female [animal];

it would not be enjoined with respect to the Agniṣomīya [sacrifice] or for one desiring cattle, nor would that [quality] be enjoined with respect to the Agniṣomīya. Likewise, in the case of "the Ājya [stotras] become fifteenfold," the state of being fifteenfold applies to the Ājyas; yet the Ājyas do not exist within the stotras unless they have been previously enjoined.

And there is no other injunctive sentence; this [sentence] alone would enjoin the *ājya* chants and their fifteenfold nature once they have been enjoined. Furthermore, the connection between the fifteenfold nature and the *ājya* chants is understood, as is the connection of the *ājya* chants with the *stotra*, though that connection and the connection with the fifteenfold nature were previously unknown. These two...

These two meanings cannot be enjoined within a single sentence. However, if it is indeed a name of the ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*), then this contradiction does not arise; in that case, only the connection with the number is being enjoined. Furthermore, [this is so].

By this word "ājyāni stotrāṇi," a quality would be enjoined only through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). Therefore, these are names of rituals that have been enjoined by other sentences such as, "They praise with the ājyas," "They praise with the pṛṣṭhas," and so forth. As for the claim that the name of the rituals is not well-known, [the answer is]: they are called *ājyāni* because of "going to the race" (*ājigamana*). How is there a "going to the race"? From the words of the explanatory passage (arthavāda): "That which they went to the race... [and so on].

"The state of being *ājya* belongs to the *ājyas*. [The term] *pṛṣṭhas* [is used] because of the mention of touch. [The term] *bahiṣpavamāna* [is used] because it consists of mantras for the *pavamāna* [laud] and because of its connection with the exterior. *Citrā* [is so called] because it consists of curds, honey, milk, clarified butter, parched grains, rice, and water. Therefore, such types [of words] are names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*). Now, why are the *ājyas*, qualified by the number fifteen, not enjoined as ritual acts among the *stotra* rites? Because they are qualified...
Because of the absence of a denotative word.
But surely these two words will constitute the denotation: "the fifteen ājya[-stotras]. [89] {1/}
Thus [it refers] to those that are qualified;

this [the Sūtra] will prescribe among these very stotras. Neither of these two words is prescriptive. One here is prescriptive and one is referential (uddeśaka). If both were prescriptive, there would be no mutual connection between them. If neither were prescriptive, the connection with the stotra would not be enjoined. Nor, in this case, does one word function as a qualifier toward [the other].
The hymn ought to be prescriptive. Therefore, because of the difference in the mode of expression, this is not a valid solution.
