They record in the sacred texts: "One who desires heaven should offer the Agnihotra," and "He should pour the Āghāra libation.
In this regard, there arises a doubt: do the words *agnihotra* and *āghāra* prescribe accessory details (*guṇavidhi*), or...?
Or is it the name of a ritual action? We say: they are injunctions of accessory materials (*guṇavidhi*). Why?

Because it is understood that "in this [rite] there is an oblation (*hotra*) for Agni. Likewise, there is a substance capable of flowing, such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*), in the expression "he pours the *āghāra*. In this way, common usage (*prasiddhi*) will be upheld. And [the same applies] to the *āghāra* offering in the *upāṃśuyāja*. In that case, these two [sentences] possess purposefulness and produce a specific mode of activity. Furthermore, in the view that they are injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*), there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as in the case of "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*. In the *agnihotra*, the injunction of an accessory quality is understood through the compound; likewise, in the *āghāra*, the accessory quality is enjoined by the direct expression (*śruti*) itself in the form "he performs the *āghāra*. Therefore, [the conclusion is reached] that these are indeed injunctions of accessory qualities. Thus the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) stands.

We reply: "And another scriptural passage is that which makes [the quality] known" (*tatprakhyaṃ cānyaśāstram*). Regarding the two qualities that might be suspected to be enjoined by these [two passages], they are both understood from elsewhere. The injunction regarding the deity is found in the text: "One offers in the evening to Agni and to Prajāpati. And the text: "This [oblation] was indeed fourfold; having poured the *āghāra*-libation for it... [establishes the quality].

Furthermore, there is an injunction regarding the substance in relation to the locus (*ādhāra*). An injunction is defined as the making known of what was previously unknown. In this case, however, the prescription of the quality is already known from another source; therefore, these are not injunctions of qualities. Rather, they are possible as names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*), in which the oblation (*hotra*)—that is, the sacrifice—is offered to Agni.
That is the *agnihotra*. The *āghāra* is well known as the act of pouring out a long stream [of ghee]; therefore, it is a name for a ritual action.
Furthermore, the reasons such as "well-known usage" (*prasiddhi*) have already been stated as rebuttals. If it is argued that the mention of "Agni" is intended to exclude Prajāpati, this is not so;
for this [word] is capable of enjoining Agni.

It is not possible to negate Prajāpati; furthermore, if Prajāpati were negated, the injunction [regarding him] would be purposeless, and it is understood that Prajāpati is the deity (*devatā*). And that which is so understood cannot be conceived as false. Therefore, this is not a valid solution. It is said in reply: "He pours the *āghāra* libation"—this injunction is directed toward a substance (*dravya*), whereas those [other passages] for which a substance is intended to be prepared...

For by this act, the substance is sprinkled (*kṣāryate*). And once sprinkled, it accomplishes the sacrifice (*yāga*). Of which principal action, then, is this the name? It is said: this very act of pouring (*āghāraṇa*) is the principal action. But surely it lacks both a substance and a deity? We reply: it does have them. For that [action], the substance is clarified butter (*ājya*), as indicated by the words "having poured the *āghāra*."

The deity is known from the wording of the mantra: "Indra, lift up!"—for the mantra, "He offers the *āghāra* oblation," denotes either the action itself or its instrument as being inherent in the ritual act. And this mantra is capable of denoting Indra. If that Indra were to be the instrument of that [action], [then he would be the deity].
Thus, by means of this mantra, the *āghāra* (sprinkling) can be performed. Therefore, Indra is the deity;
the *āghāraṇa* is conjoined with both the substance and the deity. Consequently, it is a sacrifice (*yajati*), and this [mantra] is the name of that sacrifice.

It has been stated that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*). By what means, then, is its function (*vyāpāra*) enjoined? Therefore, the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) applies with respect to both the person desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājyakāma*) and the accessory (*guṇa*). Consequently, it is connected to both.
If there were an injunction in both cases, the *vājapeya* would not be connected to the sacrifice for the one desiring self-sovereignty; for in that case, there would be two separate sentences.
There is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between the injunction of a subordinate element (*guṇavidhi*) and the sacrifice for one who desires self-sovereignty (*svārājyakāma*).
If it is argued that there is a connection between the one desiring self-sovereignty and the sacrifice by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), we say no;

for [the subordinate element] is enjoined with respect to the sacrifice in general by means of the sentence (*vākya*). If it is argued that let there be a connection with the sacrifice in general, we say no.

Because it is understood that there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between the sacrifice and one who desires self-sovereignty (*svārājya*). Thus, the sublation of both context (*prakaraṇa*) and sentence (*vākya*) is appropriate only if [Vājapeya] is a name for a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*). For if it were the position that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), all these defects such as syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would arise. Therefore, the word *vājapeya* is a name for a ritual action.

The following and other such passages are heard in scripture: "That which is dedicated to Agni, consisting of eight potsherds, is unswerving on the new moon day and the full moon day. In this regard, there is a doubt: are [the terms] *āgneya*, *agnīṣomīya*, and so forth, injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*), or are they names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*)? What, then, is the prima facie position? If they were injunctions of accessory qualities, multiple accessories would be enjoined—namely, Agni, the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and the eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*). Therefore, they are not injunctions of accessory qualities.

This being the case, we reply: both that action and its qualities would be enjoined. For they are inseparable from the action when the word ending in a *taddhita* suffix is intended for the injunction of the action. For in that context, the state of being dedicated to Agni (*āgneyatā*) is enjoined for the eight-potherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*). This very cake becomes "dedicated to Agni" only if it is offered after being mentally resolved upon for Agni.

Therefore, this sacrifice is enjoined in this manner. When it is being enjoined in this way, it cannot be enjoined without enjoining both the fire and the cake on eight potsherds; for a relationship being enjoined cannot be said to be enjoined without enjoining its two relata. Therefore, these are injunctions of accessories (*guṇavidhi*). A sacrificial cake made of rice or barley, when prepared upon eight potsherds, is indeed the *puroḍāśa* itself.
That is a restatement (*anuvāda*). And here, the *aṣṭākapāla* (the cake on eight potsherds) is already established by the statement "he bakes it on potsherds" (*kapāleṣu śrapayati*);

therefore, they do not take what has been baked by another means. Consequently, in this view, there is no split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). If [the qualities] were not enjoined by another [text], then it would be a name; however, where the qualities are enjoined by another statement, there it is a name. For example: "He performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*).
In the case of *barhis* and *ājya*, because the word is obtained even when there is no consecration, it is not a term for that [consecrated object].
Regarding *barhis*, *ājya*, and *puroḍāśa*, there is a doubt: are these words for consecrated objects (*saṃskāra-śabda*) or are they words for generic classes (*jāti-śabda*)?

We say they are words for consecrated objects. Everywhere, people apply the word *barhis* to grass that has been consecrated, not to unconsecrated grass. They apply the word *ājya* to clarified butter (*ghṛta*) that has been consecrated. Likewise, they apply the word *puroḍāśa* to flour-cake (*piṣṭa*) that has been consecrated.

But surely, [the term] is also applied metaphorically to something unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) in a certain sense. For example, speakers say, "The cows have gone taking the *barhis* grass," or likewise, "The clarified butter is for sale," or "My mother gives me a riddle with a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). Their usage toward these things is due to similarity, just as the word "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*) is used for the *upaśaya*. Why is this so?
Since the word is applied to only one part [of the whole], it follows that these are words denoting a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*).

This being the position reached, we reply: because the word is found even when applied to *barhis* (sacrificial grass) and the like, which have not undergone preparation, they are not words denoting a preparatory rite. But was it not said that they will apply to a single part by virtue of similarity? That is not so.

For it can only be said that [the term] is used "on account of similarity" once the status of these words as denoting consecrated objects (*saṃskāra*) is established; yet that is not established. How so?
Consecrations are enjoined with reference to things designated by words such as *barhis* (sacrificial grass). Therefore, since the words exist, there must be consecrations corresponding to them.

And since the acquisition of the word [barhis] occurs only when the refinement (saṃskāra) exists, there arises a mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya). Furthermore, refinements are not prescribed such that people would employ them after having observed them [in common usage]. Therefore, people do not employ words like *barhis* with respect to refined objects. Consequently, even in a single instance, they are seen to be based on the genus (*jāti*) as the cause.

In all cases, [words] ought to have their basis in genus (*jāti*). Furthermore, for things that are not worldly, it is impossible to determine their meaning from the Veda alone without depending on the relationship between preceding and succeeding words. One might postulate such a basis so that the preceding and succeeding words do not become meaningless;
however, that which is unperceived and cannot be understood is impossible to postulate.

Furthermore, your preceding and following words will be meaningful through the use of unrefined (asaṃskṛta) worldly expressions. Therefore, words of this kind are indeed generic terms (*jātiśabda*). The purpose [of the argument] is as follows: regarding the rule "one covers the sacrificial post-hole with *barhis* grass," if the prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*) holds, then it must be covered using only consecrated (*saṃskṛta*) grass.
In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), it is the opposite.
[The cause is] based on genus (*jāti*)}*
The sprinkling water [is for the purpose of the ritual] because of its connection with the purpose.

It is heard [in the Veda]: "Place the *prokṣaṇī*s. Regarding that, there is a doubt concerning the word *prokṣaṇī*: is it based on a ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*), or is it based on a genus (*jāti*), or is it etymological (*yaugika*)? In this regard, since the word is observed to be used when the ritual refinements are present, its status as a term based on ritual refinement is understood.

Because the word is applied to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is a class-term (*jātiśabda*). In a certain region, people say, "We were agitated by the *prokṣaṇī* waters even when they were unconditioned. Since it would thus follow that this is a class-term, it is stated that it is an etymological term (*yaugika*). Why?
Because of its connection with the meaning. This is because the application of the aggregate consisting of the prefix, root, and suffix as "*prokṣaṇyaḥ*" is based on the cause of a class.

It is inferred [that the term is etymological]. For, due to its connection with the act of sprinkling (*secanasaṃyoga*), it will be supported by common usage that [the word] occurs in relation to water when accompanied by a prefix, a verbal root, an instrument, and a suffix. When even other types of sprinkling are expressed by the word *prokṣaṇa*, then [the application of the term] to water will occur simply through that connection; thus, it is not possible to postulate a collective meaning for the whole. Therefore, it is etymological (*yaugika*). The purpose [of this discussion] is...
"Clarified butter is the sprinkling," it is said.

If these are words denoting a ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*), then the injunction is "Place the *prokṣaṇī* waters. If they are genus-words (*jātiśabda*), then it is "Place the clarified butter. If they are etymological (*yaugika*) terms, then it is "the act of sprinkling" (*prokṣaṇam*). [96] {1/688}

"One bakes the bricks with the *nirmanthya* [fire]. Because it is seen used for something prepared (*saṃskṛta*), the word *nirmanthya* is a term for a consecrated object. The purpose is that when the term is based on consecration, the bricks must be baked with a consecrated fire; whereas if it were a generic term (*jātiśabda*), [it would apply otherwise].

"With what is available. In the case of a derivative term, as in "he eats with fresh butter" (*nāvanītena*), it is understood to mean "with [butter] that has not long been churned"; likewise, in the case of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, there would be an option. If this is argued: MS_1,4.13.

Regarding the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice on the first festival of the Cāturmāsya rites, there is a doubt: in the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva," is the word *vaiśvadeva* an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) or the name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*)? If there is a doubt, there is no [real] doubt;
in the case of the Vaiśvadeva, there is an option. The word *vaiśvadeva* is an injunction of an accessory, for an injunction of an accessory is understood; [namely,] the Viśvedevas.

They are prescribed in the sacrifices such as the Āgneya and others. In that regard, there is an option between Agni and the others on one hand and the Viśvedevas on the other. In this way, the established usage will be meaningful.
*Not so, because of the context and because of the direct injunction; for the context does not [govern] the substance.* MS 1.4.14.
This is not so. Agni and the others are prescribed by direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) for those sacrifices;

it is understood that the Viśvedevas are [prescribed] by the sentence (*vākya*) through that very context (*prakaraṇa*), and not by any other means. Furthermore, this option (*vikalpa*) based on unequal injunctions cannot be valid. For context is not capable of subverting a substance that has been directly revealed by scripture. Therefore, [the term] is a name of the ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*).

And there is a mutual connection with what is purposeless. (MS 1.4.15)

Now, it is argued that by this term *vaiśvadeva*, the sacrificial accessory (*yāga-guṇa*) characterized by the qualities of Agni and others is indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), for the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) belongs to the Viśvedevas therein. [Objection: If the sacrificial accessory is indicated by the word *vaiśvadeva*, then the Viśvedevas are not being enjoined;
how can the word *vaiśvadeva*, uttered only once, indicate both the sacrificial accessory and [the deities]?

And because it would follow that [the sacrifice] would establish all the gods, this mutual connection of the word *vaiśvadeva* with "all the gods" (*viśvair devaiḥ*) is not tenable. Therefore, it is simply the name of the rite (*karmanāmadheya*), and not an injunction of a subordinate element (*guṇavidhi*).
This is because subordinate elements exist for the sake of another (*parārthatvād guṇānām*). (MS 1.4.16)

Furthermore, the subordinate qualities (*guṇas*) exist for the sake of another; they are not able to cause the principal (*pradhāna*) to repeat its performance. Therefore, the sacrifice must be performed once and ought not to be repeated in accordance with the subordinate qualities. Moreover, because the deity is the same, there is no contradiction. In that case, thirty oblations are offered within a single principal offering; thus, the fulfillment of the number thirty pertains to the oblations made in the *āhavanīya* fire.
It is not tenable [that they are injunctions]. Therefore, it is established that they are names of rites.
"Those which possess a prior [basis] are for the purpose of non-injunction; their capacity lies in the traditional recension (samāmnāya). (MS 1.4.17)

It is heard in scripture: "One should offer an oblation on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when a son is born. In that context, alternative options for the number of potsherds are heard, such as: "When it is on eight potsherds, by means of the Gāyatrī he purifies him with sacred luster," and so forth.
Regarding these, there is a doubt: are the numbers eight and so on injunctions of subordinate qualities (guṇavidhi), or are they merely explanatory passages (arthavāda)?

In this regard, we say that these are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*). How so? For those [words] which have a prior basis (*pūrvavat*)—that is, whose referents are already known—are not for the purpose of enjoining; rather, the capacity of this sentence within the recited collection (*samāmnāya*) consists in its expression of what has not been enjoined before. What is that?

This is the capacity of an injunction (*vidhānasāmarthya*). In this way, it will enjoin a matter not previously enjoined. Otherwise, being merely explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), they would be purposeless. Furthermore, the twelve potsherds cannot be regarded as a mere subordinate element (*śeṣabhāva*). For the praise of the eight potsherds is direct (*pratyakṣa*), whereas that of the twelve is indirect (*parokṣa*). And where there is no direct [praise], there may be an indirect one. Therefore, these are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhis*).
previously enjoined}*
But for the purpose of enjoining a quality (*guṇa*), those qualities would be meaningless in actual usage, for there is nothing that possesses meaning with respect to that [quality]. (MS 1.4.18)

This is not the case that these are injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*). If these were for the purpose of enjoining an accessory quality, they would enjoin a number of potsherds (*kapāla*) for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). However, they are not able to enjoin the performance of the sacrifice itself. For the state of having twelve potsherds belongs to the sacrifice by virtue of the direct statement (*vākya*), whereas the eight potsherds and so forth belong to it by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, those [eight potsherds, etc. will not apply to the sacrifice. Furthermore, since the number eight and so forth are syntactically connected with the sacrificial cake, they set aside the context and—

They cannot belong to the sacrifice; for if they were unrelated to the sacrifice, they would be meaningless, as there is no fruit in their connection with the *puroḍāśa* cake alone. However, it is appropriate that they serve as an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) for the Vaiśvānara sacrifice.
Therefore, they are *arthavādas*;
thus, their status as a supplement (*śeṣa*) to that [sacrifice] is not tenable.
"What has been stated thus must be refuted"—this is the sūtra ending with the introductory phrase [ābhāṣānta].
[The answer is: "Because there is no distinction, they would be applicable for the purpose of praise within the context of an injunction. (MS 1.4.20)

But when it is understood that the passages concerning the eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) and so forth are purposeless as mere incitements (*prarocanā*), then, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the praise of the twelve potsherds will serve as an incitement for the Vaiśvānara sacrifice. For within the number twelve, there exist specific numbers such as eight and the rest.

[The parts] are not separate. Therefore, since it serves as a praise for the twelve-potherd [cake], the praise of its constituent parts is appropriate—just as one might say, "The rim and hub of this wheel are beautiful," or "The elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry of this army are beautiful. Thus, the praise is logically established.
If it is argued that there must be a cause, [we reply: MS 1.4.21.

If you view these as *arthavādas*, why should the fruit of *brahmavarcasa* (spiritual luster) and so forth not result from the eightfold [cake] and the rest? "One desiring *brahmavarcasa* [should offer] a cake on eight potsherds.

Likewise for the subsequent [offerings], according to one's desire. What would happen in this case? Even if it were an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), it would still be purposeless.
It will not be the case that the praise of the twelve potsherds is imagined through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, the injunctions will pertain to the desires.
Because [otherwise] they would be purposeless, the agent's motives are not the cause; for an injunction is prescribed for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*). (MS 1.4.22)
If the injunctions were for the sake of the desire, there would be separate sentences. But this is a single sentence:
"Upon the birth of a son, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara"; thus, the fact that it is on twelve potsherds is already included within this.

"In this very world, he bestows cattle upon him in whom, once born, one performs this sacrifice; he becomes purified, radiant, powerful, possessed of sensory vigor, and rich in cattle"—thus ends [the passage]. If the qualities such as "eightfold" (*aṣṭatva*) heard in the middle of that [passage] were not connected [to it], then they would constitute separate sentences. [100]

For the causes of the agent would indeed be qualities such as purity (*pūtatva*) and so forth. It is this purpose of the quality that is prescribed here in the Vaiśvānara sacrifice, namely, "he becomes purified" (*pūta eva*), and so on. And by means of that, these [qualities] such as the number eight are connected directly as causes:
because he purifies him with the *gāyatrī* verse through spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), therefore he is indeed purified.

Because he places brilliance in him by means of the *trivṛt* [stoma] itself, he is brilliant; because he places food in him by means of the *virāj* itself, he is an eater of food; because he places sensory power in him by means of the *triṣṭubh* itself, he is possessed of sensory power;

because he places cattle in him by means of the *jagatī* itself, he is possessed of cattle. Therefore, since injunctions for specific desires are impossible [in this context], [the results follow automatically].

If even the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) were not to exist, these [passages] would indeed be purposeless. Therefore, the possession of Brahmanic luster and so forth is not the reason for the number eight and the rest. Consequently, the number eight and the rest are merely explanatory passages.
The establishment of that [is as follows]: MS_1,4.23.
"The sacrificer is the *prastara* (grass-bundle);
the sacrificer is the single-pot-sherd," and so forth, is recited in the tradition.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is the statement "the sacrificer is the *prastara*" an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), or...

"What is the purpose of an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*)? For example, [the statement] "The sacrificer is the one-potsherd cake" (*yajamāna ekakapālaḥ*). What, then, is the prima facie view? That it is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*). Why so? Because in this way it will enjoin a previously unknown matter; otherwise, the explanatory statement would be purposeless. And it is logical that it should have a purpose. Therefore, it is an injunction.
This is not so;
for if it were an injunction (*vidhi*), then [it would apply] to the function of the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*).

The sacrificer would be restricted [to the role of the *prastara*]. Or else, the *prastara* performs the functions of the sacrificer; for it is said, "He places the *juhū* on the *prastara*, or all the ladles (*sruva*)," and thus the *juhū* would have to be placed upon the sacrificer, or all the *sruva* ladles [would likewise be placed there].
If that were the case, it would not be possible to perform the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*),
because from the time of initiation (*dīkṣaṇa*) until the ritual is completed, both the Brahman priest and the sacrificer sit [in their respective roles].

Furthermore, the *prastara* (grass-bundle) cannot perform the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). Likewise, if the sacrificer were enjoined to perform the function of the single-potsherd cake (*ekakapāla*), it would have to be offered entirely as a burnt oblation (*sarvahuta*); in that case, there would be a total abandonment of the entire ritual system (*sarvatantra-parilopa*).

Moreover, the single-potsherd cake cannot perform the duties of the sacrificer. Therefore, this is not an injunction (*vidhi*). There exists another injunction: "He places the *prastara* above the *barhis* grass; he makes the single-potsherd cake a complete offering."

Thus, for this reason as well, it is not an injunction. Rather, it is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). For it is already known that the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), and that the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) is the sacrificer.
But how is their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) understood? For the sacrificial grass-bundle or the cake on one potsherd is not the sacrificer;
nor is the sacrificer a sacrificial cake prepared on a single potsherd, or the first sheaf of cut grass. How [is this so]?
The word "other" (*para*) refers to something else;
for what purpose, then, is that which is already known being mentioned? It is said in reply: it is mentioned while being known in order to offer praise.

The *prastara* grass-bundle is to be placed above the *barhis* grass because it is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Likewise, the one-pot-sherd cake (*ekakapāla*) is the sacrificer when it is offered in its entirety.

"Heaven is to be made the *āhavanīya* fire; thus it becomes established therein. [Objection: How can a word for one thing apply to another? [Response: It is a figurative statement (*guṇavāda*). This statement proceeds on account of a quality (*guṇa*). [Objection: How can a word that does not denote a quality express a quality?
[Response: We say it is by denoting its own primary meaning. None of these words are figurative in the sense of abandoning their own primary meaning.

[The word "lion"] applies to the qualities [of a lion]. For in that case, there would be the abandonment of what is well-known and the conceptualization of what is unknown. Moreover, not all words denoting a collection apply to the individual qualities; for it is observed even in one devoid of the qualities [of a lion]. Indeed, even a son of a lioness who is incapable of performing the [typical] actions may, when occasionally afflicted by disease, still be a lion. Furthermore, a word denoting a collection cannot properly apply to a single part [of that collection]. [It refers rather to] that universal (*sāmānya*) which exists in all individual lions.

The established principle that "a word is that which expresses its own meaning" would then be overturned. Furthermore, one would not apply the term "lion" through mere conceptual construction in the absence of an actual lion, because such a construction would be impossible. If it is asked, "How then is the determination of the cognition [of the lion] established by the expression of its own meaning?"—it is due to the connection with the object. When it is recognized as a "lion," since violent action is generally present therein, it is understood as a "violent actor."

The meaning [is understood] through the power of the cognition (*pratyaya*). For one who thinks, "I shall cause the cognition of a forceful agent," if he utters the word "lion" (*siṃha*), his intention is accomplished. Because the meaning "lion" is understood as being connected with the quality of being a forceful agent, it causes the cognition of the other meaning. Thus, by the expression of its own primary meaning, there is a connection with its qualities.

It is understood [in those cases]. But here, in the statements "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*)" and "The sacrificer is the single-pot-sherd (*ekakapāla*"), what kind of connection of qualities is understood? It is the quality of "being that which effects its accomplishment. For everyone brings about the accomplishment of their own purpose. Furthermore, whatever else effects the accomplishment of one's purpose comes to mind when that person is mentioned; just as, for example, a king [brings to mind] his troop-leader.

Thus, the foot-soldier accomplishes the king’s business; when the word "king" is uttered, he is understood [as being included]. Likewise here as well, the *prastara* (grass-bundle) and the *ekakapāla* (single-pot-sherd cake) accomplish the sacrificer’s business; they are understood when the sacrificer is understood. Therefore, those two are conveyed by the word "sacrificer. How so?

These two [passages] would be praises regarding the placing of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) above and regarding the offering of the whole oblation; therefore, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) of this kind are not injunctions (*vidhi*).
It may take the place of the function of the *prastara*;
therefore, it may [be used] in the function of the *prastara*.

The Brāhmaṇa belongs to Agni;
the Rājanya belongs to Indra;
the Vaiśya belongs to the Viśvedevas—and so forth.

They are heard [in the texts]. Regarding this, there is a doubt as to whether these are injunctions of secondary qualities (*guṇavidhi*) or explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). We say they are injunctions of secondary qualities. In this way, they will enjoin a new matter (*apūrva*);

otherwise, being merely explanatory passages, they would be purposeless. There is no further injunction [required], because another injunction already exists. Therefore, there is agreement. Their mention is for the purpose of praising the injunction. By what means do words such as "related to Agni" (*āgneya*) apply to those [offerings] that are not related to Agni?
By way of figurative praise (*guṇavāda*). What is this figurative praise? It is the connection with fire (*agni*). How so?
Because they belong to the same class (*ekajātīyakatva*). What is this belonging to the same class? Prajāpati desired, "May I create offspring. He drew forth the *trivṛt* [stoma] from his mouth.
Agni was emitted as the deity after him,
the Gāyatrī as the metre, and the Rathantara as the Sāman.
The Brāhmaṇa is [the foremost] of men; the goat is [the foremost] of animals. Therefore they are preeminent, for they were created from the mouth.
From the chest and the two arms, he fashioned the fifteenfold [Stoma].
From him Indra was created as a deity,
the Triṣṭubh as the metre, and the Bṛhat as the Sāman.
The Rājanya among men, the sheep among animals. Therefore they are full of vigor, for they were created from vigor. From the two thighs, from the middle, he fashioned the seventeenfold [Stoma].
The Viśvedevas were created as its deities;
the Jagatī was the metre; the Vairūpa was the Sāman.
"The Vaiśya among humans, the cow among animals.
When this has been stated, once such a thing of that kind is understood, another thing of that same kind also comes to mind. Therefore, these are words that are explanatory praises (*arthavāda*).

Homogeneity. (MS 1.4.25)
"The sacrificer is the sacrificial post (*yūpa*);
the sacrificial post is in the sun," and so forth is heard in scripture. In that regard, there is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).

There is a doubt as to whether this is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise). It is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) because it possesses meaning. However, it is not an injunction because the sacrificer is incapable of performing the function of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), nor is the sacrificial post capable of performing the function of the sacrificer; furthermore, there is no other injunction [to that effect]. This correspondence serves the purpose of praising the injunction. The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) arises from figurative description (*guṇavāda*). What is the quality?
Similarity. What is similarity?
Verticality and brilliance. Therefore, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) of this kind [are to be understood] in this way.
Other animals than cattle and horses are indeed no-animals;
cattle and horses are [true] animals. That which is without the *sāman* is indeed no-sacrifice.

It is heard in scripture: "That which is without *chandoma* is indeed without sacrifice. Regarding this, when there is doubt as to whether these are injunctions (*vidhi*) or explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), the initial position is that they are injunctions because they possess purposeful meaning. To this, it is replied: if they were injunctions, [the following would occur].
Cattle and horses alone would be the sacrificial animals; the Sāman-chanting alone would be the sacrifice;
and the Chandomas alone would be the sacrificial session. As for other animals, other sacrifices, and [104] the [other] sessions...
Furthermore, the origin of the *satra* sacrifices would be purposeless, and another injunction (*vidhi*) would not be possible. Therefore, this correspondence is for the sake of praise.

There is a deprecation of other animals in order to praise cows and horses; a deprecation of those without *sāman* chants in order to praise those with *sāman*; and those without *chandoma* meters are deprecated in order to praise those with *chandoma*. For example: "That which is without clarified butter... [and so forth].
That is non-eating; that which is soiled is "without clothing."

It is heard in the scripture: "He lays down the *sṛṣṭi*-bricks. Regarding this, when there is a doubt as to whether this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) or an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is an injunction because it conveys something not previously established. To this, it is replied: if it were an injunction, the meaning would be "he lays down bricks with the *sṛṣṭi*-mantras. In that case, no specific distinction among the bricks would be required.
"Such are the *sṛṣṭi*-mantras, not such are [others]. In that case, all mantras containing the characteristic marks of creation (*sṛṣṭi*) would be applicable.

Consequently, other unconnected mantras would become purposeless. Therefore, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of those mantras already obtained through the traditional recension (*samāmnāya*) for the act of piling (*upadhāna*); it is a mention of the *sṛṣṭis*.

It is for the purpose of establishing [the creation] and providing an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*). Furthermore, if it were an injunction (*vidhi*), there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*);
in the passage "They praise with one," it would have to indicate those things that were not created. But surely, there is also figurative indication in a restatement (*anuvāda*)?

There is no fault in resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*). But how can the word "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) apply to both non-creations and creations? By way of predominance (*bhūman*). There, many mantras possess the characteristic marks of creation, while only a few possess the opposite marks.
The proclamation of creations within the creations.
Regarding the passage "They praise with one [verse]," one should understand that those which are not created [verses] are indicated there.
But is it not the case that even in a restatement (anuvāda), there is indication (lakṣaṇā)?
[The answer is: It is a collection of indicative marks (liṅgasamavāya).

Regarding the injunctions "he places the *prāṇabhṛt*s" and "he places the *ājyānī*s," if these were intended as mere injunctions, then while the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks are being placed with their respective mantras, those mantras possessing different indicative marks (*viliṅga*) would be rendered purposeless.
Therefore, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Due to the association with a characteristic mark (*liṅgasamavāyāt*), a word for one thing is applied to another, as in "the umbrella-bearers are going," where all are indicated by the single umbrella-bearer. However, this word *prāṇabhṛt* and the word *sṛṣṭi* do not indicate the group of mantras by abandoning their own primary meaning (*jahatsvārtham*). And since [the terms] *sṛṣṭi* and *prāṇabhṛt* [occur] in the group...

Those two are also included. For example, by the word "umbrella-bearer" (*chatri*), through the function of indicating its own primary referent (*svārtha-lakṣaṇārthena*), that person who is not currently holding an umbrella is also understood as a "bearer."
Because it would be purposeless, [the sacrifice] is not the cause; for the causes belong to the agent, since the ritual injunctions are prescribed for the sake of the constituent qualities.

In cases of doubt, [the meaning is determined] from the remainder of the sentence.

"One places smeared pebbles" is [the injunction], and it is heard in scripture that "clarified butter is indeed splendor. In this regard, there is a doubt: should they be smeared with any one of the substances—clarified butter, oil, or fat?

"Either with sugar or indeed with ghee. How is there doubt? Because the sentence begins with the general term "ointment" (*añjana*) and concludes with the specific term "ghee. In a single sentence, the conclusion must correspond to the beginning. In that case, either the general term at the outset is intended to indicate the specific, or the specific term at the conclusion is intended to characterize the general.

There arises the doubt: "Which is more appropriate, the beginning or the conclusion? When such a doubt exists, since there is no contradiction when the opening statement is general in nature, one should not assume a specific meaning [at that point]. However, at the conclusion, because a general cognition has already arisen, there is a contradiction;

thus, the mention of *ghṛta* (clarified butter) serves to indicate its specific definition (*lakṣaṇārtha*). This is just as the word "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) is used both for actual creations and for non-creations.

In this way, even that which is not ghee is called "ghee. When such ambiguity arises, we say: the commencement of a sentence by means of a general term depends upon a specific instance, while its conclusion is determined by the specific instance. Why?

Because no general rule has been prescribed, whereby there would be a contradiction with the conclusion. How is it that nothing is prescribed? Because, in cases of doubt, there is an absence of any word of prescription.

For there is no word of injunction [here], because the expression "he places down the smeared pebbles" (*aktāḥ śarkarā upadadhāti*) is an indication in the present tense. Nor is there a direct praise of the general category; rather, there is an explicit praise of the clarified butter (*ghṛta*). The praise of the clarified butter is by means of direct denotation (*śruti*), whereas the praise of the general category is by means of indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And direct denotation is more authoritative than indirect indication. Therefore, it is an injunction of clarified butter. Likewise, "he puts on the garment."

"Indeed, linen cloth belongs to all the gods; thus, having touched this [earth], he should sing the *udgītha*, for all beings subsist upon this *audumbarī* [pillar]. **NOTES:** 1. *Kṣauma*: Linen cloth, made from flax (*kṣumā*). 2. *Sarvadevatyam*: Belonging to or dedicated to all the deities. 3. *Udāyet*: He should sing forth; refers to the chanting of the *udgītha*. 4. *Audumbarīm*: The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) made of *udumbara* wood. 5. *Upajīvanti*: They live upon, subsist by means of. This refers to the ritual significance of the *audumbarī* as a source of sustenance and vitality. The connection between the linen cloth and the earth is established through their shared association with all the gods (*sarvadevatya*), while the *audumbarī* is linked to the earth because it is planted in the ground and supports the sacrifice. By touching the earth, the priest symbolically connects the ritual act to its universal foundation. The commentary suggests that the linen garment represents the cosmic order pervaded by all deities, and the act of touching the earth serves to ground the ritual in the reality of the world. The *audumbarī* is praised as the support for all living beings. Thus, the passage integrates the material elements of the rite—the garment and the pillar—with the metaphysical principle that the sacrifice is sustained by and connected to the totality of existence. The mention of the *udgītha* indicates that the specific act of chanting must be performed with this awareness of universal connection. The phrase "all beings subsist upon this" (*imām hy audumbarīm viśvābhūtāny upajīvanti*) emphasizes the sacrificial post's role as a conduit for life-force (*ojas*) and nourishment, derived from the *udumbara* tree’s association with strength and abundance. The ritual logic here is to ensure that the performer remains in harmony with the cosmic substrate while executing the sacred function. The use of the term *upajīvanti* implies a reciprocal relationship: just as the post supports the sacrifice, the sacrifice in turn sustains the world. This reflects the broader Vedic view of the interdependence between the microcosm of the ritual and the macrocosm of nature. The instruction to touch the earth before singing the *udgītha* serves as a meditative preparation, aligning the singer’s consciousness with the foundational reality of the universe. The commentary further suggests that the linen garment, being "of all the gods," acts as a protective covering that shields the priest from worldly impurities while maintaining his divine status. The parallelism between the garment and the pillar underscores the unity of the ritual space, where both the personal attire and the central sacrificial object participate in the same cosmic resonance. Ultimately, the passage functions as a *mantra*-like injunction to sanctify the ritual environment by invoking the presence of all deities and affirming the sacrificial post as the axis mundi of life. The connection between the linen cloth and the earth is not merely symbolic but ritualistically necessary to establish the integrity of the *yajña*. "With the hand of those who are able. Since this is stated without qualification, there would be no fixed rule.

Verbs denote actions; from them, the performance of action is understood, for it is this meaning that is enjoined. (MS 2.1.1)
In the first chapter, the definition of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) was established;

therein, injunctions (vidhi), explanatory passages (arthavāda), mantras, and traditional texts (smṛti) were determined according to their true nature, and subsidiary injunctions (guṇavidhi) as well as names (nāmadheya) were examined.

It has been stated that the determination of the meaning of doubtful matters is achieved through the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). That must not be forgotten. Immediately thereafter, the primary and secondary [elements], as well as those that are distinct and non-distinct, will be examined.
This alone is the meaning to be described, and nothing else;
this indeed is the connection of the chapter. Therefore, sixfold differentiation of action will be explained here: difference of words, repetition, [and so forth].
Number, quality, and grammatical derivation.

The term "name" (nāmadheya) refers back to what is about to be stated. It is mentioned here so that the happiness being demonstrated may be easily grasped, and thus the listener's intellect is composed; this very thing is called the "chapter on the characteristics of various actions" (nānākarmalakṣaṇa), in its essential purport.
Apart from this, there is the introduction (*upodghāta*) and what follows from the introduction (*prasaktānuprasakta*).

Among these, first this is considered: it was stated in the first chapter that "Dharma is a matter characterized by an injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ*), and an injunction is a sentence that expresses an action.

And regarding the meanings of words within a sentence, there arises this question: is the dharma expressed by each individual word, or is it expressed by all of them together as one? What, then, is the prima facie position?
"Regarding the statement 'dharma at every step': this being the position reached, it is said in reply— when there is a new transcendental result (*apūrva*) from one [action],
then another [action] is for that purpose."
...it will be so;
thus, there will be a much simpler assumption that avoids the undesirable consequence of postulating unseen factors (*adṛṣṭa*). Therefore, the *apūrva* is one.
When it is one, then a doubt arises: what—
Is it from words denoting action (bhāva), or from words denoting substance (dravya) and quality (guṇa)? What, then, is action?
What, then, are these words denoting action (*bhāvaśabda*)? They are "he sacrifices," "he gives," "he offers oblations," and so forth. But surely these are words for sacrifice, giving, and offering;
they are not words denoting action. This is not so; these words such as "sacrifice" and the like are both words for sacrifice and words denoting action.

And from this, the meaning of the sacrifice and so forth is understood, as well as "one should bring about. Thus one should strive so that something comes into being. Therefore, these are words denoting an action (bhāva-śabda).

From words denoting substances and qualities, there arises the cognition of substances and qualities, not of an efficient force (*bhāvanā*). Therefore, they are not "words for being" (*bhāva-śabda*). What, then, is the prima facie view?
That it applies without distinction.
To this, it is replied: "Words for action (*karma-śabda*) have being as their meaning."
From those [words] such as "one should sacrifice" (yajeta), action is understood. Why?
Precisely because they have the sense of bringing something into being (bhāvārtha). As for those who say, "one should bring something into being," [it refers to this].
Because of their connection with the term "one who desires heaven," they would state, "One should bring about heaven. Therefore, from them, an action is understood;

for the action is the instrument (*karaṇa*) by which the result is accomplished (*niṣpatti*). And these [actions], being connected with sacrifice, giving, and oblation, declare the production of heaven. Why?
Because this is the meaning that is enjoined.
For example: "How should one who desires heaven bring about heaven by means of sacrifice and so forth? [The answer is:
"By means of sacrifice and so forth. And that word by whose meaning the result is accomplished does so by first producing the *apūrva* (the unseen potency).
Since it is not otherwise,
an unprecedented [meaning] is understood from that;
therefore, whatever word expresses it, [that is the apūrva].

Therefore, it is understood that the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is what is produced. For this reason, we say that words denoting action (*bhāva-śabda*) are the indicators of the *apūrva*. However, there is no word whatsoever that directly denotes the *apūrva*. [The general understanding derived from] words denoting action is that "something must be brought about" and "for one who desires heaven, something must be brought about by means of some [action]."
The union of these two is like that of a man who has lost his horse and another whose chariot has been burned;

injunctions such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) are expectant, [asking] "What should one sacrifice? By what means? How? They become free from expectancy through the purpose expressed by the term "one desiring heaven. But this is not the case for words denoting substances or qualities. Therefore, words expressing action, having existence as their meaning, enjoin the *apūrva*.
Now, why is it said that "action-words have being as their meaning"? It is replied: some action-words do not have being as their meaning, such as *śyena*, *aikatrika*, and so forth.

8*. Some words expressing an action (*bhāvārtha*) are not verbal roots denoting action (*karmaśabda*), such as "being" (*bhavana*), "existence" (*bhāva*), or "coming into being" (*bhūti*). What, then, is the example here?
[The sentence] "One seeking to perform malevolent magic should sacrifice with the Śyena."
"One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā.
[One asks: "Is it that one practicing sorcery should sacrifice with the Śyena, or that one practicing sorcery should sacrifice [with the Citrā]?
Likewise, "one desiring cattle [should sacrifice] with the Citrā."

Furthermore, once it is established that "one desiring cattle should sacrifice," there will be an investigation in this section as to whether [the term] is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) or a name (*nāmadheya*). Likewise, regarding the statement "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," [it must be considered whether] "Darśa" refers to a time.
And regarding the term "Pūrṇamāsa," does it mean that one who desires heaven [should perform] by means of those two, or that one who desires heaven should sacrifice?

Furthermore, [the words] "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa," "by means of the Śyena," and "by means of the Citrā" are not expressive of an action (bhāvavacana). Nor is there any connection between these [words] and the person seeking a result, because they possess different case-endings. Therefore, words denoting substances or qualities are not the enjoiners of the *apūrva*.

If it is argued that the meaning is the existence (bhāva) of all [words], [we reply: MS_2.1.2.
If one perceives it in this way—
that because they are words denoting existence (*bhāva*), words denoting substance (*dravya*) or quality (*guṇa*) do not enjoin the *apūrva*—
then the meaning of all [words] is existence.

In the injunctions "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyām yajeta*), "One practicing sorcery should sacrifice with the Śyena" (*śyenena abhicaran*), and likewise "One desiring cattle [should sacrifice] with the Citrā," the word *yajeta* (he should sacrifice) will express the connection between these two [the instrument and the result]. Therefore, these too are verbal expressions of an action (*bhāvavacana*) because they possess expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*). Among all verbal expressions of an action, there is no reason for a definitive distinction.
Only words denoting action (karmaśabda) are the enjoiners of the *apūrva*, not words denoting substance (*dravya*) or quality (*guṇa*).
Those [words] for which the form is perceived at their own primary usage during their origination are "names" (*nāman*).
Therefore, there is no further expectation regarding them, because they have already been realized in their own application.
Those words whose form is perceived when they are uttered and produced for their own meaning—
[that form] which, once arisen, persists for a period of time.
The meaning is not that it perishes immediately upon arising like an action;
those are the names,
those are the words for substances and qualities.

Such is the meaning of words for substances (*dravya*) and qualities (*guṇa*). While it should have been stated that "those are words for substances and qualities," it was formulated in the Sūtra as "those are names" (*tāni nāmāni*); therefore, "names" is a synonym for these. How is this known? Because their case-endings (*vibhakti*) are called "nominal" (*nāmikī*). Which are they? *Vṛkṣaḥ*.

"Tree," "trees," "white," "white [two]," "white [many]," and so forth. Therefore, it is correctly formulated: since their referent is not momentary, there is no further expectation—no primary expectation—from them; thus, their production need not be brought about.
"Because of its being real" means because it exists during its own application— that is, at the time of its own employment.

But those words for which no usage is found when their own meaning has arisen are verbal roots (ākhyāta). Therefore, the action should be understood from them, because usage depends upon them. (MS 2.1.4)

However, those words whose application to their own meaning is not found at the time of their utterance—meaning that at the time of usage, their referent is not perceived—these are called *ākhyāta*. [The author] teaches these as synonymous terms for *bhāvaśabda* (action-words). How is it that *bhāvaśabda*s are synonymous terms? Because their case-endings (*vibhakti*) are said to be verbal (*ākhyātika*). Which are they?

[Examples] such as *pacati*, *pacataḥ*, *pacanti*, and so forth. Therefore, from these [verbs], the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) would be understood. These [verbs] have meanings that are yet to be accomplished (*bhavyārtha*), while they are uttered together with those having meanings that are already accomplished (*bhūtārtha*). When that which is already accomplished serves the purpose of that which is yet to be accomplished, its purpose is seen; for the production of that which is yet to be accomplished, being purposeful, is brought about by that which is already accomplished—this is a perceived purpose. On the other hand, when that which is yet to be accomplished serves the purpose of that which is already accomplished, nothing is perceived.
And the unseen (adṛṣṭa) is postulated [as the result]. Therefore, the sacrifice is not for the sake of the substance.

Furthermore—because the performance is dependent, the performance of these [substances] becomes dependent upon the person; it is the productive activity (bhāvanā) connected with the person that is expressed.
For it speaks of a person, saying "one should cultivate [the mind]," and by that, the person who desires heaven is also understood in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice."
The sacrifice as well as the relation [are understood]. In the expression "one desiring heaven [should sacrifice] with a substance," both the substance and the person are perceived,
but not the relation.
Is it not the case that this has already been stated?

One will say "one should sacrifice," which expresses the relationship between the seeker of the result and the substance, meaning "one should bring about [the result] by means of the substance. Therefore, the production of the result through the substance would be understood.

And there is the requirement (ākāṅkṣā). It is understood that "one should effect [the result] by means of a substance" through the sentence, but "one should effect [the result] by means of a sacrifice" through direct audition (śruti). However, when...

When it is enjoined that "one should bring about [the result] by means of sacrifice," the connection with the sacrifice is what is prescribed, not at that time the connection with the substance as in "one should bring about [the result] by means of a substance. And when the connection with the substance is being prescribed, there can be no connection with the word "yajeta" (he should sacrifice). However, such a connection is possible when [the sacrifice] is being restated, and yet that is not the case here.
Simultaneous injunction and restatement are not possible. Therefore, there is a contradiction between the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and the syntactical connection (*vākya*);
and in the case of a contradiction, the direct statement is more authoritative.

Consequently, the substance is not connected with the person desiring the result. In that case, it is untenable to claim that the substance—given the absence of a connection with the one desiring heaven—will serve the purpose of attaining heaven.
This is the reason for the definitive conclusion that only words denoting actions (bhāva-śabda) are the enjoiners of the apūrva,
and not words denoting substances or qualities.

When it is said, "one should perform by means of sacrifice," then it is simply a statement regarding the sacrifice. By the term "by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (darśapūrṇamāsābhyām), it is indicated through figurative usage (lakṣaṇā) that the sacrifice is prescribed for both the New Moon and the Full Moon.

Furthermore, an injunction (*codanā*) is a new undertaking (*ārambha*). (MS 2.1.5)
By "injunction" (codanā), we mean the *apūrva*;
moreover, the *apūrva* exists because an undertaking is enjoined, such as: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice."
Otherwise, the injunction would be purposeless because the sacrifice would perish;
for if the sacrifice were to perish without producing something else, [the injunction would be futile].

If, however, it is further imagined that this [production] is not determined precisely because of the force of the statement regarding the fruit, such a thing is impossible. because of its destruction, it is understood that [the other] has also perished. If it is argued that the substratum has not perished, we say no, because ashes are perceived. If it is argued that the mark [of inference] is the operation of the result (*phalakriyā*), then, such being the case, an explanation must be given for its non-perception. Therefore, sacrifice (*yajati*) is of a perishable nature (*bhaṅgin*); because of its perishable nature, the *apūrva* exists.
What is the purpose of this deliberation?
If even words denoting substances and qualities enjoin the *apūrva*, then in the event of the loss of a substance or a quality, no substitute should be taken.
Thus, according to the prima facie view; and thus, according to the established conclusion,
the performance should be carried out by substituting either a substance or a quality.
Now,
those [words] are twofold, being either subordinate (*guṇa*) or principal (*pradhāna*). (MS 2.1.6)
This has been understood: that words denoting action (bhāvaśabda) are expressive of the action;
and words denoting action are of many kinds.
He sacrifices,
he offers oblations,
he gives; thus [is it].
There are nineteen such types, including "milks," "grinds," "melts," and so forth. Regarding these, there is a doubt: do they all enjoin a primary action?

Or rather, some [actions] are of the nature of preparatory acts (*saṃskārakarman*). Since there is no difference in their being denotative of an action (*bhāvārthatva*), it follows that all [verbal roots] denote primary actions (*pradhānakarman*). To this we reply: they ought to be divided into two classes; some denote primary actions, while others denote preparatory acts. In this way, all [verbal roots] remain meaningful.

Since they possess a visible purpose (*arthavattva*), it is not possible to postulate an unseen potency (*apūrva*) for all of them; therefore, not all of them denote a primary ritual act (*pradhānakarman*).
[This applies to those] by which the substance is not intended to be processed (*na cikīrṣyate*).
These [substances] are primary, because the substance is subordinate to them. (MS 2.1.7)
This being the case, it is logical that there be a minimal assumption of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), yet we do not perceive any reason for a definitive selection; from where [could such a reason arise]?

"Previously, it was asked: 'Why not? To this it is replied: Those verbal roots (*bhāva-karman*) by which a substance is not intended to be refined or produced are primary; they denote the primary object (*pradhāna-karman*)."
Because the substance is subordinate [to the action]. For the substance is indeed subordinate,
since it is that which is most desired to be reached through the accomplishment of the action.
But in cases where a substance is intended to be prepared, a quality should be understood [as subordinate], because that [action] has the substance as its primary object. (MS 2.1.8)
But in those cases where a substance is intended to be prepared, there the action should be understood as a subordinate quality (guṇa). Why?

Because that [action] has the substance as its primary purpose. Since substances are not intended to be prepared by such [injunctions] as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), therefore [the action is subordinate].

These [words] denote the principal action (*pradhānakarman*), because the substance (*dravya*) is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*). By means of such [verbs] as "he grinds" (*pinaṣṭi*), the substance is prepared;

therefore, they are expressions of a subsidiary action (*guṇakarman*). This is precisely the reason for the definitive determination. As for the purpose: according to the former position, even in the case of a *caru* made of *praiyaṅgava* grains, rice (*vrīhi*) would have to be produced for the sake of threshing (*avadhāta*).
In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), [the *apūrva*s] are not to be produced.

When [an action] is not separated by another word that requires it, there is a distinction of actions because of the connection with the verbal suffix (kṛt). (MS 2.2.1)
There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice; regarding it, it is heard in scripture: "One should sacrifice with Soma," "He offers the sacrificial fees," and "He gives gold to the Ātreya."
Regarding the acts of sacrificing (*yajati*), giving (*dadāti*), and offering oblations (*juhoti*), there arises a doubt: do they perform their function collectively or individually?
For it is observed that means of accomplishment (*sādhaka*) are seen to accomplish their ends even when acting collectively.
Even when separated. To begin with, when joined together, three stones are seen supporting a single beam;
however, pegs are seen even when separated.
For it is possible to suspend the sling from each individual [post]. Therefore, a doubt arises as to whether one should sacrifice, give, or offer oblations by acting together or by acting separately.
What, then, is the prima facie position?
That they are combined. Why?
Because it is logical that the assumption of assistance for those things whose purpose is unseen should be as minimal as possible. How so?
An object that is neither seen nor heard is understood to be non-existent;
when that [non-existence] is absent, what is seen or heard is not contradicted.
If there were a contradiction, [the object] would have to be postulated; by that means, it becomes meaningful.
However, if no distinction [between the objects] were perceived, then not even a single one would be postulated.

And a distinction is indeed perceived: that from many [actions] a single *apūrva* arises. Therefore, the collection [of actions] is what is intended to be performed; for it is from that [collection] that the unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) is to be postulated.

Since the parts possess meaning with respect to the whole, a single *apūrva* will be postulated from the whole. Nor is the whole "non-verbal," because the whole is expressed by the very words that denote its parts. Therefore, it is the whole that is intended to be performed. Alternatively, the prior portion of the word *yajeta* [is as follows]: [138] {2/2}
The former [injunction] expresses the meaning "one sacrifices," while the latter restates that very same thing,
saying "one should bring that into being."

The phrase "one offers thus" (*evaṃ juhoti*) prescribes the first part as the act of offering (*juhoti*), while the latter part merely restates that same act. Thus, by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), three means—namely, sacrificing (*yajati*) and so forth—are prescribed for a single productive operation (*bhāvanā*). Therefore, the productive operation of the transcendental result (*apūrva*) is qualified by these acts of sacrifice, gift, and offering; hence it is said that they, acting in combination, accomplish a single *apūrva*. Alternatively, the act of giving (*dāna*) prescribed by the word "sacrifices" (*yajati*) is restated by the words "giving" and "offering" for the purpose of connecting it with a specific accessory (*guṇa*).
Therefore, it follows that there is a single *apūrva*.
This being the position reached, we reply: there is a distinction of *apūrva* for each word;
because when there is a different word, there is a difference of action, due to the connection with a distinct [verbal] element (*anubandha*).
By the word "yajeta" (one should sacrifice), the necessity of performing the sacrifice alone is expressed, and not that of what is denoted by the words "juhoti" (he offers) or "dadāti" (he gives),

because these are different words. For it is through the status of being a supplementary part of the injunctive sentence (*prayogavākya*) that the connection with existence is understood for the aggregate.

Regarding the constituent element of direct assertion (*śruti*), although both giving (*dāna*) and offering (*homa*) are proximate by virtue of the sentence (*vākya*)— as in "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*)—
it is understood through direct assertion that the connection with existence belongs to the sacrifice alone.

It does not apply to both *dāna* (giving) and *homa* (offering). Furthermore, direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is more authoritative than syntactical connection (*vākya*). Therefore, the word [denoting the sacrifice] is not a collective term;

for if it were assumed to be so, it would have to be assumed as such only after being brought into a single syntactical unity with the injunctive statement of performance (*prayogavacana*), and moreover, *dadāti* (he gives) is a different word from *yajati* (he sacrifices). In this regard, although the subsequent portion expressing the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is common to all [the constituent acts], [the specific verbal roots remain distinct].

Nevertheless, for each [word], the preceding constituent part is one thing, and the aggregate formed by it is another; thus, the aggregate is a different word from any other aggregate, and in that case, a distinct meaning is clearly manifested.

In the expression "one should give" (*dadyāt*), it is understood that one should accomplish [the result] through giving; thus, giving alone is perceived as the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), and it does not require sacrifice (*yāga*) and oblation (*homa*) as auxiliaries. Likewise, in "one should offer oblations" (*juhoti*), [the word] expresses a productive activity whose instrument is oblation, and it does not require giving and sacrifice. In this regard, so much is understood from the verbal root itself.

The notion that success is achieved by giving alone, or that success is achieved by offering oblations alone—such as when it is said "he offers"—does not exclude the possibility that success may also be achieved by giving alone; rather, the cognition [of the act] remains. Thus, when one gives, it is accompanied by its own set of causal factors (kāraka-grāma) and does not depend on the sacrifice or the oblation as an auxiliary. Therefore, these are distinct sentences.
"For every word there is a distinct apūrva.

Nor can "dāna" (giving) be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of "yajati" (sacrifices) or "juhoti" (offers oblations), because that would entail the undesirable consequence of the sacrifice and the oblation not being intended as primary meanings. Nor is "dāna" a restatement of the other two, because the root *dadāti* has as its purpose the transfer of ownership to another.

And because the other two [words] have the meaning of "abandoning" (tyāga). The purpose [of this discussion] is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the transcendental result (*apūrva*) arises from the collection [of the three acts];
whereas according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), since the sacrifice possesses the fruit, the other two are subordinate (*guṇabhāva*).
In this way,
the repetition of what has already been stated regarding a single [subject] would be purposeless, since there is no distinction [between the two instances]. (MS 2.2.2)

Does the word *yajati*, which is repeated five times in such passages as "he offers the fuel-sticks" (*samidho yajati*) and "he offers to Tanūnapāt" (*tanūnapātaṃ yajati*), enjoin a single unseen potency (*apūrva*), or [multiple ones]?
Is there a distinction of *apūrva* with each repetition? It has been stated that a difference in action (*karmabheda*) occurs when there is a different word;

here, however, that very same word is uttered again and again. Therefore, there is only one *apūrva* here. [Objection: But surely, if it does not produce another *apūrva*, it becomes purposeless. [Response: True, it would indeed be purposeless;
yet even when uttered many times, it does not acquire a different meaning.

What is understood at the first utterance is understood exactly the same even at the hundredth; therefore, the word *yajati*, though repeated five times, enjoins a single *apūrva*. Furthermore, the repetition will not be purposeless.
The deities beginning with Tanūnapāt will be enjoined;
therefore, there is only one *apūrva*.
This being the position reached, we reply: such a repeated mention would pertain to the same [action] alone.

The meaning is that one would effect a division of the ritual action (*karmabheda*). If only that much were prescribed, and no specific distinction were made, the restatement (*punaḥśruti*) would be purposeless. Now, was it not said that [the sentence] cannot enjoin another matter? It is replied: even "He offers the *samidhs*" is merely an initial reiteration (*anuvāda*).
In the injunction "One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices," the act of sacrifice (*yāga*) is already established. In that case, a deity cannot be enjoined,
for the deity there is already obtained through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), whereas this [proposed deity] would be derived from syntactical connection (*vākya*) or context (*prakaraṇa*).
A conceptual distinction between those two is not logical;

for this connection between the deity and the sacrifice, being enjoined, cannot be established if the sacrifice is not performed, and thus it would be purposeless. But when the sacrifice is performed, it can be established. Therefore, the sacrifice must be repeated.
And because there is a difference in the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) with each repetition,
that which is performed in connection with the *samit* is not the same as that which is performed in connection with the *tanūnapāt*.
Because those two are distinct,
there is therefore no optionality (*vikalpa*). The purpose [of this discussion] is that,
according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the performance occurs only once.
In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, there is repeated performance.
*{2/191: E2,4 (v.l.): that which is being uttered for the first time}* *{2/192: E2,4 (v.l.): even a hundred times}* *{2/194: E2,4 (v.l.): or unprecedented}*
But the section [dealing with the new-moon sacrifice] belongs to the full-moon sacrifice, because its specific form has not been stated there. (MS 2.2.3)

For thus they recite: "That which belongs to Agni, offered on eight potsherds, is never omitted on the new moon and full moon days"; those two, Agni and Soma, said, "One should sacrifice to them both with clarified butter alone, silently, on the full moon day."

To those two he gave this cake for Agni and Soma on eleven potsherds at the full moon; [he gave] curd for Indra at the new moon, and milk for Indra at the new moon. In that same manner, he pours the libation.
He offers the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga),
he cuts off the portion for Sviṣṭakṛt,
and he performs the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings.
He offers the *samiṣṭayajus*.
Likewise, he who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the full moon day,
and he who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the new moon day— so it is said.

In this regard, there is a doubt: are all these [rites] equally primary, or are those beginning with the Āgneya and ending with the Payas offering the primary rites, while the Āghāra offerings and so forth are merely auxiliary acts that provide indirect assistance?
Likewise, the two phrases "he who, knowing thus" (*ya evaṃ vidvān*) are either restatements (*anuvādau*) of the previously mentioned rites,

or they are injunctions (*vidhātārau*) for two new rites, namely: "he who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the full moon day" (*paurṇamāsīm yajate*) and "he who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the new moon day" (*amāvāsyām yajate*).

In this regard, [the opponent argues that] the others are injunctions of subordinate qualities (*guṇavidhi*). What is the prima facie view? Because they are different words and because of repetition, they are equally primary (*samapradhāna*). To this we reply:
but the context (*prakaraṇa*) pertains to the Full Moon sacrifice.
The two [sentences] connected with the full moon and the new moon are restatements (*anuvāda*) of the rites under discussion, namely the Āgneya and the others. Why?
Because there is no mention of their specific forms (*rūpa*);
for instance, in the statement "He who, knowing thus, performs the sacrifice named Paurṇamāsī," it is not all the sacrifices that are intended.
They are said [to be mentioned] as such; that which is designated by the name "Full Moon" (Paurṇamāsī) is what is being enjoined.
However, we do not understand this in such a way, for we do not know what the specific form of a sacrifice bearing such a name might be. Therefore, they... [are not so].

We might understand something [from it]. Therefore, we say: if they were the enjoiners of something previously unestablished (*apūrva*), they would be meaningless. But if, on the other hand, they are restatements (*anuvādau*) of those [actions] already under discussion, then the form [of the sacrifice] is understood as being the sacrifices connected with the *Paurṇamāsī* and *Amāvāsyā* festivals that are present in context;

thus, the statement possesses purpose (*arthavattā*). If it is asked, "How then can a word ending in the singular number denote many [sacrifices]?"—it will be explained by its being a term for a collective whole (*samudāyaśabda*).
For the sacrifices previously mentioned possess form,
and there exists a collective aggregate of them established by their accumulation; this word "arūpa" (formless) is used with reference to that [aggregate],
therefore the use of the singular ending is not a fault.

For there are indeed many words ending in the singular number that refer to a collective aggregate, such as *yūtha* (herd), *vana* (forest), *kula* (family), and *pariṣad* (assembly). When these two [words, *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa*] denote the aggregate of the Āgneya and other sacrifices, then they are designated by the term *darśapūrṇamāsa*. Consequently, it is these [sacrifices] that are connected with the fruit.
But because they are proximate to that which possesses the fruit, the Āghāra-libations and so forth are remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*).
*{2/197: E1,6; E2,5: not in a low voice; E4: not in a low voice}* *{2/198: Cf. Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.6.2.14}* *{2/199: Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.4.1}*
