E2,4: by that; E6: by that}*
And because of the perception of a distinction, there would be a lack of activity toward all [objects] that are otherwise equal. (MS 2.2.4)

And if all [the rites] were equally primary, the *prayāja*s would not be seen to be present in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*); yet they are indeed seen—[as in the injunction]: "At each *prayāja*, one offers a *kṛṣṇala* grain.
This would not be possible if the *prayāja* did not possess the quality of being subordinate to the *āgneya*.
Therefore, not all [factors] are equally primary. NOTES: *{2/207: E2,4 (v.l.): of the preceding ones}*
"But it is a subordinate quality (guṇa), because of its connection with the Vedic text. (MS 2.2.5) *{2/208: Tait.S. 2.3.2.3}* *{2/209: E2,4: nopapadyeta*}
This is not the case; the two terms "paurṇamāsī" and "amāvāsyā" are not names for the two collections [of rites],
but rather they are the enjoiners of two previously unknown (apūrva) rituals.

In that case, the word will not function as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). But is it not the case that "form" (*rūpa*) does not exist? We shall understand the form through another sentence: "On the full moon day, there is the cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni. This is the form of that rite which is called the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*).
"Agni is the deity;
the *puroḍāśa* cake is the substance. Therefore, by means of the [mantras] such as "pertaining to Agni" (*āgneya*), a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) is enjoined.
Or rather, there is an injunction of the qualities simultaneously, because when [the rite] is enjoined by the scripture, each [quality] is taught as being for the sake of that [rite]. (MS 2.2.6)
The injunctions regarding ritual action would consist of the Āgneya and other such sacrifices. Why?
Because of the simultaneous teaching of multiple qualities;
for you intend to enjoin several qualities here by means of a single sentence alone.
Furthermore, when an action has been enjoined by one word, it is not possible to enjoin multiple subordinate factors (guṇas) unless they are mutually related. How so?
If, first of all, the intended connection were "on the full moon day, there is a cake on eight potsherds" (*paurṇamāsyām aṣṭākapālo bhavati*), [then the following would apply].
In that case, the meaning is not that "the eight-potherd [cake], being existent, is connected with that";
rather, what is it that the eight-potherd is connected with—the full moon sacrifice?
In that context, the verb *bhavati* (it exists) is operative.

In that case, the term *āgneya* would fall even closer to this [word *aṣṭākapālaḥ*], and due to the absence of a connection, it could not enter into a relationship with it, such that "the eight-potherd cake is for Agni. If, on the other hand, one intends to express "the *āgneya* [cake] occurs at the full moon," then there would be no connection whatsoever between the *āgneya* and the *puroḍāśa*. Alternatively, if the fact that the eight-potherd cake is for Agni (*āgneyatā*) is prescribed in relation to the full moon, then it must be stated:

[Question: By what [rule] is the eight-potherd [cake] prescribed for that [Full Moon sacrifice]? [Answer: It is because the eight-potherd nature belongs to the offering to Agni (āgneya) in that [sacrifice]. Even so, this same fault remains. Furthermore, if the term "Full Moon" were connected with both [the substance and the deity], there would be no connection at all between the substance and the deity with one another.

It might be so. Now, if it is argued that the substance and the deity, being mutually qualified, would be connected with the *paurṇamāsī* sacrifice—namely, that "the cake on eight potsherds which belongs to Agni occurs at the *paurṇamāsī*"—this too is incorrect because that [cake] is not established [as such]. Or, if it is argued that something intended for Agni by someone [is offered] at the *paurṇamāsī*...

It is so prescribed. Nevertheless, because no deity is enjoined, there is simply an absence of form (*rūpa*). If someone were to say, "Agni shall be the deity," he should be told: "And there would be a mutual lack of connection with the purpose."
For the word *āgneya* cannot simultaneously be a restatement (*anuvāda*) and an injunction (*vidhi*). If it is argued that one will postulate a deity [for the clarified butter], we say no;

for in the absence of an injunction, there is no deity. This term "deity" is a relative term; thus, Agni alone is the deity of the eight-potherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*), not of the clarified butter. Therefore, the connection between the *āgneya* and the eight-potherd cake must necessarily be enjoined.

"This is that sacrifice" means that another sacrifice related to the Paurṇamāsī sacrifice is enjoined by it, not a substance or a deity. And one sacrifice cannot constitute the form of another sacrifice. Therefore, because no form [of a new sacrifice] is stated, [the term refers to] the Paurṇamāsī.

The terms *āmāvāsya* and *paurṇamāsī* are not enjoiners of two previously unknown rites. As for what was said—that the words *paurṇamāsī* and *āmāvāsya* are unable to refer back to the rites under discussion directly, but can only do so through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—this is not a fault;
for when the literal meaning of a word cannot be logically sustained, [indirect indication is permissible].
Then, even when conceived through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), it becomes correct,
as in the expression "he stands in the fire" (agnau tiṣṭhati).
There is common usage such as "he stands in a pit," "near the fire," or "near the pit. For even figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is indeed worldly.

And designation is likewise [based on that]. (MS 2.2.7)
Indeed, these formidable oblations are collected on the new moon day:
"The first is for Agni, the latter for Indra"—this indicates their conjunction;
for if the offerings to Agni and the others were merely subordinate qualities, there would be an option between them. In that case, the offering to Agni comes first.

Furthermore, the designation "the two northern [cups] belong to Indra" would not be possible; and in the case of an option (vikalpa), the sequence of the preparatory rites (saṃbhāra) would be untenable.
This is also because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga). MS 2.2.8.
And an indicative mark (liṅga) is also seen: "Fourteen oblations are offered on the full moon day; thirteen on the new moon day. [144] NOTES:
The silent sacrifice (upāṃśuyāja) should be like that of the full-moon sacrifice.
"That which is done [when] two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are offered consecutively is indeed a repetition (*jāmi*) of the sacrifice; therefore,
one should sacrifice to Viṣṇu in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) to avoid repetition, and one should sacrifice to Prajāpati in a low voice to avoid repetition."

"Agni and Soma are to be sacrificed to in a low voice (upāṃśu) for the sake of avoiding monotony. Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the statement "he performs the upāṃśuyāja between [the two offerings]" refer to the collection of the previously mentioned sacrifices characterized by Viṣṇu and the others, or rather to a previously unmentioned sacrifice? To this it is replied: the upāṃśuyāja ought to be like the Paurṇamāsī sacrifice. Why? Because of its connection with a name;
for a specific sacrifice connected with a name is heard in the scripture.

It is designated as the *upāṃśuyāja*, and neither the substance nor the deity constitutes its form; furthermore, there exist sacrifices characterized by the quality of being performed silently (*upāṃśu*) which have been introduced in the context. Therefore, it is a term denoting a collective. But [one might object]: what about that which is characterized by the quality of being silent?
Another sacrifice is enjoined as having "whispering" (*upāṃśu*) as its characteristic form. A word of this kind is not capable of expressing a sacrifice qualified by whispering;
for its expresser is the term *upāṃśuyāja*.
By the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*, there ought to be a substitution of *k* for [the *c* of] *yaja*;

however, the word *upāṃśuyāja* is an un-derived (avyutpanna) term. Therefore, it is not a distinct sacrifice possessing its own form (*rūpa*). Furthermore, even if it were connected with a name, it would be merely a general act of sacrificing (*yajati-sāmānya*).

Nevertheless, we cannot consider this to be a different sacrifice, as it lacks a specified deity and substance. But if that were the case, would it not follow that the term is non-denotative even of the sacrifices under discussion? Let the word *upāṃśuyāja* itself not be denotative;
the word *yajati* (he sacrifices) will suffice.
This being so, even if the word *upāṃśuyāja* is not literal because it is a restatement (*anuvāda*), there is no fault.

E5: kughiṣṇatoḥ}
Or rather, it is an injunction, because [the subject] has not been previously introduced. (MS 2.2.10)
Or it would be expressive of another action, namely, "he performs the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice. Why?
Because there is an absence of previously mentioned sacrifices.
If the archetypal sacrifices do not exist, of what would he speak as having a composite form?
But was it not just stated that the sacrifices possessing qualities such as Viṣṇu and so forth do exist as archetypes? They do not exist.
No, for those injunctions such as "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a whisper" and so forth are indeed explanatory passages (arthavādas). Why?
Because in this sentence there exists another injunction.

In this sentence, "He performs the *upāṃśuyāja* in between," it is this [the *upāṃśuyāja*] that is enjoined. If these [Viṣṇu and the others] were also enjoined here, then the sentence would be split (*vākya-bheda*).
Furthermore, in this sentence, the relationship between the sacrifice and Viṣṇu and the others is understood, and not the injunction of the sacrifice itself. But surely, [one might object:]...

In the statement, "He performs the *upāṃśuyāja* in between," a connection with the interval is also understood. Certainly; however, what is being enjoined there is the connection with qualities such as being performed in a whisper (*upāṃśutva*). For this single sentence cannot enjoin multiple things. How so?
This sentence begins with, "This indeed creates a flaw (*jāmi*) in the sacrifice," and concludes with, "for the sake of avoiding the flaw."

The statement concerning Viṣṇu and others, which is recited in the midst of that [passage], cannot constitute a separate sentence when connected with it; therefore, statements such as "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a low voice" are not injunctions, but rather *arthavādas* (explanatory or commendatory passages). What, then, is an *arthavāda*?
It is that in which the defect of *jāmitā* (monotony or redundancy) is stated regarding the *Āgneya* and *Āgnīṣomīya* sacrifices when they are performed in immediate succession.
To heal that [defect], it is prescribed: "One performs the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice in between. How will one be healed by that?
When it is performed, it is indeed known.
Just as Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to, as are Prajāpati and Agni-Soma; and because of that separation, non-redundancy (*ajāmitā*) is indeed understood.
Therefore, thinking "I shall state the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding non-redundancy," the connection with Viṣṇu and the others is restated.
But there is no other purpose for the connection with the intermediate stage than this injunction. How, then, is it understood that Viṣṇu and the others are to be sacrificed to?
It is understood that the text mentions Viṣṇu and the others—whether they are already established as objects of sacrifice or not—in order to praise the *upāṃśuyāja*.
Regarding this, some say: "They are indeed already established. Why?

"Because of the injunction in another recension. Even if [the deity] is not otherwise established, nevertheless, due to the commonality of being whispered (*upāṃśu*), Prajāpati and Viṣṇu are merely restatements (*anuvāda*); for both Viṣṇu and Prajāpati possess the property of being whispered.

Therefore, because of such declarations as "whatever is performed for Prajāpati in the sacrifice is performed only in a whisper" and because of the recitation of the mantra collection, one might speak of Viṣṇu as if he were established [as a deity], even though he is not [explicitly] established there. However, the injunction for Agni and Soma is cited as follows:
"These two should say... (*etāv abrūyātām*).
"One should sacrifice to Agni and Soma with clarified butter in a low voice at the full moon;
therefore, this is a separate sacrifice.

6 (correct): they exist;
{it is divided};
{certainly}.
5: "They both spoke thus [that it is] because of the connection with qualities (*guṇopabandha*). (MS 2.2.11)
As for what is said— that it is not known which sacrifice this is, designated as the *upāṃśuyāja*,
to which this accessory has been attached—
"One should sacrifice in a whisper on the full moon day. Therefore, there is no fault; for this is because the statement refers to the general rule (*prāya*).
This statement occurs in a context where the primary object (pradhānakarman) predominates; it reinforces the status of the primary object,
as for example:
Having seen that which is written in a preeminent [text], the thought arises, "This is preeminent. Therefore, it is not a term denoting a collective whole.
[The case of] the Āghāra and Agnihotra is so because they lack a specific form (arūpatvāt).
It is heard in the scripture: "He pours the libation," and likewise these others:
"He pours the libation upwards."
"He pours the oblation continuously; he pours the oblation straightly," and so forth. And this Agnihotra he offers.
Likewise, there are such injunctions as "He offers with curd" and "He offers with milk. In this regard, a doubt arises: is it [the case that] subsequently...?

By such injunctions as "he pours the libation" (*āghārayati*) and "he offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), the *āghāra*-libations and the *homa*-offerings are prescribed; of these, [the text says] "he pours the *āghāra*."

Regarding the statements "He offers the Agnihotra" and [the other], are these two restatements (*anuvāda*) of existing complexes, or are they the injunctions (*vidhi*) for two previously unknown *āghāra* and *homa* offerings? What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That they are not injunctions for two new acts. Why?
Because they lack a specific form;

for these two do not possess a distinct form different from the preceding oblations (*homa*) and libations (*āghāra*), by virtue of which they could be determined to be separate rites. Therefore, because they are the subject under discussion, they are merely restatements of what has already been introduced.
5: Because the subjects under discussion possess form, and because of the application of the technical designation [saṃjñā]. (MS 2.2.14)

Pouring out is *āghāra*,

Therefore, there are two restatements. And furthermore, [it is not so].

Since that distinction is understood, the injunctions for the *apūrva* (unprecedented result) and the *āghāra* libation are not tenable. Furthermore, how could an action be expressed by a word denoting an instrument (*sādhana*)?
For that instrument which is the most desired (*īpsitatama*) is expressed by a word ending in the accusative case.
"Action" [is expressed] by a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). In the view that it is a restatement (*anuvāda*), the collection of actions constitutes a distinct entity;
that will be the most desired object (*īpsitatama*) and thus the means (*sādhana*).
And because they are not the subject under discussion. (MS 2.2.15) *{They are understood as such.}

Furthermore, even the substance and deity relevant to the context are not present in the *āghāra* offering, by virtue of which it might possess a specific form (*rūpa*). Therefore, these two terms as well are collective designations (*samudāya-śabda*). [150] {2/231} NOTES:
Or rather, it is an injunction (*codanā*), because the meaning of the word constitutes the basis for its performance.
Because of its proximity, there is a restatement for the sake of a specific quality. (MS 2.2.16)
And this is not the case; these two cannot be words denoting a composite whole, for they would then be injunctions of separate ritual acts. Why?
Because the meaning of the word consists in its being put into practice, as in "he pours out" (āghārayati) and "he offers" (juhoti).
The meaning of the words is that the *homāghārau* (the oblation and the pouring) are to be performed;
therefore, we understand that they are enjoined as distinct rites. Furthermore, the terms *āghāra* and *agnihotra* are well-known to denote the general acts of pouring and offering;

As for what was said—that these are merely restatements because they have already been enjoined by such injunctions as "he pours the oblation upwards" and "he offers with curd"—this is not so; for these [sentences] are unable to enjoin the *homa* and the *āghāra*. "He pours the oblation upwards..."
And by the statement "one offers with curd," it is not meant that "the Āghāra-libation must be performed" or "the oblation must be performed."
What then?

A connection with the *ūrdhvapātra* (upright vessel) must be established, and a connection with the curd-offering (*dadhi-homa*) must be established. Therefore, because they are not already obtained [from elsewhere], these two are not mere restatements (*anuvāda*). But surely, once the connection has been enjoined, the offering and the pouring out will follow by implication. This is not so.

For when this [injunction] exists, there is a connection through the rule of prescription. Therefore, the *homā* and *āghāra* do not follow merely from the sense of the passage; hence, we say that these two are prescribed as something new (*apūrva*).
But [one might object]: "He pours the *āghāra*..."

The verbal root *juhoti* (he offers) is heard as denoting an activity pertaining to the oblation and the pouring, not a connection with curd, upwardness, and so forth. True, it is not so heard; however, in that case, the hearing of the activity will be understood for the purpose of [establishing] a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) within that [act]. But surely, a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) cannot express an activity residing in another word-meaning. This is indeed true.

He will state that [the word] refers to its own object; however, it might be argued that the quality-word will qualify that very object of its own, and thus that qualified [object] alone will be understood.
The quality-word (*guṇaśabda*) would qualify its own referent, but this operation pertaining to the quality would not be perceived. What would happen in that case?
Even if the quality were not being operated upon, the word and its meaning would be established. Now, what is the purpose of the proximity of the quality-expressing word?
But it is purposeless. How, moreover, can the Veda possibly be purposeless?
If the meaning [is already established] by direct statement (*śruti*), it is not purposeless;

but if the meaning is not [established] by direct statement, what else could be said? [Objection: In that case, it will be obtained from the sentence (*vākya*). [Reply: When the meaning is present in the direct statement, the meaning of the sentence cannot be assumed. [Objection: This is true. [Reply: But it will be assumed when [the meaning] is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*). How is there non-intention to express?

Because the word expressing the quality (*guṇavacana*) is recited without error, and because its own specific meaning has already been enjoined by another word, it is established that the repeated mention in such passages as "one offers with curd for the sake of the quality" (*guṇārthena dadhnā juhoti*) is a restatement (*punarśruti*). Furthermore, the utterance of the root *juhoti* (to offer) is a restatement intended to connect the action with the quality. If "he offers" (*juhoti*) is indeed a restatement, [it serves this purpose].
By what means, then, is the quality (guṇa) enjoined?
Do not say "by the word *dadhi*. But was it not just stated that the operation regarding the quality is understood from the sentence (*vākya*)? That is true.

But if it were not being enjoined, from what source would it be known? Its authority would not be understood. In the absence of authority, there would be delusion. If that is so, then the words *juhoti* and *āghārayati* are injunctive. Of what, then, is this a restatement (*anuvāda*)? We reply: it is a restatement of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
If they are injunctive,
since their own meaning has already been enjoined previously, for what purpose are they uttered again?

There is no fault in [the view] that this is intended to establish the meaning of the sentence. Therefore, there is an injunction for a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*). As for what was said—that in the *āghāra* offering, the substance and deity are not established from the archetype (*prakṛta*)—what is the use of a substance and deity in this case, when its form is already fully known through the expression of well-established meanings? Moreover, since it is stated, "Having taken four portions, he pours the *āghāra*," clarified butter (*ājya*) is its substance.
The injunction regarding the deity is derived from the wording of the mantra:
"O Lord of the Sacrifice, may the lofty sacrifice, accompanied by Indra, reach the heavens; Svāhā!"—thus he pours the *āghāra* offering.
In this way, it is "accompanied by Indra" (indravān) only if Indra is its deity.
Therefore, if this were a designation of the deity for the *āghāra*,
then by this [mantra] the *āghāra* would be performed; consequently,
it is established that these are two distinct rituals and not words denoting a collective whole.

"The Adhvaryu draws these ten cups at the morning pressing"—thus a collection [of cups] is observed. Likewise, there is a sequence: "The Aśvin cup is drawn as the tenth;

"He binds with a *khadira* tree," "He binds with a *pālāśa* tree," and "He binds with a *rohitaka* tree. In that case, the observation of both sequence and combination (*samuccaya*) would not be possible.
Furthermore, in this statement referring to a collective whole, this is properly established when there is a sacrifice (*yajati*). Therefore, these two are restatements of a collective whole.
This being the position reached, we reply: there is an injunction prescribing two previously unknown rites, namely the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) and the Soma sacrifice (*soma*). Why?
The word *soma* is well-known to denote the milky creeper and not the juice;

for the word *soma* expresses a generic form (*ākṛti*) and does not denote an individual instance (*vyakti*). Likewise, they employ the word *paśu* (animal) as denoting a generic form with respect to a specific substance that has horns, a tail, hair, and four feet.

Furthermore, there are no sacrifices under discussion here that consist of substances possessing such a form (ākṛti), for which these two [words] could serve as restatements of a collective whole. [Objection: But surely the heart and other organs, which are modifications of the animal, are restated by means of the word "animal" (*paśu*) for the purpose of establishing their connection with Agni and Soma.

If [the reference were] to the heart and so forth, then it would be a secondary derivative by virtue of its connection with a modification (*vikāra*).

In the injunction "He draws the cup for Indra and Vāyu," what is expressed is merely that he intends [the offering] for Indra and Vāyu; since it is not logical to intend [something] without a sacrifice, a sacrifice must be inferred,
and that very sacrifice is what is traditionally handed down in the scripture.

Because there is an absence of previously mentioned sacrifices, the word *yajati* is not a term denoting a collective.

Because of that distinction, there would be repetition of the action; for [the action] would be purposeless due to the separateness of the substance, since the distinction [of the action] results from its being subordinate to the substance and the quality. (MS 2.2.19)

The discussion regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) will arise again in the tenth [book], whereas now the Soma sacrifice is under consideration. How can there be both sequential order (*krama*) and combination (*samuccaya*)? The deities such as Indra-Vāyu are not heard of in this way [in the injunction]:
"A sacrifice is to be performed for Indra and Vāyu."
"The sacrifice must be performed for Mitra and Varuṇa"—
if they had heard this,
they would have been conceived as deities with respect to the sacrifice.

For then it would have been prescribed that the sacrifice is accomplished by the deity alone. But if, on the other hand, one takes these [cups] for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*), and the deities are enjoined with respect to a preparatory act (*saṃskāra*), then the intention directed toward Mitra and Varuṇa is distinct from the intention directed toward Indra and Vāyu;
thus, through the act of taking [the cup], it produces another unseen result from the unseen result produced by that [former intention].
The same applies to other measurements as well;

therefore, there is a cumulative total. However, this [cumulative] measurement is not appropriate for the entire Soma, prepared in ten handfuls, when it is contained in upright vessels of fixed dimensions measuring one span (prādeśa) each, or in water-jars of fixed dimensions.

Even if it were possible [to perform them as alternatives], nevertheless, since the injunction regarding the performance would be subverted if there were an option between deities who are permanently prescribed, it is more logical to accept only the *avaśya* (inevitable) ones.

For if the entire [Soma] were taken at once, it would not be possible to think, "This very same [portion] is intended for Indra and Vāyu," and "That very same [portion] is intended for Mitra and Varuṇa. Therefore, because of the difference in mental allocation (*kalpanā*), the Soma remains distinct;
and precisely because of its multiple deities, it cannot be made into a single unity. Furthermore, when there is no offering to the deities, it is not possible [to satisfy] the deities.
It is impossible to conceptualize [otherwise]. Therefore, one must necessarily sacrifice to the deity as it was intended;

and when those deities are being sacrificed to, the sacrifice enjoined by the scriptural text "one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" becomes fully accomplished, and it does not require any other deity.
Furthermore, the sacrifice is prescribed with the entire Soma consisting of ten handfuls;
since that would not be possible without repetition, the sacrifice must be repeated by implication so that this quality may be fulfilled,
for without repetition, [the offering] cannot be made for all the deities and with the whole [quantity].
He will become endowed with the Soma sacrifice. And while that [Soma] is being practiced, both sequential performance (*krama*) and combined performance (*samuccaya*) are indeed appropriate;
therefore, the observation of those two is entirely logical.
But the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) would not be differentiated.
Because a substance exists for the sake of another, it is subordinate in nature. (MS 2.2.20)

As for what is also said— that just as in the injunctions "he binds with a khadira post" and "he binds with a palāśa post," the khadira and other materials are optional alternatives for the ritual preparation (saṃskāra),

And that is not logical, because in that case, *khadira* wood and other materials are prescribed for the purpose of bringing about the ritual preparation (*saṃskāra*). If the deities of the cups (*graha*), such as Indra and Vāyu, were also prescribed for the purpose of bringing about the sacrifice,

But these [subsidiaries] are not heard of in connection with the sacrifice; therefore, they should be combined. Because they reside separately, there would be a distinction of actions on account of the number. (MS 2.2.21)
There is the Vājapeya sacrifice, [enjoined by the text]:

In that [sacrifice], there are animals dedicated to Prajāpati.
He immolates seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati;
for Prajāpati is seventeenfold, [this being] for the attainment of Prajāpati. The hornless goats are dark-colored and uniform in appearance.
In this very way, Prajāpati [is the means] for prosperity.
Regarding this, a doubt arises: are these seventeen separate rites, or is there one single rite characterized by seventeen animals as its accessory? What, then, is the prima facie view?
"One rite. Why?

Because seventeen animals are dedicated to Prajāpati. When the doubt arises as to whether they are intended to accomplish one sacrifice or many, it is logical that there is one; for he who postulates many sacrifices [commits a fault].
He postulates one [sacrifice];
once that single sacrifice has been postulated, the postulation of exactly seventeen animals becomes logical;
by what means, moreover, could we postulate a second and subsequent sacrifices? This being the case...
The assumption that there is a minor consequence of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and inference would be simpler. Therefore, a single sacrifice is accomplished by means of seventeen animals.
This being the position reached, we reply: there must be a distinction of rites (*karmabheda*) on account of the number, since the number seventeen can only be applied when the animals are separate.
And that distinctness of animals is feasible in the case of many sacrifices, not in the case of a single one. How so?
The extended injunction (codaka) indicates that this sacrifice is to be accomplished by means of eleven portions (avadāna); thus it applies to each.

And since those [limbs] are obtained from just a single animal, the immolation of a second or subsequent animal cannot be for the purpose of completing the required portions; rather, while one animal is being immolated, others would be immolated for the sake of some unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Such being the case...
Because they would not have that as their purpose, they would not be *prājāpatya*;
in that case, the scriptural mention of "the *prājāpatyas*" would be contradicted.
Consequently, the number seventeen, which resides in plurality, could not be appropriately applied to a single animal.
In many sacrifices, there is a requirement for many sets of sacrificial portions (avadāna-gaṇa);
therefore, they should take seventeen animals for seventeen sacrifices, whereby the numerical congruity will be achieved; thus, there are seventeen sacrifices.
[Objection: But surely, even in a single sacrifice, one will sacrifice with seventeen sets of cuttings (avadāna) because of a scriptural injunction. [Reply: This is not so;
for the number is heard in relation to the animals, not in relation to the sets of cuttings. The cuttings are the oblations (havīṃṣi), which are the means of accomplishing the sacrifice.

The form of the animal is not [the primary factor], for since that form, by qualifying the substance which is the source of the portions to be cut off (*avadāna*), has assisted the primary rite in the archetype (*prakṛti*),
it will likewise assist the primary rite in the ectype (*vikṛti*) by qualifying the substance which is the source of the portions to be cut off.
And in that case, the number seventeen is a modification of the animal, not of the group of portions; therefore, it follows that one animal should be sacrificed for each group of portions.
In that case, the number seventeen would not be appropriate;

rather, it should be understood in this way: if they were intended as horns, or intended as colors, or intended as physical forms—such as the seventeen animals being white, black, red, and so forth—and if any one of these were to be taken, [then the number would be consistent].
Alternatively, [it refers to] hornless ones, horned ones, single-horned ones, and so forth; [the animal] is one of these,
for they are heard of in scripture as being dark-colored, hornless, and uniform in appearance.

Therefore, this [number] applies to many sacrifices, not to a single one. Consequently, there are seventeen sacrifices. The practical purpose is that if one [animal] is lost or defective, the entire group of animals would have to be repeated;
they would have to touch all [the others] following the one being sacrificed.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it serves an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), only a single animal is repeated; for when there is a difference in ritual acts, one animal does not require another animal.

perception is obstructed because it is conjoined with arising. (MS 2.2.22)
"Now this is Jyotis, now this is Viśvajyotis, now this is Sarvajyotis.

Here there is a doubt: do these names merely refer back to the previously mentioned Jyotiṣṭoma to enjoin qualities such as a sacrificial fee of a thousand [cows], or are they teaching distinct rituals characterized by the features about to be described? What is the prima facie view?

"By virtue of favoring the context, these are injunctions of qualities for that which is under discussion. But surely, by the power of the sentence, these qualities will be enjoined for the Jyotis and the others? This is not a fault;

"Jyotis" is employed as a synecdoche (pratīka) for the Jyotiṣṭoma.
The term "Viśvajyotis" refers to the Trivṛt and other such [stomas] which are mentioned in the supplementary passages as its lights;

This being the case, we reply: there are indeed three designations that differentiate them—the Jyotis and the others—since these are heard in the originative injunctions. Of these...
Furthermore, these scriptural passages—namely, "Therefore, this is the Jyotiḥ"—are injunctions of a new ritual action;

for if they were merely restatements (*anuvāda*), they would be purposeless as they would not produce any specific activity. Furthermore, the *jyotis* and other [names] are not designators of the Jyotiṣṭoma,
for these are distinct composite wholes;
nor does a different composite whole, by virtue of sharing a common component, come to have that same meaning as the original.

Just as the word *śālā* denotes a house, the fact that the word *mālā* and others do not also denote a house simply because they share the commonality of being the word *śālā* [is irrelevant]. As for the point that the term *jyotis* is taken as a synonym (*pratīka*) for the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, it is indeed by virtue of the power of the context (*prakaraṇa*) that the word *Jyotiṣṭoma* [is understood there].
There would be syntactic unity with that which is remote;
this would subvert the direct syntactic unity with the word "light" (jyotis),
and this is not logical.

For direct statement (*vākya*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*). Now, this [term] might apply to another ritual action either because it has the sense of "illuminating" (*dyotana*) or because of its connection with the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.
And if it is argued that "Viśvajyotis" and "Sarvajyotis" are terms denoting the totality of those "lights" (*jyotis*) such as the *Trivṛt* and so forth—[we reply: no, we say;
for the word "light" (*jyotis*) is not well-known (*prasiddha*) in the sense of the *Trivṛt* and other such [stomas].

Speaking thus, one would contradict what is well-established. It cannot apply there,
just as in the case of "Devadatta is a lion," where the word "lion" refers to Devadatta based on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but not in a case such as "one should sacrifice a lion."

But in that case, there is no other means of valid cognition for it. Therefore, those who speak of the *viśvajyotis* and the *sarvajyotis* as being the *jyotiṣṭoma* would not be speaking of the *jyotiṣṭoma* at all [if it were distinct].
All other ritual acts [are to be performed];
it is heard in scripture: "One should sacrifice with this *sarvajyotis* [rite] accompanied by a thousand sacrificial fees (*sahasradakṣiṇa*). In this regard—
"Other actions [are enjoined]" because, when there is a connection with a new transcendental result (*apūrva*), the two sentences are equal in status regarding their quality. (MS 2.2.23)
In the Vaiśvadeva section of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, they recite:

Regarding this, a doubt arises:

"It is an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi). Why? Because, having referred to the Viśvedevas as "the Vājins [by means] of this whey (vājina) and the curd-mixture (āmikṣā)," the whey is enjoined; therefore, both are dedicated to the Viśvedevas.

There are both *āmikṣā* and *vājina*. And in that very same ritual action, there is an injunction regarding the quality of *vājina*. Just as when it is said, "One performs the *agnihotra*," it is then stated, "One performs it with curd," or "One performs it with milk.
This being the prima facie view, we reply: since the quality (*guṇa*), when connected with a deity not mentioned in the original context, would enjoin a different ritual action.

For at that time, these two sentences are identical, as both are enjoiners of two previously unknown sacrifices. But how can there be a designation of a previously unknown deity? For it has just been stated:

There is a restatement regarding the Viśvedevas in the word "vājinam. This is explained as follows: here, the status of the Viśvedevas as deities is established sometimes by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and sometimes by syntactical connection (*vākya*). In the case of an indication based on their benefit, it is established by direct statement.

In the *Caturthīnirdeśa*, it is by means of the sentence (*vākya*). Where the status of being a deity is established by direct statement (*śruti*), there is syntactic unity with the *āmikṣā*; where there is the dative case (*caturthī*), there is syntactic unity with the *vājina*.

In that regard, in one case their status as deities is established by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), while their connection with a specific material is established by syntactical connection (*vākya*). In another case, both are established by syntactical connection. Thus, here there is a conflict between direct statement and syntactical connection regarding the status of being a deity;
and since direct statement is more powerful in the event of a conflict, the status of deity belongs to the Viśvedevas in the sentence concerning the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture).

Nor is it determined that this is a statement regarding the horse-sacrifice; rather, it is understood from this that its connection is with a deity not mentioned in the context. Therefore, it is a distinct ritual action.

Now, as for what was described— that when it is said, "One performs the Agnihotra," statements such as "One offers with curd" are injunctions of accessories (*guṇavidhi*)— to that it is replied: [158] {2/270} NOTES:
*{2/266: Cf. Mait.S. 1.10.1}* *{2/267: E2,4: "a different ritual action" (*karmāntaram*)}* *{2/268:
Cf. Tait.Br. 2.1.5.4}*
But when the word denoting the action is devoid of a quality, then a quality would be understood there [from the context]. (MS 2.2.24)
It is appropriate that there is an injunction of a quality therein;

for there is no connection with any quality not already under discussion, whereas there is a connection with the sacrifice which is under discussion. Therefore, this [previous] explanation is incorrect.
Alternatively, this is a separate topic:

[the claim that] acts such as "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) are distinct rituals, postulated out of a desire to avoid the fault of optionality (*vikalpa*). However, it is understood from the word *juhoti* that it is indeed that same ritual action.

It is not a separate action. Therefore, it is established that this is an injunction of an accessory (guṇavidhi) regarding that very same [action], and that there is an option (vikalpa) due to the scriptural statement.
However, because of the mention of a fruit, it might be considered a separate action.
Because the fruit is connected with action. (MS 2.2.25)
With reference to the *agnihotra*,
they recite such passages as, "One desiring sensory power should sacrifice with curd," and so forth.
In this regard, there is a doubt:

Is the offering of curds and so forth a separate oblation from the Agnihotra oblation, or does the fruit result from the accessory (guṇa) of the curds and so forth? What is the prima facie view? That it is a separate oblation. Why?
Because of the mention of the fruit; for a fruit is mentioned here,
and that is logically appropriate to the ritual action.
What indeed is seen as the fruit of action?
Rice and so forth from agriculture and the like. We say: no;
for this is not established by such visible means.
If perception were the cause for the knowledge of a result,
then that perception would apply to objects such as agriculture and the like.

It is not in the oblation (*homa*). Now, if it is argued that what is seen in agriculture occurs elsewhere as well, then it would follow [absurdly] for the substance (*dravya*) too. If it is said that it arises from something similar to agriculture, then the oblation is similar to agriculture because it is an action (*kriyā*), whereas the substance is not.

"For that is indeed dissimilar. Sacrifice (*homa*) is also dissimilar [to agriculture], because sacrifice has mantras, deities, and so forth as its means (*sādhana*), whereas agriculture has the plow and so forth as its means; furthermore, because sacrifice consists essentially in relinquishment (*tyāga*).

Furthermore, because agriculture consists of the act of plowing. Now, if some degree of similarity is being considered—since even a substance possesses some similarity such as "being existent" or "being impermanent," and so forth—and if, on the grounds that there is something more similar than a substance, it is said that a substance is not similar;
then, since there is something more similar to agriculture than the *homa* sacrifice, insofar as it has a visible purpose, the *homa* too [would not be similar].
It would be dissimilar. Nor is it established that whatever is seen in one place ought to exist—
even if unseen— in another place that is merely similar.
For when something is observed to be the cause of another in a proven case,
if it is understood to be the cause of that same thing in the case to be proven as well, it becomes the means of establishing it.

That which is not known to have been the cause is not a means of accomplishment even if it is similar [to what is effective]. Therefore, one must examine whether something, though similar, is a means of accomplishment or not. Now, whatever is an action is seen to be fruitful; and the oblation (*homa*) is also an action.

"By that [action] as well, there must be a result. Since it is observed that when an action has ceased, another substance is the result of substances and their conjunctions, the substance itself should also possess a result. Furthermore, since agriculture does not have an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*), by analogy with that, even from the oblation (*homa*) there would be no unseen result.

Or, due to its similarity to agriculture, it would be merely rice, not a sense organ. Therefore, in cases of this kind, one cannot establish the unperceived from the perceived. How, then, is it logical that there is a fruit [resulting] from the oblations? It is said:
that fruit is understood through the word.
Since the word "fruit" expresses this, it is logical;
and that the fruit arises from the oblation is understood through the direct statement (śruti) of the word.

By the sentence "the fruit [arises] from the curd," and since direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is more powerful than syntactical connection (*vākya*), it is logical that the fruit arises from the oblation (*homa*),
and it is illogical that the fruit arises from the curd.
Moreover, curd is incapable of both:
producing the fruit and accomplishing the oblation.

[Objection: But surely this will be like the washing of a woolen blanket; for washing performs both functions: the purification of the blanket and the cleanliness of the feet. [Reply: We do not say that.

It is not that a single [sentence] lacks the capacity to accomplish both purposes; rather, it is incapable of expressing a single sentence stating that curd is subordinate to the fruit [of the rite] and also to the oblation (*homa*). If it were to say, "One should effect the fruit by means of curd," it could not say, "[one should effect] the oblation by means of curd."

If one were to say that the oblation should be accomplished with curd for the sake of the result, rather than the result itself, then the statement would be split if both [the substance and the result] were mentioned; yet this [statement] is perceived as indivisible. Therefore, the result does not arise from the accessory substance, and thus the curd-oblation is a distinct ritual act (karmāntara) from the Agnihotra oblation.
NOTES: *{2/271: Tait.Br.
2.1.5.6}* But because the two sentences are not equal, that [quality] should be understood as a subordinate element (guṇa). (MS 2.2.26)
By the word "tu" (but), the position is reversed:
it is not a different ritual action, but rather the fruit arises from a subordinate quality (guṇa). How so?
For these two statements are indeed unequal:

in the case of "one desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra," the fruit is expressed in grammatical coordination with the action, meaning "one desiring heaven should bring about [the result] by means of the oblation"; whereas in "one desiring sense-power should offer with curd," the fruit is expressed in coordination with a subordinate quality (*guṇa*). For here, it is not understood that the oblation is to be performed for the sake of sense-power.
Rather, [the statement] "one desiring sensory power should offer with curd" establishes a connection between the oblation and the curd for the sake of sensory power;
it does not constitute the origination of the oblation itself.
"One who desires sense-faculties should perform the oblation with curd. In this context, which word expresses the human effort? We say it is "juhuyāt" (he should sacrifice).
But does it not express this human effort as being connected to the oblation by direct denotation (*śruti*)?
[The word "dadhi"] establishes a connection with curd through syntactical connection (*vākya*),
and syntactical connection cannot override direct statement (*śruti*). Nor...

"The simultaneous connection with both is not contradictory, for otherwise the sentence would be split. To this it is replied: Those who would resort to your position would subvert the revealed scripture (*śruti*) in the interim.

In our position, however, only the meaning of the verbal root *juhuyāt* (he should sacrifice) is set aside; in your position, on the other hand, the entire word *dadhnā* (with curd) is set aside. And it is understood that they recite this without negligence, for it has been stated that "this is not the singing of one who is demented, since the traditional transmission is equal. Therefore, the fruit is not mentioned in syntactic coordination with the ritual action.
But when [the verb] is uttered in connection with a quality (*guṇa*), there can be no instance of a careless recitation;

for it must necessarily be stated that "one should sacrifice" (*juhuyāt*) in order to enjoin the relationship between the curd (*dadhi*) and the desire for sensory power (*indriyakāma*). [Objection: Even if it is so stated, the mere meaning of the action (*karoty-artha*) is not understood.
"It is not merely for the sake of speech;
moreover, that [speech] is connected with the oblation;
therefore, it is inconsistent. We say: "No."
Even though this [act] is connected with the oblation, it indeed effects a purpose;
however, its connection with the oblation is merely a specific qualification,
and it does not subvert its status as something that effects a purpose.

"One who desires sense-powers should make an effort connected with the oblation and connected with the curd. But if this is so, is it not the same fault—that the fruit is mentioned in grammatical coordination with the oblation? It is said in reply: the capacity of the word "juhuyāt" (he should sacrifice) is such that it expresses an effort qualified by the oblation.
But here, the oblation (homa) is not enjoined as the means;
rather, it is understood from the sentence that a specific effort, characterized by being the end to be accomplished, is based upon the curd.
For this very reason, the Vṛttikāra stated: "The accessory (guṇa), being based upon the oblation, will accomplish the fruit."
Just as a king’s servant, depending upon the king, performs the king’s work; therefore, the result belongs to the curd:
"He who desires sensory power should produce sensory power by means of curd. How so? By means of this procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the Agnihotra. Why is this so?
Because the curd, which is the means to the result, requires a procedure (*itikartavyatā*);
because this procedure is in close proximity;
and because the meaning of the root *hu* (to sacrifice), which serves as the indicator of the injunction, is observed. And for this very reason, this meaning of *juhoti* is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Therefore, it is not injunctive.
Nor is there any other injunction for the oblation; therefore, it is not a separate ritual action.

Therefore, the fruit [accrues] from the curd. Alternatively, because the word "curd" (dadhi) has its intended meaning expressed, this connection between the curd and the oblation is enjoined by the sentence;
thus, the fruit will arise from the curd as it is connected with the oblation.
6: [The view that] they would exclude [the sacrificer] more strongly [is incorrect];
rather, it should be connected with the ritual action in the case of equals.

"The Agniṣṭut is a threefold Agniṣṭoma; having made the twenty-one-fold [stoma] its Agniṣṭoma-sāman with verses addressed to Vāyu, one desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should sacrifice with it.
Having made the Vāravantīya the Agniṣṭoma-sāman upon the Revatī verses, one desiring cattle should indeed sacrifice with this. Here, this matter is subject to doubt:
is it that cattle are the fruit resulting from the quality of the Vāravantīya applied to that very Agniṣṭut Agniṣṭoma?
The statement "one should sacrifice with this" is a restatement (anuvāda).

Now, is it that "one should sacrifice with this" refers to a different ritual action? What is the prima facie view? It is not a different ritual action; rather, the fruit results from an accessory (guṇa). Why?
This is a statement concerning that which is already known through the injunction "one should sacrifice with this," not concerning that which is unknown;
therefore, it is not a separate injunction.
It is said that "one who desires cattle should sacrifice in this manner," not simply "one should sacrifice"; how so?

"Having performed the Vāravantīya [sāman]," and furthermore, the phrase "of this very [sacrifice]" is a clear statement that there is no separate rite. Therefore, the prima facie view is that the fruit results from the accessory (guṇa).
This being the position, we reply: in the case of such similar instances where the sentences are distinct, the fruit must be connected with a separate ritual action.

Regarding the statement, "Having performed the Vāravantīya on the Revatī verses for this very [sacrifice]," it is because he does not possess the Revatī verses upon which his Vāravantīya would otherwise be performed.
In that case, there would be the *revatī* verses, and the *vāravantīya* chant would have to be enjoined upon them; thus, the sentence would be split. Now, if it were argued:
"Having first taken up the *revatī* verses for this [sacrifice], and having performed the *vāravantīya* upon them..."

By this [statement], "one should sacrifice with this," it is restated; thus, the term "having the Agniṣṭoma-sāman" would not be appropriate. If it were said that it exists for the purpose of the Agniṣṭoma-sāman, then the phrase "of this very [sacrifice]" would be unintended. If both were intended, there would be a syntactical split (vākya-bheda);
therefore, it is a distinct ritual act.

Now, how is there no syntactical split (*avākyabheda*) in another instance of ritual action? In the case of the injunction, "Desiring cattle, one should sacrifice having performed the *vāravantīya* chant upon the *revatī* verses," a previously unknown (*apūrva*) sacrifice is enjoined as qualified by all its qualifiers;

thus, there is a single purpose, and since there is mutual expectancy when divided, syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*) is established. But is there not a difference in meaning, for in this way a sacrifice must be performed that is otherwise unprecedented?
"In the *revatī* verses, the *vāravantīya* [sāman] is something unprecedented. We say: no;
rather, a sacrifice characterized by the *vāravantīya* as a quality of the *revatī* verses is enjoined, not the production of the *vāravantīya* itself.

By implication, the Vāravantīya will be produced in connection with the Revatī verses, and it is indeed possible to produce it there. It is argued: if no specific relationship between the Revatī verses and the Vāravantīya were enjoined, then other Sāmans might occur in the Revatī verses, and the Vāravantīya might occur in other Ṛks as well. This is not a fault.
Having performed [the action], the connection that has been brought about is expressed for the sake of the sacrifice;
by that, the connection is understood,
for this word "having performed" (kṛtvā) is capable of expressing both of these meanings.
[It expresses] manifestation and priority in time;
for example, in the command "Bring the red one," the horse connected with the quality of redness is enjoined by the word itself as the object to be brought.
There is no split in the sentence;
it should be understood in the same way here as well.
But even so, there are many meanings.
The Revatī verses, the Vāravantīya chant,
and their connection.
"The sacrifice" and "one desiring cattle"— this is not a fault,
for many [words] are heard [in the text].
In this case, only one thing is enjoined:
a sacrifice qualified [by specific elements]. But surely the *revatī* verses are also enjoined, as well as the *vāravantīya* chant?
If they were not enjoined,
the sacrifice qualified by them would not be understood at all; for one cannot enjoin a qualification without first enjoining the qualifier itself.

It is possible to prescribe [them] as distinct; therefore, when many things are being prescribed, there is not a single purpose. To this it is replied: "purpose" (artha) here denotes the objective (*prayojana*).
As many words as there are that express a single objective—[164]—
That many [syllables] constitute a single sentence, and there are not many purposes here.
For here, there is no single word that prescribes multiple intended [elements];
the phrase "in the Revatīs" does not prescribe the Revatīs alone.
Regarding the statement, "The Vāravantīya [chant] is [to be performed] during the Revatī verses," here too, in these two words, the word *vāravantīya* ends in the accusative case;
yet from this, no intended relationship is understood,
because the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) does not deviate [from its inherent nature].

Even the verb "having made" (*kṛtvā*) does not terminate in mere connection; it expresses a connection with another purpose. Thus, however, the sacrifice (*yajati*), being thus qualified, is not for the sake of another;

that is the single purpose of these word-meanings. Therefore, there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*). On the other hand, when a fruit is postulated for a subordinate element (*guṇa*), the *vāravantīya* chant is [to be performed] as the function of the *agniṣṭomasāman*.

Furthermore, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the statement "and this [rite] has the *agniṣṭomasāman*. Now, if it is argued that a sacrifice qualified by all the particulars beginning with the *revatī* verses is enjoined for this *agniṣṭut*, even so, the sentence would be split due to its connection with the desire for cattle (*paśukāma*). Or, if it were said:
"One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *vāravantīya* performed upon the *revatī* verses," this cannot be maintained.

There would be a deficiency [of the rite] due to the singing of a different *ṛc* and the loss of its specific quality. But was it not just stated that it is indeed possible to perform the *vāravantīya* on the *revatī* verses? It is possible only when there is an explicit scriptural injunction; in the absence of such an injunction, they are not included by the mention of the *vāravantīya*. Well then, there will be such an injunction.
"One desiring cattle should produce the Vāravantīya chant upon the Revatī verses;

then he should sacrifice"—here, the term "sacrifice" (yajati) is a restatement (anuvāda). If there is a scriptural statement regarding the connection between the Revatī verses and the Vāravantīya chant, then a distinct ritual act (karmāntara) is established.

The *agniṣṭut* is not an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*). [Objection: But surely, because of the restatement of the sacrifice in the phrase "one should sacrifice with that," there will be a connection between this [quality] and the sacrifice as its constituent part and purpose (*aṅgaprayojana*). [Reply: This cannot be so;
for while it would be enjoined as a subordinate part (*aṅgabhāva*) in relation to the sacrifice, it would have no connection in relation to one who desires cattle (*paśukāma*).

If there were a connection with both, the sentence would be split. If, on the other hand, the connection with the sacrifice is a restatement (*anuvāda*) and its status as a subsidiary (*aṅgatā*) is established by context (*prakaraṇa*), this is not tenable; for syntactical connection (*vākya*) is more powerful than context.

Therefore, it is either a distinct ritual action characterized by the *vāravantīya* chant performed upon the *revatī* verses, or a sacrifice characterized by that [chant] performed upon those [verses].

In that regard, we perceive the verbal suffix following the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) as the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that prescribes the relationship between the sacrifice and the desire for cattle;
however, nothing is directly perceived that prescribes the relationship between the *revatī* verses and the *vāravantīya* chant. Therefore, the sacrifice is qualified by all its qualifiers.
It is established that [the *vāravantīya*] is enjoined for one who desires cattle.
Now, however, when it is enjoined in relation to a specific sacrifice, how does that *vāravantīya* on the *revatī* verses become the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*?
It is said: [The injunction] will apply to the function of the Agniṣṭoma-sāman because of the scriptural statement; for what indeed could a scriptural statement not accomplish?
There is no burden too heavy for a scriptural statement. As for what was said regarding "of this very [sāman],"...

Since the statement refers to what follows immediately [in the sequence], there is no contradiction even in that case; thus, the word "characterized by" (*lakṣaṇā-śabda*) will mean "possessing this quality. Therefore, the result does not arise from a subordinate factor (*guṇa*), but rather from a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*) characterized in this way.
Consequently, it is established that in such similar cases, the result is connected to the ritual action itself.
