The rite would not be performed because its purpose has been lost.

This is not so; it has already been stated that "not all [auxiliaries] are to be employed everywhere," for those which do not provide assistance in a particular case do not merit being employed there. [Objection: But surely, by the force of the injunction itself, all will provide assistance everywhere. [Response: We say no. [213] {3/22}
NOTES:
But the fruit [of action] occurs together with the effort; the meaning of the word would be [the result] in the absence [of the effort], that is, upon separation. (MS 3.1.10)

There is no rule by which all [words] would assist in every instance; nor do we perceive such assistance through perception or other means of knowledge. Presumption (*arthāpatti*) too must necessarily occur only where there is an injunction by means of a word.

Not otherwise. And if the recitation of the *prathanā* and other acts within the context of the *ājya* and *sānnāyya* offerings were illogical even though they do not assist them, then an invisible benefit (*adṛṣṭa-upakāra*) would have to be postulated by implication;

however, those acts must necessarily be recited for the sake of the *auṣadha* (grain-offering). For the result—such as the removal of husks—is understood to occur together with the physical activity of threshing and so forth.
And there is a purpose served by it, for without it the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is not accomplished;

and when this [purpose] exists, the recitation within the context is meaningful. Since that [recitation] is meaningful, there is no authority for assuming an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*); therefore, it cannot be so assumed. Moreover, if [the assumption were made] that the production of rice grains and so forth occurs therein—

If the visible [benefit] had not existed, then, due to the absence of rice and so forth in their separation, the benefit would have to be considered as consisting of the mere word-meaning, independent of any visible benefit; consequently, even for the *ājya* and *sānnāyya*, the benefits produced would have been invisible (*adṛṣṭa*). Therefore, the acts such as spreading [the flour] and so forth do not [produce a visible benefit].
In all cases, it is thus with the winnowing and so forth, as well as the fetching of the branches and so forth. Therefore, not everything is to be performed everywhere;
the spreading [of the grass] and other such acts are not to be performed in the case of the clarified butter (ājya) and the sacrificial pap (sānnāyya).
The acts of purifying and so forth belong only to the clarified butter (ājya), not to the medicinal herbs (auṣadha) or the cooked milk offering (sānnāyya).
It is established that the fetching of branches and so forth pertain to the *sānnāyya* offering, not to the clarified butter (*ājya*) or the vegetable offerings (*auṣadha*).
Furthermore, because of its connection with the originative injunction, the substance is for the sake of that [offering].
And it should be urged in this very way. (MS 3.1.11)
There are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices;

regarding them, they recite: "The wooden sword (sphya), the potsherds (kapāla), the Agnihotra-ladle (agnihotrahavaṇī), the winnowing basket (śūrpa), the black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina), the yoke-pin (śamyā), the mortar (ulūkhalam), the pestle (musalam), the large millstone (dṛṣad), and the small millstone (upalā)—these indeed are the ten sacrificial implements (yajñāyudha)."
In this regard, a doubt arises: are these [mantras] recited for whatever object can be accomplished by these [means] here,
or rather for that which is connected with whatever [means]?
"To that very one" means: what, then, is the prima facie position?
That [the injunction applies] to one by whom it can be performed. Why?
Because the injunctions will be thus meaningful.
Otherwise, those restatements would be purposeless, as there is no distinction in the context regarding all the items;

furthermore, the connection with the sacrifice expressed by the term "sacrificial implements" (yajñāyudhāni) is common to all. Therefore, the prima facie conclusion is that all [implements] are to be used in every [sacrifice].
This being the case, we reply: the substance, because it is connected with the act of production, should be enjoined for that very purpose;

whatever substance is connected with a particular ritual act by means of a sentence regarding its production, that substance must be used for that very act—just as, for example, the *sphya* (wooden sword) is for the purpose of digging, according to the sentence "one digs with the *sphya*."

That digging out must not be performed with anything other than the wooden sword (sphya). Since this is the case, the wooden sword is already established [as the required tool]; therefore, this statement must be understood as a restatement (anuvāda) of it.

"These indeed are the ten sacrificial implements. This is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what has been established by various individual scriptural injunctions, such as: "He cooks [the oblation] on the potsherds," and "He pours out the sacrificial offerings with the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle."
He winnows with a winnowing basket;
he spreads a black antelope skin beneath the mortar; he places [the pestle] upon the yoke-pin.
"One threshes with the mortar and pestle;
one grinds with the lower and upper millstones. Due to the context (*prakaraṇa*), all [actions] would apply everywhere;
however, by virtue of the specific statement (*vacana*), they apply only according to that statement.
Furthermore, even the word *yajñāyudha* (sacrificial implements), while enjoining a purpose in a general sense, would necessarily be set aside;

for the prescription of a particular is indirect when expressed by a general term, whereas the prescription of a particular is direct when expressed by a specific term. Therefore, whatever is connected with something by way of its origin, [that is what prevails].
Thus it is established that it is employed for that very purpose. [215] NOTES:
{3/23: E2: artham}

When there is a single purpose, there should be a restriction [of the substance and the quality] because they perform a single function. (MS 3.1.12) [Note: The variants for *dṛṣadam* are *dṛṣadam* (E1,6), *dṛṣad* (E2,4), and *dṛṣad* (E4 v.l.). The variant for *bādhyetaiva* is *bādhyetaiva* (E2,4,6).]
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, with reference to the purchase [of Soma], it is heard in scripture: "One purchases Soma with a reddish-brown, yellow-eyed, one-year-old cow.
In this regard, there is a doubt: does the quality of redness (aruṇimā) pertain to the entire context?

"Or rather, [the redness] belongs to the one-year-old cow alone. But how can there be a doubt when the connection with the purchase is so clearly understood from the statement, "He purchases with the red one"? It is said in reply: For here, the word teaches that the quality of redness, being formless, is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the action.
Since he indicates [the quality] by connecting it with the third case-ending— which denotes an instrument— as in "aruṇayā" (by means of the red one),
and since an immaterial object cannot serve as the means for an action,
we understand that the quality of redness has no connection with the act of buying. Nor should it be suspected that this meaning is not authoritative.

The conceptual construction that "the word will express [the meaning]" might perhaps be tenable; for when one seeks the basis for the authority of a statement, the thought arises that there is a connection by some means or other.
If that is the case at most, [then...]

By investigating the capacity for a connection with the action, we shall understand that through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), we must enjoin the quality of redness (*āruṇimā*) within the act of purchase itself. However, if, despite being sought by those who are not negligent, no such connection can in any way be established,
then we shall admit a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) and determine this to be a property of the context (*prakaraṇadharma*).
Therefore, this must necessarily be investigated.
What, then, is the prima facie position? That it should be inserted into the entire context. Why?

Because there is no distinction in terms of connection and because there is no distinction in terms of context. [Objection: But surely a syntactical statement (*vākya*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*); therefore, due to their forming a single syntactical unit, the quality of redness (*aruṇimā*) shall be connected with the act of purchase (*kraya*). [Response: This is not how it is understood, for even by a hundred declarations, [it cannot be so] if it is not commenced... [213] {3/3}
A purpose cannot be established for those [elements] beyond this;
for if someone were to say, "One should burn with water" or "One should moisten with fire," would he achieve consistency in the utility of his statement?

Furthermore, it is not logical for an immaterial object to be the means of accomplishing an action. Therefore, because there is no connection [between the two], the sentence "He buys with a red one" does not constitute a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*).
Now, one might object: this word is certainly not expressive of a quality (*guṇa*); rather, it is expressive of a substance (*dravya*). Why?
Because of the connection with the feminine gender. For these are specific substances— namely, "female," "male," and "neuter"—
and the feminine suffix occurs after that nominal stem which denotes a female.

"And we perceive that [the word] *aruṇayā* (red) is based on a feminine suffix; therefore, it denotes a substance. This is not correct, for that very same substance, when delimited by redness (*aruṇiman*), becomes the denotatum of the word *aruṇa*.
Even when it acquires those other qualities, the word *aruṇa* is not able to denote it;
this word does not deviate from the quality of redness (*aruṇimāna*).

Furthermore, a substance (dravya) is subject to deviation, whereas for those who possess causes, a cause is held to be non-deviating. Therefore, it is understood that its own meaning is a quality (guṇa);
thus, its status as a word denoting a quality is understood through direct perception.

However, from the observation of the feminine suffix, there is the inference that the nominal stem *aruṇā* denotes a substance (*dravyavacana*). Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is stronger than inference;
therefore, it is a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*). How, then, is there a connection with the feminine suffix?
For even a word denoting a quality can possess a feminine gender.

Just as the cognition [arises] from "aruṇā," so too does it arise from "aruṇeti. If it is a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*), it cannot be syntactically connected with the verb "to buy" (*krīṇāti*). Therefore, having created a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), its application must be within the entire context (*prakaraṇa*).
Now, if it is not connected with "to buy,"...
"In that very same sentence, it will be connected with the word *ekahāyanī*, and there will be no split of the sentence. That is not so;
for the word *aruṇā* [expresses] the quality alone.
It expresses neither a substance nor a quality; rather, the word *ekahāyanī* denotes only the substance, not the substance accompanied by a quality.
Without a genitive case-ending—which would express the relationship between the two—how can that relationship be understood?
He said: Even without the sixth case-ending,
we shall understand the coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) from the indication by a single case-ending.
As in the case of "a blue lotus. That is untenable,
because the word *aruṇa* (red) denotes a quality (*guṇavacana*) distinct from the color-form (*rūpa*).

However, because of the connection with a single case-ending and the proximity of the word *ekahāyanī*, one must assume syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) and thereby establish grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *ekahāyanī*;

moreover, syntactical connection (*vākya*) is not stronger than indicative power (*liṅga*). Therefore, that [previous argument] is incorrect. To this, it is replied: when a word functioning solely as a denotation of a quality does not obtain a connection with anything else, [it must be understood otherwise].
In that case, lest it be rendered meaningless due to its lack of injunctive force (*anupadeśakatva*), it attains the status of being subordinate to a substance (*dravyaparatā*).

In that state, becoming syntactically unified (*ekavākyatā*) with the proximate word *ekahāyanī*—which is joined with the same case-ending—it becomes a term in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). And having done so, [the sentence functions as follows].
It is appropriate [to say] "the blue lotus. And this word *aruṇā* (red) functions in that particular state;
for if it were to express its own primary meaning [as a color], it would have no semantic value even within the context when separated from this [lotus]. Why?
Because of the very same reason by which it is connected [to the lotus].

[The word] does not [denote] that which is bought by the act of purchasing, nor does an immaterial object become the means (*sādhana*) for an action. Nor [is it denoted] by substances which are the means of action;

for a word expressing a quality alone is not capable of denoting a substance—this is the very same reason [it cannot denote the substance], even in the absence of a connection with the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Even there, if it were to be connected, it would have to be connected either with actions or with the substances that are their means;

however, both of these are untenable. Therefore, in order to avoid meaninglessness, the word *aruṇā* (“red”) is connected with the proximate word *ekahāyanī* (“one-year-old [cow]”). There is no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).
This is not so;
for this word *aruṇā* cannot function as a qualifier of the *ekahāyanī*. What is the reason? Because it is uttered with the third case ending, which is the instrumental case.

Therefore, by the force of this instrumental case-ending, it must function as an adverbial modifier of the action, for grammatical factors (*kāraka*) are connected with an action, not with a substance. Thus, by the force of direct audition (*śruti*), this [word] is an adverbial modifier of the action;
[yet], it is also an adjectival modifier of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*). And direct audition is more authoritative than syntactical connection (*vākya*).
Therefore, there is no connection between this [the word *aruṇā*] and the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*).

But surely, since a quality cannot be connected with an action, the case-role (*kāraka*) is not intended to be expressed; thus, this connection with the one-year-old cow has been determined. Even so, this is not tenable.

If the expression of the *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is not intended, and this word [ending in the third case] is desired to denote the substance (*dravya*) by means of its quality-suffix (*guṇaśabda*), then—since there is no deviation from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*)—the nominative case (*prathamā vibhakti*) would result. For a word ending in the third case is not able to express that relationship; nor can another meaning be postulated for it on the grounds of "impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*).

Just as when it is said, "The boy stands in the fire," since [standing] is impossible in a blazing fire, one does not conceive of it as being in a horse or a cow, but rather determines it to mean "in the vicinity of the fire"; so too here, a word that is not in the nominative case cannot in any way exist without its meaning being distinct from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Therefore, let it be understood that [the suffix] is indeed purposeless.
One should not determine that this [the quality of redness] has a connection with a one-year-old cow.
He says: we do not say that the factor (kāraka) is not denoted by the word *aruṇā* (red).
Clearly, by this [word], the factor (kāraka) qualified by the quality of redness is denoted. However, sometimes something is intended to be enjoined;
sometimes the subordinate meaning is what is intended to be enjoined, while the predominant meaning is a restatement (anuvāda). For example:
The word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) is understood as a term in which the person is primary and the staff is subordinate;
however, when the person is already known, it is uttered for the purpose of prescribing the attribute of the staff—as in: "The staff-bearer recites the injunctions. Likewise:
"The priests proceed wearing red turbans. In the same way, here too, if [the word] is not subordinate...

The quality "red" (*aruṇa*) is subordinate, while the factor of action (*kāraka*) is primary. Nevertheless, it is appropriate for this statement to be made for the purpose of enjoining the quality of redness with respect to the factor of action that has already been restated. Therefore, its connection with the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) is logical, and there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). This argument is not sound;
for here, this word *ekahāyanī* is uttered in order to make known the previously unapprehended relationship between the one-year-old cow and the act of purchasing.
How is this very term "aruṇā" connected with the word "krīṇāti"?
This, though already stated, is being questioned again and again.
But how, then, is the word "ekahāyanī" connected with "krīṇāti"?

Furthermore, when there is a co-utterance (samabhivyāhāra) with the term "buys" (*krīṇāti*), it must be accepted that the connection is with the quality of redness (*aruṇa*) as a whole, and not merely with the quality of redness alone. This is because of the authority of the word (*śabdaprāmāṇyāt*);
for indeed, there exists a case-ending expressive of the connection with the action which is attached to the word *ekahāyanī*.

But it does not express a connection with a quality (*guṇa*). What, then, expresses a connection with an action (*kriyā*), and what expresses a connection with a quality? When the connection with an action is intended to be expressed, the second case (*dvitīyā*) and so forth occur, characterized by the grammatical factor (*kāraka*);
but when the *kāraka* is not intended to be expressed, [the suffixes expressing quality occur].

The genitive case is used when one intends to express a mere relationship; however, we do not see a genitive here, but rather we clearly see an instrumental. Therefore, we accept that the word *ekahāyanī* has a connection with the verb *krīṇāti* (he buys), and not with the word *aruṇā* (red).
How, then, does the connection "the lotus is blue" arise? It is said: it does arise, but not by way of direct denotation (*śruti*).
Rather, it is characterized by a sentence;

for when the word "lotus" (*utpala*) is in proximity, the word "blue" (*nīla*), depending upon it and accepting syntactic unity with it, is uttered as being intent on denoting a specific kind of lotus while not abandoning its own primary meaning, and thus [the two] enter into a relationship. But surely here too, just like that, a relationship with the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) is joined with the redness (*aruṇimā*) through the characteristic of a sentence? We say: no.
For direct statement (śruti) is stronger than syntactical connection (vākya), and this direct statement expresses its connection with the action,
not its connection with a subordinate quality (guṇa). If, however, by the force of the direct statement...

If it were admitted that there is a connection with the action, then there would also be a connection with the subordinate element (guṇa), as in the case of a single syntactical unit (ekavākya). This is not possible;
for that which is uttered to be connected with one thing [cannot simultaneously be connected with another].

Even though another [word] is in proximity to it, it cannot be connected with that [other word]. Just as in the expression "the king's wife" (*rājño bhāryā*) and "Devadatta's man" (*puruṣo devadattasya*), the word *rājan*, which is uttered for the purpose of qualifying the wife, is not connected with the man;
likewise here, the word *ekahāyanī*, which is uttered for the purpose of qualifying the purchase (*kraya*), cannot be connected with the word *aruṇā*.
He said: "This is indeed true;
in the absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is not a cause [for syntactic connection].
However, when the meaning of each word has been made known, the meaning of the sentence is established."
Not otherwise;
for a word functions with reference to the universal, whereas a sentence functions with reference to the particular.
The settling of general categories of things that have been set forth in a general manner into their specific particulars is the meaning of a sentence.

This has been stated: "The recitation of words already formed [into a sentence] is for the sake of action, because the meaning [of the sentence] is caused by that. In this regard, the meaning of the word (*padārtha*) is perceptible, whereas the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) is inferential.
Let this be understood:

a word functioning solely for its own meaning is not self-instructive; it enters into syntactic unity with another proximate word, and not otherwise. Therefore, in this case, although the word *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow), being connected with the verb *krīṇāti* (buys), has fulfilled its purpose and does not require a connection with another word, [it nevertheless does so].

But the word *aruṇā* (red), not obtaining a connection with another word [within the sentence], would be meaningless; therefore, it enters into syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the word *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow). Now, it was argued that its purpose is to connect with the action, not to connect with the [cow].
To this we reply: we say that its purpose is to connect with both, in order to avoid the word *aruṇā* being meaningless.
Even that which is performed for one purpose can also serve another purpose;

for example, irrigation channels are dug for the sake of rice, yet from them water is both drunk and used for ritual rinsing. Likewise here, the word *ekahāyanī*, though uttered for the purpose of establishing a connection with the act of purchase, is combined with the word *aruṇā*.
Nothing is faulty; therefore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). This is not so.

Even if this word *aruṇā* were connected with the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) so that it might not be meaningless, nevertheless, it ought to apply to the entire context (*prakaraṇa*). And the expression "he buys Soma" (*somaṃ krīṇāti*) is not able to qualify it. For this [latter expression] is not uttered as a qualifier.
What then? This is enjoined as something not previously established (*apūrva*).
But even when enjoined as something new, will it not be connected with the other [element], just like the word *ekahāyanī*? How so?
For a word being uttered for a specific purpose conveys its meaning only through that [connection].

It is for that purpose alone that [the word] is postulated, and it becomes present in the intellect; therefore, by means of what is present in the intellect, a word possessing expectancy can be connected. This is not so.
For that which, when not connected, would be meaningless, is what is connected, and nothing else. Why is this so?
Because when it is connected, the universal is established within the particular.

In that case, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) would be contradicted by the syntactical connection (*vākya*). Furthermore, this [word *aruṇayā*], which is not connected with the verb *krīṇāti*, is not meaningless; it will be connected [with it].
But has it not been said that even in the context (*prakaraṇa*), its connection is untenable? It is not untenable;
for when one meaning is being enjoined within a single sentence, it does not connect with another, because of the difference in the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*).

For the mode of expression is indeed different for that which is being enjoined and different for that which is being connected with a subordinate quality (guṇa). An object being enjoined is made known as if it were unknown; whereas, for the sake of connecting it with a subordinate quality, it is restated (anūdya) as if it were already known.
Furthermore, a word being uttered only once cannot be both known and unknown;

the word *ekahāyanī*, when enjoined in connection with the purchase (*kraya*), would be as if unknown, yet when connected with the word *aruṇā*, it would be as if known. However, there is no fault if there is a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).

In the context (*prakaraṇa*), however, other actions and other substances have been obtained through other sentences. This [action] enjoined by one sentence is connected with those; thus it is logical that it is enjoined in one case and restated (*anūdyate*) in another sentence. Therefore, because there is no distinction in the connection and no distinction in the context, [the rule applies].
"In every case, there is a connection with substances.

This being the position reached, we reply: "When there is unity of purpose, there should be a restriction because of the single function of the substance and the quality," where the unity of purpose of the substance and the quality is heard in the scripture.
In that case, substance and quality would be restricted to a single category. Why?
Because of their having a single function—that is, because they have a single purpose;
for a single purpose is heard in scripture regarding substance and quality, namely, the connection with purchase. How is this understood?
Because they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*). How is there a single syntactical unit?
The meaning of "with a red, tawny-eyed, one-year-old [cow]" is not yet complete because the speaker and the listener have an expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*);
however, it reaches completion with the words "he buys Soma."
Because of their lack of such eagerness [for activity], one might ask: "If they have a single function, why does no conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) occur? This is not so.

Since it is said that things with a single object may be conceptually differentiated, these two would consequently possess the property of being subject to conceptual differentiation; therefore, this objection is improper. How so?
An objection is indeed such [only when it is valid].
He who establishes his own position and acts in opposition to the opposing side, yet whose conceptual construction does not act in opposition to our own position—

Our position is that the connection of *aruṇimā* (the quality of redness) is with the act of purchase (*kraya*). Nor is there an option (*vikalpa*) [between them], because they have different functions.
But was it not just stated that they have a single function?
And that too is contradictory,
for it was previously stated thus:
"Because it is formless, a quality is not connected with action."
Now the opposite view is stated: both the substance and the quality accomplish the purchase as having a single purpose. It is said in reply:
this is not contradictory, nor is there an option between them.
The purpose is one and the same, yet there is a difference in their capacities;
for substance assists the action directly, whereas a quality is the means of accomplishing specific [actions]. If this is so, [then...]
In that case, the quality (guṇa) does not bring about the action, for it is a qualifier of the means (sādhana). This is not so;
this very capacity belongs to the quality as it brings about the action.
That which qualifies the means (*sādhana*). Furthermore, an action requires a qualifier of its means;

for a quality (*guṇa*), acting as a mark, indicates the means. If the mark were absent, it would not be indicated—namely, which means belongs to the action. Consequently, we would not determine that the action is to be performed; thus, the quality becomes the means of the action. And this being so, there is no optionality (*vikalpa*).
Just as it is with the locus and the agent and so forth— the locus indeed supports the agent and the rest;
for if they were not supported, they would be unable to bring about the action— so too [is it with the mind].
The agent coordinates the instruments and so forth;

if they are not coordinated, they are unable to accomplish their respective purposes. However, when another means is prescribed for that very same assistance toward the effect which is to be accomplished, there is an option (*vikalpa*) in that case.
Just as in the cases "one should sacrifice with rice" and "one should sacrifice with barley," both are intended for the purpose of producing the rice-grains.
In that case, it follows that this very thing has come into being as the injunction for the one-year-old cow,
and the quality of ruddiness is its qualification.

In that case, the same fault would follow, namely, a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). We do not say that the word *aruṇā* (red) is connected with the word *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow); rather, it is connected with the verb *krīṇāti* (buys) itself. For it is heard [in scripture] thus: "One should accomplish the purchase by means of the quality of redness," and in whatever manner it is accomplished by that [quality].
Thus, one must strive accordingly. And since a quality does not bring about an action without qualifying its means,
it follows by implication that it functions as a qualifier of that means.

Just as in the case of the instruction "one should cook in a pot," when the pot is designated as the instrument for accomplishing the action, one naturally employs it for both containing and supporting [the food], so too should it be understood here. Therefore, there is no contingency of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
But even so, would the sentence not still be split? How so?

It is observed that the completion of a sentence occurs with each individual [word], just as in the case "Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra should be fed," where the act of eating is completed for each one;
and just as in "He whose father and grandfather did not drink Soma. So too here: "He buys [the cow] with a red one."
"One purchases [the Soma] with a one-year-old cow. This does not contradict our position;
for even in this way, the quality of redness (āruṇimā) will be restricted to the act of purchase alone, and not to the entire context. True, this fault does not arise.
However, the purchase would also apply to a one-year-old cow that is not red,
as well as to a multi-colored cow that is red;
therefore, regarding what was stated— that there is a restriction between the substance and the quality— [it is not so].
That proposition is abandoned. In that case, we do not say there is a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). How so?
For it is the purchase (*kraya*) to which the substance and the redness (*aruṇimā*) are taught, not the purchase to them. And furthermore, [it is not the case that...]
The subordinate element differs according to each principal element, for indeed the subordinate element differs with each principal element;
and there is this illustrative example: "the completion of the sentence occurs within the aggregate."

Just as in the case [of the statement], "Let the Gargas be fined one hundred," so too [in the case of], "Having pressed [the Soma] and having offered it, they consume it. Therefore, the purchase is enjoined as qualified by both qualifiers.
But how, when both examples exist, can it be determined with absolute certainty?

"Or rather, the completion of the sentence occurs only in the aggregate, not in each individual part. To this we reply: here, both the substance and the quality of redness are perceived as connected to the action, yet they are not connected to one another;
furthermore, the purchase is perceived as qualified by both the substance and the quality of redness, and not by either one alone.
In that case, if this statement were intended to have the substance as its primary referent and the quality of redness as secondary, [the following would ensue].

Consequently, there is an inseparable connection with the purchase for every individual part. Now, if it is stated with the intention of prescribing the purchase, then—just as this [animal] is qualified by the "one-year-old" (ekahāyanī) quality—likewise it is qualified by "redness" (aruṇimā); thus, a necessary dual connection must be admitted. Furthermore, neither the substance nor the redness is intended as the primary object of desire here.
But the purchase is what is desired,
for by it the substance *soma* belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma is obtained; thus,
both the substance and the quality of redness, being for the sake of the purchase, would be what is desired.

Not otherwise. Therefore, the purchase is enjoined, and since it is not perceived as qualified by either [the cow or the goat] individually, it is determined here that the completion of the sentence occurs with the aggregate. And when this is the case, then [it is] not...
Since there is no other substance besides the one-year-old cow that serves as the means of purchase,
and no quality other than the red color that qualifies the means,
the restriction is established.

To this we reply: if the quality enters into a connection with the means of purchase (*kraya-sādhana*), then, even though the sentence is split, because it serves as a means of purchase, the redness (*aruṇimā*) would not be restricted to this particular substance;

for what purpose, then, is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) so laboriously established? This is explained as follows: for if the sentence were split, the purchase would be understood as having the one-year-old cow (*ekāhāyanī*) as its means.
The procurement of the *aruṇa* (red) quality is also a separate act of purchase;
it is not the case that the redness is enjoined within that very same act of purchase which has the one-year-old cow as its means.
In that regard, there is another act of purchase characterized by the quality of redness.

In that case, another means of accomplishment (sādhana) would also be obtained by implication; and if the quality *aruṇa* were to qualify that as well, it would become connected with it. However, this difficulty is avoided when there is syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*). Therefore, it is rightly stated: "When there is a single purpose, there should be a restriction because the substance and the quality serve a single function."

It is connected with oneness because of its connection with the singular [number] in the Vedic revelation.

There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, concerning which it is said: "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with Soma. In that context, it is heard: "He cleanses the cup with the fringe-filter (*daśāpavitra*)," and likewise, regarding the Agnihotra, it is heard: "He sweeps away the grass-blades from the fire."

Likewise, in connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "He carries fire around the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa). Regarding this, there is a doubt: [does this apply] to one cup (graha), or to one fire (agni)?

Should the cleansing and other rites be performed for one cake-offering (puroḍāśa), or for all the cups (grahas), all the fires (agnis), and all the cake-offerings? What is the prima facie view? One cup, one fire...
Only one sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is to be taken here. Why?
Because of the connection with the scriptural statement;
these items are connected with the scriptural mention of singularity.
For this is heard as a single substance; and in the matter of defining sound, that which the word itself declares regarding its own nature is our authority.

Just as when it is said, "One should sacrifice an animal," only one male animal is sacrificed; so too here, only one cup is to be cleansed, only one fire has its grass-blades removed, and only one sacrificial cake is to be carried around with fire.
Or rather, it is common to all because a characteristic is indeed non-distinct [from the thing characterized].
This is not so— that which was said, that these ritual items should be performed as being associated with singularity in the case of the cups and so forth,
meaning all the cups are to be cleansed.
"Grass is to be removed from all the fires, and the sacrificial cake alone is to be carried around with fire. Why?
Because, having indicated the substance by means of the class of the vessel (*graha*), the cleansing and other rites are enjoined.
Furthermore, the characteristic is undifferentiated across all substances;
in that case, no distinction is perceived as to which vessel should be wiped.

"Which one?"—this cognition arises because there is a general understanding [of the class] but no understanding of the specific [individual]. The same applies to the fire and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). But surely a singular number is heard; that will specify [the referent]. This is not so.
For if singularity were being heard, it would express singularity in the case of the cups (*graha*) and so forth,
but it could not exclude a second or more;
that word is the designator of singularity, not of a second or more.

[He is] the prohibitor. Therefore, since the second [instance] and so forth are not prohibited, why should acts such as sweeping—which are applicable to them by virtue of the general statement—not be performed?
In this regard, it might be argued that the singular number heard here applies only to that single substance which is actually present.
And regarding the second and subsequent [syllables],
what else could it do other than exclude them,
if it were not to exclude the second and subsequent ones by means of the singular number?
It would indeed be purposeless,
yet it is capable of excluding the second [animal] and those following it, just as in the expression "he takes the horse's halter," which excludes the donkey's halter.
As it is explained in that context, so it should be understood here as well.
This is not so.
In that regard, the statement which is intended to express the relationship between the mantra and the horse's halter is: "He took this [rope]," namely, "the horse's halter."

In that case, because the act of taking is already established by the very indicative mark (*liṅga*) "he has taken," it is appropriate to treat the mantra as a restrictive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*). However, here, as for the singular number heard in reference to the substance,
even though it is heard, it cannot function as an exclusion because it is not being enjoined.
For example, suppose someone were to point out a heap of cooked rice and say, "If any dog or cat should eat this,
it must be driven away. In that case,
if the act of eating were prescribed as the causal condition (*nimitta*), it would not be so.

The connection between the dog and the cat is such that even a crow arriving there is excluded; for although the dog or the cat may be heard, their connection is not enjoined as the cause [of the exclusion]. Likewise here, since the connection with oneness is not being enjoined, even when [the singular number] is heard...
"Even in the case of singularity, one would only cleanse the cup.

Furthermore, there is no word here that prescribes a connection between the substance and singularity. [Objection: But is it not "he cleanses" (*saṃmārṣṭi*)? [Reply: For this does not prescribe a connection between the substance and singularity. What, then, does it prescribe?
It prescribes a connection between the substance and the cleansing.

In this way, its own meaning is enjoined by direct statement (*śruti*); otherwise, the meaning of another word would be enjoined by syntactical connection (*vākya*). And syntactical connection operates only when direct statement is impossible, not when direct statement is possible. Therefore, [the object] is not being enjoined as a qualifier.
Oneness cannot serve to negate a second and so forth. This being the case, when the cleansing and other rites are performed upon a second and so forth, they do not become unenjoined or prohibited.
For just as that [word] is heard and understood by one person,
so too it is by a second and others.
And this is another fault:
That singularity of the substance would not be restricted to objects such as the act of cleansing;
for there is no cleansing or similar act to which singularity could be restricted with respect to a particular substance.
It functions as its qualifier; for here the cleansing and so forth are enjoined,
and it is not mentioned as a substance serving merely as a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) that was already established.

For it is not possible to enjoin [the action] and utter [the word] as a defining characteristic simultaneously. Indeed, only that which has a well-known relationship can function as a defining characteristic;
and a word-comprehended object of this kind cannot have a well-known relationship if it has not been enjoined. Yet, the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) and so forth are indeed enjoined.
Therefore, it is not a qualifier; and if it is not a qualifier,
one cannot maintain that the oneness of the substance is thereby determined.
Now, singleness is stated [as the purpose] for the cleansing. In that case as well, there would be two possible courses:
either singleness is primary, or the cleansing is primary.

And both of these [positions] are untenable. First of all, the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) of oneness cannot be performed. Nor does an action performed upon a substance benefit oneness in any way through that context (*prakaraṇa*). Furthermore, there is no purpose served by benefiting oneness, for it is not heard in the scripture as being a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*). If it is argued that oneness is subordinate with respect to the cleansing, that too is not the case. Why?
Because it is formless,
it does not indeed effect the cleansing; for even if another formless thing effects an action by qualifying the instrument,
this [the *saṃmārga*] cannot be such [an agent].
For here the cup is not for the purpose of wiping; rather, the wiping is enjoined for the sake of the cup,
since that [cup] possesses a purpose.

The purpose of the purification (*saṃmārga*) is to be determined through conceptual construction. If the cup (*graha*) were to benefit the purification, then—since it would be benefiting that which benefits [it]—oneness (*ekatva*) would be a benefactor of the purification. But this is not the case. Therefore, there is no connection between oneness and the purification.
But surely even that which is subordinate, such as the cups (*graha*), certainly accomplishes the cleansing (*saṃmārga*);
therefore, by qualifying its means, it will assist that [cleansing],
just as the properties of the *praṇītā* water assist the cooking when the curd and milk are for the purpose of sacrifice, and [they assist] the act of wrapping.

"In the case of the *paridhi*, the characteristics of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) apply because it serves as a binding; therefore, this is not a valid solution. To this it is replied: We do not say that things which do not serve that purpose are incapable of providing assistance. What then?
When the principal element, such as the *graha* and so forth, is mentioned as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), [it is for the sake of that].
At that time, oneness has no connection with the act of grasping and so forth, nor with the act of cleansing and so forth. How so?
Because whatever is mentioned here as a defining characteristic [of the relationship]—
A connection occurs there, but it is not prescribed for the sake of cognition. For what purpose, then, is it uttered?
It is because something else will be prescribed for it.

Having thus characterized the cup (*graha*) and so forth, its cleansing (*saṃmārga*) and other such actions are enjoined. If, however, a further connection with singularity were enjoined either with respect to the substance of the cup or with respect to the ritual act of cleansing and so forth, the sentence would be split due to the enjoining of two distinct relationships. Now, it might be argued: "Having characterized the cup and so forth, the connection with singularity is enjoined for that [cup]."
There is no connection with the act of wiping (*saṃmārjana*) and so forth;

and if that were the case, it would have to be admitted that the study of the wiping and other such acts is merely negligence. But this is not so. Therefore, the singular number has no connection with either [of the two]. Thus, this singularity of the cup (*graha*) does not provide any assistance whatsoever.
It is not [the case that] the cleansing applies [only] to that [specific one];

rather, it is the existing state that is being restated. Therefore, nothing at all is intended to be enjoined here; thus, the cleansing and so forth must be performed for all the cups and other items. Why?
Because there is no distinction in their connection [to the rite] and because there is no distinction in the context (*prakaraṇa*).
If unity is not intended to be expressed, why is the singular number uttered?
Surely, when plurality is intended, the plural number ought to be used. It is said in reply: we do not deliberate upon this matter.
"One should pronounce the singular number, or one should not pronounce it"— if it is being pronounced, what should be understood [from that]?

Whether the sweeping and other rites apply to one [altar] alone or to all—this has been established as applying to all. Furthermore, the expression of the case-ending does not have only a single purpose; what then?

The connection with the *kāraka* (grammatical participant) as well—though not intended to be expressed—is for the sake of connecting it with the *kāraka*, and its utterance will serve that purpose. Therefore, it is not meaningless.
Furthermore, the base (*prātipadika*) denotes the cup (*graha*), while singularity is the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*). What follows from this?

If this is so, then this follows: for a case-ending expresses its own meaning—which resides within the meaning of the nominal stem—by means of direct denotation (*śruti*) itself. Now, if this is the case, why would it not be connected with the act of cleansing (*saṃmārga*)? For if it were connected by that [cleansing], it would be connected through syntactical connection (*vākya*), and not through direct denotation.

A word being connected with one [element] deserves to be connected with another only after breaking its connection with the former. However, the act of cleansing (*saṃmārga*), which is not [naturally] connected [with a specific number],
incurs no deficiency whatsoever if it is not performed as qualified by singularity (*ekatva*).
Furthermore, since the act of cleansing and so forth is not qualified by oneness (*ekatva*),
and is enjoined for the cups (*graha*) and other items in their entirety, why should it not be performed for the second and the third as well?

*{3/73: E2,4: by way of assistance}* *{3/74: E2: 4,86; E4: 3,602; E6: 1,156 (l.Z.)}* *{3/75: E1,6, E4 (v.l.); E2,4: in the case of a substance}*
But when [an act] is enjoined for the sake of another, it should be understood according to the scriptural statement, because it exists for the purpose of that other. (MS 3.1.15)
Now, as for what was said— that just as when it is commanded "one should sacrifice an animal," only a single animal, specifically a male animal, is sacrificed, so it is here too—
there is a reversal in this case: here, the cleansing is for the sake of the cup (*graha*).
In that case, however, the animal is for the sake of the sacrifice. What follows from this being so?
He who appropriates [the animal] for the sake of the sacrifice benefits the sacrifice.

A sacrifice cannot be performed with that which is undelimited; however, the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) is not to be performed by means of some specific cup (*graha*), such that by qualifying the cup it would assist the cleansing.

And this singleness of the animal is taught in relation to the sacrifice. But was it not said: "The case-ending expresses its own meaning, residing in the meaning of the nominal stem, by direct denotation (*śruti*) itself"?
The sacrifice will be enjoined by this sentence;
however, it has been stated that direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is stronger than syntactical connection (*vākya*). This is true in cases where a direct relationship is intended to be expressed.
And when something is not intended to be expressed, it remains unexcluded as it is understood from the sentence; therefore, "one male animal is to be sacrificed.
Just as the singularity of the cup does not assist the cleansing and thus cannot qualify the cup, so too [the number] is not intended to be expressed. [230]

Or else,
if [the term] "existent" were not excluded [from the definition], there would be no distinction between conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and qualities (*guṇa*). (MS 3.1.16)

There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice; therein it is heard: "He cleanses the cup with the fringed filter. Regarding this, the following point has been established: all cups (grahas) are to be cleansed. Now, this is being deliberated: are the chalice-cups (camasas) also to be cleansed, or not?
What, then, is the prima facie view?
That everything, including the *camasa* cups and so forth, must be cleansed. Why?
Because there is no distinction in the connection [of the injunction] and because there is no distinction in the context.
For just as there is a previously unestablished connection for the *grahas*, so too it is for the *camasas*; and just as the *grahas* [are mentioned] in this context, so too are the *camasas*.
The same applies to the cups (*camasa*). Therefore, the wiping (*saṃmārga*) is to be performed in all cases.
[Objection: But the *graha* vessels are explicitly mentioned in the scripture;
they will therefore serve as the substitutes for the cups. [Reply: It is said in response: the mention of the *graha* vessels is for the purpose of illustration.
The *graha* and other vessels are Soma-cups,
concerning which there arises this apprehension: "In which [vessel] the Soma being drawn might be spilled."
All of that must be swept clean. Just as when the time for a meal has arrived and it is said, "Let the vessels be swept," whatever items are fit for use at the meal [are to be cleaned].
It is understood that all those various items are wiped clean;
the mention of the "pot" (sthālī) is for the purpose of illustration. It should be seen that the same applies here as well.
It is said: in the world, conventional usage is characterized by its practical purpose.
Whatever object is to be purified,
whether it has been mentioned or not mentioned, that very thing must indeed be purified. But here in the Veda, [the purification] is characterized by the word.
And the word [“saṃmārṣṭi”] expresses the cleansing of the cup;

in that case, why, while a direct Vedic statement (śruti) is possible, is the word “cup” assumed through indirect indication (lakṣaṇā)? It is said: this word is capable of enjoining human effort toward the act of cleansing itself, whereas it would require syntactical connection (vākya) to establish a relationship with the cup.

Moreover, direct statement (*śruti*) is stronger than syntactical connection (*vākya*). Therefore, the word "cup" (*graha*) is explained through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and not according to its literal sense;
by that [principle],...
Whichever thing is fit for the refinement of sweeping must be swept; it does not follow that such a quality as this would be restricted solely to the planets (*graha*). [231] NOTES:
Or rather, there is a fixed determination of the meaning because of its connection with the Vedic revelation,
since that [revelation] has the word as its means of valid cognition.
Or rather, the wiping should apply only to the cups (graha), and it should not extend to the goblets (camasa). Why?
Because the purpose [of the action] is connected directly with the Vedic text.
For a *graha* that is explicitly heard in the scripture must not be abandoned;
if it were abandoned, the scriptural statement "the *graha*" itself would be contradicted,
and thus it would be understood that what your honors have said is merely the singing of one who is intoxicated.

And this is not logical. Therefore, having indicated the cup (*graha*) by means of the word "cup," the connection of that [cup] with the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) is enjoined. And one cannot enjoin its connection without enjoining the cleansing itself;
therefore, this very word enjoins the cleansing. Nor will the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) be sublated. Why?

The word "he cleans" (*saṃmārṣṭi*) is able to enjoin through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) the human effort involved in the act of cleaning; there is no distinction therein whether that cleaning is being produced for the first time or is already established.
Or, [it may be argued that it is] connected with something else. Therefore, even when there is a connection with the *graha*, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is not sublated;
thus, the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) ought to be restricted to the *grahas* alone.

[Objection: But surely, because there is no difference in the connection with the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) and because there is no difference in the context (*prakaraṇa*), it would follow by implication that it applies to the *camasa* cups as well.

It has been stated that the injunction does not apply to the cups alone. To this it is replied: [The injunction] can enjoin something there by forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the context (*prakaraṇa*), but not without forming such a single syntactical unit. And that [unity] is inferred from the context;
however, this [connection], on the other hand, is directly perceived (*pratyakṣā*) together with the word "cup" (*graha*).
Therefore, there is no injunction within the context;
furthermore, having abandoned its own meaning in connection with the singularity of the cup, it is not able to enjoin [it]. Therefore, this is dissimilar.

As for what was said— that just as the expression "the pots are to be scrubbed" is indicative (lakṣaṇā), so it is here— that has been refuted by the fact that in the world, indication exists for the sake of the action.
Furthermore, he knows the definition of sound.
[232] NOTES:
*{3/88: E2: saṃmṛjā, E4: saṃmṛjām}* *{3/89: E2,4: vaiṣamyaṃ}* *{3/90: This sentence is missing in E6}*
The definition of action is by its purpose;
[the subsidiary parts] are for that purpose because they would otherwise be meaningless. (MS 3.1.18)

In the Vājapeya sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of the Vājapeya is seventeen cubits long. Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the measurement of seventeen cubits apply to the upper vessel of the Vājapeya, or does it apply to the sacrificial post for the animal victim? What, then, is the prima facie view?
That it applies to the upper vessel. Why?
Since there is no sacrificial post (yūpa) for the Vājapeya sacrifice,
whatever vessel belonging to the Vājapeya resembles a sacrificial post, it is appropriate that [the ritual act] should take place there.
Furthermore, there exists the sixteen-cup vessel, which, because it is made of khadira wood and is upright, resembles a sacrificial post (yūpa);
if [the term 'sacrificial post'] were applied to that, the word *vājapeya* would be used in its primary sense.

Otherwise, it is understood that in the animal sacrifice which is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the Vājapeya, the word "Vājapeya" is employed through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). [Objection: But even in your position, the word "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*) must apply to the tall vessel through secondary indication. [Reply: It is said in response: in any case, we cannot escape the use of words by way of secondary indication. However, in my position, the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Vājapeya is upheld.
"Therefore, it should be placed in the upper vessel.
This being the position reached, we reply: because it would otherwise be purposeless, it applies to its constituent parts;
for the word "Vājapeya" denotes a specific type of Soma sacrifice.

For that [Vājapeya sacrifice], there is no direct requirement for a sacrificial post (*yūpa*); however, it has as its constituent part the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*), and for that [animal sacrifice], the purpose of the post is to tether the animal. If, therefore, the measurement of seventeen cubits were prescribed directly for the Vājapeya post itself—

In the absence of that [animal sacrifice], the statement would become meaningless; lest it be meaningless, it deserves to find its place in the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) used in this animal sacrifice. And in the case of the upright vessel, the word *yūpa* would apply through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). But [one might object]: "Even in the other view, the word *vājapeya* would involve secondary indication. We say: no.
The word "vājapeya" will apply to the vājapeya sacrifice itself,
and it will be able to qualify the animal-sacrifice post; thus, it is an auxiliary that benefits this subsidiary rite.
And when one person benefits someone who has already been beneficial to him,
he becomes connected to that person by a primary connection itself; nor does he become unconnected on the grounds that there is an intervening step,
as in the case of "Devadatta’s great-grandson."
Moreover, he is separated from his son, yet he is connected to Devadatta by the primary relationship itself. Therefore, this very position is the one that should be adopted.
For in this view, there is not even a single word that functions as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
(Note:
*In the animal sacrifice which is a subsidiary of the Vājapeya.*)
But if [the qualification] pertains to the agent, there would be a split of the sentence because of the lack of inherence in the object. (MS 3.1.19)
In the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard in the injunction regarding the *prayāja* offerings: "He offers while stepping forward, for the sake of victory.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the stepping forward belong only to the *prayāja* offerings, or does it pertain to the entire context? What, then, is the prima facie view? We say that since stepping forward is a quality of the agent, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) [if it were restricted to the *prayājas* alone].
Because one action does not coalesce with another action. Walking forward is an immaterial action;
it cannot accomplish the act of offering, and therefore it does not form a single syntactical unit with it. Consequently, it is inserted into the entire context.
"Because of the lack of distinction in connection and because of the lack of distinction in context.

[Objection: But surely, by this very reason, it would not be enjoined even in another case. [Reply: It is said: in another case, it will be connected with persons. [Objection: But then it would also be connected with persons in the case of the *prayāja* offerings. [Reply: This is not so;
for the word "he offers" (*juhoti*) is an act of pouring (*havana*), and it is capable of enjoining human effort.

It is not [connected] with the person’s stepping forward (*puruṣābhikramaṇa*). But surely, in other cases as well, there is no injunction of a connection with the person’s stepping forward? This is not a fault; for in those other cases, since its status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) is already established through its mention within the context (*prakaraṇa*), the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) will express its necessity of being performed. Therefore, the stepping forward finds its place within the entire context. *Notes:* The opponent argues that the stepping forward is not connected to the person because it is not explicitly enjoined as such elsewhere. The proponent replies that while it may not be enjoined elsewhere, its subsidiary status is determined by its inclusion in the ritual context (*prakaraṇa*). Once this is known, the general injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) dictates that it must be carried out. Thus, the stepping forward is integrated into the whole ritual procedure.
"But that which is expectant [of completion] shall constitute a single sentence, for it is not finished by the preceding. (MS 3.1.20)
This is not so—that which was stated, that the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) belongs to the context [of the *prayāja*s]. It ought to belong to the *prayāja*s themselves. Why?
Because it forms a single syntactical unit with them.

Since this sentence is expectant and incomplete with respect to the preceding word, it concludes at the point "he offers while stepping forward" (*abhikrāman juhoti*); and because a direct syntactical statement (*vākya*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*), the stepping forward is to be included within the *prayāja* offerings themselves. Now, it was argued that stepping forward, being immaterial, is incapable of accomplishing the sacrifice; to this it is replied:
That which is incapable by itself will be able to accomplish its purpose when connected with the agent. How so?
By means of the approaching, the agent draws near to the Āhavanīya fire.
Two things are the means for the oblation: one may offer it either by extending the hand from a distance, or...

One should sit down by means of successive stepping forward (*anvābhikramaṇa*). Therefore, it is understood that stepping forward assists the *homa* (oblation). Consequently, its application is restricted to the *prayāja* offerings alone.

But when there is doubt, a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would occur due to intervention. (MS 3.1.21)
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the Sāmidhenī verses are taught in the seventh and eighth Brāhmaṇa sections;
the Nivids are in the ninth; and the optional (kāmya) forms of the Sāmidhenī verses are in the tenth.

"One should recite so many [verses] for this desire, so many for that desire," and in the eleventh [book], the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is prescribed: "He invests himself with it; he thereby makes it the mark of the gods."

In this regard, there is a doubt: should one wear the *upavīta* while reciting only the *sāmidhenī* verses, or should it be worn by one who performs all the constituent acts within the context (*prakaraṇa*)? Why is there this doubt?
Because the *upavīta* is mentioned in the context of the *sāmidhenīs*.
Now, it is not known whether their context has ceased or not.
[Objection: But surely this context belongs to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices themselves;
the Sāmidhenī verses are heard in another context. [Reply: True, they are heard in another context. Nevertheless, there is a further intermediate context for them.

For there exists the statement, "One should recite the *sāmidhenī* verses," which requires a specific object; by virtue of this, that which is mentioned in proximity to it is understood to belong to it. But how is it suspected that the context (*prakaraṇa*) of those verses has ceased? [235] {3/}
99*} "The *nivit* verses interrupt their context. If this is so, what is the concern that the context continues? [It continues] after the *nivit* verses.
Only those qualities of the *sāmidhenī* verses that are prescribed as optional (*kāmya*) are heard;
immediately after which the *yajñopavīta* is mentioned.

Therefore, the thought arises that the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *sāmidhenīs* has not ceased. Consequently, the *nivid*s, falling within this subsequent context, do not create an interruption. Just as:
The dharma of the twelve *upasads* belongs to the context of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. Therefore, a doubt arises.
In this doubt, what is the prima facie view?
The context of the *sāmidhenī* verses has not ceased.
"In that context, the wearing of the sacred thread (upavīta) is traditionally taught. Why?
Because of the statement regarding the immediate sequence of the optional *sāmidhenī* formulas;
while the *sāmidhenīs* are revolving in the mind, they enjoin the wearing of the sacred thread.

And for the agent, the *upavīta*—which is merely the arrangement of the garment—is a subordinate element (*guṇa*). There arises an expectancy for the constituent matter (*padārtha*) as to what must be done by the agent while performing that [act].

In that context, having entered into syntactic unity with the *sāmidhenī* passage—which is present in the mind and not remote—the word "he arranges the *upavīta*" (*upavyayate*) is understood to enjoin the *upavīta* in relation to the *sāmidhenīs*.
This being the prima facie view, we reply: No.
In this doubt, that which has been stated is the resolution: "In this doubt, there is a split of the sentence," such is the resolution. Why?
Because of the intervention; for here, the Sāmidhenī sentence, having been completed along with its connection, [is interrupted].
Furthermore, there is an interruption between this statement, "asya copavyayate," and the prescriptive passage for the *nivid*s by means of a text that is unrelated to the *sāmidhenī* verses;
and even when that statement has been concluded, they proceed to another matter that is indeed connected to it.

In that case, there is no lack of continuity in the context, for the mind turns toward what is being expressed as connected to it. However, where the speech has reached its conclusion and they proceed to another topic entirely unconnected to it, the preceding object is not present in the intellect. And yet—
The syntactic unity with the cognition occurs when it is not present;
for the meaning of a sentence is produced by two factors— the cognition and the word-meanings— and not by either one alone.
The sole purpose of this recitation in proximity is this:
how might they produce a cognition qualified by both word-meanings? For the meaning of a sentence can be established with that which has not been cognized immediately preceding it.
Furthermore, when unrelated words are uttered, the subsequent cognition does not arise [from them]. Therefore, there can be no syntactic unity with what is separated [by an interval].

Alternatively, if one were to understand the meaning of the preceding word through another means such as meditation (*dhyāna*) and thereby produce the meaning of the sentence, that sentence-meaning would be non-Vedic, being preceded by human intellect.
For example, just as when a verbal form is taken from one section (anuvāka) and a nominal form from another, a certain sentence-meaning is produced; [so it is here].
Such would be that [sentence],
wherein one might, having understood the prior word-meaning through another means such as meditation (dhyāna),
then produce the meaning of the sentence. Therefore, it is determined that there can be no syntactic unity (ekavākyatā) when there is an intervention by a disconnected meaning.

Therefore, the upavīta does not form a single syntactical unit with the *sāmidhenī* verses. But one might object: since the upavīta is recited in close proximity to the various arrangements of the *sāmidhenīs* that have just been understood, it must therefore be connected with the *sāmidhenīs*. We say: no; for the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *sāmidhenīs* has already passed away due to the intervention of the *nivit* formulas. Indeed, [the connection] would have to be by way of syntactical unity (*vākya*).
The ritual variations for the *sāmidhenī* verses pertain to optional rites (*kāmya*) and enter into a specific connection;
they do not follow the general context (*prakaraṇa*), nor do they [apply otherwise].

Furthermore, by the mention of the word "kalpa," the *sāmidhenī* verses are brought back to their original context. For it is not the case that there is an injunction there stating "they are to be recited"; rather, they are to be connected with specific numbers.

That too is by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*), not by context (*prakaraṇa*). In that regard, for a quality whose syntactical unity with the *sāmidhenī* verses is not established when those *sāmidhenīs* are not the subject under discussion, there is no connection between it and them. Therefore...
It is established that whatever is to be performed must be done by one wearing the sacrificial cord (*yajñopavītin*).

In the rite of establishing the sacred fires (agnyādheya), vessels made of *vāraṇa* and *vaikaṅkata* wood are prescribed for both non-oblation purposes and for oblation purposes: "Therefore, the sacrificial implement should indeed be made of *vāraṇa* wood, but one should not offer oblations with it."

"A sacrificial implement should be made of *vaikaṅkata* wood; one should offer with this. Furthermore, there is no connection between the *vāraṇa* and *vaikaṅkata* vessels and the *agnyādheya* (the establishment of the sacred fires). Why?
Because of the expression "sacrificial implement" (*yajñāvacara*), which indicates that these vessels belong to the sacrifice.

By means of the direct statement (*vākya*), the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside. In this regard, there is this doubt: do they find their place in the *pavamāna* offerings, or in all sacrifices such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and others? What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That they belong to the *pavamāna* oblations. Why?
It has been stated that when a matter is impossible in relation to the primary subject, it is to be attributed to its subordinate quality;
and since the Pavamāna oblations are recorded within the context of the *Agnyādheya*, they are subordinate to it. Therefore, the prima facie view is that [the rule applies] to the Pavamāna oblations.
This being the case, we reply: because the qualities are equal.

There is no mutual connection between the Pavamāna offerings and the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya). Just as the establishment of the fires is an accessory to the fire for the purpose of consecration, so too the Pavamāna offerings are accessories belonging to the fire itself. What, then, is their mutual connection? As for what was said—that they are recited within the context of the establishment of the fires—even though they are so recited, [there is no such connection].
Nevertheless, setting aside the context (*prakaraṇa*), they belong to the fire by virtue of the sentence (*vākya*). What is the sentence here?
It is: "In that one offers into the *āhavanīya*, thereby that [fire] becomes desired and pleased for him."
But surely, the *āhavanīya* fire is heard here as a subordinate element (*guṇa*) by virtue of being the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the sacrifice. True;
the *āhavanīya* is the locus, yet nevertheless, the sacrifice exists solely for the sake of the *āhavanīya*.

Because the Āhavanīya fire serves a purpose, whereas the Pavamāna oblations serve no purpose. How is it that these have no purpose? Because no fruit is heard of [in the scripture]. If it is argued that the fruit must be inferred, that is true—it must be inferred—but the fruit of those [oblations] is the consecration of the fire.
Heaven is not [the result];
for if heaven were assumed [to be the result], two unseen forces (adṛṣṭa) would have to be postulated: that heaven arises from the oblation, and [that it arises] from the sacrifice.
Furthermore, there is another unseen refinement (*adṛṣṭa-saṃskāra*) of that [fire] by means of the *āhavanīya* fire. Therefore, the *pavamāna* oblations have the fire as their purpose;

they have no connection with the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires). Consequently, what is heard in the context of the *ādhāna* cannot pertain to the *pavamāna* oblations. Rather, their application is in all sacrifices, beginning with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, which constitute the primary acts following the *ādhāna*.
juhvati} And because there is no connection with a purpose, [the action] is mutual. MS_3,1.23.
In connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "The two Vārtraghni verses are recited at the Full Moon sacrifice; the two Vṛdhanvatī verses at the New Moon sacrifice.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the duality of the invitatory verses (anuvākyā) apply to the primary sacrifice?
Or rather, [is it] "of the two ājyabhāga offerings"? What, then, is the prima facie view?
That it is [the time of] the principal [offering]. Why? Because of its mention in conjunction with the full moon sacrifice (paurṇamāsī).

And because of the mention together with the *amāvāsyā*. The principal [offerings] of the *paurṇamāsī* and the *amāvāsyā* do not have [their own] *ājyabhāga* offerings. Therefore, it follows from the direct statement that [the *ājyabhāgas*] belong to the principal [offerings].
To this we reply: there is no function for the principal [offerings] with respect to the two *anuvākyā* verses used together;
rather, where there are two *anuvākyā* verses, [they belong to the principal offerings].
In that context, the *vārtraghna* and *vṛdhanvat* qualities of those two [verses] are prescribed;

however, since there is only one invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the primary sacrifice, a sentence prescribing both duality, the *vārtraghna* quality, and the *vṛdhanvat* quality would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). As for the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, two verses are already established: one addressed to Agni and one to Soma.

In that case, one will be able to prescribe the *vārtraghna* and *vṛdhanvat* qualities exclusively. But surely, even if they pertain to the primary sacrifices, there would be two invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) for the two primary sacrifices—namely, for the offering to Agni and for the offering to Agni-Soma. It is replied: one *vārtraghna* verse pertains to Agni.
One [verse] belongs to Soma,
likewise one to Vṛdhanvat; therein, one belongs to Agni.
If it were being enjoined, it would be connected [with that sacrifice], but not with the Soma sacrifice. First of all, it does not exist at all on the new moon day;

even on the full moon day, it would have to be performed only when the Agniṣomīya is being performed, and even there, having only one deity, it would be unable to perform its function when there are two deities. [If you argue: "But both [sacrifices] are obtained in the Agniṣomīya," [we reply: no.

There is a need for two invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) for a single sacrifice. Since the invitatory verse is enjoined as something to be taken up (*upādeya*), its singularity is intended to be significant;
therefore, there should not be two in that case either. Consequently, they must find their place in the two *ājyabhāga* offerings.
There is no injunction regarding immediate retribution.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard: "He closes his fists, restrains his speech, and announces the initiated one."

Likewise, [the texts state]: "He washes his hands" and "He spreads a layer of *ulapa* grass. In this regard, there is a doubt: are the clenching of the fists and the restraint of speech for the purpose of the announcement (*āvedana*), or do they find their place within the entire context? So it is.
Is the non-trembling of the hands for the purpose of strewing the grass-bundle (ulaparāji), or for performing all the ritual acts within the context? What, then, is the prima facie view?
The non-trembling of the hands is for the purpose of purifying the hands.
Restraint of speech is for the purpose of purifying the person;
one who restrains his speech becomes single-minded,
and he carries out the ritual acts.
Because of this, there arises an expectation as to which specific entities these *saṃskāras* belong to;

and since that expectation exists, it is satisfied immediately by what follows. Therefore, due to this immediate sequence, the purpose of the vow of silence and the clenching of the fists is for the sake of making known [the intention].
"The two hands are motionless" and "to spread the *colaparāji* grass.
When this situation arises, we say: there is a connection with everything studied within the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Why? Because of the split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). How is there a split in the sentence?
Because two distinct meanings are expressed.

For [the word] "āvedayati" does not mean "to announce" in the sense of "having initiated [the sacrificer]," nor does "stṛṇāti" mean "to spread" in the sense of "having announced. Both the spreading and the washing are enjoined; likewise, the clenching of the fists and the restraint of speech are enjoined.
And there is the communication [of them]. Yet, there is no mutual connection whatsoever among these,
nor—
When there is a requirement for a word's meaning, immediate sequence becomes the cause for syntactic unity;
therefore, such types of rules are indeed *prakaraṇa-dharma*s (contextual rules).
And because these [two] sentences are complete in themselves. (MS 3.1.25)
Each complete sentence— whether it be one, another, or all those that have been cited— is fulfilled by its own respective collection of words. Therefore, the two meanings are clearly distinct.
Furthermore, there is no expectancy regarding the division [of the ritual],

and thus there is a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, because there is no distinction in the connection and no distinction in the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is established that [the rule] applies to the entire context.
