In connection with the New and Full Moon sacrifices, it is recited in the scripture: "One divides the cake dedicated to Agni (āgneya) into four parts. Regarding this, there is a doubt: does this fourfold division apply everywhere—in the offering to Agni alone, in the offering to Agni-Soma (agnīṣomīya), and in the offering to Indra-Agni (aindrāgna)—or does it apply to the offering to Agni alone? What is the prima facie view?
The remaining portion is the fourfold division;
since the term "belonging to Agni" (āgneyam) is understood as common to all [portions] by virtue of its connection with the deity as a qualifying attribute,
it would apply to the portion for Agni-Soma as well.
It applies even in the case of the offering to Indra-Agni. Why?
Because those two [deities] are also associated with Agni;
that which has Agni as its deity is [connected to] Agni.
And there is another [mother], who is the mother of both Ḍittha and Ḍavittha; that is the one who is to be praised (āgeya). For example, she who is the mother of Ḍittha and Ḍavittha.
That [rule] applies to the *ḍavittha* tree;

so it is here as well. If there were no mutual connection between the *puroḍāśa* dedicated to Agni and the one dedicated to Agni-Soma, then the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*) would be restricted to the *puroḍāśa* dedicated to Agni alone.
But there is indeed a connection;
therefore, there is no fixed restriction,
just as in the case of the rule "having divided the head of the Agneya [cake], he cuts off the Prāśitra," where the Prāśitra is taken from all [the cakes].
The same applies to the division into four parts as well.
(Note:
Or rather, because of the connection with the purpose, the mention of a quality is for the sake of definition, due to the relationship of the indicative mark (liṅga) with that purpose. (MS 3.1.27)
The word "vā" (or) sets aside the alternative view; rather, the division into four parts must apply to the cake dedicated to Agni alone, as it cannot be common to both. Why?
Because of the connection with the purpose:
there is a connection with the deity Agni through the purpose of the single-deity offering, but not with the two-deity offerings such as the Agnīṣomīya or the Aindrāgna.
And thus [it is said]. Why? For he whose deities are Agni and Soma performs a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) qualified by both attributes;
for him, Agni is a deity only insofar as it stands in relation to Soma.
It is not independent;
and since Agni, while depending on Soma, is the deity, the secondary derivative suffix (taddhita) is not produced from that [Agni].

For that [compound] is said to belong to those [words] that are semantically independent (*samartha*), whereas that which is dependent is not independent. Therefore, it is not [formed] with a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix, such as "having Agni as its deity" (*agnidaivata*), which is dependent.
Consequently, where Agni is the deity independently, [the compound is formed].

Regarding the statement "the division into four parts occurs in that very case": for the connection with the deity-indicative suffix occurs through semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) on the part of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), and not when such competency is absent.
Now, as for what was said— that just as the taking of the *prāśitra* portion is performed from all [the portions], so too is the fourfold division—
It is appropriate that the connection [of the *prāśitra*] with the act of giving is made right there, as in:
"He cuts off the *prāśitra* of the offering to Agni. How then [is it to be understood]?
Regarding the statement "having divided the head of the offering to Agni": there is one sentence, "he cuts off the *prāśitra*," and a second, "having divided the head of the offering to Agni";
from these, it is understood that he cuts [the *prāśitra*] from the head of the offering to Agni.
There is no fixed rule as to whether it is from the head of one person or from another; for if that [offering] had not been dedicated solely to the deity Agni, [it would have been otherwise].
In that case, to avoid the charge of meaninglessness, even a deity-pair (*dvidaivatya*) would have been accepted.
As for the expression "the mother of Ḍittha,"...
In that case, motherhood is appropriately applied as non-distracted [to her], since Ḍittha was born from her;
by this much alone is there a connection.
She is called "mother," and nothing else is required here. Since that much of a relationship exists there, the expression "the mother of Ḍittha" is appropriate.

[The rule applies] to that which has a single deity by virtue of the meaning of the deity [itself]; [to that which has] two deities, such as the one dedicated to Agni-Soma or the one dedicated to Indra-Agni;
[and to that which is performed] independently of the deity Agni.

If it were to be taken as having two deities, [the mantra] would have the status of a subordinate element (*śeṣabhāva*) in the mantras due to its capacity to express that meaning; therefore, there is a connection with the original [deity] because of the eternal association with the meaning. (MS 3.2.1)

In this regard, the mantras are the examples—such as "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods," and so forth. Is the application of mantras restricted solely to the primary denotation (*mukhya*), or does it extend to the secondary (*gauṇa*) as well? What, then, is the primary and what is the secondary? It is said: that meaning which is understood from the word itself is the first, the primary meaning.

It is called "primary" (*mukhya*) because it is like the face (*mukha*). That which, however, is understood from a primary meaning through some connection, because it occurs subsequently, is like the buttocks (*jaghana*); thus it is "secondary" (*jaghanya*), and it is also called "figurative" (*gauṇa*) due to its connection with qualities (*guṇa*).
If this is so, then everything is primary,
for everything is understood from the word;
for just as when it is said, "The fire burns," there is a cognition of the burning itself.

In the same way, when the word "Agni-māṇavaka" (the boy Agni) is uttered, there is a cognition of the boy. Now, if it is argued that that object for which a cognition arises from a word used without an accompanying term (*nirupapada*) is primary (*mukhya*), whereas that for which it arises from a word with an accompanying term (*sopapada*) is secondary (*gauṇa*), this is not correct. For the form of a word is the cause (*nimitta*) for the cognition of some particular object.

That same form applies both when it has a prefix (*upapada*) and when it lacks one. Furthermore, it is impossible for the effect (*naimittika*) not to exist when its cause (*nimitta*) is present. What follows from this?
If this is so, then it cannot be said that "that meaning does not exist without the prefix."

But when the *upapada* has arisen, that meaning will arise; yet this collective meaning cannot be understood. For the distinction [between word-meanings] is apprehended through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Now, if it is said that this is the meaning of the sentence (*vākya-artha*), this is not possible, for a word-meaning does not exist if it is not syntactically connected.

This is the meaning of the sentence. Let it be seen thus: this word "fire" (agni) alone denotes the flame, and this word "fire" alone designates the young boy. Therefore, there is no distinction such that one is primary and the other secondary. Now, if it is argued that that which is well-established [in common usage] is primary, then...
"That which is only slight is figurative"— this also is not tenable,
for "notoriety" (prasiddhi) is indeed cognition (prajñāna),
and there is no distinction whatsoever within cognition. Now, it might be argued:
"That which has frequent usage is primary (*mukhya*), while that which is used rarely is secondary (*gauṇa*). This is not so;
even when used rarely, a word cannot convey meaning if it lacks the capacity (*sāmarthya*) to do so. Therefore, since it is understood from the word even in such cases, it is indeed primary.
To this it is replied: there is a distinction here;
the boy is not understood from the word "fire. How is this known? It has been stated: "It is improper for a single word to have multiple meanings. Why, then, is the reverse not the case?

It is said: People are observed to understand "flame" from the word "fire" while disregarding the boy; however, they do not understand the boy from the word "fire" while disregarding the flame. Why is this so?
Because whatever is intended to be expressed as similar to fire [is understood].

In each case, the word "fire" (agni) is fixed [to its primary object]. For this very reason, because the similarity has departed, this [boy] is seen [as secondary]. Therefore, similarity to fire is the cause for the application of this [word] to him; and that similarity is not perceived unless the blazing [fire] is first perceived. Consequently, the word "fire" has the blazing [element] as its cause, not the boy. Therefore, it is primary with respect to the blazing [fire], not with respect to the boy. In exactly the same way, the word "barhis" has the grass-blade as its cause.

Not [the application] of a word whose cause is like that of grass. Thus, since duality exists, it is appropriate to investigate whether the word’s referent is primary (*mukhya*) or whether it also has a secondary (*gauṇa*) referent. What, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That there is application (*viniyoga*) to both the primary and the secondary. Why?
Since both are possible, both can be conveyed by the word *barhis*:
namely, actual grass and that which resembles grass;
[the former] being the grass directly.
It is similar to grass by virtue of being grass. And whatever can indeed be indicated by the word *barhis*, which serves as a means for the New and Full Moon sacrifices— all that must be indicated,
because there is no reason for a restrictive selection.

Moreover, if this were accepted, the mantras for Pūṣan and others would not be displaced from the New and Full Moon sacrifices; they would simply denote the deities of those very sacrifices through figurative expression.
This being the case, we reply: the mantra must be applied according to its primary sense, not its figurative one. Why?
Because both [options] are impossible;

for, since it is recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*), it enters into syntactic unity with the principal act. In that case, this follows: "Whatever one is able to accomplish by means of this mantra, one should accomplish it in that manner. And that [mantra], through its connection with the expression of meaning, is capable of providing assistance.
A secondary meaning cannot be expressed [directly];
therefore, there is no application [of a word] to a secondary sense.
But surely, a secondary sense can be conveyed through the cognition of the primary sense. This is true.

Since its purposeful utility is fulfilled solely through the primary signification (*mukhya-pratyāyana*), there is no evidence whatsoever for its application (*viniyoga*) toward a secondary sense (*gauṇa*). Indeed, by means of application to the primary sense, its lack of purpose is avoided; once the lack of purpose has been avoided, the expression of a secondary sense does not follow. For a word does not express a secondary sense without first expressing the primary one. Therefore, due to the absence of evidence, it should not be applied to a secondary sense.
Moreover, because of the capacity for conveying a secondary (gauṇa) meaning, many means of realization are obtained;
and it has been stated that this capacity resides in a single part of the word—namely, "or [the meaning is understood] from the sense, because it is a part of the conceptual construction" (3.1.132).
In that regard, when a mantra is necessarily employed with reference to a secondary meaning, there exists another means [of realization].

It would be sublated in the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is argued that the traditional recitation of the mantra (*mantrāmnāna*) is the means of valid cognition, we say no; for that [recitation] lacks the capacity to exclude other means. [Objection: But surely this same defect applies even when [the mantra] is employed in its primary sense. [Response: No, it is said—in reply—that if it were not employed even in the primary sense, [then the defect would indeed apply].

What, then, is the prima facie position?
Whatever belongs to Indra-Agni, Vaiśvānara, Agni-Soma, and Jātavedas—in all those cases, these should be the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. Why?
Because of their indicative mark (*liṅga*). But surely, sequence (*krama*) and name (*samākhyāna*) will serve as the specific determinants. True.

"Nevertheless, indicative power (liṅga) is able to override both order (krama) and name (samākhyā). This being the position reached, we reply: on account of indicative power, order, and name, it is understood that these *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses belong to those very optional sacrifices (*kāmyā*);
for whatever is the order of these rites, that same is the order of these *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses.
Therefore, those [mantras] are indeed the remainders of those [rites].
Now, it was stated that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is more powerful; this is true, but in this case, the name (*samākhyā*) is more powerful.
For these [verses] do not attain the status of being *ṛc* for these optional (*kāmya*) rites merely by virtue of their name;
nor do they belong to rites performed in different locations. Why?
Because without the name, their very status as *yājyā-anuvākyā* verses would not even be recognized.
How could there be *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for rituals performed in different locations?

Furthermore, this designation (*samākhyā*) indicates that these are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses specifically for the optional (*kāmya*) rites, not for all of them. If the designation were disregarded, [the rule would be inapplicable].
These [mantras] do not even possess the status of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* [invocatory and offering verses] unless they are so intended;
in that case, they belong exclusively to the optional (*kāmya*) rites. For it is thus designated: "The Section on Optional *Yājyā* and *Anuvākyā* Verses" (*Kāmyayājyānuvākyākāṇḍa*).

Now, for what purpose are both [criteria] taught— namely, "from the mark and the order" and "from the designation"? In that context, there exists the ritual belonging to Pāthikṛt and the ritual belonging to Vrātapati, and there is also the function of the *sāmidhenī* verses.

The function of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses must also be taken into account. If only "by means of indicative power (*liṅga*) and order (*krama*)" were stated, then those verses might be applied to the function of the *sāmidhenī* verses by virtue of their indicative power. Now, for what purpose are both indicative power and order mentioned?

All [the verses] would be employed solely for the function of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*, and there would be no application among the *sāmidhenī* verses. However, if, on the other hand, the function of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* is already fulfilled by virtue of their designation (*samākhyāna*) and their indicative power and sequence (*liṅgakrama*), then their application among the *sāmidhenī* verses becomes established.
Just as when the sequence of the Agnivāruṇī sacrifice has passed and the Saumāraudrī sacrifices have not yet arrived,
the verses of Manu are called *dhāyyās* among the *sāmidhenīs*,
so too are two *dhāyyās* prescribed for Pṛthuyājas, namely "tam saṃbādhaḥ. Therefore, both [the general category and the specific instance] must be designated.
And when there is a general heading (adhikāra), the injunction of a mantra applies even to those [rites] not designated by that [heading], because it has been taught [as such]. (MS 3.2.20)
In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard: "With a verse addressed to Agni, [one approaches] the Āgnīdhra; with one addressed to Indra, the Sadas; with one addressed to Viṣṇu, the Havirdhāna."

175* Thus it is said. In this regard, there is a doubt: should the worship be performed with verses from the present context that possess such indicative marks (*liṅga*), or should verses with such marks be brought in from the *Daśatayī* collection? What, then, is the initial position? When a mantra is enjoined in a specific context by virtue of its indicative mark, it should be brought in from the *Daśatayī* collection itself.

For it is possible to refer to the *Dāśataya* [Ṛgvedic hymns] by means of such expressions as "the Āgneyī" and so forth. And this [hymn] which is under discussion has already been employed for another purpose;
it does not deserve to be taught here as well. Indeed, the teaching of what has already been taught is not at all logical in such a case. Of what kind [of thing] would that be?
Whatever has been taught in reference to a specific [instance] does not deserve to be taught elsewhere by means of a general mark. Why?
If that mark were intended as its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), [then it would apply].
Then that [agent] would be distinguished by the mark by which one could say, "He performs this because he possesses such a mark";
thus, [the agent] would not be taught. But if it is taught that "he performs it by means of such a mark," [then the agent is indeed taught].
Therefore, it is not perceived;

thus, a further instruction of the same kind for that which has already been instructed in such a manner is not logical. Consequently, the mantras possessing the indicative marks (*liṅga*) from the *Daśataya* collection are to be taken.
[Objection: But surely, by the force of the context (*prakaraṇa*), those belonging to the present ritual (*prakṛta*) are logically to be taken. [Reply: No, it is said.
For indicative power (liṅga) is stronger than context (prakaraṇa). He says:
"In the event of a conflict, context would be sublated by indicative power;
however, there is no conflict between these two."

We do not intend to subvert the indicative power (*liṅga*) by adopting the context (*prakaraṇa*) while desiring to favor it, provided that the context refers to that which possesses the indicative mark. However, if we were to adopt a context that lacks the indicative mark, then we would indeed subvert the indicative power. We shall fulfill both: the context and the indicative power. But this is not so.

The conviction arises from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that it must be performed even with the *dāśataya* verses; for the *dāśataya* verses can also be designated by the term "āgneyī" (verses addressed to Agni).
That cognition which is produced by a sign (*liṅga*) and is conceived as false is so [conceived] in accordance with the context (*prakaraṇa*). If it conforms to the context,
it is conceived as false.

If it is argued that [the mantra] does not properly conform [to the deity], then there is a contradiction; and when there is a contradiction, the context (prakaraṇa) is weakened. It is replied: "That [deity] possessing those indicative marks (liṅga) must be assisted by this act of attendance."
The term "dāśatayī" does not refer to the individual manifestation of a mantra;
rather, when that [term] is employed in the present context, it refers to the mantra in its entirety.

However, if the term "dāśatayī" were employed to refer to the individual manifestation of a mantra, then whichever specific mantra manifestation is obtained from the context would be the one so obtained.
That [injunction] would be sublated only if there were a contradiction; however,
in this case, there is no contradiction between the indicative mark (liṅga) and the context (prakaraṇa).
From the context, the individual is understood;
from the indicative mark, the universal [is understood], and the individual is something else.
The other [alternative] is the general [application]. Therefore, that which possesses the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is what should be adopted in the present context. It is replied:
this is indeed true; when the subject matter of the context (*prakaraṇa*) is adopted, the context is not sublated, and the indicative mark is also favored.

However, a certain cognition produced by a *liṅga* (inferential mark) is conceived as being false. [Objection: But the individual (*vyakti*) is not the object denoted by the word; how then could the cognition be sublated when the individual is not being apprehended?
It is said: this very point is not [the case]. [260] {3/179}

We do not know whether the possession of gender marks (*liṅgavattā*) is a factor here or not. However, this is an injunction for benefit (*hitanirdeśa*); therein, the deity is indicated by the mantra, for it is the specific manifestation of the mantra that is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

There is no such thing as a "universal" (sāmānya) distinct from the deity itself; rather, it is the deity alone that must be characterized here as the universal. Furthermore, no distinction is perceived such that "this is this mantra" and "that is not this."

Since no distinction is perceived, all those [mantras] possessing that characteristic mark should be accepted; thus, there would be a conviction regarding the *mantra* forms even within the *Daśataya* collection, and it would be improper for that conviction to be sublated merely by conformity to the context (*prakaraṇa*). This being the case, it is not the case that only those from the *Daśataya* are to be employed.

They might even adopt what is under discussion [in another context]. But has it not been said that when something under discussion is taught for the sake of another effect, it will not be taught for some other purpose? It is replied:
it is not necessarily the case that the very same thing must function for another purpose.

That [word] and the other [word] are [connected] by means of a general indicative mark (*liṅga*). This being so, nothing is faulty. But is it not the case that this is faulty—namely, that neither the indicative mark nor the context (*prakaraṇa*) is supported? True, they are not supported; however, the context simply cannot be supported because it is contradicted by the cognition arising from the indicative mark. Furthermore, it is not the case that both the indicative mark and the context must be supported.
Activity occurs toward that which has been determined, namely, when it is understood: "This is fruitful. One engages in that [activity]. What follows from this being so?
This follows from it:

Since the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not favored anywhere else, once that [other] has been excluded, activity [toward it] cannot occur. Therefore, it is understood that the *dāśataya* [Ṛgveda] must be taken.
*Notes:
{3/173: E2,4,6: āgnīdhram}*
*upādadīmahi* (E2,4);
*upādademahi* (E6, E4 v.l. *kathaṃ* (omitted in E2,4)
Or rather, it is designated by that [name] because of both the context and logical consistency, just as in the case of a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). (MS 3.2.21)
That which is designated by that name—namely, what is known as the Jyotiṣṭoma—is precisely what must be understood [here]. Why?
Because of both the context and logical consistency.
For this [mantra] is the subject under discussion, and it is logical that the suffix refers to what is under discussion. How so?
Because it is not tenable to enjoin the operation of the mantra with respect to the Jyotiṣṭoma.

Precisely because it has already been obtained. However, the prescription of a specific function is appropriate, since that specific function has not yet been obtained; furthermore, if it were prescribed in the *Daśataya* (the ten books of the Ṛgveda) independently of the context, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), as one would have to say: "And he should perform the attendance (*upasthāna*)," and "And that [attendance] should be done by means of this [verse] according to its indicative mark (*liṅga*)."
NOTES:
*{3/182: E1 gives jyotiṣṭomasamākhyātaḥ in parentheses}* The instruction would be purposeless because of the lack of connection with that which possesses a fruit.
For attendance is not fruitful.

But would it not rather assist the Jyotiṣṭoma by virtue of the context? If the connection between the *upasthāna* (approaching) and the Jyotiṣṭoma were intended, then the *upasthāna* would be taught as belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma, and through the context, it would form a single syntactical unit with it. However, when the connection of the *upasthāna* with the mantra is intended to apply to all instances of *upasthāna*, [the mantra does not belong to the Jyotiṣṭoma].
In that case, the mantra would apply by setting aside the context (*prakaraṇa*). Context cannot serve as a specifier;
for if it were connected to both, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). In our position, however, this fault does not arise.

By whichever [mantra]—whether pertaining to Agni or Indra—a specific function is performed within the Jyotiṣṭoma, by that very [mantra] a specific function of standing near (upasthāna) is enjoined as belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma; all else is merely restated (anūdyate), and thus no fault arises. Alternatively, [one may argue as follows:]
Only the connection with the *dhānasad* is enjoined; the word "he worships" (*upatiṣṭhate*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*),
[meaning] that by means of this mantra one [worships] the *agnīdhra*.
"Upatiṣṭhate" means "he approaches. Therefore, mantras of this kind belonging to the context should be employed.
(NOTES:
*{3/184: E2,4,6: āgnīdhrahavir}*)
And because [the Agnīdhra] is prescribed for all [of them], the *agnīdhra* [is the place for the sacrificer]. (MS 3.2.23)
As for what was said—that "those [verses] under discussion have been taught as being for another purpose"—to that it is replied:

this has already been answered. Moreover, they are not untaught by anyone at all; rather, when the *vācastoma* is being recited in the *āśvina-śastra*, while the sun is still not yet risen, [they are indeed taught].
Therefore, there is no distinction in the present context. Consequently, only that which is under discussion is to be understood.
*{3/186: E2: Moreover, these alone have been taught as such;}
E4: Moreover, it is not only these [indications] that have been taught;
rather, by means of both inferential mark (*liṅga*) and designation (*samākhyāna*), the section [of the Veda] has the purpose of being for consumption (*bhakṣa*).
The mantra for consuming [the Soma] is heard: "Enter me indeed for long life, for health, for the increase of wealth, for luster, and for good progeny.
Come, O Vasu, O Purovasu; you are dear to my heart. With the arms of the Aśvins, may I hold you fast.
You, O divine Soma, who look upon men, may I, with clear sight, behold you. Impel my limbs, O Lord of Bay Horses; do not let my vital powers thirst."
Be auspicious to me; attend upon the seven seers. Do not descend below my navel. O Speech, the delightful, the overcomer, the banner of sacrifices—may you, being pleased, be satisfied with the Soma!

[O Speech] belonging to the host of Vasus, the host of Rudras, and the host of Ādityas; O divine Speech, knower of the mind, of the morning pressing, the midday pressing, and the third pressing; of the *gāyatrī* metre, the *triṣṭubh* metre, and the *jagatī* metre; [be satisfied by] the oblation offered to Agni.
"Of that which was drunk by Indra, drunk by Narāśaṃsa, drunk by the Pitṛs, the honeyed, the invited—I, being invited, partake," and so forth.
In this regard, there is a doubt: should this entire section (anuvāka) be applied to the act of consuming, or is some portion of it to be used elsewhere as well?
What is established? That the entire section (anuvāka) is for the purpose of eating, based on both indicative mark (liṅga) and name (samākhyā);
the whole section is to be applied to the act of eating. Why?

The word "I eat" (bhakṣayāmi) is clearly to be employed in the sense of eating; it is capable of expressing eating and nothing else. And its other words are indeed expressions qualifying that act of eating.
"Wherever [I] eat," they are employed in each of those places.
But is it not the case that the formula beginning with "Come, O Vasu" and ending with "to be accomplished" is for the purpose of taking up [the vessel]?

By its own collection of words, which are mutually expectant, it forms a single meaning distinct from the sentence concerning eating. The passage beginning with *nṛcakṣasam* and ending with *avakhyeṣam* is a statement regarding looking. And the passage beginning with *hinva me gātrā harivaḥ* and ending with *mā me vāṅ nābhimatigāḥ* is for the purpose of proper digestion. Because of the multiplicity of these meanings, [the mantra is used].

There are many sentences. How can it be said that all this constitutes a single sentence employed for the purpose of eating? It is replied: it has already been stated that all these are qualifiers of the specific act of eating. He says: even so, the sentence would be split, because it is impossible to express the qualifiers and the qualified simultaneously. It is replied: we do not intend to express the qualifiers as independent [entities].
A single object qualified by qualifiers such as "grasping" and "observing" is intended to be expressed. This is not correct,
because it would follow that the words expressing the qualifiers do not intend to express their own meanings,
and that they are instead subordinate to the qualifier of "eating."
However, it is understood through indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And when there is a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and indication, direct statement is the proper course, not indication;
therefore, they do not constitute a single sentence.
To this it is replied: although many meanings such as seizing and so forth are understood here, not all of them are intended;
rather, only eating is what must be communicated. For that alone is what is directly stated in the scriptural text (*śruta*).
The qualifiers have not been heard;
there is no purpose served by those [qualifiers] being understood,
for the purpose belongs to the entire collection of words as a single unit.

Thus, it constitutes a single sentence. Therefore, since this is a single sentence for the purpose of a specific consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*), it must be employed in that act of consumption. Furthermore, there is a traditional designation (*samākhyā*): "the *Bhakṣānuvāka*" (the recitation of the consumption formula);
and this refers to the entire recitation, not merely a part of it.
Now, one might object: "But the traditional designation is a worldly term; how can it restrict a Vedic subsidiary element? Even though it is a worldly term, [it serves as a guide].
Nevertheless, its connection with the *anuvāka* is beginningless. What follows from this being so?
This follows: it refers to the *anuvāka* as being mentioned in conjunction with the act of eating.
And co-utterance occurs only when there is a relationship;

as in the case of "the cooker" and "the reaper," we shall infer a relationship from their co-utterance. [The opponent] says: In matters of this kind, the status of being an auxiliary is not to be understood through inference alone, but is understood precisely from the injunction itself.
Not otherwise;

nor does a name (samākhyā) constitute an injunction. To this it is replied: the name will bring the two related entities into proximity within the mind, and the injunctive statement of performance (prayogavacana) will then enjoin them. Therefore, the entire section (anuvāka) is to be applied to the act of consuming.
NOTES:
There is a reduction [of the penance] for him through the instruction regarding his form, because the purpose has already been enjoined.

This is not so; the entire section (*anuvāka*) is not enjoined for the act of consuming. On the basis of its form, the sentence beginning with "Come" (*ehi*) and ending with "with Soma" (*sadhyāsam*) would be enjoined for the act of taking up (*grahaṇa*). And the passage beginning with "the one who watches over men" (*nṛcakṣasam*) and ending with "I have beheld" (*avakhyeṣam*) would be enjoined for the act of looking. Why?
Because in this way, that sentence retains its primary meaning.
Otherwise, there would be a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇārthatā*); and it is more logical that [the words] have a primary sense (*mukhyārthatā*) rather than a figurative sense.
It is said: regarding the denotation of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇānām abhidhāne*),...
It has been stated that there is no purpose [for these qualifiers]. To this it is replied: these are not merely qualifiers;
rather, these acts such as "grasping" (grahaṇa) and so forth are expressed as distinct entities by their respective sentences. Why?
Because there is indeed a purpose served by them.
For those [factors] have indeed been enjoined;
some by separate sentences, and some as implied by the sense.
These must necessarily be made manifest; these sentences will make them manifest. Their form possesses the capacity for that manifestation;

therefore, because they have different meanings, it is said that they do not constitute a single sentence. [Objection: But does their form not also serve as a supplement to the sentence concerning eating? [Reply: It is said: Certainly, the form exists, but these are not construed as qualifiers of that [eating]. For what reason would they become such [qualifiers] if they were for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*)?
Whether by the qualities mentioned or those not mentioned, the meaning remains exactly the same;

otherwise, [the mention of] seizing and so forth would be for the purpose of illumination, and thus they would have a visible purpose. Therefore, there would be a displacement of some [of these functions] from the description of form.
On account of the mention of qualities, there should be a single mantra beginning with the *mandra* [pitch], because those two are connected to a single purpose.

In the *Bhakṣānuvāka*, it is heard: "The delightful, overpowering banner of sacrifices, Vāk, the impeller—may she be satisfied with the Soma. O divine Soma, possessing the quality of wealth, knower of the mind, belonging to the morning pressing, having the Gāyatrī metre, offered into the fire, drunk by Indra, full of sweetness, being invited, I, being invited, partake."

In this regard, there is a doubt: is the mantra beginning with *mandra* and ending with *tṛpyatu* one mantra, while that beginning with *vasumadgaṇa* is another; or rather, is the mantra beginning with *mandra* and ending with *bhakṣayāmi* a single mantra? What, then, is the prima facie view?
There are two mantras,
for these two purposes are distinct: satisfaction is one thing, and consumption is another.

Therefore, because there is a difference in meaning, there is a difference in the sentence. As it has been said: "There is a displacement of that [meaning] due to the instruction of its form, because the purpose has already been enjoined.
This being the case, we reply: because of the mention of qualities, the mantra beginning with *mandra* should be a single mantra;
for satisfaction (*tṛpti*) is mentioned as a qualification of the act of eating.
"I shall eat; speech will be satisfied. But surely "let it be satisfied" is one word, and "it will be satisfied" is another?
This [suffix] occurs when a future action functions as an *upapada* (a subordinate word);
in that case, there is a connection between two actions, such as "I shall eat, [and thereby] my voice will be satisfied. But here, in the case of "I eat;

let [the voice] be satisfied," there is no such connection. It is replied: Indeed, this is not understood as an injunction (*vidhi*) in the sense of "let it be satisfied. Where, then, is it understood?

Whether it be in the sense of a request (*prārthanā*) or in the sense of the time being appropriate (*prāptakāla*), the connection is made either as "if I eat, then speech will be satisfied," or as "if I eat, the time has arrived for speech to be satisfied. Thus, because of the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) within a single purpose, syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) is established, and the oneness of the mantra is justified. [Objection: But these two sentences are independent; by breaking their form, they are rendered dependent. To this it is replied: even though these are two sentences...

Even if two meanings were expressed that are distinct in sense and independent of one another, nevertheless, since the visible purpose is the manifestation of the act of eating and not the act of satiating, they would indeed constitute a single purpose. How much more so, then, when it is understood that here one functions as a subordinate element (*guṇabhāva*)? Therefore, because it denotes subordinate qualities, the mantra beginning with "mandra" should be considered a single mantra.
NOTES:
Because of the specification of gender, those [oblations] not dedicated to Indra lack the status of being accompanied by mantras, even when the ritual procedures are identical. (MS 3.2.27)

This very mantra serves as the illustration: here, there exist offerings belonging both to Indra and not to Indra, and there are also corresponding consumptions (bhakṣaṇa) for them. In this regard, a doubt arises: is the mantra used for both those belonging to Indra and those not belonging to Indra, or is the mantra used only for those belonging to Indra?
"The consumption of those [portions] not dedicated to Indra is without a mantra. What, then, is the prima facie position?
That the consumption of those not dedicated to Indra is without a mantra. Why?
Because these offerings are governed by the same injunction.

In these cases, the mantra "of that which was drunk by Indra" (indrasya pītasya) is unable to denote what has not been drunk by Indra; nor is modification (ūha) possible within the same context, because in the absence of an explicit injunction, it cannot express a different meaning. Therefore, in such instances, the consumption is to be performed without a mantra.
Or rather, it is according to the deity; for it shows that this is its original form.
Alternatively, it should be indicated by modification (*ūha*) according to the respective deity. Why?
Because the *dhruva*-cups are the archetypal forms (*prakṛti*). Which, then, are the *dhruva*-cups?
Those which belong to the commencement of the pressings (*savanamukhīya*) during the performance of the *śukra* and *manthin* cups.
They belong to Indra;
of these, one is the archetype (prakṛti) offering, while the others are modifications (vikṛti). How is this understood?
For it demonstrates that this is its original nature. How so?
Because it says, "In the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* [cup] at the *atirātra* [sacrifice], one modifies the consumption mantra by [specifying] 'of the *anuṣṭubh* metre'. What is the demonstration here?
The word "modifies" (*namati*) demonstrates a transformation (*vipariṇāma*).
Surely this might be the statement. No, it is said in reply;
for it is not heard that "it bows down. How then is it "thus it bows down"?
It is because [the text] says, "with the *anuṣṭubh* metre," meaning that it bows down the *bhakṣa*-mantra.
This very modification (ūha) is applicable to the modifications (vikāra);

therefore, these are modifications, and consequently, even in the case of those [offerings] not dedicated to Indra, the mantra obtained through the rule of extension (codaka) must be modified. It is replied: "These are modifications"—this is the indicative mark (liṅga) that has been pointed out.

"Let the logical principle (nyāya) be stated. It is said: "The Soma for Indra is both drawn and measured; therefore, while Soma exists in the offerings for Indra, Soma itself does not exist in those not for Indra. Consequently, all the properties of Soma apply only to the offerings for Indra, while the others are without such properties and remain expectant [of them]. But how is it known that 'the Soma for Indra is both drawn and measured'?"
From the wording of the mantra: the mantra beginning with "For Indra, thee, accompanied by the Vasus" is capable of denoting Soma for Indra, and not any other. Therefore, the Soma belongs to Indra;
consequently, the properties of Soma pertain to those [vessels] dedicated to Indra.
But other offerings are expectant; therefore, it is the logical rule that they will receive their respective deities. Consequently, the mantra must be modified according to the deity.
Thus far, the argument remains established but not yet concluded.
Therefore, this being the case, another consideration will follow:
"Furthermore, when all [the cups] have been drawn again, there is an indication for all [of them], because they are characterized by two [qualities]. (MS 3.2.29)
Furthermore, there are Soma portions that have been drawn up— those belonging to the opening of the pressing (savanamukhīya) during the performance of the Śukra and Manthin cups.

After having offered from them four times with the goblets of the central officiants at the Hotṛ’s *vaṣaṭ* and *anuvaṣaṭ* calls, and having offered once each time at the *vaṣaṭ* call with the goblets of the Hotrakas,
Soma is again drawn up into those very vessels while they still contain remnants.
For thus the Adhvaryu gives the direction there:
"O Camasādhvaryus of the central performers, offer at the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*;
O Camasādhvaryus of the Hotrakas, having offered once, replenish with the *śukra* cup and return. There, the Hotrakas sacrifice to various deities.
The Maitrāvaruṇa [recites] for Mitra and Varuṇa: "We invoke Mitra... (RV 1.23.4);
the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin [recites] for Indra.
"O Indra, we [choose] you, the bull," [says] the Potṛ;
"the Maruts, for whose dwelling... [says] the Mārta.
The Neṣṭṛ [invokes] Tvaṣṭṛ and the wives [of the gods] with [the verse],
"O Agni, bring the wives here";
the Āgnīdhra [invokes] Agni with [the verse], "For the bull-food, for the cow-food..."
203*. In that regard, with those cups, Indra was worshipped at the first *vaṣaṭ*-call;
then, having been refilled, Mitra, Varuṇa, and the other deities were worshipped.

Thus, the remnant belongs both to Indra and to Mitra, Varuṇa, and the others. In this matter, there is a doubt: should there be a mention (*upalakṣaṇa*) of both the deity to whom the cup was originally dedicated, namely Indra, and of Mitra, Varuṇa, and the others?
"Furthermore, Indra is not to be indicated.
What, then, is the prima facie position? That in the case of the cups being filled again, there should be an indication for all [deities]. Why?
Because there is a remainder of two; for in each cup there is a remainder of two, whereas in the archetype it was offered to a single deity.

It has been stated that "that [cup] is the remnant" and "he has drunk from it. Here too, it must be stated in exactly the same way. Therefore, in each and every cup (*camasa*), there is the observation of two [deities].
*Ṛgveda 3.40.1a* *Ṛgveda 1.86.1a* *Ṛgveda 1.22.9a*
Or rather, there is no perception of the preceding [moment] due to its removal.

We consider the remnant of the deity to whom [the offering] was presented to have been consumed. Why? Because that which remains in the vessel is addressed for the sake of Mitra, Varuṇa, and the others. How is this so?
It is said: for Mitra, Varuṇa, and the others are indeed the ones being worshipped.
For example, when Devadatta is eating the remains of his teacher's meal, if he gives the remainder to Pūrṇaka, Pūrṇaka observes Devadatta and thinks, "He is eating the remains of Devadatta's meal."
It is not a remnant of the Ācārya; therefore, Indra, as the deity of the *prasthita* offering, is not to be indicated [as the deity].
Or rather, because of the taking [of the cup], there would be a removal.
And this is not the case, that Indra is not to be indicated;

for he too is directly perceived as a subordinate element (śeṣa) of that [action]. [Objection: "But has he not been removed? [Reply: It is said—He is not removed. He draws from the *droṇakalaśa* the cups (*camasa*) that have already been offered once.

The cup with its residue is the mark of another [cup] being filled. Therefore, that which is in the cup must be offered, whether it has been prompted by a call (*preṣita*) or not. As for the statement, "the *āśrāvayitṛ* [responds] toward the deities who are about to be sacrificed to," it is said in reply: there, the announcement (*āśrāvyate*) is made to the deities, but not specifying "this one" or "that one. By that...
That which is taken up for the purpose of offering is understood to be "that which has been announced" (*āśrāvita*). Furthermore, at the time of the announcement, there is no connection with a deity;
rather, whatever is connected with a deity [is what is meant].
That is what is being proclaimed;
therefore, there is a remnant for Indra, and it is also indicated.
Hence, it is an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of all [the deities]. This is a hypothetical deliberation (*kṛtvācintā*).
No further purpose need be stated here;
this very purpose is determined to be that of the preceding section itself.
Because there is no grasping;
because there is neither increase nor decrease;
and it is not so.
But for the Pātnīvata [offering], it is as before. MS 3.2.32.
There is the Pātnīvata draught;
for it is said, "One draws the Pātnīvata from the Āgrayaṇa vessel using the Upāṃśu cup," and the remnants of the dual-deity offerings have been poured into the Āgrayaṇa jar.
Then the Pātnīvata cup is drawn.

Now, when the Pātnīvata has been offered and its remnant is being consumed, a doubt arises: should Indra, Vāyu, and the others be mentioned [as deities], or not? What, then, is the prima facie view? They should be mentioned; for this remnant belongs to them just as it does to the deity for whom the offering was originally set forth.
Or rather, it would be removed by means of its apprehension.
For that remnant is removed here,
not as it was previously;
for in that case, it is mentioned by way of being a characteristic of the vessel, and not Soma as something to be taken up.

But here, in the statement "he draws from the Āgrayaṇa," it is the Soma residing in the vessel that is indicated for the purpose of offering to the deity who is about to be worshipped. [Objection: Is it not the case that the Āgrayaṇa is not [identical to] the vessel?

And furthermore, in that context, that which is drawn from that *āgrayaṇa* vessel is the *pātnīvata* cup, whereas that which is drawn from the *saṃpāta* residue is not the *pātnīvata*. It is replied: the *āgrayaṇa* is the source (*apādāna*).
Therefore, whatever has departed from the Āgrayaṇa— whether it be the Āgrayaṇa itself or not— all that belongs to the Pātnīvata;
and all of this has departed from the Āgrayaṇa.
[270] But surely it has also departed from the *āgrayaṇa*. This is not a fault;
for it has indeed departed from the *āgrayaṇa*, and therefore it cannot be said that it was drunk by the previous deities. For that portion of the Soma which was intended for Indra—

In the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is stated that "the remainder is that which was drunk by Indra. Here too, in the same manner, a portion belonging to the previous deity must be designated. But surely this is a portion of that very thing which belonged to the previous deity? We say: no.
For no part of what has been offered is seen. [Objection: But even in the archetype sacrifice (*prakṛti*), no part of what has been offered is seen. [Reply: It is said:

in that case, a part of the aggregate consisting of both the offered and the unoffered belonging to that deity is perceived. [Objection: But here too, it was the aggregate itself that belonged to that deity;
this is merely a part of that very thing. [Reply: No, it is said.
This collection formerly had that deity as its presiding deity;
now, one of its parts has come to have another deity, whereby the collection has departed from having that deity as its presiding deity.

He says: "This [cup] was a part of that which was drunk by the deity Indra; therefore, by way of its former state (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*), it shall be so designated. It is replied: "In the original archetype (*prakṛti*), the designation was not made by way of its former state;

here too, it should not be done in that same manner. Moreover, in that case, it was called 'Indra-drunk' because it had Indra as its deity, and that status of having Indra as its deity has not been removed."
Furthermore, his connection with the previous deity has ceased; therefore, the previous deity is not to be indicated here.
(Note: *'nāgrayaṇaś*)
One should not [regard] the Āgrayaṇa [cup] as [belonging to] Tvaṣṭṛ, because of the drinking.
There is the Soma for the Pātnīvata; regarding it, there is this mantra:
"O Agni Pātnīvata, together with the god Tvaṣṭṛ, drink the Soma."

213*. In this regard, there is a doubt: should Tvaṣṭṛ be mentioned as a secondary characteristic (upalakṣayitavya) or not? What is the prima facie position? He should be mentioned. Why? Because of the drinking; for the drinking is heard in the text: "In harmony with the god Tvaṣṭṛ... [271] {3/...}

"Drink the Soma," it is said. From this, it is understood that this [offering] is given to Agni Patnīvān together with Tvaṣṭṛ. And for whomsoever and with whomsoever it is given, it is given to both; in this way, it becomes a joint offering (*sahadāna*).

Just as when it is said, "Let a hundred be given to Devadatta together with Yajñadatta," it is given to both of them; therefore, since this Soma belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ as well, Tvaṣṭṛ must be indicated [as a recipient]. He too drinks, just like Indra.
"But because they are not equal, it cannot be thus. (MS 3.2.35) *{3/213: Tait.S. 1.4.27.1}* *{3/215: E2,4: eva*}
This is not so;
we take scripture as our authority,
and whatever scripture says, that is it.
Therefore, this is our authoritative position:
the word states that Agni Patnīvān has the drink, while Tvaṣṭṛ’s presence merely as an accompaniment is mentioned;
for since accompaniment cannot be established if [the act] is not being performed, the drinking is inferred to belong to Tvaṣṭṛ. But is it not the case that the drinking is enjoined for Tvaṣṭṛ? True.
It is enjoined by the wording of the mantra,
not by a direct injunction (*codanā*). For the injunction is "He takes the *pātnīvata* [cup]," whereas in the world, even that which is not enjoined is performed upon seeing a practical purpose.
This is indeed so; moreover, this is determined by worldly convention,
and not by a statement such as "the Soma has been made for Tvaṣṭṛ."
NOTES:
*{3/216: E2,4, E1 (v.l.): even that which is unenjoined is performed when enjoined}* And thirty [subsidiary acts] are for the sake of another. (MS 3.2.36)

Regarding that very *pātnīvata* offering, there is a mantra: "O Agni, come hither with these on one chariot, or on various chariots, for thy horses are powerful; bring the thirty-three gods who have wives, according to thy wonted way, and rejoice! In this regard, there is a doubt: [does it refer to] the thirty-three...?
Should the gods be mentioned as a secondary reference (*upalakṣaṇa*), or not? What is the prima facie view? One should mention the thirty-three gods. How so?

For the Soma is indeed offered to the thirty-three gods. Thus the Agnīdh priest urges Agni: "Come hither from the direction of Agni, having mounted the same chariot with the thirty-three gods," or rather, they may mount various chariots, for they possess such power.

"Those are the horses. Therefore, bring hither according to their wont; cause the thirty-three gods accompanied by their wives to come, and satisfy them. For it is understood from this that the Āgnīdhra priest directs Agni toward the satisfaction of the thirty-three gods, since this mantra is the primary one in this context.
Soma is superior to that; therefore it is said: "The thirty-three gods are to be understood.
[Objection: But in the injunction, Agni alone, as the *patnīvān*, is heard of as the deity. [Reply:
True, in the injunction, the *patnīvān* is indeed heard of as the deity.

But another deity is not being excluded. What follows from this being so? This follows: the thirty-three deities mentioned in the words of the mantra are understood as not being in contradiction with the injunction.
This being the case, we reply: the thirty-three gods are not to be understood [as the ones to be worshipped].

For in this mantra, Agni is not requested to be the invoker, the server, or the satiator. Nor is any purpose accomplished here by worshipping the thirty-three gods. Who, then, is to be worshipped? He who is accompanied by his wife (*patnīvat*). Why is this so?

For he is enjoined thus: "He takes the Pātnīvata cup. But is it not the case that there is here a mention of the thirty-three deities based on the wording of the mantra? It is said in reply: they are mentioned for the sake of another; for that [cup] does not belong to Agni until it has been offered.
Furthermore, giving away what belongs to another is not logically possible. Therefore, the statement "give these to the thirty-three deities" is inconsistent;
rather, by this [statement], the giving is declared to be for Agni alone. How so?
For it is Īśāna who causes the substance to linger.
Thus, by proclaiming this "delaying," he makes it known that you are its lord (*īśāna*).
Now, it might be objected: "It is said, 'rejoice' (*mādayasva*), not 'delay' (*vilaṃbhaya*). To this it is replied: for the deities do not become intoxicated.
Therefore, the mention of intoxication would be for the sake of an unseen result (adṛṣṭa),
whereas the mention of renunciation would be for a seen purpose through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā);
for figurative indication is superior to the postulation of an unseen result.

For that [designation] arises from authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Now, it might be argued that even when the act of addressing (*adhyeṣaṇā*) is being indicated, Agni is intended to be the agent. To this it is replied: the addressing of Agni is also solely for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*);

therefore, it is logical that this sentence indicates the exercise of sovereignty (*aiśvaryakaraṇa*) by Agni. Furthermore, Soma is enjoined in relation to the Pātnīvata sacrifice: "He takes the Pātnīvata. Now, was it not said that the injunction prohibits what is based on the wording of a mantra (*māntravarṇika*)? It is replied: it has already been stated that even such a basis in the wording of a mantra does not exist here. Moreover, it is understood that the prohibition is effected through the inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the words.

For the word *patnīvat* is not dependent [on another term] in such a way that it is perceived as having the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*); therefore, the deity is simply *patnīvat*. And the mantra must be interpreted in accordance with this injunction. Therefore, the mantra is to be explained exactly as we have explained it.
"It ought to be exactly so," [he says],

for Agni accompanied by his wives is designated in grammatical apposition as "O Agni, accompanied by your wives" (*agne patnīvan*). Therefore, it is Agni who is to be characterized, not the thirty-three deities.
And the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is like the agent.
There is a deity of the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*, for it is said:
"O Agni, accept the Soma," and thus he performs the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*.
In this regard, there is a doubt: should the deity of the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* be mentioned or not? What is the prima facie view?

Regarding the phrase "it is to be indicated," no purpose for another (*pārārthya*) is perceived therein as before; therefore, it is said that "it is to be indicated. This being the position reached, we reply: the deity of the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* is not to be indicated, just like the agent.
Just as the agent is not perceived— as in the case of "drunk by the Hotṛ"—
so too is the deity of the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*. For she was not perceived in the archetype (*prakṛti*), and whatever is performed in the archetype [does not apply here].
Therefore, this must be done here: for that reason, it should not be observed.
But there is a prohibition of desire because it leads everywhere.
To this, the following reply is stated: This is not so; that which was said—that the consumption should be performed with a mantra through modification—is incorrect.
The consumption should be performed without a mantra. Why?
It is said: because the procedure is identical, there is no relationship of archetype and ectype here. Why?
Because the context is the same.
Regarding the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) that has been stated,
it is said to be a prohibition of the *chandas* (meter);

for while the rule "because it belongs to the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), it has the *jagatī* meter" would have applied, [the text] modifies the *bhakṣa*-mantra at the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice to read "having the *anuṣṭubh* meter."
Even when the rule is the same, it is understood [that there is a single sacrifice]. As for what was said— "The Soma for Indra is drawn and measured"—
these are not distinct sacrifices, some belonging to Indra and others not.
These are specific instances of practice belonging to a single [sacrifice], and they are not properties of the specific appearances because they are qualities;
all these are properties of the sacrifice. Therefore, the entire set of Soma-ritual properties is enjoined for the sacrifice.
And as for "Soma too," and [the statement] "Indra is both taken up and measured":
since Indra is mentioned in the mantra, the taking up must be manifested by means of that mantra.

For the other deities, however, it is by means of meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth. Therefore, for those [deities] who do not have Indra as their deity, the consumption [of the soma] is without a mantra.
But in the case of the offering to Indra and Agni, it should apply because of the presence of the indicative mark (liṅga). [MS 3.2.39]
This being the case, it is considered: there is a Soma offering for Indra and Agni, according to the injunction "he draws the cup for Indra and Agni.
In this regard, a doubt arises: is the consumption accompanied by a mantra?
"Or it may be without a mantra. What is the conclusion?
There should be a mantra for the offering to Indra-Agni;
for he whose deities are Indra and Agni does not have Indra alone.
For it is possible to designate that [soma] as "drunk by Indra" (indrapīta),
since that whose other parts have been drunk by Indra is "drunk by Indra."
While Indra and Agni are drinking, another portion of it is drunk by Indra alone; therefore, the consumption [of the soma] is accompanied by a mantra.
(Note:
Or [the distinction] is like that between one deity and another deity. (MS 3.2.40)
Neither is another part of it drunk by Indra, nor does it become "drunk" by means of another part that has been drunk by Indra;
therefore, this term "drunk by Indra" (aindra) is a word used figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*). It refers to that which is intended for Indra, such that Indra is its deity.

And just as that which is expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) has no connection with the sense of "beneficial" (*hitārtha*), so too a compound such as *indrapītasya* ("drunk by Indra") is not possible for that which is expectant;
as it has been said: "Or rather, there is a fixed determination because of the connection with the meaning. (Pāṇini 2.1.49)
He says: "Is this not already settled by that very same discussion?
For what purpose is it considered again? It is replied: That which was investigated there is indeed established. But how is it investigated here? [The answer is:
"There is no connection with a deity for that which has a further expectancy"—this is the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position, namely, that here there is no connection with a deity at all.
"In this case, there is a connection with the mere act of drinking";
the subsequent position is that where two [persons] drink by means of a connection with the mere act of drinking, there the connection with the deity belongs to only one.
Therefore, it is not a repetition. [276] {3/230} NOTES:
And the meter is like the deity. (MS 3.2.41)

In this mantra, it is stated "gāyatrachandasaḥ" (of the Gāyatrī metre); regarding this, there is a doubt: does the mantra apply to Soma when it is of a single metre, or even when it is of various metres?
It is said: Just as with the deity, so too with the meter;

just as a mantra [addressed] to Indra accompanied by another [deity] would not [be considered valid], so too a mantra would not apply to a *soma* sacrifice involving multiple meters. For here, too, a compound consisting of the term "gāyatrī-meter" together with its qualifier is not possible.
NOTES: *{3/231: Tait.S.
3.2.5.2}* Or rather, [the rule applies] to all [verses], because there is no [restriction to] a single metre. // MS_3,2.42 //
Or rather, the mantra should apply to all [the Soma vessels]. Why? Because of the absence of any single-metered [Soma];
for there is no Soma at all that possesses a single meter.
Therefore, this *chandas* is a qualification according to its true nature; consequently, the mantra should belong to that *soma* which possesses multiple *chandas*.

According to Aitiśāyana, there is a single mantra for all [the priests] as they are in their true state, because [the mantra] is a drink of devotion; for it is indeed the qualification for the *savana* (pressing).
As for what was stated— that those [soma cups] not belonging to Indra are to be consumed without a mantra— that is not so; rather, all are to be consumed with a mantra.
And the mantra should be exactly as it has been handed down. It is not the *soma* that is called "drunk by Indra" (*indrapīta*); what then?

It is the *savana* (pressing), because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the term "morning pressing" (*prātaḥsavana*). But is there not also a genitive case [ending] in relation to the *soma*? True, the genitive exists, but there is no coreferentiality with that. It is not the case that this *soma* was drunk by Indra.
Nor was it given to Indra;
rather, it was something entirely different that was drunk or given, and that has already passed away. Furthermore, a past collection is not designated [as existing]. [277] {3/}

For this word is indeed used in its direct sense. However, there is no fault regarding the *savana* (pressing), because the *savana* becomes "drunk by Indra" (*indrapīta*) when it has been drunk by Indra.

Therefore, even that which is not for Indra (*anaindra*) is included within the *apīta-savana* (the pressing where [Soma] has not been drunk [by Indra]), and thus it can be designated by means of the mantra.

If it is possible [to apply it] when the rule is identical, why indeed would the mantra not occur? For even by figurative usage (*bhakti*), that which has not been drunk is called "drunk. It was the teacher Āitiśāyana who held this view; this is our opinion as well. The mention of the teacher is for the purpose of honoring him, implying that [the rule] has come from him.
NOTES:
On account of the Vedic revelation, there should be eligibility for one who has been born. MS 3.3.1.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard: "The Ṛc is recited loudly, the Sāman loudly, and the Yajus in a low voice."

In this regard, there is a doubt: do these words function with reference to the classes (*jāti*) such as the *Ṛk* and so forth, or do they function with reference to the Veda? What, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? They should have the class as their referent. Why?
From the scripture: we understand the *jāti* (class/type) from the mere hearing of these words;

therefore, the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) is connected with that which is governed by the *jāti*, since there is no word that governs the Vedas as a whole. Furthermore, for those *ṛks* that have transcended the *Ṛgveda*, their recitation in the *Yajurveda* will be performed loudly (*uccaiḥ*).

Otherwise, both properties would be optional alternatives belonging to that very same ṛc, and in that case, there would be a sublation in one alternative. Furthermore, the context (prakaraṇa) would thus be upheld;
otherwise, if there were a connection with the Veda, the quality of being whispered (upāṃśutva) would apply to the entire sacrifice. Therefore, these words have the genus (jāti) as their scope.
NOTES: *{3/234: Mait.S.
3.6.5}* "Or rather, it is the Veda [that is meant], because of the observation of its general application. (MS 3.3.2)
This is said with reference to the Veda. Why?
Because of the observation of the majority. What is this "observation of the majority"?
In a passage that consists mostly of the Veda and begins with the Veda, these words are heard as they are being concluded: "Prajāpati alone was this [universe] in the beginning."
He performed austerity;
from that austerity, through its heat, three deities were created: Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya.

They performed austerity; from their austerity, through its heat, the three Vedas were created: the Ṛgveda from Agni, the Yajurveda from Vāyu, and the Sāmaveda from Āditya—having begun thus, [the text concludes] with this summary:
It is heard in scripture: "The *ṛc* is performed loudly, the *sāman* loudly, and the *yajus* in a low voice. For this reason, these aforementioned acts must be performed in a low voice and so forth.
It is not said that [the Vedas] are produced by birth, such as the *Ṛg* and so forth. How is this understood?
Because it is heard in the conclusion of the passage:
"From whence these Vedas were born."

Therefore, since [the acts] such as the *upāṃśu* must be performed by these [means], there must also be a conclusion by means of the Vedic utterances themselves, such as the *ṛc*s and so forth. Otherwise, the sentence itself would not be possible;
in that case, they would be entirely meaningless.
Therefore, they have the right to the Vedas.
[This is established] also from an indicative mark (liṅga). MS 3.3.3.
There is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this meaning, namely that words such as *ṛc* and so forth are capable of denoting the Veda:

"By the *ṛc*s the god moves in the sky at dawn; by the Yajurveda he stands in the middle of the day; by the Sāmaveda he is magnified at sunset; with the three Vedas, never lacking, the Sun moves. (RV 10.90.5)
Having mentioned the two Vedas and the word *ṛk* in three quarters [of the verse],
he concludes in the fourth quarter with a plural form.

The phrase "the sun moves with the three Vedas not empty" (*vedair aśūnyas tribhir eti sūryaḥ*) demonstrates that the word *veda* refers to the [three] Vedas. Therefore, we also see that these words have the Vedas as their subject matter.
*Note: {3/236: Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.12.9.1}*
And because of the instruction regarding the dharma, there is indeed no connection with a substance.
Furthermore, there is the instruction regarding the *sāman* that it is "loudly" (*uccaiḥ sāmnā*);

this is appropriate under the view that the qualification belongs to the Veda. However, if the qualification belonged to the [specific] birth-class (*jāti*), then the loudness of the *sāman* would already be established by the loudness of the *ṛc*.
Its connection with the substance of the Sāman is not to be understood;
therefore, too, [the study of] the Vedas is the qualification. And the designation "knower of the threefold knowledge" applies to one who knows that. (MS 3.3.5)
He whose knowledge is the threefold [Veda] is a *trayīvidya*; he who studies the three Vedas is known by this very title.

The term *trayī* is well-known as a designation for the *Ṛg*, *Sāman*, and *Yajus* [Vedas]; if the three Vedas are called the *Ṛk*, *Sāman*, and *Yajus*, then the name "knower of the *trayī*" (*trayīvid*) is appropriately applied to one who knows them.
And it is so. Therefore, these [passages] pertain to the Vedas.
E4 (Fn.): it is declared}*
If it is argued that, in the case of a transgression, one should act according to what has been heard [in the scriptures]. // MS 3.3.6 //
Now, as for what was said— that even for those *ṛc*s that have transcended the *Ṛgveda*, there will be loudness (*uccais-tva*) in the *Yajurveda* as well—
and regarding the statement that in my view the performance will be according to the literal text (*yathāśruta*), that must be refuted. This concludes the *sūtra* with the introductory address.
NOTES:
*{3/239: E2 has enclosed the sūtra ending with ābhāṣāntam within brackets}* Because it is not included in everything. (MS 3.3.7)
This is not a fault; for there is loudness throughout the entire Ṛgveda and low-voiced recitation throughout the entire Yajurveda.
Therefore, if a verse that has transgressed into the Ṛgveda occurs within the Yajurveda, it would indeed have the quality of being recited in a low voice.
This is not faulty. For while it might be that the Veda is the *dharma* and the *Ṛgveda* is the *dharma*,
the Veda does not have a connection with two distinct *dharmas*.
NOTES:
sa na} It would not be sublated by the context because of its connection with the Veda. (MS 3.3.8)

As for what was said—that the context (*prakaraṇa*) would thus be favored—there will be no fault when the context is set aside by the sentence (*vākya*) due to its connection with the Veda. [The sūtra states: "In the conflict between the subordinate and the principal, because it exists for the sake of that, the connection with the Veda belongs to the principal. (MS 3.3.9)
There is the ritual of establishing the sacred fires, [expressed by] "He who, knowing thus, establishes the fire";
that belongs to the Yajurveda.
In that regard, they prescribe the singing of the Sāmans: "He who, knowing thus, sings the Vāravantīya;
he who, knowing thus, sings the Yajñāyajñīya; he who, knowing thus, sings the Vāmadevya."
Thus it is said. Regarding this, there is a doubt: at the *ādhāna* (the fire-consecration), is the *sāman*-chanting to be performed loudly (*uccais*), or in a low voice (*upāṃśu*)?
It follows that it should be "loudly. Why?
"That which is performed with the *vāravantīya* and other [chants] is done by means of the Sāmaveda;
therefore, these Sāmans should be chanted loudly.
This being the position reached, we reply: one may set aside the primary [element] in deference to the subordinate [quality].
Or rather, "in accordance with the primary," meaning that it is proper for the subordinate to be set aside so that the primary may be favored. Why?
Because the quality is for the sake of the primary,
one engages with the quality thinking, "How might the primary become possessed of its quality through the performance of that quality?
If, however, by the engagement with the quality, the primary suffers a loss of its own quality, [then it is not to be performed].

When a subordinate element (*guṇa*) proceeds toward its activity, the result itself is not yet attained. Now, if one thinks, "I shall make the principal element (*pradhāna*) possessed of a subordinate," and while engaging the subordinate, causes a further subordinate of that subordinate to fall away, his own purpose is not lost. He does not engage in order to make the subordinate itself possessed of a subordinate; for the subordinate is the singing of the *sāman*.
The fire-laying (*ādhāna*) is the primary act,
because it belongs to the Yajurveda;
its quality is that it must be performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
He subverts the loud chanting of the *gaṇadharma* belonging to the Sāmaveda; therefore, the *sāmans* should be sung in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
Because it belongs to the Yajurveda, [the ritual] is Sāmavedic; however, due to the predominance of both, there is scriptural authority for both. (MS 3.3.10)

In the Yajurveda, they recite the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. Likewise, there is this very same recitation in the Sāmaveda as well. And when the cognition has already been produced once, a second hearing occurs for the sake of a subordinate element (*guṇa*). In this regard, there is a doubt: is the Yājurvedic recitation intended for the performance of the action, [or for something else]?

"Is it for the sake of a quality (*guṇa*), or is it the opposite? Whichever recensional text (*āmnāna*) has the purpose of [prescribing] an action, its properties (*dharma*) will belong to that. What, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)?
It is that there is no certainty as to whether it belongs to the Yajurveda or not, because no specific distinction is perceived.
This being the case, we reply: it should be determined by the preponderance of qualities; wherever more qualities are recorded, there the purpose of the action [is to be understood].
It is understood as "injunction" (*codanā*). For where there is an injunction regarding what ought to be done, there a requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) arises;
and where there is a requirement for the procedure, [there is an injunction].
In that case, the statement regarding the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is logical. And those numerous qualities, together with the procedure— that is,
by means of the mark of the procedure, there is the injunction for what is to be done.
We infer as follows: just as when many who resemble kings are seated together, he whose umbrella and fly-whisk are white is understood to be the king.

Even though it is not explicitly stated by means of the marks of a king, in this way, by means of the mark of what ought to be performed and because of the abundance of qualities, an injunction for the Jyotiṣṭoma belonging to the Yajurveda is inferred. Therefore, the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma is in a low voice (*upāṃśu*),
for the Jyotiṣṭoma is indeed performed by means of the Yajurveda.
That which is enjoined by it cannot be performed if it is not so enjoined.
(Note:
This pertains to the Yajurvedic tradition.)
*{3/248: E2,4: pertaining to the Sāmaveda}* *{3/249:
E2,4: pertaining to the Sāmaveda}* *{3/250: E2,4: pertaining to the Yajurveda}*
*{3/252: E2: For the sake of action}* *{3/253: E2: Because of the injunction regarding what is to be done}* *{3/254: E2,4: Of that which belongs to the Yajurveda}*
It is not connected [with the general injunction] because of the context, since there is a requirement for the procedure (itikartavyatā). (MS 3.3.11)

The causes for application (*viniyoga*) have been stated: direct statement (*śruti*), indicative power (*liṅga*), and syntactical connection (*vākya*). Direct statement is the accusative case-ending, as in "with the *aindrī* [verse], [one worships] the *gārhapatya* fire. Indicative power is the capacity of the words in mantras, as in "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods."
[The statement] "one purchases [the Soma] with a ruddy [cow]" is an example of syntactical connection (*vākya*).
Now, are these the only grounds for application (*viniyoga*)?
It is said: no. With the question, "What other ground is there?", the discussion begins.
And there is even an introduction by means of a question, such as:
"What is the name of this river? or "What is the name of this mountain slope?"
"What is this result?
To this it is said: It is not connected [with the primary action] because of the context, and because there is a requirement for a procedure (itikartavyatā).
That which is not connected by direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), or syntactical connection (*vākya*) is [connected] by context (*prakaraṇa*),

because of the requirement for a procedure (*itikartavyatā*). That verbal expression which, occurring in proximity to that which requires a procedure, falls [upon it] as being capable of fulfilling that requirement— [that is what is connected by context].
It forms a single syntactical unit with that which is under discussion (*prakṛta*).
Therefore, it is applied to what is under discussion. What is the example here?
And what is the purpose? With reference to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is heard in scripture: "He offers the *samidh* oblations."
He sacrifices to Tanūnapāt,
he sacrifices to the Iḍās, he sacrifices to Barhis.
One performs the *svāhākāra* offering;
by the force of the context (*prakaraṇa*), these [mantras] are applied to that very [rite],
not to the *agnihotra* or the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
And the sequence [of mantras] is determined by the commonality of location. (MS 3.3.12)
Now, are these the only grounds for application (*viniyoga*)? No, it is said. What more?
There is also "order" (*krama*) due to similarity of position (*deśasāmānya*), [referring to] those things that are taught in a sequence according to their successive order.
In whatever context they teach a particular teaching, an expectancy toward it is inferred;
when that expectancy exists, there is the state of being a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*).
"Therefore, its application follows from that. What is the example here?
And what is the purpose?

When the mantras for the consecrations (*anumantraṇa*) of the sacrifices (*yāga*) arranged in a specific sequence have been recited, [the mantra] "Thou art the unscathed one by name" (*dabdhir nāmāsi*) occurs in the order of the *upāṃśuyāja*.
Having been thus recited, it generates an expectancy and, by attaining syntactical unity with that [other passage], deserves to be applied to that very context;
and so, there exists for one who possesses an enemy a rite dedicated to Indra and Agni belonging to the same class as the sacrifice.
For that [offering], a pair of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses dedicated to Indra and Agni is also handed down:
one beginning "O Indra and Agni, from the luminous realm of heaven... (*indrāgnī rocanā divaḥ*), and another beginning "O Indra and Agni, the ninety forts... (*indrāgnī navatim puraḥ*).
Regarding the phrase "ślathad vṛtram":
once the general application has been established through indicative mark (*liṅga*), a specific application follows;
namely, that the first pair [of verses] belongs to the first [offering] dedicated to Indra and Agni.
"Of the north, the north"—
this is both the example and the purpose.
