And the name is likewise [denotative] because it has that as its object. (MS 3.3.13)
Now, are these the only grounds for application (*viniyoga*)? No, it is said. And what else?
There would also be *samākhyā* (designation). How is it a ground for application? *Samākhyā* occurs when there is a relationship, as in the cases of "cook" or "reaper."
In that case, having perceived the word "cook" (pācaka), it is understood that it has a connection with the act of cooking;

so it is also in the case of the Veda. Having perceived a word that expresses a connection with an uncreated object, there arises conviction regarding that connection. What is the example and what is the purpose here?
The duties designated as *ādhvaryava* are to be performed by the *adhvaryu*,
and those designated as *hautra* by the *hotṛ*. This is both the illustrative example and the purpose [of the discussion].
The connection of that which has not yet performed its function [is established by these means];

when there is a conflict among direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical unity (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*), each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding because of the remoteness of the meaning. (MS 3.3.14)
The causes for application have been stated—
namely, direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyāna*).
Now it is considered which among these is stronger when they come into conflict.

Because words function toward a single purpose and cannot be connected simultaneously to two different things, there is a deliberation between each pair. In that regard, between *śruti* (direct statement) and *liṅga* (indicative power), which is stronger—is it *śruti* or *liṅga*?
What, then, is the illustrative example here? "One worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī verse."

In this regard, it is considered: is there no fixed rule as to whether the worship of Indra or of the Gārhapatya fire is to be performed, or is it the Gārhapatya alone? If these two reasons possess equal force, then there is an option;
however, if the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is more powerful—
The Gārhapatya fire alone is to be worshipped.
What, then, is the scriptural authority (śruti) here? What is the indicative mark (liṅga)?
Direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is the hearing of the word "gārhapatya"; as for the indicative mark (*liṅga*), it is:
"And when, O Indra, are you not a giver, nor do you fail the donor?"
Thus is the capacity of the word *indra* to denote a specific deity. Now, what is a sentence (*vākya*)?
A sentence consists of words that express a meaning by acting in concert. If this is so, then this too is a sentence: "With the *aindrī* [verse], one worships the *gārhapatya* fire," and this too:
"Never art thou barren... (*kadā cana starīr asi*).

In both cases, the words express their meaning by acting in combination. Therefore, this deliberation concerns the sentence as a whole and the individual word, not the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Or rather, if one were to distinguish between *śruti*, *liṅga*, and *vākya*:
"This is the distinction between direct statement (*śruti*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*);
this is the distinction between indicative mark (*liṅga*) and syntactical connection.
To that it is replied: first, as for the capacity of a word to denote its own meaning...
That indicative mark (liṅga) by which the denotation of a meaning is understood from the mere hearing of the word is understood through direct assertion (śruti).

"Śravaṇa" means "hearing. It has already been stated that a sentence consists of one or more words having a single meaning. This [definition] is seen to be both inherent in and distinct from all sentences. In this case, for instance, it is understood from the mantra "kadā cana starīr asi" (*RV 8.51.7*) that Indra is to be worshipped.

This is not understood merely from hearing this particular word; nor does any other word uttered in its proximity possess the capacity by which this could be understood. Indeed, in this *ṛc*, the word "Indra" exists, which is capable of making known a specific deity.

And there is a purpose for that [word] being understood. Therefore, the word "Indra" is employed in the act of worshiping Indra, and the remaining words [of the verse] form a single syntactical unit with it; however, in this *ṛc*, the worshiping of the Gārhapatya fire does not occur through the semantic power (*sāmarthya*) of any word therein. Rather, it occurs solely from the direct hearing (*śravaṇa*) of the word "Gārhapatya."
We understand Agni from the direct statement, not from the indicative mark. However, if the indicative mark were stronger, Indra would be the one to be approached;
if, on the other hand, there is the explicit mention of the Gārhapatya fire, [then that is the case].
Then there is the Gārhapatya fire.

In that case, it is the conflict between indicative mark (liṅga) and syntactical connection (vākya) that must be deliberated here, not the conflict between direct statement (śruti) and indicative mark;
for, due to the capacity of the word "Indra" to denote a specific deity, the worship of Indra [would follow].

If the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is more powerful, then the Gārhapatya fire is to be worshipped; for this sentence—"one worships the Gārhapatya with the Aindrī verse"—is indeed a sentence. This is not so, because although this is a sentence, there is also direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) here.
But the scriptural passage (śruti) that occurs here is contradicted by the indicative mark (liṅga), not the syntactical connection (vākya). How so?
For even though the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is stronger,
the statement "he worships with the Aindrī [verse]" enters into syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the word "Gārhapatya"; for if it did not so enter, [the injunction would be meaningless].

Consequently, it contradicts the indicative power (*liṅga*). That meaning which is understood solely from the direct statement (*śruti*) regarding the *gārhapatya* fire is set aside when the indicative power is more powerful. It is not connected with the act of worship; for in that case, the word *gārhapatya* would either denote Indra or the vicinity of the fire. Now, however, if the direct statement is the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), [then the indicative power must yield].

Consequently, the worship of Indra understood through the indicative power (*liṅga*) would be sublated. Therefore, this contradiction lies between direct assertion (*śruti*) and indicative power (*liṅga*), not between indicative power and syntactical connection (*vākya*). Alternatively, it is not because of syntactical unity that the worship has Indra as its primary object or Gārhapatya as its primary object. Why then?
Because the mantra contains the word "Indra."

There is the predominance of Indra, because of the hearing of the accusative case-ending; there is the predominance of the Gārhapatya fire, because of the hearing of the accusative case-ending. Therefore, there is a conflict between the direct statement (*śruti*) and the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
What, then, is the prima facie position?
"These two causes are of equal strength. How so? This is a cause, and this too is a cause.
Scripture also [confirms this], as does the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
For no distinction whatsoever is perceived between one consciousness and another with respect to form;
the form of this [consciousness] is just like that of something fragile.

"Of this [knowledge] which is as if firm. Now, an objection is raised: "The nature of an inferential sign (*liṅga*) is indeed fragile; for the cognition arising from an inferential sign is accompanied by doubt, whereas that arising from sacred scripture (*śruti*) is free from doubt. This is not tenable."
Since the cognition arising from a mark (liṅga) is accompanied by doubt,
there can be no definitive comparison between that and scriptural testimony (śruti); however, as for the cognition that is free from doubt, it arises from a mark.

He ought to deliberate by means of the *śruti*. But is it not the case that there is never a cognition free from doubt arising from an indicative mark (*liṅga*)? This is not so; for if this were the case, the indicative mark would not be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) at all. Granted, let it not be a means of valid knowledge; however, a doubt does arise regarding objects fully cognized through an indicative mark. Or rather, there is indeed a clear lack of validity, not merely a doubt. How so?

"It is capable of accomplishing this purpose"—only this much is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*). And that which is capable of accomplishing something does not deserve to accomplish it in the absence of an explicit statement. Therefore, the indicative mark is not the means of application (*viniyojaka*).
To this, it is replied: when there is proximity to a matter possessing a context (*prakaraṇa*), they enjoin a certain purpose.

It is understood that this [word] serves as its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). When there is doubt as to how exactly it will provide assistance, the definitive conclusion arises through functional capacity (*sāmarthya*): "Insofar as this is capable, it can be employed therein.

Therefore, indicative mark (*liṅga*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, there is no reason for deciding between them regarding the validity of the indicative mark. Consequently, these two causes possess equal force.
On account of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the mantra "Never art thou barren," Indra is to be worshipped;

on account of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), however, it is the Gārhapatya fire. Indeed, because there is no contradiction, we understand this very meaning. For even a stronger reason is capable of subverting a weaker one only when they are in conflict, not when they are not in conflict.
And there is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that one might worship Indra with this mantra and the Gārhapatya fire as well.

Is this not indeed a contradiction—that what is enjoined as a single presentation is performed repeatedly? This is not a contradiction; rather, it is simply the established principle that "subordinate elements (guṇas) are repeated for each principal element (pradhāna) according to the distinction of those to be presented. Then what is the contradiction? It is this: when the Gārhapatya fire is being presented, the word "Indra," which denotes Agni...

It must exist by depending either on a quality (*guṇa*) or on the application of an action (*kriyāyoga*). However, when Indra is to be approached, there is no dependence on anything other than the word "Indra" itself; and between the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*), the understanding rests upon the primary. We say: "No," for the secondary would be sublated by the primary only in case of a contradiction, and here there is no contradiction whatsoever.

For if they were to denote [the deity] simultaneously, they would contradict one another; here in one application it expresses Agni, while in another it expresses Indra. Therefore, these two grounds are of equal strength. This being the case, we reply: between direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), the direct statement is stronger. Why? Because of remoteness of meaning (*arthaviprakarṣāt*). What is this "remoteness of meaning"?
The remoteness of the meaning is "arthaviprakarṣa. What, then, is the meaning?
It is the meaning of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). "He worships the Gārhapatya fire" is the proximate meaning of the scriptural statement;
"Indra is to be worshipped" is the remote meaning. How so?

It is not heard in scripture that Indra is to be attended upon with this mantra, "Never art thou barren. Even though there is the capacity for the mantra to denote Indra, because of the absence of an explicit injunction, it is understood that Indra is not to be attended upon.
But was it not said: "From its recitation within the context, it is understood to be an auxiliary (aṅga)"?
"Application [of a mantra] occurs through capacity"—this is not so.

For it has already been stated: "Because Dharma has its root in the Word (śabda), that which lacks the Word should be disregarded. Both this context (prakaraṇa) and the indicative mark (liṅga) are indeed the Word. And in a matter characterized in this way, which lies beyond the scope of direct perception (pratyakṣa), [these two are the only means].

Determination [of meaning] is possible even without a word; therefore, we consider that an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is more remote than direct statement (*śruti*). If this is so, then even where there is no conflicting direct statement, there is still no determination of meaning from an indicative mark. In that case, it simply does not exist that the indicative mark is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Why?

"In this way, the Śruti would be contradicted. To this we reply: in that case, even the deliberation regarding the relative strength of Śruti and Liṅga is not possible. Here it is said: a mantra that occurs in proximity to a matter that possesses a context (prakaraṇa) and requires a specific procedure (itikartavyatā)— [The sentence continues: ...is [determined by] the context. But if there is no such requirement for a procedure, then the context is not established; therefore, the mantra is connected with the word "vākya" (syntactical connection). And since the mantra is connected with the word "barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi," it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the act of cutting the grass. Furthermore, because the mantra is recited at the time of the cutting, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the cutting. Moreover, because the mantra is recited while the grass is being cut, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the cutting. Thus, the mantra is connected with the cutting through the medium of syntactical connection (vākya). But if there is no such requirement for a procedure, then the syntactical connection is not established; therefore, the mantra is connected with the word "liṅga" (indicative power). And since the mantra contains the indicative power of cutting, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the cutting. Furthermore, because the mantra is recited at the time of the cutting, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the cutting. Moreover, because the mantra is recited while the grass is being cut, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the cutting. Thus, the mantra is connected with the cutting through the medium of indicative power (liṅga). But if there is no such requirement for a procedure, then the indicative power is not established; therefore, the mantra is connected with the word "śruti" (direct statement). And since the mantra is mentioned in the same sentence as the word "barhiḥ," it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the word "barhiḥ. Furthermore, because the mantra is recited at the time of the preparation of the barhis, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the preparation of the barhis. Moreover, because the mantra is recited while the barhis is being prepared, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the preparation of the barhis. And since the mantra is mentioned in the same section as the word "barhiḥ," it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the word "barhiḥ. And since the mantra is mentioned in the same section as the word "barhiḥ," it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the word "barhiḥ. Moreover, because the mantra is recited while the barhis is being prepared, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the preparation of the barhis. Thus, the mantra is connected with the preparation of the barhis through the medium of explanatory passage (arthavāda). And since the mantra is mentioned in the same section as the word "barhiḥ," it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the word "barhiḥ. And since the mantra is mentioned in the same section as the word "barhiḥ," it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the word "barhiḥ. Furthermore, because the mantra is recited at the time of the preparation of the barhis, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the preparation of the barhis. Moreover, because the mantra is recited while the barhis is being prepared, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the preparation of the barhis. Thus, the mantra is connected with the preparation of the barhis through the medium of direction (praiṣa). But if there is no such requirement for a procedure, then the direction is not established; therefore, the mantra is connected with the word "vidhi" (injunction). And since the mantra is mentioned in the same section as the word "barhiḥ," it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the word "barhiḥ. Furthermore, because the mantra is recited at the time of the preparation of the barhis, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the preparation of the barhis. Moreover, because the mantra is recited while the barhis is being prepared, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the preparation of the barhis. Thus, the mantra is connected with the preparation of the barhis through the medium of injunction (vidhi). But if there is no such requirement for a procedure, then the injunction is not established; therefore, the mantra is connected with the word "sāmānya" (general rule). And since the mantra is mentioned in the same section as the word "barhiḥ," it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the word "barhiḥ. Furthermore, because the mantra is recited at the time of the preparation of the barhis, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the preparation of the barhis. Moreover, because the mantra is recited while the barhis is being prepared, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the preparation of the barhis. Thus, the mantra is connected with the preparation of the barhis through the medium of general rule (sāmānya). But if there is no such requirement for a procedure, then the general rule is not established; therefore, the mantra is connected with the word "viśeṣa" (particular rule). And since the mantra is mentioned in the same section as the word "barhiḥ," it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the word "barhiḥ. Furthermore, because the mantra is recited at the time of the preparation of the barhis, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the preparation of the barhis. Moreover, because the mantra is recited while the barhis is being prepared, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the preparation of the barhis. Thus, the mantra is connected with the preparation of the barhis through the medium of particular rule (viśeṣa). But if there is no such requirement for a procedure, then the particular rule is not established; therefore, the mantra is connected with the word "nitya" (permanent). And since the mantra is mentioned in the same section as the word "barhiḥ," it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the word "barhiḥ. Furthermore, because the mantra is recited at the time of the preparation of the barhis, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the preparation of the barhis. Moreover, because the mantra is recited while the barhis is being prepared, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the preparation of the barhis. Thus, the mantra is connected with the preparation of the barhis through the medium of permanence (nitya). But if there is no such requirement for a procedure, then the permanence is not established; therefore, the mantra is connected with the word "naimittika" (occasional). And since the mantra is mentioned in the same section as the word "barhiḥ," it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the word "barhiḥ. Furthermore, because the mantra is recited at the time of the preparation of the barhis, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the preparation of the barhis. Moreover, because the mantra is recited while the barhis is being prepared, it is understood that the mantra is subordinate to the preparation of the barhis.

On the strength of the traditional injunction (*āmnāna*), one accepts that this mantra constitutes a supplementary part (*vākyaśeṣa*) for a rite that requires a specific procedure, such that "one should sacrifice with this mantra. What is being said here?
That when the desired object is being accomplished by means of a sacrifice, one should assist it with this mantra;
and this mantra cannot provide assistance without the mention of Indra. [289] {3/3}

By this it is meant that Indra is to be designated by this [word]. Therefore, this matter is rooted in scripture (*śruti*) alone. If it is rooted in scripture, it cannot be sublated by another scriptural passage. Thus, this indicative mark (*liṅga*) is either a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not at all.

Or rather, [one might argue] that it ought to be subject to option (*vikalpa*) because of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). To this we reply: it shall neither become invalid as a means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), nor shall it be subject to option. How so?
It has been established that this matter is characterized by direct scriptural statement.

Therefore, it is not non-authoritative. However, since this scriptural meaning— that "one should worship Indra with this mantra"— is understood only by depending upon an inferential syntactic unity and the force of the indicative mark (*liṅga*),
whereas the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) says "one worships the Gārhapatya fire," [the former is weaker].
This is that remoteness of meaning. First there is the cognition of the inferential mark (liṅga), and then, by implication, this meaning is expressed by the word;
this is not possible when it contradicts direct Vedic revelation (śruti).
For this is clearly understood:

"By means of this mantra, the Gārhapatya fire is to be worshipped. In that case, it is known that this mantra assists in this very way; and once this is ascertained, it is not possible for the sentence (*vākya*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*), whose functions have already been fulfilled, to assume such [an alternative] interpretation.
"The worship of Indra is expressed by the word. Therefore, because of the remoteness of the meaning, the indicative power (*liṅga*) is set aside by the direct statement (*śruti*).
Furthermore, an option (*vikalpa*) is improper;
indeed, an option is improper, for in that case there would be non-existence [of the injunction] on one side and its being as if eternal (*nityavat*) on the other.

When it is heard in the scripture, "One should worship the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī verse," if one were to postulate the non-existence [of the Aindrī verse] in a particular case, that would be something unheard,
and what is heard would be abandoned. And whatever fault there is in discarding the meaning of what is heard, [that same fault applies here].

To that same extent [the assumption] applies in the case of an unestablished [textual basis], for in both cases the established [evidence] is sublated. Therefore, because such a conceptual construction is improper, we understand that between direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), the direct statement is more powerful.
Now, as for what was said—that sublation is proper when there is a contradiction—
And it is not the case that there is no contradiction here;
rather, this is the contradiction:
that while the sentence and the context have their capacities unestablished, there is a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) expressing the worship of Indra.
But it is not possible for two things that have already established their capacity [to function] to do so simultaneously;
nor can it be the case that both the sentence and the context have simultaneously established their capacity and yet failed to establish it. Therefore, there is a contradiction.
And when there is a conflict, direct statement (*śruti*) is stronger than indicative mark (*liṅga*).

What is the example for a conflict between indicative mark and syntactical connection (*vākya*)? "I prepare a pleasant seat for thee; with a stream of ghee, I make it well-fitting. (*syonaṃ te sadanaṃ kṛṇomi ghṛtasya dhārayā suṣevam*) [Note: *suṣevaṃ* is a variant of *susévaṃ*.]
"I prepare it. Sit upon that immortal [seat]; O essence of rice, be well-disposed.

Here a doubt arises: should the entire mantra be employed both for the spreading of the underlayer (*upastaraṇa*) and for the placing of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśāsādana*), or should it be used up to the word "I prepare" (*kalpayāmi*) for the spreading of the underlayer?

The phrase beginning with "sit upon that" (*tasmin sīda*) refers to the placing of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). If the syntactical sentence (*vākya*) is more authoritative, then the entire [mantra] applies to both [the placing and the sitting]. How so? By taking into account the phrase "I fashion a pleasant seat" (*suṣevaṃ kalpayāmi*).

The passage beginning with "sit upon that" forms a single syntactical unit with the preceding one: "upon that which I prepare, sit thou. Now, if the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is stronger, then [the mantra] applies to the preparation of the interior seat. How so?

The mantra "I prepare a pleasant seat for you" is sufficient to express the preparation of the seat; the phrase "sit upon it" is likewise employed to set down the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and is thus enjoined for the act of setting it down.

What, then, is the initial position? These two reasons are of equal strength, just as it was stated that the direct statement (śruti) possesses greater force with respect to the indicative mark (liṅga).
The indicative mark (liṅga) is not said to be [contradicted] in the same way with respect to the sentence (vākya). Alternatively, the sentence itself is stronger than the indicative mark. Why?
Because that [sentence] is even set aside by direct statement (śruti), yet a stronger cause cannot be set aside. Therefore, we determine its fragility.
"But that which is set aside by one [means] can also be set aside by another.
This being the position reached, we reply: "Between indicative power (*liṅga*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*), indicative power is stronger. Why?
Because of the remoteness of the purpose (*arthaviprakarṣāt*). What here is this remoteness of purpose?

It is understood that this mantra is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) because it is recited in proximity to that which possesses the context (*prakaraṇavat*).

When [the mantra] is applied to the act of placing [the sacrificial cake]—on the basis of its capacity to denote the placing of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśāsādana*) through the words "sit upon that"—then the recitation of the mantra has fulfilled its purpose. Thus [it is concluded].

There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which it could be applied even to the act of spreading the base; likewise, the mantra "I prepare a pleasant seat for you" (*syonaṃ te sadanaṃ kṛṇomi*) has attained the status of being an auxiliary to the New and Full Moon sacrifices solely through the force of its recitation within that context.

Since it is applied to the act of spreading the base precisely through its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*), and its purpose having been fulfilled, it cannot be applied to the placing of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

For there is no purpose whatsoever for that which is being enjoined here. Thus, the phrase "sit upon this" (*tasmin sīda*) lacks the capacity [to apply] to the spreading of the base (*upastaraṇa*). Nor does the phrase "pleasant for you" (*syonaṃ te*) have the capacity [to apply] to the placing of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśāsādana*). [Rather,] it acquires the capacity for the spreading of the base by entering into a single syntactical unit with the preceding [phrase], and [the preceding phrase] acquires the capacity for the placing by entering into a single syntactical unit with the following [phrase].
But not in their own form do both [meanings] apply. This, then, is the remoteness of meaning:
that while the phrase "syonaṃ te" has the manifest capacity to denote the act of preparing a seat, [the other term lacks such capacity].

That [direct application] is primary. However, when the mantra "sit upon this" attains syntactic unity with the preceding one, its application becomes secondary. Thus, in this case, because of the expressive power (*abhidhāna-sāmarthya*) of the preceding mantra, its application to the act of spreading [the base] is stated; therefore, the meaning of the direct statement (*śruti*) is proximate to the indicative power (*liṅga*).

But when the capacity for expression has been produced in the latter [word], its meaning then follows from direct statement (*śruti*); thus, it becomes more remote than that which is mediated by indicative power (*liṅga*).

Likewise, in the case of the placing of the fire-wood (*sādana*), the former [word] is proximate while the latter is mediated by indicative power. Therefore, because of this remoteness of meaning, indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger than syntactical connection (*vākya*).
Therefore, although the word "syonam" (pleasant) is required by what follows and thus deserves to be used in the context of the settling [of the oblation],
nevertheless, having split the sentence, it must be applied specifically to the act of spreading [the base]; and the phrase "tasmin sīda" (sit upon that) is to be applied to the settling.
Now, just as the word "syonam te" possesses the capacity to denote the act of spreading [the sacrificial grass],
so too does it possess the capacity to enter into syntactic unity with what follows.
And capacity (*sāmarthya*) is said to be the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Therefore, when the sentence is split, it is precisely the indicative mark that becomes sublated. This is true;
yet even this is an indicative mark, for an indicative mark characterized in this way indeed has a remote object.

Syntactic unity arises from the indicative mark (liṅga), and from that, the capacity for denotation; from that, the meaning of the direct statement (śruti). Thus, there is remoteness of meaning, and this remoteness of meaning is the cause for sublation. Therefore, it is not [the case].
"It will form a single syntactical unit with the subsequent [verse]. In this way, "sit upon it" does not form a unit with what precedes it either.

Furthermore, for that which has entered into a single syntactical unit with the subsequent [verse], no visible purpose whatsoever is observed; however, the spreading [of the grass] and the bringing back [of the fire] are indeed observed. Why?

Because the spreading [of the grass] and the placing [of the oblation] are explicitly mentioned in the scripture. Thus, there is an indication of the placing for the subsequent [formula], but not in the sense of forming a single syntactical unit with the preceding one. Nor do these two fail to perform their respective functions individually without being part of a single syntactical unit with the preceding and subsequent [formulas]. Therefore, the former should be applied to the former context, and the latter to the latter.

Now, as for what was said—that since it is sublated even by Śruti, it must also be sublated by the Vākya—this is not so. For it is not logical that what has already been sublated should be further sublated by another;
rather, what has been sublated ought to be upheld for the sake of its meaningfulness.
With respect to *śruti*, it has a remote meaning; with respect to *vākya*, it has a proximate meaning;
therefore, *liṅga* is stronger.
Now, regarding the conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), how is it so? What, then, is called "context"?
Context is the statement of that which is to be performed, which requires an explanation of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). For it is the commencement of the act of stating that [procedure];

it does not depend on the end of the injunction (*vidhyanta*) beginning with the injunction itself (*vidhyādi*). Syntactical connection (*vākya*) has already been explained. What is an example of a conflict between these two?
The *sūktavāka* recitation. For therein the deities of the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) and the deities of the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*) are recorded;

these do not admit of syntactic unity with one another. In that case, by virtue of the force of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), the word "Indra-Agni" should be displaced from its use in the full moon ritual and employed in the new moon ritual. Now, as for the remainder of this [recitation]:

The two have increased greatly; they have accomplished a great deed. Should this [formula] be employed for both the full moon and the new moon sacrifices as many times as it is recited in the *sūktavāka*?
Is the context more powerful,
or should it be employed only where the term "Indra-Agni" has been extracted and applied?
"The statement is more powerful. Thus, there is doubt regarding all of them. What, then, is the prima facie view?
These two reasons are of equal strength. Why? [293] {3/3}
There is expectancy for the one, and there is expectancy for the other;
when the expectancy is equal, there is no reason for a decisive selection.
Therefore, they are of equal strength. Alternatively, the sentence is weak, for it is sublated by the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
This being the position reached, we reply: the sentence is stronger than the context (*prakaraṇa*). How so?
Because of the remoteness of the meaning. What here is the remoteness of the meaning?
When each individual word in a sentence is analyzed, it remains expectant [of further words], whereas the whole becomes complete.
In that case, the state of being a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyabhāva*) is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), whereas in the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is not directly perceived. How so?
Because a complete [text] occurs in proximity to that which requires a procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣa*), the expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) of that subject matter (*prakṛta*) is understood.

It is inferred that they do not constitute a single sentence. And having ascertained the capacity for expression through their being a single sentence, one conceives: "This [act], when expressed, becomes thus. This is the remoteness of meaning here:
that while *śruti* (direct statement) is proximate to the sentence, *prakaraṇa* (context) is remote. Therefore, by means of the *sūktavāka*, [one offers] the *prastara*...

Regarding the statement "he strikes": when those [mantras] denoting the deities of the Full Moon sacrifice and those denoting the deities of the New Moon sacrifice are extracted and employed separately, the remaining portions of those mantras must also be extracted and employed separately.

Therefore, although by the force of the context (*prakaraṇa*) it might be inferred that the remnants of the words denoting the Full Moon deities form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the words denoting the New Moon deities, this is actually perceived directly in conjunction with the words denoting the New Moon deities themselves.

Furthermore, inference is not possible when there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Moreover, once a context (*prakaraṇa*) has become meaningful, it is impossible to impose a requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*) upon those [words] that have already attained their own requirements. Now, as for what was said—that since it is sublated even by an indicative mark (*liṅga*), it must therefore also be sublated by the context—this is not so.

It should be understood that whatever is sublated by another is fragile even in other instances. If it were fragile, it would not be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) at all. However, the power of one thing exists only with respect to something specific.
The syntactical connection (vākya) has the power to sublate the context (prakaraṇa), but not the indicative mark (liṅga);

for while this context is remote in meaning with respect to the indicative mark, it is proximate in meaning with respect to the syntactical connection; therefore, the context is sublated by the syntactical connection.
[294] Now, what is an example of a conflict between the context (*prakaraṇa*) and the sequence (*krama*)?
In the context of the *rājasūya*, the story of Śunaḥśepa and other such elements are recorded within the sequence of the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice;
if the context were stronger [than the sequence], [then those elements would apply to the entire *rājasūya*].
Is that [rite] an auxiliary for all [sacrifices], if it is a sequence;
or is it an auxiliary for the Abhiṣecanīya alone? What, then, is the prima facie view?
"These two causes are of equal strength. Why?

Because we do not perceive any distinction by which we might understand that "this one is stronger. Therefore, these two causes are of equal strength. Moreover, the context (prakaraṇa) is set aside by the syntactical connection (vākya).
"Therefore, it would be sublated even by means of sequence.
This being the position reached, we reply: Context is stronger than sequence. Why?
Because of the remoteness of the purpose (*arthaviprakarṣāt*). What is the remoteness of the purpose here?
Because that which possesses a context (*prakaraṇavat*) has a requirement for completion,

syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) may be established even with something recited in proximity to it, provided that [proximate] thing is complete; however, this does not apply to that which possesses a fixed order (*kramavat*), in relation to what is recited according to that order.

For *krama* (order) is merely the recitation in close proximity (*saṃnidhi*) of several [elements] that are being recited. In that case, by the force of the recitation in close proximity, it must be understood that even though it is not perceived, there exists a state of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣāvatva*) on the part of that which is recited in proximity to what possesses the order. In the case of *prakaraṇa* (context), however, [the expectancy] of that which possesses the context is directly perceived.

Furthermore, it is impossible for that which is recited [in scripture] to have syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) simultaneously with both *prakaraṇa* (context) and *krama* (order); thus, there is a contradiction. In this regard, the directly perceived state of expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) within the *prakaraṇa* is capable of subverting the inferential *krama*. From expectancy arises syntactic unity; from syntactic unity arises the capacity for expression (*abhidhānasāmarthya*).

By virtue of its capacity, the meaning of the direct statement (*śruti*) is proximate to the context (*prakaraṇa*), whereas the meaning of the direct statement is remote from the order (*krama*). Therefore, between order and context, context is more powerful.
Now, as for what was said—that it is also sublated by syntactical connection (*vākya*)—[the response follows].
"Therefore, it should be sublated by something else as well. This is not so;
it is logical to support that which has been sublated, not to further sublate it.
298*} It must be set aside.
Now, what is the example for a conflict between order (krama) and designation (samākhyā)?

Which is more powerful? In the section designated as *pauroḍāśika*, within the sequence of the *sāṃnāyya* [offering], there is the mantra: "Be purified for the divine step" (*śundhadhvaṃ daivyāya kramaṇa*).

A mantra for the purpose of purification has been handed down in the sacred tradition. In this regard, a doubt arises: should it be employed for the purification of the vessels of the *puroḍāśa* cake because the name (*samākhyāna*) is more powerful, or for the vessels of the *sāṃnāyya* offering because the order of sequence (*krama*) is more powerful? What, then, is the prima facie position?
These two means of knowledge would be of equal strength. Why?
Because there is no distinction; or rather, the designation itself might be the stronger authority.
"For even by context, the order is set aside.
This being the position reached, we reply: the order is stronger. Why?
Because of the remoteness of the meaning (*arthaviprakarṣāt*). But what, then, is the remoteness of the meaning here?
When it is ascertained through context that [a passage] forms a single syntactical unit with something else, then regarding that which is recited in proximity to it, an expectancy is postulated;
it is understood that there is no [independent] syntactical unity.

And common worldly usage is a designation (*samākhyā*). However, the world alone is not an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding such matters. Therefore, the sequence (*krama*) is more powerful.
If this is so, then in cases characterized in this way, the application (*viniyoga*) occurs by means of sequence.
But sequence is not stronger because it is not more proximate to the meaning. How so?
For a deliberation regarding relative strength occurs between two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and in this case, designation (*samākhyā*) is not a means of valid cognition.
Because the word is worldly,
it is the person who possesses authority; this is not a fault,
for here the status of being an auxiliary is not understood through the authority of the person.

The word *pauroḍāśika* refers to this section (*kāṇḍa*); thus, in this matter, human authority is the means of knowledge. And in this sense, the person is the authority, just as the recitation in the order of the *sāṃnāyya* is based on human authority.

Just as there is syntactic unity according to the context, so too is this the word "Veda. For these objects, which are beyond the reach of the senses, are not logically possible [otherwise]; rather, authority regarding them belongs to those who are experts in them.
But those [names] which do not have the senses as their objects—those who are intent upon them are not authoritative. Therefore, the designation (*samākhyā*) is the cause;

and since it is a cause, its relative strength must be examined. It is replied: in that case, the remoteness of meaning (*arthaviprakarṣa*) of the designation must be stated. This is the remoteness of meaning: for the connection with the *sāṃnāyya* is taught through its position in the sequence of the recited text (*samāmnāna*).
It is not taught in the case of a name (*samākhyā*);

rather, having perceived the word being uttered, it is inferred by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) that "surely [the author] exists. Therefore, because the meaning of the earlier Veda is remote, the name is sublated in due course.
Now, as for what is said here and there—"this is sublated by that"—[it is as follows].
"‘This [is] by means of this’— in that regard, does that which is sublated reach the object of the sublater, or does it not? And what follows from this?"
If it has not been reached, what is sublated?
Or if it has been reached, [what is sublated]?
How can it be sublated? We say that the preceding cognition has reached the object of the sublating [cognition]. How so?
Because its cause, the universal, is still present. Then, how is it brought to an end?
Thus there is another cognition. But what, indeed, is the nature of non-erroneous cognition?
It is that for which no subverting cognition arises, even when it is being investigated.

That is not false. Among these—direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*)—each preceding one is stronger than each succeeding one. There is no other subsequent cognition that, when produced and examined, can sublate it. Therefore, when they coincide and there is a conflict, the latter is weaker because of its remoteness from the purpose.
He indeed approaches [it];
[the Śruti also,
and the Liṅga also].

In this regard, there is a doubt: does the state of having twelve upasads belong to the Jyotiṣṭoma or to the Ahīna? What, then, is the prima facie view? That it belongs to the Jyotiṣṭoma. Why?
Because of the context;
in this way, the context is upheld. But is it not contradicted by the direct statement? It is not contradicted;
we shall explain that the word *ahīna* refers to the Jyotiṣṭoma. Why?
It is called *ahīna* because it does not diminish (*na hīyate*).
It does not diminish in terms of sacrificial fees, ritual performances, or its fruit;
therefore, the Jyotiṣṭoma is an *ahīna*. By the word "or" (*vā*), doubt is dispelled.

In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, it is heard: "Since you two are indeed the lords of heaven, one should employ [the verse] 'yuvaṃ hi sthaḥ' as the *pratipad* for two sacrificers;
[and the verse] 'ete 'sṛgram indavaḥ'..."
"Regarding the phrase 'for many sacrificers' (bahubhyo yajamānebhyaḥ):

Because they are connected with duality and plurality, the two *pratipad* verses would have to be displaced from the Jyotiṣṭoma,

He who alone will not be able shall proceed with assistance;
since it must necessarily be performed, it should be done in whatever way possible.

Likewise, even setting aside some established rule, the sacrificer will take an assistant for the purpose that "it should be sacrificed in this manner. Thus, the two *pratipad* verses will remain within the context (*prakaraṇa*);
therefore, they should not be displaced. [This is because] it is not so, due to the singular connection with the archetype (*prakṛti*). (MS 3.3.19)
For the Jyotiṣṭoma is the archetype;
its ritual details are directly enjoined therein and are not obtained from anywhere by means of the extended application (codaka). What follows from this?

If this is so, that which is directly heard in the scripture (*pratyakṣa-śruta*) cannot be sublated. However, those [elements] obtained through the rule of transfer (*codaka*) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), being inferential (*ānumānika*), would be sublatable.

For the singularity of the agent in the Jyotiṣṭoma, being directly heard in the scripture, is not sublated by implication. Even where the necessity of performance is heard, there too only a single sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is heard—namely, "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring. Therefore, these two *pratipad* verses must be displaced from the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Now, why does this [mantra] not intend the wife?
Because when there is only one wife and the sacrificer, [the mantra] says, "For you two are... (*yuvaṃ hi stha*).

In the case of two or many wives, the mantra "these drops have been pressed" (*ete 'sṛgram indavaḥ*) is used; just as the statement "the two, wearing linen garments, should establish the sacred fire" (*kṣaume vasānāv agnim ādadhīyātām*) is intended to enjoin the wearing of linen garments, so too here this [mantra] is intended to enjoin the introductory verse (*pratipad*). It is replied: because the primary meaning is impossible in that case.

The word *lakṣaṇā* denotes a male person or a female; however, in this context, since it can apply to both a twice-born man and a many-born woman, it cannot be a term used in a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*).
Regarding the phrase "for many sacrificers," and also this dual form "for two sacrificers"— in these cases as well, there is the grammatical operation known as *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one).

The expression "man" and "woman" is likewise merely a word used figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, [if this were not the case], the two opening verses (*pratipad*), beginning with "Sing for him, O men," would have no scope at all. Therefore, it is established that these two opening verses must be displaced (*utkraṣṭavya*).
And the tail [is not a separate portion] because it is a single part.

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "They perform the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings with the tail (jāghanī). Regarding this, there is a doubt: does this injunction pertain to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, or to the animal sacrifice (paśu)? How would it apply to the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and how to the animal sacrifice? If the Patnīsaṃyājas are enjoined with the tail, then there is a displacement [of the ritual from its original context].

Now, regarding the injunction that the tail (jāghanī) is to be used in the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings, does this apply to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices themselves, or is there a displacement (utkarṣa)? What is the prima facie view? There is a displacement. Why is it displaced?
Because the Patnīsaṃyājas are enjoined with respect to the tail. How so?

The injunction for the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings arises from direct statement (*śabda*), while that for the tail (*jāghanī*) arises from syntactical connection (*vākya*); and direct statement is stronger than syntactical connection.
But surely the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings have already been enjoined. True, they have been enjoined;

however, they are now enjoined again with reference to the tail (*jāghanī*), which means it is stated that the offering must be performed in connection with that [tail]. This being the case, the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings in the New and Full Moon sacrifices are not deficient even without the tail.
However, it is the tail that is disposed of there. Therefore, its disposal occurs wherever the tail has a purpose,
and that [purpose] exists in the animal sacrifice,
not in the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
And since the tail, being offered as a single part, would not necessitate the employment of the entire animal,
this injunction must therefore be transferred [to another context].
NOTES:
Or rather, it is an injunction, because of its being something not previously known. (MS 3.3.21)
Or rather, the tail (jāghanī) is enjoined as a subordinate element (guṇa) of the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings. Why?

Because it is something not previously established (apūrvatvāt); the tail has not been previously established as a subordinate element of the Patnīsaṃyājas. In that context, while the Patnīsaṃyājas themselves are enjoined by their own words, their connection with the tail is not yet enjoined; and it is precisely where such a connection is being enjoined [that this rule applies].
In that case, when one of two things is enjoined in relation to another, their connection is inseparable; or rather, when the connection itself is enjoined, the two related members are inseparable,
wherein both function as defining characteristics.
In that case, the relationship is enjoined by its own word;
however, where one of the two is [taken] as a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa), there, having defined one, the other is enjoined.
And here, the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are indicated by way of their characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*). How is this understood?
Because of the connection with the wives (*patnī*), not every sacrifice is meant, but rather only that specific sacrifice which has wives as its instrumental means (*sādhana*) is indicated.
Now, why is it that the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are not prescribed by taking the tail (*jāghanī*) as the indicator?

It is not possible to prescribe the wives for this new sacrifice; however, if the tail were taken as the indicator while prescribing a sacrifice accompanied by wives, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). But here, there exists a sacrifice already prescribed that is accompanied by wives, which is indicated by the wives. Therefore, [the tail refers to] the sacrifice...
Having perceived [the animal], the tail is enjoined. As for the claim that the tail is enjoined by syntactical connection (*vākya*) while the sacrifice is enjoined by direct assertion (*śruti*),
it has been stated here that the injunction of the sacrifice is not possible in this case.

Because it would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, there is an injunction for the tail (*jāghanī*). If this is so, then in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings would be defective without the tail; therefore, there is no displacement [of the tail].
If it is argued that it is a "part" (*ekadeśa*)... [MS 3.3.22]
Now, as for what was stated— that because the tail is a single part, it will not cause the employment of the entire animal, and therefore there must be a displacement (utkarṣa)— that must be refuted.
Not so, because the tail is not established by the scripture regarding the archetype.

In the archetype of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the tail (jāghanī) is not mentioned in the scriptural injunction as "the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings are to be performed with the tail obtained from the animal. Rather, the tail is enjoined without qualification. Such a tail is possible in the Darśapūrṇamāsa even if it is brought in by purchase.
Therefore, there is no displacement.
The *saṃtardana* (joining together) should apply in the archetype, just like the purchase, because there is no loss of purpose. (MS 3.3.24)
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, with reference to the two pressing-boards, it is heard in scripture: "In a long Soma sacrifice, one should join them together for the sake of stability.
In this regard, there is a doubt: does the joining together apply to the Jyotiṣṭoma itself?
"Or rather, [does it apply] to the long-duration Soma sacrifices? It is said: "This is not a case where the purpose is omitted in the archetype;
therefore, it should not be displaced. He says: "But is it not also heard that there is no separation—'the two [presses] are not separated'?"
It is said: it will be treated as an option (*vikalpa*), just as there is an option in such cases as "he buys with gold" or "he buys with a cow.
In the same way, here too there will be an option: there shall be either overlapping (*saṃtardana*) or non-overlapping (*asaṃtardana*).
'the two pressing-boards'}* *{3/323:
*{3/324: O you who are without thirst, E2: asaṃtṛṇye, E4: asaṃtṛṣṇe; E6: asantṛṇṇe}* *{3/325: Cf. Tait.S. 6.2.11.3; Mait.S. 1.10.13}*
Or rather, there is a displacement [of the mantra], because of the mention of a specific [deity]. (MS 3.3.25)
Or rather, the *saṃtardana* (the joining together) is displaced,
for a specific distinction is indeed perceived in the case of the long *soma* sacrifice.
"One should close [the session]. With reference to the Jyotiṣṭoma, the sacrificial sessions (*satra*) are longer in terms of time.
[Alternatively, they differ] by way of the performers, because that [difference] is caused by them. (MS 3.3.26)
Or rather, the *saṃtardana* (joining) should not be extracted from the *jyotiṣṭoma*. In this way, the context (*prakaraṇa*) is upheld, and the term *dīrghasoma* will be based on the agent:
the *soma* of a long [tall] sacrificer is the "long *soma*."
Or rather, it may be [understood] from the perspective of ritual action (*kratu*), because the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would otherwise be untenable. (MS 3.3.27)
And this is not the case— that its placement is in the Jyotiṣṭoma;
it would be performed in a long-duration Soma sacrifice, for the lengthiness arises from the sacrifice itself.
Not from the perspective of being an agent. Why?
Because an explanatory passage (arthavāda) would be untenable; for there is an explanatory passage stating, "by means of support."
The meaning is "for the purpose of supporting";

for, when the Soma is pressed repeatedly over a long period of time by means of the pressing-stones, there arises a fear that the two Soma-pressing boards might split, and thus the explanatory passage (arthavāda) stating "for the sake of stability" becomes appropriate.
Therefore, there is excellence [of the sacrifice].
And the forms [of the rite] are like the performers, because there is no difference in their purpose of maintaining [the ritual]. (MS 3.3.28)
This is a sutra that follows upon the preceding word. What are the words?
[They are: "Now, for what purpose is there no application to the *saṃsthās*?
In that case, the context will be upheld.

And there is the expression "long *soma*. For it is said that the *soma* sacrifice in the *saṃsthās* such as the *ukthya* and others takes a long time when compared to the *agniṣṭoma*. It is replied: even though the *saṃsthās* take a long time, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the *soma* is not applicable;

for in those cases, the *soma* remains exactly the same, according to the scriptural statement, "He measures out ten handfuls of *soma*. There is no difference whatsoever in the quantity of the *soma* held there;
therefore, the passage must indeed be transferred (*utkarṣa*).
NOTES:
[This is so] because the meaning exists in the Ukthya and other [sacrifices]. (MS 3.3.29)

And this is not the case— that there is an "exaltation" (utkarṣa); rather, because it conforms to the context, there is no exaltation, and the term *dīrghasoma* is appropriate because of its long duration.

In that case as well, the Soma is greater than in the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, for the offerings indeed increase. Those [offerings] cannot be increased unless the substance to be offered increases. When a vessel is full, it receives the designation "graha" (cup);
therefore, it is impossible to take up smaller vessels. Consequently, when there is a danger of bursting, one must ensure that the vessel is capable of containing the liquid.
In this regard, it is argued that [the term] "by steadfastness" implies "it is established.
If it is objected that praise is useless because there is no distinction [between the two], [we reply: MS 3.3.30.

If you think that even in the case of the *saṃsthās* (the sacrificial forms), the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) is appropriate because it serves to increase the quantity of the offering material, this is not so;
for the praise would then be entirely purposeless. Why?
Because there is no distinction regarding the Soma;
as much Soma as is used in the Agniṣṭoma, so much is used in the other sacrificial terminuses (saṃsthās) such as the Ukthya and others.

In the Ukthya and other sacrifices as well, exactly ten handfuls of Soma must be taken. [Objection: "Surely the amount to be offered will increase according to the requirements. [Reply: How could those ten handfuls be increased? Furthermore, because of the rule regarding the number of joints in the phrase "having three joints" (*triparva*), it is not possible to take one with many joints;
therefore, due to this specific restriction on the measure, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would be untenable in the case of the *saṃsthās*.
Therefore, there would be an increase [of merit], because of its impermanence. (MS 3.3.31)
This is not so— that there would be an increase [of the sacrificial substance]— for it would apply to the *saṃsthās* (the completed forms of the sacrifice),

as this favors the context (*prakaraṇa*). Furthermore, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is appropriate because, due to the increase in the quantity of the offering material, there is a concern that the vessel might break.
In what manner should it be offered so that it will increase?

The Soma with widely spaced joints (*viprakṛṣṭaparvan*) shall be taken. Furthermore, at the third pressing (*savana*), only one *aṃśu* stalk is pressed, and its measure is not specified; he shall take that which has many joints and thick joints. [304] {3/3}
Therefore, there will be an increase in what is to be given; thus, the explanatory statement (arthavāda) will be consistent.
Consequently, it is established that [the rule] applies to the completed sacrifices (saṃsthās).
NOTES:
That which is associated with a number [should belong] to the sacrifice because of the context. (MS 3.3.32)

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, with reference to the Pravargya rite, it is traditionally recited: "One should not perform the Pravargya at the first sacrifice; one may perform it at the second or the third. Regarding this, there is a doubt: should the Pravargya not be performed in all performances of the Jyotiṣṭoma, or is the prohibition restricted to the first performance? What, then, is the prima facie view?
There is a prohibition in the Jyotiṣṭoma. Why?
Because of its connection with sacrifice;
by the word "first," the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is denoted, for it is that which has the first connection.

It is thus handed down in tradition: "This indeed is the first of sacrifices, namely the Jyotiṣṭoma; having sacrificed with this, one may then sacrifice with another. Since it is the first among sacrifices, the word "first" denotes the Jyotiṣṭoma;
and in this way, the context (prakaraṇa) is upheld.
If this statement refers to the sacrifice (*kratu*), then that prohibition accompanied by a number would prohibit the *pravargya* rite for the Jyotiṣṭoma.
*Note:
{3/330: E2,4: [The sacrifice] among sacrifices.*}
Or rather, it is occasional (naimittika), because of its connection with an agent, since the indicative mark (liṅga) has that as its cause.
And this is not the case— that this is a discourse on sacrifice;
for even among the four Vedas, there is no sacrifice known by such a name.

However, the first performance of the sacrifice occurs because of its connection with the agent; the word "first" is applied to the preceding [performance] only in relation to a second and subsequent ones.
That [consequence] applies to the performance,
not to the sacrifice. The performance is understood from direct scriptural statement, whereas the sacrifice is understood only through its connection with the performance.
Direct denotation (*śruti*) is more powerful than secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); therefore, one should not perform the *pravargya* rite at the first performance.

As for what was said—that because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the *jyotiṣṭoma*, it is a statement regarding that [sacrifice]—that has been refuted by the point that the coreferentiality is established through secondary indication. As for the coreferentiality with the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) in the phrase "at the first sacrifice" (*prathamayajñe*), [it is likewise explained].
Even that does not contradict our position, because the word "sacrifice" (yajña) denotes the act of sacrificing (yāga).
The grinding of the Pūṣan-oblation should be understood as applying only to the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), because it is not enjoined in the model sacrifice (prakṛti).
Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, they recite: "Therefore Pūṣan has a portion that is ground, for he is toothless.
In this regard, there is a doubt: does the grinding of the offering to Pūṣan belong to the archetype (prakṛti), or to the ectype (vikṛti)? What is the prima facie view?

"In the archetype. Why? Because of the context (*prakaraṇa*). But is it not the case that in the archetype they do not mention Pūṣan as the deity of any oblation? It is said in reply: the word "Pūṣan" will denote some archetypal deity.
This being the position, we say: where there is an oblation for Pūṣan (*pauṣṇa-havis*), [the rule applies].

In that case, it is possible for him to perform the grinding; however, since Pūṣan is not present in the archetype (prakṛti), the grinding must be displaced [to another context]. As for what was said—that the word "Pūṣan" will refer to some deity—[that is incorrect].

One might say: "If Pūṣan were not primary elsewhere as well. [Objection: "But if it were performed elsewhere, the context (*prakaraṇa*) would be obstructed. [Reply: "Let it be obstructed, for the syntactical connection (*vākya*) is what obstructs it. Or rather, there is no doubt at all in this matter.
In the same way, it is stated that the grinding of the *pauṣṇa* offering applies to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) and not to the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*),
because there is no deity named Puṣan in the archetype.
"An injunction (codanā). For what purpose is this stated?
The subsequent discussion will proceed [based on this].
That [offering] is for all purposes, because there is no distinction [stated]. (MS 3.3.35) *{3/333: Cf. Tait.S. 2.6.8.5} *{3/334: E2,4,6: of Pūṣan}

It has been stated that the grinding (peṣaṇa) prescribed for the sacrifice to Pūṣan in the archetype applies to the ectype as well. In this regard, there is a doubt: does it apply to the cooked rice (caru), the animal victim (paśu), and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa)?
"Or rather, only in the case of the cooked rice (caru). What, then, is the prima facie position?
That [the mantra] should apply everywhere—in the case of the cooked rice, the animal sacrifice, and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa). Why?
Because there is no distinction; no specific qualification is introduced.
Therefore, "in all cases":

whether it be in the case of the *caru* or the *puroḍāśa*, [the rule] is stated according to the purpose; however, in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), it would not apply because of a contradiction in purpose.

In the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), the grinding (*peṣaṇa*) would be enjoined for the offering to Pūṣan (*pauṣṇa*). As for the cake (*puroḍāśa*), grinding is already obtained by the very nature of the thing; since it is not possible for a cake to exist otherwise, a scriptural statement to that effect is unnecessary. Furthermore, [grinding] would not apply to the animal sacrifice.
If the heart and the other organs were being ground, their specific forms would be destroyed. What fault would there be in that?
[The rule] "he cuts off from the heart first" would not apply, as nothing would be cut off from the heart.
Likewise, another illustration (*avadāna*) will not be extracted [from this] as it was heard.
But is it not possible to extract [the essence] even from flour made of hearts and other organs? We say: no;
for "heart" and the rest refer to specific shapes (*ākāra*).
There are no [actual] meats;
for it has been stated that the meaning of a word is the generic form (*ākṛti*).
Even if, however, something possessing that form is produced, [it is still not meat].
Nevertheless, they might be confused regarding the place for its destruction;
therefore, this statement is for the purpose [of clarifying] that the grinding of the offering to Pūṣan shall take place in the *caru*.
If it is argued that [the rule] applies even in the case of the *caru* offering. (MS 3.3.37)
If you think thus— that because there is a contradiction in meaning, it does not have the sense of "animal"—
is it not the case that there is also a contradiction in meaning regarding the *caru*?
For they apply the word *caru* metaphorically to rice-gruel (*odana*) that has been clearly prepared.
For when being ground, it would indeed become either flour, or gruel, or bran.
(Note:
Not so, because [the word] is a name for the cooked product. MS 3.3.38.

To this it is replied: It is true that the word *caru* is employed when rice (*odana*) has been clearly cooked, as in the expression "the *caru* that has been clearly cooked is given"; however, its clear cooking is not the primary cause (*nimitta*) for its application. If its clear cooking were the cause, [then the term would not apply to other cases].
It would not be employed for the sake of what is already accomplished by flour; yet it is indeed employed there as well, because a *caru* made of flour is prepared.
Therefore, this is another point of similarity between these two.
That is the reason;
this is what is said: "Not because it is the name of a cooked offering," for there is no contradiction regarding the *caru*. How so?
Because it is a name for cooking;

this is a name for cooking, namely "caru. The word *caru* is expressive of that which is produced by internal steaming without being drained away. Therefore, speakers apply the term to both ground rice (*piṣṭa*) and solid boiled rice (*viśadaudana*).
Regarding the term *caru*: the purpose is exactly as stated for the *pakṣa* (the prima facie view);
according to the *pūrvapakṣa*, grinding (*peṣaṇa*) applies even to the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), whereas according to the *siddhānta* (the established conclusion), it applies only to the *caru*.
Because of the conjunction with one [of the two] in a single [locus]. (MS 3.3.39)

It has been stated that the grinding of the offering for Pūṣan occurs only in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) when it is a *caru*. Now, a doubt arises: does this apply only to a *pauṣṇa* offering dedicated to a single deity, or also to one dedicated to two deities? What is an example of a two-deity offering?

In the Rājasūya, there are the two offerings connected with the three [deities] on the northern altar: a cake on eleven potsherds for Soma and Pūṣan, and a *caru* for Indra and Pūṣan, with a dark-colored animal as the sacrificial fee.
In this regard, the offering to Indra and Pūṣan serves as the example. What is the prima facie view?
That grinding applies only to that which has a single deity. Why?
Because of the connection with [the deity] alone.
And as in the case of the fourfold division. {308} NOTES: And because of the contradiction with the Dharma. MS_3,3.40.
In the case of an offering to two deities, the rule would be contradicted:
there would be grinding for Pūṣan, but not for the other.

In that case, if Pūṣan’s portion were ground, the other’s would remain unground. Thereupon, the cooking would be uneven, and the term *caru*—which is based on the act of cooking—would be contradicted. Alternatively, if they were to avoid this contradiction and grind the portion of the other [deity] as well, there would be a confusion of portions. What fault would there be in that?

The portion of one [deity] might be offered for another; thus it would be done contrary to what was heard [in the scripture]. For this reason also, there should be grinding even when there is only one deity.
Or rather, it should apply when there is a second [deity], because [the grinding] is caused by the deity.
This grinding is heard as being for the sake of a deity: "Pūṣan is to have his portion ground.
And that portion becomes "one whose portion is ground" even when it is ground while belonging to two deities, unlike in the case of the fourfold division.
For in that case, it belongs to one who is independent, not to one who has a companion;
likewise, the compound *indrapīta* also belongs to one who is independent.

It does not apply to that which has a companion. Here, however, the *bahuvrīhi* compound "prapiṣṭabhāga" (one whose portion is ground) is a compound with another word (*anyapadārtha*) [as its referent], and this too occurs only when the two words are semantically related (*samartha*).
Yet, there is no such defect here in the case of an offering for two deities. Therefore, whether it is an oblation for a single deity or for two deities, its portion must indeed be ground.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark. (MS 3.3.42)

An indicative mark (*liṅga*) is likewise as follows: "Therefore Pūṣan has a portion that is ground, for he is toothless. This shows that the grinding is for the sake of the deity. Similarly, [the text] shows the state of being half-ground in the passage: "One desiring cattle should offer a *caru* to Soma-Pūṣan, half-ground. Likewise, it shows that the grinding is indeed for the sake of the deity in the passage: "Half is ground and half is unground, because it belongs to two deities."

Because of the explicit statement, there is grinding of all [grains] in that case, since it is governed by the scripture; however, due to the absence of purpose, there is no grinding in the case of the two-caru offering.
This is a sutra that follows upon the previous statement;
why is it not said that "it does not become ground sesame paste"?
It is replied:

If this statement were intended merely to refer back to the offering to Soma-Pūṣan (*saumāpauṣṇa*) and then enjoin grinding in all cases— namely, in the *caru*, the animal sacrifice, and the *puroḍāśa* cake— then, since both the connection with the *caru* and the connection with the "half-ground" (*nemapiṣṭa*) would have to be enjoined regarding that offering to Soma-Pūṣan, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, wherever there is an offering to Soma-Pūṣan, in each such case there must be the state of being half-ground.

With respect to that [sacrifice], the rule of partial grinding applies only to the offering dedicated to Soma-Pūṣan; for while total grinding would follow by implication in the case of the *puroḍāśa*, and no grinding at all would follow by implication in the case of the animal sacrifice or the *caru* due to the absence of purpose, this specific injunction must exist. In that context, the word *caru* would not have its literal meaning intended.
It might be assumed that [the mention of grinding] is for the sake of illustration;
however, under the view that it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of grinding, this contradiction does not arise.

Therefore, it is indeed an indicative mark (*liṅga*). Now, one might argue that the animal is not to be ground for fear of destroying its limbs. We say: no; in the case of partial grinding, there is no destruction of the limbs, as the portion will be cut off from what has been ground.
And the grinding has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
(Note:
Regarding the offering to Soma and Pūṣan:

because it is a property of the object (the sacrificial animal), it would not apply to both [Soma and Pūṣan] simultaneously—as in the case of the offering to Indra and Agni—since there is no scriptural injunction to that effect. (MS 3.3.44)
Or rather, the grinding should apply to the offering dedicated to Pūṣan alone, not to the one dedicated to Indra and Pūṣan. Why?
Because this is not prescribed as a property of the deity.

"The portion of Pūṣan, which is ground flour, is to be consumed. For whom, then, is it? It is a property of the purpose (artha). But what is the purpose? It is the sacrifice (yāga). How is this understood?
"It is not the property of the deity. It is replied: "For she has no share [in it]. [Objection:
"Is it not the case that what is given to a deity becomes her share? It is replied: "For this is renounced with reference to the deity."
Nor does ownership by the deity arise through mere relinquishment alone. For it is through appropriation (*parigrahaṇa*) that the relationship between owner and owned is established;
and there is no evidence whatsoever that anything has been appropriated by the deity. Furthermore, he who serves another...
That [portion] is his share; however, the deity does not partake of the oblation,
and therefore there is no share for Pūṣan.

Furthermore, even if some portion were somehow to exist [in the deity], nevertheless, grinding cannot be the duty (*dharma*) of the deity, for it would be purposeless in that case, as it is not a property of the sacrifice (*yāga*). How then can that which is recited in a different context become a property of the sacrifice? It is said in reply:

Because of the connection with the sentence. Now, an objection is raised: "But this connection is heard to be with the deity, not with the sacrifice. It is replied: It has already been stated that there is no connection with the deity because [the deity] lacks a share and because [the mention of the deity] would otherwise be purposeless.
Nevertheless, it must be explained how the connection with the sacrifice actually occurs. To that it is said: Here, that which is renounced with reference to Pūṣan is the share of Pūṣan.

In the case of that substance whose deity is Pūṣan upon its relinquishment, Pūṣan is not the deity in the offering to Indra and Pūṣan; therefore, that *caru* is not connected to Pūṣan by way of ownership. Consequently, in the offering to Indra and Pūṣan, there is no connection whatsoever between Pūṣan and the *caru*.
But when Pūṣan alone is the deity, the portion intended for him belongs to him. How so?
It is a well-known principle that whatever one has in mind when making a dedication (saṃkalpa) is the share of that [deity];

And the determination of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) depends upon the connection [of the action with a result]. The remainder, being of indefinite measure, applies to all ritual acts because there is no specific context or distinction.

And the remainder [is established] from the traditional designation (samākhyāna).
From this as well, we see that they are subsidiary to the Vedic rites. Why?
Because of their designation (*sāmakhyāna*).

For since the *jayā* and other offerings are recited in the Veda designated as "pertaining to the Adhvaryu" (*ādhvaryava*), they will be performed by the Adhvaryu priest. There is the Aśvapratigraheṣṭi sacrifice: "Varuṇa indeed seizes him who accepts a horse; as many horses as he may accept..."

"Or what constitutes the Vedic case? In common worldly practice, whether one is begging or not begging, wherever one receives a horse, that is the worldly acceptance of a horse. He says: "The mention of the fault is not for its own sake, but for the purpose of praising the expiation. It is replied: This would be so only if it were for the purpose of removing the fault, for this ritual is a "release from Varuṇa."
That [penance] ought to apply to the worldly case,
because the mention of Varuṇa exists in the world; however, in the Vedic case of accepting a horse, that would not apply,
for it is by the specific statement of the scripture [that the penance is determined].
Its status as something to be performed is understood. And if it were sinful,
its status as something to be performed would not be understood,

But surely, even in the case of a Vedic acceptance of a gift, there is sin for one who accepts from someone from whom one ought not to accept? It is said: this would indeed be so if the act of accepting were intended by the agent;
