We shall explain this further in the subsequent section (*uttarādhikaraṇa*). Therefore, it is established in this present section that there is no sacrificial offering (*iṣṭi*) in the case of the acceptance of a horse as enjoined by the Veda. *Notes:* The term *uttarādhikaraṇa* refers to the following section of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*. The point here is that the ritual injunction regarding the acceptance of a horse (*aśvapratigraha*) does not imply the performance of a specific expiatory sacrifice (*iṣṭi*), as might be inferred from other scriptural passages. Thus, the conclusion of this specific discussion is that no such offering is required when accepting a horse in accordance with Vedic law.

It is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) because it is not logically possible [otherwise]; therefore, it should be understood as pertaining to the sacrifice. *MS* 3.4.29. *{3/424: Tait.S. 2.3.12.1}* *{3/426: E1 gives vacanena in parentheses}*

And this is not the case, as it has been stated: "He who in this world accepts a horse from a Śūdra or from any other evildoer should perform this sacrifice; for he is said to be seized by Varuṇa, that is, seized by dropsy."

That whose abdomen swells due to the increase of water is well known in the world simply as *jalodara* (water-belly). And it is not recognized that the acceptance of horses is its worldly cause; nor is this [cause] enjoined by this [text]. Therefore, the occurrence of *jalodara* does not result from the acceptance of horses. Now, if "sin" is what is expressed by the word *varuṇa*, [then the passage means: "He who accepts a horse becomes afflicted with sin. This is the meaning. If, however, *varuṇa* refers to the god Varuṇa, then the meaning is: "He who accepts a horse is seized by the god Varuṇa. In this case, the connection between the two is established through the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Thus, the statement "He who accepts a horse becomes afflicted with *jalodara*" is a figurative expression based on that [causal relationship]. It is not a direct injunction. Consequently, there is no contradiction [with the Vedic injunctions]. Furthermore, since the acceptance of a horse is prohibited by the Smṛti, one should avoid it even out of fear of a worldly penalty. On the other hand, since the acceptance of a horse is not prohibited by the Śruti, it is permissible for one who seeks merit (*puṇyakāma*). Thus, there is no contradiction. Therefore, the prohibition of the acceptance of a horse is indeed established by the Smṛti. Hence, it is proven that the Smṛti possesses the authority of the Veda. Thus, the Smṛti is authoritative because it is based upon the Veda. This concludes the section on the authority of the Smṛti. Now, the author of the Bhāṣya states: "And because there is no contradiction with the Śruti... What is meant here by "contradiction"? It is when one thing is enjoined by the Śruti and another is enjoined by the Smṛti, and these two are mutually incompatible. For example, the Śruti prescribes the performance of the *Agnihotra* throughout one's life (*yāvajjīvam*), while the Smṛti prescribes the renunciation of action (*saṃnyāsa*). Since these two are incompatible, they contradict each other. Or, for example, the Śruti prescribes the drinking of Soma, while the Smṛti prohibits intoxicants (*madya*). Since these two are incompatible, they contradict each other. Or, for example, the Śruti prescribes the killing of animals in the *Vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, while the Smṛti prohibits the killing of all living beings. Since these two are incompatible, they contradict each other. In such cases, how can there be non-contradiction? To this, he says: "Because there is no contradiction with the Śruti. That is to say, there is no contradiction with the Śruti. Why? Because the Smṛti is based upon the Śruti. If the Smṛti were not based upon the Śruti, then there would be a contradiction. However, since the Smṛti is based upon the Śruti, there is no contradiction. How so? For instance, the Smṛti which prescribes the renunciation of action is based upon those Śrutis that prescribe renunciation. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Similarly, the Smṛti which prohibits intoxicants is based upon those Śrutis that prohibit intoxicants. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Likewise, the Smṛti which prohibits the killing of all living beings is based upon those Śrutis that prohibit the killing of animals outside the sacrificial altar (*paridhi*). Therefore, there is no contradiction. Thus, the Smṛti is authoritative because it is based upon the Veda. This concludes the section on the authority of the Smṛti. Therefore, it should be understood as pertaining to the sacrifice. For in the case of a worldly act, a result would have to be postulated;

whereas in the Vedic context, it will become a subsidiary part of that rite in which the acceptance of a horse occurs. In that case, its connection is established through its being construed as a single syntactical unit with the injunction of performance.

Since it is simpler for an indirect statement to form a single syntactical unit with the declaration of its result, it is logical that the offering (*iṣṭi*) is [the act] in the case of giving in the Vedic context.
And [the injunction] is not prompted [by another], because of the distinction between actions. (MS 3.4.30)
"For as many horses as one might accept, for that many one should offer cakes on four potsherds to Varuṇa.

Regarding this, it has been established that the sacrifice is to be performed in the case of accepting a horse according to Vedic injunction. Now, however, a doubt arises: should the sacrifice be performed by the person who accepts [the horse], or...
To whom it is given, or by which causal agent—
who is the one that gives. What is the prima facie view?
And because the action is distinct,
the sacrifice is not enjoined for the giver;
we understand it to belong to the recipient— of as many horses as [there are].
"One should offer as many four-potherd oblations to Varuṇa as [the number of those] one might accept";
therefore, it must be performed by the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) who accepts [the gift].
On account of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), it should belong to the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*).
This [result] does not belong to the one who performs the acceptance;
rather, it must belong to the one who performs the causal act. Why?
Because of an indicative mark (liṅga). What is the indicative mark?

The preceding words are to be connected with the subsequent words according to their respective meanings. This is what is heard: "Prajāpati gave a horse to Varuṇa," and so forth; here Prajāpati is celebrated as the giver of the horse, and Varuṇa as the recipient.
"He reached his own deity. The word "he" (saḥ) is dependent and requires the previously mentioned remainder of the sentence;

it refers back to Prajāpati, thereby forming a single syntactical unit with it. Furthermore, due to grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), this reference must be understood as referring to Prajāpati alone, and not to Varuṇa.
Because of the difference in grammatical subject (vaiyadhikaraṇya). The phrase "it burst asunder" also refers back to Prajāpati himself who was the subject under discussion previously;
thus, it forms a single syntactical unit with him. Therefore, [the statements] "he saw this four-potherd offering to Varuṇa" and "he offered it"—these refer to Prajāpati alone.

Thereupon Prajāpati was indeed released from that noose of Varuṇa. "Varuṇa seizes him"— this is a statement of the reason (*hetvapadeśa*), because Prajāpati, having given the horse to Varuṇa, became afflicted with dropsy.
Therefore, Varuna seizes whoever accepts or gives away a horse; he is torn asunder. But since he has been released by means of an offering to Varuna, [he is not seized].

Therefore, even by one who gives a horse, a sacrifice to Varuṇa must be performed; thus, the *vāruṇī* sacrifice for the giver of a horse is praised by means of this verb, which states: "Therefore, having given a horse, one should perform the *vāruṇī* sacrifice.

[The opponent] says: But surely it is stated that he who receives the horse should perform it. If that were so, since the sentence would begin in one way and conclude in another, the opening statement itself would be rendered meaningless.

There is also the conclusion. Therefore, whether at the beginning or at the conclusion, the meaning of the word must be determined in accordance with the other; that is, either the conclusion must be interpreted in light of the beginning, or the beginning in light of the conclusion.
In this regard, it says: "Prajāpati led the horse to Varuṇa."
It might be inferred in accordance with the concluding statement, "He received a horse from Varuṇa," or else the conclusion might be adjusted according to the opening statement,
"Whoever receives a horse."

"Who causes the horse to be accepted. In this regard—according to the principle that "the primary meaning comes first because of the injunction, as in common worldly usage," the primary sense must first be accepted because there is no contradiction; however, the secondary (figurative) sense must be postulated for the rest only where there is a contradiction. Furthermore, [if one were to take it literally], one would have to assume many inconsistencies, such as: "Prajāpati led the horse to Varuṇa" and "he accepted the horse from Varuṇa. This word is "pratigṛhṇāti" (he accepts/causes to be accepted).

One can express the meaning "he causes [another] to accept" by whatever means possible; for it refers to one who performs that action, and by which the action is accomplished even through an indirect sequence.
He can be called the agent of that action,
just as one who arranges [the plowing] is said to "plow with six plows" even though he does not perform the actual scratching of the soil,
because he performs what is conducive to it; so too here, he who gives performs what is conducive to the act of receiving.

Therefore, it can be said that "one who gives is one who receives. Consequently, this has been determined with certainty: it is stated that "one who gives is one who receives," and for him there is the Vāruṇī sacrifice.
He offered it as a sacrifice;
Varuṇa indeed [seized] him.

And likewise, there is [the offense of] causing intoxication by drink. MS 3.4.32.
They prescribe this: "One who has vomited *soma* should offer a *caru* oblation of *śyāmāka* grain to Soma-Indra.
In this regard, there is a doubt: does the *saumendra caru* apply to the vomiting of worldly *soma*-drinking, or to that of Vedic *soma*-drinking? What is worldly *soma*-drinking?
And what is Vedic?
It is said: Vedic Soma-drinking occurs in the Jyotiṣṭoma and its modifications;
worldly Soma-drinking is that which occurs during the seven-night sacrifices.
When Soma is being consumed during the ten-night rites for the purpose of balancing the bodily constituents (*dhātu-sāmya*), what is the prima facie view?
"And the mishap in drinking is like that."
The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is pointed out as follows: "Just as in the case of worldly vomiting, there ought to be an *iṣṭi* sacrifice, but not in the case of Vedic [vomiting]."
Just as in that case [of the horse-sacrifice], because of the mention of a connection with a fault,
it was stated regarding the worldly act of "accepting a horse" (*aśvapratigraha*),
so too here there is a mention of a connection with a fault.
"He who drinks Soma loses his sensory power through his vigor"—

in common worldly experience, when [emetics] are used for the sake of balancing the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) and then destroyed by vomiting, there occurs a loss of sensory power due to the impairment of the balance of the constituents.

For according to the scripture, there would be no fault in the Vedic case. Since the injunction "the remnant is to be drunk" has been enjoined by the word and fulfilled, there is no fault. Even if one vomits, the act of drinking has nonetheless been accomplished therein; since the purpose of the scriptural statement has been achieved, there would be no fault. Therefore, in the event of an accident involving the drinking of worldly soma, the offering to Saumendra should be performed.
And for the sake of balancing the bodily constituents (*dhātusāmya*), [it is said]:
"Soma vomits," or "He vomits Soma."

But in the case of Vedic [mantras], there would be a fault [if the word order were changed], because [the meaning] is fixed by the text; for in the case of worldly [speech], there would be no fault on account of the sense.

This [consequence] may occur in the case of a Vedic drink, but not in the case of a worldly one. Why? Because of a fault; for here a connection with a fault is heard: "He is indeed deprived of his sense-organ and his vigor. However, in the case of a worldly drink, which is prepared for the purpose of balancing the bodily humors (*dhātu-sāmya*) and so forth, nothing is defective.

For indeed, in the world, people drink that [medicine] precisely for the purpose of vomiting. Moreover, even though this is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), nevertheless, in order to avoid the postulation of a separate result, it is logical to assume that it refers specifically to the Vedic context;
for there is no distinction made in all cases. (MS 3.4.34)

This ritual dedicated to Soma and Indra (*saumendra*) is to be performed in the event of a mishap involving the drinking of Soma; it should apply in all cases of vomiting, whether occurring during the officiant’s (*ārtvijya*) or the patron’s (*yājamāna*) performance. Why?
Because there is no distinction, no specific qualification is adopted such that it would apply to one person's vomiting and not to another's.
Therefore, it should be present everywhere.
NOTES: *{3/445: E2,4: somendraṃ}*
Or rather, it belongs to the owner, because it is for his purpose.
Or rather, it should apply to both masters. Why?
Because it is for their sake;
the ritual action is for the sake of the sacrificers.
Where Soma is vomited,
that which is the ritual for Soma-Indra (*saumendra*) here is also for that very purpose. For this is heard in the scripture as being for the benefit of one who has vomited Soma.
That [penance] applies to one who has vomited the Soma;
it does not apply to the officiating priest (ṛtvij),
for that ritual act is not for the sake of the priest.

Where Soma is vomited, it is then argued: "The priests belonging to the Adhvaryu or the Hotṛ who have vomited Soma shall perform [the rite] in their own fires. If that were the case, then [the rite] would either not be a constituent part of the ritual action for one whose Soma has failed, nor would it belong to the Adhvaryu or the Hotṛ who have vomited Soma.

In that case, the Adhvaryu and others, who are entirely subordinate [to the sacrificer], do not obtain the fruit while having the rite performed by their own officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Furthermore, that which is performed for their sake does not contribute to the benefit of the sacrificer;
therefore, the act [of vomiting] should not be performed by the officiating priests.

And because of the observation of an indicative mark. (MS 3.4.36)
And there is an indicative mark [in the scripture]: "This belongs to the sacrificer who has vomited the Soma. How so?
"He who vomits the Soma is deprived of the drinking of Soma"—this refers to the sacrificer.
If the preparation of the *soma* were ruined, his ritual action would become defective and thus fail;

however, there can be no failure on the part of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). If the connection were with vomiting, it would be "the officiating priests whose *soma* they vomit," and not "he who vomits the *soma*. Therefore, we see from this also that the offering to Soma-Indra pertains to the vomiting of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

There are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices;
therein it is recited: "That which belongs to Agni, the cake on eight potsherds, is never omitted on the new moon day and on the full moon day.
In this regard, there is a doubt: is the entire oblation [to be offered], or...
Should it be given entirely to Agni,
or should some portion be set aside and some portion be given? What is the prima facie view?

The entire oblation should be offered. Why? Because it is for that purpose. There is the scriptural injunction: "The cake (puroḍāśa) dedicated to Agni must be prepared. Therefore, everything must be given.
But because of the taking of the portion, there should be a remnant.

The extraction is the *avadāna*; it is without further extraction. For this is heard [in scripture]: "He cuts off twice from the oblation. There is also another statement: "He offers the two-fold *avadāna*.
Therefore, only the two-fold *avadāna* is to be offered; the rest is to be left remaining.

*{3/453: E2 om. tena}* Or [the word "means" (*upāya*) is used] because it has that as its purpose. (MS 3.4.39)
And this is not the case— that only two portions should be offered;
rather, whatever one offers must be prepared by cutting it twice.

When it is to be offered, the rule is prescribed that it should be cut twice; it is not prohibited that what has been cut twice be offered, and the whole must be offered— this alone is logical, and not otherwise.
But because the action has been performed, it should occur only once, since the substance is subordinate to it.

It is said: when it is heard in the injunction for the oblation (*homa*) that there is a specific qualification of "twice cutting," then everything has been performed exactly as it was heard, even if [the action] occurred only once.
In that case, since no other substance exists, the sacrifice should not be repeated. Why?
Because that substance is for the purpose of accomplishing the sacrifice;

it is not the case that the substance must be connected with the sacrifice. For if the oblation were to be connected with the sacrifice [as a primary requirement], [then repetition would be necessary].

Then, once the sacrifice has been connected with the two portions (*dvayavadāna*), since there is yet another [portion] to be connected, the sacrifice would have to be repeated for the sake of connecting that. However, the sacrifice is not for the purpose of connecting the substance; rather, what is it for?
The substance is subordinate to the sacrifice;

it is taken up so that the sacrifice may reach completion. Therefore, once the sacrifice has been completed and the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) has been accomplished, it is not logical for the primary act to repeat itself merely out of necessity or in conformity with the subordinate factor.
How is it that substance (*dravya*) is not the primary factor, such that there would be no repetition? Because the fruit arises from the sacrifice (*yāga*);

for when an accomplished entity (*bhūta*) and a thing to be accomplished (*bhavya*) are mentioned together, the accomplished is taught for the sake of the thing to be accomplished. Furthermore, no perceptible benefit to the substance is produced by the sacrifice.

Therefore, having performed the offering of two portions, a remainder must be left over. As for what was said— that because of the statement "the oblation belongs to Agni," it is understood that everything must be offered—
therein, the connection with the act of offering is merely inferential.

But here, the direct perception is in the case of the double-portioning (*dvir-avadāna*). Furthermore, even when there is no connection with the whole, the application of the suffix *-taddhita* is possible; therefore, it must be understood [that way]. Indeed, "belonging to Agni" (*āgneya*) is the general rule, while "he offers the double-portion" (*dvyavadānaṃ juhoti*) is the specific injunction. Therefore, something must be left over.

There are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices;
therein are the subsidiary rites (śeṣakāryāṇi).
Regarding this, there is a doubt: should these rites be performed for each individual oblation (havis)?
"Or rather, from a single oblation"? What is the prima facie view?

They should be performed from a single [oblation], because the subsidiary rites for the remnants do not serve as the motive for the oblations. If they were motivated by the subsidiary rites for the remnants, [then they would apply to all].

"All [the remaining rites] should be performed" means they should be performed for all [of them]; however, these have other purposes, so they need not necessarily be employed in the remaining rites (*śeṣakārya*). And because the principal [act] has been consecrated by such a subsidiary act performed even once, it should not be performed again from another [act].

Or rather, the rites with the remnants should be performed from all the oblations. Why?
Because there is no distinction in the cause;
that which is the reason for performing the rites with the remnant of one oblation [is the same for all].
That [remainder] belongs to all; for that is the remainder which must be presented.
If it were not presented to someone, that person would be deprived of the refinement produced by it.
Therefore, [the rites] must be performed for all;
this is also because of the observation of indicative marks.
And an indicative mark is seen: "The gods indeed said to Sviṣṭakṛt, 'Carry our oblation. He replied, 'Let me choose a boon; let there be a portion for me.
'Choose,' they said."

He said, "One should cut [the portion] for me from the northern half once each"; this shows the use of repetition (*vīpsā*). Therefore, the remaining rites are to be performed from all [of the portions].

Now, let us consider the following hypothetical case: if [the fruits] were to arise from a single [moment], would they then arise from any [moment whatsoever], or from the first one? What is the conclusion?

thus, when they are to be performed, there is no obstruction of the causal condition (*nimitta*).

"When there is no obstruction of the occasion (nimitta), the rite occasioned by it (naimittika) must be performed. Therefore, when the [first] rites have been performed, there is an obstruction of the occasions for the second and subsequent ones; thus, they are not performed. Consequently, they should be performed from the primary [rite] itself.
Because there is no mention of "eating" (bhakṣa), the word "giving" (dāna) refers to a purchase (parikraya).

"This [is for] the Agnīdh," it is said.

"Or for the purpose of consumption. What is the prima facie view?

It is not heard [in the scripture] that "it is to be eaten. Whatever fault there is in abandoning what is explicitly stated, that same fault applies to the postulation of what is not stated. Furthermore, it is given to the laborers;
therefore, this is a purchase (parikraya).

Now, as for what was said— that it is not heard [in the text] that "one must eat"— [the response follows].

"And as great is the fault in the abandonment of what has been heard, so great is the fault in the postulation of what has not been heard. It is replied: through such statements as "this belongs to Brahmā," there is a connection of the parts with Brahmā and the others.

thus, it will apply even in cases where there is no purpose of purchasing.

"It must be purified. Why?

"Choose [a boon]," they said;
because of the word *samavatta* (collected) in reference to one [portion]. (MS 3.5.3)

In the *prāyaṇīya* offering of cooked rice dedicated to Āditya, it is heard in the scripture: "He makes a combined portion for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," "He makes a portion from the clarified butter and from one sacrificial oblation," and "He makes a combined portion with another oblation. Therefore, when the portions of clarified butter (ājyāvadāna) are being offered according to the rule of extension (codaka), it is logical that one "cuts off [the portions] together" (samavadyati). Otherwise, it would have been stated that one cuts off from the sacrificial porridge (caru) from only one [place].

And because the explanatory passage (arthavāda) concerning the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is seen in the case of clarified butter (*ājya*).

Regarding the *dhruvā* butter, there is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) concerning the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering: "Having made each successive portioning, one replenishes the *dhruvā*; having made the portioning for the *sviṣṭakṛt*, one does not replenish the *dhruvā*. This demonstrates the purpose of the replenishing: namely, that he will offer no other oblation after that [which is for the *sviṣṭakṛt*]. Once the *sauviṣṭakṛta* rite has been completed...

Therefore, since there is no subsequent offering (*parāhuti*), one should not perform the re-anointing (*pratyabhighāraṇa*). This indicates that the re-anointing takes place in the *dhruvā* vessel for the sake of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
(Notes: *3/474: E2,4: 'vatte*)
But because it is not without remainder, it would not be thus; its state of being without remainder results from the taking of everything.
It is not so; the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā* must be cut from the constant clarified butter (*dhrauvājya*). Why?
Because there is no remnant. Why does it have no remnant? Because of the taking of the whole.
Because it is common [to all], it would not apply to the *dhruvā* vessel.
Now, it might be argued that what remains in the *dhruvā* vessel after the portion for the *upāṃśuyāja* has been taken is a remnant (*śeṣa*). This is not so;
for that [remaining substance] is common to all.

For the *upāṃśuyāja* and for other purposes: as much clarified butter (*ājya*) as is to be offered, that much clarified butter he employs. For whatever [offering] has clarified butter, [he employs it].
"Each of those [portions] must be taken and prepared in this manner;

therefore, the clarified butter in the *dhruvā* vessel is common [to all]. And the scripture shows: "Indeed, that which is the clarified butter in the *dhruvā* is taken for the sake of the entire sacrifice.
What follows from this if it is so? That the clarified butter in the *dhruvā*, which has been portioned out for the *upāṃśuyāja*, is common [to all].

Therefore, other purposes and tasks are to be performed, but that which has already fulfilled its purpose should not be further expounded; for that which remains after its function is completed becomes a mere distraction.

That [meaning] is what must be explained. And in some cases, it is that which is to be explained, and how it is to be explained. However, that which is taken up because it possesses a purpose need not be explained. Therefore, [the purpose] is not [stated] in the case of the *upāṃśuyāja* in the *dhruvā* vessel.
And some remnant of the *sauviṣṭakṛta* offering must be presented; for example, where rice has been cooked for many people at a single primary meal.
In that case, when one person has eaten, it is understood that there is no remnant of his portion to be distributed to the servants in the vessel,
for that [portion] serves a specific purpose. The same should be understood regarding the clarified butter used in the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice.

He says: "In that case, there will be a remnant of the clarified butter (ājya) in the juhū-ladle, just as there is [of soma] in the cups (camasa) and goblets (graha) due to the injunction regarding the soma. To this, he replies:

And because the substance of the *sauviṣṭakṛta* offering has already been portioned out, it is [placed] in the *juhū* ladle.
And because that [offering] is connected with the oblation (homa).

It has already been stated that there is no remnant in the *dhruvā* vessel because the *upāṃśuyāja* is common to all [the offerings]. Now, why is it that the remnant-rite is not performed with what remains in the *juhū*?
As in the case of the cup used for the oblation, where there is no remnant. It is said: that which has been taken into the *juhū* ladle is entirely connected with the oblation;
therefore, there is no remnant in the *juhū*.

Thus, that which was stated again must be refuted:
"Because it would contradict the injunction and because it would involve the preparation of an oblation. (MS 3.5.9)

therefore, even the *vaṣaṭ*-utterers and others should consume [the soma] from the cups.
And because another [use] is seen in the case of the *camasa* cup.

Furthermore, [the text] indicates other *camasins* in connection with the *camasa*: "He hands over the *camasas* to the *camasādhvaryu*; he carries them to the *vaṣaṭkartṛ*. For only one's own *camasa* is carried to the *vaṣaṭkartṛ*;
therefore, the observation of the carrying away of many [camasas] would not be possible if the *vaṣaṭkartṛ* and others did not consume [the soma] from the *camasas*. Consequently, they do consume it.
Now, as for the case where many eat from a single vessel, what is the sequence there? It is said:
in a single vessel, the Adhvaryu should eat first according to the sequence.
For the sequence for consuming belongs to him in whose hand the Soma is;
or rather, it belongs to the Hotṛ, according to the wording of the mantra. (MS 3.5.37)
Or rather, the *hotṛ* priest should consume it first, because of the wording of the mantra;
for the wording of the mantra is as follows: "Even before the *hotṛ*, they have attained the eating of the oblation."
Likewise: "O Indra, being thus, protect us as our first [protector]" (RV 10.94.2d).
And because of the scriptural statement: *MS_3,5.38*.

This statement occurs: "The first draught belongs to the one who utters *vaṣaṭ*. This is indeed a direct scriptural injunction; it should not be thought that the priority [of the first draught] is not intended because multiple qualities are being prescribed, for that priority is something not otherwise established.
This is not a restatement (anuvāda),
but rather an injunction (vidhi) itself. And for one who enjoins by means of a compound, it is not difficult to enjoin multiple qualities.
And because of the sequence of causes. (MS 3.5.39)

For the first *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is the occasion for the Hotṛ, and from that, the oblation is the occasion for the Adhvaryu. And because of the sequence of the occasions, there is adherence to the order in the sequence of the things occasioned.
According to the scriptural statement, the consumption [of the portion] is permitted after authorization.
Now, when the Soma in a single vessel is consumed by more than one person,
should it be consumed there after having requested permission, or without having requested permission?

Regarding the question of whether one may consume [the Soma] even without having asked for permission: since there would be no fixed rule due to parsimony, it is stated that "one must consume it after having asked for permission.

Why? Because of a scriptural statement; this statement exists: "Therefore, Soma is not to be drunk by one who has not been invited (*anupahūta*). And "inviting" (*upahvāna*) is synonymous with "asking for permission. This is a sūtra establishing a general rule (*prāpti*). Now, once it is established that one must consume it after being permitted:
Should one seek permission using worldly speech or Vedic speech?
Since there is no fixed rule, the prima facie view is that it may be done with worldly speech; however, the following is stated [in response]:
NOTES: *{3/530: E2,4: eating what is unknown}*, *{3/531: E1 provides "this is a sūtra of attainment" in brackets}*
One should seek permission with the formula "He has been invited; may you invite," because of the indicative mark [of the text]. (MS 3.5.41)
This mantra has the characteristic of requesting permission; because of this characteristic, it is traditionally recited for the purpose of requesting permission. [359] {3/3}
It is excluded by implication; when the worldly [expression] has accomplished its purpose therein, it ceases.
In that case, the response "upahvayasva" (invite [me]) follows by implication. MS_3,5.42.
This has been understood: "When that [person] is invited, [the other] says, 'Be invited'.
Now, there is a doubt regarding the response: is the response a worldly one, or is it this very [Vedic formula]? What is the prima facie view?
This [formula] is Vedic.
It has been applied to the question. One might think that some other worldly response ought to follow. This being the case, we say: in this instance, this very [response] is the answer.
But is it not the case that "upahūyasva" (be invited) possesses the characteristic marks of a question?
It is said in reply: that which precedes it—

The phrase "upahūta" (invoked) is capable of being a response; therefore, it will serve the function of a response. He says: this traditional recitation is inverted, for the question ought to come first.
Then it is said by way of a reply:
"By implication; first there will be the performance of the reply, for the purpose (artha) is stronger than the sequence."
NOTES:
*{3/534: E2,4: "upahvayasva" (you should invite)}* *{3/535: E2,4: "with this [formula] he should request permission"}*
"*{3/536: E2,4: upahvayasva}" [is used] because of the collection of those [cups] that have a single vessel. MS_3,5.43 //

This is doubted: should anyone at all be asked for permission, or only those who share the same vessel (*samānapātra*)? Since no specific distinction is stated, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it may be anyone; to this, it is said: "That request for permission should indeed be made by those who share the same vessel. Why? Because the request for permission is an auxiliary element (*aṅga*) here.
This is the form of requesting permission:
when one person desires to do what ought to be done by another, he says, "Please grant me your consent," as in the case of eating together.

Or, one who desires to practice [austerities] such as eating from a single vessel makes his mind conform to that of another. This is simply not possible with various vessels, for in that case, it is not something to be done by one person, nor does another desire to do so.
Or, in the case of an object such as eating together (*sahabhojana*), etc. [this would be impossible].
He shows honor. However, when the Soma is common to all and must be prepared in a single vessel, an equal division follows as a matter of course;
in that case, if it were drunk without being divided, it might happen that one person drinks what was intended for another to drink.
In such a situation, the act of requesting permission is possible.
"You should drink half, and I shall drink the other half. It is possible that I might drink more or less; you should grant me permission for that."

"Or, while drinking from a single vessel with you, I might obstruct the clarity of your mind"— this is a possible request for permission. Therefore, this [rule] should apply specifically to those who drink from a single vessel.
The portion to be consumed is removed by the removal of the *yājyā* verse, just like the *pravara*. (MS 3.5.44)
There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice;

therein, regarding the seasonal offerings (ṛtuyāga), it is heard in the scripture: "The sacrificer [performs] the *yājyā*; he gives the direction, 'O Hotṛ, recite the offering prayer for this,' and having himself performed [the ritual action], he sacrifices. When he sacrifices himself, then there arises a doubt: does he have a portion to consume (*bhakṣa*)?

"It does not exist. To this it is said: when the *yājyā* verse is removed, the act of consuming (*bhakṣaṇa*) would not be removed; rather, the consumption would belong to the *hotṛ* priest alone, and not to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Why?
For the *yājyā* is one thing and the consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*) is another;
and when one thing is removed, another is not thereby removed. Just as, even when that very *yājyā* is removed, the *pravara* is not removed.
"This case is likewise.
But [it may be objected]: "He utters the *vaṣaṭ* over the *yājyā*";
where there is a *yājyā*, [there the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered]."
In that case, there is the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance;
where there is the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, there is also the consumption. Not so. [351] {3/3}
Thus it is said; however, the *vaṣaṭ*-call is not a constituent part of the *yājyā* such that it would be included by the mention of the *yājyā*.
As for the statement, "He utters the *vaṣaṭ*-call over it," [it refers to something else].
Even when another person is performing the recitation, the Hotṛ priest shall utter the *vaṣaṭ* call over it;
for, according to the scriptural injunction, there is the removal of the *yājyā* verse, but not the removal of the *vaṣaṭ* call. This is as far as the scriptural statement extends.
It is indeed based on scriptural authority,
for the statement has that very [subject] as its object.
Or rather, [the sacrificer is the agent] because of the arrival of the cause for sacrificing. (MS 3.5.45)
Or rather, the consumption [of the portion] should belong to the sacrificer. Why?
Because of the arrival of the cause;
for the cause of the consumption is the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
And he [the Hotṛ] arrives when the *yājyā* verse is being recited; for thus it is heard in scripture: "He utters the *vaṣaṭ* over the *yājyā*.
But has it not been said that even while the *yājyā* is being employed by the sacrificer, the Hotṛ utters the *vaṣaṭ*? This is not a valid solution.
One must offer without drawing breath;
the sacrifice is performed with the *vaṣaṭ* call, not by the *yājyā* mantra alone. Therefore, the sacrificer must not draw breath until the *vaṣaṭ* call.

If another were to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call, the sacrificer would be excluded [from the result] and would not perform the sacrifice. Furthermore, he is enjoined to perform the sacrifice when it is actually to be performed, not merely for the purpose of reciting the *yājyā*.
This is because the injunction "having sat down himself, he sacrifices" prescribes the performance of the sacrifice together with its auxiliary parts (*sāṅga*) by means of sitting down.
NOTES:
*{3/543: Even though it is being employed, the Hotṛ [is not]}* *{3/544:
E2,4 omit "adhi"}*
Because it has already begun, there is no cessation of the excellent [tradition].

Now, as for what was said—that just as the *pravara* (the ancestral lineage invocation) is not removed, so too the *bhakṣa* (the consumption of the portion) is not removed—it is replied: the *pravara* is not removed because it is impossible;
for how could that which has already passed away be removed from the *hotṛ* priest?

If performed at an inappropriate time, it would be deficient for the sacrificer; and that which is deficient cannot accomplish its purpose in any way. Nor is it obtained here by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer). Now, if it is argued: "That which is possible is obtained by the *codaka*, but that which is impossible is not."
"It has not been attained" means that this is the natural state; here there is the prescription of what was previously non-existent,
exactly as it has been stated.

If such a thing can be done, it should be performed; if it cannot be done, it should be performed wherever it is possible. It is not to be performed where it would be defective. Therefore, it is logical that there should be no omission of the *pravara*, but not of the *bhakṣa*.
NOTES:
The fruit-cup (phalacamasa) is a contingent modification of the consumption [of Soma], because of its connection with the Vedic text. MS 3.5.47.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard: "If he should officiate for a Rājanya or a Vaiśya,
and if he should desire to consume the Soma..."

"Having brought three Nyagrodha fruits, having ground them, and having mixed them with curd, one should offer that as the *bhakṣa* (consecrated food) to him, not Soma. In this regard, there is a doubt: is the *phalacamas* a modification of the *bhakṣa*, or is it a modification of the sacrifice (*ijyā*)? Does the meaning of the text imply "one should consume the *phalacamas*," or does it mean "one should sacrifice with the *phalacamas*"?
What is the prima facie view?
The fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) is a contingent modification of the act of consumption,
because it forms a single syntactical unit with the scripturally enjoined act of consuming.
"One should offer him the portion to eat"— there is no word stating "one should sacrifice with that";
therefore, it is a modification of the act of eating.
NOTES:
*{3/547: E1 provides "kiṃ phalacamasaṃ bhakṣayed ity arthaḥ" (the meaning is: "Should one eat the fruit-cup?")}.

Or rather, [the statement] "one should sacrifice with the fruit-cup" (uta phalacamasena yajeta) constitutes a modification of the sacrifice (ijyāvikāra), because the consecration has that [sacrifice] as its purpose. (MS 3.5.48)
Or rather, the fruit-cup is a modification of the sacrifice; the meaning is that one should sacrifice with the fruit-cup.
How so? Because this act of consuming is for the purpose of consecrating the Soma.

If the consumption of the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) were for the purpose of consecrating the fruit-cup itself, it would be purposeless, because the fruit-cup has no other application. If, on the other hand, the consumption were the primary act, then the restatement (*anuvāda*), "not Soma," would not be possible. However, if it is a modification of the sacrifice (*ijyāvikāra*)—
If that were the case, then the preparation of the *phalacamasa* would be logically consistent. Therefore, it is a modification of the sacrifice (*ijyāvikāra*).

[The opponent] asks: "How can there be a modification of the sacrifice when there is no connection with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice)? It is replied: There is indeed a connection with the root *yaj*. How so? If [the rule applies to] a *rājanya*... [text fragment]

Or, if one were to officiate at a sacrifice for a Vaiśya, one should crush the shoots of a Nyagrodha tree and offer that to him as food; it is understood that this is for the purpose of officiating at the sacrifice. For, when there is a connection with "food," the preceding [action] does not connect with the subsequent [one].

If one should wish to consecrate the Soma by means of consumption, one might think it could be consecrated by means of Nyagrodha-stems; therefore, there is no connection with consumption. For the sacrifice is the subject under discussion, and [the stems] will be connected with that;
thus, there will be no fault.

[Objection: Is it not understood from the statement "one should offer the *bhakṣa* to him" that it is a means for consumption (*bhakṣa-sādhana*), and not a means for sacrifice (*yāga-sādhana*), because of its immediate proximity to the word *bhakṣa*? [Reply: It is said: since the expressed connection would otherwise be meaningless, it is stated that it is connected with the context (*prakṛta*). But how is there a connection with consumption? For that which... [text fragment]
The sacrificial substance is to be consumed,
and that [consumption] occurs by virtue of the *codaka* (extended injunction);
therefore, it obtains a connection with consumption.
And by means of the connection with eating, the very connection with sacrifice is indicated: if one sacrifices with that [substance], then it becomes an object of consumption.
Therefore, from the mention of "eating" (bhakṣa), it is understood even more clearly that he is impelled by it;
this is the conceptualization of an exclusion. The meaning is: "one should offer the eating to him," or "one should make him the eater."
One should act in such a way that he becomes a consumer [of the offering],
provided that he is indeed worshipped by means of it.
Therefore, this [fruit-cup] becomes the sacrificial food; for that reason, one should sacrifice with it.
(Note:
This means "one should sacrifice with the fruit-cup.")
*{3/550: E2,4: the form of sacrifice}* *{3/551: E2,4 omits "or"}* *{3/552: E2,4: if}*
From the oblation.

There is a statement regarding a specific modification of the oblation: "When they offer the other cups, then, having taken [a portion] from this one with a young blade of darbha grass, he offers it. Since there is a modification of the sacrifice (*ijyāvikāra*), the mention of the "young blade of darbha grass" as an accessory (*guṇa*) in relation to the act of offering is appropriate. Therefore, this too is a modification of the sacrifice.
And because they are simultaneous with the cups (*camasa*), [the Soma] belongs to those [cups]. (MS 3.5.50)
"When they draw up other cups,
then they draw up this cup"— this observation of the drawing up is appropriate when there is a modification of the sacrifice (*ijyā*),
not when there is a modification of the consumption (*bhakṣa*). Therefore, it is also a modification of the sacrifice.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark. (MS 3.5.51)
Moreover, we see from this that it is a modification of the *ijyā* (sacrifice). Why? Because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*). What is the indicative mark?
It is the restatement of the prohibition of *soma*.
One should offer him the sacrificial food (bhakṣa), not the Soma;
since there is a modification of the sacrifice (ijyāvikāra), the Soma is not consumed. Therefore, we see that there is a modification of the sacrifice.
Because of the commonality among those who follow after.
In the Rājasūya sacrifice there is the Daśapeya;
therein it is heard: "A hundred Brāhmaṇas consume the Soma; ten by ten they approach each individual cup. Here, regarding the cup of the Rājanya, a doubt arises: what [is the case]?
Should the kṣatriyas approach him, or the brahmins? What is the prima facie view? That it is the kṣatriyas. How so?

The number of those who should approach is prescribed by the rule: "Ten by ten, they should each approach one cup. For the single Kṣatriya caste, the number ten is prescribed. That same Kṣatriya caste remains; therefore, ten Kṣatriyas should indeed approach that cup. In this way, there are one hundred Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas. Among them, the word "one hundred" is a restatement (*anuvāda*). And it has the form of a restatement, as in "they consume one hundred. Therefore, the Kṣatriyas should approach the Kṣatriya's cup. Some say: "The consumption [of the Soma] in a single cup belongs to both Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas."
"It is contradictory. That is not a fault,
for it is not heard in scripture that "they become defiled by Soma."
Or rather, it refers to Brahmins, because the word is used in the same sense.
Or rather, the Brāhmaṇas should follow after the Rājanya’s cup. How so?

The injunction, "A hundred Brāhmaṇas consume the Soma," by means of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), expresses a number pertaining specifically to the Brāhmaṇas. Therefore, there are a hundred Brāhmaṇas;
for the purpose of their consumption, as they approach, ten are assigned to each individual cup. Consequently, from among the hundred Brāhmaṇas, ten Brāhmaṇas should follow after the Rājanya’s cup.
Thus. NOTES:
[The word *sarva*] refers to all objects, because it is not the subject under discussion. MS 3.6.1.
Without reference to any specific context, it is said: "He whose *sruva* ladle is made of *khadira* wood cuts [the portion] with the very essence of the *chandas*;
his oblations become full of essence. And: "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood does not hear an evil report," and so forth.
In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the *khadira* nature [prescribed] for the *sruva*,...
The *pālāśa* wood [is prescribed] for the *juhū* ladle;
does it apply to the archetype (*prakṛti*) alone, or to both the archetype and the modified form (*vikṛti*)? What is the prima facie position?
It is for the sake of all [the archetypes and ectype], because it is not within the context [of a specific ectype];
such a rule is for the sake of both the archetype and the ectype. Why?
Because it is not within the context [of a specific ectype].
They are not heard in connection with any specific context;
therefore, by virtue of the direct statement, they would apply everywhere.
Or rather, it belongs to the archetype, because it has not been restated.
Or rather, the vessels mentioned as independent injunctions (anārabhyādhīta) should find their place in the archetype (prakṛti). Why?
Because of the avoidance of redundancy;
in this way, there will be no redundancy. What is the fault in [admitting] redundancy?

We say that it is impossible: for whatever exists both in the archetype (*prakṛti*) and in the ectype (*vikṛti*) exists in the archetype; and if it exists in the archetype, it reaches the ectype by the force of the injunction (*codaka*) alone.
Therefore, it does not require an *anārabhyavidhi* (independent injunction). Consequently, because there is no such requirement, the *anārabhyavidhi* does not enjoin anything therein;
thus we say that it pertains solely to the purpose of the archetype (*prakṛti*). Let that [injunction] be set aside, as it is already established by the explicit statement (*vacana*).

Because it does not belong to the specific context [of a particular sacrifice], it is stated that it applies only to the archetype and its modifications (*prakṛti-vikṛti*). As for what is obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), since it is already established by the *anārabhyavidhi* (a general rule not connected to a specific rite), it does not require the *codaka*. Therefore, the *codaka* will effect the transfer with the exception of the *anārabhyavidhi*;
for the quality of being made of *khadira* wood in the *sruva* ladle is directly established by the *anārabhyavidhi* statement itself.

In the case of a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), [the rule] is established by an inferential injunctive statement (*codakavākya*). And that which is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) is more powerful than that which is inferential. Therefore, the unattached injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*) pertains to both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modified sacrifice.
NOTES:
If it is argued that this is because [it is so] observed (*darśanāt*)... [MS 3.6.4]

If the general injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*) is stronger than the transfer injunction (*codaka*), then once [the rite] has been established by the general injunction, it does not require the transfer injunction; and when the modified rite (*vaikṛta*) is thus devoid of requirement, the transfer injunction does not apply at all. In that case, the observation of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth would be entirely untenable.
Furthermore, the *prayāja*s and other such elements are seen in certain cases, as in the injunction: "At each *prayāja*, one offers a *kṛṣṇala*.
Now, [one might argue that] the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) is more powerful.
Therefore, this view is tenable. Consequently, the injunction not stated in a specific context (anārabhyavidhi) pertains to the meaning of the base form (*prakṛtyartha*).
NOTES:
[The opponent's view: "Because they have the same purpose as the injunction, [the subsidiary acts] are stronger. (MS 3.6.5)

It does not have the sense of the *prakṛti* (archetype); we say it has all meanings (*sarvārtha*), because it is recited outside of any specific context (*aprakaraṇa*). As for what was said—that there is no *codaka* (transference of details) for that which is already satisfied by an independent injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*)—[that is not so].

That is not tenable. For an independent injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*) does not satisfy the expectancy of a mandatory rule (*codanā*); for when the mandatory rule is already established, the quality of being made of *khadira* wood cannot be enjoined by an independent injunction with respect to the *sruva* ladle. If the mandatory rule is absent, the independent injunction itself does not exist;
nor does the independent injunction bring about the *sruva* ladle.
And its [the ladle's] quality of being made of khadira wood. Why?

Because of the unity of the injunction. For the injunction has a single purpose, namely: "He whose sruva-ladle is made of khadira wood. And here, neither the sruva-ladle nor its quality of being made of khadira wood are both enjoined.
This word [“sruva”] expresses that the *sruva* ladle is made of *khadira* wood, and that [quality] is obtained through the *codaka* (extended application). Therefore, the *codaka* exists;

for, because the sentence of the independent injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*) is directly perceived, it causes [the quality] to apply to others while excluding that [specific case]. Thus, the independent injunction serves the purpose of both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*).
NOTES: *{3/561: E2: sarvārtham, E4: sarvārthe, E6: sarvārtha}*
If it is argued that there is origination, [we reply: MS 3.6.6.
If you think thus: "The origin of these [subsidiaries] is similar to that of the primary injunctions;

in the primary rite, the subsidiaries are stated both concisely and in detail—the concise statement being 'he offers five fore-offerings' (*pañca prayājān yajati*), and the detailed statement being 'he offers the *samidh* [fore-offerings]' and so forth; here too, there is a detailed expansion such as 'for whom a ladle made of *khadira* wood exists'."
The summary is as follows: "For whom the *sruva* ladle is of such a form. Such a rule is observed in the archetype (*prakṛti*);

this one is also of such a form; therefore, it is archetypal. This is an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭānumāna*). Therefore, the unattached injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*) has the archetype as its purpose.
NOTES:
*{3/563: Tait.S. 2.6.1.1}* No, because they are equal. MS_3,6.7 //
This is not so. For an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) of this kind is not a means of proof;

there is merely a similarity here with the procedure of the archetype (*prakṛti*), but there is no authoritative evidence that this [specific detail] occurs in the archetype. Furthermore, even in the case of the ectype (*vikṛti*), whether in brief or in detail...
The constituent parts are prescribed;
"he offers three oblations" is the summary; "Thou art the support of this support, O gods."

Therefore, even the modified (*vaikṛta*) injunctions are equal to those not specifically prescribed for a particular context (*anārabhyavidhi*); consequently, this is not a valid reason for [the rule's] application to the archetype (*prakṛti*).
NOTES:
*{3/564: E2,4: by way of summary and detail} *{3/565:
of the modified form}*
But because the purpose of the injunction is fulfilled in its entirety, and because there is a contradiction with the primary meaning, the sense of the root [is what is intended].

The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position. We maintain that this injunction not stated in connection with a specific context does not apply to all rites; rather, it is for the sake of the archetype (*prakṛti*). Why?
Because of the completeness of the purpose of the injunction.

The *codaka* (archetypal injunction) extends the entire [procedure]; it does not [extend] a modified (*vaikṛta*) and unprecedented (*apūrva*) rite by means of an isolated injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*), for that [latter] is already devoid of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*).

For that [modification] applies to the vessels by virtue of that statement, not to the sacrifices. The sacrifices, because they are connected with the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the original injunctions (*codanā*), depend upon the archetype (*prakṛti*);

they enter into syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with it. And the archetypal elements are able to render those [sacrifices] free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣīkartum*), for they are the prescriptive rules (*vidhi*). Therefore, the extended application (*codaka*) must necessarily be produced. If it is produced, then—

There is no purpose served by an unattached injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*). Furthermore, even if it were to apply due to the absence of a specific context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, it could not be connected with a modified sacrifice (*vaikṛta-yajña*). Therefore, the unattached injunction is not connected with a modified ritual act. Of that modified primary [act]...
In the event of a conflict between an unattached injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*) as a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) and [the rule] "or in the archetype" (*prakṛtau vā*),
[the former prevails] by virtue of the force of the extended application (*codaka*).

Since the ordinary remainder of the sentence would otherwise apply, there will be no "unattached injunction" (anārabhyavidhi). Therefore, the unattached injunction is for the sake of the archetype (prakṛti).
"In the case of a conflict, however, [the rule] would apply to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) because of the specific context. (MS 3.6.9)
Without reference to anything specific, the number of *sāmidhenī* verses is traditionally taught: "One should recite seventeen *sāmidhenīs*.
In this regard, there is a doubt: does this apply to the archetype (*prakṛti*)?
"And in the modification? What is the prima facie view?
By the previous reasoning, it is established that [the rule applies] to the archetype;
and in the archetype, the number fifteen is prescribed.
"Therefore, it is an option. This being the position reached, we reply: such an injunction would apply only to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*). Why?

Because the archetype (*prakṛti*) has no further expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) due to its fifteen-fold nature (*pāñcadaśya*). But was it not said that there will be an option? There is no option because of the specific context (*prakaraṇaviśeṣāt*), owing to the fifteen-fold nature.

From Viṣamaśāsana: however, in the case of a modification (*vikṛti*), having set aside the fifteen-fold nature (*pāñcadaśya*) which is based on inference, the seventeen-fold nature (*sāptadaśya*) is established by means of a direct injunction (*pratyakṣa-anārabhyavidhi*). And this has been stated without contradiction;
it will be subsumed under the performance-injunction (*prayogavacana*). Therefore, that which belongs to this class is for the sake of the modification.
NOTES: *{3/573: Ai.Br.
1.1}* But that which is contingent applies to the archetype.
That modification [of the body] results from a particular conjunction.
It is prescribed in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices: "One desiring cattle should fetch [the water] with a milking vessel.
Likewise, regarding the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) in the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, it is heard:
"One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should make it of *bilva* wood."
Regarding matters of this kind, there is a doubt: is it to be applied to the archetype (*prakṛti*) or to the ectype (*vikṛti*)? What is the prima facie view?
Regarding the phrase "in the modification" (*vikṛtau*):

the archetypal sacrifices (*prakṛti*) are already satisfied by means of another vessel and sacrificial post. This being the prima facie view, we reply: the occasional element (*naimittika*) finds its place in the archetype, because it is enjoined in connection with a specific occasion (*nimitta*).
The *khadira*, *pālāśa*, and *rauhitaka* woods, as well as the *camasa* cup, are mentioned without distinction;
however, the *godohana* and the *bilva* wood are specifically prescribed.
And a specific injunction overrides a general injunction. Context is general.
The connection with a specific indicative mark (*nimitta*) constitutes a distinction;
that which is obtained by way of a general rule is understood indirectly through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), whereas that which is obtained by way of a specific rule [is understood directly].
That is directly stated by the Vedic text, and direct statement is stronger than indirect indication;
moreover, what is directly perceived is stronger than what is mediated. Therefore, it should apply only to the archetype.
NOTES:
The establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya) is for the purpose of the sacrifice, because of the context.
There are the Pavamāna sacrifices: "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pavamāna,
to Agni Pāvaka,
and to Agni Śuci."
In the context of those [rites], it is recited in the traditional text: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in the spring.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is the establishment of the fires for the sake of the Pavamāna offerings?
Or rather, "no. What is the prima facie view?
That it is for the purpose of the *iṣṭi*. Why? Because of the context (*prakaraṇa*).
In the context of those [offerings], it is heard in scripture: "Therefore, for that purpose.
Or rather, it is not so, because those [rites] have that as their purpose. (MS 3.6.12)
For the Pavamāna sacrifices have the fires as their purpose;
if the fires were for the sake of the sacrifices, then the establishment of the fires (agnyādheya) would benefit the sacrifices. However, the sacrifices are themselves fruitless.
For that reason, even the *agnyādheya* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires) would be fruitless. But how can the *pavamāneṣṭis* have the fires as their purpose?

Precisely because they themselves lack a purpose, whereas the fires possess one. Even though the *iṣṭis* are things to be brought into being (*bhāvayitavyā*), they should be performed for the sake of the fires which already exist (*bhūta*). Therefore, the *agnyādheya* is for the purpose of the *pavamāneṣṭis*.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark. (MS 3.6.13)
It indicates the indicative mark (*liṅga*), namely that the *pavamāna*-offerings have fire as their purpose. What is the indicative mark?
"This animal, once established, indeed decays, which is the fire."
Therefore, one should offer these very oblations of the Agnyādheya at the end of a year;
by this he does not decay, and by this he makes him new again; thus it is not a subtle matter.
NOTES:
*{3/580: E2,4: And it shows the indicative mark (liṅga):}* *{3/581:
E2,4: Therefore, in this way}*
That is for the sake of the original context, just as other independent injunctions (*ārambhavāda*) [function]. (MS 3.6.14)

Regarding this *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires), there is a doubt: does it serve the purpose of the archetype (*prakṛti*), or is it for the purpose of all rituals (*sarvakarman*)? What is the prima facie view? It is said: it serves the purpose of the archetype. How so?
Just as other uninitiated injunctions (*anārabhyavāda*) pertain to the archetype (*prakṛti*), for that very same reason;
or rather, because the offering of the *adhāna* (fire-consecration) belongs to its own specific time, it serves all purposes. (MS 3.6.15)
The establishment [of the fires] is for the sake of all ritual acts. What is the meaning?

The meaning is that the establishment of the fire-substances is for the sake of all ritual acts, not for the sake of the archetype (prakṛti). It is not heard as being dependent upon the archetypes. Not [372].

Furthermore, in this case, there exist direct scriptural statements (*śruti*) and other means of proof that establish its status as a subordinate element (*aṅga*). In other *anārabhyavāda* passages, once the status as a subordinate element is known from another source, an inquiry follows—namely, whether these elements are subordinate to the archetype (*prakṛti*) or the ectype (*vikṛti*). Therefore, in those cases, such an inquiry is appropriate. But here, there is no reason for it to be a subordinate element.
Therefore, the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) is prompted by the fires themselves, not prompted by ritual acts;
for the fires exist for the sake of all ritual acts.
Thus, it is said that [the word] "all" (sarva) signifies every object.
Furthermore, its own time is prescribed; however, that [time] need not be prescribed.

When the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma takes place, then this [rite] must be performed; and at that time, it is spring. Likewise, when the performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa takes place, then it must be performed; and at that time, it is either the full moon or the new moon day. However, for the sake of what is not part of the archetype (aprakṛti), it should not be performed during the performance of the archetype (prakṛti).
In that case, the expression of time is appropriate. Therefore, it does not refer to the meaning of the base [word].
(Note:
*All the fires, however, have all ritual actions as their purpose.*)
For these [offerings], Agni should be the deity by default, just as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings.
There are the Pavamāna-iṣṭis, beginning with "To Agni Pavamāna," and so forth.
In this regard, there is a doubt: should the Pavamāna-iṣṭis be performed in a fire that has been consecrated by the Pavamāna-iṣṭis, or not? What is the prima facie view?
Indeed, for those Pavamāna sacrifices, the fire consecrated by the Pavamāna sacrifices should be understood as the archetype (prakṛti). Why?
Because of the force of the extended injunction (codaka), just like the fore-sacrifices (prayāja).
Just as the *prayāja* offerings occur by virtue of the extended injunction (*codaka*),
so too should the fires be consecrated by the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices.
Or rather, it is not so, because those [mantras] have that as their purpose. (MS 3.6.17)
The *veṣṭi* consecration should not apply to the *pavamāneṣṭis* of the sacred fires. Why?
Because those [consecrations] are for that purpose.

It has been stated that those Pavamāna sacrifices are for the purpose of consecrating the fire (agni). And whatever is indeed a subordinate constituent (aṅga) is grasped by the extended application (codaka). Furthermore, the consecration of the Pavamāna sacrifices is prompted by the fire, not prompted by the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa);

therefore, it is not drawn [to the modified sacrifice] by the extended application. Moreover, the Pavamāna sacrifices require a primary model (prakṛti) that is devoid of sacrificial consecrations, because at that stage the Pavamāna sacrifices themselves have not yet been prescribed.
NOTES:
The ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice is common to all [the deities], because there is no distinction in the context. (MS 3.6.18)

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma—as it is said: "When one who has been initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma"—likewise, there are the Savanīya and the Anūbandhya animals; and there exist the ritual duties pertaining to these animals.
The preliminary rites, the leading forward, the inexhaustible [offering], the binding,

the tying to the sacrificial post, the immolation, the dismemberment, and so forth— do these apply to all three, namely the Agniṣomīya, the Savanīya, and the Anubandhya, or only to the Agniṣomīya or the Savanīya?
Or is it only for the Agniṣomīya animal? What is the prima facie view? Because there is no distinction, it applies to all animals. How is there no distinction?
Because all animals are mentioned within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
Because they fall within that same context, all the ritual rules pertaining to the sacrificial animal (*paśudharma*) are connected [to it],
and there is no distinction among them in that regard.

This being the case, we reply: these ritual details should belong to the Savanīya [offering], for the procedure regarding the animal sacrifice would be common to all, were there no distinction within the context (prakaraṇa). However, there is indeed a distinction within the context.
In the context of the Savanīya offerings, the characteristics of the animal sacrifice are recited:
"The animal dedicated to Agni is to be offered at the Agniṣṭoma, for the Agniṣṭoma belongs to Agni; the animal dedicated to Indra and Agni is to be offered at the Ukthya."
For the Ukthya sacrifices belong to Indra and Agni. At the Ṣoḍaśin sacrifice, a bull dedicated to Indra is to be offered;
for the bull belongs to Indra, and the Ṣoḍaśin belongs to Indra. At the Atirātra sacrifice, a ewe dedicated to Sarasvatī is to be offered;
for Sarasvatī is indeed Speech.
Since the animal rites are prescribed by nature, it follows that [the offering] must belong to the *savanīya* due to its context.
NOTES:
And because of the position [of the word], it belongs to the preceding [section]. (MS 3.6.19) [Citations: *paśudharmaiḥ* (E2,4); ŚB 4.2.5.14]
As for what was said— that [the mantras] are for the sake of the *savanīya* due to the context— we accept that;
however, they belong to the *agnīṣomīya* by virtue of their sequence, for its sequence is indeed recited on the day of preparation (*aupavasathya*).
Therefore, [the rule] applies to both as well.
But for some, the prior mention in that context on the following day is for the purpose of indicating a subordinate quality (guṇa).
For some reciters of the Vedic branches, there is a scriptural injunction for the *savanīya* animals [to be offered] on the following day;

with reference to that, this repeated mention of them is for the purpose of a subordinate element (*guṇa*). But what is the subordinate element for the sake of which this scriptural statement exists? It is said: having enumerated the animals—

"Just as a fish, when unrecognized, shakes off the people [who catch it], so too these, when not being recognized, shake off the people"— having thus stated the fault in their lack of recognition, [the text continues].
By means of these questions—"How do [the sacrificers] perform the Soma-pressings so as to possess animals?"—the subsidiary rite of the offering of the omentum (vapāpracāra) is enjoined;
this scriptural passage exists for that purpose, because it forms a single syntactical unit with the offering of the omentum. What follows from this?

If this is so, it is not the case that the animal-rites (paśudharma) belong to the Savanīya offerings by virtue of the context (prakaraṇa); rather, by virtue of the sequence (krama), they belong specifically to the Agniṣomīya. What, then, is that scriptural mention (āmnāna)?
Having drawn the Āśvina cup and having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-twisted cord, he dedicates the Savanīya animal to Agni.
He shakes off [the dust],
or [he does not].
[The text reads] "paśum" (cattle), while E6 reads...
If it is argued that this is an injunction regarding the time for the Savanīya animal which has been postponed.
This is not the case— that they serve solely the purpose of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice—
because, by virtue of the context (prakaraṇa), they serve the purpose of the Savanīya;
the recitation on the preceding day is for the sake of its injunction.
The statement regarding the Āśvina cup is for the purpose of prescribing a specific time. How so?

By means of that performance of the omentum-offering (*vapāpracāra*), this time is prescribed for what has been drawn out; since the performance of the omentum-offering is enjoined at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), the immolation of the animal (*paśvālambha*) would also follow there. Since an uncertainty regarding the time would otherwise arise, [the text specifies it].

By the statement "having taken the Āśvina draught," only the time is prescribed. The phrase "the sacrificial post with the threefold cord" is a restatement (anuvāda). For otherwise, the time for the encircling of the post would be what is being prescribed.

And regarding the *upākaraṇa* (the ritual act of bringing the animal forward): since multiple qualities would have to be enjoined therein, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, the characteristics of the animal (*paśudharma*) are for the sake of the *savanīya* [animal].
*Note:
{3/596: E2,4: "Having bound it around, he performs the upākaraṇa."}*
[The reason] is not [valid], because it is only a part [of the subject]. (MS 3.6.22)

This is not so; these [acts] belong solely to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice according to their sequence. For the mention of the time of the Āśvina cup is for the purpose of injunction. If this were for the purpose of a subordinate quality (guṇa), the sentence would be split;

it is not for the purpose of an injunction. Indeed, an injunction regarding time is not possible for that which has been displaced by the performance of the omentum-offering (vapāpracāra). For the substance of the omentum is only a part [of the animal], and therefore, because of its direct connection (saṃnipātin) with the refinement of the omentum, [it cannot be displaced].
There is no introductory rite by way of excellence.
If it is argued that this is so because of the purpose. (MS 3.6.23)

He said: "In that case, the time for the one who has been elevated is prescribed by the purpose. For it is heard in the scripture: 'Having covered [the wound] with his fist, he should remain seated until the offering of the omentum (*vapā*). On the previous day, having covered the wound with his fist, he would not be able to remain seated for such a long period of time."
He must necessarily perform such acts as eating and moving about.
Not so, because of the contradiction with the Vedic revelation. (MS 3.6.24)
This is not so;
it would be thus, and there would be no contradiction with the Śruti.

It will be covered with a handful of grass or a handful of leaves. Now, does the verb *āste* (he sits) necessarily mean "sitting down"? No; it is not restricted to sitting down alone, as it is also seen in the sense of remaining indifferent or inactive. For example: "He remains having taken possession of his household duties," or "He remains having taken possession of his fields"—it occurs even in the absence of the act of sitting.

Upon the cessation of the activity. Here too, having covered [the vessel] with a handful of grass or a handful of leaves, it will remain set aside until the offering of the omentum (*vapā*). Therefore, the mention of the time of the Āśvina cup is for the purpose of an injunction;
the characteristics of the animal sacrifice do not belong to the context of the *savanīya* offerings.
Therefore, they are not for the sake of the Savanīya offerings. (376) {3/601} NOTES: *{3/599: In case of conflict with direct Vedic statement (śruti)}*
But [the result] follows from the standing position, because the preceding refinement (*saṃskāra*) is for that purpose; [this is established] by the very fact of sitting down. (MS 3.6.25)

Since there is no *prakaraṇa* (contextual setting) for the *savanīya* offerings, this being the case, by the very same reason as before, [the preparatory rite] must belong to the preceding *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice by virtue of its position (*sthāna*). This preparatory rite is prompted by the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*), not prompted by the *jyotiṣṭoma*;

for if it were prompted by the *jyotiṣṭoma*, there would be no distinction regarding the animals. For the animal sacrifices themselves are also capable of prompting the ritual duties (*dharma*) because they possess their own unique originality (*apūrvatva*).
And they possess a specific context; therefore, by virtue of that sequence, the properties belong to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark. (MS 3.6.26)
From this also we see that the animal-rites belong to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice. Why?
Because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga). There is an indicative mark for this meaning:
"They proceed with the omentum at the morning pressing."

The statement, "With the *puroḍāśa* at the midday pressing," indicates the *paśupuroḍāśa*. Otherwise, if all animals were subject to the same rule (*samānavidhāna*), the *puroḍāśa*— being for the purpose of consecrating the two deities Agni and Soma— would, by its own capacity, belong to the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice and not to the *savanīya*.

Because of the absence of those two deities, and because [the scripture] shows [this], therefore they are for the sake of the Agniṣomīya [sacrifice]. "There is no injunction for the sake of a subordinate element. (MS 3.6.27)
This is the subsequent section of the Sūtra.

[The opponent] says: "But is it not the case that the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) is for the purpose of covering the openings? We reply: "No," because there is no injunction for it as a subordinate element (guṇa).
It has been stated that, for the purpose of covering its defects, this is not an injunction (*codanā*), but rather an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Therefore, it serves to consecrate the deity;
consequently, it pertains to the purpose of the Agniṣomīya [sacrifice].
The observation of the *puroḍāśa* at the *savanīya* sacrifice is logically consistent,
but not if it were common to all. Therefore, the ritual duties pertaining to the animal belong specifically to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice.

*{3/602: E1 gives this subsequent sentence in brackets}* *{3/603: E2,4: regarding its being for the purpose of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice}* Because of the difference in time between the two milkings, the boiled [milk] would be unconnected [to the rite]. MS 3.6.28.
There is the evening milking,
and likewise there is the morning milking; however, the duties pertaining to the milking include the fetching of branches and the driving forth of the cows.
The *prasavana* [vessel],
the *godohana* [vessel], and so forth— do these serve the purpose of the evening milking,
or do they serve both purposes? What, then, is the prima facie position?
Of those two milkings, that which is performed on the Upavasatha day would be connected with the ritual details (*dharmas*) of the evening milking. Why?
Because they prescribe the sequence for the evening milking—beginning with the fetching of the branch (*śākhāharaṇa*)—on the very day of the Upavasatha;
therefore, the evening milking takes place on that same day. Consequently, by virtue of this sequence, the ritual details of the milking pertain to the purpose of the evening milking.
Or rather, because there is no distinction in the context, the scriptural injunction regarding time applies to that which is connected with it. (MS 3.6.29)
For the context (prakaraṇa) is common to both; just as it applies to curd, so too does it apply to milk.
Moreover, context is more powerful than sequence (krama).

Therefore, the rules regarding milking apply to both [the morning and the evening]. Furthermore, the milking for the evening is not prescribed on the preceding day; when then? On the following day. How so?
Thus they prescribe: "Sour milk for Indra on the new moon day;
milk for Indra on the new moon day," for on the new moon day both [are offered].
The [sacrificial act] is enjoined together with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*). This very evening milking (*sāyaṃdoha*) is performed on the previous day by implication;

for this is the inherent nature of curd (*dadhi*), that what is commenced on the previous day is completed on the following day. Therefore, the claim that the sequence of the evening milking is established [by the text] is simply not the case. Consequently, the properties of the milking (*dohadharmāḥ*) serve both purposes.
E2,4: both}*
In the same way, there is the scriptural injunction for the cups at another pressing.
There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma.
In that context, ten cups (grahas), beginning with the Aindravāyava, are prescribed for the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana).
Regarding them, certain ritual duties (dharmas) are heard: "The other cups are set down on a leveled spot."

"The cups are fixed when the [Soma] has been poured. "He cleanses the cup with the *daśāpavitra*. There are other cups at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*) and others at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*).
Regarding those cups belonging to the midday and third pressings, a doubt arises:
should the ritual duties pertaining to the cups be performed for all of them?
"Or rather, [they belong] to those cups which are at the morning pressing. What is the prima facie view?
They should belong to the cups of the morning pressing, for they follow its sequence.

Not for the others.
