This being the case, we reply: the mention of the cups (*graha*) in the other pressings—the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina*), and the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*)—must be understood in exactly the same way. For the context (*prakaraṇa*) is equal for all of them, wherein these ritual duties (*dharma*) are prescribed.

By the sentence, the properties are enjoined for the cup (*graha*) alone. Furthermore, sequence (*krama*) is weaker than sentence (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, the properties of the cup are for the sake of all [the cups].
*{3/609: And there is a doubt regarding the [cups] belonging to the third pressing}* *{3/610: For their sequence}* *{3/611: is recited in the sacred text}*
And the girdle [is also included] because of the observation of its indicative mark.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, as it is stated: "When one who has been initiated offers the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. In that context, a rope is mentioned, as well as the properties of the rope: "It is threefold."

"It is made of darbha grass" and "it must be made"—regarding this there is a doubt: are these ritual properties common to both the rope of the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice and the rope of the Savanīya animal sacrifice, or do they belong to the rope of the Agniṣomīya alone? What is the prima facie view?
On account of the context, [it might be argued that it belongs] to the rope of the Agniṣomīya [animal sacrifice].
This being the position reached, we reply: it is common to both. Why?
Because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga).
There is an indicative mark;
thus it says: "Having drawn the Āśvina cup and having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-strand rope, he dedicates the animal for Agni. [379]
In the context of the binding of the sacrificial animal at the *savanīya* sacrifice, the text shows the rope;
this observation is consistent if that rope is common [to all three animals], but not if it were intended solely for the *agnīṣomīya*.

Therefore, it would exclude the ordinary *parivyāṇa* (encircling) of the *savanīya*. And at the *savanīya*, there is another *parivyāṇa* that is not the original one, wherein a threefold nature (*trivṛttva*) is observed. How so?
"Having taken the *āśvina* cup and gone out, he encircles the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). In that case, if the rope were not common [to both], [the threefold nature would not apply].

[The text] prescribes the wrapping with a cloth, but it indicates the girdle. Therefore, the girdle is common [to all], and because of that commonality, its properties are also common. This commonality of the girdle is established through an indicative mark (*liṅga*). What, then, is the underlying principle here? It is said: [the girdle belongs] to the Agniṣomīya [animal sacrifice] by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*).
"From the sentence [it follows that it applies] to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) in general.
(Note:
*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 6.1.11.6)
The *savanīya* animal sacrifice belongs to the *pratiṣṭhās*,
as it is remote and unconnected with the others due to its proximity [to them]. (MS 3.6.32)
That which remains from afar belongs to the Jyotiṣṭoma, as in the section on the *aupasadānuvākyās* concerning the Aṃśu and Adābhya cups.
In this regard, there is a doubt: should the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the cups (*graha*) prescribed in the Jyotiṣṭoma be performed?
Or rather, "no. What is the prima facie view?
They should not be performed, because they are not present.
Just as, according to the statement "he mixes the offering for Mitra and Varuṇa with milk," the mixing is heard as applying only to the offering for Mitra and Varuṇa,
and not to all; so too, this collection of ritual properties applies only to those [rites] situated within the specific context.
"Not for all. (NOTES: *{3/616:
E2,4: 'śvadābhyau}*)
Or rather, it is connected [to the primary act], because the subsidiary is for the sake of that [primary] and is dependent upon it. (MS 3.6.33)
Or it may be associated with other dharmas; such would be its nature, even if it is not situated within the specific context. Why is that?

Since a direct statement (*vākya*) is stronger than the context (*prakaraṇa*). [Objection: But would those [rites] being performed elsewhere not be of benefit to the Jyotiṣṭoma? [Reply: It is said: they will indeed be of benefit, because the Aṃśu and Adābhya vessels are for its sake—that is, for the sake of the Jyotiṣṭoma.
This is the nature of the *graha* (cup):

being caused by the *graha*, it is an auxiliary to the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. Whatever *graha* assists the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, for all of that [the *graha*-dharmas] ought to exist. Therefore, the *graha*-dharmas must also be performed for the *Aṃśu* and *Ādābhya* cups.
NOTES:
*{3/619: E1 gives jyotiṣṭomārthatvāc in parentheses}* Because of the specific mention, it should be restricted [to that purpose]. // MS_3,6.34 //
As for what was said— that "one mixes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk"— that is correct, because there is a scriptural injunction regarding the mixing.
In that case, the specific context (prakaraṇa) sets aside the general rule (vyavasthāna). Here, however, it is the reverse:
there, the context applies to all cups (graha), while the syntactical statement (vākya) applies to specific ones; here, however, the syntactical statement applies to all cups.
The context pertains to specific [rites]. Therefore, these properties (dharmas) belong even to that which is not situated within the context.
It is the same in the context of the subsidiary parts of the fire-altar (agnyaṅga). MS 3.6.35.
Without reference to the fire-altar, it is said: "He lays down the *citriṇī* bricks;
he lays down the *vajriṇī* bricks; he lays down the *bhūteṣṭakā* bricks."
However, in the specific context (*prakaraṇa*), there are duties pertaining to bricks, such as:

"One should make the brick unbroken and not black," and likewise, "One should join the bricks with ashes. In this regard, a doubt arises: should these duties be performed for those [bricks] mentioned outside of the specific context?
Or rather, not so. What is the prima facie view?
They should not be performed. Why?
Because they are not present.
This being the position, it is replied:

an accessory of the fire-altar (*agni*) of such a kind should be treated exactly like that, just as the cups (*graha*) are. For syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*), since these bricks have the fire-altar as their purpose.
The occasional rite would have a different procedure because it is unequal [to the regular rite]. (MS 3.6.36)
In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard: "If he should officiate for a Rājanya or a Vaiśya,
and if he should desire to consume the Soma..."

"Having fetched Nyagrodha shoots, having ground them, and having mixed them with curds, one should offer that as food to him, not Soma. In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there are ritual properties (dharmas) pertaining to Soma, such as measuring, pouring down, purchasing, pressing, and so forth. In this regard, there is a doubt: are these ritual properties common to both the Soma and the fruit-cup (phalacamasa), or are they properties belonging solely to the Soma?

"But because the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) is a modification of that. The purpose of the deliberation in this section is whether those who desire specific results (*guṇakāma*) are entitled to perform the rite. What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It is obtained that they are equally entitled to the injunction (*samānavidhāna*), because there is no division from the context (*prakaraṇa*). This being the position reached:
It is said: An incidental [act] of this kind would have a different ritual procedure. Why? Because of inequality; the fruit-cup is not equal to the *soma*.
The *soma* is prescribed as a permanent (obligatory) element, whereas the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) is occasional (contingent). What follows from this?
If it is so, then the ritual details (*dharma*) also, being prescribed as permanent, cannot be performed as if they were non-permanent. If they are common [to both],...

In that case, an independent purpose would have to be enjoined. Furthermore, the *phalacamas* (fruit-cup) is contingent upon a specific occasion; as such, it adopts the characteristics (*dharma*) of the *soma*.
In that situation, those characteristics, being common [to both], would be said to be redundant. Therefore, they do not share the same injunction (*asamānavidhāna*).
*{3/623: E2,4 omit "vā"}* *{3/624: E1 provides "guṇakāmānāṃ pravṛttir vā prayojanam adhikaraṇacintāyāḥ" in parentheses}* *{3/625: E2,4: "evañjātīyakasamānavidhānam"}*
And the substitute is likewise [to be treated] in that same manner.

There is a substitute when the prescribed substance is unavailable, just as when rice (*vrīhi*) is unavailable, wild rice (*nīvāra*) is used. In this regard, there is a doubt: are the *nīvāras* subject to the same injunctions?
Or rather, "no. What is the prima facie view?
That the substitute is also like that, just as in the case of the Naimi... [382] {3/3}
The *ṣaṣṭikaudana* rite has a ritual procedure that is not identical with that of the *nitya* rite;
likewise, the substitute (*pratinidhi*) is not identical, because of their inequality. What is this inequality?
These [rites] are prescribed for *vrīhi* rice, not for *nīvāra* wild rice. This is the inequality:
they are prescribed for *vrīhi* rice.
The wild rice (*nīvāra*) grains [are used] by implication,
because the purpose is the same. (MS 3.6.38)
This is not so— the substitute does not have an identical injunction;
it should be like that,
just as it is heard in the scripture.
There is no relationship of original material (*prakṛti*) and modification (*vikāra*). Why?

Because the nature of rice (*vrīhitva*) is the cause for the properties of rice to apply to a specific individual instance of rice. Furthermore, it is not heard in scripture that the nature of wild rice (*nīvāratva*) takes the place of the nature of rice;

therefore, there is no relationship of original material and modification. How then do the properties apply to wild rice? It is said: those individual instances of rice which are delimited by the nature of rice—

They exist in the wild rice (nīvāra). Those ritual acts are performed for their sake; and this rule applies equally to those individual instances and to other instances residing in the cultivated rice (vrīhi). What is the equality? Both are characterized by the generic property of being rice (vrīhitva). Therefore, they are subject to the same injunction.
NOTES: {3/627: E2,4: na tadvat} And because it is not characterized by the scriptures. MS_3,6.39.
For this reason as well, there is no relationship of original and modification between the substitute and that which is prescribed by scripture. Why?
Because the substitute is characterized by its purpose;
for a substitute is employed on account of the purpose. And this cannot be understood through the purpose alone.

"In place of *vrīhi*-ness, *nīvāra*-ness occurs. Therefore, there is no relationship of original and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) between the substitute and that which is directly prescribed by scripture.
The mention of the quality is for the purpose of restriction.
Now, regarding a substitute that is prescribed by scriptural injunction (*śruta-pratinidhi*), is there an equal application of the ritual rules (*sāmāna-vidhya*) to it, or not?
For example: "If one should not find *soma*, one should press *pūtīka* plants."

We say that there is no commonality of ritual procedure (*asāmānavidhya*), for this is the opposite of what is not explicitly heard in the scripture. This being the position reached, it is said: the mention of the quality (*guṇa-śruti*) is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*);
here too, the substitute (*pratinidhi*) is characterized solely by its functional purpose (*artha-lakṣaṇa*).

In some cases, "when a substance similar to Soma is obtained, and a very similar substance has been obtained, one prescribes a slightly similar one; when another is to be substituted, something else is substituted in place of what was heard [in the scripture], but not as a substance for the sacrifice itself. **Notes:** This passage concerns the principle of substitution (*pratinidhi*) in Vedic ritual. When the prescribed primary material (such as Soma) is unavailable, a substitute may be used. The rule states that if a highly similar substance is available, one should not settle for a less similar one; rather, if a different substance must be substituted, it should be substituted in the specific place where the original was mentioned in the scriptural injunction, and not merely as a general sacrificial material. This ensures that the ritual integrity is maintained through the specific correspondence of the substitute to its designated position in the rite.
But the sacrificial forms (saṃsthās) have the same injunctions, because there is no distinction in their context (prakaraṇa).
There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice; therein the terminuses (saṃsthās) are enumerated: the Agniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, and so forth.

The *ṣoḍaśī* and the *atirātra*. In this regard, there are ritual duties (*dharma*) such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others. Concerning these, a doubt arises: were the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other duties taught with reference to the *jyotiṣṭoma* in all its forms (*saṃsthā*), or were they intended [only for specific ones]? What is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)?
The procedure is the same for all forms [of sacrifice]. Why?
Because there is no distinction in the context;
there is no difference in the context.
By this it would be known that [the rule] refers to the Agniṣṭoma as the archetype. Therefore, the various terminuses (saṃsthās) are subject to the same injunction.
*NOTE:
{3/630: E2,4,6: Or [it refers to] the Agniṣṭoma terminus}*
And there is a designation as if they were equal. (MS 3.6.42)
The designation occurs as if it were common to the entire context: "If it is an Agniṣṭoma, he offers the oblation; if it is an Ukthya, he anoints the enclosing-sticks;

if it is an Atirātra, he should proceed to the Havirdhāna shed while muttering this very Yajus. This is understood from the specific statement regarding the rite in all its states, even though it is a general [injunction].
That too applies only to one who is in every state. For if the rule were not common [to all],
it would apply only to that which has the *agniṣṭoma* as its concluding form.
It would be so. One need not mention the *agniṣṭoma* here;

for even when it is not mentioned, there is a connection with its ritual properties (*dharma*), because it is mentioned in all its states, and thus it constitutes the context (*prakaraṇa*) for all its states.
Thus we understand.
Moreover, it is heard in scripture: "At the Agniṣṭoma, one should sacrifice a goat dedicated to Agni; at the Ukthya, a second one dedicated to Indra and Agni."

The observation that "the third [animal] for Indra, the bull, is for the two Ṣoḍaśins" is consistent with a common rule (sāmānavidhya) regarding the second and third [sacrifices]. For in the Ukthya sacrifice there are two causes:
the Agniṣṭoma-stotra and the Ukthya-stotra; therein, there are two contingent animals, the one for Agni and [the others].

And because there is the [offering] to Indra and Agni (*aindrāgna*), the observation of a second [offering] is appropriate there. The same applies to the *ṣoḍaśin* and the *atirātra*. However, if there were a relationship of original form (*prakṛti*) and modification (*vikāra*), the offering to Agni (*āgneya*), which is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), would be sublated by the offerings to Indra and Agni and others that are directly heard in the text; in that case, the observation of a second [offering] and so forth would not be possible. Yet it does occur. Therefore, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are the properties of the Jyotiṣṭoma in all its states.
NOTES:
*{3/631: E2 and 4 give "na" in parentheses} *{3/633:
E2, 4: the section on that which exists in all states}*
But modifications [arise] when there is a connection with desire, because that [desire] is constant and equal [to all].

This is not so; they do not have the same injunction. What then? The Ukthya and other such forms would be modifications (*vikāra*), while the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other ritual duties (*dharma*) are recited [as common]. Why?
Because the Ukthya and other rites are heard of in connection with specific desires: "One desiring cattle should take the Ukthya;
one desiring vigor should praise with the Ṣoḍaśin;
one desiring progeny should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice with the Atirātra. A quality heard as being for a specific desire enters by modifying the permanent rite. How so?
In the case of an optional rite of this kind, the accomplishment of the fruit results from the accessory alone;
for instance, "one desiring cattle should take the Ukthya," not one desiring the Jyotiṣṭoma, nor one desiring the taking of the Ukthya itself.
The meaning is that one should grasp [the object] in the same manner as the animals do. How so? In this regard, a specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*) must necessarily be expected;
it is understood that, due to proximity, it is the procedure of the permanent rite (*nitya*) that is intended.
But how is it determined that this *itikartavyatā* (procedure) belongs to the obligatory (*nitya*) rite, and not rather to this very optional (*kāmya*) one?

"Or it is common. It is said: wherever there is a desire for a quality, there it occurs when the action is being accomplished, and not otherwise. That which invariably presents itself is the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) in that case.

Being in doubt as to whether that [excellence] belongs to the means (*sādhana*) or to the goal (*sādhya*), it must belong to the goal. For if it did not belong to the goal, it would not be connected with the means;
for in this way, that specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is enjoined by means of this [means].
"One should assist the agent"—

but there is no such mode by which the agent could be made such [an agent] while the action remains unaccomplished. Therefore, even for the agent, one who accepts a specific set of procedures (*itikartavyatā*) must likewise accept [the necessity of those procedures].
This must also be accepted:
that the object of proof is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, and the *saṃsthās* (concluding rites) are its means of accomplishment.
Therefore, it is established that the Jyotiṣṭoma indeed possesses its own specific procedure (itikartavyatā).
Now, why is it not common [to all sacrifices]?
Because it is prescribed as if it were obligatory (nityavat).
Whenever there is the Jyotiṣṭoma,
at that very time there is the initiation (dīkṣā). But when one desires cattle in the Jyotiṣṭoma, then it has the Ukthya as its concluding form (saṃsthā).
The ritual procedures (dharmas) of the Jyotiṣṭoma are to be performed at all times;
[there are also] the one-day Ukthya terminuses; therein, the ritual procedures of the Jyotiṣṭoma are to be performed at all times.

And the statement that "they are for the sake of those [sacrifices] whose form is the Ukthya and so forth" contradicts what was previously stated by the subsequent [argument], if it were not always for the sake of the Ukthya and so forth. Or, if they were for the sake of the Ukthya and so forth but not always, both [positions] would be contradictory. Therefore, it is not common [to all]. Furthermore, if the scriptural injunction were as if permanent (nityavat), yet [the thing enjoined] were non-permanent (anitya), [it would be a contradiction].
If that which is prescribed as permanent were to be performed as non-permanent,
then its prescription as permanent would be contradicted. Therefore, this applies to the Jyotiṣṭoma established as a permanent rite,
not to the optional form established with the Ukthya and other extensions.
NOTES:
*{3/634: E2,4: he who [is the cause] of the eternal} *{3/635:
having accepted the final dissolution}
Alternatively, one might argue that the proof (*sādhana*) will apply to the base form (*prakṛti*) because it has been stated twice. (MS 3.6.44)
But surely the Agniṣṭoma terminus is also heard of as being optional; for two [versions] are prescribed therein:
one as obligatory and one as optional.
In that case, by the force of the two statements, one who desires [the result] will certainly become [an Agniṣṭoma];
since there is no sublation of its obligatory nature, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma in its Agniṣṭoma form will take place.
But because of the statement in the traditional teaching (*āmnāna*), there is a combination (*samuccaya*). (MS 3.6.45)
Now, as for what was said— that the second and third observations are possible only if the rule is uniform and not otherwise— that statement will be fulfilled.
It is not a case of mere observation. In the Ukthya sacrifice, the offering to Indra and Agni is prescribed as the second;
likewise, in the Ṣoḍaśin, the offering to Indra is the third.
Furthermore, this is because of the prohibition of the preceding indicative marks.
From this also we see that there is a relationship of original material and its modification (prakṛti-vikāra). Why?
Because of the negation of the previous indicative marks. For if [the view were otherwise], when it is said, "If it is an Agniṣṭoma he offers;

if it is an Ukthya he anoints the enclosing sticks and does not offer," the observation of the absence of the oblation would not occur. This is because, when the occasion has arisen, there would be uniformity of rule (sāmānavidhya) due to the authority of the explicit statement.
The designation of one [among many] is due to a distinction of qualities.

Now, as for what was said regarding "designation": this designation by means of a quality that is not itself entitled [to the rite] belongs to the single person who is entitled, according to the reasoning already stated. Furthermore, the mention of the *agniṣṭoma* is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
[MS 3.7.1: "Because of the distinction of the context, that which is unconnected [with a specific subsidiary] belongs to the principal [rite]."

There are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices; therein are the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and the properties of the sacrificial grass, as well as the altar (*vedi*) and the properties of the altar. In this regard, a doubt arises: do the sacrificial grass and its properties, and so forth, belong to the principal sacrifice alone, or to both the subsidiaries and the principal? What, then, is the prima facie position?
Because of the specific context, it is not connected with the subordinate; such qualities belong to the principal alone. Why?
Because of the specific context.
For the context belongs to the primary acts, not to the subsidiary acts; and since their connection is established through the context,
it therefore belongs to the primary act.
Or rather, because the status of being a subsidiary (śeṣatva) belongs to all [the rites], it is not prompted by that [specific rite].
These properties (dharmas) belong to all [elements], both the subsidiaries and the principal;
here, subsidiarity does not arise from the context (*prakaraṇa*), for that is characterized by the notion of assistance (*upakāra*). Whatever assists something [is its subsidiary].
That [subordinate act] is a remnant of that [principal], and these ritual elements (dharmas) assist all the subsidiaries and the principal acts. How is this understood?
From the syntactical connection (vākya); for from the statement, "He places the oblations on the altar," it is understood from the sentence that this applies to oblations in general.
The principal oblations [belong] to the context (*prakaraṇa*). And syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than context;
therefore, "he places the oblations upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
He says: if the context is set aside by syntactical connection, [then what?]

In the world as well, these rules (dharmas) are said to apply to the sacrificial grass (barhis). What fault is there in that? It would follow that these rules must be performed in all cases. It is replied: by virtue of the context (prakaraṇa), it is understood that they serve as auxiliaries only for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa). Therefore, they are not to be performed in worldly matters.
If this is so, then the auxiliary rites (aṅgas) themselves are also not denoted by the word "darśapūrṇamāsa."

Therefore, [the ritual duties] do not apply to those [auxiliaries] either. It is said in reply: although the auxiliaries are not denoted by the words "Darśa" and "Pūrṇamāsa," they are indeed benefactors of the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices;
thus, the ritual duties performed in relation to them will benefit the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa. Consequently, [those duties] must be performed for both the auxiliaries and the primary sacrifices.
NOTES:
"If it is argued that [the suffix] *ārāt* is also [governed by this rule]," MS 3.7.3.

In the Piṇḍapitṛyajña as well, it would be connected with the properties of sacrificial grass (*barhis*); that [offering] also takes place upon the sacrificial grass, and there is a purpose for that [grass] as well. That too would be like the *ārācchiṣṭa* properties.
For that [Veda] is not a sentence, because its purpose is that [meaning]. (MS 3.7.4)
The *barhis* grass is not possessed of these properties by virtue of those properties themselves;
for the single sentence [prescribing them] is connected with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices,
and therefore these properties are auxiliaries to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
Since they apply only to that which is for the sake of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and not elsewhere, the sacrificial grass (barhis) used in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña will not be included.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark.

There is an indicative mark (liṅga), which says as follows: "He indeed first pours butter over the *dhruvā* ladle, for from that point he is about to offer the two initial *ājyabhāga* portions. This shows that the purpose of the pouring is for the sake of the *ājyabhāga* offerings.
But because of the connection with the fruit, that which is joined with the owner belongs to the principal [act].

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the shaving of hair and beard, the observances of consuming only milk, and ascetic practices are prescribed. Regarding these, there is a doubt: do they serve the purpose of both the subsidiary and the principal rites, or do they serve the purpose of the principal rite alone?
What, then, is the prima facie position? That they serve the purpose of both the subsidiary and the principal rites; this is established by the preceding principle.
This being the case, we reply: this is connected with the owner;
therefore, it belongs to the principal. Why?
Because of the connection with the fruit.
This relationship belongs to the person through the sacrifice:
the sacrifice is the giver of the *apūrva*, and the person is the recipient. But is there not yet another relationship?

The sacrifice is that which is to be accomplished (*nirvartya*), and the person is the accomplisher (*abhinirvartaka*). It is for this purpose—that there will be a connection with the fruit—that the person is mentioned in the scripture. For he does not bring the sacrifice into being; rather, the sacrifice will connect [with the fruit] through its very existence. Why, then, does the fruit accrue to one who accomplishes [the sacrifice]? And it is said that the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) "purify" (*saṃskurvanti*). That which is to be purified by them...

In that regard, they produce capacity. And the purpose for a person is to obtain the fruit, not to bring about the sacrifice. Therefore, those purificatory rites of the person render the person capable of receiving the fruit, not capable of accomplishing the sacrifice. He says:

If they do not produce capacity for the accomplishment of the sacrifice, how then are they properties of the sacrifice? It is said: they exist to provide assistance to the sacrifice as it accomplishes its own purpose. And what is its own purpose?
That by which its agent becomes connected with the fruit. Therefore, the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) pertaining to the master [of the sacrifice] are for the sake of the primary act.
NOTES:
And because of the connection with the desire to act. MS 3.7.7.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice it is heard: "Thirty-six steps long toward the east, twenty-four at the front, thirty at the back—this much we are able [to construct]. Regarding this, there is a doubt: is this altar for the sake of both the subsidiaries and the principal rite, or is it for the sake of the principal rite alone? What, then, is the prima facie view?

"And because of its connection with the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), it is for the sake of the primary [act]. What is this "desire to act"? It is the thought, "I shall be able to do so much. That which is desired to be done—for the sake of that, this [Vedic injunction] is heard: "We shall be able to perform this. And that which is desired to be done by him is the primary act.
They are not the primary members. For it is the principal that possesses the fruit, not the members.

He asks: "If the members are not intended to be performed, for what purpose are they performed? It is said in reply: Even though they are not intended to be performed, the members are nevertheless performed.

Even though those [other things] are not intended to be performed, nevertheless, by means of those which are not intended to be performed, something else is intended to be performed. Therefore, those are performed; that which is intended to be performed—
The altar belongs to that [sacrifice]. Therefore, it is for the sake of the primary [rite];
this much remains established for now, though not yet concluded.
By means of such a designation. (MS 3.7.8) [Note: 3/644: Cf. Tait.S. 6.2.4.5; 3/646: E1 provides "sthitaṃ tāvad aparyavasitam" in parentheses.]
There are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices;
regarding them, it is heard in scripture: "One should touch the Paurṇamāsī [offering] with the Caturhotṛ formula, and the Amāvāsyā [offering] with the Pañcahotṛ formula."
In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the touching for the sake of both the subsidiary and the principal acts, or is it for the sake of the principal act alone? What, then, is the prima facie view?
That it is for the sake of the principal act.
Furthermore, these names— *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā*— are primarily designations of the principal [rites]. Therefore, the touching [of the offering] pertains to the principal rite.
"But when [the act] is joined [with the result], there is the scriptural declaration of the fruit; therefore, there should be a desire to perform it in its entirety. (MS 3.7.9)
The answer to this established position is as follows: As for what was stated— that the principal rite is what is intended to be performed, not the subsidiaries,
and therefore the altar belongs to the principal— this is not so.
Therefore, there is a declaration of the fruit when [the rite] is joined;
the fruit is heard as resulting from the rite together with its auxiliaries.
Consequently, it is intended to be performed along with its auxiliaries, even if the auxiliaries themselves are not what is directly intended to be performed.

Even though [the rites] have been performed by the Ṛṣis, they must nevertheless be performed on the altar (*vedī*). Otherwise, what has been performed on the altar would not be complete with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*).
*Notes: {3/649: E1 gives "sthitād uttaram" in parentheses}*
Because it denotes qualities, the denotation [of a word] applies to all its meanings. (MS 3.7.10)

As for what was said—that because the words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* denote the primary [sacrifices], there is the touching (*abhimarśana*) of the primary oblations—that is not so; for there would also be the touching of the subsidiary oblations. Why?
Because of the mention of a quality (*guṇa*);
for there is a mention that "the touching (*abhimarśana*) is a quality. What is that mention?

It is that which says, "the touching is a quality. And since the words *paurṇamāsīm* and *amāvāsyām* end in the accusative case, the touching must be performed for the sake of the *paurṇamāsī* sacrifice.
The touching (abhimarśana) must be performed for the sake of the new moon sacrifice;

therefore, wherever its performance is beneficial to either the full moon or the new moon sacrifice, it should be performed there. Whatever is connected with either the full moon or the new moon [must be performed accordingly].
Whether directly or indirectly,
that which is performed here and there benefits those two. Therefore, it must be performed for both the primary oblations and the subsidiary oblations.
But the sacrificial fee for the initiation belongs to the principal [offering], because of the scriptural statement.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the initiations are heard in the text: "There are three initiations"; likewise, the sacrificial fees are heard: "Its sacrificial fee is one hundred and twelve. Regarding this, there is a doubt: are the initiations and the sacrificial fees for the sake of both the subsidiaries and the primary sacrifice, or are they for the sake of the primary sacrifice alone? What is the prima facie view?

Since the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) serve the purpose of both the subsidiary and the principal rites for the persons [performing them], it follows that the initiation and the sacrificial fee also serve the purpose of both the subsidiary and the principal [in this context]. This being the position reached, we reply: the initiation and the sacrificial fee belong to the principal [rite] alone.
Why? Because of a scriptural statement; for there is indeed a scriptural statement: "The initiations are for the Soma [sacrifice]."

"The sacrificial fees belong to the Soma," for indeed there is no burden too great for a scriptural injunction anywhere. Therefore, by virtue of this statement, the initiation and the sacrificial fees belong to the Soma.
NOTES:
And because cessation is observed. (MS 3.7.12)
It demonstrates the cessation of the initiations. How so? [The text says:
"O Adhvaryu, since you have purchased the animal, what is its initiation? "When he offers the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ oblation, that is its initiation.
Even though there is no actual initiation, this statement occurs. Therefore, the initiation and the sacrificial fee belong to the auxiliary parts.
Likewise, the altar belongs to the sacrificial post.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, concerning which it is said: "When one who is consecrated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. In that context, with reference to the sacrificial post (yūpa), it is heard: "The sacrificial post is indeed a thunderbolt; if one were to fix it within the altar, it would burn him up; if it were outside the altar, it would not be secured. Therefore, he fixes half within the altar and half outside the altar, so that it is secured."
"It does not burn.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is the altar (*vedi*) enjoined as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) by the phrase "within the altar" (*antarvedi*), or is it stated for the purpose of defining a location, namely, "half within the altar and half outside the altar"? How is it a subordinate part of the sacrificial post, and how is it a definition of location? [This would be the case] if [the phrase referred to] half of the sacrificial post being inside the altar...
And this connection is intended;

Furthermore, if one were to teach that even the area outside the altar (*bahirvedi*) is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the sentence would be split (*vākya-bheda*). In this context, ritual actions (*karman*) are cited as examples: "One desiring heaven should offer the *agnihotra*," "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*," and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *jyotiṣṭoma*. 664* Should these be performed [by the preceptor],

Or rather, another person [should perform] the remainder. What is the prima facie view? It should be performed by oneself. Why?
Because the fruit accrues to one who performs it oneself. How is this understood?
Because it is characterized by that [word], the word is the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) of this meaning;

Regarding the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," it is said that whoever desires heaven is the one [authorized] to perform it.
One who becomes the agent in a sacrifice shall accomplish the fruit; and by becoming the agent with respect to the sacrifice together with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), one attains the fruit.
Therefore, the performance should be carried out by oneself.
But in the case of the disposal (utsarga), because it is subordinate, the performer of the subsidiary acts is the same as the performer of the principal act;
therefore, it may be performed by another or by oneself.
There is primacy in the act of relinquishment (utsarga). How so?
He who performs the relinquishment has accomplished everything. How so?
Relinquishment is equivalent to hiring (parikraya).

Therefore, [the priests] perform everything through that [purchase]. Consequently, for one who performs the purchase, everything becomes performed by himself alone. Therefore, he should perform the mere relinquishment (*utsarga*) himself;
as for the remainder, it may be performed either by another or by himself.
Or rather, there should be another [performer], because of the scriptural injunction regarding purchase and because of the prohibition against [acting for] one's own self (*pratyagātman*).

The agent for the remainder must be someone else. Why? Because hiring (parikraya) is prescribed. When many types of persons are applicable, hiring is restricted [to one]. Therefore, all ritual items (padārtha) are to be performed by those engaged through hiring. Furthermore, hiring oneself is contradictory; for if one were to perform it oneself, [hiring would be impossible].

If it were performed by one who has not been hired, then the scriptural injunction regarding hiring would be rendered meaningless, or else an invisible (transcendental) result would have to be assumed. Therefore, the remaining ritual acts must be performed by others who have been hired; however, for one who performs the *utsarga* himself, everything becomes performed by himself.

And because [the action] exists with respect to the injunction (*codanā*). (MS 3.8.7)

By "injunction" (codanā), we mean the *apūrva*—the unseen potency. With respect to that *apūrva*, the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are prescribed. Since they are impossible with respect to [certain] substances, they are postulated for others;
and in the absence of proximate substances, they would apply to remote ones.
However, when they are possible with respect to a proximate substance, [they must be applied there].

In that case, they should not be employed for those who are remote [from the sacrifice], because their purpose has already been fulfilled. Therefore, they belong to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). Because they are unequal, they would not have the same injunction (*asamānavidhāna*).
This is a sūtra following upon the preceding word.

Now, why are they not of equal application? For, because the rule is laid down without distinction, it would apply to every man whatsoever. To this it is replied: This is not a rule of equal application for all men. Why?
Because they are unequal;

these [priests] are unequal with respect to this procedure. What is the inequality? It is that [the fees] are prescribed for the sacrificer, not for the officiating priests. How is it understood that they are prescribed for the sacrificer?
That is to say, they would apply to the agent himself.

But surely, since there is no distinction, they are prescribed for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) as well. We observe that they are not prescribed [for them] because there is no purpose [in their doing so]. How is there an absence of purpose?
When performed by the officiating priests, they are neither performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) nor caused to be performed by him.
Because the purchase [of services] does not have that as its purpose; and those things performed by oneself do not assist one who is seeking [assistance]. Therefore, they are useless;
hence, they are not prescribed for the officiating priests (ṛtvij). This is the point of inequality. Therefore, they are not subject to the same injunction. [415] {3/717}
