for if it were stated [as a rule], the reason [for the practice] would remain unestablished.

For in this case, one is not about to perform the after-offerings (anuyāja). When it is understood that the act of pouring together (samānayana) is not for the sake of the fore-offerings (prayāja), then there is the statement. When there is the statement, then the absence of the after-offerings is not the reason.

For if the cause were absent, the explanatory statement (*nigada*)—"for here one will not be about to perform the after-offerings (*anuyāja*s"—would not be appropriate. Therefore, the act of pouring together for the sake of the fore-offerings (*prayāja*s) is the motivator (*prayojaka*) of the clarified butter (*ājya*) contained in the *upabhṛt* ladle. What happens when there is a pouring together for the sake of the after-offerings?
[It occurs] only to the extent required for the fore-offerings.
In that case, everything should be brought together;
half of what is in the *aupabhṛta* ladle [is brought],
because if it were useless, there would be no necessity for either half or that much.
In that case, the origination would be undifferentiated. (MS 4.1.42)
In connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "One takes four [spoonfuls] in the Juhū; one takes eight in the Upabhṛt.
Regarding this, there is a doubt:
are both the substance for the Juhū and that for the Upabhṛt intended for both purposes?
From both the *prayāja*s and the *anuyāja*s;
or rather, from the *prayāja*s the *jauhava* [ladle], and from the *anuyāja*s the *aupabhṛta* [ladle]?
Or rather, [the butter] in the *aupabhṛta* ladle is for both the *prayāja*s and the *anuyāja*s. What is the prima facie view? Both [portions of butter] are for both purposes. Why?
Because whatever is performed with clarified butter [is served by it].
It ought to belong to each of those [offerings] without distinction.
NOTES:
In that context, the *jauhava* [ladle] is for the purpose of prohibiting its use in the *anuyāja* offerings. MS 4.1.43.
It is not so; both serve both purposes: the *jauhava* is for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings, while the *aupabhṛta* is for both purposes. How so?
When he takes [the butter] in the *juhū* ladle,
he takes it for the seasons; since the *prayāja* offerings are indeed the seasons, this statement regarding the *juhū* mentions the *prayājas* for the purpose of excluding the *anuyājas*.

He said: "Is it not the case that there is no statement here for the purpose of prohibiting the after-offerings (anuyāja), since this [statement], 'he draws it from the fore-offerings (prayāja),' is an instruction regarding the fore-offerings?"

"It has no capacity to prohibit the *anuyāja*s. To this it is replied: We do not say that this [text] is a prohibition. Rather, in the original injunction (*utpattivākya*), there was no connection with a specific purpose for the *ājya* offerings;
by this statement, the status of being the purpose of the *prayāja*s is established for the *jauhava* [clarified butter].
Since it is not understood from the mere absence of a statement that this [offering] serves the purpose of the *anuyāja*s,
it is said that the statement is intended for the purpose of prohibiting the *anuyāja*s.
If it is argued that the same applies to the *aupabhṛta* [ladle], [we reply: no. *MS_4,1.44*
If it is argued that [the latter] is seen [in the text],
such that the *jauhava* is prohibited from the *anuyājas*,
while the *aupabhṛta* serves both purposes;
Let the *jauhava* butter be for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings, but let the *aupabhṛta* butter not be for both purposes. That too should be as the *jauhava* is. How so?
This [portion] is also heard as being for the sake of the after-offerings (anuyāja) alone:
"That which he takes in the *upabhṛt*—he takes it for the after-offerings; for the after-offerings are the meters. Its purpose is for the after-offerings.
It might be argued that because of the prohibition regarding the *juhū*, this is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*).
This is not so;
for the *aupabhṛta* [ladle] serves both purposes, as it is heard in scripture: "When he takes eight [spoonfuls] in the *upabhṛt*, he takes them for the *prayāja*s and the *anuyāja*s."
[Objection: But was it not stated that "he takes it for the after-offerings (anuyāja)," and thus its purpose is for the after-offerings? [Reply: It is said:

because of the prohibition regarding the *juhū*, this is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*). Since both—the portion in the *aupabhṛta* and that in the *jauhava*—are applicable for both purposes, the *jauhava* portion is prohibited for the after-offerings.
It is not the *aupabhṛta* [clarified butter];
since that *aupabhṛta* serves both purposes, the statement regarding its purpose for the *anuyāja*s must be considered a *nityānuvāda* (a constant restatement).
It is not possible to deny its purpose for the *prayāja* offerings, for that is directly stated in the scripture;
therefore, the butter in the *aupabhṛta* ladle serves both purposes. Furthermore, the pouring back from that [ladle] into the *juhū* is prescribed in the scripture.
Therefore, even for this reason, it is not possible to set aside its status as being for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings.
(Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.3.2.9)
That [offering] consists of eight portions, because it is so heard in the scripture. (MS 4.1.46)
It is heard in the scripture: "He takes eight [spoonfuls] in the *upabhṛt*. Regarding this, there is a doubt:
is that butter in the *upabhṛt* consecrated by the act of taking it eight times?
Or rather, is it that the number four is subordinate to the two acts of grasping? What, then, is the prima facie position?
That the number eight is subordinate, not two numbers of four. Why?
The number eight is heard directly from the text;
the number four is indicated by the number eight, and when there is a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the direct statement is the proper course.
Therefore, this is a grasping consisting of eight items.
And because of the favor conferred by the clarified butter from the *juhū* ladle.

And there is a statement of favor (*anugrahavāda*): "This [clarified butter] was indeed fourfold; having poured the base for it, he performs three fore-offerings from here and pours it together because it is fourfold. How might this be a favor toward the fourfold [butter]? Is it the case that it becomes fourfold by means of the pouring together? We say: no.
That [offering] was indeed "fourfold-drawn" (caturgṛhīta) from the very beginning;

even when the *āghāra* libation had been poured, what remained was taken as being precisely fourfold in number. Why, then, is it called "fourfold-drawn"? It is for the sake of favoring that which is fourfold-drawn.
For a small amount taken four times is insufficient for the oblation;
how, then, might it become sufficient? Thus, by the word "four-times-taken" (*caturgṛhīta*), "smallness" is indicated;
and smallness exists only in relation to something larger.
For if the eightfold portion in the *aupabhṛta* ladle were indeed small when measured as four *graha*s, then the term "four *graha*s" could indicate that smallness. Therefore, we see this also.
In the *aupabhṛta* [ladle], the number eight is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*).
(Note:
*trīnitaḥ*)

Regarding the two [offerings], there is the mention of the causal capacity and the act of bringing together in the formula *prācīnān*. Furthermore, in that case where the four-fold ladled portion (*caturgṛhīta*) is small, [the same applies]. MS 4.1.48.
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position;
these two [portions] are each four-fold-drawn,
and thus the reason is established for the *ātithyā* [offering].
The clarified butter is taken four times;
for here one will not be about to perform the after-offerings (*anuyāja*).
Even if the after-offerings were not present, this *aupabhṛta* portion would still consist of eight takings. This is because the number eight is a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).

In that case, when there are two [portions] each consisting of four ladlings, the plural form "ājyāni" (clarified butters) applied to the "caturgṛhītān" (four-ladled portions) would be inappropriate. Therefore, there are two [sets of] four-ladled portions. He says:
"This is an indicative mark; let the basis for its application be stated. To this it is replied:
It is stated without reference to a specific context that "one offers with four ladlings" in all homas;
therefore, even in the case of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings, that [rule] cannot be set aside by the rule for eight ladlings.
Because they have different objects: for eight portions are taken at the drawing, while four portions are taken at the offering;
indeed, such a possibility exists.
If that which is taken eight times were to be taken, it would be offered as four times-taken;
thus, this eightfold nature occurs here in the taking. How, then, could one accomplish two four-times-taken portions for the offering?

Therefore, these two [portions] of four ladlings each are taken when an eight-ladling portion is being taken. No one can produce an eight-ladling portion without first taking two portions of four ladlings each. Therefore, these are two portions of four ladlings each.
Now, as for what was said—
that "eightfold-drawn" is heard in the scripture,
and that direct scriptural statement (śruti) is more authoritative than indirect indication (lakṣaṇā)— [that remains to be addressed].

It is replied: We have already stated the purpose of the number eight—namely, how there might be two *caturgṛhīta* (four-drawn) portions. Furthermore, since the rule says "he takes eight in the *upabhṛt*," if the *upabhṛt* were brought [separately], how could there be two *caturgṛhīta* portions? Otherwise, in the absence of the word "eight," they would be taken in separate vessels. Therefore, there is the hearing of the word "eight."
This is well said:
"There are two fourfold portions in the *upabhṛt*. This is the purpose.
When there are two portions of four spoonfuls each, half must be poured together;
however, when there is a portion of eight spoonfuls, it is not necessarily half. Likewise, where there is no drawing for the sake of the after-offerings (*anuyāja*), there too it is eight spoonfuls.
Just as in the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) and just as in the established conclusion (siddhānta),
so too in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, there is a fourfold-drawn portion (caturgṛhīta) in the upabhṛt ladle.
[fourfold] portions}* *{4/188:
E2: for one cannot take an eightfold portion without first taking two fourfold portions}*
But the *svaru* is not produced for multiple purposes, because its own word denotes its specific function.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, concerning which it is stated: "When one who has been consecrated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma," and therein this is traditionally taught: "He binds [the animal] to a post made of Khadira wood."
"One binds [the animal] to a *pālāśa* tree; one binds it to a *rohita* tree. In proximity to that, this other [text] is handed down:
"One anoints the animal with the *svaru*; one makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)."

Now, this is being deliberated: should the *svaru* be produced separately from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), or should a splinter (*śakala*) be taken as a byproduct while the post is being fashioned? In this regard, first we must examine this point.
Is the *svaru* the motivator for the production of the cutting and so forth?
If it were the motivator, it would have to be produced separately from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). If it is not the motivator, [then...]
"The chip (śakala) will be taken up as it is produced in accordance with the sacrificial post (yūpa) being produced. How could that [chip] be the motivator (prayojaka)?
Or how could it not be the motivator? If this is the mode of expression, then that which is denoted by the word *svaru* is what is to be brought into being. How so?

"By means of specific procedures such as selection (*joṣaṇa*) and so forth. Therefore, that which is understood as "the *svaru*"—namely, [the wood] from which [the sacrificial post] was fashioned—will be taken up [as the object]. Thus, [the rule] "he anoints the animal with the *svaru*" will apply.
Then there is the instigator (*prayojaka*). Now, if it is understood in this way—"He anoints the animal with the *svaru*"—the *svaru* remains unestablished.
All that is understood of it is simply that "anointing is performed by means of it."
This also [is the case]:

the statement "he makes a *svaru* from the sacrificial post" (*yūpasya svarum karoti*) assigns a portion of the post to the function of the *svaru*, namely, the act of anointing; therefore, it is not a motive for the action.
What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)?
The *svaru*, however, has a single production because it is denoted by its own action-term;
the *svaru* would not have a single production with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), for the *svaru* exists independently of the sacrificial post.
The production [of the *svaru*] occurs from the wood of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Why?

Because it is the word for its own action. For its own word for action is the injunction for the *svaru*, namely, "he makes the *svaru*. And thus, the state of being a *svaru* is produced from a portion of the sacrificial post's wood.
In the statement "he makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)," the word *yūpa* is used figuratively;
the meaning is "from a part of the *khadira* tree or other [specified wood]. Why?
Because the production of the nature of a *svaru* is understood through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
"He makes the *svaru*" means he produces the *svaru*. The taking up of a portion from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is established by syntactical connection (*vākya*);
and since direct statement (*śruti*) is more powerful than syntactical connection, this being the case, the *svaru* need not necessarily be produced from the wood of the sacrificial post itself;
rather, it may be made separately even from another tree that is independent [of the post].
NOTES: *{4/140: Tait.S. 6.1.11.6}* *{4/141: E2: utāprayojaka iti}*
"This much [is] necessarily [the case]," and he suspects [it] because of another birth. (MS 4.2.2)
From this as well, it is understood that the *svaru* originates independently. Why?
Because there arises a suspicion [of its origin] even from a different genus.
How so? "One should not make the *svaru* out of anything else."
If one were to make the *svaru* from another tree, others would ascend after him to the world;

therefore, it says, "one makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). For when something is mentioned as being produced in accordance with the sacrificial post, it is not possible to suspect that it belongs to a different species.

For the splinter of the sacrificial post (*yūpa-śakala*) is employed at that time for the function of the *svaru*. Therefore, for this reason as well, the *svaru* must be produced separately from the sacrificial post.
*Note: {4/144: E2 gives vṛkṣāntarāt in brackets}*
Or rather, it is a part of that [quality], because the state of being *svaru* is caused by that. (MS 4.2.3)

The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position. For a fragment produced as a byproduct of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)—that is, a portion of the post itself—is to be taken as the *svaru*. Why? Because it is so recorded in the scripture: "If one were to make the *svaru* from another tree, others would ascend after him to his world."

"One makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). In this case, the meaning being enjoined is not "one produces the *svaru*"; rather, it is that one takes up whatever [wood] is necessary to perform the function of the *svaru*.
"From that [wood] for the sacrificial post. Why?
Because the status of being a *svaru* is caused by that;
for here, the status of being a *svaru* is heard in reference to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
"One makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). To which does "of the sacrificial post" refer? It refers to its own; and a part belongs to the whole of which it is a constituent.
Therefore this is said:
for inanimate objects, the genitive case functions in the sense of the ablative,
as in "give some vegetables."
"Give vegetables," as well as in some cases in the sense of the instrumental case,
such as "he sacrifices with ghee."
"He sacrifices with ghee. This is used in the sense of the ablative:
"He sacrifices from ghee," or "He sacrifices of ghee"; or it is used in the sense of the accusative.
"He drinks from the Soma," "he drinks the Soma," or "he drinks from the Soma."

But has it not been stated that here a part of the sacrificial post (yūpa) is enjoined by the syntactical connection (vākya), while the production of the *svaru* is [enjoined] by direct assertion (śruti), and direct assertion is stronger than syntactical connection? To this it is replied:
True, it is so;
however, in the phrase "of the sacrificial post" (*yūpasya*), the word *iti* would have its meaning unintended. In that case, even the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) would be contradicted.
This applies to the sentence as well. However, in our position, nothing is intended to be non-expressive;

the statement "he makes the *svaru*" will be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of its own meaning, and a splinter from the sacrificial post (*yūpa-śakala*) will be enjoined. It is understood that the word *svaru* is used figuratively for the splinter by virtue of its purpose, namely, anointing.
The well-known meaning of the individual parts will convey this sense. For there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "Now, why is it called *svaru*?
Because from this [sacrificial post] the sacrificial garment (*veṣa*) is cut off."
Therefore, this [wood] of his becomes like his own body;
that is why it is called *svaru*.
And because of the scriptural mention of "shavings" (*śakala*). (MS 4.2.4)
Moreover, there is the taking of what is produced from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Why?
Because of the scriptural mention of a "chip" (*śakala*);
for there is a scriptural mention of a chip of the *svaru*.
"That first chip which falls away should be made into the *svaru*. Now, a "chip" (*śakala*) is a single part,
and a single part is not something that can independently serve as a purpose.

Because it is a relative term, and because linguistic usage occurs to that extent with respect to the whole; therein, by virtue of the context, there is syntactic unity between this [term] and the previously mentioned material such as *khadira* wood—which serves another purpose [as the sacrificial post], is characterized by actions such as selection (*joṣaṇa*), and is intended for the sacrifice—as in:
"one selects, cuts, [and prepares] *khadira* wood for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)."

And he hews it. In that context, the first chip that falls off is made into the *svaru* for the purpose of anointing; and by merely repeating the word *svaru* there, he figuratively designates it. Therefore, this is not a separate production of a *svaru*, such that one might suspect it could be made from another tree as well. Consequently, the statement regarding the possibility of other species is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*) intended for the praise of the *yūpa*-chip.
NOTES:
And because it is seen [to be repeated] for each sacrificial post (pratiyūpam). MS_4.2.5.
For this reason as well, the *svaru* is not produced separately. Why?
Because it is observed in the context of the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice that there is one for each sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
Just as,
having anointed the animals in succession with the sacrificial stakes, [one binds them] to their respective loops of rope on the middle [stake].
The statement, "one hides each respective chip of the sacrificial post (*yūpaśakala*)," indicates a multiplicity of *svarus*.

Furthermore, if the *svaru* were produced separately, then in the case of the set of eleven posts (*ekādaśinī*), a single *svaru* would suffice to accomplish the purpose through the principle of ritual extension (*tantra*). However, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is the taking of that which is produced concomitantly with the sacrificial post.

Since the collyrium is made from a chip of one's own sacrificial post (*svayūpaśakala*), the extended injunction (*codaka*) in the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice brings about precisely that same chip of one's own post;

thus, the plural number is justified. Furthermore, the mention of "a chip of one's own post" is determined to refer to the archetypal (*prākṛta*) chip, because it is of the same nature as that which exists in the archetype.
Such a person is to be censured,
not one who is distinguished. Therefore, the *svaru* is not the motivator (*prayojaka*) for its production.
In the sense of taking up, the word "karoti" [is used] for each respective [act]. (MS 4.2.6)
Now, as for what was said— that its production is expressed by the word, "he makes the *svaru*":
And thus the word "karoti" (he makes) will be appropriate. It is said:
the word "karoti" will apply to the act of taking up;
one "makes" the *svaru*.
"He takes up the *svaru*. Just as the word "makes" (*karoti*) occurs in the sense of taking up— as in "he makes [fuel] from wood" or "he makes [fuel] from cow-dung"—
so too should it be understood here.
NOTES:
*{4/151: The editions repeat MS 4.2.1–6 once more between MS 4.2.6 and 4.2.7, accompanied by a shorter commentary that differs very little in content.}
Because that [the *śākhā*] is the primary element in the *śākhā*.
In connection with the *śākhā* (branch) used in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture:
"He brings it from the east, he brings it from the north, he brings it from the northeast."

In this regard, there is a doubt: is this a discourse on the directions (*digvāda*), or is it a discourse on the branches (*śākhāvāda*)? It is initially concluded that it is a discourse on the directions, because the word "direction" (*diś*) is used in the scriptural text.
"In the case of the mention of branches, it is a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). Therefore, it is a statement regarding direction. This being the position reached, we reply:
"It is a statement regarding branches. Why?
If first of all this is the meaning:
"If it is said that 'the eastern direction is to be brought,' then that is an impossible matter;
however, if it is said that 'one should bring [something] toward the eastern direction,'"

In that case, as for the question "whence should it be brought?", this connection is untenable because the word "branch" (śākhā) is absent from the sentence. If, however, the branch under discussion is intended, then its connection with the word "eastern" (prācī) alone is logical. Why?
For the word "east" (prācī) has a direct syntactical connection with the verb "to carry" (harati);

it would have a connection with the word "branch" (śākhā) only by virtue of the context. In either case here, the word "east" would indicate either the branch under discussion through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), or else it would indicate the direction, since that is not what is intended to be achieved.
It is improper [to claim] that the location of the monastery (*vihāradeśa*) is the most desired object. Furthermore, "eastern" (*prācī*) is a relative term,
and all relative terms are dependent [upon something else].
Without another word, they do not express a complete meaning; moreover, if there were a connection with a general category as the referent, practical linguistic usage would be impossible.

Because every place indeed exists prior to something [else]. Likewise, the word "branch" is also a relative term; it requires the phrase "of the tree. When it requires the phrase "of the tree," then [the expression] is "the eastern branch of the tree."
The connection is that it is either "northerly" or "north-easterly," and in this way, common worldly usage is rendered possible. As for the statement regarding the branch [473]:

154* Regarding the term "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇā*): it is said that even by means of a characteristic, the meaning of a word is established. Therefore, [the expression] "one who possesses branches" (*śākhāvān*) is used.
NOTES:
*{4/152: Tait.Br. 3.2.1.3}* *{4/153: E2: connected with that which is most desired; E6, E2 (Fn.): not connected with that which is desired; E2 (Fn.)}
That which is most desired [to be separated] is connected [with the action];
because that is the primary factor in the case of the branch, there would be a separation by means of the *upaveṣa*, and thus there would be an inequality. (MS 4.2.8)
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is recited in the scriptural tradition:
"Having trimmed the branch from its base, he makes the *upaveṣa*. Regarding this, the following point is subject to doubt:
is both [the trimming and the making] a result of the cutting of the branch?
Is the branch the motive for both the *upaveṣa* and the [other],
or is the branch the motive for [the *upaveṣa*] alone?
"The *upaveṣa* is a by-product. What is the prima facie view? Both the branch and the base of the branch are produced from the act of cutting.
Both [the root and the tip] serve a purpose. The tip will be used for driving away the calves and so forth, while the root serves as the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick);
since there is no distinction [in their utility], both are motivators.
This being the position reached, it is said in reply:
we state [the conclusion] regarding the branch,
because that is the primary factor.
The separation [of the branch] should be performed with the *upaveṣa*. The *upaveṣa* is understood as being produced from the branch. How is its predominance established?

By the use of the accusative case in the expression "having stripped off the branch" (*śākhāṃ parivāsya*). But is it not also the case that in "he makes the *upaveṣa*" (*upaveṣaṃ karoti*) there is likewise an accusative?
It is said in reply: that [accusative] is not the object of the verb *parivāsayati* (to strip); of what then? Of the verb *karoti* (to make).

He asks: why does the connection not occur thus—"having trimmed the branch, he makes the *upaveṣa* from the root"—and because the word "branch" (*śākhā*) applies just as much to the tip as it does to the base? To this, the following is the meaning:
One should divide [the cord] at the top and the root using a thread.
What is the purpose?
Having divided the root, [one proceeds].
"It is said: 'I shall make the *upaveṣa*.
[To this] it is replied: not so;
for in this way, there would be the assumption of an intervention."
The parivāsana (cutting) is performed by means of placing the branch-parts;
once that is completed, the upaveṣa is made from it.
Now, one might object: since the root is the subject under discussion, it should be connected with the word *upaveṣa*. To this it is replied:

If there were a connection with both, there would be a contradiction. And when there is a contradiction, the syntactical statement (*vākya*) is stronger than the context (*prakaraṇa*). Now, if it were connected with what is proximate, even so it would follow that it is employed by the branch (*śākhā*). Therefore, it is already established: [the *uvaveṣa*...].
"He does not cause the cutting. This is the point of difference here.
(Note:
Both [the cutting and the resulting action] pertain to the cutting of the branch.)
*{4/156: E2 gives śākhāpradhānatvād in brackets}* *{4/158: E2: karotīti}* *{4/159: E2 omits ataḥ}*
And [the term] *upaveṣa* [is used] because of the departure from the Vedic text. (MS 4.2.9)
He drives away the calves with a branch, he leads the cows forward with a branch,
and he milks them with a branch.

By means of the Niriṣṭaka}*
"They come into being.
"It was opened up previously.
"It was in the Ātithyā [offering]."

Or rather, because of the connection with their origination even at the time of the *upasat*, the relationship of meaning among those [actions] that are not distinguished would be the cause for the unity of their performance.

The alternative view (*api vā*) is rejected. This connection of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is solely with its production; for if the sacrificial grass produced for the *ātithyā* were specifically qualified [for that rite], then its ritual properties (*dharma*) would be extended (*atidiśyeran*) to the sacrificial grass of the *aupasadā* rites, but there is no such statement by any scriptural text. Thus...

By its very nature, a specific distinction regarding the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) will be stated: "The *prastara* [bunch] is made of *aśvavāla* grass, and the two *vidhṛti* [separators] are made of *ikṣu* grass. Therefore, it is not the sacrificial grass prescribed elsewhere that is being referred to, nor is it that which has already been used for another purpose (*niriṣṭika*).
No dharmas are assigned from anywhere. What then?
That which is prescribed for the *ātithyā* [offering] is called the common *barhis* of these [offerings].
That very [barhis] is prescribed for the Upasads and for the Agniṣomīya; thus,
there is a connection with the barhis for all of them without distinction, by means of a single [act].
When the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is first cut, that cutting is for the sake of all [the rites];
the employment of the *barhis* is common [to them all]. Such is the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) regarding the word.
It will be taken in its primary sense;
otherwise, it would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

And when there is a conflict between the primary sense (*śruti*) and a figurative indication, the primary sense is the more appropriate, not the figurative indication. Therefore, the *barhis* grass is common to all three.
The purpose stated for the position [is as follows].
(Note:
*By the sentence: "When [the mantra] is used in the Atithyā-rite," and so forth.*)
In the case of substances, preparatory acts, and rituals, because they are for the sake of another, the mention of a fruit should be considered a mere explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*). (MS 4.3.1)
He whose *sruva* ladle is made of *khadira* wood cuts [the portion] with the very essence of the meters; his oblations become full of essence. He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood...
"He hears no evil report"—this applies to him for whom the *upabhṛt* ladle is made of *aśvattha* wood;
by means of the Brahman itself he secures food for himself.
For him whose *dhruvā* ladle is made of *vaikaṅkata* wood, [the same holds true].
The oblations stand ready for him; moreover, he is indeed propagated, for whom there are such offering-spoons (*sruva*);
all the forms of cattle attend upon him.
"No form other than this is born from the self.
Likewise, there is a scriptural declaration of results regarding the consecration of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
When he anoints his eyes, he thereby appropriates the sight of his rival;
likewise, he shaves his hair and beard and cleanses his teeth.
He pares his nails and bathes;
for this skin is indeed dead, or rather, it is impurity and defilement upon his self; by removing that very thing, he becomes pure and thus attains the sacrificial essence.
The fruit of the ritual action is heard [in scripture]:
"These two Āghāra libations are indeed the two reins of the sacrifice;
these two Ājyabhāga portions are indeed the two eyes of the sacrifice."
"In that the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s are offered,
a coat of mail is indeed made for the sacrifice; it is a coat of mail for the sacrificer, for the sake of overcoming his rival."
In this regard, there is a doubt:
are these injunctions of results, or are they merely explanatory passages (arthavādas)? What is the prima facie position?
There are injunctions regarding results,
because an injunction concerning a result produces a specific mode of activity, as in: "One desiring vigor should make a sacrificial post of khadira wood."
"A vessel made of *pālāśa* wood for one desiring Vedic splendor,
one made of *bailva* wood for one desiring food"— just as these are injunctions regarding results (*phalavidhi*), so it is here.
The same should be understood here as well. This being the case, we reply: these are *arthavādas* for the sake of the fruit. Why? Because they are for the sake of another;
these are for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). The *juhū* ladle is subordinate to the act of offering.
The *upabhṛt* is for supporting; the *sruva* ladles are for holding the clarified butter; and the application of ointment, the shaving [of the beard], and so forth are for the sacrificer.

The two *āghāra* libations, the two *ājyabhāga* portions, and the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings belong to the [sacrifices] beginning with that to Agni. If there were also a state of being subordinate (*guṇabhāva*) with respect to the fruit, it would have to be asserted that those [elements] enjoined elsewhere are again enjoined as subordinate elsewhere; and this is not logical, for subordination consists in being for the sake of another.
And their purpose is for the sake of the sacrifice, as expressed by the word:
"He offers with the *juhū*"; that is, he brings about the oblation by means of the *juhū*.
This applies everywhere. Therefore, these are not for the sake of the person.
*{In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, regarding the preparatory rite} *{Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.1.1.2} *{Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.1.1.2}*
*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.6.2.1;
*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.6.1.5; *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* 2.1.
And because the production [of the fire] is not for its own sake, [the mantra is subordinate]. (MS 4.3.2) *{4/248: E2: dhruvā}*, *{4/249: E2 gives "juhvā homam abhinirvartayati" in brackets}*

Now, it might be argued: "The subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) [of the *juhū*] with respect to the person is also taught by such statements as, 'He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa-wood* hears no evil report. But that is not so. Why?
Because the origin [of the injunction] does not have that as its primary purpose. In that regard—*{4/}*
No word at all says that the hearing of ill-repute is performed with a ladle made of *pālāśa* wood.
This much is heard:
he to whom this belongs does not hear an evil report.
This much is understood here by the word:
"the *juhū* ladle" and "the hearing of its evil reputation. In that regard, it is performed with the *juhū*, or the *juhū* is for that purpose.
The scripture does not state this.
But surely it is understood through inference: "Surely that act is performed with a ladle made of *pālāśa* wood."
"Because when that [cause] exists, this [effect] comes to be. To this it is replied: No, an inference regarding the relation of cause and effect does not function in such a manner;
rather, what is called the "relation of cause and effect" is as follows:

The causal relationship exists precisely when, something being present, another comes to be, and when that [first thing] is absent, the [second] does not come to be; however, in this case, while that is present...
Existence is known [through perception],
not non-existence through non-existence. As for the claim that "he who does not possess a palāśa-sacrificial ladle has no hearing of ill-repute," there is no such statement.
Therefore, it is not understood with necessity that "this is done by that."
This characteristic is perceived as belonging to the person;
therefore, it is not inference.
Furthermore, even for one whose *juhū* ladle is made of *pālāśa* wood, [the same applies].
Even for that [person], there occurs the hearing of evil verses. How is this known?

Through direct perception. [Objection: If this were so, then even the *agnihotra* would not produce its fruit. [For] the fruit is not seen merely by the act of offering. [Response: This is not a fault.

For it is not stated there that the result comes about by that alone. Here, however, there is a prohibition against hearing ill-repute while the existence of the *juhū* ladle is present. Therefore, there is no inference here that "this must be done."

"This is the cause. In the case of the Agnihotra and other such rites, however, the relationship between cause and effect is expressed by the word itself. Therefore, even though the fruit is not perceived at that time, it is understood that the fruit will come into being at another time;
but this is not the case with things of this [other] kind.
Therefore, there is no fruit from such [injunctions].
But is it not the case that when it is said, "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *pālāśa* wood does not hear an evil report," it is understood that that very thing is the fruit?
Therefore, one might argue that even in this case, the fruit will arise at a later time. It is replied:
True, it is understood;
however, we must investigate what the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that is. First of all, it is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
It is not inference, nor any other means of knowledge such as comparison whose object is perceived, nor indeed is it verbal testimony; this has been stated.

The meaning of a sentence, moreover, arises from the meanings of the words, and not otherwise; as it has been said: "Of those [words] which have attained their respective states, there is a recitation together with a word denoting action. (JS 1.1.25)
Therefore, because it is not rooted in a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), this is a false cognition (*mithyājñāna*). However, among worldly statements, it is understood in this way:

for those [statements], when employed once the object is already known, are used with words that must be supplied (*adhyāhārya*), are figurative (*gauṇa*), and have meanings that are modified or separated. Therefore, due to similarity to those [worldly statements], even regarding objects to be understood from verbal testimony, there arises a false notion (*mithyāpratyaya*) that takes the form of reality (*tattvarūpa*).
As in the case of a mirage and so forth.
Furthermore, this is a statement concerning the present,
and it is not...
This matter concerns the present;

therefore, even when sacrificial ladles (*sruva*) made of *khadira* wood and so forth exist, that result would not occur. Thus, it follows that while the result occurs when there is [a ladle] made of *khadira* wood and so forth, it does not occur [when such a ladle is absent].

"Whether it exists or not" [is a statement] even when [the thing] is non-existent. It is not understood in this way: "From where does that result come? Therefore, when such [statements] are uttered, there is neither engagement with anything nor withdrawal from anything; thus they are purposeless because they do not have action as their object. But when there is an *arthavāda* (explanatory passage), there is a purpose for [the use of materials] such as *khadira* wood.

Regarding the *sruva* ladle and other implements used for ritual purposes, which possess a specific utility: if these were not useful with respect to the sacrifice (*kratu*), then one might deliberate whether this very result arises from some verbal function or not. However, since they serve another purpose (*pārārthya*), no such verbal function can possibly be maintained; for such a function would only be postulated if there were a question of "for what purpose" (*kaimarthya*). Therefore...

Explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are of this nature; and since they function as explanatory passages, the word "present" (*vartamāna*), though not denoting actual present time, will be appropriate through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the purpose of praise.

But the fruit [belongs] to that [action] which has it as its primary purpose. (MS 4.3.3)
Now, as for what was said:
"One should make a sacrificial post of khadira wood for one who desires vigor."

Regarding the statements, "The sacrificial ladle made of Bilva wood is for one desiring food; that made of Palāśa wood is for one desiring spiritual luster," it is appropriate that in these cases there is an injunctive suffix, as it enjoins the performance [of the act] which establishes the connection between the *vīrya* (potency) and the *khadira* wood.
And it is not a statement referring to the present; therefore, there is no contradiction in that case. For those who know the logic of word-meanings and sentence-meanings recite this verse:
"One should act," "it should be done," "it must be performed."
"Bhavet" means "it would be"; this is the fifth [form].
This is the fixed characteristic of an injunction found in all the Vedas. Thus [it is said].
For those who consider the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) to be the expressive element of an injunction (*vidhi*), they recite this verse:
"And here there is an injunctive suffix; therefore, this [explanation] is not a description [of the true nature of the Veda]. [491] Notes:
Thinking thus, they recite:
"In the case of a specific characteristic (*naimittika*), because it is a modification (*vikāra*), there would be another primary sacrifice (*kratu*). (MS 4.3.4)
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is an incidental rule:
"One should perform the Bārhadgira as the Brahman-sāman for a Brāhmaṇa;
the Pārthuraśma for a Rājanya."
The *rāyovājīya* [chant] is for a Kṣatriya, and the *vaiśyasya* [chant] is for a Vaiśya;
likewise, there is a contingent rite (*naimittika*) regarding the fire.
One who is building for the first time should build a thousand-fold [altar]; for the second time, a two-thousand-fold;
for the third time, a three-thousand-fold.
Likewise, it is heard in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices:
"One desiring cattle should fetch [the water] with a milking vessel;
one desiring spiritual luster should fetch it with a bronze vessel."
"With an earthen [vessel] for one desiring consecration"—these are the occasional (naimittika) rites. Regarding them, there is a doubt:
are these very occasional rites intended for the sake of the obligatory (nitya), or is there something else [required] for each respective case?
Regarding the phrase "the meaning of permanence":
what is the prima facie conclusion? That these very [days] are meant. Why?
Because here there must necessarily be the Brahmasāman and so forth.
For those [actions], being enjoined,
require the means of accomplishment to be present; yet, for these [actions], no enjoined means of accomplishment exist.

And since the occasional rites (naimittika) occur in proximity, it is logical that these [permanent rites] are rendered complete by those [occasional ones] which are already present and relevant. How so?
For the occasional rite is indeed present.
Nothing other than what is understood from the sentence is heard;
and whatever fault there is in abandoning what is heard, exactly the same fault exists in the postulation of what is not heard.
He says: "But surely those [elements] mentioned in the context have the purpose of being signs (nimitta). It is replied:
This is not a fault;
even that which is mentioned in the context for one purpose may be connected with something else.
Just as irrigation channels are constructed for the sake of rice, and from them water is drunk, so it is here.
And it is touched upon; so too should it be understood here. Or rather, there is indeed an intermediate sentence here, as for example:

Regarding the injunction "one should carry [the water] with a *godohana*," this brings about the act of carrying by means of the *godohana* even though it is not connected to a specific desire. Furthermore, it is not possible to abandon what is directly stated in the scripture (*śruti*). As for this expression, "for one desiring cattle" (*paśukāmasya*), it...
He would be able to establish the connection with the desire for cattle,
neither to set aside the meaning of the subordinate sentence nor that which is being understood.
Without a reason,
it cannot be said that [a statement] is unintended; for there are indeed sentences that have two referents, such as:
"The white one runs;
Alambusās are going. Therefore, it follows that occasional rites (naimittika) are capable of serving the purpose of obligatory rites (nitya).
This being the position reached, we reply:
"When an occasional (naimittika) [injunction] is heard, something else must be for the sake of the sacrifice. Why?
Because it is a modification (*vikāra*) and because it is heard in reference to a specific [case]; this is the meaning.
For in that instance, the occasional [injunction] is indeed heard in reference to a specific [circumstance]."
Therefore, in the absence of that specific [injunction], it ought not to come to pass. As for what was said—that they must necessarily be performed—this is no fault;
because they are necessary to be performed, they will indeed be performed. As for the point that no other means for these has been prescribed:
There is no fault, as it will be prescribed by a general rule. What is that?
The *abhīvarta* is the *brahmasāman*, and Agni is the one contained in the eighteen mantras.

The *vāraṇa* is the vessel for pouring. Now, as for what was said—that the *brahmasāman* and other such elements will be connected with the occasional (*naimittika*) rites that are present and form part of the context—we say: no, for there is no context (*prakaraṇa*) for the *bārhadgira* and the rest. If it should be argued:
The claim that they are connected with the prescribed stotras and so forth is also untenable; for even though the stotras and so forth are prescribed as permanent (nitya),
nevertheless, the Bārhadgiras and other such hymns are heard in the text as being connected with specific conditions (nimitta) by means of syntactical connection (vākya).
And a sentence is stronger than context.
As for what was said—that this meaning is understood from the sentence due to proximity—it is not so;
a sentence-meaning of such a kind [cannot override] the general word-meaning.

It ought not to be set aside. For it is through connection with a specific occasion (*nimitta*) that the *bārhadgira* and other such verses possess purposefulness. Therefore, in each case, there is something other than the occasional application.
Now, as for what was said—that even the *godohana* vessel has been brought forward by the intermediate sentence and cannot be discarded—[that is not so].
Without a reason,
it is improper to postulate something unintended,
for that would result in a dual status. It is said in reply:
It is not intended [to be stated] for a specific reason. What is the reason?
Because these two do not occur simultaneously:
namely, the complete expression of the meaning and the expression by means of an intermediate sentence. How so?
The term *praṇayati*—derived from the root *nī* preceded by the prefix *pra*—expresses an injunction (*vidhi-vibhakti*) that directly (*śrutyā*) enjoins the meaning residing within its own word.

Furthermore, it enjoins by direct statement (*śruti*) and by syntactical connection (*vākya*) such things as the *godohana* vessel, even though they are connected to the act of carrying forward (*praṇayana*). The actual relationship, however, is between the result and the *godohana* vessel; for that [relationship] sets aside the direct meaning of the [primary] verbal statement.

[If it is argued that] it is by means of a single sentence [that both are expressed]: namely, that it expresses the connection of the *praṇayana* with the *godohana* vessel and so forth, and the connection of the *godohana* and so forth with the result—[we reply:
no, because of the expression of two distinct matters, the sentence would be excessively split.
And this is not logical.

As for cases such as "the white one runs," there might be an understanding of both meanings because no specific distinction is perceived; however, in the present case, a specific distinction is understood through the utterance of the word expressing desire (*kāmin*).
This is the meaning heard directly from scripture (śrauta). One might think:

if the connection of the *godohana* vessel and so forth with the action were intended to be expressed, then the word expressing the desired object (*kāmapada*) would be a mistake. Yet, this is not a mistake.

If the meaning of the intermediate sentence were intended to be expressed, a connection with the word *kāma* (desire) would not be possible. Therefore, the sentence is not directed toward two objects;
rather, it is here the connection with the desire for the *godohana* vessel and so forth that is denoted, and it cannot pertain to the obligatory duty (*nityakārya*).
Thus it is in all cases.

*That is not so; rather, when one [substance] possesses both [qualities], there is the distinctness of conjunction.* (MS 4.3.5)
In the Agnihotra it is heard: "He offers with curd," and again:
"One desiring sensory power should offer with curd. Likewise, regarding the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, it is recorded:
"He binds [the animal] to a post made of khadira wood," and furthermore:
"One should make a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of *khadira* wood for one who desires vigor. In this regard, there is a doubt:
is there also something else here for the sake of the obligatory (*nitya*) rite, or is it only occasional (*naimittika*)? What is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)?

"By the previous reasoning, it is otherwise. This being the position reached, we reply: when a single [act] possesses both [characteristics], namely permanence (*nityatva*) and occasionality (*naimittikatva*), the cause is the "separateness of conjunctions" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*). That separateness of conjunctions exists here;
there is one conjunction in the injunction, "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*).
"One [should offer] curd for one desiring sense-power," and likewise,
"He binds [the animal] to a post made of khadira wood."

Another [scriptural passage] states, "The *khadira* wood for one desiring vigor. Therefore, curd, *khadira* wood, and so forth serve both as a constant requirement and for the sake of a specific desire.
If it is argued that the remainder [is implied]—whether it be permanent (*nityatva*) or occasional (*naimittikatva*)—[then the following applies].
MS 4.3.6: *śeṣa iti cet* //
If you see it thus, why does this [subsequent statement] not also become a supplement (śeṣa) to the preceding one?
As for that which was said:
"One offers with curds," "One binds [the animal] to a post made of khadira wood";
yet the fruit of those very curds is sensory power (indriya).

Likewise, there is the potency of the *khadira* wood; and since that [potency] and this [injunction] constitute a single sentence, it is not [the case that they are separate], because there is no difference in their purpose (*arthapṛthaktva*). (MS 4.3.7)
This is not so;
these two matters are distinct:
namely, that which is the connection with curd and the oblation.
And there is the connection between curd and the sense organ,
as well as the connection between the *khadira* wood and the act of binding (*badhnāti*) with vigor; these are two matters,
and both are intended to be enjoined.

And it has been established that a sentence is one because of its unity of purpose. Here, however, the sentence would be split by reason of two purposes. How so? The injunctive suffix has been set aside, since the direct Vedic injunction for the oblation is impossible.

A quality [guṇa] mentioned in proximity [samabhivyāhṛta] ought to enjoin something; in the absence of that, it establishes a connection between the quality and the result. For in that case, the direct Vedic statement (śruti) would have to be abandoned entirely for the sake of conforming to the syntactical connection (vākya);
and it is not possible for both possibility and impossibility to coexist simultaneously. Therefore, that which is contingent (naimittika) is itself for the sake of the obligatory (nitya).

*{4/275: E2: regarding the prescription for Vedic oblations} But the consecration (saṃskāra) of substances intended for ritual action should be considered a property of the sacrifice (kratudharma). MS 4.3.8.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, they prescribe: "The milk-vow for the Brāhmaṇa,
rice-gruel for the Rājanya,
and curdled milk for the Vaiśya."
In this regard, there is a doubt:

is this a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*), or rather of the sacrifice (*kratu*)? Since it is enjoined by the syntactical connection (*vākya*) setting aside the context (*prakaraṇa*), it belongs to the person. This being the position reached, we reply:

This sacrament called a *vrata*—which serves the purpose of action for men and has the purpose of maintaining the body and providing strength—is fit to be a duty of the sacrifice (*kratudharma*), in order to favor the context (*prakaraṇa*). [Objection: But surely, on account of the syntactical connection (*vākya*), it is a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*). [Reply: We say, "No."
If that were the case, the result would have to be postulated;

however, it is already established in the other instance. For that [result] is subsumed by the injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*) under the primary [sacrifice]. Therefore, it is a property of the sacrifice (*kratudharma*).
On account of its distinctness, it would remain separate. (MS 4.3.9)
Now, for what purpose is the association with a person?
We say it is for the purpose of establishing a rule:
"The milk-vow belongs to the Jyotiṣṭoma."
But that [result] belongs only to one whose agent is a Brāhmaṇa, not to one whose agent is another. This applies everywhere. [496] {4/278} NOTES:

In the case of an injunction where no fruit is mentioned, only the ritual act itself would be prescribed; for that which is not expressed by the word [of the Veda] is not understood [as part of the injunction]. (MS 4.3.10)
They prescribe this;
therefore, one performs [the rite] for the ancestors on the preceding day.
Likewise, he pledges himself to all the gods, to all the meters, and to all the *pṛṣṭha* chants.

When there is a scriptural injunction characterized as follows: "He who resolves to undertake a sacrificial session (sattra) should sacrifice with the Viśvajit Atirātra, which has all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras, all the Stomas, and the giving away of all one's possessions (sarvavedasa) as the sacrificial fee."
A doubt arises:
is this merely a fruitless action, or is it fruitful? What is the prima facie position?
"It is fruitless. Why?
Because no fruit is heard mentioned in the case of such types of rites, which have scripture as their sole authority; for nothing that is not based on scripture is recognized [as authoritative].
But was it not stated that Vedic rituals possess fruits? It is replied:

it was stated that they possess fruits because fruits are observed from them, not because they are Vedic. If that is so, then we determine that they possess fruits because they are understood to be things that ought to be performed.
"For that which has happiness as its fruit must be performed. To this it is replied:

the duty of such a thing is directly contradicted by perception, for we perceive that it results in suffering. And a statement of this kind, being in direct contradiction with perception, does not constitute valid authority (*pramāṇa*).
Just as gourds sink in water,
stones float,
and fire is cold; and furthermore:
In this case, the fact that it has happiness as its fruit is based on inference, [namely] because it is something to be performed, therefore it must have happiness as its fruit;
however, perception is more powerful than inference. Therefore, an action of this kind is indeed fruitless.
For in this way the fruit would be postulated here, if this [teaching] were possessed of a fruit;
thus the instruction becomes meaningful. It is said in reply:
Granted, it would be logical to say that the statement is meaningless,
for there are indeed statements that are meaningless,
such as "ten pomegranates" or "six cakes."
Such are the types of [objections]. Now, is it not the case that the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the Viśvajit sacrifice has happiness as its fruit? The answer is:
it is indeed the *apūrva* (unseen potency) that has happiness as its fruit, not the operation.
Nor does this [injunction] state the necessity of performing something previously non-existent; for that is understood only when there is a necessity to perform the result,
and it is the meaning of the sentence that states the necessity of the result.

It is not a [denotative] word-meaning (*padārtha*). Nor is there here a sentence connected with a result. Therefore, this word is not an injunction (*vidhi*) for the *apūrva*; it enjoins only the mere activity (*vyāpāra*), and that activity does not have happiness as its result at the time of its occurrence.

A word that expresses all human goals, being a general term, is not restricted to a specific [instance], for it can indeed be connected even with the word *svargakāma* (one desiring heaven), though situated at a distance. [The opponent] says:
