this very sentence is the originative injunction for the Vaimṛdha offering. It would either form a single syntactical unit with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices due to the context (*prakaraṇa*), or it would be directly connected to the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*).

In this matter, direct connection (*pratyakṣasaṃyoga*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*); and the connection with the *paurṇamāsī* (Full Moon sacrifice) is direct, whereas the connection with time is indirect. Therefore, the *vaimṛdha* is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *paurṇamāsī*.
But time would apply to non-arising, because of its connection with a purpose. (MS 4.3.36)

In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard: "They proceed with the after-sacrifices (anuyāja) after the Āgnimāruta [offering]," and "Having thrown the enclosing sticks (paridhi), he offers the Hāriyojana. In this regard, there is a doubt:
what is being enjoined as a subsidiary element?

"Or rather, it is time. In the case of enjoining an auxiliary (*aṅga*), there is direct scriptural statement (*śruti*); in the case of enjoining time (*kāla*), there is indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is an injunction of an auxiliary, we reply: in a sentence concerning non-origination (*anutpatti-vākya*), it must be time.

The Āgnimāruta [offering] is a subsidiary of the Soma sacrifice, while the after-offerings (anuyājas) are subsidiaries of the animal sacrifice; in that case, there is no mutual connection between those two. Likewise, the enclosing sticks (paridhis) are subsidiaries of the animal sacrifice, whereas the Hāriyojana [offering] is a distinct primary rite. Thus, the after-offerings and the Āgnimāruta are established as being obtained [in their respective contexts], but their immediate sequence (ānantarya) has not been so established.
That is prescribed, as it is for both the Hāriyojana cup and the throwing of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).

This being the case, no benefit is conferred by the throwing of the enclosing sticks upon the Hāriyojana cup, nor by the Hāriyojana cup upon the throwing of the enclosing sticks. [Objection: But surely, because it occurs subsequent to the throwing of the enclosing sticks, it might benefit that act? [Reply: It is said:

For the act of throwing the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) upward is not to be performed for the sake of its being on top; rather, it exists solely for the sake of the animal sacrifice. And since that [act] exists, its being on top is indeed established. Therefore, the connection is for the purpose of time (*kālārtha*).
Regarding the time of origin, the time [of the sacrifice] would be [the meaning] of the sentence, because that is its primary subject. (MS 4.3.37)
This is handed down in tradition:
"Having sacrificed with the Soma, one should sacrifice [again].
Regarding this, there is a doubt.

Is this an injunction regarding the subsidiary element (aṅga), or regarding the time? What is the prima facie view? It concerns the subsidiary element, because of the direct scriptural statement (śruti).
This being the case, it is replied: in this doubt regarding whether there is an injunction of an auxiliary (aṅga) or of time, it must be time.
Because that is the primary purport of the sentence. For this sentence has time as its primary purport;
it is not intended to enjoin a sacrifice, because it does not state the ritual form (*rūpa*). How is it that it does not state the ritual form?
Because of the absence of a deity. How is there an absence?
Because it is not heard [in scripture]. For that which is heard as belonging to someone becomes his deity; indeed, a deity is understood through scriptural revelation (śruti).
It is not established by means of perception and the other sources of knowledge. Therefore, this is not an injunction of a previously unknown sacrifice;

rather, there is no fault here because it is a restatement for the purpose of specifying the time, for that which has already been enjoined with a deity is what is being restated. Therefore... [511] {4/}
In this context, the relationship is one of time (*kālārtha*). He demonstrates this: "The New and Full Moon sacrifices are indeed the chariot of the gods;

when, having performed the New and Full Moon sacrifices, one sacrifices with Soma, one rests at the end of the journey on the excellent path made manifest by the chariot of the gods. Thus, once the path has been shown, one may proceed by chariot.
It becomes easy. Likewise, having performed the New and Full Moon sacrifices, it becomes easy to sacrifice with Soma.

For him, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, which have the New and Full Moon sacrifices as their archetype (*prakṛti*), become well-mastered. Thus, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) becomes meaningful.
[Regarding] the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.5.6.1):
how can it be that this [text] does not have them as its primary purpose?
Or how [is it] that there is no mention of the nature of speech,
the goer,
or the sacrificer?
But there would be no connection with the result in that which is not enjoined, because it does not constitute the entirety [of the rite]. (MS 4.3.38)

Regarding the injunction, "One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when a son is born," there arises a doubt: is it for one's own supreme welfare, or for the supreme welfare of the son? We say: it is for one's own supreme welfare.
These ritual acts do not bear fruit for another. Why? Because of the use of the middle-voice (*ātmanepada*) in the injunction; for example:

"If one potsherd should be lost, one month of the year would have passed away. Then, if the sacrificer should die, he should offer a cake on one potsherd to Heaven and Earth. If two should be lost... [and so forth].

Two months of the year would have passed. Then, if the sacrificer should die, he should offer a cake on two potsherds to the Aśvins. He removes it [from the fire] after counting [the potsherds], for the protection of the sacrificer. This shows that when there is the occasion of the destruction of the potsherds, there is a rite whose fruit is the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) for oneself. It should be understood in this same way here as well.
Therefore, it is for the sake of the self's supreme good.
This being the case, we reply:
there would be no connection with the fruit for the father.
The statement regarding the fruit is supplementary to the son, not to the father. How so?
It is heard thus:

When a son is born, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. In that it is on eight potsherds, he purifies him with the Gāyatrī through spiritual luster; in that it is on nine potsherds...
By means of the *trivṛt* [stoma], he bestows brilliance upon him. In that there is a cake on ten potsherds, by means of the *virāj* he bestows food-eating upon him.

In that there is a cake on eleven potsherds, by means of the *triṣṭubh* he bestows sensory power (*indriya*) upon him. In that there is a cake on twelve potsherds, by means of the *jagatī* he bestows cattle upon him. He for whom, once born, one performs this sacrifice, becomes indeed purified, brilliant, an eater of food, possessed of sensory power, and rich in cattle.

Regarding that which has been born, the fruit is heard [in scripture] there; there is no overburdening of the word. Therefore, the fruit belongs to the son. As for what was said—that these actions do not bestow fruit upon another—it is replied:
Since the fruit belongs to the son, that joy is one's own; therefore, the use of the middle voice (ātmanepada) is not contradictory.
It is with reference to this very joy of the self that the statement occurs:
"The self, indeed, is the son.
"From limb by limb you are produced; from the heart you are born."
"You are indeed the self named 'son'; live for a hundred autumns. (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.2.5.4)
Having thus prescribed [the rite], it is traditionally taught:
"In whomsoever born one offers this sacrifice, he indeed becomes purified, radiant, an eater of food, possessed of sensory power, and rich in cattle. Regarding that [passage]:
But the connection with injury to the limbs is for the purpose of indicating the cause [of the penance]. (MS 4.3.39)
Now, as for what was said— namely,
"if one potsherd should be lost," and so forth— it is replied:
the connection of the subsidiary parts with their impairment is logically understood as being for the purpose of an occasioning condition (*nimitta*).

Not otherwise. For when the potsherd has been destroyed, a sacrifice for the purpose of searching for it is not appropriate. Indeed, when a farthing (kākini) is lost, its search is not conducted with a kārṣāpaṇa coin.
Or rather, the connection of the auxiliary parts with injury is for the purpose of a specific occasion (nimitta).
"One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when a son is born.
Regarding this, there is a doubt:
[does it apply] immediately upon birth?

"Or rather, after the birth-rite has been performed. We say it is "immediately upon birth," for when the occasion has arrived, the rite pertaining to that occasion must take place. This being the position, we reply:
"after the birth-rite has been performed. Why?

By implication. For it is after the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) has been performed that the consumption [of the sacrificial food] is prescribed for him. If the *iṣṭi* were performed before the birth-rite, the time for the consumption would be postponed; in that case, he would not have the means to sustain his body.
Now, as for what was said— that when the occasion has arrived, that which is contingent upon it must necessarily occur— it is replied:
the connection of the subsidiary parts with impairment is intended as the occasion.

The birth of a son is an injury; that is the established cause (*nimitta*). Time is not a constituent part of it, nor is it the cause. Even when the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) has been performed, [the impurity] does not depart. In the other case, time would cause it to depart.
And in this view, there would have to be figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). Therefore, [the rule applies] "when the birth-rite has been performed.
Now, does this mean on any day within ten days, or rather at its own proper time? What is the prima facie position?
"In whichever [day] it may be" implies that there is no fixed rule. To this it is replied:
on either the full moon day or the new moon day. Why?
From scripture; for it is thus heard in the scripture:
"He who, having sacrificed with an animal or with Soma, should sacrifice on the full moon or the new moon day. There is no overburdening of the scriptural statement.

In the other case, the time would be lost; moreover, there would be a figurative interpretation (lakṣaṇā) in this view. If one were to perform it on another lunar day or within ten days, one would not be able to bring together all the auxiliary parts (aṅga). One would fail to observe both the proper time and the state of ritual purity (śauca). Therefore, one should perform it after the ten days have passed, either on the full moon day (paurṇamāsī) or the new moon day (amāvāsyā).
NOTES: *{4/355: E2 does not repeat MS 4.3.39}** *{4/356: Tait.S. 2.2.5.4}**
Because of their connection with the principal [act] through the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*), the subsidiaries share the same time as the primary. (MS 4.3.40)

It has been stated that there is a relationship between the subsidiary and its purpose in such injunctions as, "Having piled the fire-altar, one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī," and "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava. Now, this is being deliberated:

Is it to be performed merely upon the accumulation [of the required number], right in the middle of the *tantra* (the central ritual procedure), or should it be performed at its own proper time? Likewise, in the case of the *vājapeya*, is it [to be performed] in the *bṛhaspatisava*...
Or rather, it is at its own time. These two [the *agnicayana* and the *soma* sacrifice] would have their primary time. Why?

Because the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) do not have a time other than that of the principal (*pradhāna*). For it will be stated [later]: "There is indeed one time for both the principals and the subsidiaries. And since the subsidiaries are taught by way of injunction, they are to be performed together with the principal, according to the rule: "Having performed the *agnicayana*, one should not stop there alone."
Another sacrifice known as the Sautrāmaṇī should be performed. Likewise, having accomplished the Vājapeya, one would not have finished merely by that;
one should also perform the sacrifice known as the Bṛhaspatisava.
But when [the time for the original injunction] has passed, there is an injunction [for a substitute] because of its similarity; it should take place at its own proper time.
Once the sacrifice has been concluded, this other sacrifice is enjoined;

however, that conclusion does not occur until all the constituent parts of the sacrifice have been performed. It is not as you think—that it occurs merely upon the completion of the primary act of sacrificing. Why?
Because of the connection with the instrumental case-ending,

it is understood that by means of the *vājapeya* sacrifice— one having performed the operation upon the fruit through the *vājapeya*— the operation is accomplished together with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*).
The application within the middle of the tantra would not be without its constituent parts;
for if it were said that "the Vājapeya is to be accomplished," then the intended state of the Vājapeya would belong [to that whole],
and from that, it would be understood that only the principal element designated as the Vājapeya is to be accomplished.

But this is not the case. Therefore, the meaning is that one must perform all the constituent parts (aṅgas) exactly as described. If this were so, then once the preparatory ritual (prayoga) has been completed and the time for the Vājapeya has passed, the sacrifice would be performed; and since the general injunction (codanā-sāmānya) establishes that the ritual procedure (vidhyanta) of the Jyotiṣṭoma applies, it would have to occur at its own time as obtained through the *codaka* rule. This applies to the Sautrāmaṇī as well.

"By the time of the Darśapūrṇamāsa. He says: In the case of the Vājapeya, because of the statement "having sacrificed," it is understood that one must first complete the sacrifice; however, this is not applicable to the fire-altar (agni). In that case, because of the statement "having piled [the altar]," the meaning would be that one must first complete the piling. It is replied:
This is not so; for it is heard in the scripture, "having piled the fire" (*agniṃ citvā*), which means having consecrated [it] by means of the piling of the fire (*cayana*).
By "fire" (*agni*), the blazing [element] is designated. Merely placing it upon a spot of ground does not constitute a service to it.

If the sacrifice takes place when [the fire] is situated on the ground, then there is benefit to the fire by means of the piling (cayana). The phrase "having brought that about" is understood as "having brought about the sacrifice when the fire is situated on the ground. As long as the sacrifice does not take place while the fire is situated on the ground, the fire is not benefited by the piling. It is by this [benefit] that the fire assists the sacrificer.
Thus, the assistance rendered by the fire is not merely its placement on the ground; therefore, it is understood that even in that case, one must first bring about the sacrifice.

Because of the commonality of the context and the words, the injunctions do not constitute subordinate elements [of the fire-altar construction]. (MS 4.4.1) *{The meaning is: "having consecrated the fire-altar by means of the piling," according to E1 in parentheses.}
There are sacrificial rites such as the Anumati and others; animals such as those with dewlaps and others;
and Soma-pressings such as the Pavitra and others.
The oblation in the ant-hill mound and so forth are the *dārvihomika* (wooden-spoon) rites. Likewise, one gambles with a cow that has calved for the first time,
defeats a Kṣatriya, and causes [him] to proclaim [the victory].
Regarding the statement "he is consecrated," it is heard in the proximity of these [texts]:
"One desiring self-sovereignty should sacrifice with the Rājasūya."
This very word "Rājasūya," being heard as formless in the proximity of sacrifices that possess form, is understood to denote the entire collection [of rites]. In this regard, there is a doubt:
does the word "Rājasūya" denote the collection of all [the constituent rites] beginning with Anumati?
Or rather, is it expressive of some [mantras] and not of others? What is the prima facie view? That it is expressive of all. Why?
Because of the commonality of the context and the word.

The term *prakaraṇa* (context) is common to all [the rites] in the case of the Rājasūya. A king (*rājā*) is consecrated (*sūyate*) therein; therefore it is called the Rājasūya. Alternatively, it is the sacrifice (*yajña*) of a king that is the Rājasūya. Since this context is present and there is no distinguishing factor [to the contrary], the word must be expressive of all [the rites]. And since the fruit arises from that which is designated by the word "Rājasūya," therefore all [the rites] are primary (*pradhāna*).
NOTES:
In the presence of those who are beautiful}.*
Or rather, the subsidiary acts would not be sacrifices, because they are distinct from that [primary sacrifice].

The phrase "or rather" (*api vā*) serves to set aside the previous position. Those acts which are not sacrifices (*anijyā*) are auxiliary (*aṅga*), such as gambling (*videvana*) and so forth. When it is stated, "One should effect self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) by means of the sacrifice named Rājasūya," it is understood that self-sovereignty is accomplished by the sacrifice itself, and not by what is not a sacrifice. And acts such as gambling are not sacrifices; therefore, they should be considered auxiliaries.
"Of those sacrifices which are fruitful and whose results are heard [in scripture].
That which is situated in the middle belongs to that [sacrifice] which is in the midst.

In the Rājasūya sacrifice, within the context of the Abhiṣecanīya [rite], the gambling with a pregnant cow and other such acts are prescribed. Regarding these, there arises a doubt: are they subsidiary (aṅga) to the Abhiṣecanīya alone, or to the entire Rājasūya? It is said in reply:

[The opponent argues: "Because it is mentioned in the middle [of the section] regarding the Abhiṣecanīya sacrifice, its immediate sequence will thus be favored. [The siddhāntin replies: "Or rather, because all [the rites] are equal due to the injunction, [the sequence] would not apply; for its context is not stated for the purpose of location in the middle. (MS 4.4.4)
Furthermore, acts such as gambling would be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to all the injunctions (*codanā*), beginning with the *anumati* sacrifice. Why?
Because of the equality of the injunction;
these injunctions, beginning with the *anumati*, are equal.

All of these are fruitful and constitute the primary elements. This is the context for all of them, not for the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice alone. Nevertheless, they apply to the *abhiṣecanīya* by virtue of their sequential order.
By virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it applies to all [the rites];
and context is stronger than sequence (*krama*). Therefore, it does not apply to the *abhiṣecanīya* alone. Rather, the position of the gambling (*videvana*) and so forth is within the *abhiṣecanīya*;
thus, when performed there, they assist all [the constituent rites].
NOTES: *{4/368: E2: Of the solitary [rite]. [It is] because of desire for the solitary consecration (abhiṣecanīya). Because of desire; E6: Of the solitary. Because of desire}*
And if there were no distinction between the contexts, both [theories] would indeed be contradictory.
With reference to the *upasads* of the Rājasūya, it is heard in the scripture:
"Before the *upasads*, they proceed with the offering to Soma; in the interval, however, with the offering to Tvaṣṭṛ."
Regarding the statement "by means of the Vaiṣṇava [offering] above," there arises a doubt: are the Saumya and other offerings auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the *upasads*, or...
"Are they subordinate to the *upasads*? We say: they are subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the *upasads*. Why?
Because the connection with the *upasads* is directly stated in the scripture (*śruti*).
If it were a prescription of time (*kāla*), there would be an implied figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, they are subordinate members of the *upasads*.
But surely the limb will be like time; if that were so, both would be favored, as well as the connection with the *upasad* rites.
The word "purastāt" (before) is a designation of time;

through its connection with the word "upasad," it will become an auxiliary element (*aṅga*) of the *upasads*. Furthermore, by the force of the word "purastāt," its application would be in the eastern direction and so forth. It is replied:
for both [conclusions] are contradictory.
The word "of the Upasads" is not able to qualify both [the Upasads] and those beginning with the Saumya within a single sentence.
And [the words] "east" and so forth [are not auxiliary]. For in that case, the sentence is split; therefore, it is not an auxiliary like time.
(Note:
Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.8.1.2)
Or rather, it may be merely a matter of time, because no specific distinction is observed.
The phrase "or rather" (api vā) serves to set aside the previous position. There would be a mere connection with time, not a connection between the subsidiary act and its purpose. Why?
Because no specific distinction is observed.

No specific distinction of this [time] is perceived through other designations of time, such as "they perform the after-offerings (anuyāja) after the Āgnimāruta [offering]," and so forth; for here too, the *saumya* and other offerings as well as the *upasads* have been prescribed. This sequence, however, has not been prescribed, and it is that which is now being enjoined. Therefore, it is merely a matter of time.
NOTES:
Because the reason stated possesses its fruit, the other [the *pradhāna*] would be primary. (MS 4.4.7)
"One desiring a village should offer the *vaiśvadevī* *sāṃgrahāyaṇī* sacrifice. In that context, the *āmana*-offerings are heard:
"He offers three oblations. Here there is a doubt:
are the *āmana*-offerings equally principal with respect to the *sāṃgrahāyaṇī* sacrifice?
"And as for its limb"—what is the prima facie view?
That they are equally principal. Why?
Because the other has an equal cause; for the possession of sacrifice (*yajimattva*) is equal. But surely the oblations (*homāḥ*) are without fruit. It is said in reply:
The phrase "desiring a village" is supplied here.
Therefore, [the acts] are of equal primary importance.
This being the position reached, we reply:

The subsidiary would be primary because its stated cause is like that of the fruitful; but this is not the case, for the oblations are equally primary with the sacrifice. For that which is fruitful is primary to that which is fruitless, and the sacrifice is indeed fruitful.
The oblations are fruitless. But was it not said that there will be an ellipsis (anuṣaṅga)? It is replied: ellipsis does not apply here. Why?
Because of the intervention. As it has been said:
"On account of the intervention, one should not connect [the subsequent]. By what is there an intervention?
By the *paridhi* mantras.
Having recited these mantras in sequence, beginning with "Ugro 'si," "Ugras tvam deveṣv adhi," "Ugro 'ham sajāteṣu bhūyāsam," "Priyaḥ sajātānām," and "Ugraś cet tā vasuvid."
They prescribe: "One offers three oblations. Therefore, the *āmana*-oblations are auxiliary to the *Sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice.
"O gods, for the sake of mental well-being, for the sake of mental well-being..."}*
Thus it follows [from the context]:
"The gods are both mental distress and non-distress.
The *dadhigraha* (curd-offering) is occasional (*naimittika*), because of its connection with a scriptural injunction (*śruti*). MS_4,4.8 //
In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard:
"Whatever deity the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer may exclude, from that [deity] they would be cut off."
"In that he draws the *dadhigraha* belonging to Prajāpati,
he indeed pacifies it.
Regarding this, there is a doubt:

Is the curd-offering (dadhi-graha) obligatory (nitya), or is it occasional (naimittika)? What is the prima facie view? The curd-offering should be occasional, because of its connection with a specific scriptural injunction.
It is heard that an obstacle caused by a deity is the occasion [for the rite], and an obstacle is not constant; therefore, it is occasional (naimittika).
And [the fire] is eternal because of the word "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*).
As for what was said—that it is occasional—that is accepted;
however, it is also permanent. Why?
From the word "eldest" (jyeṣṭha), the word "eldest" arises;
for he for whom this [cup] is drawn is indeed the eldest among the cups.
"He attains preeminence (*jyaiṣṭhya*) itself.
And the word *jyeṣṭha* may refer either to preeminence or to primacy. This [Self] is the first, not the preeminent. If it were eternal, [it would be the preeminent].
Since it is thus praiseworthy, it is logical;
for they never praise that which is unstable or wavering. Therefore, it is both permanent and occasional.
It should be apprehended even without a sign, and furthermore, it should be apprehended by means of a sign as well.
And because of its possessing all forms.
And it is heard [in scripture] that it possesses all forms:
"This cup which is drawn is the form of all these gods; all the forms of the sacrificial animals attend upon him.
For no other form of a deity is perceptible to us.
Other than this, it is due to its permanence. Therefore, it is both permanent and occasional.
Or rather, it must be a permanent explanatory statement (arthavāda), because those two have no connection with the ritual act and because an obstacle is by nature transitory. (MS 4.4.11)
As for what was stated— that [the rite] is both obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*)— in that case, it must be only obligatory,
because of the word "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*) and because of its universal form (*sārvarūpya*). As for what was stated...

It is heard that "the obstacle caused by a deity" is the cause. However, an obstacle caused by a deity is not understood to be the cause [of the sacrifice's failure], because the connection is with the obstacle to the ritual action of those two—the *adhvaryu* and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). For it is not heard [in the scripture] that "the deity must be obstructed by the *adhvaryu* or by the sacrificer."

For an obstacle is impermanent. Furthermore, there is no such statement as "when an obstacle exists, the curd-cup (dadhi-graha) is to be drawn. Thus, the drawing of the curd-cup occurs even without a formal injunction of connection.

"But the purpose of this [instruction] is the removal of obstacles. This would mean that the instruction is treated as permanent, while the purpose is impermanent. It is not logical that one should grasp what is permanent for the sake of removing an impermanent obstacle. In that case, because the purpose is impermanent, the scriptural statement regarding the permanence of the instruction would be contradicted.

But if it is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), it is not contradicted. For it is not taken up there to remove an obstacle; rather, it is stated for the purpose of praising it, since it has another purpose altogether. However, the purpose of the *dadhi-graha* (curd-offering) is simply its being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the Soma sacrifice.
Furthermore, because the obstacle is transitory, [the injunction remains uncontradicted].

The mention of the impermanent is for the purpose of praising the permanent; it is a figurative expression and an indirect means (antarāya). Therefore, this is not a fault, and the *dadhi-graha* is indeed permanent.
And the Vaiśvānara [offering] should be obligatory, because it has the same number as the obligatory offerings. (MS 4.4.12)
"There is the fire; he who, knowing thus, piles the fire.
In that regard, it is heard [in the scripture]:
"He who, indeed, having not carried the fire for a year as the *ukhya*, [piles the fire]..."
He accumulates [sin] such that he perishes like a fetus stillborn;
he would thus meet with affliction.
One should first offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara. For Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year.
Just as one gives birth when the year has been reached and the time has arrived,
even so, having waited for a year, he piles the fire-altar when the time has arrived; thus he shall not come to ruin.
"Vaiśvānara is indeed the dear body of Agni;
thus one secures his dear body.
Regarding this, there is a doubt.
Is Vaiśvānara obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*)? What is the prima facie view? Here too, it is indeed obligatory; it is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
The defect incurred by the failure to maintain the fire in the *ukhā* for a full year is remedied by the *vaiśvānara* oblation. Furthermore, its number becomes equal to that of the obligatory rites,
for there are these three oblations.
"These three worlds are for the purpose of ascending to these worlds," [it is said];
there is no commonality between the worlds and the oblations. If, just as the three worlds are eternal, so too these three oblations were eternal, [then...]
In this way, association with the worlds is possible; therefore, Vaiśvānara is eternal.

Or [the fire-altar is not eternal], because it is connected with that which has arisen, as in the case of "having previously not existed, [one builds] the fire" (abhūtvāgnim) [Tait.S. 5.5.1.7]. MS 4.4.13.

The connection with the destruction of faults occurs upon the arising of the sign (nimitta) consisting of the wearing of ornaments. There is no purpose in the destruction of faults for that which has arisen without such a connection. Therefore, there is no contradiction here as there is in the case of the *dadhi-graha* (curd-offering);
thus, it is not a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), but rather something contingent (*naimittika*). Now, as for what was said:
"The identity of number with the worlds is possible because of their eternity, and not otherwise. To this we reply:
"Because of the commonality of the number three between the worlds and the oblations, it will be a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda)."
The sixfold consciousness [is not the self], because it is as before.

"There is the fire; he who, knowing thus, piles the fire. Regarding this, it is heard in scripture: "The year indeed drives away from its foundation him who, having piled the fire, does not find a firm footing."
"There are five preceding layers; then one piles the sixth layer. Regarding this, there is a doubt:
is it that very same fire which is permanent that is here said to consist of six layers?
Or is it that this [sixth layer] is occasional, pertaining to a specific occasion? What is the prima facie view?

This sixth layer is prescribed for that very same permanent fire; this is a commendatory statement (arthavāda) regarding that very permanent sixth layer. Even one who is not worthy of a firm foundation [is so described].
"He too ought to be established with this sixth layer"—this is a praise of the layer (*citi*). Why is it described in this way?
Because of the hearing of the word "sixth" (*ṣaṣṭhī*). For the word *ṣaṣṭhī* is the ordinal that completes a group of six;
indeed, the word *ṣaṣṭhī* would not be appropriate in reference to a single layer. Therefore, the fire-altar (*agni*) is eternally composed of six layers.
And because they are enumerated as being equal in number to those [qualities]. (MS 4.4.15)
And by means of those preceding [layers], there is a corresponding enumeration for this one. How so?
This earth, indeed, is the first layer; the plants are the loose soil (purīṣa). The intermediate space, indeed, is the second layer.
The seasons are the loose soil. Yonder sky is indeed the third layer;
the stars are the loose soil. The sacrifice is indeed the fourth layer; the sacrificial gifts are the loose soil. The sacrificer is indeed the fifth layer.
"Progeny is the loose soil; the year indeed is the sixth layer, and the seasons are the loose soil. For there is a sequential enumeration of equals as equals.

For example: "The gods, the seers, and the Gandharvas were on one side; the Asuras, the Rakṣases, and the Piśācas were on the other. By means of this genitive case, there is an enumeration of these layers (*citī*) as equals. Therefore, this [genitive] must be equivalent to that. And if those [layers] belong to a particular sacrifice, then this one must belong to that same sacrifice.
Therefore, it is equal to these; for that very reason, that same eternal fire consists of six layers.
And because the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is logically consistent [with this view]. (MS 4.4.16)
And there is an explanatory passage (arthavāda):
"There are six layers;
there are six fillings of earth."
These amount to twelve;
twelve months are a year;
verily, he finds firm support in the year.
Therefore, that statement is not consistent with regard to a single-pile fire. Consequently, the six-pile fire is indeed permanent.
Or there may be a single altar, for it is enjoined by means of a specific occasion when [the altars] have been separated.
Or rather, the single piling (*ekaciti*) would be occasional (*naimittika*).
Why? Because it is enjoined when the sacrifice has been completed, triggered by the occasion of non-establishment (*apratiṣṭhā*). It applies to one who does not attain stability.
This piling of his is said to be occasional;
it cannot be permanent.
Moreover, it is enjoined only when the sacrifice has been completed.

It cannot occur while it is present. But surely, the word "having piled" (*citvā*) refers to the completion of the piling (*cayana*), not the sacrifice. It is said in reply: this word "having piled" does not refer to the completion of the ritual act (*padārtha*). What then?

Regarding the meaning of the sentence: "having piled the fire" (*agniṃ citvā*) means "having accomplished the purpose [of the rite] through the piling of the fire. And when the sacrifice has been performed, the purpose of the fire is accomplished by means of the piling, and not otherwise. Furthermore, there is the word in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīśabda*).
Five previous layers have been mentioned; with reference to them, this [single layer] will be determined as appropriate.
Therefore, it is said that the sacrifice is completed [when this is done]. Consequently, by virtue of this scriptural statement, the fire-altar consists of a single layer.
NOTES:
*{4/393: E1 gives naimittikaḥ in parentheses} Because of the conflict [of rules], there is equality of number with them. (MS 4.4.18)
This is the answer regarding the two sūtras,
because they correspond in number with those [senses] and because the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is logically consistent.
By means of those [five] eternal [deities],
there will be equality in number,
and the explanatory passage (arthavāda) will be justified: "There are five preceding layers."

Since he does not find firm support through those previous layers, this sixth one is for the purpose of providing support. And by referring to those [previous layers] together with their soil-fillings (*purīṣa*), there will be a praise in terms of the number twelve. This is because of the contradiction between the number six and the number twelve regarding one and the same thing. Furthermore, even things that are unequal may be enumerated as if they were equal.
For example: "Gods, humans, and ancestors—they were from elsewhere.

And because they are equal in number to those [mantras],
and because the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is thus rendered consistent;
and because of [the reading] "with the eternal ones" (*nityābhiḥ*) in the margin.
The Pitṛyajña, because it has its own specific time, should not be a subordinate part [of the Soma sacrifice].
In the ritual of the new moon (āmāvāsya), there is the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña);
for it is said: "On the new moon day, in the afternoon, they perform the piṇḍapitṛyajña.
Regarding this, there is a doubt:

Is the Piṇḍapitṛyajña an auxiliary (aṅga) of the New Moon sacrifice, or is it not an auxiliary? What is the prima facie view? It is an auxiliary, because it occurs in proximity to that which possesses a fruit, and because of the statement regarding its redemption (niṣkraya).
He says: "Is it not the case that what is without fruit becomes a subsidiary part (aṅga) of that which has fruit when it is in its proximity;
and this [sacrifice] could be conceived as having heaven as its fruit? It is replied:
True.
"Because it forms a single syntactical unit with *amānāsyā*, heaven cannot be postulated [as its meaning]. He replies:
"Since it expresses time, its status as a single syntactical unit with the ritual action is not possible. It is said in response:

"Even by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), its status as a single syntactical unit with the ritual action is indeed possible. If heaven were to be postulated [as the primary meaning], there would be no secondary indication."
It is not based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). For they recite thus:
"When one performs [the rite] for the ancestors on the previous day, having thereby ransomed the sacrifice from the ancestors, the sacrificer extends it toward the gods."
Furthermore, it is heard that [the *anvārambhaṇīyā*] is to be performed for the purpose of redemption on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*); therefore, it is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of that [sacrifice].
This being the position reached, we reply:
The *piṇḍapitṛyajña* should not be an auxiliary (*anaṅga*) because it has its own specific time;
thus, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is not an auxiliary. Why?
Because it has its own time;
its connection is with the time denoted by its own word, not with the action indicated [by that word].
For example: "Having sacrificed with the New and Full Moon sacrifices, one should sacrifice with Soma";
and for example:
"Prior to the Upasads, they proceed with the offering to Soma."

Furthermore, this word "time" (kāla) is primarily used in its primary sense (*mukhya*), not in the sense of an action; its application to an action is merely figurative (*lakṣaṇā*), and direct denotation (*śruti*) is more powerful than figurative indication. As for what was stated:

It might be argued that through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) there will be syntactic unity with the action; but that is not so. Why? Because figurative indication is appropriate only in the case of a restatement (anuvāda).

This is not a prescriptive injunction (*vidhi*); rather, this is a prescription (*vidhi*). Therefore, there is no connection with the ritual action of the new moon (*amāvāsya*), for two distinct ritual actions would exist at one and the same time without being mutually connected.
E2: pratanitum}*
*{4/405: Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.8.1.2; cf. also Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā 4.4.5–6}* *{4/406: E2,6: [the] time here}* *{4/407: E2 omits "in the ritual action"}*
And because it is enumerated as being equal [to other things]. (MS 4.4.20)
And it is enumerated as equal to other principal [acts]:
"There are indeed four great sacrifices: the Agnihotra,..."
The New and Full Moon sacrifices,
the Jyotiṣṭoma, and the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.

It is enumerated as being equivalent to the great sacrifices (mahāyajña). What would constitute its status as a great sacrifice, other than its fruitfulness? Therefore, it is not an auxiliary part [of the ritual].
And because it is seen even when [the ritual] is prohibited. (MS 4.4.21)
For this reason also, it is not a subsidiary part:
the scripture shows the Piṇḍapitṛyajña as belonging to the New Moon sacrifice;
"One who has rivals should perform the Full Moon sacrifice alone."
On the new moon day,
having struck down his rival, he should sacrifice with the Amāvāsyā [offering];
indeed, by means of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña itself, he gratifies [the ancestors] on the new moon day.

Since the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is prescribed even when there is no new moon day (amāvāsyā), it follows that it is not an integral part [of the Darśa sacrifice]. Therefore, for this reason as well, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is not an auxiliary (aṅga).
What is the purpose of this deliberation?
If the establishment of the fires (ādhāna) takes place on the full moon day,
then it is not performed on the immediately following new moon day,
just as in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa). However, according to the established conclusion (siddhānta),...
It should be performed in that manner. Furthermore, there is this other purpose:
"At the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana, one performs the Agnihotra for a month;
for a month, [one performs] the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. (527) {4/}

"One should sacrifice"—according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* should be performed in that manner; according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it should not be performed in that manner. They also cite this verse:
"If the establishment of the fires (ādhāna) takes place on the full moon day after the new moon sacrifice has already occurred,
and if the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña) is not an integral part [of that rite], then it shall not be performed on that very same day."
for it is prohibited} *{4/409:
And in the *sattra* sacrifice, the cord should be a limb of the animal, because it is prescribed upon the arrival of that [animal].
In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard:
"Having taken the Āśvina cup and having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-twisted rope, he dedicates the Savanīya animal to Agni. Regarding this, there is a doubt:
is the rope a subsidiary part of the animal?
Or is it an auxiliary of the sacrificial post? What is the prima facie view? It is an auxiliary of the animal sacrifice. Why?
Because it is prescribed upon the arrival of that [animal].
For it is prescribed in the animal sacrifice ritual. The connection of the animal with this [rite] is heard in the originative injunction:
"Having performed the encircling, he dedicates the animal, and not otherwise. Such is the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*);
if it were a statement of time, there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
"The time [of the sacrifice] should be indicated by the act of encircling," [says the opponent].
[The Siddhāntin replies: "Rather, it is a subsidiary part of the sacrificial post (yūpa), because it is a refinement (saṃskāra) of that."
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the refinement of the sacrificial post (yūpa) is indeed directly perceived;

for the rope (raśanā), whatever it may be and to whatever degree of firmness it produces in the post, serves the purpose of providing that firmness to the post. Therefore, the rope should belong to the post itself for the sake of its firmness. Furthermore, the accusative case-ending occurs precisely when that [the object] is predominant.

And the third [case-ending] is used for the girdle (*raśanā*). Since that third case indicates its status as a subordinate element (*guṇatva*), it is therefore an accessory (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). As for what was stated, "because it is prescribed upon the arrival of that [post]," [that argument is refuted].
That must be refuted. It is said:
there is an injunction regarding its arrival, and the accusative case-ending is both a direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*) and a perceptible fact.
[Otherwise] the two statements would be contradicted. As for the point regarding "indication" (lakṣaṇā):
when direct denotation (śruti) is impossible, indication is indeed logical.
And the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is meaningful because it has that [injunction] as its purpose. (MS 4.4.24)
And in this way, the explanatory mantra (*arthavāda*) will be meaningful:
"The youth, well-attired and girt with the cord, has come; he becomes even more excellent as he is born. The wise poets, seeking the gods, uplift him with their minds in pious devotion.
Therefore, the rope is an accessory (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
What is the purpose of this reflection?
It is heard in the Śruti regarding the fire-altar: "Eleven animals are to be bound to a single sacrificial post. A rope must be prepared for each animal.
If the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is maintained, then according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), there must indeed be two ropes. They also cite a verse:
"If the rope is an accessory of the animal, then if one were to yoke many animals with a single [rope]..."
"A rope should be made for each animal; if there is a single sacrificial post, there should be two ropes. (Notes:)
And the *svaru* [wooden chip] also [is not a separate offering], because it is a single part [of the same substance].
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal victim dedicated to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya*), which is an auxiliary part of the Soma ritual, as stated in the text:
"When one who has been consecrated (*dīkṣita*) sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. Regarding this, it is heard in the scripture:
"One anoints the animal with the *svaru* or with the axe. In this regard, there is a doubt:
is the *svaru* an accessory (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), or is it an accessory of the animal (*paśu*)? What is the prima facie view?
We say that it is an accessory (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Why?

Because it is a part (*ekadeśa*). It is heard in scripture that the *svaru* is a part of the sacrificial post, as in "one makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post" (*yūpasya svaruṃ karoti*); the meaning is that one should make the sacrificial post such that the *svaru* is its tip.
"Thus that sacrificial post (yūpa) comes to be,
just like the top-ring (caṣāla). [529] {4/417} NOTES:

And the ransoming [of the sacrificial post] is like its subsidiary parts. (E1: "He makes the *svaru*"; the meaning is that one should make the sacrificial post such that the *svaru* is its end. MS_4,4.26.
The statement regarding the purchase [of the Svaru] shows it to be an accessory of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), like the Svaru itself:
"In ancient times, the seers who brought the post to the altar used to feel remorse and regret after having divided it."
Thinking, "This ritual act would indeed result in the destruction of the sacrifice," they saw that the *prastara* [grass-bundle] was the ransom for the *sruva* ladle,
and the *svaru* [wooden chip] from the sacrificial post was for the sake of preventing the destruction of the sacrifice.
Because its redemption is heard [in the scripture], it is understood to be a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of that [sacrifice]. Therefore, it is a subordinate part of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
Or rather, it is a subordinate part of the animal (*paśu*), because it is a purposeful action (*arthakarman*).
Or rather, it is a part of the animal, for its purpose is to serve as the *svaru* for the act of anointing. For it is so stated in scripture:
"He anoints the animal with the *svaru*. That anointing belongs to the animal.

It serves as the purpose for the production of the *svaru*. If this *svaru* is for that [specific] purpose, then its purpose is visible (*dṛṣṭa*). But if it is for the sake of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), then its purpose is invisible (*adṛṣṭa*).
Therefore, it must be so conceived; hence, it is a limb of the animal.
(Note:
E2 omits "prayojanam")
Through devotion, there may be the doctrine of ransom.
With what devotion?
He spoke thus: "The sacrificial post (yūpa) is indeed to be cast into the fire;
that which is thrown as the *svaru*—by that [it is done]."
"The sacrificial post is being thrown in"—this is like a ransom;
by this figurative expression, it is a praise.
What is the purpose of this?

When eleven animals are tied to a single sacrificial post, according to the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa), the anointing is performed for only one animal; according to the final conclusion (siddhānta), it is for all of them. And there is a verse:

If it is argued that the *svaru* is an accessory (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), then there would be an anointing for only one [post]; however, when there are many [posts] with a single *yūpa*, there must be an anointing for all of them. Thus [it is said]. [530] {4/420}
NOTES: *{4/419: E2: tena tena}* The sacrifices of the New and Full Moon rites are the primary acts, because there is no distinction [among them]. (MS 4.4.29)
There are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices;
therein are heard [the injunctions for] the Āgneya, Agnīṣomīya, Upāṃśuyāja, Aindrāgna, and Sāṃnāyya sacrifices. Likewise,
The two libations (āghāra), the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), the fore-offerings (prayāja) and after-offerings (anuyāja),
and the offerings to the wives (patnīsaṃyāja).
The *samiṣṭayajus* and the *sviṣṭakṛt*. In this regard, there is a doubt:
are all these sacrifices primary acts?

And some [might argue] that they are subordinate (*guṇabhūta*). What is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That all the sacrifices whatsoever belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are principal (*pradhāna*). For it is heard in the text "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*) that the fruit results from the sacrifices without distinction;
and that which possesses a fruit is principal.
And all these are sacrifices; therefore, all of them are primary.
Alternatively, some are subsidiaries, in which there is praise as being subsidiary, for the praise is common [to both].
Or rather, there may be certain auxiliary elements (*aṅga*). Which ones, then?
Those for which there is praise by way of being an auxiliary element, as for example:
These two Āghāra libations are indeed the two reins of the sacrifice;
these two Ājyabhāga portions are the two eyes of the sacrifice.
When the Prayājas and Anuyājas are offered, the armor of the sacrifice is thereby fashioned.
"The armor is for the sacrificer's overcoming of his rival," it is said.
The reins are a part of the chariot;
they are the eyes of the one who possesses eyes.
The armor belongs to the one possessing armor; for a common praise is appropriate. And if those limbs are praised, then the praise becomes meaningful. Therefore, the limbs are praised as limbs.

Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.2.1}* *{4/423: Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.1.5}*
And likewise, there is the observation of another [scriptural] passage to that effect. (MS 4.4.31)
And by taking it thus, the observation of another purpose becomes logical, namely:
"At each *prayāja*, he offers a *kṛṣṇala* grain," whereas [otherwise] one would not be performing the *prayāja* sacrifices.
And [the text] says, "He does not perform the after-offerings.
But the cause is non-distinct [in all cases], because the quality exists within the primary elements.
This reason called "praise" (saṃstava) is not distinctive;
for even the Āgneya and other offerings are praised as being constituent parts [of the sacrifice], as in:
"The Āgneya is indeed the head of the sacrifice."
The Upāṃśuyāja is the heart,
the Agniṣomīya is the two feet;
for the head is a limb of that which possesses a head.
"The heart [belongs] to that which possesses a heart;
the feet [belong] to that which possesses feet"—this is a praise of everything as being a limb. Consequently, everything would become a limb.
In that case, there would be no principal element (*pradhāna*). If there is no principal element, of what would anything be a limb?
Therefore, this is not a factor [of that].
NOTES: *{4/426: E1 (Fn.): tatra}*
An observation of another purpose does not [constitute a reason] when [the reason] has not been stated, because it serves a different aim.
Now, as for what was said—
that the observation of another purpose does not prove [the point] because it is for the sake of another— that sentence is indeed for the sake of another.

It is not for the purpose of enjoining the *prayāja* offerings and the like which are already being observed. Therefore, another means of knowledge must be sought for this—either another scriptural statement (*śruti*) or a logical principle (*nyāya*). In the absence of such a means, that [observation] becomes like the sight of a mirage; even so is the case with praise when there is no underlying logical principle.
It is indeed not established.
NOTES:
However, there is the application of two distinct designations.
On account of scriptural statement and designation;
furthermore, that which possesses fruit is the primary characteristic [of a rite],
and that which is not connected by a specific injunction in its proximity should be an auxiliary to it.
Because the cause possesses a share [in the result], and because no connection with anything else is heard [in the scripture]. (MS 4.4.34)
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position.
It was stated that all [the constituent acts] are equally primary; however, this is not so.
The primary rites are those denoted by the term *darśapūrṇamāsa*. Why?
Because of the connection with the fruit:
from those [texts] containing the term *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the fruit is heard, namely,
"One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa."
What, then, are those [rites] designated by the term *darśapūrṇamāsa*?
They are those in whose scriptural injunctions the word *paurṇamāsī* (full moon) or the word *amāvāsyā* (new moon) occurs;
these are the *āgneya* and the others. But is it not the case that for those rites designated by the word *amāvāsyā*, no fruit is heard [in the scripture]? It is said in reply:
If these two designations, "paurṇamāsī" and "amāvāsyā," were to apply separately to the two collections,
then [the name] would refer to whichever collection exists among the three [offerings], beginning with the Āgneya.
In that context, the word "paurṇamāsī" [is used] for one [day], and the word "amāvāsyā" for the others.
How is it that the dual form "paurṇamāsyāmāvāsye" is heard?
And because it is designated as having two meanings. How is it so designated?
By means of a dual-number designation, namely, "by means of the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]."

The words *darśa* and *amāvāsyā* have the same meaning. How so? *Darśa* is the first of these two, and *pūrṇamāsa* is the latter; therefore, if one begins with the *pūrṇamāsa* first, it is performed out of its proper sequence.

One who is about to undertake the New- and Full-Moon sacrifices should offer a *caru* to Sarasvatī and a cake on twelve potsherds to Sarasvant; for Sarasvatī is indeed the New Moon, and Sarasvant is the Full Moon. Having thus prepared both of these in their proper order, he undertakes [the sacrifice] for the sake of prosperity; verily he prospers, for this purpose is through the state of being a productive pair.

In this context, by using the word *darśa* as a synonym for the word *amāvāsyā* (the new moon day) in its primary sense, he demonstrates their identity of meaning. Furthermore, it is possible to define the *amāvāsyā* as *darśa* based on the non-seeing (*adarśana*) of the moon;
just as one who lacks eyes is designated "one with eyes" (*cakṣuṣmān*) by means of his two eyes despite their absence.
This is established both from this designation and from the scriptural tradition heard in the world.
We determine that they indeed have a single purpose. Furthermore, that which possesses fruit is the primary characteristic;
whatever else is heard in proximity to it [is subordinate].
That is its subsidiary. How so?

That which is heard in proximity to something that requires a procedure (*itikartavyatā*), being capable of fulfilling it by way of specifying that procedure, ought to be its subsidiary. Otherwise, if the remainder of the sentence were not supplied, one would have to postulate a separate result.
He says: "But surely, the fruit of the Darśapūrṇamāsa itself is here attached [to these subsidiary rites]. It is replied: "It is possible for it to be attached;

however, the sentence concerning the Darśapūrṇamāsa would remain expectant (sākāṅkṣa). Another procedure (itikartavyatā) would have to be postulated for that [Darśapūrṇamāsa], and another [procedure] would have to be postulated for these [subsidiaries] such as the Prayājas. Thus, the procedure already understood from this [Darśapūrṇamāsa context] would be abandoned."
Therefore, it possesses the status of an auxiliary;
the cause is that it "participates" [in the result]. The connection of these with any other fruit is not heard in the scripture. Consequently, not all of them are equally primary;
rather, the *āghāra* and other such acts are subordinate rituals (*guṇakarman*).
NOTES:
Furthermore, qualities associated with names are prescribed; they are not applicable to the subsidiaries (*aṅga*). (MS 4.4.35)
Furthermore, specific qualities are prescribed in conjunction with specific names,
as for example: "One should touch the Pūrṇamāsī [day] with the Caturhotṛ [formula]," and "the Amāvāsyā [day] with the Pañcahotṛ [formula]."

If there were no knowledge of the distinction that "among all the principal [offerings], this group consists of the Caturhotṛ [mantras]" and "this [group] consists of the Pañcahotṛ [mantras]," then this [application] would not be possible. Yet, such an injunction of subordinate qualities (guṇavidhāna) does indeed exist. Therefore, it is only our position that holds true. Furthermore, because the Āghāra and other [acts] are subordinate...
The praise will be appropriate. (534) {4/433} NOTES:

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the mantra-text for the Āgneya offering comes first, while the Brāhmaṇa-text follows later. Regarding this, there is a doubt: which [is authoritative]?
"The reading is more authoritative. It is replied:
there is no fixed rule, because there is no scripture that establishes such a rule.
This being the case, we reply:
the recitation of the mantra is more powerful. Why?
Because of the capacity of its form for application. The mantra possesses the capacity of its form for application; that is its capacity by which the mantra is employed.
And for that which is being employed, the sequence is observed for the sake of perception.
But is it not the case that the very same purpose applies to the recitation of the Brāhmaṇa as well? It is said:
that [recitation] is the place of origin.
Furthermore, its purpose will also be for the sake of the arising of karma.
*{4/499: E2: iṣṭāv abhavati}* According to that statement, in a modified sacrifice (vikṛti), it should be performed according to the principal element. 5.1.17.
There is a sacrifice named Adhvarakalpā;
one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu,
Sarasvatī should have a portion of clarified butter, and there should be a pap for Bṛhaspati.
In this regard, there is a doubt:
should the ritual details (*dharma*) of the *bārhaspatya* sacrifice— which is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *āgneya*— be performed first, since the original injunction (*codaka*) is more powerful?

Because of the injunction for performance (*prayogavacana*). Or rather, the injunction for performance of the modification of the *upāṃśuyāja* is stronger than the extended application (*codaka*). What is the conclusion?
In this modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), [the former applies].

It would follow the order of importance, because that is what is stated; for in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there is a direct statement regarding their sequence. Therefore, it is the injunctive statement of performance (*prayogavacana*) that brings together those [elements] which are proximate, for that is directly perceived.

And the properties of those [elements] are established through inference, for they are obtained by means of the *codaka* (the extended application). Therefore, the directly perceived *prayogavacana* (the injunction of performance) is more powerful;
by it, the inferential *codaka* is sublated.

Or, in the case of a deviation, [the result follows] according to the nature [of the cause], because of the continuity of that nature. 5.1.18.
Or, in the case of a contradiction regarding the sequence of the primary parts,
it ought to be exactly as it is in the archetype (prakṛti), so too in the ectype (vikṛti). Why?
Because of the continuity of the archetype (*prakṛti*). Whatever properties exist in the archetype, those same must exist in the modification (*vikṛti*);

therefore, if they were performed according to the order of the primary [rite], they would not be performed as they are in the archetype. For the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) [governs] the performance...
It is more powerful than the statement, for it both produces and brings about [the result]. Having observed those things brought about, the statement of application (prayogavacana) summarizes them;
having arisen with respect to what has been brought about, it subsequently has the bringing about as its cause.
The *codaka* (the general rule) cannot invalidate what was previously obtained,
even though it is directly perceived,
because it is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*).
He will prescribe exactly as they have been obtained. Therefore, first come the rules of Bārhaspatya,
and after that those of Ājya.
A modification (*vikṛti*) should take place at the same time as its archetype (*prakṛti*), because it possesses the nature of the archetype; this is according to the rule of the learned. 5.1.19.
Among the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the Sākamedha is the third seasonal festival; its constituent parts are as follows:
in the morning, an eight-potherd cake for Agni Anīkavat.
"At midday, there is a *caru* offering for the *Sāṃtapana* Maruts;

That the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) ought to follow the time of its archetype.
Just as it has been stated regarding the archetype (*prakṛti*),
so should it be for the ectype (*vikṛti*); for the latter possesses the characteristics of the former.
Therefore, whatever modification there may be,
it ought to have a duration of two days.
"Whichever modification there may be,

Alternatively, if [the rite] were to be performed immediately, even though it is connected with a specific sequence and time, there would be a loss of the characteristics of the archetype (prakṛti) because the injunction is merely inferred in that case. //5.1.20//
Those things which are spoken of as occurring at the times of the day—
namely morning, midday, and evening—
are understood to occur sequentially within a single day.
Just as when it is said, "Devadatta eats cake in the morning,

eats various foods at midday, and eats sweetmeats in the afternoon," it is understood to occur within a single day; therefore, modifications (*vikṛti*) of this kind have the same immediate timing (*sadyaskālā*).
For the performance at two times, obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) and thus inferential,
would be sublated by the *sadyaskāla* (immediate) form, which is perceptible.
If it is argued that there is an extension of time. //5.1.21//
If you think thus,
[you must admit that] it is heard as being accompanied by its constituent parts (sāṅga),
both at midday and in the evening.
There will be an extension so that [the ritual] remains complete with its constituent parts during these times; nor is there any contradiction regarding the two-day duration,
for one will commence with the *Anīkavant* [offering] on the morning of the first day.

On the second day, he shall sacrifice in the morning. In this way, the Sāṃtapanīyā will be commenced on the previous day at midday and sacrificed on the following day at midday. Likewise, for the Gṛhamedhīya, the commencement is on the previous day in the evening.
"The sacrifice in the evening is on the following day. Now, it was argued that a single day is understood from the sentence. It is replied:
for the meaning of a sentence arises from the capacity of the meanings of its constituent words. And here, there is no such capacity of the word-meanings by which a single day could be understood.

*{4/507: E1 (Fn.): sāṃtapanīyāḥ}* [The suffix -ya-] does not occur because of connection with that [the action], [as in the case of] *sāṃtapanīyāḥ*. //5.1.22//
This is not so. Why?
Because of their connection;
the principal acts are heard in scripture as being connected with the auxiliary acts at one and the same time. How so?

For it is heard that the primary rite together with its auxiliaries (*sāṅga*) is to be performed at the morning time, and likewise at midday and in the evening; the auxiliaries are not [to be performed] at the morning time and so forth [separately]. In that case, if the auxiliaries were at different times and the primary rites at different times, the rite would not have been performed with its auxiliaries at those [prescribed] times. Therefore, these modified forms (*vikṛti*) are indeed of immediate performance (*sadyaskāla*). Moreover,
It is heard in the scripture: "One should perform the Sākamedha sacrifices for two days. This is consistent with the view that they are performed on a single day (*sadyaskāla*).

Because the limbs have their primary time [of performance], there would be a displacement [of the main act] as previously stated. (5.1.23)

"They proceed with the after-offerings (anuyāja) after the Āgnimāruta [offering]"; thus there is an upward displacement (utkarṣa), as is the case in the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice.
"The animals being standing, they perform the fore-offerings (prayāja)"—this is a case of anticipation (apakarṣa). In this regard, there is a doubt:
when there is postponement (utkarṣa), is only the after-offerings (anuyāja) postponed; and when there is anticipation (apakarṣa), is only the fore-offerings (prayāja) anticipated?

Furthermore, [the sequence] is from the *anuyāja* onwards in the case of postponement (*utkarṣa*), and up to the *prayāja* in the case of anticipation (*apakarṣa*). What, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It is as much as has been stated.

There would be [an adjustment] in cases of advancement (utkarṣa) and postponement (apakarṣa). Why? Because the subsidiaries have the time of the principal as their time. In this way, there will be for others the time of the principal. In that case, the injunction of performance (prayogavacana), which establishes simultaneity, will be favored.
Or rather, because of the connection starting from that [point], there would be postponement up to the end of that. (5.1.24)
In that case, [the sequence] beginning with that would be understood as the progressive development (*utkarṣa*), and ending with that as the regressive development (*apakarṣa*). Why?
Because of the connection. That which...
It is recited after the *anuyāja* offerings;

although it would have been performed before the principal sacrifice as obtained through the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), it is instead performed after the *anuyāja* offerings by virtue of the force of its textual position (*pāṭha*).
Likewise, that which is beyond this is beyond that. In this way, when one [element] is elevated, it elevates the entire category of qualities;
likewise, when it is lowered, it lowers it.

For those whose time has been fixed by their engagement [in a ritual], [the death-impurity lasts] until the completion of that engagement. //5.1.25//
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard at the time of the Prātaranuvāka:
"O Pratiprasthātṛ, offer the Savanīya oblations"—thus he gives the command; this is the time for the offering of the Savanīyas. And there is also [a rule] when the Bahiṣpavamāna has been chanted.
"O Agnīdh, distribute the fires;
strew the sacrificial grass;
prepare the sacrificial cakes. In this regard, there is a doubt:
At the time of the *prātaranuvāka*, should the Soma-related ritual items such as the *pracaraṇī-homa* and others be performed after the *savanīya* offerings have been set aside,

There is no fixed rule, because there is no scripture that establishes a restrictive rule.
This being the position reached, we reply:
for those [rites] whose time is determined by the commencement [of the main rite].
There would be a restriction based on the sequence of items known through their performance;

However, in the case of the Soma sacrifice, the sequence of the *pracaraṇī-homa*—which is an item belonging to the Soma ritual—is set aside by a specific scriptural injunction. Therefore, the preceding ritual items for that [offering] end with the pouring out (*nirvapaṇa*) and so forth; after that, the subsequent ritual items belonging to the Soma sacrifice (*saumika*) are to be performed.

And because of the contradiction with the verbal testimony [of scripture]. 5.1.26.

for if one were told "decorate," one might instead perform acts such as sprinkling water [on the materials]. In our view, however, when told "decorate," one will understand only the act of decorating. In that regard, concerning the decoration, the *loṭ* suffix ending in the verb—which expresses the present time—will be favored as denoting the appropriate time for action. Therefore, in this case, the meaning follows the context of the activity (*prāvṛttika*).
But because there is no connection [with the original], that modified [element] alone should be transferred. 5.1.27.
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, which has the New and Full Moon sacrifices as its archetype, there is a modified rite concerning the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

That rite is brought forward [to an earlier point], according to the rule: "During the initiations, one cuts the sacrificial post. When that rite is brought forward, it also brings forward the subsequent rites, such as the carrying forth of the fires for Agni and Soma.
When there is a doubt as to whether it draws [the result] back or not,

that which is additional in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), when it is postponed, cannot cause even those elements preceding it—such as the carrying forward of the fires and Soma—to be postponed. Why is this so?

Because there is no connection: the ritual activity concerning the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) belongs to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*), while that which precedes it belongs to the Soma sacrifice (*saumika*). There is no mutual relationship between these two; a rite belonging to the Soma sacrifice does not assist either the animal sacrifice or the animal itself. Therefore, even the sequence of that which assists [the sacrifice], while providing assistance, would be subordinate; however, this is not the case.

Consequently, there is no restriction regarding their mutual sequence. Thus, only the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is drawn forward. Moreover, once the word has fulfilled its purpose by drawing forward only the sacrificial post, there is a sublation of the natural sequence of the Soma-related rites.
And one should not extend a secondary application (*prāsaṅgika*) because there is no connection [to the original context]. 5.1.28.

[The answer is: because of their connection, they do displace them.

these two are not at all entitled to be displaced, for those which belong to them...
The *anuyāja* offerings are connected [to the sacrifice], not employed by others;

Not [is there a sequence] among the word-meanings and their purposes,
for we shall explain that word-meanings assist [the cognition] simultaneously. Furthermore, the arising of word-meanings occurs in a sequence, because their arising is expressed by distinct words.

It is not for the sake of the purpose of the ritual substance (*padārtha*), because it has already been expressed by the injunction of simultaneous performance. Therefore, since there is no cause for the postponement (*utkarṣa*) of the *anuyāja* offerings, the two oblations in the southern fire (*dākṣiṇāgnika*) should not be postponed. Moreover, once the word has fulfilled its function by merely postponing the *anuyāja*, [the postponement of] the two southern-fire oblations...
There will be no subversion of the respective order of the two oblations.
The altar belongs to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; this is the connection.

The offering of the oblation (*havir-abhivāsana*) is prescribed as occurring after [the preparation of the altar]. On the new moon day, it is drawn forward [to the previous day], according to the rule: "On the day before the new moon, one prepares the altar. However, there arises a doubt: when that [offering] is drawn forward, does it draw forward the ritual items (*padārtha*) that precede it, or not? It is said in reply:
"Because of the connection, he draws [the offering] back.
This being the position reached, we reply:
likewise, it is something not previously established (apūrva).

In the previous [sacrifice], the preparation of the altar (*vedi*) on the preceding day was prescribed for the preceding new moon day, while the covering of the sacrificial offerings (*havir-abhivāsana*) is prescribed for both [days] on the following day. There is no basis—neither direct statement (*śruti*) nor any other means of proof—for the view that the altar must be prepared on the new moon day after having performed the covering of the offerings. Therefore, the rites ending with the covering of the offerings should not be postponed. Furthermore, if the covering of the offerings were postponed, the sacrificial materials would be reduced to ashes.

Among the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, there is an offering called the Sāṃtapanīyā, which is a constituent part of the Sākamedha;

That when one warp is extended, another warp is perceived [therein].

Therefore, there is no superiority [of the later time] either. it is the efficient cause.

This is because [the term] is heard as something not to be adopted (*anupādeya*). Repetition [of a word] occurs because of a specific cause. 5.2.3.

tat}* repetition [of a word] occurs because of that reason. 5.2.3.

And in the cases of the handfuls, the potsherds, the portions, the collyrium, the ointment, the shaving, and the purification, it is done with a single [action]. (5.2.4)
Regarding the fist and so forth, there is a doubt:
is there a sequential performance with a single fist, or with four fists? What is the prima facie view?
"By a handful. Why?
Because the offering of one handful is indeed a single ritual act (*padārtha*), not the offering of four handfuls. How so?
When a single handful has been offered, the state of being a *yati* (ascetic) is fully established. It cannot be said that "nothing at all has been offered," nor can it be [otherwise].
If it were already poured out, the act of pouring would not have been performed;
nor is there any purpose served by pouring out merely a handful. For if one [handful] is not poured out, the four [required portions] cannot come into being.
For the word "four" has the fist as its coreferential basis; therefore, the sequential performance (anusamaya) must be carried out by means of the fist. Likewise, [it is said]:
"He places the potsherds. Similarly, [it is said]:...
He cuts from the middle, he cuts from the eastern half;
likewise, he anoints, he smears, he shaves, and he purifies.

*{4/543: E2: nirvapatibhāvaḥ}* But all [the offerings] are [of one kind], because they have a single purpose and because they possess that quality. //5.2.5//

But having completed all [the grains], one should perform the pouring out; the pouring out of a single handful is not the ritual act (padārtha), because the pouring out possesses the number four. How is there the number four?
Because the word "four" is connected with the act of offering (*nirvapati*),
it is thus logical that multiple qualities are enjoined together with the ritual action; otherwise, [it would not be so].

If there were a connection with the fist (*muṣṭi*), a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) would result, and it would become a subordinate part of the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*). The same applies to the placing [of the potsherds] and so forth, because of the instruction:
"He pours out [the grain] on eight potsherds, on eleven potsherds. He cuts off twice;
he anoints three times.

"In that 'he purifies with twenty-one [verses],' number and the other [factors] possess the nature of being subordinate to the action (*kriyāguṇatva*). Therefore, there is a simultaneous performance (*anusamaya*) by means of the aggregate."
But when [an action] is connected [with another], it should be a subsidiary part of that [other] because of the commencement [of the procedure]; for the other is for the sake of that. (5.2.6)
In connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture:
"He cuts off two portions of the oblation.
Regarding this, there is a doubt.

Is the sequence [of offerings] according to the portioning-off (avadāna), or is it according to the portioning-off followed by the final offering (pradānānta)? What is the conclusion? We say it is according to the portioning-off. Why?

Because of the mention of "cutting off" (avadāna). This being the position reached, we reply:

Just as, according to the order of the direct textual recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), the preparation of the fire-pan (*ukhā-sambharaṇa*) and other rites come before the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering,

The *sāmidhenī* verses are to be meditated upon. Why?

Because there is such a statement by the venerable Pāṇini: "The forms *pāyya*, *sāṃnāyya*, *nikāyya*, and *dhāyyā* [are used] in the senses of 'measure,' 'oblation,' 'dwelling,' and 'sāmidhenī' [respectively]" (*Pāṇini 3.1.129*).
From this statement, we infer the corresponding Vedic revelation (*śruti*). In which *sāmidhenīs* [is this intended]? It is said: [in those that are recited].

It is understood that, because there is no distinction, [the term *dhāyyā*] applies to all [verses]. The statement is indeed applicable even to those that are qualified. If they are qualified, then which ones? It is said: those in which the word *dhāyyā* is heard.

Those, then, are the *dhāyyā* verses. And it is only when those *dhāyyā* verses exist that the statement becomes meaningful. Since the statement is meaningful, there are no other *dhāyyā* verses, because there is a lack of authoritative evidence [for them].

"These two are of equal strength, for both the textual order (*pāṭha*) and the direct statement (*śruti*) as well as the meaning (*artha*) are causes [of application]. Furthermore, there is no distinction whatsoever regarding their authority;

Recollection according to the order of the text is understood as follows: "It should be brought about in this manner. What is the example and the purpose? [In the case of] the direct statement (*śruti*)...

And for some [schools], Soma [is the time for the establishment of the sacred fires], because of the statement regarding the passing over of the seasons and constellations for the *agnyādheya*; for otherwise, that [statement] would be rendered meaningless by the end of that [period]. (MS 5.4.6)

The statement regarding the transgression of the proper season and lunar mansion would be meaningless if immediate succession were not intended; for if no regard were paid to immediate succession, it would imply that disregard for those two applies only to whichever specific season and lunar mansion were mentioned.
Therefore, there is immediate succession between the Soma sacrifice and the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya). Moreover, the verbal suffix clearly indicates the present tense.
Regarding the phrase "one who is about to sacrifice with the Soma," that [phrase] intends to express [the state of being about to sacrifice] after having permitted the precedence of the *iṣṭi*.
