In the absence of a specific distinction regarding the Soma sacrifice, there would be no basis for it being intended for the Soma. This specific distinction would be that there is immediate succession between the Soma and the establishment of the fires (agnyādhāna).

When something is for the sake of that [other], it takes precedence over the Soma sacrifice.
This sūtra concerning the purpose is now explained. The subject matter has been exhausted. What is the purpose of this inquiry?

The establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) exists; therein, this principle has been established: that it must be preceded by an iṣṭi sacrifice and preceded by a soma sacrifice. Now, there arises a doubt.
Is it that for all three social classes (varṇas) there is the option of being preceded by the *iṣṭi* or preceded by the *soma*,

That for the three castes, there is either the precedence of the *iṣṭi* or the precedence of the *soma*. Why? Because there is no distinction; we perceive no specific difference whatsoever. This being the position reached, we reply:
For a Brāhmaṇa, there should be the precedence of the Soma sacrifice. Why?
Because of its elevation; for an elevation is heard in scripture:
"The Brāhmaṇa is indeed related to Agni by deity."

Having sacrificed with Soma, he becomes one for whom Agni and Soma are the deities. Since that very oblation which belongs to the full moon sacrifice is to be offered there as a subsequent offering (*anunirvāpa*), at that time he becomes one whose deities are both. For what indeed would a scriptural injunction not accomplish? Therefore, for a Brāhmaṇa, the Soma sacrifice must necessarily come first.

Regarding the statement, "This very oblation which belongs to the full moon," whatever is stated according to the wording is based on that explicit declaration;

But from the context, it should be time. (MS 5.4.14)

Where no fruit is heard mentioned, the meaning of the sentence itself is grasped there; and here, there is no hearing of a fruit. As for what is said—that a fruit must be postulated—[it is not so].

therefore, the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) have an immediate time of performance (*sadyaskālā*).
*{5/137: E2: Not by sacrifice}* The modifications of the *sāṃnāyya* and the *agnīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice] after the *soma* [sacrifice] follow the model of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
In this context, the modifications of the *sāṃnāyya* and the modifications of the *agnīṣomīya* serve as examples.
First, regarding the modifications of the *sāṃnāyya*, such as the *āmikṣā* and the animal sacrifice; [and] the *agnīṣomīya*...
"One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), a Brāhmaṇa should offer śyāmāka grain on eleven potsherds in the spring"—
such is the first [example]. In this regard, there is a doubt:
Are these [rites] both before and after the Soma sacrifice, or only after it? What is the prima facie view?
Both before and after.
Because no specific distinction is understood. This being the case, we say: they should come after the Soma sacrifice; for their archetype (prakṛti) indeed occurs after the Soma sacrifice.
By the injunction, even by these [means], it must take place after the Soma sacrifice; that is, the *sānnāyya* offering is after the Soma sacrifice because of the scriptural statement:
"One who has not sacrificed with Soma should offer the *saṃnayya*. This applies to the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice as well.

"The Brāhmaṇa belongs to Agni by deity; having sacrificed with Soma, he becomes [one who belongs] to Soma. Therefore, one should subsequently offer that very oblation which is the Full-moon offering."
In that case, since it belongs to both deities,
its modified form (*vikṛti*) also ought to occur after the *soma* sacrifice.
E2: modifications of the Agniṣomīya, the Agniṣomīya}*
2.5.5.1}* *{5/142: Having sacrificed with Soma, one becomes connected to the Agniṣomīya [offering]};
likewise, the modifications of Soma [are performed] after the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. // MS_5,4.26 //
The one-day sacrifices (*ekāhas*) such as the *Gavām-ayana* are modifications of the Soma sacrifice. Regarding them, there is a doubt:
are they to be performed before or after the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), or only after them? What is the prima facie view?

There is no fixed rule, because there is no distinction. This being the position reached, we reply: likewise, the modifications of the Soma sacrifice should take place after the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

The Jyotiṣṭoma occurs after the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, according to the injunction: "Having sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa, one should sacrifice with Soma. By means of this extended application (codaka), this rule also applies to the one-day sacrifices (ekāha) such as the Gava-ekāha and others. Therefore, those too must be performed after the Darśapūrṇamāsa.

*{5/144: Tait.S. 2.5.6.1}* When substances are connected with an action, they are related as subordinate factors (guṇa). //6.1.1//

It is traditionally taught: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," and so forth. In this regard, there is a doubt:
is heaven a subordinate factor?
Is action the primary element, or is action subordinate while heaven is the primary element? Whence arises this doubt?

In this context, both "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) and "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) are indicated. Here, a relationship between the desire for heaven and the sacrifice is understood. Regarding that relationship, an inquiry arises as to whether the sacrifice is connected as the means (*sādhana*) or as the end to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
In this regard, if the sacrifice is enjoined as something to be performed for a person desiring heaven—
meaning "the sacrifice is to be performed by one who desires heaven"—
it is understood that it is accomplished for one characterized by the desire for heaven; thus, the desire for heaven is taught there as being directed toward the sacrifice by the person.
Therefore, that [result] is accomplished for him and not for another. A person who desires heaven is able to accomplish the sacrifice.
Now, if it is argued that the desire of one who desires heaven is enjoined as something to be performed, [that is incorrect].

Therefore, since the performance of the sacrifice is what must be accomplished as something distinguished by the sacrifice, the sacrifice is accepted as the means of achievement (*sādhaka*). And this [fact that] both [the sacrifice and the desire] are the object [of the injunction] is understood from a single uttered sentence—namely, that "either the sacrifice is to be performed" or "the desire is [to be attained]. But this cannot occur simultaneously;
for when there is the desire, [the sacrifice is not yet the object].
When there is the sacrifice, that is not when the desire exists; when the desire exists, that is not when the sacrifice exists.
Because of the difference in the mode of expression, doubt is justified.
Likewise, this other point is also doubtful: is heaven pleasure (*prīti*), or is it a substance (*dravya*)? If heaven were a substance, [then...]
Therefore, the action is primary and the substance is subordinate; furthermore, if heaven is pleasure,
then the sacrifice is subordinate to it.
"Heaven is the primary [result]. From what source does this doubt arise?
There is no scriptural statement here regarding desire as being either subordinate or primary;
rather, its mere connection with the sacrifice is understood.
But the material substance has action as its purpose by its very nature,
and human effort has the fruit as its purpose. What, then, is the prima facie view?
"Heaven is by way of its qualities,
while action is by way of its predominance. Regarding this,
they explain as follows:
"Swarga is a substance. How is this understood?
For all words, common usage (*laukika-prayoga*) is the means for knowing their meaning;
and in that common usage, the word *svarga* is observed to denote a substance, as in the case of "kauśikāni" (silken garments).
"Fine garments are heaven; sandalwood is heaven;
women of sixteen years are heaven"—whatever object is a source of pleasure [is considered heaven].

Each of those things is expressed by the word "svarga. Because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [word], we consider that *svarga* is a substance characterized by pleasure;

if it is argued that the application of the word [to these things] is based on analogy, [we reply that] it is not so, for [the word] is not established as referring to anything in the world that is without a counterpart (*anupamita*).
That for which this would be an analogy is not an analogy; therefore, heaven is a substance.
To this he says: no, heaven is pleasure.
It is not a substance (*dravya*), because of the deviation;
for that very same substance, in certain states, the word "heaven" does not denote it. But [the word] pleasure (*prīti*) there is never, in any state, not denoted by it.
It does not denote [anything else]. Therefore, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is understood that the word "heaven" (*svarga*) applies to pleasure.
This is not so.
The word "heaven" (svarga) is a designator of pleasure. Why?
Because that which is a qualifier is not expressed by the word itself. For example: [text fragment]

The word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) is a designation for a person based on the staff; the staff is its cause (*nimitta*), not its denotation (*abhidheya*). Likewise, this word "heaven" (*svarga*) is not a designation for pleasure itself, but rather a designation for the means of achieving pleasure.
[Objection: But surely the word "heaven" is well-known in common usage as referring to a specific place, in which there is no heat...
There is no cold, no hunger, and no thirst.
There is no discontent, nor is there exhaustion;
only those who have performed meritorious deeds go there after death.
Not others. To this it is said:
if some there go without dying, then they come without being born.
In that case, such a place is not perceived directly (*pratyakṣa*), but is rather understood through inference (*anumāna*).
But surely some other accomplished ones (*siddha*) have seen it?
If it is argued that they have indeed told us so, we reply: there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that;
for while there may well be established entities of such a kind, and they might have seen them and reported them, such a place simply does not exist.
But surely, it is understood from common worldly experience, from narratives, and from the Veda that heaven is a place of such a kind. That is not so;

because humans have no connection with such a place, their word is not authoritative. Even a narrative is to be disregarded because it is composed by humans. Even the Vedic narrative concerning heaven is intended solely for the purpose of injunction.

Rather, it forms a single syntactical unit with another injunction and is intended for praise (*stuti*). Even if such a place were to exist by virtue of the presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) arising from the hearing of the word "pleasure" alone, there would still be no contradiction with our position, because the word *svarga* refers to a means of attaining joy (*prītisādhana*). This is because there is no linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) associated with that [physical] place.
"How then could the word 'heaven' (svarga) be its designator? To this we reply: when heaven is a substance consisting of pleasure, then [the word applies].
"In the connection of substances with an action, there is a relationship as a subordinate factor (guṇa).
Here, it is heard in scripture that "a sacrifice is to be performed by one who desires heaven. In that case, a relationship between heaven and the sacrifice is necessarily established;
therein, the substance is something already existent.

[The word] *bhavya* [denotes] action (*karman*). And it is logical that that which has come into being (*bhūta*) has for its purpose that which is yet to be (*bhavya*), because its purpose is perceived; however, it is not the case that that which is yet to be (*bhavya*) has for its purpose that which has come into being (*bhūta*), for in that case, the perceived benefit would be abandoned.

But how is it understood that the sacrifice is enjoined as something to be performed, when from this very sentence the desirous result (*kāma*) is also understood as something to be performed? It is said in reply:

The obligation to perform the desire arises from the sentence, whereas the obligation to perform the act of sacrificing arises from the direct Vedic statement (śruti); and the direct statement is more powerful than the sentence. Therefore, this is the meaning:
"One who desires heaven should perform a sacrifice" means that for one who desires heaven, the sacrifice is to be performed. And that which is to be performed is accompanied by happiness;
that which is not to be performed is accompanied by suffering. Since the scripture declares it "to be performed," the sacrifice will therefore have happiness as its fruit;
and that [happiness] belongs to whoever has the desire.

It is understood that this succeeds for him and not for anyone else. Therefore, the desire for heaven is subordinate to the sacrifice; indeed, for every ritual action, the desire for the material substance is subordinate, and one exerts effort to procure that substance by means of it.
By means of the visible [purpose] alone. But here, it is precisely the desire for the substance designated as "heaven" that is restricted;
just as that [desire] was obtained as a subordinate factor (guṇabhūta), so too, when it exists, it is restricted by means of the visible purpose alone.

Not by means of an invisible benefit (*adṛṣṭa*). Therefore, with heaven as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*) due to the desire for heaven, one will strive toward the substance of heaven in order to accomplish the sacrifice. Even if it were by means of an invisible benefit, there would still be no fault.
*{5/146: E2: it is understood}* *{5/148: E2:
in that case, first thus}* *{5/149:
E2: silken garments}*
"No," he said, "for there is nothing whatsoever that is without a point of comparison.
[This is] because joy is a qualifying attribute.
They do not go [there];
nor is it apprehended through inference;
nor by any other means. But is this not so?
"But that [inference] is not effective, because it has that [same object] as its purpose. (6.1.2)
By the word "tu" (but), the [opposing] position is set aside. Therefore, they describe it as follows: pleasure (*prīti*) is heaven (*svarga*). Why?
Thus it has been stated by you:

that the word "heaven" (svarga) applies to a substance distinguished by pleasure. If this is so, then it ought to apply first to pleasure itself; for it does not deviate from that [pleasure], whereas it does deviate from the substance. Indeed, the word "heaven" is a designator of whatever substance serves as the means to pleasure.
When that very thing does not become a means for pleasure, then it is no longer denoted by the word "heaven. Therefore, this word expresses pleasure.
As for what was said—that it is like the word "staff-bearer"—[that is incorrect].
That [word] also,
through the word "stick" (daṇḍa) being present within it, produces a cognition of the "one with the stick" (daṇḍin), because the word "stick" is contained therein.
That [word] denotes the staff. Here, however, the word "heaven" (svarga) itself is the designator of pleasure.
If it is a word denoting pleasure, then the sacrifice is subordinate and pleasure is the primary element. Why?
Because human effort is directed toward that end—

since a person exerts himself for the sake of pleasure— it is understood that pleasure itself is not the means of accomplishing the sacrifice; rather, it is the material substance (*dravya*) that is the means of accomplishing the sacrifice.

A sacrifice does not arise from the substance alone, because the word *yajati* (he sacrifices) applies to the triad of substance, deity, and action. Even in the absence of pleasure (*prīti*), the sacrifice occurs. Furthermore, if the sacrifice were not for the sake of pleasure, it would be an ineffective ritual act.
One would not find anyone who could accomplish it. For that which is for the sake of pleasure is what is accomplished, and nothing else.
But surely, the sacrifice is heard of as something to be performed? It is said in reply:
Truth is heard as something to be performed; desire is also understood as something to be performed. [The opponent] says:
[This applies] to the sacrifice by virtue of direct scriptural statement (śruti).
[The injunction applies] to desire by means of the sentence, nor to both [desire and the sacrifice], because that would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*). It is said:
although the sacrifice is heard as something to be performed, [it is not so in this context].
Nevertheless, it should not be performed;
for while that which bestows happiness should be performed, sacrifice bestows suffering. Therefore, it should not be performed according to direct perception.

And [the sacrifice] gives pain through direct perception. It is argued that it becomes a giver of pleasure through inference because of the statement regarding its being "to be performed. To this it is replied:
inference is not a valid means of knowledge when it contradicts direct perception. Therefore, the sacrifice is not to be performed if it does not have pleasure as its purpose.
[Objection: "But it will be connected with another statement of the fruit. [Reply: It is said:

even if it were not being enjoined, it would not be understood as having a fruit merely by virtue of being mentioned in proximity. Therefore, so that it may not be purposeless, the fact that heaven is to be accomplished (*kartavyatā*) is understood;
and since human effort is qualified by the sacrifice, the sacrifice must be its instrument (*karaṇa*). Thus, it has been well stated that the sacrifice is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*).
Heaven is the primary [goal].

*{5/161: Because it would result in a split in the sentence}* *{5/162: Or, if [the word] were connected with another [meaning] imagined for the sake of avoiding meaninglessness}* *{5/163: Then [it would be] connected [with that]*}
And because there is a connection with each respective object, for the relationship indeed arises from the action; therefore, there should be an instruction regarding the action. //6.1.3//
We do not assert that the sacrifice has the status of a subordinate element (guṇabhāva) merely out of fear of its being purposeless. What then?

The sacrifice is enjoined as the instrument (karaṇa) with respect to the object designated as heaven. But surely the sacrifice is enjoined by direct scriptural statement (śruti) as something to be performed (kartavya). True, it is so; however, in that case, it would indeed be purposeless.
If the sacrifice were not enjoined for the sake of heaven,
then even if one who desires heaven were enjoined to perform it, that injunction would be purposeless, as the act would be fruitless. In that case, for him— [603] {5/...}
The instruction would be rendered useless, and there would be the fault of *vākya-bheda* (splitting of the sentence) because two things being enjoined would be mutually unrelated.
Therefore, the word "one who desires heaven" does not enjoin its own primary meaning. What then?

It is being pointed out: therein, from the sentence, the desirability (kāma) understood is apprehended as that which is to be accomplished (*kartavyatā*), and the sacrifice (*yāga*) as the instrument (*karaṇatā*). And thus, regarding the desirability of the sacrifice, there will be no contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, it must be an instruction for ritual action (*karmopadeśa*).
Action is taught with reference to heaven,
not heaven with reference to action. What follows if heaven is not taught [as the goal]?

This is what follows from this: for a quality cannot be both untaught and yet attained through the primary object. Therefore, heaven is the primary element, while the ritual action is subordinate. Moreover, for one who desires heaven—
"To complete the sacrifice" would thus be as if incoherent,
for he desires one thing but performs another.

Now, if it is thought that this is understood from the connection "from that, heaven arises," [we reply: for those who hold verbal testimony (*śabda*) as their authority, comprehension without the word is not logical. We understand this very connection from this sentence alone, just as if one were to say, "One desiring to fetch firewood should go to the forest."
One might say this:
"In that case, it is observed by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that the capacity for fetching wood exists upon entering the forest.
Now, suppose one thinks thus:
[Objection: "Let there not be the futility of the instruction; therefore, there will be an implication (arthāpatti) [of a result]. [Response: It is said:
this is not the capacity of the futility of the instruction, such that—without a statement of a result—[an implication could arise].

The pleasure resulting from the sacrifice would be understood as its fruit. Granted that this [injunction] might be purposeless, it can never produce an inherent capacity [for the sacrifice to yield a result]. For the taking up of water by one desiring to burn does not, simply because burning does not occur, generate a power of burning in that water. Alternatively, its purposefulness will be established by resorting to another position, namely, that the sacrifice is enjoined for one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*).

[Objection: But surely, even in the other view, a sacrifice is enjoined for one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*), not that heaven arises from the sacrifice. [Reply: This is not so. For in that view, having referred to the performance of one who is seeking heaven, the sacrifice is enjoined as its means;
thus there is no fault. If it is argued that there is no statement that "that performance [leads] toward heaven," [we reply: the performance occurs with respect to the desired object.
And for one who desires heaven, heaven is the desired object;

thus, the inclusion of the qualification "one who desires heaven" is solely for the purpose of specifying the particular performance of that [action], which is therefore faultless. Consequently, there would be an instruction regarding the sacrificial act for one who desires heaven;
hence, heaven is the primary objective.
"Karma by way of its quality" refers to the injunction "one should sacrifice" with respect to one who desires heaven; thus, this definition of qualification (*adhikāra*) is established.
*{5/165: The consequence of a split in the sentence}* *{5/166: Jha (2,969) suggests with a manuscript reading "evam ayāgakartavyatāyām"* *{5/167:
E2 omits "iti"}*
It is understood from the connection;
you think so;
it would be so.
Since action is for the sake of its fruit, the scripture must apply to all who are qualified. 6.1.4.
They recite this: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," and so forth. In this regard, there is a doubt:
Does this statement refer to every single sentient being whatsoever,
or does it refer only to those who are capable? What is the prima facie position?
There is eligibility for all, because there is no distinction. [Objection: But trees and the like do not desire anything;
how could they have eligibility?
It is replied: let it not be so for insentient things;
however, with reference to animals, one might say, "one should sacrifice. But do not animals also desire nothing at all? We say: no, they do desire happiness.
For it is observed thus:
those tormented by heat seek shade, and those afflicted by cold seek sunlight.
He says: "But surely animals intend for immediate results; they do not pray for results at a later time, yet Vedic rituals have results at a later time. It is replied:
They are observed to desire results even at a later time;
we see dogs fasting on the fourteenth day and hawks on the eighth day. And there is no suspicion of disease in these cases.

Because the cause is fixed, for we observe that even those who consume various kinds of food [produce the same result] at that time, while even those who consume the same kind of food do not produce it at another time. Furthermore, there are indicative marks (liṅga) in the Veda.
Passages such as "The gods indeed performed a sacrificial session" (*devā vai satram āsata*) demonstrate the eligibility (*adhikāra*) of deities, sages, and trees.
[Objection: But since they are unable to carry out the ritual procedure in its entirety, they are not eligible. [Response: It is said in reply:
Some are able to perform the sacrifice;

therefore, injunctions such as "one should sacrifice" will apply to those who are capable, but will not apply to those who are incapable. In that case, one who has not been instructed in the Viṣṇu-steps and other such details will perform only the basic sacrifice.
What is his fault? Even the possession of property, such as a village belonging to the gods or a village of elephants.

Because of the metaphorical usage "the village of Ṛṣabha," [the village] certainly exists. Therefore, even non-humans who are capable [of performing the rites] possess the entitlement [to perform them].

Or rather, because of the connection with the Vedic revelation regarding the agent, the injunction is understood as applying in its entirety, as in the case of the Viṣṇu-strides and other such acts. (6.1.5)
The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position. It is not the case that animals and the like also have the qualification [for ritual action]. Then for whom [does it apply]?
For one who is capable of fully accomplishing the ritual act. And these animals and the like are not able to fully accomplish the ritual act.

Therefore, for these [gods], action is not the means to happiness. How could that which cannot be performed be a means? It is not for the gods, because there is no other deity [to whom they could offer].
For it is not possible to renounce that which one has taught as the self;
that would not be a true renunciation at all,
nor would it be [the teaching] of the seers (ṛṣis).

Because of the absence of a Ṛṣi lineage. Bhṛgu and others do not share the same *gotra* as other Bhṛgus and so forth, nor is their capacity perceived through direct observation. Moreover, animals do not seek results that occur at a later time.
For they desire what is near at hand.
But has it not been said:
"We observe that even animals seek fruits whose results occur at a later time"?
"Regarding the statement that 'the Śunaḥśyenāḥ fast on the fourteenth and the eighth [lunar days],' it is said:
those who fast do not do so for the sake of results in another birth. How is this known?
Because of the absence of Vedic study."
Those who study the Veda know this:
that having performed this action, one attains this fruit in the hereafter; yet these [others] do not study the Veda.
Nor do they understand it from the treatises on memory (smṛti-śāstra), nor do they learn it from others. Therefore, they do not know dharma. How could those who are ignorant practice it?
Consequently, they do not dwell for the sake of dharma.
For what purpose, then, is their fasting? It is said: it is because they have a distaste for food due to illness. But how can illness occur at a fixed time?
It is said: there are indeed illnesses that occur at fixed times.

As in the cases of tertian and quartan fevers. Therefore, human beings possess the qualification [for ownership]. Furthermore, animals do not possess property, for they are never seen to utilize goods according to their own will; thus, they lack mastery over wealth. As for the expressions "the village of the gods" and "the village of the elephants," [these are metaphorical].
That is merely a figurative expression; therefore, for that reason as well, animals have no entitlement [to Vedic rites].
As for those indicative marks, such as "The gods indeed performed a sacrificial session," and so forth—
Those are explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) intended for the purpose of praising the injunctions (*vidhi*);

for in all of them, another injunction exists. Moreover, an injunction does not form a single syntactical unit with another injunction, because their modes of expression differ. Rather, that [explanatory passage] is praise.
Thus indeed must sacrifices be performed, that even the gods remain seated once their purpose is accomplished,
and even animals remain seated with their consciousness close at hand.
Even trees are insentient; how much more so, then, are learned humans?
But surely those who are not authorized for the Viṣṇukrama and other such rites will simply perform the sacrifice.
It is not so; the qualities (*guṇa*) are taught in relation to the sacrifice, not in relation to the agent.

Therefore, if the sacrifice were performed merely as such [without those qualities], there would be a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*), and thus there would be no connection with the fruit (*phala*). But how [is it known that they relate] to the sacrifice?

If it is argued that they are taught as supplements (*pratyupadiśyante*): [we reply that] because they occur in proximity to the injunction of sacrifice which requires a description of the procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣa*), they are capable of satisfying that requirement.

Otherwise, while the words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*) were enjoining the agents, the statement of the result (*phalavacana*) would remain unsatisfied in its expectancy and would thus be entirely purposeless; therefore, there must be *anuṣaṅga* (syntactic connection).

And if the statement regarding the fruit were to apply [to both], then, because of the resulting expectancy, the sentence would be interrupted. Now, if it is argued that this very sentence will enjoin the qualified action for those who are capable and the unqualified action for those who are incapable— that is not so.
If [the word] were uttered only once, the sentence would be split due to the conflict between its two capacities;

for it remains expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) with respect to the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Therefore, that [sentence] is an instruction regarding the sacrifice together with its subsidiaries (*sāṅga-yāga*), and there is no instruction regarding a sacrifice devoid of subsidiaries (*niraṅga-yāga*). Consequently, only humans possess the qualification (*adhikāra*).
The purpose [of this discussion] is as stated in the respective positions.

Some say that the rite of a thousand years need not necessarily be calculated in days, because there exist deities and others whose lifespans reach such a duration; however, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), even though it is possible in that case—
It should be prepared on the very same days; we shall explain that further below.
*{5/177: E2: by way of connection}* *{5/178:
E2: it should be formulated; in the prima facie argument}* *{5/179: E2: because of possibility}*
"In the established doctrine (siddhānta), that is impossible" (MS 6.7.31–40).
"Because of the mention of a specific gender, [the sacrifice] is connected with a male, according to Aitishayana" (MS 6.1.6).
It is traditionally taught: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices," and so forth. In this regard, there is a doubt:
was this word "should sacrifice" uttered with reference specifically to a man who desires heaven, or is there no such restriction?
"Whether it be a woman or a man"—what is the conclusion?
Ai-ti-sha-ya-na (Aitishayana) held that the masculine gender is the one under discussion. Why?
Because of the specification of gender. There is a specification by means of the masculine gender, as in:
"One who desires heaven should sacrifice.
Therefore, it is said that a male should sacrifice, not a female.

And because it is a statement of that [author], the mention of defects applies only when [the author's intention] is not understood. //6.1.7//

When an embryo is killed while it is not yet discernible, there is the designation "feticide" (*bhrūṇahatyā*); therefore, by killing an undiscernible embryo, one becomes a feticide. A feticide is the worst of evildoers;
whereas he who benefits both worlds [is the best].
The slayer of that [sacrifice] is a destroyer of the embryo; the destroyer of the sacrifice is a destroyer of the embryo,
for he is one who commits the killing of the means of the sacrifice.
Therefore, he designates the sacrifice by the word *bhrūṇa*. For it either sustains (*bibharti*) everything, or it brings about prosperity (*bhūti*).
Consequently, a "killer of a *bhrūṇa*" (*bhrūṇahā*) is one who commits the destruction of the sacrifice.

Because it is connected with a male, this [term] is understood as a restatement (*anuvāda*). When an embryo that is not yet known [as male or female] is being killed, it is possible that a male might be killed.
In that case, because the one authorized for the sacrifice has been killed, the "sacrifice-murder" would constitute the killing of an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*). Otherwise,
if both were authorized [for the act], [it would not].
In that case, there would be a "sacrificial slaughter" (*yajñavadha*) whether [the victim] is recognized or unrecognized.
One might then assume that the inclusion of the term "unrecognized" is not restrictive. Therefore, the masculine gender-ending is intended to be expressive.
Likewise: "Having killed an *ātreyī*, one becomes a killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahā*)."

"One should give a hundred [cows] along with a chariot to one who has a daughter, and a pair of cattle in the Ārṣa form. even that is not her own.

The master must have his work performed by her;

"Or rather, they two should sacrifice together. What is the prima facie view? [They should not. Why? Because the singular number is intended to be significant. "In matters of dharma, artha, and kāma..."
"One must not transgress [this vow]," it is said; likewise, "one should practice the Dharma together" and "one should procreate offspring together. To this it is replied:
It is not proper to set aside a scriptural statement (śruti) by means of a Smṛti statement. We say: no;
for in this context, some ritual acts have only women and men as their performers, such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa and the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Where a libation is prescribed with clarified butter (ājya) that has been inspected by the wife and inspected by the sacrificer, there is a deficiency in the rite if either one is absent.

"It will be looked upon by the wife who is performing the sacrifice as the patroness. "No," he says, "this is not a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the beholder; if it were a refinement of the beholder,"

In that case, it would be as follows: this is a consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*), and the two observers are subordinate factors; therefore, if either one is absent, a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) necessarily occurs.

And the injunction for the performance involves the inclusion of all constituent parts. In this regard, it might be argued that a woman acting as the sacrificer will hire a man to look at the clarified butter (*ājya*), and a man will hire a woman to look at it. But that is not so.

For the word *patnī* (wife) is said to mean the mistress of the sacrifice, not one who has been purchased. The term *patnī* is a relative term, and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is its counterpart as the master.
It is not purchased. Therefore, for a man and a woman, the action is of this same nature.
In that regard, by the force of the scriptural statement (*śruti*), whoever [performs it] together with whomever—
Since it might be concluded that "one should sacrifice by gathering together," this is said:
whatever dharma you must perform with anyone at all, [that should be done].
Thus, it is understood that because she accompanies him, there is no contradiction between the Smṛti and the Śruti. Now, as for what was said—

And as for the argument that "one should sacrifice with a woman alone" because the singular number is intended to be significant, that must be refuted. First, he should be asked this:
if the singular number in "one should sacrifice" (yajeta) is indeed intended to be significant, [what follows?]
How is it that the sacrifice is performed together with sixteen officiating priests? It is explained thus:
there is a distinction of actions according to each causal factor (*kāraka*); [the priest] performs the very duties of the sacrificer himself, such as the act of hiring (*parikraya*) and so forth.
The sacrificer is called "he sacrifices" because he performs the duties of the *adhvaryu*;

just as a cooking pot is said to "perform the cooking" while merely performing the act of holding [the contents], so too the *adhvaryu* is said to "sacrifice" while performing the duties of the *adhvaryu*.
Furthermore, whatever is the specific function belonging to a particular agent,
that must be performed by one [agent] alone when singularity is intended. If this is so, then whatever the extent of the sacrificer’s function may be, it is not to be performed collectively.

One [sacrificer] is officiated by one [priest], another by another; or twelve [sacrificers] by one, and fifty-six by another, and likewise fifty-six by the other. But here, however, the activity of the wife is entirely different; the wife, while performing her duties there, does not destroy the singleness of the sacrificer.

Just as the Adhvaryu priest proceeds with his duties in the Adhvaryava rites, so too must one necessarily sacrifice together with one's wife; for this property of the couple belongs to both equally, and therefore the sacrifice must necessarily be performed by the husband together with his wife.

Otherwise, in the absence of the desire of either one, the renunciation itself would not take place; for indeed, without a second wife, renunciation is not at all possible for one who has a second wife.

In that regard, she will perform them once for those acts intended for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). There is no fault whatsoever regarding those acts intended for the purification of the agent (*kartṛsaṃskārārtha*),

*Why? Because [it] is heard as distinct.* *It is not heard together.*
And because of the observation of indicative marks. 6.1.18.

"He girds the wife with the yoktra and the sacrificer with the girdle for the sake of forming a couple."

the distinction between the yoke-strap and the girdle is understood from the statement,
as is their union as a couple.
This is applicable in the case of a ritual action performed by means of both a woman and a man, and not otherwise.

Since the gift of a hundred chariots has a visible purpose, therefore,

Just as Pūrṇaka is the master of our oxen,

For that Smṛti, being intent on its own result, would not be respected;

It possesses its own [result], because it conforms to the Vedic revelation;

"May the husband and wife go together by means of their good deed; yoked as the two bearers of the sacrifice, being in harmony, may they cast away their enemies; may they attain the undecaying light in heaven"—this shows the fruit for the couple. And the double-consecration (dvyādhāna) is like the double-sacrifice (dviyajña). //6.1.22//
There is the injunction for the establishment of the sacred fires: "He who, knowing thus, establishes the fire. In this regard, they prescribe:

It is said: here it is heard [in the scripture], "The two, wearing [the skins], should perform the *ādheya*. In that case, the statement is heard again even though its meaning was already established [by implication].
Is this for the purpose of connecting it with the masculine gender, or for the purpose of enjoining the linen cloth? Since both [possibilities] exist, a doubt arises;

Therefore, because there is no distinction [between them],

for what is understood through direct audition (*śruti*) is indeed understood from the hearing itself.

The connection with another word is understood from the syntactical context (*vākya*), and direct statement (*śruti*) is more powerful than syntactical context. He said: "The word *vasānau* is not exclusively masculine; it denotes both a male and a female, just as *kukkuṭaś ca kukkuṭī ca* [a cock and a hen] is expressed by the dual form *kukkuṭau*."
"A boar and a sow are 'two boars'; likewise, a man and a woman are 'two people'. To this it is replied:
where there is no specific meaning or context that serves as a qualifier [to distinguish gender], [the dual form applies].
And the word is injunctive;

Just as when one says "bring two," a man brings two men; and when one says "bring two," [it refers to] two women—thereby it is understood that the dual ending in *e* denotes women, and likewise the dual ending in *au* denotes two men. As for the fact that the dual ending in *au* is now seen being used for both women and men:
In this regard, is it the man who has a companion that is the cause, or is it the woman who has a companion? It is said: [the cause] is seen when the man has a companion.
Just as in the case of the command "Bring two brahmins," here too the meaning is a male accompanied by another [male]. Therefore, it is understood that this is based on the cause of a male.
To this, he replies: if usage were the observed means of valid cognition, then [the word] would be observed in the case of two males.
How could it exist in a single [entity]? To this it is replied: one can say that it is observed in both the masculine and in duality, but not in two distinct substances.

This word does not deviate from its masculine gender and its dual number, whereas it does deviate from its substance (*dravya*). And because of the observation [in the Veda] that "of Mitra and Varuṇa" (*pra mitrayor varuṇayoḥ*), since the formation of a compound is prescribed for the sense of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) expressed by *ca*, and since the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) is an exception to the *dvandva* (copulative) compound,
just as the example "two *khadira* trees and two white ones" (*khadirau ca dhavalau ca*) is given.
The same should be understood here as well. Therefore, it is understood that [the word] applies to the masculine and to the dual number; however, it is not observed to apply to the feminine dual.
To this, he says: "But surely, because it is observed right here, it is understood to denote both the feminine and the masculine. To this, it is replied:
This has been stated:

"It is illogical for there to be multiple referents. Thus, the meaning of this [term] will be "a man accompanied by another," and it would be illogical for it to mean "a woman and a man. Now, in the injunction regarding a man who is accompanied by another, what else could that companion be?
Thus [it is said]. Since a woman cannot be the subject of the statement,

In this way, since one is accompanied by the other and the other is also accompanied by the first, only two males are taken as the referents. Therefore, it is said that two males are enjoined here in the context of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration).

It is replied: "The word of Pāṇini does not state that the long vowel *au* in the form *kukkuṭau* denotes both male and female. How then?"

Where there is a co-utterance (*sahavacana*) of a female and a male, one might expect that, taking it as "a man accompanied by another," the *au*-vowel would apply to the stem ending in *-a*; or, taking it as "a woman accompanied by another," the *ī*-vowel would apply. It is the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the word *ādadhīyātām*.
He asks: "Will she indeed enjoin it?

If it were meaningless,

In that case, one's own purpose would not be abandoned entirely; however, when the connection with wearing linen (*kṣauma-vasana*) is to be enjoined, by discarding the act of kindling (*ādadhīyātām*) and enjoining [the linen-wearing] instead, one would utterly abandon the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). [The injunction] is not able to enjoin [the linen cloth], because of the remoteness of the meaning. He asks: "In that case, what meaning is intended by the quality of being a subordinate (*vaśānaguṇatā*)?

for this very reason, this position is abandoned. He asks:
Regarding the mention of wearing linen (*kṣauma*), how is it to be understood now?
It is said: it is not possible to enjoin both the linen and the gender marker (*liṅga*), for in that case the sentence would be split. Therefore, [it applies] to those who do not wear linen.

The word *kṣauma* (linen) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), since clothing is already established by the context; thus the meaning is "two men wearing [clothing]. And these [garments] are generally soiled and resemble linen for one who is engaged in manual labor.

For in this way, a previously unestablished matter is enjoined, since a specific restriction is indeed understood. "It should be established"—this it will enjoin. Now, one might object: "Is this [text] capable of enjoining the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) by means of direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*), and nothing else? It is replied:

On account of common renown and from the wording of a mantra; for there is a wording of a mantra:
"The *Ṛbhus*, sons of Sudhanvan, who possess the vision of the sun."
Thus [it is said]; "ṛbhūṇāṃ tvā" is the consecration mantra for the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*). Therefore, the Ṛbhus are the sons of Sudhanvan, and the Ṛbhus are chariot-makers. Moreover, it says:
"The Ṛbhus lead the felly as [they do]."

Those who lead the rim [of the wheel] are called the *ṛbhus*. And chariot-makers lead the rim. Therefore, this establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) belongs to those who are not of the three [higher] castes, provided they are not *śūdras*.
On account of the force of the word, the *sthapati* (chief carpenter) should be a *niṣāda*. (Pāṇini 6.1.51)

"One should offer a *caru* oblation to Rudra in the center of the site, where Rudra might afflict the subjects"—having introduced this sacrifice (*iṣṭi*), it is stated: "One should cause a *niṣādasthapati* to perform this [sacrifice]. Regarding this *niṣādasthapati*, there is a doubt.
Is it one among those authorized,
or is it someone else entirely? We say it is one among them,
for he alone is capable.
Because he possesses learning and fire, whereas the other lacks learning and fire and is thus incapable. [Objection:
But surely the term *niṣādasthapati* would not be applicable there. [Reply: It is said: No.
This is not tenable;

rather, the compound "sthapati of the Niṣādas" will be a genitive (ṣaṣṭhī) compound, meaning "the most excellent among the Niṣādas. Therefore, this scripture concerns those who are already entitled [to Vedic study]. This being the position reached, we reply:
The *sthapati* should be a *niṣāda*; indeed, only a *niṣāda* is fit to be the *sthapati*. Why?
Because of the force of the word itself.
For the word "Niṣāda" is indeed capable of denoting the Niṣāda person by means of hearing alone.

One might, however, speak of the "chief of the Niṣādas" by means of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And when there is a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and figurative indication, direct statement is the proper course, not figurative indication. Now, it might be argued:
This is not a fault;
the word *niṣāda* denotes the *niṣāda* caste itself, while the genitive case expresses the relationship [between them]. That is not so.
Because the genitive case-ending is not heard; we do not perceive the genitive here. He says:
"The meaning of the genitive is understood through the power of elision. True, it is understood, but not by means of elision. By what, then?

It has been stated that [the word *niṣāda*] functions through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and that such [indication] is weak. However, a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*) is stronger; for in that case, both words function in their own primary sense (*svārtha*). Since the accusative case ending applies by *tantra* (simultaneous application) to both, the *niṣāda* is understood as being designated by the accusative.
In that case, one who would assume the sense of a genitive would be grasping what is not heard in the text. Therefore, the *niṣāda* himself must be the *sthapati*.

The word *viṣāda* [takes the suffix *ghañ*] when it denotes the act of lamenting;
and because of the observation of the grammatical indicator (*liṅga*), [the suffix *ghañ* is applied] after the root *nad*. (Pāṇini 6.1.52)

Since the accomplishment of the human goal is the sole purpose, there should be the qualification for each respective [means]. (6.2.1)

"One desiring offspring should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice with the twelve-day rite; those desiring prosperity should undertake it. Likewise, in each such case, those having such a desire should undertake the sacrificial session (*sattra*)."
"Seventeen at the minimum and twenty-four at the maximum should perform the sacrificial session (*sattra*). Regarding this, there is a doubt:
does each individual who desires the entire fruit have the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the *sattra*, or is the entitlement for the assembly (*parṣad*) as a whole that desires it? He says:
But surely, those who seek [the goal] are specified as being distinguished by a large number;
how then will there be entitlement for them individually? It is said in reply:

When injunctions such as "those desiring supernatural power" (*ṛddhikāmāḥ*) and so forth are prescribed, they apply to all those characterized by supernatural power, both collectively and individually; since it is not possible to restrict them to a specific [individual] by means of the plural number, a doubt arises as to whether one should apply the rule to each individual or to the assembly (*parṣad*).
What, then, is the conclusion reached?
Each individual is not capable of performing a *sattra* sacrifice that requires many agents;
however, we understand that the assembly (*parṣad*) is the agent seeking the result. And a fruit does not accrue to one who is not the agent.
Nor is a single agent declared;
therefore, the fruit belongs to all together. For each individual there is a portion of the fruit, whereas the middle [agent] would possess the entire fruit.
This being the case, we reply:
for each individual seeker, the entire fruit is accomplished through the sacrificial session (satra). Why? Because from it, the fulfillment of each person's purpose occurs.

When performed together, every single one accomplishes the human goal through a common ritual procedure (*tantra*), and the fruit belongs to all the performers; moreover, each individual here is a performer.
He said: "But has it not been stated that a single individual cannot perform an action involving multiple agents? It is replied:
"A single individual is capable [of doing so] when there is an intention to express his independence."
When each one acts independently,
then he will employ others through conciliation and other means for the sake of accomplishing the number [required]. One person achieves one human goal,
and another achieves another.
Therefore, all agents will be dependent upon one another. And if all are agents,
they will each be connected with their own respective fruits individually.
Moreover, because they arise in conjunction one by one, just as there is the perception of a being (*sattva*),
so too would the entity (*bhāva*) exist in its undivided state. (6.2.2)
Furthermore, it is not contradictory that a single action is performed by many. If it is argued that this is contradictory, [we reply: it is not.
"If one [agent] has performed the action, what could a second do? To this it is replied:

such a fault applies only when the action is performed sequentially (*paryāyeṇa*); however, when the action is performed simultaneously (*tantra*), there is sometimes the possibility [of both agents acting].

If there were a perception of a single being (*sattva*), then there would be a state of non-distinction (*avibhāga*); just as the perception of each individual being— whether an elephant or a horse— is accomplished in its entirety by each individual [observer], even so the state of a ritual procedure (*tantra*) would exist in a collective sacrifice (*satra*),
with the substance belonging to the center of all.
The Adhvaryu throws [the offering] over the middle Āhavanīya fire.
In that case, all the performers act by way of a common procedure (*tantra*).
Furthermore, there is no connection with what has arisen here.

But the action is connected with the number at the very moment of its origination. For if it were connected after having originated, then the statement "for the sake of multiple connections" would be understood;
however, this is not the case when the connection occurs at the time of origination. Therefore, each individual [action] is connected with the entire fruit.
NOTES:
Since the word "man" (puruṣa) is heard in reference to the performance [of the rite], there should be freedom of choice regarding the performance. 6.2.3.
It is heard in scripture: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. Regarding this, there is a doubt:
Is it without restriction—
that one, two, or many may sacrifice—
or rather that only one should sacrifice? But has this not already been addressed in the third [book]?
"The fruit of the treatise belongs to the practitioner. When it belongs to the practitioner, we shall explain how the intended singularity [of the agent] applies, just as it is.
But here, that very point is raised as an objection and will be resolved once again.
What is the prima facie position?
The application would be according to one's desire. Why?
Because of the mention of the person; for the person is mentioned in the scriptural text.

Having made known the sacrifice in relation to the person, the word has fulfilled its purpose; it does not preclude the performance of the sacrifice by one, two, or many persons. That person is not heard of in the injunction as "he shall accomplish the sacrifice" or "he shall bring about the fruit through the sacrifice. How then?

"One should obtain the fruit through sacrifice. In this regard, the person is not a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) either of the sacrifice or of the production of the fruit. For if he were a subordinate factor of the sacrifice or of the production of the fruit, then the number—as a subordinate quality (*guṇabhūta*)—would delimit the person who is that subordinate factor. However, on the contrary, by manifesting the person as a subordinate factor, it would be connected to the person only as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatvena*).
It is not by virtue of expressing a quality (*guṇavacanatayā*). Furthermore, the expression of number (*saṃkhyāvacana*) is not intended there;

since this [injunction] is spoken with reference to every person who is a seeker and capable, it cannot be qualified by a single number. And how could there be primacy of the person (*puruṣaprādhānya*)?
There is no purpose whatsoever served by the production of a result (*phalotpatti*).
Not by the production of the sacrifice;
rather, the self is universally accepted as that which is connected to the fruit,
and for its sake the ritual action must be performed.
Otherwise, even if it were stated, it would not be performed; in that case, the statement would be purposeless,
and therefore there would be freedom of choice.
"One, two, or many should sacrifice. And thus it shows:
"Since you two are the lords of heaven," one should employ this as the *pratipad* for two sacrificers; these...
The mantra *asṛgram indavaḥ* ("the drops have been poured forth") indicates a sacrifice for many sacrificers; that is, it demonstrates the performance of a sacrifice for two or for many.

If it is argued that there is a distinct auditory perception for each object. (6.2.4)
If you say this, and if you perceive it thus,
there would be the state of being based on scripture (*śrutibhāva*).
One should perform the sacrifice and thereby obtain the fruit. Why?
Because both of these are understood from this very source.
"We do not decide which of these two we should abandon; therefore, both are to be accepted. He says:
"But surely it is not logical for them to express a single meaning. It is replied:
"That which is understood is what is logical."

Both [the singular and plural] are perceived; therefore, it is logical that it expresses both meanings. Furthermore, because it is subordinate to the sacrifice (*yāga*), the singular number is intended to be significant.

If you should consider that unity is not intended to be expressed, [we reply]: no, because [the suffix] is for the sake of each respective object (*pratyartham*); it does not have the quality as its purpose since the purpose has not been stated, and because the agent is the primary element due to being a distinct entity. 6.2.5.
This is not so;
for when the person is the primary factor for the sake of that [purpose], the person is not perceived as a subordinate member,
since we do not perceive it in the absence of an explicitly stated logical principle.
Since a different meaning arises from the state of being subordinate to the state of being primary,
and since the agent here is the primary factor so that the statement may be meaningful, it is therefore not possible for the agent to be in a subordinate state.
Because the injunction is one. For there is indeed a single injunctive injunction;
if it enjoins either the production of the fruit or the production of the sacrifice, then the agent does not act for his own sake.
When, however, it is for one's own sake,

then either the sacrifice or the fruit exists for that purpose. And this does not occur simultaneously, for [in the former case] it is for another's sake, while [in the latter] it is for one's own sake.

Whether that purpose is served by one [hand] or by the other in the opposite manner— as when it is understood from the expression "Devadatta shoots arrows with both arms" that it is not done simultaneously— so it is here.
When he throws with the right hand, then he bends the back of the bow with the left;
it is understood that he does not throw with that [left hand] either.

Because he is occupied therein. Thus, when the person is primary, then the sacrifice or the fruit is understood to be subordinate. Because he is occupied therein, their primacy is not understood either. Therefore, the person does not have a subordinate status toward the sacrifice or the fruit; hence, there would be freedom of choice (yāthākāmya).
"One, two, or many may perform the sacrifice. [638] {5/312} NOTES:
Or rather, because it is connected with a specific desire (*kāma*), it should be taught as being for the purpose of performance.
For each individual object, there is indeed a separate scriptural injunction, just as in the case of the two horns. 6.2.6.
The phrase "or rather" (api vā) serves to set aside the previous position:
the agent would be taught for the sake of the performance [of the ritual], not for his own benefit. How so?
The meaning of the injunction "one should sacrifice" (yajeta) is either "one should perform a sacrifice" or "one should effect [something] by means of a sacrifice"; thus,
it is understood merely as the manifestation of existence.

There is neither an agent nor a creator of the fruit; furthermore, the word "one who desires heaven" (svargakāma) refers merely to one who desires heaven and does not depend upon any specific qualification.

"Whether it belongs to oneself or to another"—for in such matters, we rely on verbal testimony as our authority. How, then, is the connection of desire with the self understood? It is understood through that very connection.
One who desires the fruit, even when the word is not explicitly stated,
desires the fruit for himself alone,
not for another. But where both meanings must be expressed, [the word is used].
In that context, the injunction is heard with respect to each individual object,
as for example:
"He scratches himself with the black antelope horn."
"One throws the black antelope horn into the *cātvāla* pit.

Where there are two such injunctive scriptural statements (*śruti*), there both a subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) and a primary status (*prādhānya*) are understood. But here, there are not two such injunctive scriptural statements; rather, the person is heard as being subordinate in the sense that "one should bring it about" (*bhāvayet*).
In that context, the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is either the instrument or the object; however, due to the connection [with the result], the person is primary,
for no one has a need for pleasure merely as it arises.

But the purpose of the self is through its connection with happiness. Therefore, from that connection, the predominance of the person (*puruṣa*) is understood, not from the Vedic text (*śruti*). Consequently, the number of the person, who is here a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*), is intended to be significant.

"The fruit of the treatise belongs to the agent. [639] Notes:

It is not the case that one should not sacrifice because [the injunction] says "one who desires heaven for another"; nor is it that the word "desirer of heaven" does not denote another person. How, then, is it to be understood?
"He does not obtain the fruit. But how is there a non-attainment of the fruit?
Because of the hearing of a specific qualification [in the injunction], namely, "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), or in the case of the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*).
Regarding the injunction "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in spring," the mention of the agent (*upagraha*) in that desire-based scriptural statement is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
If it is argued that one who desires heaven [is not the agent], nor indeed anyone else, but rather the desire for the fruit is the cause; 6.2.9.
If you think thus— that the word "desirer of heaven" is not denotative, and therefore another person would not sacrifice due to the absence of a result— then [we reply]:
"If it is not his sacrifice, then he should sacrifice;
this sacrificer prays for long life, he prays for [long life]."
The Hotṛ priest will point out the instigator;
furthermore, there is an injunction regarding the fruit, namely "He casts the prastara [grass-bundle] with the *sūktavāka*.
If this injunction regarding the fruit is based on the wording of the mantra, then...
The *prastara* grass-bundle is offered with the *sūktavāka* mantra;
otherwise, an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) result would have to be postulated. Therefore, for the sake of the incidental fruit, one person desiring heaven should sacrifice on behalf of another.

Not so, because of eternality. 6.2.10.
This is not so;
for that very person who possesses the fruit of the primary action, it is also fitting that they possess the incidental fruit as well.
In this way, the installation is performed for one's own sake. For there is no distinction in the fact that the installation is for one's own sake;
whether it be the primary fruit or a secondary incidental result, everything must accrue to the installer.
Furthermore, the status of being both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) would be contradicted.
If one should sacrifice desiring long life and so forth, then it is not obligatory;
if it is obligatory, then one does not desire long life and so forth. Therefore, the established principle should not be overturned.

And the person, being the primary factor, is enjoined; however, because he is subordinate [to the sacrifice], his singularity is intended [by the author]. Therefore, one alone should sacrifice. (640) NOTES:

If it is argued that action is likewise [momentary], [we reply: no. 6.2.11.
Now, as for what was said—that it shows the sacrifice of two and of many:

One should employ the *pratipad* "ete asṛgram indavaḥ" for two sacrificers; one should employ the *pratipad* [beginning with] "ete asṛgram indavaḥ" for many sacrificers.
In a ritual involving two sacrificers or many sacrificers, the rite would have to be performed according to the injunctions for a single sacrificer; therefore,
that objection must be refuted.
That which is thus associated [is not perceived] because of its inherence. 6.2.12.
This is not so;
for there exists a combined ritual performed by two sacrificers and by many sacrificers, according to the scriptural injunction.
Just as in the case of those who are deficient [in limbs], the prescription of the ritual procedure (*pratipad-vidhāna*) for them will be meaningful. Therefore, "one should sacrifice" [is the rule].
However, [the number] shall be restricted by the initial undertaking (*prakrama*), because the commencement is the cause for the performance [of the rite]. (6.2.13)
Rites such as "one desiring offspring should sacrifice" and "one desiring a village should sacrifice" are recorded in the tradition. In this regard, there is a doubt:
must that which has been commenced necessarily be brought to completion, or may it be performed according to one's desire, or even abandoned? What is the prima facie view?
"It must necessarily be brought to completion. Why?
Because it is heard [in scripture] thus:
"One who desires this should sacrifice."

Thus they explain the meaning of that spoken word: "He has said [it] from the beginning until the end," meaning that its specific function (vyāpāraviśeṣa) consists in this much: starting from the commencement up to the final completion.

"It is not as in the case of 'cooking' or 'giving. For in those cases, only the existence of the action is indicated, without reference to its being commenced and brought to completion. And even worldly people understand the meaning of the verb in this way.
In that case, it is understood that human effort is not enjoined with respect to the undertaking; for while they do not necessarily undertake what is enjoined, they do necessarily complete it.
Therefore, neither the undertaking nor the completion [is subject to injunction].
This is not the meaning of the word. What, then, is it?

Completion is the meaning of the word, because the undertaking [of an action] reaches its fulfillment in completion. Therefore, it is understood that completion is the meaning of the word. And if that [completion] is the meaning of the word, [then...]
That [action] is enjoined as something to be performed;

however, at the very commencement, there is no statement that it must be performed. Therefore, the undertaking is not mandatory, but the completion is mandatory. Consequently, if the desire for the fruit should fail once the rite has been commenced, [the obligation remains].
Or even if one obtains the fruit,
in that state as well,
the completion of what has been commenced must certainly be performed.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the object desired by the seeker is what is stated here as something to be performed? [Reply: This is not so, for that would be the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*).

The necessity of performing the sacrifice, however, is understood from the direct Vedic injunction (*śruti*). Therefore, a sacrifice undertaken by one desiring a village must be brought to completion. At that time, the mention of the desire for a village and so forth serves as the occasion (*nimitta*); and when an occasion has arisen, it is stated what ought to be done.
Even when that cause has perished, the rite must indeed be performed;
the commencement must be brought to completion, for what has perished does not become as if it had never arisen. And its arising is the cause.

It is not a positive entity. Therefore, even when the desire for the fruit has ceased, what has been commenced must be brought to completion. For the motive for an action is its commencement, and that [motive] also [persists] until its completion.

The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position. Or rather, there is no fixed rule. Why?
Because of the desire for results; this means that for one who desires a result and wishes to bring it about, this [practice] is prescribed as the means.

It is not [the object] to be performed (*kartavyatā*), for if that were being enjoined, it would pertain either to the fruit or to the sacrifice. First of all, it need not be stated in regard to the fruit; for it is not necessary to teach that "whatever someone desires, that must be performed" by him.
Thinking, "This must be accomplished by me alone," one does not know the means and thus desires it; this is what is being taught.
The sacrifice is the means,
in the sense that it is performed by means of the sacrifice; yet there is no "to-be-done-ness" (kāryatā) inherent in the sacrifice itself,
because that would contradict direct perception.
But sacrifice is a directly perceived affliction;
if the duty belongs to something else by means of the sacrifice, then there is no contradiction. If the duty belongs to the sacrifice itself, then a fruit must be postulated.

Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that which is being conceptualized. And an instruction regarding what is to be done (*kartavyopadeśa*) applies only to matters that are possible and so forth;

therefore, the sacrifice (*yāga*) is not something that must be performed. Rather, having referred to (*anūdya*) that which is desired by one who seeks a fruit, the status of the sacrifice as a means (*sādhanatā*) is enjoined according to how it is already established; consequently, it does not necessarily have to be brought to completion.

Just as one need not necessarily begin what has been prescribed in sequence, so too one need not necessarily complete what has already been begun. As for the claim that the meaning of a sentence is sublated by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), this applies only where the meaning of the direct statement is impossible.
It has already been stated that in those cases the meaning of the sentence is apprehended; therefore, there is no fixed rule.

Alternatively, if it is accepted that "eating is not to be performed," or that "eating qualified by the negative particle is to be performed," then the suffix -tavya prescribes non-eating through direct denotation (śruti).

The negative particle (*nañ*) denotes the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). And because of its function, the negative particle does not connect with [the action] as something to be performed (*kartavyatā*). If, however, the meaning of the negative particle were to be performed, then the placing [of the firewood] would be [understood] through the sentence.

And *bhakṣayati* (he eats) is qualified by the negative particle (*nañ*), and direct statement (*śruti*) is stronger than syntactical connection (*vākya*). Therefore, it is understood that "non-eating" is what must be performed;
and non-eating is the absence of eating.

There is nothing further to be done for him. Therefore, that mental operation which occurs therein is what is taught here—the means by which eating becomes qualified by the negative particle (*nañ*). First, there is a connection between the negative particle and the verb "to eat."
Next is the rule of procedure.
For example, regarding the vows of Prajāpati such as "one should not look at the rising sun," there is a fruit for one who performs them;
for one who does not perform them, there is neither fruit nor fault.
In the same way here as well,
because actions are distinguished [from other things],
it is not action that is prohibited here.
Only non-action is being taught here;
for action, namely eating, which is being prohibited, is one thing, while non-action, which is a mental resolve, is another.

The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice is prescribed as being performed with a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), and it is heard in the scripture that this sacrificial cake must be made of rice. In this regard, the following is considered:
what if the sacrifice were performed with a sacrificial cake made of wild rice (nīvāra)?
Is it that very same sacrifice, or is it another? What is the prima facie view? There would be a division [of the ritual] because of the different substance; therefore, it is another sacrifice.
Why? Because it is dependent;

for a distinction is understood from the difference in the substratum. This [grain] which has *nīvāra* as its substratum is different from that which has *vrīhi* as its substratum. The difference in the substratum is indeed quite clear;
because of that difference, the form (*rūpa*) is also understood to be distinct. Therefore, the sacrifice is different when the substance is different.
NOTES:

*{5/402: E1 gives anyo yāgaḥ in parentheses}* Alternatively, because there is no difference [in the action] and because there is no distinction in the word for its form, there would be identity of action like the universal "cowness" (gotva); and it would be a name [of the sacrifice], like the word "existent" (sattva). 6.3.12.

The phrase "or rather" (api vā) serves to set aside the previous position. There would be a single action even when there is a different substance; for when the action occurs—whether it be moving or falling—that object remains exactly the same.
And therein there is no distinct quality, either superior or inferior;
nor indeed is the form itself something else, nor is there another word that expresses it.
"Is it not the case, then, that the difference in substrata is perfectly clear? It is replied:
We indeed maintain that the substrata are distinct, but we do not hold that there is a distinction in the supported [quality] due to that difference in substrata.

Because of their difference. For when a garland or a cloth is divided, a division of the person is not perceived as a result of that [division]. If it is argued that he too has a distinct self, this is not so;
for only those who perceive a distinction could speak in such a manner, and no distinction is perceived in this case.
But is it not the case that this very thing is the distinction, namely, that even though [the self] is one...?
Even one [of them] remains undestroyed.
That which is said, "it is not destroyed," is not so.
Prior to its perception, there is no means of valid cognition for its existence;
therefore, it has perished. And yet, [it is not the case that...].
That [object] is recognized as distinct from its substance, because no difference [between them] is perceived. If it is asked, "How then does the cognition 'it moves' arise?", it is said:
because one observes its arrival at another location.
That which goes to another place and comes back is said to "move"; in that case,
both the mover and the other place are perceived through direct perception.
Therefore, it is said that he has "gone," and it is also said that he has "come. This is true:
that which has not perished is other than that which has perished.
But even that other [action] is indeed denotable by the word "yajati" (sacrifices);
the generality of "yajati" is not divided.
Nor is it expressed by the word [itself]. Therefore, even one who should perform the sacrifice with wild rice (nīvāra) has indeed performed what was enjoined;
and for one who performs what is enjoined, the desired result comes to pass.
It is not something previously uncreated. Furthermore, it indicates a name—
either "Darśa" or "Pūrṇamāsa"— which belongs to this very generality,
just as there are names for a generality among sentient beings.
[This applies] to universals, not to individuals. What is the purpose of this inquiry?
This will be examined in the subsequent section.
