Because the Veda is the authority, there is no tradition from others in the absence of cultured persons (śiṣṭa), since others are not cultured. 6.3.13.
The obligatory rites, such as the Agnihotra and others, serve as the examples. When there is a substitution of the prescribed substance for these rites, a doubt arises:
should the performance be carried out by taking a substitute, or should the rite be abandoned at that point? What is the prima facie view?
In the absence of what is prescribed, there is no authority for anything else; that alone must be abandoned. Why?
Because it is not prescribed.
That which is prescribed as having rice and barley as its constituent qualities is fruitful;
however, when it is performed with wild rice (*nīvāra*) as its constituent quality, it becomes fruitless. Therefore, it must be abandoned at that very point.
And because [the rite] is prescribed in certain cases [only with specific materials]. 6.3.14.

In some cases it is prescribed, as in: "If one does not find Soma, one should press Pūtīka plants. If the performance were to be carried out by taking a substitute, this would not have been prescribed.
But it is indeed prescribed. Therefore, that which is not prescribed has no substitute. [660] {5/409} NOTES:
*{5/408: E2: Just as, if}* scripture [is authoritative], because there is no difference in the meaning of the injunction. 6.3.15.
Or rather, there is the scriptural authority for the substance to be substituted. Why?

Because there is no difference in the meaning of the injunction; for the purpose enjoined by the injunction to sacrifice is not distinguished whether it is performed with rice or with wild grains (nīvāra).
Sacrifice must necessarily be performed when obligatory rites and occasional rites have been commenced;
in some cases, an injunction is for the purpose of restriction. (6.3.16)
Now, as for what was said— that [the rule] is due to an injunction in some cases— it is replied: in some cases, an injunction is for the purpose of restriction.

In the absence of *soma*, when several similar substances are available, a restriction is made that only *pūtīka* plants are to be pressed. Therefore, the performance of the rite must be carried out by taking a substitute.
That [action] is constant, for it is the desire to perform that very [action]. 6.3.17.
But how is it understood that this statement is intended solely for the purpose of restriction? It is said:
because the *pūtīka* plants are already obtained. And how are they obtained?
For that is the desire to act;
we shall explain this as the desire to act toward similarity in that regard.
And because they were obtained through the desire to perform that [substitute], the *pūtīka* plants are [therefore] permanent.
Therefore, this statement is understood as being for the purpose of restriction; it is permanent.
NOTES:

[The word *sādṛśya* (similarity) refers to] the desire to perform [an action]. [This is] not [the case for] the deity, the fire, the word, or the action, because of their connection with another purpose. (6.3.18) [Vgl. MS 6.3.27]
The deities are those such as "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" and so forth;
[and] Agni.
"In that they offer into the Āhavanīya fire, by that his desired [deity] becomes pleased"—
this is the word, which is the mantra,
such as "I cut the sacrificial grass, the seat of the gods," and so forth.
The ritual acts are those such as "he offers the fuel-sticks," "he offers to Tanūnapāt," and so forth. In this regard, there is a doubt:
When there is a deficiency in the deity, the fire, the word, or the action, should a substitute be adopted or not? What is the prima facie view?
That one should adopt something else by applying the principle of the preceding section.
"The ritual application must be performed.
This being the position reached, we say:
there should be no substitute for a deity, fire, a word, or an action when they are absent. Why?
Because of its connection with a different purpose, that which is substituted would be something other than these [original items],
and it would not be able to perform their specific function. And what is their specific function?
First of all, a deity accomplishes the purpose by way of being the objective; for instance, with reference to Agni,
an offering on eight potsherds is abandoned at both the full moon and the new moon sacrifices, as well as that which is prescribed among other oblations.

The New and Full Moon sacrifices do not take place [if a substitute is used]. In that case, another deity being designated would not fulfill the purpose of the deity prescribed by the scripture; for when another deity is designated, the New and Full Moon sacrifices do not come into existence.
Therefore, a deity is not substituted.
Likewise, regarding the rule "one offers in the Āhavanīya fire," if the Āhavanīya fire is lost, no other fire should be substituted.
"Or another substance. Why? Because of its connection with a different purpose; that which is substituted does not function for the purpose of the *āhavanīya*. How so?
The effect of the Āhavanīya fire is unseen;
that which occurs when an offering is cast upon the Āhavanīya does not occur when it is cast upon anything else. For indeed, it is not so.
By the word "yajati" (he sacrifices), that [substratum] is understood through implication— that upon which the offering is cast;
for it is not otherwise.
The location where the sacrifice is being performed provides some assistance; therefore, there can be no substitute for the fire.
Likewise, in the event of a lapse regarding a mantra, another mantra is not substituted for it. Of the mantra...
For this is indeed the purpose:
that it causes one to remember either the action or the means;
for if there were no remembrance, the action would not be accomplished.
If, when the original mantra has been displaced, one utters another word for its sake— uttering a word for a meaning already understood—

one would not perceive the meaning through that word. For if one were to perceive even what is already understood by uttering a substitute word, one would be producing a cognition from the word itself [rather than from the meaning].
And thus, compliance with the utterance of a substitute term would be purposeless; for there is no authority whatsoever that it must be made known by means of a word. What there is, is this:
that it must be made known specifically by this particular word, such as "barhis" and so forth.
In the absence of that [original substance], compliance with another word would be meaningless. Therefore, there is no substitute for the word.
In the case of a lapse in the ritual action, there is no other ritual action [that can serve as a substitute].

The *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices must be performed with the two fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and the two oblations (*yajus*). If these are performed using something else [as a substitute], they do not possess those two components. Therefore, there can be no substitute for the ritual action itself.

Therefore, it is not a substitute for Agni. Why?} *{5/420: E2: [It is] substituted. From what?}*
Because of the connection with another purpose, one should produce understanding from the mantra.
One should substitute another action, because it is connected with a different purpose; and also because the deity exists for that purpose. 6.3.19.
There is another specific characteristic regarding the deity, by virtue of which it cannot be substituted; for that which is called a "deity" [is unique].

Whatever is enjoined for a specific purpose—that [is the deity]. Another, being substituted in its place, would not be the deity; for that which is enjoined is the deity, not that which is not enjoined.
Furthermore, this term "deity" (devatā) is a relative term. Whatever [substance] is enjoined for the sake of a particular [deity], that substance belongs to that deity alone, and not to another.
Thus, "deity" is a relative term, not a generic term. For this reason as well, there can be no substitute for a deity.
And that [eating] is prohibited without distinction, for so says the scripture. (6.3.20)
Now, as for that which has been prohibited— namely,
"varaka and kodrava grains are unfit for sacrifice" and "māṣa beans are unfit for sacrifice"— what is the rule regarding that when there is a deficiency of the prescribed substance?
Or rather, "no. What is the prima facie view? [It is that] "there is indeed [a transfer], because there is no difference in the meaning of the injunction.
This being the prima facie view, we reply:
And that which is prohibited must not be substituted;
for this is stated without qualification,
and it is not said specifically, "Māṣas, Varakas, and Kodravas are unfit for sacrifice."

The connection of these [substances] with the sacrifice is prohibited; that is to say, they are not to be brought into the state of being constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice, for if they were substituted, they would thereby be brought into the state of being constituent parts. Therefore, these are not to be substituted.
Likewise, [the fruit belongs] to the owner, because of the connection with the fruit and because the fruit is linked to the ritual action. 6.3.21.
Ritual acts such as the Agnihotra and others serve as the illustration. Regarding these, when the master (svāmin) fails to perform them, a doubt arises:
should another be appointed as a substitute, or not? What is the prima facie view? That a substitute should be appointed. Why?
"Or rather, it is scripture, because there is no difference in the meaning of the injunction.
This being the position reached, we reply: "In that case, it would belong to the owner. What is the meaning?
There is no substitute. Why?

Because of the connection with the fruit. For he who, being desirous [of the result], hires the priests by means of his own relinquishment, and he who relinquishes that which is his own to be given—[for him alone does the result accrue].
He is the master. If he is represented by a proxy,
he should perform everything that ought to be done by the master.
If one were to perform all of that, he would be the master himself,
not a representative; for he alone is connected with the fruit— he who performs the relinquishment.
He becomes the possessor of the fruit. As it has been said:
"The fruit of the treatise belongs to the performer.
Therefore, there can be no substitute for the master.
But when many [priests] have already begun, one may bring another, provided there is no deficiency in the ritual performance. //6.3.22//
Sacrificial sessions (*satra*) are the example, as in the rule:
"At least seventeen persons should perform a sacrificial session. When one of those masters commits a transgression, a doubt arises:
should another be substituted in his place?
Or rather, not so. What is the prima facie view? That there can be no substitute for the master. This being the position, we reply:
when many sacrificers have commenced the ritual act...
If some master has failed in his duty, one may bring another [master]. Why?
Because in this way there is no deficiency;
for in that case, the number seventeen and so forth residing in the master is an auxiliary element (*aṅga*).
Without her, the ritual action is deficient;
therefore, another must be brought in to accomplish it.
But is it not the case that the number resides in the master?
But we shall say that one who is not yet arrived cannot be the master; therefore, it is impossible to adopt that number. It is replied:
it will not belong to the master, for it is impossible to make it so. However, this can be done:
those things which belong to the masters—
It will thus be established that these [sacrifices] are to be performed here by at least seventeen persons. Therefore, a substitute must be appointed there.
He would be the master [of the sacrifice], because of his connection with it. (6.3.23)
Now that he has arrived, there is a doubt:
is he the master or a laborer? What is the prima facie view?
He would be the owner. Why? Because of that connection, namely, through that ownership.
It is a conjunction. For that which is brought in is made the owner;
if the owner has passed away, another is made the owner.
Therefore, he becomes a representative. For that reason, he is called "the master" (*svāmī*). [665] {5/432} NOTES:
{*5/431: E1 gives *svāmitvena* in parentheses*}
Or he may be a laborer, because of being hired for wages. 3.3.24.

Or he would be a laborer. Why? Because of being hired; for he has been employed by those cultured masters as a hired servant, and one who is being paid for his work does not become the owner. He who obtains the fruit [is the owner].
He who acts for the benefit of another is the master;
he who acts for his own benefit is the servant.
He does not obtain the fruit at all. Why?
For he who, having begun [an action], brings it to completion, is one who possesses the fruit.
For this is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*);

it expresses [the action] from its commencement until its completion. But do they not perform that [action] with a deficiency, due to the absence of seventeen masters? Therefore, they too are not masters.
If they do not belong to the master, they do not obtain the fruit. It is said in reply:
it is heard in scripture that "there should be no fewer than seventeen" in the attainment of the fruit.
The number is not subordinate with respect to the inclusion of the result; rather,
it is subordinate with respect to the ritual acts, in the sense that "the ritual acts to be performed by the sacrificer must be done with at least seventeen persons."
And those [rites] are performed by a substitute;

even though there is no fruit [in the case of the substitute], they bring in another person in order to fulfill the intention (*saṃkalpa*). Furthermore, that which is brought in has no purpose for him [the original sacrificer], because the fruit is seen to belong to him [the original sacrificer]. (6.3.25)

And when he has gone to his destined state, [the text] shows the fruit, indicating that even for one who dies while consecrated (dīkṣita), there is a fruit. Therefore, he is a performer of the ritual action; he would possess those qualities because of his connection with the ritual action. 6.3.26.
It has been established that when any one among many has committed an offense, another person should be substituted in his place. Now, however, there is a doubt regarding this matter:
would such a substitute possess the same duties as the original master?
Are these the duties of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*)? What is the prima facie view? They are the duties of the officiating priest. Why?
"For he sacrifices for the sake of another;
and he who sacrifices for the sake of another is an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). This being the position reached, we reply:
He would possess those qualities,
for it is heard that he presides over his effects;
and whoever presides over someone's effect, [he possesses that person's qualities].
It is connected with those properties,
just as an axe is [connected] with the properties of its handle.

For that desire to act is indeed common [to all]. (6.3.27)
It has been established that when a prescribed substance is unavailable, the ritual should be performed by taking a substitute. In this regard, there is a doubt:
should the performance be carried out by taking any substance whatsoever, or should it be one that is similar? What is the prima facie view?
"Whatever may be taken"—this being the position reached, we reply:
that which is grasped as a general property (*sāmānya*) must be taken as something similar. Why?
For all words denote a generic form (*ākṛti*);

and although the generic form is heard as being subordinate (*aṅga-bhāvena*), nevertheless its subordination toward the action is not direct. Rather, it is the substance (*dravya*), which is the means of accomplishing the action, that is obtained as subordinate by implication (*arthāt*).
In the act of delimiting that [universal], it becomes a subordinate factor (*aṅga*);
and by means of the universal (*ākṛti*), the particulars (*viśeṣa*) of the individual (*vyakti*) are delimited.
Those particulars are the subordinate factors. Now, when that universal has been set aside, the substance (*dravya*) which is obtained through implication must indeed be grasped.
And when a substance similar to that [original] is being taken up, some of those specific qualities are included;
thus, the benefit is obtained therein, and therefore a substance similar to it must be adopted. Consequently, in the absence of rice (*vrīhi*), wild rice (*nīvāra*) is to be used as a substitute.

But when there is an option [between two rules], that which has already commenced [applies] because of the specific instruction (nirdeśa). 6.3.28.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, concerning which it is stated:

regarding this, it is heard [in the scripture]:

"One binds the animal to a *khadira* tree, one binds it to a *palāśa* tree, one binds it to a *rauhitaka* tree. In this regard, suppose that once a ritual procedure involving the *khadira* as its specific quality has been commenced, the *khadira* is destroyed.
There arises a doubt:
should there be the adoption of an optional alternative (*vaikalpika*), or [should one use] something similar to the *khadira*? What is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)?
"Of that which is optional. Why?
Because that [wood] is indeed heard [in the scripture], whereas something similar to *khadira* is not heard.

That which is similar to that is to be accepted;
that [practice] in which it has been engaged is specified.

that which is optional is not a constituent part. In a performance where the *khadira* tree has been resorted to, the *palāśa* and *rauhitaka* trees are not constituent parts;

To perform [the action] at that very time is impossible and has not been prescribed. Therefore, when the *khadira* tree is employed, the other two [trees] are not to be adopted, because they do not constitute constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the rite. One must seek something similar to the *khadira*.

If you think that what is similar to *khadira* wood is to be adopted,

for it would be understood as contingent upon a specific cause, provided that such a cause were stated.

whereas this [substitute] is indeed prescribed.

In this context, the statement regarding "one for whom" [suffering occurs] as being caused by a specific sign (*nimitta*) is invariably untenable.
It is understood. Therefore, the *ārti* (calamity) must necessarily be qualified. And that [calamity] is qualified by the oblation (*havis*).

Thus, the accomplishment of the connection between the oblation and the calamity is not the cause for the five-platter offering (*pañcaśarāva*). For the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is capable of expressing that connection; however, the connection of the oblation with both [the calamity and the deity] would have to be expressed by syntactical connection (*vākya*).
And the statement is weak compared to direct Vedic utterance (śruti).
[Objection: But surely the connection with the damage to the oblation is also established by sentence alone (vākya). [Reply: It is said in response:
there, the cessation of the damage is also understood; and that [cessation] is established by direct utterance (śruti).
If the oblation were connected to both [the new moon and full moon sacrifices], the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) would be completely set aside.

Therefore, it is not indicated that the connection [to both] is being brought about. How then is the word "both" (*ubhaya*) used? The term "both" is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*), applicable even when only one has been spoiled and even when the other has been. Thus it is said: "For whom both oblations should meet with ruin."

Now, why is it that suffering qualified by two words is not understood as the *nimitta* (condition), namely: "for whom the sacrificial offering, qualified by both qualities, should suffer ruin"? To this it is replied:
First of all, what do you think?

"An extraordinary affliction (*viśiṣṭārti*) is the cause by virtue of its being an extraordinary object. He said: "Because of the proximity of an extraordinary object, the extraordinary object is present as the affliction. What, then, would happen if it were so?
From that, there would be an affliction distinguished by both."
It is understood that this refers to the *nimitta*.

To this it is replied: first, this "Beloved of the Gods" (*devānāmpriya*) must be questioned. For even in the case of one for whom a specific object is present in close proximity, is that which is not specific driven away by sticks? What follows from the fact that it is not driven away? This is what follows from it:
The affliction (*ārti*) is the cause for the *pañcaśarāva* [offering]. [Objection: But will not the word "both" (*ubhaya*) qualify the oblation (*havis*)?
[Response: No; since it is not syntactically connected with the word "oblation," it cannot qualify it. It will be connected [with the oblation] due to proximity (*ānantarya*).
Even so, it is still not capable [of producing the result]. For it does not bring about cessation.
He says: "Because it expresses a specific quality, it will bring that about, just as when one says, 'Bring a white cow. No.
When this has been stated, they bring forward the black cow. [The opponent argues: "The word 'white' excludes this cow from the black ones and so forth.
It is replied: "This is an unequal comparison."
In that case, it is not by characterizing the substance through the form of a cow that its bringing is enjoined;
for if it were so even there, this [objection] would not apply at all.

[The verb] would have been [conjugated] in the potential mood (*vyaśekṣyata*). However, in that case, the act of bringing (*ānayana*) qualified by both adjectives is stated as the primary element. Here, however, the *pañcaśarāva* [offering] pertains to a substance characterized by distress (*ārti*) and being an oblation (*haviṣṭva*).

What, then, is the reason? When the meaning of the verbal root (*ākhyātārtha*) is the primary element, the qualifiers function collectively; but when it is for the sake of another [element], they function separately.
It is said: whether the primary element is the form (*ākṛti*) or the quality (*guṇa*), it is stated for the purpose of establishing its connection;

this is understood from a single sentence. Having performed [the action] as qualified by that, one’s duty is fulfilled. If one were to perform it as qualified by only one of the two, one would be doing what was not prescribed in the scripture. However, where the meaning of the verb is declared with respect to a substance (*dravya*) characterized by its form, [that is the case].

In that case, it is stated to apply to all members of that same class. One should not think that [the rule] is fulfilled when it has been performed with respect to only one; for since it is characterized by the generic form (*ākṛti*), it is indeed stated to apply to another as well. Why then should that which is stated there and not prohibited not be performed? Furthermore, when the meaning of the verb is the primary element, it does not have a connection with that which is characterized by the generic form.

In that case, even if an object of that same form is not brought forward, the primary requirement is indeed fulfilled, and the primary requirement remains endowed with its qualities; thus, nothing that has been heard in the scripture is lost. Therefore, a qualification is appropriate there, but not so here. For here, it is stated that when the substance having the form of the oblation is lost, there is the "five-platter" (pañcaśarāva) offering. That [offering] cannot be set aside by a specific statement that does not express a prohibition.

Moreover, even though the word "both" (*ubhaya*) is connected with the oblation (*havis*), an affliction (*ārti*) qualified by "both" is not at all understood. What is the reason? The word "both" is connected with the oblation, not with the phrase "he should not suffer affliction. In that case, although the word "both" is present, the meaning of the word "oblation" remains [unqualified].
Affliction (*ārti*) is connected with that alone; and the meaning there is not qualified [by anything else]. Therefore, affliction qualified by both is not the cause.
Now, if it is argued that the word "both" (*ubhaya*) is used because of its connection with the case-ending of the substratum of affliction, [we reply:]...
It is said that there is suffering characterized by both; but that is not so,
for the word "both" (ubhaya) can qualify the oblation (havis) only through its connection with the case-ending,
because of its co-occurrence [with it].
It is not a qualifier of *ārti* (calamity). For there is no co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of this [word *havirvināśa*] with *ārti* such that it would qualify it.
If it is argued that even in the absence of co-occurrence, the object qualified by that [destruction] will be understood due to the proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) of the word *ārti*, that is not so;
for when there is no expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity is not a cause [for syntactic connection].

As in the cases "the wife of the king" or "the man of Devadatta. If it is argued that because these occur within a single sentence, [the referent] is understood as qualified by that [other term], this is not so. For even within a single sentence, there is no [understanding of qualification] for that which is a constituent part but is not required, as for example:
In the expressions "he goes by horse" and "covered with a white cloth," whiteness does not function as a qualifier for the horse unless it is itself expected [as a relevant attribute].

Now it might be argued that the connection of both [the offering and the expiation] with the oblation is qualified by the distress (*ārti*). That too is not tenable. For the phrase "should suffer distress" (*ārtim ārcchet*) is not employed as a qualification of the oblation; rather, it serves as the occasion (*nimitta*) for the five-platter offering (*pañcaśarāva*). If one were to accept a simultaneous connection of the distress of the oblation with both [the original offering and the five-platter offering], the sentence would be split (*vākya-bheda*).

Now, if one were to say that "one should recite" [the verse] when connected with that which is characterized by the form of the oblation (*havis*), then it would again be connected with the word "both" as qualified by the oblation; even so, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Therefore, the recitation is not declared as being qualified by both.

Just as when the meaning of the verb is primary, it is expressed as qualified by both and not understood as qualified by either one alone, so too in the other case, although it is qualified by the two qualifiers, it is not qualified in its own essence.
Nevertheless, being qualified by either one [of the two], it cannot serve as the cause. What is the distinction?
This is explained:
in my position, there are two qualifications by way of being the object of appropriation (*upādeya*).
In your view, however, it is [the cause] by virtue of being a definition (*lakṣaṇa*). He asks: "What follows from its being a definition? It is replied: {6/}
This follows from that: the substance is indicated by its generic form (*ākṛti*), and something must be said regarding it.

If it were mentioned without being so indicated, it would not be understood to which [substance] it would belong; or else, it might be understood as belonging to every substance whatsoever. Since both of these [consequences] are equally undesirable, [the specific substance must be specified].

When that [affliction] exists, the form of the oblation (*havis*) is mentioned in order to characterize its basis. In that regard, two possibilities arise: either that which has the form of an oblation is afflicted, or else, that which has the form of an oblation...

Regarding the phrase "that both": if, first of all, it is intended that "whatever has the form of an oblation is spoiled," then both—that which has the form of an oblation and that which does not—is understood as the cause of the spoilage.

Alternatively, if "that which has the form of an oblation is both," then the spoilage is not qualified by the oblation. In this case, since the spoilage is not qualified by the oblation, the word "both" will qualify the oblation.
This is not tenable. How so? It would indeed be qualified in this way:
"that which has the form of the sacrificial oblation (havis) is both";
however, in that case, it must further be stated:
Regarding the statement, "If both [offerings] which have the form of oblation-material (*havis*) are damaged," how could the damage be connected with that which is thus qualified? It is not,
however, the case that the two words "both" and "oblation-material" are for the purpose of qualifying the damage.
79*} They should be uttered. Now, if the utterance is not performed again,
then even if the word *havis* were not uttered by way of *tantra* for the purpose of indicating the characteristic based on both [the substance and the deity],
it would remain undistinguished.

The characteristic of the *ārti* (calamity) would be common to both; however, if a specific [calamity] is intended, a repetition must be made. In that case, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Thus, if the word "both" (*ubhaya*) were connected with the verb "to suffer" (*ārchati*), [the fault remains].
The oblation would not be qualified;

in that case, the destruction of the unqualified oblation would be the occasion [for the rite]. Alternatively, if it were connected with the word "oblation," then for the sake of connecting it again with "destruction," it would have to be uttered together with the word "oblation."

Or it might be indicated by the pronoun "this" (*etad*); in that case, too, there would be the same syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Furthermore, if they were to be taken as things to be enjoined (*upādeya*), there would be no purpose in their being mutual qualifiers; rather, both would be uttered for the sake of qualifying *ārti*.

In that case, suffering qualified by either one [of the two] cannot be the cause (*nimitta*). However, if it were a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), it would be qualified by either one; this is the distinction.

Furthermore, when every word is connected with another word, if there is a possibility [of connection] through a third word, a connection with even the proximate [word] is not appropriate without [the intervention of] the word [itself].

For it does not occur that in the expression "the king's wife" or "Devadatta's man," the king is a qualifier of the man. However, when no other way [of interpretation] is possible, even if there is an intervention, the connection of several subordinate elements with the principal element is admissible;
for the meaning is more powerful than the word-order.

However, if it were a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), then upon the conjunction of two characteristics, one of them would necessarily have to be abandoned; either the [other] characteristic or the quality (*guṇa*) that is mediated by it would have to be relinquished.

And likewise, the offering, the pressing, and the consumption [of the soma] take place in one or the other [of the two fires]. MS 6.4.24.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard:

"Having pressed [the Soma] with the stones in the Havirdhāna shed, having offered it in the Āhavanīya fire, and having gone back westward, they consume the portions in the Sadas. Therein, the pressing is enjoined by another statement.

The *yajati* [denotes] the *homa* (oblation). Those two [the *yajati* and the *juhoti*] are not prescribed here, nor is their sequence; for that [sequence] is obtained through the very nature of the matter (*arthāt*). Therefore, what is prescribed is the consumption by the same agent as the pressing and the oblation: "Once the pressing has been performed and the oblation offered, the consumption must be carried out by those who performed them."

In this regard, there is this doubt: must he alone who performs both [the acts] consume [the remnant], or may it be consumed by either one as well? What is the prima facie view? The consumption following the oblation and the pressing should be likewise;
that is, it should be exactly like that.

It is like the defect of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*). How so? It is not connected in this way—that one should press [the Soma], and then offer it, and then consume it. By this, the sequence of the pressing and the offering is not being stated;
rather, it refers to those who, having pressed [it], offer it.
"They consume them"— for in this way the sentence would be split:
"having pressed [the juice], they consume it," and "having offered [the oblation], they consume it."

Therefore, since there is no mutual connection between the offering (*homa*) and the pressing (*abhiṣava*), the act of consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*) would be connected with even one of them, and likewise with the other— as in the case of "having pressed [the Soma], they consume it. Consequently, the consumption occurs by means of either one of these two conditions.

"Having offered [the oblation], they eat"—
this applies to both [the father and the son], for there is no separate Dharmaśāstra for those two.

Or rather, one should consume [the soma] on account of both causes. The act of consumption is not prescribed as a property (*dharma*) of either the oblation (*homa*) or the pressing (*abhiṣava*). For what would happen if it were prescribed as a property of those two? Since the oblation and the pressing are the primary acts (*pradhāna*), the consumption would be a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), and being subordinate to each primary act, it would have to be repeated for each. However, if the consumption is instead prescribed on account of both causes, then when that [single act of consumption] has been performed, a single purpose is achieved.
It is thus prescribed. Therefore, it constitutes a single sentence, which concludes with this much:
"having pressed [the Soma], having offered [it], they consume [it]. In that context, there is this intermediate sentence:
"Having offered, they eat. And when there is a great sentence (*mahāvākya*), a subordinate sentence (*avāntaravākya*) does not constitute a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
because it is sublated by the other words [of the greater context],
as for example:
From the great sentence (*mahāvākya*), the prohibition "one should not look at the rising sun" is understood;

from the intermediate sentence (*avāntaravākya*), the injunction to look is understood. Therefore, eating [the soma] would have no stated cause. From the great sentence, it is understood that there are two causes for eating. Otherwise, one who performs the eating differently would abandon what is explicitly stated in scripture.
Therefore, the consumption [of the soma] is by both.

When a substance has been destroyed, the re-establishment of that very same substance constitutes the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Its visible purpose is this:
"How might the substance be restored?"—thus the re-consecration (*punarādheya*) is performed.
In this regard, the rule is as follows:
two fires arise together, not separately. Therefore, if one of them has gone out, it is not possible to establish only one; it would be deficient in its qualities.

95*. Now, one might also establish a second [fire]. If that [second fire] were the Āhavanīya, then since another Āhavanīya already exists there for the purpose of the oblation, it would not serve for the oblation. And that which is produced for the purpose of the oblation is the Āhavanīya, because this is a term denoting a consecration (*saṃskāra*).

And the word "preparatory act" (*saṃskāra*) does not occur even in the absence of a single preparatory act. Moreover, this very [act] is a preparatory act, namely that which has the purpose of the oblation (*homārthatā*), as expressed in the statement:
"One offers into the *āhavanīya* fire."
In that case, when one [element] has followed and another is being superimposed, there is a deficiency,
for [the result] depends on both.
It is simply a defect. Therefore, once [the fire] has been transferred to one [location], there is no re-establishment [of the fires], because it is impossible.

But the five-śarāva offering should be a substitute because of the mention of a specific substance.
Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture:
"If both sacrificial offerings of one should meet with ruin, he should offer five *śarāva*-measures of cooked rice to Indra.
In this regard, there is a doubt: is the five-portioned rice a substitute for the ruined offering?
Or is it a different rite on account of the occasion? How is it a substitute (*pratinidhi*), and how is it a different rite? If the connection is thus:
"One should offer the five-portioned oblation (*pañcaśarāva*)," one should perform it.

Thus, [it is said]: "Therefore, in the case of the *sāṃnyāya* sacrifice, the five-platter offering (*pañcaśarāva*) is the substitute. Now, it is not that the five-platter offering is connected with the act of offering (*nirvapati*), but rather it is connected with the deity.

"One should prepare a *pañcaśarāva* offering for Indra"—thus, the sacrifice is enjoined with reference to that occasion (*nimitta*). What, then, is the prima facie view? "But the *pañcaśarāva* should be a substitute (*pratinidhi*) because of the scriptural mention of a substance.
The *pañcaśarāva* is a substitute for the *sāṃnāyya*. Why? Because of the scriptural mention of a substance.
The scriptural statement [occurs] in connection with the pouring out of the substance.
Why? Because in this way the injunction for the pouring out will be established;
therein, the direct Vedic word (*śruti*) is the enjoining authority.
Otherwise, there would be a syntactical connection (*vākya*) between the substance and the deity, and that is weaker than direct statement (*śruti*). Therefore, it is a substitute (*pratinidhi*).

The Viśvajit sacrifice is prescribed as a contingent rite (*naimittika*). In this regard, there is a doubt:

does the Viśvajit apply to one who, having resolved to perform all [sacrifices], actually performs them all, or to one who does not perform them? What, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That it applies to both him who performs them and...
And [the word "no"] applies because there is no distinction. Alternatively, it applies to one who employs [it].

Why? Because it has been stated that such a thing is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the ritual action only when it serves as a cause (*nimitta*). How then could it be a constituent part for one who does not employ it?
This being the case, we reply:
But the Viśvajit should take place when [the sacrifice] has not commenced;

"He shall sacrifice with the Viśvajit Atirātra"—this means that he who makes a formal resolve (*āgurate*) saying "I shall perform a sacrificial session (*satra*)," he should accomplish his purpose by means of the Viśvajit sacrifice. because both are already present.

[This is] the division. For by this sentence, "One should divide the rice into three parts," the removal of the deity is effected;

"This and this belong to it. Even for that substance for which no specific division exists, one should still divide it; this is the general division. Therefore, just as there is a division for the others, so too there is a division for the *upāṃśuyāja*. Alternatively, [the meaning is as follows:]

Āśmarathya maintains that if the moon rises before the oblation has been poured out, one should offer the *prākṛtī* [portions], because the removal occurs once the rice grains have been prepared.

It is established that the *nimitta* (the causal occasion) is merely the occurrence [of the event]. As for the *naimittika* (the ritual consequent), namely the removal of the original deity and the connection with another deity:

The teacher Āśmarathya held that one should offer from the original (*prākṛtī*) oblations when the moon has risen while the rice has not yet been poured out. Why? Next, he speaks of the division of rice. That [division] is not possible when [the grains] have not yet become rice. But Ālekhana [holds that] it belongs to those [rites] whose results pertain to the higher worlds, because the removal of the deities is caused by that [act].

The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position. The teacher Ālekhana held that one should offer [the oblation] to those deities who partake in the action after [the time has passed]. Why? Because the removal of the deity is caused by that;
for the removal of the deity is caused by the commencement of the ritual procedure at an improper time.

Therefore, since the deity has been removed, the portions should be offered to those [deities] who occupy the upper positions. Once the portions have been set aside, there is no removal of the handfuls, because they are subordinate to that [act of setting aside].

The deity belongs to the act of offering (*nirvāpa*), not to the handfuls (*muṣṭi*). And that offering has that [deity] as its recipient. Why? Because it is for the purpose of completing the number four, only a repetition (*abhyāsa*) is to be performed. And that mere repetition is performed again.

Since that offering was already performed previously, the deity was not removed. This very same act is being performed again; therefore, as it is being performed once more, it stands to reason that the deity remains unremoved. Thus, the offering must be made to the original deities. Furthermore, the subsequent handful is not a separate ritual act (*padārtha*) such that it would cause the removal of the deity. This is merely the completion of the number for the offering already performed. Therefore, there is no removal.

"Having undergone the consecration on the fifth day.

Regarding the measure of initiations, one may act according to one's desire; there is no fixed rule. Why? Because of the lack of distinction; no specific distinction is prescribed. It is that "for twelve nights, having been consecrated, one should seek the sacrificial fee" (*dvādaśa rātrīr dīkṣito bhṛtiṃ vanvīta*), which is recorded as an obligatory rule (*nityavat*).
It is not optional. One who performs that very [twelve-day rite] constantly is unable to adopt any other measure. Therefore, the twelve-day period alone should be fixed as the measure;

And [the rite is performed] because of the favor granted in the event of an offense against the initiation (dīkṣā).
They should undergo initiation on the Ekāṣṭakā;

having prescribed the initiation four days before the full moon, their purchase of the Soma is completed on the Ekāṣṭakā.

Regarding the statement, "They do not perform the Ekāṣṭakā in a superficial manner," this indicates that by taking the Ekāṣṭakā— which has fallen away from the period of initiation (*dīkṣā*)— through the act of purchase (*kraya*), one demonstrates authority over the full moon day of Māgha. May she whom people greet with joy as the night approaches like a cow coming home,
she who is the consort of the year— may she be auspicious to us.
With the words, "Svāhā to Aṣṭakā,
the giver of wealth," he indicates that very eighth day of the month of Māgha as the Ekāṣṭakā.
NOTES:
And because it grows again upon being cut down. (MS 6.5.36)
And he shows the subsequent growth following the rising [of the sun]: "When they rise, the herbs and the trees rise after them.
Thus, he shows the rising in spring; for it is in that season that the herbs and the trees rise. Therefore, she too is restricted by that [season].
And in this [verse], all the characteristic marks are present. (MS 6.5.37) *{6/213: Tait.S. 7.4.8.3}*
"Those who undergo initiation on the Ekāṣṭakā day undergo initiation for the sake of one who is afflicted during the year.
As for those who are afflicted at that time:
That time is afflicted; they are afflicted by the cold. Therefore, the eighth day of the month of Māgha is called *ekāṣṭakā*. Likewise, it is said:
"Those who undergo initiation on the *ekāṣṭakā* undergo initiation at the end of the year. By the word "end" (*vyasta*), the turning of the solstice is meant. And so, too:

Regarding the statement, "They descend for the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) without rejoicing in the waters," those who have been consecrated (*dīkṣita*) on the full moon of Caitra should descend while rejoicing. Therefore, it is also the full moon of Māgha.
Because the time for initiation remains, there is no postponement of the obligatory rites even upon its lapse, since their time has already arrived.
This is heard [in scripture]:
"Therefore, one who is consecrated does not give, nor does he cook."
They recite in the Jyotiṣṭoma: "He does not offer. However, if by force of divine or human circumstances the time for initiation is postponed, [the rule applies].

In this regard, there is a doubt: is there a displacement (utkarṣa) of the giving, the oblation, and the cooking, or not? What is the prima facie view? There is no displacement, for the giving, the oblation, and the cooking are indeed fixed.

The prohibition of these [daily rites] is established by such scriptural injunctions as "One should offer the Agnihotra for as long as one lives," which prescribe the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice with all its constituent parts on specific days.

One should perform [the rites] on other days, excluding those many days [of the sacrifice]. Since they are not prohibited after the time for the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma, they should therefore be performed, for their proper time has arrived. NOTES: * *tāvanty ahāni*: "those many days" refers to the days occupied by the Jyotiṣṭoma. * *muktvā*: "excluding" or "leaving aside. * *anyeṣv ahaḥsu*: "on other days," meaning the days following the conclusion of the Jyotiṣṭoma. * *jyotiṣṭomavidhānakālāt parataḥ*: "after the time for the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma. * *apratiṣiddhāḥ*: "not prohibited"; since there is no rule forbidding them at that point, they remain obligatory. * *prāpto hi teṣāṃ kālaḥ*: "for their proper time has arrived"; this establishes the obligation to perform them.
[The texts] recite:
"There are three initiations," and so forth.
If there is a displacement [of the rites], it is due to the state of being initiated, for the reason is no different.
By the word "or" (*vā*), the position is reversed. As for what was said—that there is no such excellence—that is not so; they are indeed to be excelled.
Why? Because of his consecration;
these [acts] are prohibited for one who is consecrated, not for one who is not consecrated at that time. For in this way, there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
However, according to our view, scripture is the authority; moreover, prior to the avabhṛtha bath,
this person is indeed consecrated (dīkṣita), for the reason is no different.

Whatever [is prescribed] at the time of the injunction for the Jyotiṣṭoma, that very same applies even when it has passed. For in both cases, the state of being consecrated (dīkṣitatva) is the cause. Therefore, there is an extension (utkarṣa) of those [rites].
*{6/217: They are to be postponed}*;
in that case, no supplementary oblation (*pratihoma*) is prescribed, as was the case for the previous ones. MS_6,5.40 //

In that context, when the Jyotiṣṭoma is being extended and the oblations have not yet been performed, should the oblations be performed by counting [the days], or not? What is the prima facie view? The oblations should be performed by counting. For what reason? Because they are necessarily to be performed.

For those oblations have been prescribed for you; even if they have passed their time, they must certainly be performed. In this way, their necessity will be upheld. However, only the principal act is fixed; here, one need not adhere to the specific timing.

Because they are like the current of a river. Even though the times have passed, one should calculate those that have passed and perform only the principal duties, such as what must necessarily be done, for example, providing food and wages.
Whatever has passed away is performed after being fully enumerated;
so too is this [case].
This being the case, we say:
in that situation, there is no substitute oblation (pratihoma),
just as in the previous cases.
One should perform what ought to be done,
not what ought not to be done; and these [actions] are not to be performed,
because they are prohibited.
Just as there is no compensatory oblation (*pratihoma*) for the rites of the predecessors when they have not been performed due to the lapse of time,
so it is also for these [rites].
And because of the predominance of time, [it applies] at the time of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. MS 6.5.41.

Furthermore, time is of primary importance, because it is heard [in the scriptures] as the causal condition (*nimitta*). In its absence, that which is prescribed simply does not come into being. Even if only the principal act were to be regulated, it would still be so in relation to the time as the condition; and that time, which is comparable to the current of a river, has already passed.
Therefore, a *pratihoma* (a remedial oblation) should not be performed.
This is because of the prohibition [stated] after the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), prior to the *iṣṭi*.

Regarding those oblations which occur after the *avabhṛtha* bath and before the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice, if they have been omitted due to some divine or human obstacle, a doubt arises as to whether a compensatory oblation (*pratihoma*) should be performed or not. What is the prima facie view? It should be performed.

For at that time he becomes one whose initiation has been released, since the *avabhṛtha* bath is for the purpose of releasing initiations. Therefore, they ought to have been performed; yet they were not performed.
This being the case, we reply:
from after the *avabhṛtha* bath until the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice.
For those [offerings] that have been omitted, there should be no *pratihoma*. Why? Because of the prohibition;
for there is indeed a prohibition:
"By means of this *iṣṭi* performed together with the re-establishment of the fires, one [performs] the *agnihotra*..."
"One must offer," [this refers to] the prohibition of the oblation prior to the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice; as long as the *udavasānīyā* is postponed, [the prohibition remains].

This is a prohibition; thus is the direct scriptural statement (śruti), otherwise there would be figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). Therefore, they are not to be performed, and thus they were not performed.
"There would be no *pratihoma*.
NOTES:
If there is a compensatory offering (*pratihoma*) after having sacrificed for the sake of measuring the receptacle, the evening *agnihotra* and the subsequent offerings should be performed.

Regarding these very examples, a doubt arises: in the case of a re-offering (*pratihoma*), should the rites begin with the evening *agnihotra* and so forth, or with the morning *agnihotra* and so forth? Now, it has already been established that there is no such thing as a re-offering at all. It is replied: we are considering this on the assumption that there is one. This is a hypothetical consideration (*kṛtvā-cintā*).

It is considered whether there is a purpose for this [rule] in other similar principles and examples. What is the prima facie view? There is no fixed rule, because it is established by the purpose. This being the case, we reply:
If a compensatory oblation (*pratihoma*) is performed, the evening *agnihotra* and the subsequent rites should be offered. Why?
Because the rites were omitted starting from the evening *agnihotra*.
"In that very same sequence, they are to be offered."
The evening *agnihotra* and the subsequent offerings should not be performed. Why? Because [they are performed] in the morning at the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice. (MS 6.5.44)

When the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice has been established and the *soma* offerings have been completed, a doubt arises regarding the evening *agnihotra*: should it be performed [with the *soma* remnants] or with the regular evening *agnihotra*?
Now, regarding the phrase "or in the morning": what is the prima facie position? It was stated in the preceding section that [the rite] is performed with the evening *agnihotra*;
thus, it follows as a general rule that this applies everywhere. To the one who has reached that conclusion, the following is said:

But in the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, since the morning *agnihotra* and other rites have been passed over when the *ṣoḍaśin* is performed, they should be commenced starting from the very morning *agnihotra*.

[In the case] of the Jyotiṣṭoma, when [the offerings] have been omitted, should one perform the Agnihotra, or should one perform the morning Agnihotra? [The answer is: There is an expiation (prāyaścitta) because the fault is common to all cases within the scope of the ritual injunction.

In connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "One offers when [the vessel] is broken; one offers when [the grain] has spilled. In this regard, does this expiation apply only to the breaking and spilling occurring during the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices themselves, or to wherever [a vessel] might break or [grain] might spill? What is the prima facie view? [720] {6/}
Whatever penance of this kind has arisen in this context, it shall apply everywhere, wherever [the substance] is split or spilled. Why? Because the fault is common.

The cause is the same—whether it be spilling or breaking—and that alone is intended here as the fault. Due to the context (*prakaraṇa*), this expiation (*prāyaścitta*) would apply to the New and Full Moon sacrifices;
however, due to the direct statement (*vākya*), it applies elsewhere as well.
And since the direct statement is more powerful than the context, therefore the expiation applies everywhere in the case of spilling or breaking.
NOTES:
Or rather, [the word] is used in its primary sense because it is the cause of the verbal expression. (MS 6.5.46)
The expiation occurs only when the vessel is broken or spilled within the context of the ritual procedure. Why? Because of the verbal authority;

for these oblations form a single syntactical unit with that archetypal purpose. Therefore, the word "one should sacrifice" (yajeta) from the archetype is the authority for conveying the sacrifice as possessing those oblations. If this is so, it will be meaningful by way of assisting that [archetype].

Otherwise, in the absence of the sentence, one would have to postulate a result. Therefore, since the sentence is sublated precisely by the absence of a result, the context (prakaraṇa) must be upheld.
And [this applies to] that which is not a modification of it (atadvikāra).

Furthermore, neither the Agnihotra nor the Jyotiṣṭoma is a modification (*vikāra*) of those [two sacrifices]; nor is it a modification of the Darśapūrṇamāsa. If it were a modification of them, then there would also be an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in that case when [the offering] has been spilled or broken.
When that which is spoiled goes into the water, one should understand that it is something unfit for the Aryas to eat.
It is heard in the scripture: "One should cast what is spoiled into the water. To the question, "What is called 'spoiled'?", this is explained:
that which is spoiled, that is, corrupted by some action.
It is performed. What is that? That which is unfit for the Noble Ones (*ārya*), such as food contaminated by hair or insects, or otherwise defiled by some form of damage.
"That has perished.
NOTES:
*{6/230: E1,6; E2: abhidhīyate,}
Food that has fallen into hair or insects, or that has been damaged by some other form of defilement, is not to be eaten by the noble ones.
Since there is a scriptural injunction for partitioning even in the case of a child and an insect, there is no expiation when [the offenses] occur simultaneously.

231* Or, where there is a simultaneous interruption (*apaccheda*) of both the *udgātṛ* and the *pratihartṛ*, what expiation (*prāyaścitta*) should there be? Is there none? Such is the doubt that arises. What, then, is the prima facie view? There is no expiation when [the interruptions] occur simultaneously. Why? Because of the scriptural statement regarding their separate [occurrence].
They prescribe an expiation when there is a separation resulting from a disjunction; and this disjunction is a separation,
which is accomplished by both [the priests],
yet here an expiation is heard of when it is being accomplished by one.

[The expiation applies] to either the *udgātṛ* or the *pratihartr*. And that which is performed together with another does not become something performed by one alone. For if it were performed by one alone, then since it would have been accomplished by him, what could the other do? Therefore, there is no expiation for two who have been cut off simultaneously.
NOTES:

Where there is a simultaneous suspension [of both]}*
Alternatively, because the cause has been established, there may be only a single time-period. (MS 6.5.50)

Or rather, there may be an expiation even in the case of simultaneity, for the occasion [for expiation] has indeed occurred when both the Udgātṛ and the Pratihartṛ have been cut off. For where there is a cutting off of two,
both are indeed cut off.

It is both one and the other. For "severance" (*apaccheda*) is the state of being separate from that which is conjoined, and that exists in both [the agent and the object]. Severance is effected there by one even without depending on the other, and likewise by the other. However, in that case, time alone is one; and [it is not... [722] {6/}
Because of the identity of time, there is an identity of the two disconnections (*apaccheda*). Therefore, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) applies even when the disconnections occur simultaneously.

In that case, because there is a contradiction, there should be an option.
If the simultaneous disqualification of both the Udgātṛ and the Pratihartṛ occurs,
there is a doubt: is it the absence of sacrificial fees (*adakṣiṇya*), or is there an option between the giving of all one's possessions (*sarvasva*)?
[The question is: "Or is it a combination? What is the prima facie view? In that case, because of the contradiction, there should be an option (*vikalpa*). For these two options are contradictory:
giving away one's entire property and the absence of sacrificial fees (*adākṣiṇya*). Therefore, an option ought to prevail.
Or rather, there may be an option (*vikalpa*) [between the two], or else there would be a simultaneous application (*ubhayānugraha*) in another usage. (MS 6.5.52)

The word "or" (vā) sets aside the alternative position. This is not the case, namely that there is an option (*vikalpa*), because both are prescribed. Only in this way is the injunction regarding the performance (*prayogavacana*) justified as one that incorporates all constituent parts (*sarvāṅgopasaṃhārī*). For if there were an option, there would be a contradiction in one of the two cases.
Therefore, there is a combination [of the two]. Now, as for what was said—that because of contradiction there is an option—it is replied:
in another application, both may be accommodated.

Furthermore, it is stated that "one should sacrifice again. There are two performances of that [sacrifice]. In one performance, there is one ritual procedure (*kalpa*); in the other, there will be another. Thus, there is no contradiction; therefore, both are expiations (*prāyaścitta*).
Nor [is it established] from a single conjunction. (MS 6.5.53)
But this is not so. Why? Because of the single conjunction;

that very same sacrifice would have to be performed again. If it were determined that there is a deficiency (vaiguṇya) in the absence of either one [of the two], then when the entire property is given away, the sacrifice would be deficient due to the absence of the fee (adakṣiṇya). One performance being carried out does not benefit another performance.
Neither lack of courtesy nor the giving away of all one's possessions possesses primacy;
rather, an action must be connected with a performance endowed with excellence. Therefore, there is an option.
NOTES:
When two rules apply in a sequence, the earlier one is weaker, just as in the case of the original form (*prakṛti*). MS_6,5.54 //

Where there is a sequential occurrence of two disconnections, a doubt arises as to whether the expiation is for the prior cause or for the subsequent cause. What is the prima facie view? That the prior one is stronger.

When a contingent rule (*naimittika*) has been reached due to a prior interruption, it is impossible to perform that which is contrary to it. And what is impossible cannot be the subject of an instruction; there is no doubt that the prior cognition has already been attained. Therefore, another action must be performed in a way that does not contradict it. Where, then, would that [contrary rule] apply? Only where the contingency exists alone. Thus, the prior cognition [remains].
This being the case, we reply:

in a sequence of prior and posterior, there would be weakness of the former. Why? Because regarding the matter that is stated by the verb as "that which is to be done," this [subsequent element] is understood in such a way that it may be possible [to perform it].

"So be it. That [subsequent cognition] can [arise] by subverting the preceding cognition, and not otherwise. Therefore, the meaning of the word is that "this must be done after having subverted the preceding cognition.
But is this not possible even while the preceding cognition [remains]?
Whatever other contradictory cognition may arise,
that is false; for since it is unreal, it cannot be relied upon.
"This is that.
And yet, as long as that [future existence] is not yet established, the prior consciousness cannot occur. Therefore, it must remain unestablished;
but when that [existence] comes to be, [the consciousness arises].

At that time, the prior cognition arises precisely as something being sublated. Now, having been sublated, it is unable to sublate the subsequent one, just as in the case of the original (prakṛti). For even when the original is sublated by the modified (vaikṛta), this is the very reason: the modified cannot come into being without having first sublated the prior cognition.
And the archetypal (*prākṛta*) is prior, because the modified (*vaikṛta*) depends upon it;
since the modified is based on inference while the archetypal is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), the former sublates the latter.

If [it is argued that] even though it is perceptual, it would not sublate [the prior cognition] if this meaning of the verbal suffix were not as described; however, since it is impossible [to act] while the prior cognition exists, it would necessarily sublate the ordinary [cognition]. Therefore, it is indeed logical that the subsequent [cognition] possesses superior force.

If the Udgātṛ should be the last [to finish], one should give away all one's possessions (*sarvavedasa*) at a repeated sacrifice (*punaryajña*), just as in the other case.

Since it was previously stated that [the gift] is to be given,

[725] But surely even his entire property would be forbidden; thus, he might not give even that.

In a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*),
that day upon which an interruption (*apaccheda*) occurs would have to be repeated, because each ritual act is distinct.

When there occurs on some day of a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*) the interruption of the Udgātṛ, then a doubt arises: does the entire multi-day session repeat, or only that specific day? What is the prima facie view? The entire multi-day session [repeats]. Why? Because without the other days, that [interruption] [cannot be remedied].
"Therefore, he should indeed turn back to the group. This being the position reached, we reply:
in whichever [sacrifice] the interruption occurs, [that is the one to which he should return].
That very [rite] should be repeated. Why? Because of the distinctness of the actions;
these are separate actions, such that one day is not a subordinate element of another.

And by the word "having sacrificed" (*iṣṭvā*), it is understood that the sacrifice has been completed, not that it is accompanied by its constituent parts (*sāṅga*). Those other days which will assist through their cooperation certainly exist; therefore—
"Thinking that they will provide assistance, therefore that very thing would recur.
NOTES: *{6/259: E2: asau; E2 (v.l.), E1,6: tadā}*
NOTES:
In a combined performance (saṃnipāta), because there is no deficiency, those of equal ritual procedure (tulyakalpa) should sacrifice just as in the original model (prakṛti). MS_6,6.1 //

The *satras* are the examples: "At least seventeen should perform a *satra*," "Those who, knowing thus, perform a *satra*," and "Those who, knowing thus, enter upon a *satra*. Regarding this, there is a doubt.

Is there a joint entitlement for those of the same *kalpa* as well as those of different *kalpas*, or only for those of the same *kalpa*? Who, then, are those of the same *kalpa*? For the Rājanya, Atri, Badhryaśva, Vasiṣṭha, Vainya, and Śunaka, as well as the Kaṇvas, Kaśyapas, and Saṃkṛtis, the second *prayāja* is the *nārāśaṃsa*.

*Tanūnapāt* [is the deity] for the others. Thus, some have the *Nārāśaṃsa* ritual procedure (*kalpa*), while others have the *Tanūnapāt* ritual procedure. In this regard, what is the prima facie position? When many sacrificers assemble, only those who have identical ritual procedures (*tulyakalpa*) should perform the sacrificial session (*satra*) together. Why? Because of the absence of deficiency (*avaiguṇyāt*).
Otherwise, for that person whose ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is not brought to completion,
there would be a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*); just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself, there is an absence of fruit due to the lack of perfection, so it would be here as well.
NOTES:
*{6/264: E1,6; E2: tulyāḥ}* Or, because of the statement, it should be like the head. // MS_6,6.2 //
Because of the word "or," the position is reversed. It is not the case that those belonging to different *kalpas* lack qualification;
they too would be qualified. Why? Because there is no distinction.

The attainment [of the result] belongs to all sacrificers (*yajamāna*), and there is no prohibition against those who follow different ritual manuals (*kalpa*). Now, an objection is raised: "But surely there is a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) for those following different ritual manuals. To this it is replied: Because of the explicit statement, even those following different ritual manuals are included by the general declaration. In that case, there would be a sublation (*bādha*) as in the case of the "head" [sacrifice], just as, for example: [727] {6/266} ...by virtue of the scriptural injunction, even those with different ritual manuals are encompassed by the general statement. In that context, there would be a sublation, like the "head" [sacrifice], just as...
By the force of the scriptural statement, "He places the human head," even the touching of corpses' heads—which is prohibited by the Smṛti—is performed;
so it is here as well. Or else, [it is explained differently].

It will be so because of this statement, just as in the case of the *ṛtapeya* sacrifice, where, due to the injunction "he has clarified butter as his vow," when the cow used for the vow-milk is set aside, they provide another cow for the *āśira* mixture. So too shall it be here because of the statement.
NOTES: *{6/265: E1,6; E2: from where? because there is no distinction. [This applies] without distinction}* *{6/267: Tait.S. 5.2.9.2}*
Or rather, it is not so, because it is a general statement (anārabhyavāda).
This is not so, as was stated:
that those belonging to different kalpas also possess the qualification.

Only those belonging to the same ritual manual (*samānakalpa*) should be authorized. Why? Because of the absence of deficiency (*avaiguṇya*). As for what was said—that it will succeed even with deficiency because of a scriptural statement—that is not so.
Because it is an unattached statement (*anārabhyavāda*);

for that [rule] is established by virtue of the scriptural declaration, since without it being postulated, the declaration would be purposeless. For if [the rule] were made contingent upon those of different ritual procedures (*bhinnakalpa*), [it would lose its universal application].
If this were said, then the statement would be purposeless, and one would have to accept that a *sattra* sacrifice is permissible even for those of different ritual manuals (*kalpa*).

However, this is not stated with reference to those of different ritual manuals; rather, the purposefulness of this statement will apply to those of the same ritual manual. Therefore, there is no entitlement for those of different ritual manuals.
NOTES: *{6/268: E2 (v.l.): even in the case of a defect}* It may be so, because it is for the sake of the sacrifice, as in the case of the Audumbarī pillar. MS_6,6.4 //

Or rather, there may be eligibility for those belonging to different *kalpas*. Why? Because the *kalpa* exists for the sake of the sacrifice. For Vasiṣṭha and others, the *Nārāśaṃsa-kalpa* is the means of accomplishing the sacrifice; and since that sacrifice is common to all, it becomes accomplished even when performed according to another's *kalpa*.
Just as, for example:
Regarding the statement, "Having measured the Audumbarī post, they shave it," the sacrifice established by the measurement of one person becomes established for others as well.

It is argued: "But surely, by the sentence concerning the *prayāja*, there is a connection with the person; and that will sublate the fact that the *prayāja* serves the purpose of the sacrifice, which is obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*). We say: no. [Because] there is a result...

For then that [unseen force] must indeed be postulated. But surely, even otherwise, an unseen force must necessarily be postulated. To this it is replied: True, it must be postulated; however, it is by means of the authoritative injunction as a single syntactical unit that it is established, whereas in the second position, one would have to postulate an additional verbal element.
Thus, there would be syntactic unity with that [text]. Now, it might be argued:

"There will be syntactic unity with something recited elsewhere. Even so, a construction based on what is not the subject matter at hand and separated by an interval would be more cumbersome than a construction based on what is the subject matter at hand.
No, because that [the Udumbara wood] is the primary factor. MS 6.6.5. *{6/269: E2 (v.l.): for the sake of success} *{6/270: E1,6,E2 (v.l.); E2: made of Udumbara wood}.

This is not so, because that [the person] is the primary factor. For this ritual procedure has the human purpose as its goal. How so? Because for Vasiṣṭha and others, the *nārāśaṃsa* is a constituent part of the sacrifice (*yajñāṅga*). And whatever is a constituent part of someone's sacrifice, [that belongs to them].
In conjunction with that [recitation], his action becomes fruit-bearing. Thus, the connection is made in this way:
"The action accompanied by the *nārāśaṃsa* [recitation] becomes fruit-bearing."
[The mention of] the Vāsiṣṭhas and others [is merely for the sake of praise],
because the Audumbarī post exists for the sake of another, just like the potsherds.
Now, as for what was described—
that "as with the *audumbarī*, so it is here"— the *audumbarī* exists for the sake of another (*pārārthya*).
The sacrificer is mentioned as a subordinate factor (*guṇatvena*). But even there, would not the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) establish the primacy of the person? This is not a fault;

for although this [measurement] is measured by a single sacrificer, it becomes "measured by the sacrificers" for all of them. However, in the present case, when one person is included, all are not thereby included. Therefore...
The Audumbarī post exists for the sake of another,
like the potsherds;
as, for example, [in the case of the sacrificial vessels].
"Just as in the case of the injunction, 'One should scatter the husks with the sacrificial cake-pan,' where the pan—
being for the sake of another— is taken up as the instrument for scattering the husks,
so too is this [the present case]."
