If it is argued that [the cognition] is produced by something else as well; // MS_6.6.7 //

If you view it thus— that the honor belongs to the sacrificer, or rather, that it belongs to the sacrificer through the performance— then by that same logic, the honor would also accrue to whoever happens to be the sacrificer in another performance.
NOTES:
*{6/279: E1,6; E2: not by itself nor by another; E2 (v.l.): by that itself or by another}*
Because it is not one, because it lacks qualification, and because the word is indivisible. (MS 6.6.8)

To this it is replied: the sacrificer does not become attached to another performance. However, there is no specific distinction in the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) from which a restriction could arise. What then? Because singularity is intended to be expressed, the duties of the sacrificer are not to be performed by two people; therefore, no other person is brought in. He says:

"In that case, let it be someone else for all the duties of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Not so; for the statement regarding the sacrifice with its subsidiaries is made with reference to one who has a desire [for a result]. Moreover, the word 'sacrificer' here, in the context of the wiping of the *audumbarī* post, is not differentiated [from the primary sacrificer]. Therefore, there shall be no other."

But from their combination there would be a destruction of the respective causes, as in the case of the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans], because they are taught as distinct [alternatives] when performed by Vasiṣṭha.

The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position. When there are many sacrificers, there would be a failure of the occasion (*nimitta*) due to the coming together [of multiple priests]. Why? Because [the offices] are assigned by division: in a performance accomplished by a Vasiṣṭha, the *nārāśaṃsa* is the occasional [priest]; in another case, the *tanūnapāt* is the occasional [priest]. Since both are now the performers through mutual assistance, the accomplishment [of the office] does not occur by one alone. Therefore, one alone is not the performer. And if the Vasiṣṭha is not the sole performer, [then the occasion for the *nārāśaṃsa* does not arise].
Therefore, one should not perform that [action] for the sake of the former, nor for the sake of the latter; for in both cases, there would be mutual interference.
It is like the case of the Bṛhat and Rathantara;
for instance,
when it is said, "The Pṛṣṭha-stotra consists of the Bṛhat and Rathantara," it does not mean that the Bṛhat is the means of accomplishment [for the stotra].
"It does not have the *rathantara* as its means," meaning that in that case, neither the *bṛhat* nor the *rathantara* serves as the cause. It is the same here as well.
NOTES:
Or rather, because of the connection with the whole, there should be understood to be no contradiction, since the relationship is one of ownership. MS 6.6.10.
The phrase "or rather" (*api vā*) sets aside the previous position. There is a connection with the whole [of the sacrifice] through the agency of the individual alone;
therefore, there is no obstruction to the occasional rites (*naimittika*). But how is there the necessity of performing them in their entirety?
Because of the connection by way of ownership (*svāmitva*).

With respect to action, there is a connection with Vasiṣṭha and others alone by virtue of their ownership; action is beneficial to persons, for it is capable of producing the fruit for each individual. Therefore, since each one is the agent of the whole, all that [result] which is occasioned by the action accrues to him. It is as if [one says]: "Let it be given to the tip of the mouth."

Thus it is said. Even though she is the mother of both Tuṇḍa and Piṭṭha, nevertheless [the offering] is given to her; for she is his mother in its entirety. Maternity is not something that is distributed [partially]. It should be understood in the same way here as well. Therefore, those who do not follow the same ritual manual (*kalpa*) have no entitlement [to participate].

When there is a connection with a part [of the chant] due to the increase of the ritual action (*karma*) of the two *sāmans*, there is a relationship as a subordinate element (*guṇa*); therefore, in that case, there would be an obstruction. MS 6.6.11.

Now, as for what was said—that it is "like the Bṛhat and Rathantara"—that must be refuted. In the case of the two Sāmans, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara, there is a connection with a portion [of the rite] through the increase of the occasional (naimittika) action; for in that case, both are the means of accomplishment, not just one. [This applies] by means of a portion of the Stotra.

However, in that case, the connection is with the two *sāmans*, not with the entire *stotra*; for there the *sāman* is heard as a subordinate element (*guṇa*), while the *stotra* is the primary element (*pradhāna*). Therefore, in that instance, there would be an obstruction.
But because of the scriptural statement, there is a twofold conjunction; therefore, one [hand] possesses the nature of a hand.
They prescribe this:
"By this, a king and his domestic priest, desiring union, should sacrifice. In this regard, there is a doubt: should two domestic priests of the king perform the sacrifice?

"Or rather, [the compound refers to] the king and the domestic priest. What is the prima facie view? That there are two domestic priests for the king. Why? Because the dual number is heard after the word *purohita*; that [dual number] is able to express duality of the referent of that word. And by direct statement (*śruti*), it is the domestic priest who is denoted by that word, not the king. The word *purohita* denotes the domestic priest. [If one were to argue that it denotes both] through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in a simultaneous expression of the substratum, [that would be incorrect].

For that is indeed the case. But surely there cannot be two domestic priests (*purohita*) for one person; since the singular number is intended for the *purohita* being enjoined by the rule "one should choose a *purohita*," it must be one. It is replied: this will come about through the force of the scriptural statement. For what scriptural statement would not effect such a thing? By that very reason, there shall be two.

Just as in the case of the injunction "one offers with speech and with joined palms," there are two hands for a single person— even though the left hand is not [explicitly] prescribed, it is nonetheless [included].
"But because of the non-existence of the object, it could not be so, [even] if the left [hand] has not reached [it]. (MS 6.6.13)
By the word "but" (tu), the position is reversed.
It would not be thus that there are two domestic priests. Why? Because of the absence of purpose.
This meaning—that there are two domestic priests—is not at all the case; for it is heard in scripture that only one domestic priest is to be appointed for a single king, in the statement:
"He appoints a domestic priest."
Unity is intended to be expressed. But was it not said, "because of the word"? It is replied:
this cannot be established by the word alone, because the term *purohita* is based on a consecration (*saṃskāra*). Even if one were being appointed, he would not be a *purohita*.
NOTES:
*{6/285: E2 (v.l.): vyāvartyate}* Because meanings are distinct, there is no connection with that which is heard [in the Veda]. MS_6.6.14 //
Furthermore, the distinction between the objects [of the rites] is heard in scripture:

there is a praise of *tejas* for the Brāhmaṇa, and a praise of *vīrya* for the Rājanya. By these two castes, their connection with those respective fruits is restated. Therefore, for this reason as well, there are not two domestic priests (*purohita*).

NOTES: *{6/286: E1,6; E2: "The two domestic priests belong to one king."} Because the hand is a subordinate part [of the body], it would be understood that there is no connection [between the two priests]. MS_6,6.15 //
Now, as for what was said—
that for this very reason a single person has two hands— that is appropriate there,
because the hand is a subordinate limb (pratyaṅga).

The right hand itself constitutes the counterpart to the left hand in the *añjali* gesture; without that [left hand], there would simply be no *añjali*. Indeed, an *añjali* is not said to be formed by two right hands. Therefore, there should be both a king and a domestic priest (*purohita*). But is it not the case that in that context [the term] is "king-priest" (*rājapurohita*)?
And the royal priest and the king—these two, the royal priest and the king, should perform the sacrifice. It is said in reply:

those two do not both desire union (*sāyujya*). That king has a single purpose with the priest, but the priest does not have that same purpose with another priest. For when both of them perform malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) against the king, they are called "two priests," for they are not [simply] two priests [in the ordinary sense].

"Desiring," for the word *saṃskāra* means "domestic priest" (*purohita*). [Objection: But in your view, there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). [Reply: It is said: even by way of figurative indication, linguistic usage occurs in the absence of direct denotation (*śruti*), as for example:
"He stands in the fire;
he stands in the pit. Therefore, "the king and the domestic priest" are called "the king-priest" (*rājapurohita*).
*{6/288: In the joined palms, they became the individual limbs; E2: [they became] the individual limbs in the joined palms}* *{6/289: Him}*
Sacrifices belong to all social classes without distinction.
In this context, the *satras* (sacrificial sessions) serve as the example: "Those who, knowing thus, perform the *satra*;

those who, knowing thus, enter upon the *satra*. Regarding this, there is a doubt: do the *satras* belong to all three social classes (*varṇas*), or only to Brāhmaṇas? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? The *satras* should belong to all classes.
Why? Because there is no distinction;
for no specific distinction is maintained, such as that "sacrificial sessions (satra) belong to these castes, but not to those. Therefore, all three castes have the entitlement [to perform them].
NOTES:
And because of the observation of an indicative mark. (MS 6.6.17)

And for this reason we see that there are three *satras*. Why? Because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*). What is the indicative mark? It says thus: "One should perform the *bārhadgira* as the *brahmasāman* for a Brāhmaṇa."

In the context of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), there occurs the statement: "The *rāyovājīya* for a Kṣatriya, and [the *vaiśyastoma*] for a Vaiśya. This statement is intended as an injunction regarding the *brāhma-sāman*.
In that context, the mention of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas occurs. Therefore, for this reason as well, all social classes (*varṇas*) possess the qualification [to perform the sacrifice].
The *pārthuraśma* [sāman] belongs to the Brāhmaṇas, because the other two [classes] lack the office of officiating priest (*ārtvijya*). (MS 6.6.18)
The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position. This is not the case for all three social classes (*varṇa*).
What then? It would belong to the Brāhmaṇas alone. Why? Because the other two [classes] lack the office of officiating at sacrifices (*ārtvijya*). As for the other two...

For the performance of the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) is prohibited for the two castes, the *rājanya* and the *vaiśya*. Furthermore, there is a deficiency [in the sacrifice] when one performs the *ārtvijya* oneself [without a priest].
Therefore, it should belong to the *brāhmaṇas* alone.
If it is argued that this is because of the statement: "The qualification belongs to the [three] castes" (varṇānām adhikāraḥ) with respect to the other two [Vedas]. (MS 6.6.19)

If you think thus—that a deficiency would result for the *rājanya* and the *vaiśya*—[we reply]: by virtue of the scriptural statement, they shall be the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) while being the sacrificers (*yajamāna*), according to the rule:
"Those who are the sacrificers, they are the officiating priests. But who, then, are the sacrificers? Those who [seek] the fruit therein.

Those Kṣatriyas and even those Vaiśyas who, desiring [the results], have engaged in the performance of a sacrificial session— for them the office of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is prescribed. In this regard,
it might be argued that this [office] belongs only to those Brāhmaṇas for whom the performance of the priestly duties is possible.
"For it is prohibited for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas; this injunction regarding the office of the officiating priest (*ārṭvijya*) does not apply to them. This is not so.
Just as for Brāhmaṇas who are sacrificers [the performance of the Sattra] occurs even when not explicitly prescribed by a direct injunction,

so too it ought to occur for non-Brāhmaṇas who are sacrificers solely on the basis of the authority of the scriptural statement. Therefore, even Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, when consecrated for the office of the officiating priests (*ārlijya*), may perform the Sattra.
The fruit of sovereignty belongs to the Kṣatriyas; for it is not prescribed that Brahmins may possess lordship.

This is not so. By this statement, ownership [of the fruit] is enjoined; it is enjoined that "those who desire such [results] should perform the sacrificial session," and not the office of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). If it is argued that the office of the officiating priests is enjoined by the statement "those who are the sacrificers are the officiating priests," it is replied:

That too is not correct. Why? Because this is not the way the sentence is structured here: "those who are the sacrificers" (*ye yajamānāḥ*) is the subject term (*uddeśapada*), and "the officiating priests" (*ṛtvijaḥ*) is the predicate term (*vidheyapada*). If that were the case, the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijyam*) would be enjoined as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) that effects a refinement (*saṃskāraka*) of the sacrificer.

The sacrificers are not a constituent part of the priestly functions (*ārtvijya*). In that case, these priestly functions would lack their original purpose, and a transcendental purification (*saṃskāra*) would have to be postulated; moreover, since that [purification] would pertain to the sacrificer, it would again be something unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). Therefore, the priestly ritual acts are not enjoined for those who are already sacrificers. What then? It is the non-delegation of the performance of the priestly acts to anyone other than [the priests themselves]. And this is the explicit form of the statement:
"Ṛtvijas" is the term of reference (uddeśapada). "They" is what is prescribed (vidhīyate): those who are the sacrificers (yajamānas) are themselves the officiating priests (ṛtvijas), and no others.

In the ritual acts belonging to the officiating priests (*ārtvija*), the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) are prescribed as the agents by way of substitution; consequently, others are excluded. This being the case, the ritual acts of the officiating priests retain their original purpose (*prākṛta-prayojana*).

It is not the case that an unseen refinement (*adṛṣṭa-saṃskāra*) of the sacrificer is being prescribed. Even if one were to assume the sacrificer as the agent of these acts, there would still be an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*).
If it were to be so postulated, we reply:

even in the other view, one must necessarily postulate that this unseen refinement (*adṛṣṭa-saṃskāra*) has the sacrificer as its object. And a defect that applies to both sides cannot be charged against only one.
NOTES:
{6/297: E1,6; E2: uddeśyapadam} They may belong to the Gārhapata fire, because there is no prohibition. MS_6,6.21 //

The Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya will be eligible for the duties pertaining to the householder (*gārhapata*), and there is no requirement for officiating priests (*ārtvija*) therein. Therefore, there is no prohibition against them [performing those duties].
NOTES:
*{6/299: E2 (v.l.): at the Gārhapatya fire} *{6/300: E2 (v.l.): at the Gārhapatya fire}
Or rather, it is not [the case], because it contradicts the ritual manual (kalpa). MS_6.6.22.

And this is not the case, that the two— the Rājanya and the Vaiśya— should [participate] in the ritual act belonging to the Gārhapatya; for there would be a contradiction with the ritual manual (kalpa),
as according to some, the sacrificer’s cup consists of Soma.
According to some [teachers]: likewise,
the *brahmasāman* is the *bārhadgira* for the Brāhmaṇas,
while it is the *pārthuraśma* for the Rājanyas.
The Rāyovājīya belongs to the Vaiśyas. Therefore, even this [notion] that "the establishment [of the fires] takes place in the Gārhapatya" does not exist.
*Notes:
{6/301: E1,6; E2: phalacamasamaya}*
Because of the ownership [of the sacrificer], there is the observation of an indicative mark regarding the others in the Ahīna sacrifice.
Now, as for what was stated—that it is because of the observation of an indicative mark—that must be refuted. To this it is replied:
he will refer to the *ahīna* sacrifice itself by the term *sattra*.

Since the status of being a master (*svāmitva*) is prescribed for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), therefore, because the priests possess this status, a sacrificial session (*satra*) is not possible for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. Consequently, the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*) applies to the *ahīna* sacrifice.
Or [it applies] to the Vāsiṣṭhas, because of the restriction regarding their role as the Brahman priest.
"This has been established: this sacrificial session belongs only to Brāhmaṇas, not to Rājanyas or Vaiśyas.
Now, however, this is a point of doubt:

Is it for all Brāhmaṇas, or for those of the Vasiṣṭha lineage, or for others excluding the Bhṛgus, Śunakas, and Vasiṣṭhas? What is the prima facie view? It is for all, because there is no distinction; for no specific distinction is resorted to, such as "the sacrificial session (sattra) is for these Brāhmaṇas" or "for those."
"No," [says the opponent]. "Therefore, it belongs to all.
This being the position reached, we reply:
because of the restriction of the office of Brahman to the Vāsiṣṭhas.

The sacrificial session (sattra) should belong to the Vāsiṣṭhas, not to others. Why? Because there is a restriction regarding the office of the Brahman priest: "The Brahman priest must be a Vāsiṣṭha."
Therefore, this sacrificial session (sattra) should belong to the Vāsiṣṭhas and to those who share their ritual manual (kalpa).
Or rather, because there is a counter-exception for all of them.

Or rather, the sacrificial session (*satra*) should belong to all [the officiants], because there is no distinction made. But is it not said that "one who is a descendant of Vasiṣṭha is the Brahman priest"? No, he says. It is restated again:

"Whoever should study the *stomabhāga* [text], he alone shall be the Brahman priest. If it is asked, "What is the purpose of the instruction regarding the descendant of Vasiṣṭha now?", it is for the purpose of praising the *stomabhāga*.
"One who studies the *stomabhāga* formulas is capable of performing the duties of a Vasiṣṭha even if he is not a Vasiṣṭha by birth.
Because of Viśvāmitra’s restriction regarding the office of the *hotṛ*, those of the Bhr̥gu, Śunaka, and Vasiṣṭha lineages are ineligible [for that office].
There would be no entitlement for Bhṛgu and others. Why? Because the office of the *hotṛ* priest is restricted to one belonging to the lineage of Viśvāmitra, according to the rule:
"Viśvāmitra is the *hotṛ*. Therefore, the entitlement belongs to those of the Vaiśvāmitra lineage and to those who share the same ritual manual (*kalpa*) with them.
NOTES:
Because of the ownership of the monastery, this [prohibition] would apply even to those who do not maintain sacred fires. MS_6.6.27.

The sacrificial sessions (*satra*) themselves are the examples, as in the passages: "Those who, knowing thus, perform the sacrificial session" and "Those who, knowing thus, enter upon the sacrificial session. Regarding these, there is a doubt: do they belong to those who possess the sacred fires (*sāgnīnām*) and to those who do not (*anagnīnām*)?

"Or rather, [it applies] only to those who possess the sacred fires (*sāgnīnām*). What is the prima facie view? It applies to both those with fires and those without fires. Why? Because of the sovereignty of the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*). For even a sacrificial ground belonging to another is capable of benefiting everyone.
As it is said: 'For by that [ground], success is achieved';
whether it belongs to him or to someone else, one attains success through it. Therefore, it ought to apply even to those without fires."
NOTES: *{6/304: E1,6,E2 (v.l.); E2: kratvartho}* Because it is observed in the case of the Sārasvata [sacrifice] as well. MS_6,6.28 //

And there is a scriptural observation regarding the Sārasvata sacrificial session: "Those who perform a sacrificial session without having established the sacred fires go to the heavenly world by means of others' chariots. This indicates that there is a sacrificial session for those who have not established the sacred fires; therefore, [the rule applies] to all.
Furthermore, it is because of the prescription of expiatory rites.
An expiation is prescribed:
"One whose consecrated fires have become mixed with other fires should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vivici."

It shows the expiation for the mixing of fires: it should be thus [only] when [the fires] have not been formally established (anāhita), and not otherwise. For this reason also, there are *satras* for those without fires;
because for those with fires, the *iṣṭi* must come first.
The sacrificial sessions (*satra*) belong to those who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgnī*), not to those who do not. Why? Because they must be preceded by an *iṣṭi* sacrifice;
for it is traditionally taught that the *soma* sacrifices must be preceded by an *iṣṭi*.

"Having performed the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, one should sacrifice with Soma"—this establishes that the Jyotiṣṭoma is preceded by an iṣṭi. That [requirement] is extended to the Satras through a succession of scriptural injunctions. Therefore, those [Satras] would belong to those who do not maintain the sacred fires (anagnīn).
And because it is motivated by its own purpose. (MS 6.6.31)
Furthermore, the fires are employed for one's own purpose. How so? Because of the specific verbal suffix;

for there is a specific verbal suffix [indicating the agent], namely, "one should establish the fires" (*agnīn ādadhīta*). Therefore, the accomplishment of another's purpose by means of another's fires does not occur.
"Even though the fires are for the sake of the sacrifice, [the text] also shows their combination. (MS 6.6.32)

Regarding the statement, "Those intending to offer the *sāvitra* oblations should combine [the fires]," it is understood from this that those possessing the sacred fires (*sāgnayaḥ*) perform the *satra* sacrifices. Thus, having resolved the doubt concerning the indicative mark (*liṅga*), another matter is considered in the remaining section of the discussion:
since the *juhū* and other implements are not specifically prescribed, there would be a doubt; in such a case, one should understand that there is freedom of choice (*yathākāmī*).

Are the sacrificial vessels, such as the *juhū* and others, to be taken from the possession of some specific sacrificer for the performance [of the rite], or should other, common vessels be used? What [is the correct view]?

It follows that [the ritual] must be performed by taking up whatever vessel belongs to any sacrificer whatsoever. Why? Because a sacrificer does not employ his own vessel; rather, the performance must be carried out with one's own vessel. Therefore, others should sacrifice using the vessels belonging to another.
NOTES: Regarding the doubt—*{6/306: E1,6; E2: "They are to be performed. In this doubt, it is said: What?}*—*{6/307: E1,6; E2:
"In the case of the *juhū* and other vessels, one may act according to one's desire. For whom?}*, [the answer follows].
Or rather, they may make other vessels common to all, because there is no prohibition and it is established by the sacred texts.
The phrase "or rather" (*api vā*) serves to set aside the previous position. This is not so;
for other vessels must be made that are common [to all]. Why? Because there is a contradiction;
indeed, a contradiction arises.
It may happen that those vessels have been taken up [for use]. Now, if the death of some sacrificer should occur, there would be a conflict [of rules], for it is said:
"They burn one who has maintained the sacred fires with the fires and with the sacrificial vessels."
If they were to cremate him with those [sacrificial fires],
the sacrifice of the others would be obstructed. On the other hand, if they were to complete the sacrifice with those [fires], the funeral rites for the body of the other would be neglected.
Furthermore, when other common [factors] are being adopted, nothing at all would be contradicted. Therefore, it should be done in that manner. NOTES: {6/308: There is indeed a contradiction.}
They would increase that faction;
the funeral rites for the body would be neglected.
In times of distress, the performance of expiatory rites need not be carried out in that same manner. MS 6.6.35.
Now, the refutation of the previously mentioned objection is stated: an expiation will be prescribed for our position.

How so? When those traveling or staying in a forest or wilderness experience terror due to fear of bandits or wild beasts, or if they should be overtaken by a forest fire—[in such cases, an expiation is required].

Or rather, that subject matter will be the expiation for one another. [740] {6/312} NOTES: Or, by way of the person's qualification, there may be a restriction on the agent in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), because the sacrifice has that as its quality; due to the absence [of such a restriction], there would be entitlement for others in each individual case. MS 6.6.36.
The illustrative examples are rituals characterized as the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi, the animal sacrifice, and so forth,
in which there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.

Regarding these, there is a doubt: do all three social classes have the entitlement to perform these rites, or is it the Vaiśya alone? What is the prima facie view? In this modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the performer should be restricted by the rule concerning the person. Why? Because this is a sacrifice such as the *adhvarakalpa* and others.

This [sacrifice] has number as its quality. And since this number is stated for the Vaiśya, only the Vaiśya is capable of performing this ritual in its entirety. This ritual has seventeen as its quality;

and that state of having seventeen [components], if performed by one who is not a Vaiśya, is improper. For that [number] is not enjoined with respect to others. Therefore, because of the lack of capacity [implied by the rule] "one should sacrifice," it will not entitle Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas [to perform it].
NOTES: *{6/313: E1,6; E2: adhvarakalpā}* *{6/314:
E1,6; E2: kutaḥ. Because the sacrifice possesses those qualities. The sacrifice}*
"Because of the indicative mark [in the text], 'One should recite seventeen for a Vaiśya,' which was stated regarding the Vaiśya, it is like a specific sacrifice. (MS 6.6.37)
And there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*),
namely that for a Vaiśya there is a group of seventeen;
for the Vaiśya is indeed seventeenfold.
Thus [it is said]. Therefore, for the Vaiśya there is the number seventeen. Hence, such are the duties of the Vaiśya; just as there is a specific sacrifice belonging to the Vaiśya.
"A Vaiśya should sacrifice with the Vaiśyastoma," because of the connection with the Vaiśya; likewise, the number seventeen belongs to him alone.
"The Vaiśya is indeed the seventeenth" [MS 6.6.37];
"not for one who is not a Vaiśya" [MS 6.6.38].

Or rather, it is not so, because of the distinctness of the connection (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*); since the subordinate quality (*guṇa*) has the sacrifice as its primary purpose, the injunction is indeed unconnected [to that status].
And this is not the case; these two conjunctions are distinct:
one sentence is "He should recite seventeen for the Vaiśya," while another sentence is "In the Adhvarakalpa and other rites, he should recite seventeen."
And that quality has sacrifice as its primary purpose;
it is not that sacrifice exists for the sake of the quality. What follows from this?
If this is so, then wherever there is sacrifice, it must be accompanied by that quality; but it is not the case that wherever there is a quality, there is sacrifice.
In that context, there is sacrifice;

for the Vaiśya as well, sacrifice occurs in accordance with his specific qualities. Sacrifice belongs to the three social classes (*varṇas*). Since that [sacrifice] requires a quality, there is also another injunction regarding that which has become subordinate to sacrifice.

That [text] is not connected with the Vaiśya; rather, it conveys a quality that excludes the Vaiśya. If it is argued that it first includes the Vaiśya, we say no, because the Vaiśya is the primary subject. There, the Vaiśya is heard as the principal figure. Therefore, there is eligibility for all [classes].
NOTES:
Moreover,
that which is another injunction regarding the quality [of the sacrifice] would be specifically restricted by virtue of being a quality of that sacrifice. (MS 6.6.39)
Now, as for what was said—
that it is just as in the Vaiśyastoma,
so it is here too— that is appropriate in that case.
Sacrifice is indeed prescribed for the Vaiśya. In that case, it should be restricted by the specific rule explicitly stated in the text. Therefore, there is no fault in that regard.
{MS 6.7.1: In the giving of one's own [gift], everything [is included] because there is no distinction.}
Regarding this, they prescribe for the Viśvajit sacrifice:
"He gives away his entire property. In this regard, there is a doubt: does "entire property" refer to whatever is denoted by the word *sva* (property)?

Just as [the gift of] a mother or father, so too everything else should be given; or rather, only that which is designated by the word "one's own" (*sva*) through the connection with ownership should be given. What is the conclusion? Because there is no distinction, even a mother, a father, and so forth, should be given. But is it not said that "giving" is the cessation of one's own ownership (*svatva*)?
And [giving] consists in the transfer of ownership to another. In that regard, it is impossible to remove the ownership of the father and others; for in no way does a father cease to be a father.

It is replied: True, he does not cease to be a father; however, he can be made subject to the authority of another, and giving (*dāna*) is the act of transferring ownership to another. This follows from the sense of the matter.
And there is the relinquishment of one's own ownership. Therefore, everything is to be given. (NOTES: *{6/322:
E1,6,E2 (v.l.); E2: api tat sarvaṃ}*)

Or rather, [the suffix] occurs after that which one is the master (*prabhu*) of, because [giving] anything else would be impossible; for the meaning of the root *dā* is "to give" (*dadāti*), and [the object] must be something that has a purpose (*artha*). (MS 6.7.2)

By the word "or" (vā), the position is reversed. That which possesses ownership by virtue of being subject to one's authority is alone to be given, and not anything else. Why? Because that which is subject to one's authority is possible [to give], whereas the other is impossible. For it is not possible to relinquish one's ownership of one's father and so forth.
But was it not said that making [the property] subject to another's control is possible? It is replied:

here, "everything" refers to one's own property that is being given while one possesses sovereignty. There is no giving of one's own property when one lacks sovereignty, and this [latter case] is not logical.

That which consists in the state of being an attendant to one's father and others; and whoever it may be for whom this is even appropriate, he might indeed give it. Here [the opponent] says: But surely, where the word "one's own" (*sva*) occurs...

When it is said, "that is to be given," fathers and so forth are understood as being the things to be given. Therefore, one should strive for mastery over them even by setting aside the *smṛti* (tradition). To this, it is replied: this word *sva* denotes each of one's own wealth and kinsmen individually, not the collection as a whole. In that regard, when mastery over one's own wealth has been achieved, the purpose of the scripture has been fulfilled;
however, this does not apply to kinsmen who are impossible [to control].

The totality (*sarvatā*) must be conceptualized, nor should the traditional rule (*smṛti*) be subverted. Furthermore, when the [animals] belonging to oneself, such as cows and so forth, are obtained through the *codaka*, the totality residing in those belonging to oneself must necessarily be adopted. And once that has been adopted, the purpose of the teaching is fulfilled; thus, [the animals] belonging to one's kin are also included.
There is no reason [for this],
therefore fathers and others are not to be given away. Consequently, wherever ownership exists by virtue of authority, [that person is the owner].
That alone is what should be given.
NOTES:
*{6/325: E2 (v.l.): not [to be given] among kinsmen who are incapable [of receiving it]}*
The mother, father, and so forth would not be the [basis], because they are indistinguishable with respect to all [sentient beings]. (MS 6.7.3)
In this very context, there is a doubt regarding all forms of giving:

should land be given, or not? What, then, is intended here by "land"? It is that globular mass of earth which is composed of clay and is not contained within other substances. Not [that which is...]*6/6.

"Is it merely the field or the soil? What is the conclusion reached here? It should be given without distinction, for the word 'one's own' (*sva*) applies there by virtue of the connection with ownership, and one's own property can be relinquished through a mental act. This being the position reached, we reply:
"The earth is not given. Why? Because humans are seen as the lords of specific fields, not of the entire terrestrial globe.
He says: "Whoever is now a sovereign of the whole earth..."

"In that case, he will give it. We say: "He too will not. Why? Because whatever enjoyment the sovereign ruler possesses over the earth, another possesses to the same extent; there is no distinction in that regard.
But in his status as a sovereign ruler (*sārvabhauma*), this is additional:
namely, that he provides protection for the rice and other crops produced upon the earth.
He has authority over some portion that has been enjoyed, but not over the land itself. And as for those humans who have enjoyed it,
they [have authority] over everything else, such as the sustaining and traversing of all living beings.

Regarding that which is established upon a specific level (*bhūmi*), there is no distinction whatsoever with respect to mastery (*īśitva*) therein. Therefore, the level itself should not be given away.
*{6/327: E1,6,E2 (v.l.); E2: called the "earth-globe," not}* *{6/328: E1,6,E2 (v.l.); E2: by its own nature}* *{6/329:
E1,6,E2 (v.l.); E2: by the enjoyment of the earth}*

And because it is not something to be produced (*akāryatva*), there would therefore be a further distinction [between the two], such as its being universal (*sārvabhauma*) and its being maintained through movement and so forth (*dhāraṇa-cakramaṇādi*). (MS 6.7.4)

Regarding the Viśvajit sacrifice itself, there is a doubt: should horses and other such items be given, or not? What is the prima facie view? Since everything has been prescribed [as the sacrificial fee], the horses should be given. This being the position, we reply:
And for whom giving is improper, that should not be given, such as in the case of horses; for giving them is improper. This indeed is the specific characteristic of horses.

Regarding other substances, their giving is prohibited; for it is specifically recited in the context of the Viśvajit sacrifice: "One does not give a maned horse, nor does one accept that which has two rows of teeth. Therefore, horses are not to be given.
And because it is eternal, there is no connection with things that are impermanent.

Regarding the Viśvajit sacrifice itself, there is a doubt concerning the injunction "he gives away his entire property" (*sarvasvam dadāti*): does this mean all the implements a person has already acquired, or as many as he is capable of acquiring?
Should he give all those things, such as prepared vessels and so forth,
or rather only those which he actually possesses—
all of those should be given?
"Those that do not exist are not to be performed. From where does this doubt arise? Because both modes of expression are possible; for instance, if the statement is expressed in this way:
"all those which are one's own..."
It is prescribed that one should give all those things which are beneficial to a person, such as beds and so forth; or rather, whatever things of one's own are capable of being given to a person.

The phrase "all of them" prescribes totality. If giving were being prescribed, then there would be giving even of those things not previously intended for gift, such as finished vessels; however, if totality is being prescribed, then it applies only to those things that are already present.

What, then, is the conclusion? Prepared vessels should be given; for in that case, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) regarding the method of giving is upheld, whereas otherwise, it would be a mere syntactical sentence (*vākya*). And between these two, the direct statement is more authoritative. Therefore, prepared vessels should be given.
This being the case, we reply:
because [the Veda] is eternal, there can be no connection with non-eternal things; the word "ca" (and) is used for the sake of reference. It has been stated that "horses should not be given."

And "finished articles" (kṛtabhāṇḍaka) are not to be given. For in the Viśvajit sacrifice, the giving that is constant is restated as being obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction). Finished articles, however, are non-constant; it is impossible to bring all of them together when the Viśvajit is being performed. In that case, there might be giving of finished articles, but it would not be constant; and yet, that [giving] is enjoined by the *codaka* as something constant.
It is not by way of connection with the indicative mark (*nimitta*). Therefore, this must necessarily be accepted:
that the *sākalpya* is prescribed for those gifts that have been obtained; and when a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is impossible, the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) must indeed be adopted.
Therefore, finished articles should not be given.
[In] all respects [one should give];
[regarding] "made vessels," [it is said]:
"In the Viśvajit sacrifice, one should expect a gift; therefore, it is not occasional."
And the Śūdra [is excluded] because he is not part of the Dharmaśāstra.
Regarding the Viśvajit sacrifice itself, a doubt arises:
should a Śūdra servant be given as a gift, or not? What is the prima facie view? That everything belonging to oneself [should be given].
"Because it is prescribed, it should be given.
This being the position reached, we reply:
"And a Śūdra should not be given"—this is a supplementary injunction (*anvādeśa*). Why? Because it is a treatise on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*).

In this way, when he has been offered to that member of the three higher castes, he will, by serving him, be bound to him through righteousness (*dharma*). Even if he does not wish to be given to another, [the giver] has no power over him if he is unwilling, nor should he be taken by force. However, one who should take him by unjust means—
He might even give it away; however, it cannot be given away merely by the act of offering it as a religious gift (*dharmopanatamātra*).
*Note:
{6/338: E2 (v.l.): of his entire property}*

At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), whatever belongs to oneself should be recognized [as the object of giving], because it is connected with the act of giving, as established by the teaching of the Dharma.

In the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice itself, there is a doubt: must that which exists prior to the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) necessarily be set aside at the time of the fee, and must that which will exist after the time of the fee— even if it is not yet present— also be given at the time of the fee?

Or rather, only that which exists at the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given. What is the prima facie view? Even that over which one's ownership existed both before and after [the time of the fee] should be given.
Since the rule for giving applies to one's own property, this being the case, we say: at the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), whatever property exists [at that moment],
that alone is to be given.
It is not that which exists before or after. Why? Because here, having referred back (*anūdya*) the giving of one's own property, its completeness (*sākalya*) is enjoined.

And since that giving is already established at the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇākāla*), it is referred back at that very time. Therefore, only what is present at the time of the sacrificial fee is to be given.
It should be prescribed that [the gift] be given at the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*),
because it is not otherwise complete; for the ritual act reaches its conclusion through the accomplishment of the material substance.
Regarding that very Viśvajit sacrifice, there is a doubt: should the Viśvajit be abandoned at the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) itself, or not?
Or [should it be performed] with everything?

"It must be given; it must be brought to completion. What is the conclusion? It should be relinquished. Why? Because there is nothing remaining. How is there no remainder? In the Viśvajit sacrifice, one gives away "all one's property," and it is impossible to complete [the rite] without material substance.
Therefore, that [substance] should constitute the end [of the ritual].
NOTES:
*{6/343: Because it is without remainder, it is the end}* *{6/344: Because it is established as a substance}*
[Objection: Even in the Viśvajit sacrifice, after having given away all one's possessions (*sarvasva*),
there should still be a remainder of the ritual action (*śeṣakarma*), because it is directly enjoined for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratoḥ pratyakṣaśiṣṭatvāt*).
The phrase "or rather" (api vā) serves to set aside the previous position. There may be a remaining ritual act;
at the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one's entire property need not be given, but only as much as is required to complete that act.
It should be left over for that long. Why? Because the sacrifice is directly enjoined [to be completed]. The completion of the sacrifice is directly enjoined;
having begun with "One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," the meaning is that one should complete it. By one who completes it, whatever can be given—
The meaning is "all [of that]"; therefore, one must not abandon it until the end. And thus there is a scriptural indication of another purpose.
And by taking it in this way, the observation of another purpose becomes logical;
for the statement, "Having emerged from the *avabhṛtha* bath, he covers himself with a calf-skin," is only possible if there is a remainder.
However, if there were no remainder, the subsequent ritual acts would be rendered inconsistent due to the complete consumption [of the substance].

The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position. This is consistent with reason: that which is understood in its entirety, such that the expression "he gives away his entire property" becomes logically appropriate. As for the claim that the completion [of the act] is perceptible, to that we reply:
"It will be through grasping that the remaining karma will come to be. It is said in reply:
No, because grasping is not eternal.
The taking up [of the substance] is non-permanent, whereas the remaining rite is permanent; for a connection between these two is not logically possible. Therefore, something must be left over.
But because of the specific assignment during the initiations, there is a connection with that which is not for the sake of the sacrifice; therefore, there would be no contradiction.

The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position. It is not the case that something must remain as a residue; rather, the specific assignment occurs during the initiations within the archetype itself, namely the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. That [assignment] is obtained here by means of the extended application (*codaka*).
"This is for the sake of the ritual," "this is for the sake of consumption," and "this is for the sake of propitiation. Now, in this context, that which is to be given for the sake of propitiation—

This modification of it is called "universality" (*sarvatā*). Why is this so? Because the statement "he gives his own" is restated (*anūdyate*) and then enjoined (*vidhīyate*). Therefore, what is enjoined is not the giving of that which ought not to be given, nor for the purpose of eating.
And that which is for the sake of the sacrifice must be given. Therefore, there will be no contradiction.
(Note:
*This is for the sake of my sacrifice.*)
*{6/349: E2 (v.l.): the state of being all}* *{6/350: E1,6; E2: for the sake of eating; E2 (v.l.):
for the sake of liberation}*
And in the case of a multi-day sacrificial session (ahargaṇa), that [single-day] rule should apply, because there is no distinction among all [the days].
There is an eight-night sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*).
Now, regarding this eight-night session: on both sides are the one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*) of Viśvajit and Abhijit;
in the middle is a six-night period (*ṣaḍaha*) with light on both ends.

"One desiring cattle should indeed sacrifice with this. In this regard, there is a doubt: should the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consist of one's entire property even for that [Viśvajit] which occurs as part of a multi-day session (*ahargaṇa*), or should it be one hundred and twelve? What is the prima facie view? It should be one's entire property. Why? Because there is no distinction among all Viśvajits. Whatever is the characteristic (*dharma*) of the Viśvajit in its original form (*prakṛti*), [that applies here].
And that very [gift] shall be his by virtue of the injunction (*codaka*). Therefore, "the entire property is to be given.
(NOTES:
*dakṣiṇāḥ*)
Or else, one hundred and twelve [stomas] are used, as in the case of the natural state.

"Or rather, one hundred and twelve [cows] should be given. [The opponent argues: "It should be performed according to the archetype (*prakṛti*); and the Jyotiṣṭoma is the archetype. The ritual properties (*dharma*) are prescribed therein, but they are not perceived in their entirety in the Viśvajit. Therefore, one hundred and twelve [cows] should be given here. [The Siddhāntin replies: "But this cannot be so, because it does not possess those qualities (*atadguṇatvāt*)."
The word *tu* (but) sets aside the previous position. It cannot be thus. Why?

Because the quality of one hundred and twelve [cows] does not belong to the Viśvajit sacrifice. For here, the adoption of the ritual details (*dharma*) occurs by means of the name. Therefore, it will belong to the Viśvajit, and not to the Jyotiṣṭoma.
NOTES: *{6/353: E1,6; E2: naiṣa}* *{6/354: E1,6,E2 (v.l.); E2: grahīṣyati}*
And because of the observation of an indicative mark. (MS 6.7.17)
An indicative mark (*liṅga*) also demonstrates this. What is the indicative mark? It is as follows:

"He who does not give everything in the Viśvajit is deprived of his cattle. This shows that the giving of one's entire property (*sarvasvadāna*) is mandatory in the case of a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*).
NOTES:
*{6/355: E1,6,E2 (v.l.); E2: sarvasvaṃ}* Being a modification, it is [the same] on both sides because there is no distinction. MS_6,7.18 //
"In the Viśvajit sacrifice, one gives away all one's possessions. Regarding this, there arises a point of doubt:
does this apply to one who possesses more than twelve hundred [cows], or even less?

Does the entitlement to the Viśvajit sacrifice belong to that person as well, or only to one who possesses the full amount or more? What is the prima facie view? Since it is a modification (*vikāra*), there is no distinction between the two cases; no specific qualification is relied upon, such as "one who has one hundred and twelve [cows] or less. Therefore, the entitlement to the Viśvajit belongs to everyone.

"Regarding the term *kriyā*: in this way, the statement will be meaningful. Mere talk is useless, whereas this [term] possesses the capacity for injunction (*vidhi*). Therefore, there is an injunction regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) entities."
This [is the rule] for all [cases] without distinction, because it applies equally to everyone, including those who have not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*).
He said: "This is understood as an injunction. As for the statement, "of those that are not subsidiary to a sacrifice," that is not so.

[This rule applies] to all *caturhotṛ* oblations, whether they are subsidiary to a sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*) or not subsidiary to a sacrifice. Why? Because there is no distinction; it is not stated that this rule pertains only to those subsidiary to a sacrifice and not to those not subsidiary to a sacrifice. Therefore, it applies to all.

NOTES: *{6/417: E1,6,E2 (v.l.); E2: because there is no distinction. This is the rule for the Caturhotṛ formulas.} *{6/418: E1,6; E2: there is no distinction between those that are remnants of a sacrifice and those that are not. Therefore...}
Alternatively, because of the absence of the ritual (*kratu*), there is a designation of all beings for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*).

The phrase "or rather" (*api vā*) serves to set aside the previous position. This rule applies only to those acts that are not subsidiary to a sacrifice (*akratuśeṣāṇām*), and not to those that are subsidiary to a sacrifice (*kratūśeṣāṇām*). Why? Because for one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgneḥ*), there is an absence of sacrifices. Indeed, no sacrifices exist for one who has not established the fires. Furthermore, a subsidiary part of a sacrifice employed in isolation could not serve any purpose; nor can any other fruit be postulated for it.

Because there is no authoritative means of knowledge [to that effect]. For speech has other purposes as well; moreover, it is not possible to assume a ritual (*kratu*) for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) on the basis of this statement alone. Therefore, this is a duty (*dharma*) for those [acts] which are not subsidiary parts of a ritual.
Or else, a fruit might be postulated for this [recitation] because it is a recitation that lacks connection with fire. (MS 6.8.6)

By the word "or" (*vā*), the position is reversed. Such oblations as these would not take place in the case of fires that are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Why? Because the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is a subsidiary element for all [rituals].
But is this not a direct scriptural statement: "This [is for one] who has not established the fires"?

"It is a sacrifice. We say: no; this will be an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) like those concerning *japa*. It is an explanatory passage for those [formulas] that have the nature of *japa*, not for all the *caturhotṛ* formulas.
In this way, statements such as "one offers in the Āhavanīya fire" will possess meaningful purpose.
Regarding those [acts] which are recitations (*japa*), this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of them.

However, since it is praised as a sacrifice (*iṣṭi*), it must be a fire-oblation (*homa*), because of its connection with the fire that is not introduced for a specific purpose (*anārabhyāgni-saṃyoga*); otherwise, it would be inexpressible for the others. (MS 6.8.7)

As for what was said—that "this rite of one who has not established the sacred fires is equal to an *iṣṭi*, and this statement refers to the *japas*"—that is not so; this is not the correct interpretation of the sentence. [The correct interpretation is: "This rite which belongs to one who has not established the sacred fires is equal to an *iṣṭi*. What is the reason? A mere restatement of similarity would be purposeless. In the other case, the injunction is meaningful. As for this *iṣṭi*:
Regarding the phrase "this [is for] one who has not established the sacred fires," this is a reference to *homa*s alone because of the praise of the *iṣṭi*. How so? An *iṣṭi* is a sacrifice (*yāga*);
that very same thing is a *homa* when it includes the act of pouring. As it has been said:

"The Āhavanīya fire is for the purpose of all oblations (*homa*). This is not so; for it is stated specifically with reference to the *caturhotṛ* offerings. However, since [the rule] applies without distinction to all oblations, it will apply to others as well because it is impossible for it to apply to the *caturhotṛ* offerings [alone]. Furthermore, when the *caturhotṛ* offerings are being performed by one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), the Āhavanīya fire is not a required constituent part (*aṅga*).
NOTES:
*{6/424: E1,6; E2: na. katham. naiṣā}* [This is] like the sacrifice to the ancestors (piṭṛyajña) for both. MS_6,8.8 //
This is not so; it is not the case that the Caturhotṛ formulas belong only to one who has not established the sacred fires. They should belong to both, just as in the case of the Pitṛyajña.

Just as the Pitṛyajña belongs to both one who has established the sacred fires (āhitāgni) and one who has not, so too do the Caturhotṛ-homas. How is this understood? This has already been explained: when they are taken as a restatement (anuvāda), then they belong to the āhitāgni.

When it is the position of the injunction (*vidhipakṣa*), then [the rule applies] to one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*). In both cases, the syntactical expression (*vacanavyakti*) is understood. And a meaning that is clearly understood cannot be denied. Therefore, the *caturhotṛ* formulas belong to both.
Or rather, it is an instruction for one who has not established the sacred fires, because there is no connection with the fires mentioned without reference to a specific context.

And this is not the case, that there should be *caturhotṛ* offerings for both [the one who has established the sacred fires and the one who has not]. How so? For this is a specification regarding one who has not established the sacred fires. By the statement "this *veṣṭi* is for one who has not established the sacred fires," it is the one who has not established the sacred fires who is authorized, not the one who has established them.

This is due to the force of the specific instruction (*nirdeśa*). Furthermore, since [the injunction] is exhausted as a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), it does not contradict that very point. It has already been stated that the statement "one offers in the *āhavanīya* fire" is not spoken solely with reference to the *caturhotṛ* offerings.
Therefore, such types of oblations belong exclusively to one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*).
[The opponent says: "It exists, because it is like the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña); [the text] is a restatement of that which is already connected [to both]. MS 6.8.10.
Now, as for what was said— that it is "like the Pitṛyajña"—
that is appropriate in the case of the Pitṛyajña; for there, this statement applies again specifically to one who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni).

"Should it also be performed by one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*)? This statement—"even for one who has not established the sacred fires"—refers to the *anvāhāryaka* [offering] being performed for one who has not established the sacred fires;

however, here there is no such statement. There is only one mandatory injunction: "This is for one who has not established the sacred fires. Here, too, the word "also" (*api*) does not exist. Therefore, this is not equal to the *pitṛyajña*.
NOTES:

They prescribe this: "One should offer with three verses while bringing [the ladle]. In this regard, there is a doubt: is this oblation to be performed in fires consecrated by the rite of establishment (*ādhāna*), or...

"And regarding the unconsecrated fires. What is the prima facie position? That one should establish [the fire] while removing [it from its former place]. Why? Because of the connection with the *āhavanīya* fire in the injunction:
"One offers in the *āhavanīya*."
Because he is pleased by that which is desired by him, it is established that these oblations (*homāḥ*) take place after the time of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*).

As in the case of the Sthapati sacrifice, [the ritual] is performed according to worldly practice, because it follows the sequence of learning and action. (MS 6.8.12)

And this is not the case, that one must offer after having performed the fire-laying (*ādhāna*) of such a kind. What then? That they should proceed with the worldly fire alone. Why? Because of the sequence of knowledge and action. These oblations are for the purpose of acquiring knowledge; for one who possesses knowledge, [they follow] by virtue of capacity. Therefore, their occurrence subsequent to the fire-laying is not tenable.
As in the Sthapati-isti.
NOTES: *{6/431: E1,6,E2 (v.l.); E2: cādhānādhikāraḥ}*
And the establishment of the sacred fires is connected with [the taking of] a wife.

Furthermore, the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is heard in scripture as being connected with a wife; and the taking of a wife occurs after the acquisition of knowledge. For this reason also, the priority of the *ādhāna* is not tenable.
Moreover, there is no ritual action prior to the *ādhāna*, for its connection with ritual acts exists only subsequent to it.
To this he replies: that marriage which takes place prior to the establishment of the sacred fires will be for the sake of ritual action,
and [marriage] after the establishment of the fires is due to a specific scriptural injunction.

"It is for the sake of offspring; since it occurs at both times, there will be no such fault as in the case of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. To this it is replied: "And marriage is not a ritual act (*akarman*)."

Why? Because the conjunction with the Āhavanīya and other fires occurs through ritual acts, and there is a rule that the sacred fires must be established for one's own sake. Therefore, the taking of a wife at either of these two times is not possible.
NOTES: *{6/432: E1,6; E2: dārakriyāyā ādhānottarakāle}* If it is argued that [the rite] is like the *śrāddha* [offering]. MS_6.8.16.
It is not so, for there would be a contradiction with scripture (*śrutivipratiṣedha*).

If this rite of marriage were performed after the time of acquiring knowledge—as it is heard [in scripture]—then to say it is performed earlier is contradictory. If it is argued that this is something entirely different from that [marriage], we say no.
This restriction of time applies only to that which has already attained its purpose. And initiation is for the sake of ritual action; therefore, it would be prohibited on the second day.
Furthermore, because it serves all purposes, one should not employ it solely for the sake of a son.

Now it is argued: "Before the *ādhāna* (consecration of the fires), it is for the sake of ritual action (*karma*), and after that, it will be for the sake of offspring; thus, this being so, nothing will be contradictory for him. To this it is replied:
This is not so; for that [marriage] is for one's own benefit and does not serve the purpose of offspring alone. As it has been said:
"Because there is no difference in the zeal for the fruit. Therefore, for this reason as well, there is no taking of a second wife. Moreover, it is thus recorded in the Smṛti:

"One must not transgress in regard to duty (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*). If this were the case, there would be a transgression; therefore, one does not take a second wife. There is only one wife, for the sake of ritual action (*karman*) and offspring (*apatya*). And she is to be taken after the acquisition of sacred knowledge (*vidyā*). Therefore, these *homa* offerings are not to be performed in fires consecrated by the *ādheya* rite.
Therefore, because the attainment of a second [offspring] does not result from the drinking of Soma, one should therefore marry [again]. MS_6,8.18 //
This is accepted:
that prior to initiation there is no wife. As for what was said—that there is only one wife—that is not tolerated, according to the Smṛti.

"One should not transgress in respect of duty (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*)," and "one should not take another wife while one's current wife is endowed with both virtue and offspring. Thus, this too is indeed recorded in tradition: "In the absence of either [quality], one may take another. Therefore, for one whose wife is neither endowed with virtue nor endowed with offspring, [it is permissible].

"He should take another," he says; and he cites "because of drinking soma" as an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). By saying "the drinker of soma did not desire a second wife," he indicates that there was indeed a second wife.

But in the case of the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), it should be understood as occurring before the establishment of the sacred fires (prāgādhāna), because it is so observed [in scripture].
Now, how is it that there are two times for the *pitṛyajña*? It is said:

for a statement is seen there [in the scripture], namely, "It should be performed even by one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*). Therefore, the *pitṛyajña* takes place prior to the establishment of the fires.
The *sthapatīṣṭi* should cause the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) to be performed, like the *prayāja* offerings; and because it serves that purpose, it would conclude [the rite].
There is the Sthapati-iṣṭi sacrifice, concerning which it is said:

"One should cause a Niṣāda-Sthapati to sacrifice with this. In this regard, there is a doubt: should it be performed in fires consecrated by the *ādhāna* rite, or in worldly (unconsecrated) fires? What is the prima facie view? It should be in the consecrated fires. Why? [769] {6/}

Because of such statements as, "When one offers in the Āhavanīya fire," [it follows that the Śūdra has no Vedic revelation]. Now, it may be argued: "Since the Śūdra lacks an Āhavanīya fire, he cannot have the Śruti. To this it is replied: That [injunction] would indeed necessitate the Āhavanīya fire, just as it necessitates the Prayāja offerings even though they are not explicitly mentioned in his case. This is due to the force of the extended application (codaka). Furthermore, the fires would be extinguished because they serve that purpose; for the fires were kindled for the sake of the Sthapati-iṣṭi, and once that sacrifice is completed, they are extinguished.
[The mantras] would be discarded. For their maintenance is prescribed for the sake of a visible purpose; once that purpose has been accomplished, [the need for them] would cease to exist.
Alternatively, it may take place in the worldly fire, because the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is not a subordinate element of everything.

The phrase "or rather" (api vā) serves to set aside the previous position. [The fire] would exist in worldly fires, not in consecrated ones. Why? Because the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) is not a subsidiary part of everything. The fires are subsidiary parts of all ritual acts;

their establishment is a subsidiary part of those [fires], not a subsidiary part of the ritual acts themselves. Since there is an absence of direct scriptural statement (śruti) and so forth, the establishment of the fires is not prompted by the ritual acts.

Furthermore, by the force of the statement, [the sacrifice] is prompted by the fire; and that which is prompted by the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices is obtained through the *codaka* (extended injunction), not that which is prompted by the material. Therefore, the *sthapati-iṣṭi* is performed in worldly fires.
And likewise, the animal sacrifice for one who has broken his vow of celibacy [is not performed] because the time for the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) has not yet arrived.

There is the animal sacrifice for one who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇi-paśu*), prescribed as follows: "A student who has broken his vow of chastity shall immolate a donkey dedicated to Nirṛti. In this regard, there is a doubt:

should the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) be performed for that purpose, or should it proceed with ordinary (worldly) fires? And [the rule concerning] the animal sacrifice for one who has broken his vow of chastity...
"Like that" (*tadvat*) indicates an extension of the preceding section. Whatever was the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the previous section, that is the prima facie position here;
whatever was the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), that is the conclusion here. The installation of the fires (*ādhāna*) is for the sake of all [rituals].

Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that [the rite] applies to those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that this is because the time for the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) has not yet arrived. It has been stated that "this time for the establishment of the fires has not arrived. Therefore, this ritual action also pertains to those who use common (non-sacrificial) fires.

pūrvapak�śaḥ}* Rites for the gods are to be performed during the northern course of the sun, during the first half of the month, and on auspicious days; this is based on traditional authority (smṛti) and because other scriptural passages indicate this meaning. MS_6,8.23 //

Divine rites (*daivāni karmāṇi*) are exemplified by those beginning with the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). Regarding these, there is a doubt: should divine rites be performed at an unrestricted time, or during the northern course of the sun (*udagayana*), the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*), and on auspicious days (*puṇyāha*)?

Since the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that they may be performed at any unrestricted time, it is stated that they should be performed during the northern course of the sun and so forth. Why? Because the traditional authorities (*smṛti*) record it thus:
"At those times, [it is] the way of the gods. And there is a figurative statement regarding form: "This indeed is the form of the gods, namely the northern course (udagayana)."
"The prima facie argument is 'I am [the deity]'.

Furthermore, we do not know the form of the gods and so forth. However, since divine rites are performed at these times, it is on the basis of this connection that the mention of "form" becomes intelligible. Moreover, this sentence demonstrates another purpose.
"The forenoon belongs to the gods, midday to humans, and the afternoon to the ancestors. Therefore, rites for the gods should be performed at these times."

*By this [statement],
there is the completeness of the ritual action on the day.* MS 6.8.24.
Furthermore, there is a specific distinction regarding the day: since the entire ritual action can only be performed during the day,
one will not perform it at night.

But in the other cases, there are paternal [rites]. MS_6,8.25.
The *śrāddha* and other rites are to be performed during the latter fortnight and in the afternoon,
because of the observation of other scriptural passages that have the nature of *smṛti*.
*{6/445: E1; E2,6: pitryāṇi}* Begging and purchasing [the sacrificial materials] when they are not available, as is common in the world. MS_6,8.26.
This is recited in the Jyotiṣṭoma:
"For twelve nights, the consecrated one should seek his fee," and likewise, "He purchases the Soma. In this regard, there is a doubt: should it be sought by one who does not already possess a fee?

And for one who does not possess Soma, it must be purchased—whether it exists or not. What is the conclusion? There should be begging and purchasing even when the wealth for the fee (*bhṛti*) and the Soma are absent. Why? Because [the rule] is for the purpose of securing the substance.

Begging and purchasing are useless when [the required items] are already present; and what is stated to be useless should not be performed even if it has been prescribed. Therefore, they should occur when [the items] are absent, as is the case in the world. Just as...
In this world, one who possesses no goods begs and buys; it should be understood that the same applies here as well.
*{Either in both ways,
or even both together}* *{for the purpose of the existence of a substance}*
The act of begging for the purchase [of Soma] will thus become purposeful; therefore,
it must necessarily exist because of its purposefulness.
Alternatively, begging and purchasing must be mandatory;

that [practice] would apply whether the substance is present or absent. In this way, begging and purchasing become purposeful, for it is heard in scripture that they are enjoined as part of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
It is not contingent upon the substance; and that [sacrifice] belongs eternally to the Jyotiṣṭoma. There is no such statement as:
"When the substance is absent, then it should be performed. [772] {6/6}

Furthermore, since it has been stated that the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice has a permanent auxiliary (*nitya-aṅga*), and that the absence of a substance (*dravyābhāva*) is stated as the occasion (*nimitta*), one might suppose [the latter].
However, in such a supposition, the literal word would be contradicted. Therefore, the substance here must be employed after having been consecrated by the act of begging and purchasing.

Otherwise, there would be a deficiency. Therefore, whether the substance exists or does not exist, the purchase (*yāñcākrayaṇa*) must be performed. Now, as for what was said—that it is "like the world"—in the world, action is characterized by its purpose (*artha*), not by its verbal expression (*śabda*).
It is performed according to the actual meaning, not according to the literal word; however, in the Veda, the meaning is understood solely through the word.
It should be performed in exactly that manner. Therefore, it must be done even when [the object] is already present.

[One should offer] either gruel or curd;
furthermore, [this applies] even when [other food] is available. Likewise, he who has been sent but does not carry out the purpose of the command must be sent again.

"Or even when [the animal] is present. Likewise:

He should offer oblations with this mantra; or even another person may do so. Likewise, whoever hates anything... [773] {6/}

he should recite the mantra:

"Or rather, even one who hates and one who is not hated.

In this regard, this is an extension of the legal topic (*adhikaraṇātideśa*). Whatever was the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the preceding topic, that is the prima facie view here; whatever was the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) there [is the conclusion here].

This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) here. "One should perform [the rite] even when [the object] is not present" is the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*). "Or rather, it is restricted because it possesses purpose" is the reply. This same logic applies here that was applied previously.

He should observe the vow; he should be sent forth, or else he should strike with his feet.
"But that which is purposeless would be non-eternal. (MS 6.8.29)
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture:
"At midday or in the latter part of the night, one takes the vow. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is the vow restricted to the latter part of the night?
"And what about the indefinite [case]? What is the conclusion? It would be definite because it possesses meaning.
This being the position reached, we reply:
"But that which is indefinite would be meaningless. If one should think thus:
At this time, thinking "my vow will be digested," one should then observe the vow; but when one indeed thinks,
"it will not be properly digested," [one should act accordingly].

In that case, performing that vow would be useless. For if the sacrificer were to die due to indigestion, there would then be a failure of the ritual procedure (*tantra*); and when the ritual procedure fails, there is a total failure of everything. Therefore...
At that time, the vow is to be observed.

Because [the word] has a meaningful purpose;
otherwise, at that time, there would be the loss of the entire system. Therefore, it is not fixed.
In the injunction regarding the sacrificial animal, there is no restriction, because there is no specific qualification.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, according to the text: "When one who has been initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. Regarding this, there is a doubt: should any animal whatsoever be sacrificed, or specifically a goat? This doubt arises from the intention that will be explained later. Now, is it not the case that for some [schools] it is recited in the tradition...?

"The animal [victim] belongs to Agni and Soma. And it is held that the ritual act (*karman*) is one and the same, as evidenced across all Vedic branches (*śākhā*). To this, it is replied: this is an investigation conducted on the assumption that the rituals are distinct for each branch. What, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? There is no restriction regarding the injunction for the animal sacrifice. When the act of relinquishment (*utsarga*) is to be performed, the substance can be relinquished, but not the "animal-ness" (*paśutva*). For it is the substance that is the means of accomplishment. Therefore, since relinquishment is not possible here without a substance, a substance is employed. When that substance is being employed, there is no restriction.

"Whatever [animal] is to be released. Why is this so? Because there is no distinction. Indeed, among those things connected with the state of being an animal (*paśutva*), no specific distinction is perceived. Therefore, it refers to "whatever animal" [is available].
*Note: This is heard in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice: "He who..."*
Or rather, it is a goat, because of the wording of the mantra.

The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position. It is not the case that the animal-nature (*paśutva*) is to be employed in just any substance whatsoever. There exists a restrictive cause for what is to be offered, namely the wording of the mantra: "Recite for Agni the fat of the goat's belly."

A Vedic mantra-text capable of indicating a goat is handed down in the tradition. If the goat were not to be taken [as the victim], then the inclusion of that which is capable of indicating it would be purposeless. Therefore, it is understood that [the injunction] ordains the sacrifice with reference to the goat. Thus, there is a restrictive rule regarding the substance based on the wording of the mantra.

No, because it would contradict the Vedic injunction. (MS 6.8.32)

This is not so. A word in a mantra cannot restrict the substance when there is an opposing injunction. For where no word expressive of the substance is heard, it must be performed even without being expressed by a mantra. Therefore, a restrictive injunction regarding what is to be expressed is not inferred from the wording of the mantra, such that "in this case, only this specific thing to be expressed should be expressed. [775] {6/}

Furthermore, it is understood from the word here that [the animal] is to be manifested as "paśutva" (animal-ness). Therefore, the wording of the mantra is not capable of establishing its existence [as a goat]. For the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) regarding the performance would have to be inferred from the wording of the mantra;

however, in this case, that which is already established by the scriptural statement of performance must be integrated [into the ritual]. The meaning of the word *paśu* is simply "animal-ness," whereas the goat is restricted by the wording of the mantra. Therefore, the wording of the mantra...
It ought to be restricted without contradicting the injunction.
