*{6/501: E1,6,E2 (v.l.); E2: bhaviṹṣyati. tasmāt tatprāyavacanam}* Adhyāya 7:

[1] Since the remaining [subsidiary rites] have scripture as their authority, their performance should occur according to one's qualification when there is a distinction in the primary [rite]. MS_7.1.1.

By the first six chapters, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for rites such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), whose specific duties are directly prescribed, has been considered. Now, by the subsequent [six chapters], it is intended to consider those rites such as the sacrifice to Indra and Agni (*aindrāgna*) for which no procedure has been prescribed.
In that regard, if there are duties prescribed within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, etc.,...

They are prescribed for all ritual acts; therefore, by means of those very same properties, even the sacrifices to Indra-Agni and others are said to possess those properties and must be performed accordingly. Thus, there is no purpose for the subsequent group of six. Now, as for those [properties] which are mentioned in the context of a specific [sacrifice],...
They are stated to be right there; after that come the *adharmaka* [rites] such as the *aindrāgna* and others. Regarding them, a deliberation arises.
Do these [beings] possess the dharmas, or not? And when they do exist, which ones, how many, and how are they to be practiced? For that purpose, the subsequent six chapters should be undertaken.

In this regard, first, by the seventh [chapter], it is stated that "there are dharmas"; by the eighth, that "these belong to him"; by the ninth, that "they are to be applied in this manner"; and by the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth, that "only this many are to be applied, and no more than this. Concerning this, the following is investigated:

Are these ritual properties (dharma) enjoined by the sacrifice—meaning they are prescribed for the purpose of making the sacrifice possess its specific qualities—or are they enjoined by the *apūrva* (the unseen transcendental result)? That is, are they for the purpose of "how the *apūrva* might come to be"? If they are enjoined by the sacrifice...

3*} Therefore, all purposes [are served]. Now, if they are prompted by the *apūrva*, then they are established according to the context. What, then, is the correct view here? That they are prompted by the *apūrva*. For the *apūrva* possesses a fruit; the sacrifice itself is without fruit. And an effort being enjoined toward that which possesses a fruit becomes purposeful. Therefore...
Ritual duties (*dharma*) are prompted by the *apūrva*.

Beyond this point, the Teacher provides the scriptural citation (*sūtra*), because the remaining [elements] have scripture as their authority; thus, there should be a manifestation according to their respective functions within the primary distinction. The *apūrvas* are the primary ones, for they are the principal factors due to possessing the fruit.

And the primary term refers to the principal [action]. Their distinction has been stated through reasons such as the difference in verbal expression (*śabdāntara*). When that primary distinction exists, there would be a connection [of the subordinate elements] according to their respective spheres of application (*adhikāra*), [namely] for the remaining [elements]. Those which are taught within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the sphere of a particular *apūrva*, they would belong to that very [apūrva] alone. Because the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is the authority, this is the subordinate element of this specific *apūrva*.

In the case of the statement "this belongs to this," scripture (*śruti*) alone functions as the authority; none of the other means of knowledge, such as perception (*pratyakṣa*), does so. And by scripture, those [details] which are heard within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of a particular [rite] must belong to that very rite. An object stated for one thing cannot belong to another; for what belongs to Devadatta, such as his house or clothing, does not belong to Yajñadatta. Therefore, the determination of the ritual properties (*dharma*) is according to their respective contexts.

Because of the production of the *apūrva*. We call the *artha* (the purpose) the *apūrva*, because it is the objective of the sacrifice (*yajati*). There is no distinction between these two. Now, the word "but" (tu) serves to set aside the previous position. It is not the case that ritual duties (*dharma*) are prompted by the *apūrva*;
rather, they are prompted solely by the sacrifice (*yajati*). Why? Because there is no separation. There is no separation of the ritual duties from the sacrifice.
Some [details] are heard directly regarding the substance,
some regarding the deity,
and some regarding the mantras; and this is the sacrifice.

That substance which is relinquished by means of a mantra with reference to a deity—this is the perceptible connection of the ritual properties (*dharma*) with the sacrifice (*yajati*). However, their connection with the *apūrva* is inferential. Regarding the fruit as well, the connection of the sacrifice is heard directly in the Veda in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," whereas its connection with the *apūrva* is inferential. And the perceptible is stronger than the inferential. Therefore, the ritual properties have the sacrifice as their purpose.
But surely, because the sacrifice is transitory, it is incapable of yielding a fruit at a later time; thus, the properties performed in that regard would be ineffective.
Thus it has been stated. Against this established principle (*nyāya*), an objection is raised: "This will be like the drinking of oil.

Just as the drinking of oil or the drinking of ghee, although it is perishable, produces results such as intelligence, memory, strength, and nourishment at a later time; in the same way, the sacrifice (*yajir*) will also produce [its results]."
"What is the use of postulating something unprecedented that has neither been seen nor heard?
[And] the state of having two meanings is contradictory. (MS 7.1.6)

This being the case, all ritual elements (*dharma*) serve all purposes. Thus, since the *prayāja* offerings and other such rites exist in sacrifices such as those dedicated to Indra-Agni, their appearance in the solar (*saurya*) rite is logically consistent, as in the injunction: "At each *prayāja*, he offers a *kṛṣṇala* berry. Otherwise, one would have to enjoin both the *prayājas* themselves and the offering of the *kṛṣṇala* within them; in that case, the text would have a dual purpose.
Moreover, having two purposes is contradictory. Therefore, the ritual properties (*dharmas*) are prompted by the sacrifice (*yajati*).

This is not so;
that the ritual properties (*dharma*) are prompted by the sacrifice (*yajiprayukta*). For there would be engagement in the injunction (*codanā*). By "injunction," we mean the *apūrva*.

Because they serve the purpose of an injunction (*codanā*) and because they serve the purpose of the *apūrva*, the ritual properties (*dharmas*) are prompted by the *apūrva*. "Because they possess fruit"—this has been stated as the reason. As for the claim that the connection of the ritual properties with the sacrifice (*yajati*) is directly perceived, we reply:

because there is no injunction regarding their origin (*utpatti*). By "origin," we mean the sacrifice. There is no injunction regarding the sacrifice in its origin [to the effect] that "the ritual properties are for the sake of the sacrifice. They are merely heard and performed in relation to the sacrifice; yet, by this much alone, they do not become for its sake. It is just as when a dye is heard of in relation to a garment.
Just as one says "it dyes the cloth," yet the action is performed upon the cloth and not for the sake of the cloth itself— since it serves the purpose of the woman or the man— so too here,

the acts heard of and performed in connection with the sacrifice would be for the sake of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) in order to possess meaningfulness; and from that follows the distinction between ritual acts (*karmabheda*).

It may be so, because they have an unprecedented (apūrva) purpose. As for the fact that the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is directly perceived to have a subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) with respect to the fruit—that it does not exist without having produced the *apūrva*—this is understood through a mediated process (*praṇāḍikā*). And even by way of such a mediation, that by which [the result] is brought about [is the means].

That is the reason. For example, as when one cooks with cow-dung, the grains become cooked by the husks. As for the claim that "the fruit arises for the sacrificer just like the drinking of oil," to this we reply:

Even in the case of drinking oil, the fruit does not arise at a later time. Its fruit is the balancing of the bodily constituents (*dhātusāmya*), and that occurs at that very moment. As for the fruit consisting of strength, nourishment, and so forth, that arises from the proper digestion of food. Therefore, the comparison is unequal.
If it were perceived [directly],
it would not exist without having produced its own unseen potency (*apūrva*);
or else, like a verbal designation, it would apply to all phenomena by virtue of its generality.
Even though the *apūrva* is the motivator of the ritual duties (*dharma*), nevertheless every duty would apply, for each of those constituent elements (*padārtha*) is [motivated by it].

Because of the commonality with the designation. To begin with, the designation for these is the same: "the unprecedented" (*apūrva*). Just as there is this common designation, so too must there be a common property (*dharma*) for it, like the case of a Vāhīka.
For example, when it is said, "A Vāhīka guest has arrived;
let barley-food be prepared for him," [the word "Vāhīka" refers to a specific person, yet it functions through a shared characteristic].
Whatever Vāhīka there may be, for each of them barley-food is prepared. Or, for example, in the case of an eye disease, mung-bean rice should be eaten;
in the case of a stomach disease, milk.

"It is to be drunk. For in all cases of eye disease, rice cooked with mung beans is eaten, and even in cases of stomach disease, milk is drunk. Likewise, here too, those properties which are heard in connection with one *apūrva* ought to belong to all *apūrvas*.

Furthermore, there is a school of Vedic reciters named the Aruṇaparāśaras; among their ancillary texts, there exists a Brāhmaṇa in the form of a Smṛti [tradition] concerning those properties belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

Starting from "all those [dharmas] of the *iṣṭis* and of the *agnīṣomīya*," up to "all the archetypes (*prakṛti*) and ectype (*vikṛti*) sacrifices, including those whose end is not explicitly stated"— this enumeration indicates this very principle. Therefore, even though they are prompted by the *apūrva*, all the ritual properties (*dharma*) serve all purposes.

"But because the meaning is indivisible, it would be so in the case of denotations, since the usage is as before; because the action is to be brought about by the word, there would be no application of the remaining [auxiliaries] due to their division. To this we reply:
because the object is undivided, it would be so in the case of designations; the object is "Vāhīka-ness."

The connection with that region is indivisible; the meaning is that it is pervasive across all Vāhīkas. And the specific affection caused by that [region] is not caused by the person. How is this known? Because the usage is as before. Here, the usage is "as before."

Many Vāhīkas and non-Vāhīkas have been fed [yava-grain]. There, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is understood that this dislike for *yava*-food is caused by the region, not by the person. Therefore, it should be so in the case of designations such as "Vāhīka" and the like. Now, in this context, the action is to be brought about by the word, and not by anything else.

It is possible to know this: "Of which *apūrva* are these the properties (*dharma*)? For properties are established and understood through verbal testimony (*śabda*), and there is a distinction among the various *apūrvas*.

For it is by this logic that the systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) of the properties occurs.
Since the object is brought into being by the word, its manifestation must occur elsewhere solely through the word as determined by the context.
This is the sūtra of conclusion (*nigamana*). Conclusion is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*). This is stated as follows:

because it is thus, therefore, since the purpose—such as the placing of the firewood (*agnyanvādhāna*) and so forth—is to be accomplished through words (*śabdabhāvyatva*), [the injunction must be understood accordingly].

And because it is connected to each specific section, the existence [of the offering] would be based on the word itself in other instances. For example: "Or the Gandharvas and Apsarases drive him mad;

The injunction "he offers" (*juhoti*) refers to the teaching of the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings—which have arisen within the context of the fire-altar (*agniprakaraṇa*)—in relation to the wedding ceremony (*udvāha*). [This is seen in such texts as: "He offers these *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations; he offers the *abhyātāna* oblations. There exists this statement that the ritual properties (*dharma*) should be restricted according to their respective scopes (*yathādhikāram*). In this regard, it is first stated in the seventh [section] that the ritual properties (*dharma*) exist for the rites such as those dedicated to Indra-Agni (*aindrāgna*), and that these are established through extension (*atideśa*).

"Extension" (*atideśa*) means the application (*deśa*) of those properties which have been prescribed elsewhere, by extending them beyond that [original context] to another. For example, having established the rule for eating for Devadatta, [one applies it to others].
"Devadatta is to be fed with rice, soup, meat, and cakes"—this very rule is extended (*atidiśati*) to Yajñadatta:
"Yajñadatta is to be fed just like Devadatta. They also cite a verse:

"The established rule is that *atideśa* (extended application) is that by which a portion of the *dharma* (ritual duty) from a primary rite is applied to rites similar to it. It is the derivative (yaugika) designation for actions and formative forces (saṃskāra). Furthermore, speech is of two kinds.

[There are two types of scriptural authority: that which is directly heard (*pratyakṣa-śruta*) and that which is inferential (*ānumānika*). Of these two, the inferential will be discussed later; however, the directly heard is being considered right now.
There exists a one-day sacrifice (*aikāha*) named *iṣu*.
There is another Śyena sacrifice; both of these two are for malevolent purposes (*ābhicārika*). Having prescribed certain ritual details (*dharma*) regarding the iṣu sacrifice therein, the text says:
"The rest is the same as the Śyena. This is now considered: is this a restatement (*anuvāda*) or an injunction (*vidhi*)?
If it is an injunction...

From that, there is an extension (*atideśa*). It extends the characteristics of the *śyena* sacrifice to the *iṣu* sacrifice. Now, as for the restatement (*anuvāda*), it is not so. In this regard, what is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That is introduced by the sūtra itself.

The meaning is that the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma applies here. In this case, the Jyotiṣṭoma-related properties have arisen through the extended application (*codaka*). The Śyena also has the Jyotiṣṭoma as its predecessor; therefore, those [properties] exist there as well. Those [properties] which are in the *iṣu* and the Śyena... [12]... [7/48]

Furthermore, the phrase "what else" would not be possible in the absence [of something else]. Moreover, the word "other" (*itara*) is not applicable when [the referent] is not present.
It is indeed present. For example, when one says,
"Let another support be given," or "Let another blanket be given," that which is present is what is given.

It is not merely a cloak or merely a blanket; rather, the *jyotiṣṭoma* elements are present. Therefore, it is a statement concerning them, and this [text] is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of them, for they are indeed enjoined by the *codaka*.

The phrase "or rather" (*api vā*) indicates the adoption of an alternative position. the other [term] has a specific purpose, while the other is common.
"Equal" (samānam) means "additional" (adhika).

Now, one might object: "This term refers only to what is proximate; it does not have the meaning of 'additional'. It is replied: This term does not denote only what is proximate. For when garments are enumerated, the word *itarat* [is used for those not explicitly listed].
Let a woolen blanket be given to Devadatta,
silk to Viṣṇumitra,
and linen to Yajñadatta.
In the case of "to Caitra," only cloth is given,
not gold or silver. Here, [one should understand] the additional *dharma*s belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma.
The word *itarat* (the other) is employed in succession; therefore, it ought to denote even more [elements] here as well. Thus, it becomes a term denoting something additional.

Alternatively, if it speaks of those belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma, then it is a term denoting what is proximate. In that case, one of the two meanings must necessarily be abandoned. If, setting aside the sense of "additional," the sense of "proximate" is adopted...

A mere restatement would be purposeless, and the word *śyena* would have its meaning unintended. However, if one sets aside the sense of what is merely proximate and adopts the sense of something additional (*adhika*), no fault arises. Therefore, the author of the Sūtras says:
"The other is of additional meaning. Consequently, those specific features belonging to the *Śyena* sacrifice which are additional to the procedure of the Jyotiṣṭoma—
These are extended here by analogy. That which expresses it should be common; the meaning is that the word should be common. And the word *śyena* is intended to be expressed.
Among the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, in the Vaiśvadeva [parvan], there are the Āgneya and the others.

The sacrificial oblations have been prescribed with their accompanying explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and their ritual rules (*dharma*) have been stated. In the Varuṇapraghāsa rites, having recorded only the oblations themselves,

"These five oblations are indeed for the Brahmins, because the others are for the Brahmins. In that regard:

Is this extension (*atideśa*) intended for the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) alone, or for the entire section (*kāṇḍa*) including both the explanatory passages and the injunctions (*vidhi*)? But how can there be an extension of the explanatory passages alone? For example: "And the trees are like the nests of the *pampā* birds. What, then, are the injunctions?

What are explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)? "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is tied in three bundles," "the fuel (*idhma*) is tied in three bundles," "there are nine fore-offerings (*prayāja*) and nine after-offerings (*anuyāja*)"—such as these are injunctions (*vidhi*). They are not methods for attaining *dharma*. What follows from this?

By what means are they enjoined? Those things which are enjoined by the injunctions of dharma are not the oblations. Therefore, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the *arthavādas*, but not of the injunctions of dharma.

Moreover, even in the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, certain Vaiśvadeva ritual details are prescribed, such as "they churn the fire" and "the *prasū* stalks are present. It is logical that by the hearing of the word "brāhmaṇa," there is an extension (*atideśa*) of everything; [this refers to] the extension of the entire section (*kāṇḍa*), including its explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
And because of the observation of indicative marks [to that effect]. (MS 7.1.19)

"Having adorned it and filled it, it should be offered silently; the back should be made manifest."

[The examples] beginning with these [are given]. However, the Vāruṇapraghāsika [rite] is devoid of specific ritual rules (*adharmaka*). And he demonstrates this: that which one performs as a *sarvahuta* sacrifice is a single reproach; for every oblation offered, it turns back.

That is the second [reason]. In the sentence, "Sacrifice to Heaven and Earth with clarified butter alone," which is intent upon prescribing the *ājya* sacrifice, it shows that the offering of the entire cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) and the non-repetition [of the offering] are established. From this observation, and because of the statement regarding the single double-portion (*dvayavadāna*) at the *avabhṛtha* bath, there is a restrictive determination in the case of the *avabhṛtha*.

"From this very [offering] one cuts twice from the single-potherd cake (*ekakapāla*). From this it is known that, surely, elsewhere there is no double-cutting. And all of this has been prescribed for the single-potherd cake belonging to the Vaiśvadeva [parvan].

Therefore, the Vaiśvadeva single-potherd cake is the archetype (*prakṛti*) for all single-potherd cakes. What follows from this? Even for the single-potherd cake in the Sākamedha [parvan], the ritual properties (*dharmāḥ*) of the Vaiśvadeva [cake] are obtained by extension.

For them, an extended application (atideśa) would be purposeless. However, for those specific characteristics (vaiśeṣika-dharma) of the Vāruṇaprāghāsika [offering] that have not yet been obtained, an extended application is meaningful. Therefore, this refers to the one-potsherd (ekakapāla) cake belonging to the Vāruṇaprāghāsika. It is replied: this is merely an indicative mark (liṅga). From what [source] is its actual application derived? We shall explain the source of its application later.

Regarding the passage "the *svarasāman*, the one-pot-sherd cake, and the curd-mixture" (*svarasāmaikakapālāmikṣam*), what then are those ritual properties (*dharmāḥ*)? They are such as "a ladle made of gold" or "made of *śamī* wood," and so forth.
The *sruva* ladles are made of *śamī* wood;
the application [of the term] "Sāman" should occur by way of a designation for that which is taught as such.
This is heard:
"He sings the Rathantara on the two following [verses]," and "He sings the Rathantara on the Kavati verses."
Thus, these and other such [passages] are recited. Regarding this, there arises the inquiry:
what is it that is extended here by way of analogy?
Now, is it not the case that what is expressed by the words *rathantara* and so forth—
That is extended by analogy. Certainly; however, it is not yet known what is expressed by these words.
[Objection: But this is already established, that the designation "Sāman" applies to the songs (*gīta*).

89*. Thus, an objection will be raised against what has already been established; that very [objection] shall be the final determination (*nirṇaya*). If that itself is the final determination, for what purpose is the objection? It is for the sake of strengthening [the position], like the driving in of a pillar. What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) in this regard? That is stated:

For the term "Sāman" is used by experts as a designation for a song (*gīti*) consisting of a Ṛc verse that possesses the *hiṅkāra*, *praṇava*, *prastāva*, *udgītha*, *pratihāra*, *upadrava*, and *nidhana* sections, and which undergoes modification through *stobha*, tone, and temporal practice. Therefore, there is a doubt.

It is said: But has it not been stated that, since singing exists, these words are denoters of a purificatory act (*saṃskārakarma*) called "being" (*bhāva*)? That very point is now being challenged. These are not denoters of a purificatory act. Why? Because they are employed at a time when no ritual action is being performed. At a time when no ritual action is being performed, the *sāman* is employed; and in the case of a purificatory act, [actions such as] sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), throwing down (*avakṣepaṇa*), or carrying fire around (*paryagnikaraṇa*) are not [performed].

They are employed outside of the time for ritual action because there is no purpose [for them] then. However, if these are indeed *mantras*, then their employment outside of the time for ritual action is justified by the rule that "one should study the *svādhyāya* day after day. Therefore, they are names of the *ṛcs*.
Furthermore, because of the difference in designation; and there is indeed a difference in designation.

[The objection is: "The Rathantara, the Bṛhat," and so forth. Since the preparatory act (*saṃskārakarma*) is a single entity, [the mention of multiple names] would be purposeless; for in that case, one name alone would suffice, just as with "song" (*gīti*). Now, if these are the names of the *ṛc* verses, then their distinctness of designation is appropriate because of the difference between those verses.
Furthermore, if the Rathantara were the singing and the Bṛhat were the singing...

The assignment of distinct names, such as "this is the *rathantara*" and "this is the *bṛhat*," would not be possible [if they were identical]. However, this is possible if they are names of specific *ṛc* verses. Furthermore, because of the distinctness of the modifications (*vikāra*). For each *sāman*, a distinctness of modification is observed. Since the singing (*gāna*) is one and the same, that [distinctness] would be untenable. Indeed, a distinctness of modification is seen when there is a difference in the refinement (*saṃskāra*). For example:

The state of becoming rice-grains results from threshing, and powder results from grinding; however, for a single entity, there can be neither the state of becoming rice-grains nor the state of being powdered simultaneously. These are names of *ṛks*. Therefore, due to the distinction between the *ṛks*, the diversity of their modifications is logical. Consequently, they are names of *ṛks*. To this, he recites the following reply:

"The application of the term *sāman* should be according to what has been taught by the learned. The application of the term *sāman* to the *ṛc* should be according to what has been taught by the learned (*śiṣṭa*). What has been taught? That which was taught by the teachers to their pupils: that the *ṛc*, distinguished by its *stoma* and other features, is the *sāman*;
that [term] should be applied. What is the reason? Because "Rathantara" and so forth are the names of that [ṛc].
NOTES:
But because words enjoin a purpose, there would be no application to another purpose; for the connection [of the word] is indeed with the action, since it is distinct from it.

The word "tu" (but) serves to set aside the previous position. It should not be the case that the *ṛc*s proceed [in their own form]. How so? Here, in the injunction "one sings the *rathantara* on the *kavatī*s," either the *abhivatī*s would be extended by analogy (*atideśa*) to take the place of the *kavatī*s, or [the *rathantara*] would [be applied] to the *kavatī*s themselves.
94*} Or rather, [it applies] above [the verse]. 96*.

In that regard, first of all, an extended application (*atideśa*) regarding the ritual action (*kārya*) is not possible. Why? Because words have the function of enjoining meanings. The function of words is to enjoin meanings. And it is not the case that the meaning expressed by the *kavatī* verses in the statement "one sings the *rathantara* on the *kavatī* verses" [is what is extended].

The *abhivatya* verses are able to express that [relationship]. Therefore, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the effect. Even in the case of being a locus (*ādheyatva*), it is not possible, because of their distinctness. For a word does not inhere in a word;
rather, it remains entirely separate. [As in the examples: *abhi tvā* and *kayā na*.

For it is the action—namely, the act of singing—that has a connection with the word, not the word itself. Therefore, there can be no extension [of the rule] even by way of being something to be contained. Consequently, this is not an application of the *ṛc*.
NOTES:
*{7/96: as the state of being that which is to be contained} *{7/97:
ṚV 7.32.22 and 4.31.1} *{7/98: E1 has "gānakriyāyāḥ" in parentheses}
Or, if there were a purpose for the action in its own right, then [the details] would be taught as being subordinate members (*aṅga*) of that action. (MS 7.2.3)

Or, if they were proceeding for their own sake, the *abhivatīs* would be taught as being subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the *kavatīs*. But how can subsidiarity be taught in the case of "he sings the *kavatīs*"? It can be taught just as in the rule:
"In whatever rite one desires success, there he should offer the *jayā* oblations.
What, then, is the purpose of the *abhivatīs* effecting the *kavatīs*? It is said:
An unseen purpose (adṛṣṭa) must be postulated. Why? Because of the action; for an action is heard [in the text]:
"One sings the Rathantara on the Kavatī verses.
This is just as the purpose of the fore-sacrifices (prayāja) and so forth consists in the action itself.
It is said: this very point is the defect in this position, namely, that one must postulate a purpose for the action. Therefore, this position as well is untenable.
If it is argued that [the object] is a mere word, [we reply: MS 7.2.4.
If you think that the instruction of the *abhivatī* verses as being subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the *kavattī* verses is difficult to reconcile,
then let only the mere sound (*śabdamātra*) be prescribed. [22] {7/}

One should employ the word *rathantara* in the *kavatī* verses; that is, one should designate the *kavatī* verses by the term *rathantara*. What is the reason? When a word is uttered, the primary understanding is directed toward it.
In the case of a word, the action is understood to apply to its referent, as in "Bring the cow. But here, the action is possible only with respect to the word itself.
It is not for the sake of the meaning; therefore, we shall understand the word in this context [based on its conventional usage].
NOTES:
Because it is not innate. // MS_7.2.5 //
This [second] position is worse than the former. Why? Because it is innate (*autpattika*). For the relationship between a name and its referent is innate.
A word that is established through an innate relationship with a particular object cannot convey anything other than that. Indeed, a horse cannot be denoted by the word "cow."
And thus, the treatise would be rendered purposeless.

And this being the case, the rule of extension (*atideśa-śāstra*) would be purposeless, because its object would be impossible to achieve. Therefore, it is not logical that there should be an extension even for the word. However, the author of the *Vṛtti* thought that the science of chanting (*gāna-śāstra*), pertaining to the *Aukthikas*, would otherwise be purposeless. His intention was as follows:
Since there is a possible interpretation, it is not right to assume that such a great effort on the part of the learned would be fruitless;
[if you object] that this refers to the accent (svara), [we reply: MS_7.2.7.

If you think thus—that the extension (*atideśa*) of the name is improper—then let there be an extension of the accent (*svara*). In common usage, the word *sāman* denotes the accent; for example: "Devadatta has a beautiful *sāman*" means "Devadatta has a beautiful voice. The accent is the resonance, the sound.
102* These [terms] have the same meaning. That [sacrifice] is expressed by the word *sāman*, and the *rathantara* is a *sāman*. Therefore, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of its [properties].
NOTES:
*{7/102: Cf. Nighaṇṭu 11}* There is no lack of connection between the Vedic revelation and its meaning because of the absence of an object [to denote]. MS_7,2.8 //

This is not so; it is not a transfer of the *abhivatī* accent. Why? Because of the absence of the referent; that is, because of the non-existence of the referent. Since the accent of the *abhivatī* verses does not exist in the *kavati* verses, [one might object]: "But surely that [accent], though non-existent, is brought into being by the transfer. It is said in reply: it cannot even be brought into being. For the resonance (*nāda*) that manifests the phonemes of the *abhivatī* verses cannot be brought into being within the *kavati* verses. If it were to be brought into being, [the following would occur].

The *kavatyas* would not exist [if they were not produced]. If it is not brought into being, it has not come into existence. There would be no syntactic connection with another word for this scriptural statement, "He sings the *Rathantara* on the *kavatyas*. Therefore, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the accent.
NOTES:
*{7/103: E2: The mutual connection of the words of the Veda}*.
But the natural accent (*svara*) would belong to the [phonemes] at their point of origin, because they are not divided by *mātrā* or phoneme (*varṇa*). (MS 7.2.9)

The word "tu" (but) is used to introduce an alternative position. If the application of the *abhivatī* melody to the *kavatī* verses is not logically possible, then let it be a restatement (*anuvāda*), namely:
"He sings the *rathantara* on the *kavatī* verses. How so? That is explained as follows:

Regarding the sentence, "He sings the Rathantara on the *kavatī* verses," there are two possible modes of expression (*vacanavyakti*). One is: "That which is the Rathantara, he sings it on the *kavatī* verses. The other is: "The Rathantara, that he sings on the *kavatī* verses. Of these two, this is the second.

Regarding the statement, "He sings the Rathantara upon the *kavatī* verses," it has already been stated that this is not possible if the *svara* (melodic accent) is considered an intrinsic property of the *sāman*.

For the accent of the *abhivatī* verses cannot be superimposed upon the *kavatī* verses. However, the former [interpretation] is possible: namely, that he sings the Rathantara which [ordinarily] belongs to the *kavatī* verses.
But surely that too is not possible; for the *rathantara* does not exist within the *kavatī* verses. To this, it is further stated:
"But the *svara* should be in the original [verses]. The *svara*, however, is the *abhivatī-svara*.

It would apply to the occurrences and utterances of the *kavatī* verses. How so? Because of the non-distinction of their morae and syllables. Many morae and syllables belonging to both the *abhivatī*s and the *kavatī*s are undifferentiated; they exist in the *abhivatī*s and also in the *kavatī*s. That very accent of the *abhivatī*s exists in the *kavatī*s as inherent in the common syllables;
thus, this reference (*anuvāda*) to it is appropriate.
"One sings the Rathantara on the *kavatī* verses. Therefore, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the musical tone (*svara*).
[This is also supported] by the observation of indicative marks (*liṅgadarśanāt*).
And an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is seen in this matter: "The *rathantara* [sāman] is in the two later [verses].
What is that indicative mark? It says thus:
"I do not see the *rathantara* in the two later [verses]."
106* Thus Viśvāmitra performed austerities,
thinking, "I do not see [the power] of Vasiṣṭha's great northern [sacrificial fires]. And regarding that which exists but is not seen,
an effort is made for the sake of seeing it.

Just as one turns on a lamp because one says, "I do not see the jar," and not because one says, "I do not see a rabbit's horn"; therefore, the *rathantara* and the *bṛhat* exist [as primary injunctions], and the [other] two are merely restatements (*anuvāda*) of them.
But when there is no mention of a modification in the subsequent [verses], it is according to what is heard [in the original]. (MS 7.2.11)
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position. This is not so;
it is a restatement of the *svara* (accent). Why? Because if that were the case, no modification would be heard in the subsequent verses (*uttarā*).

Therefore, the subsequent verses should be employed exactly as they are heard, just as they are heard at the time of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). In that regard, the *rathantara* [is applied] to the two subsequent verses.

The statement "he sings" is merely a restatement; since it does not produce any specific activity, it is criticized as being entirely purposeless. Therefore, a restatement of the accent is not appropriate. [25] {7/107} NOTES:
And there is an inconsistency regarding words. (MS 7.2.12)

Furthermore, there would be an inconsistency regarding the application of the terms *sāman* such as *rathantara* and so forth, in cases such as "the *rathantara* on the two following [verses]" and "the *bṛhat* on the two following [verses]. How so? This is explained:
this word *rathantara* or the word *bṛhat*, if the term *sāman* were to refer to the musical tone (*svara*), would have to refer to a collection of tones established in a specific sequence.
When applied to a specific accent, it becomes inconsistent either in part or in its altered sequence;
therefore, this is not tenable— that the word *sāman* refers to the accent and that [the passage] is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of it.

Here it is asked: "In this way, you have refuted all positions; therefore, does it follow that there is simply no application [of the mantra]? It is replied: "Let the *ṛc* itself be the object of application. [The opponent asks:
"But was it not said that it is impossible to apply one *ṛc* to another *ṛc*? [The respondent says: "Certainly."

It will be a designation by way of location (*deśalakṣaṇā*). It is said, "One sings the Rathantara on the *kavatī* verses. And it is not possible to sing the Rathantara on the *kavatī* verses [in their literal sense]. In that case, there is a designation by way of location, namely, "the location of the *kavatīs*.
Just as, for example, one says, "He stands in the fire."

"It stands in the well. This may be a characteristic of the *dharma*. Or rather, the *dharmas* of the *rathantara* [sāman] are extended by means of the word "rathantara" to the *kavatī* verses, such as:
"While the *rathantara* is being chanted, one should meditate on the earth with the mind," and so forth. It is also like when a teacher has gone abroad...
"The teacher's wife is your teacher"— thus, service toward the teacher is extended by analogy to the teacher's wife.
*{7/108: E2: while it remains}* *{7/109: E2:
and it would be inconsistent}* *{7/110:

ĀDhS 1.2.7}* But rather, it should be a word denoting action (*karmaśabda*), having "being" (*bhāva*) as its meaning, because of the acceptance of what is well-known; for [the meaning] is not distinct from others.
But it cannot be thus:

that the word "sāman" refers to the *ṛc* (verse), and that there is a "placement" (*pradeśa*) of that [verse]. In that case, one would have to resort to a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based either on location or on the ritual property (*dharma*). And this recourse to figurative indication is a lack of a direct path [to the literal meaning]. What then? It should be a word for the action; the *rathantara* and so forth refer to what is called "singing."

It denotes the act of preparation (*saṃskārakarman*). Why? Because the principle was stated in the passage: "The designation 'Sāman' applies to the songs. In that context, [it refers] to the *ṛc* verse as qualified by the song.

This word has been observed [as a name]. And a cognition of a qualified object does not arise unless its qualifier has been apprehended; therefore, the qualifier is denoted first. From the cognition of the qualifier, there arises a cognition of the qualified object as it occurs in association with it. Consequently, there is no contact of the *ṛk* with the word [itself]. By this very reasoning, we say that [the word] is a name for the melody (*gīti*).

Furthermore, because it refers to what is well-known: this word "he sings" (*gāyati*) is well-known in the sense of the act of singing. What, then, is that? It is a particular kind of vocal utterance. "He sings" means he performs singing; and words such as *rathantara* are used to denote that [act]. This is the meaning of the phrase "expressing that. Therefore, because of its being uttered together with that [act], and because of the force of the accusative case, as in:
"he sings the *āsāritaka*."
"One sings the *vardhamānaka*. But surely, utterance also occurs by means of the word "sound" (*śabda*), as in "he sings a verse" (*gāthāṃ gāyati*).
"One sings the Ṛc"—this is true, provided that the word is modified;

for [the statement] "one embellishes the Ṛc by means of singing" does not connect with the literal sense of the word as it stands, namely, "one performs singing upon the Ṛc. Therefore, [the term *gāyati*] denotes the melody (*gīti*).

And for this reason, it is a term denoting singing. Why? Because the modification is not distinct from others. And here, a modification of the vocal substance is observed: the lengthening of short syllables and the shortening of long ones; the closing of open vowels and the opening of closed ones. This is not distinct from other transformative acts, just as rice grains are turned into rice-powder by threshing.

The state of being ground is the grinding of rice grains. Therefore, the refinement of words known as "singing" (gāna) is expressed by terms such as *rathantara* and so forth. This [text] is the application of that [refinement], such as:
"One sings the *rathantara* on the two [verses] beginning with *uttare*" and so on.
And even that which is not a substance (adravya) is observed [to be denoted by a word]. (MS 7.2.14)

Moreover, *sāman* is seen to be non-substantial (*adravya*). The word "substance" (*dravya*) is used by the Chāndogas with reference to the *ṛc*s; thus, "non-substantial" means "without an *ṛc*. A *sāman* without an *ṛc* is observed, as in:
"He sings the *Prajāpati-hṛdaya*, which is without an *ṛc*.
[The *Prajāpati-hṛdaya*...]
The term *sāman* refers to a chant. That [chant] arises even in the absence of a *ṛc*. If the word *sāman* were restricted to the *ṛc*, how could the *Prajāpatihṛdaya* be without a *ṛc*?
On the other hand, if the word *sāman* refers to the melody (*gīti*), [then it applies here].

Therefore, even without a *ṛc*, there is singing (*gīti*). In this regard, it is appropriate [to say]: "He sings the heart of Prajāpati without a *ṛc*. For this reason also, the *sāman* is the singing.
But was it not stated that if it were a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarman*), its performance at a time other than the ritual action would be purposeless?
To this we reply: [NOTES:

And its function is for the purpose of apprehension, because it assumes various forms with respect to multiple objects; for their object is indeed non-worldly (*alaukika*) due to [the Veda's] injunction. (MS 7.2.15)

At the time of its performance and ritual action, it is for the purpose of grasping [it] in order to learn and practice it. Regarding "in various meanings" (*nānārtheṣu*), this means in meanings that have become manifold, that is, distinct;

because they are diverse in form due to the difference in their bases (*āśrayabheda*), that singing becomes of various forms. That [singing] must be learned and practiced verse by verse (*pratyṛcam*) for the sake of achieving fluency in performance, like a charioteer on the ground.

For example, a chariot-rider on the ground practices by drawing a chariot on the ground. That practice produces ease for him at the time of actual performance. For the meaning of these names, such as *rathantara* and so forth, is not established in worldly usage.

As in the case of the *vāhanti* and other such [terms]. Why? Because of their being prescribed (*vidhāna*). For this [term] is prescribed through the relationship between pupil and teacher, in the form:
"The *rathantara* becomes of such a nature. It is not understood as something worldly. Therefore, this objection—that it is used at a time when there is no ritual action—is not valid.
Now, as for what was stated, namely,
"because of the distinctness of designations," it is said in response to that: [Notes:]
In that [case], there would be specific designations due to the distinctness of the modifications. (MS 7.2.16)

Even though there is only a single refinement (*saṃskāra*) called "song," there may be distinct designations for it. Why? Because of the diversity of modifications. Even when the song is identical, a distinction arises;
and from the distinction in the song comes the distinction in designation. For example, the *āsāritaka*.
Regarding the term *vardhamānaka*:

it is a chant (*gīti*) characterized by different characteristics (*anyathālakṣaṇa*). A *vardhamānaka* chant has different characteristics; likewise, here too, the *rathantara* chant has different characteristics, and the *bṛhat* chant has different characteristics. Therefore, there is a distinction in their designations (*saṃjñāpṛthaktva*).
NOTES:
*{7/120: E2: A specific type of song within the category of singing}* *{7/122: E2: The Vardhamānaka melody}*
And those which are prescribed in a systematic manner as being equal to the others. (MS 7.2.17)

That which is both a source (*yoni*) and praiseworthy is "praiseworthy as a source" (*yoniśasyā*). Discussions concerning what is praiseworthy as a source are treated as equivalent to other discussions concerning what is not praiseworthy as a source. He recites the verses addressed to Yama;
he recites the verses containing the word *śipiviṣṭa*;
he recites the verse that is the source of the *rathantara*.
"He recites according to the womb of the Bṛhat" [Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.2.10]. What is the similarity there? It is the denotation by the word *śaṃsati*.
Here, although these two words, *stauti* and *śaṃsati*, have the same purpose—praise—their domains are distinct. The word *stauti* applies to mantra-texts that are set to melody (*pragīta*).
The word *śaṃsati* is used for those [hymns] that are not sung,
as in:
"He recites the *praüga*."

"He recites," it is said; "they praise with the *ājya* [stotras]," and "they praise with the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras]. Therefore, because of the injunction by means of the word "recites" (*śaṃsati*), it shows that the *rathantara*’s source (*yoni*) is a verse (*ṛc*) not set to chant. And if the *rathantara* is indeed the chant, then its source is that unchanted verse. Otherwise, this designation would not be tenable.
"The source of the Rathantara," it is said. Therefore, the designation "Sāman" applies to the melodies.
the ordinance}* *{7/126: E2:
the absolute state}*
And likewise, that which is not born from a womb is seen even in what is not a womb.

And the *sāman* is seen in an improper source (*ayoni*). They say, "Flour is being ground in a pot," when the *bṛhat* is performed upon *gāyatrī* verses; moreover, it breaks them. And it is not possible for it [the *bṛhat*] to exist in them, for the *bṛhatī* is the source (*yoni*) of the *bṛhat*. Thus, there is no attainment of it in the *gāyatrīs*, provided that the word *sāman* refers to the *ṛc*.
But if, on the other hand, it refers to the singing (*gīti*), [then it is possible].
Therefore, that *bṛhadr̥ti* was obtained among the *gāyatrī* verses by virtue of the injunction;
thus, this restatement is appropriate:
"that which is the *bṛhat* is performed upon the *gāyatrī* verses. Furthermore, it shows that the *sāman* does not have its own source; for whatever the source of a thing may be, [it is not so here].
Then, in another case:
he who indeed applies a *sāman* to a non-verse (*vicchandas*) destroys the verse.
He either divides the *sāman* or joins the *sāman*,
or he divides the *ṛc*; whichever is the longer [he does so].
Its modification (*saṃśara*) is applied only to the *gīta* (the chanting) within the *sāman*, not to the *ṛc* (the verse). Furthermore,
the term "modification" (*ūhati*) is capable [of application] only with respect to the *gīta*.

If it were a *ṛc*, then it would be recited exactly as it is handed down in the tradition; in that case, there would be no occasion for modification (*ūha*). Therefore, for this reason as well, the word *sāman* refers to the chant.
[Objection: "The opening belongs to that [roof] which is larger; the filling-in belongs to that which is more extensive.

Therefore, if these were preparatory acts (*saṃskārakarma*), their performance during non-ritual times would be illogical.
Thus, while the proposition that the word "Sāman" does not denote a preparatory act remains established, [the opponent] challenges it with a Sūtra.
It might be so because [the cause] does not produce other effects, just as in the case of cooking. (MS 7.2.20)

There may be a change of form (*vairūpya*). Why is this? Because it is not established when there is no difference in the object; because, among different *ṛc*-verses, there is a difference in the basis (*āśrayabheda*).

Just as in the case of cooking: although this single object called "cooking" is one and the same, its form changes when applied to different objects. The cooking of rice has a different characteristic [from other forms of cooking].
The characteristic of molasses is different [from that of rice];
one who has mastered the cooking of rice does not know how to cook molasses without training. Therefore, its application at a time when it is not being worked upon is also logically consistent.

133* Thus it has been established that this is a distinct ritual act from the regular *agnihotra*. Now the word *agnihotra* is considered:

The ritual properties belonging to the regular *agnihotra* should be extended to this [new rite] by means of this name. What is the reason? It is said:
this is a word for another that is applied to something else;

when a word for one thing is applied to another, the state of being like that [original] is understood. Where that [state of being like the original] is already known, it is merely restated (*anūdyate*).

Just as in the case of "Devadatta is a lion. Where it is not already known, there an injunction is made; for example, "Let these balls of flour be made into lions. And here, the nature of this *juhoti* [offering] as being like the *agnihotra* is not known; therefore, that is what is enjoined:

by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it is capable of conveying the possession of those properties such as milking that are associated with that act. And if it is capable of conveying this, it is also capable of enjoining it.

the meaning of the suffix *vat* can be understood.

This is not tenable. Why?

For the relationship between a name and its referent is innate (*autpattika*). Whatever name is well-established for a particular object through an innate relationship, it should always be understood as referring to that very object and not to anything else. If such a fixed rule did not exist, there would be no confidence in the meaning of words. It has been said:

And it is illogical for a word to have multiple meanings. Since it cannot denote both meanings simultaneously, it first expresses the obligatory sense. If its application elsewhere is justified for the purpose of enjoining similarity to that [obligatory rite], then there is no reason for it to denote the other meaning. Therefore, it should be a case of a transferred injunction (*vidhipradeśa*).
The designation of action would arise from the connection with qualities perceived through direct perception; in the absence of that [perception], it would be unestablished.

In the *naiyamika-agnihotra*, there is a direct connection with auxiliary elements (*guṇa*). There are duties (*dharma*) prescribed directly: "One should milk in this manner," "one should cook in this manner," "one draws up four times," and "the fuel-stick for the *agnihotra* is made of *khadira* wood."
In this way one offers;
thus, from the direct perception of the connection with the quality.

That name belonging to the *naiyamika* [offering], when employed here, would denote actions such as milking and so forth; the meaning is that it would indicate the application of ritual properties (*dharma*). However, for this *juhoti*, there are no such ritual properties. In the absence of those—meaning, in the absence of those ritual properties—[the name does not apply].
It would be unestablished and not understood why this word "agnihotra" is employed here.
Or rather: the connection with a quality is directly perceived,
whereas the connection with a substance and a deity is obligatory— as in "He offers with curd" and "He offers with milk."

"One offers the evening oblation to Agni and to Prajāpati"—from this direct connection with a quality (*guṇa-saṃyoga*), there must be a designation of the action. It is a name for the ritual act (*karmanāmadheya*), meaning that the *juhoti* (offering) of such a form is called "Agnihotra. Otherwise, it would lack the form of the other *juhoti*, and in its absence, it would remain unestablished.
It would not be known what kind of Agnihotra that is.
[Objection: But surely the month will be its form. [Reply: No.
The month is a constituent part of the ritual;
it is a property of the agent. Moreover, the Agnihotra is enjoined with reference to the month.
The Agnihotra is not defined by the month; therefore, this is the name of the obligatory rite, and in other cases there is an extension (atideśa) of that same [name].
Is this the general rule?

Every name of an action, when heard elsewhere, is a designator of phenomena (*dharma*). This is indeed how it is established. Since this is established, the following is undertaken: [34] {7/144} NOTES:

Thus it is possible. This word has the sense of a quality (*guṇa*). This section concerns those hymns that have arisen, namely those which are called *pṛṣṭhas*. And it is only when their status as *pṛṣṭhas* is known that this [designation] is appropriate. But that status is not known there. How then is this a restatement (*anuvāda*)?
Because of the presence of the characteristic mark (*liṅga*). Among them, one is a *pṛṣṭha*.

"What is the fault? [The opponent] says: "It is impossibility. If the word *pṛṣṭha* enjoins the *pṛṣṭha* chants, they cannot be qualified by the word "all" (*sarva*). Now, since the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] are here obtained as alternatives, what is enjoined is their mere combination, as expressed by the statement:
"He becomes one for whom all the Pṛṣṭhas are performed";
thus, both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara are employed.
"It is not one. Therefore, this fault does not occur. Consequently, there is an authority over both. NOTES: {*7/161: E2: 'is accepted'}*

Because the word "all" (*sarva*) would otherwise be purposeless. (MS 7.3.11) [Cf. Tait. S. 3.7.1]

This is not so. Why? Because the word "all" (*sarva*) would be rendered meaningless. This being the case, the word "all" would be useless and devoid of meaning; for this term refers to a wide range of objects and is not applicable to only two. However, there is no such fault in the injunction regarding the six-day rites (*ṣāḍahika*). [Objection: But even there, the word will have a dual function. [Reply: It will not. It will enjoin the "all-ness" (*sarvatva*) of the *pṛṣṭha* chants alone.
[They are] not the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras]. But was it not said:
"If the *pṛṣṭhas* do not exist, for what is this 'all-ness' (*sarvatva*) prescribed? It is replied:
Indeed, the "all-ness" of the *pṛṣṭhas* has been prescribed.

That must be accomplished. And it cannot be accomplished by one who does not perform the *pṛṣṭha* chants; therefore, by implication, he will perform the *pṛṣṭhas*. In this way, the word will not have two meanings, and the term "all" (*sarva*) is justified. Therefore, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the elements belonging to the six-day rite (*ṣāḍahika*).

Likewise, the final purificatory bath follows from the Soma sacrifice.
In the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture:

What is the correct view? It is a subordinate injunction for the New and Full Moon sacrifices; in this way, the cognition of what is proximate is upheld, for that [pouring] has been brought near by the extended rule (*codaka*). But is that not the *avabhṛtha* itself? It is said: no. It is said: [it is a subordinate injunction].
"There is the word *avabhṛtha* there [in that context]: 'This indeed is the *avabhṛtha* of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
This being the position reached, he says this:
likewise, the *avabhṛtha* follows from the Soma sacrifice."

Just as there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the *pṛṣṭha* chants from the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*), so too here is there an extension of ritual properties (*dharma*) from the Soma sacrifice’s purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). Why? Because the principle has been stated;
it was said that when a name of an action is heard in one context, there should be an extension of the injunction (*vidhipradeśa*) to another.
If it is argued that [the soul is active] because of primordial matter (prakṛti), [we reply: MS_7,3.13.
Now, as for what was said—
that there might be an injunction regarding a subsidiary element (guṇavidhi) in the *avabhṛtha* of the New and Full Moon sacrifices—
what is the refutation of that? This is the end of the introductory portion (*ābhāṣānta*) of the Sūtra.
Not so, because it is devotion. (MS 7.3.14)

This is not correct. Why? Because there is no *avabhṛtha* (concluding purificatory bath) for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. But is it not heard in scripture: "This indeed is the *avabhṛtha* of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*"? [38]
It is indeed heard [in scripture], yet its status as an *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) does not actually occur in this manner. How so? It is said:

there are two possible modes of expression for this sentence, "This indeed is the *avabhṛtha* of the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsayoḥ*). Either it refers to a ritual element whose status as an *avabhṛtha* is already established [elsewhere] and is now connected with the New and Full Moon sacrifices; or...

It is said: just as when it is stated, "Devadatta is the son of Yajñadatta," the relationship of Devadatta—who is already known to be a son—is expressed in relation to Yajñadatta; or, when the relationship is already known, the status of being the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) is expressed for that which is not yet known to be the *avabhṛtha*, as in:
"This mango tree is the son of Yajñadatta."

The status of being a son is predicated of the mango tree whose relationship to Yajñadatta has already been established. Similarly, the connection of this sprinkling of water with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices is already established by the context (*prakaraṇa*), not its status as the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath).
Therefore, its status as the *avabhṛtha* is now being predicated. Yet, this is not actually the *avabhṛtha*. [Objection:
Let it be that this too is the *avabhṛtha*. [Reply: This is not correct, for it is illogical for a single thing to have multiple functions. How then?

The application of the word [‘avabhṛtha’] is due to similarity. What is the similarity? It is the connection with water. This is a figurative statement of praise regarding the sprinkling of water, saying "this is like the avabhṛtha," just as one speaks of a son in relation to a mango tree. Therefore, there is no avabhṛtha in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; consequently, this is not an injunction of a subordinate element (guṇavidhi).
[The connection of] a ritual act whose status as the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) is already known with the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*)}*
And because of the observation of an indicative mark. (MS 7.3.15)

"He does not offer the *āyurdā* oblation; he does not chant the *sāman*."
"Or he does not mutter the *gamana-mantra*.

By stating this prohibition of the ritual duties (*dharma*) belonging to the Soma-related *avabhṛtha*, it indicates that those duties are applicable here. Therefore, there is an extension of the ritual duties from the Soma-related *avabhṛtha*.

When a specific substance is prescribed, that very substance [is to be used] because of its connection with the Vedic text; however, when no substance is prescribed, the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is used because it is the primary material for that rite.

The *avabhṛtha* of the *Vāruṇapraghāsa* is rightly considered a receiver of the ritual characteristics (*dharma*) from the *avabhṛtha* of the Soma sacrifice. In this regard, the following is considered:
is this [rite] one that has the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) as its substance?

"Or rather, does it have husks and scrapings as its substance? What is the prima facie view? That it has the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) as its substance. Why? Because the cake is obtained by name. when there is a substitution of a substance, it should consist of that very substance. In this instance of substituting a substance—namely, "they go to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) with the husked grain"—it should consist of that very substance.
The substance for removing the husks [is the flour]. Why? Because of its connection with the Vedic text;
the removal of the husks is directly stated in the scripture (*pratyakṣa-śruta*), whereas the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is merely inferential (*ānumānika*).
It is obtained through extended application (atideśa).

But the husks-and-fragments (tuṣaniṣkāsa) specifically [are intended]. And the general is set aside by the specific. Moreover, the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is understood through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), whereas the husks-and-fragments are understood through direct statement (śruti). And between direct statement and secondary indication, direct statement is the more authoritative. Therefore, it has the husks-and-fragments as its substance. Now, as for what was said—that the husks-and-fragments are not connected with the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha)—[that is incorrect].
"Because it would result in a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). To this we reply:

if the *tuṣaniṣkāsa* (the husks and scrapings) were enjoined while setting aside the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), then there would indeed be a split in the sentence. It is not contradictory. Furthermore, if the removal of the husks were not being enjoined, the mention of them would be entirely purposeless. Therefore, it has the removal of the husks as its substance.

As for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), in the absence of a specific injunction, it follows that very material because it is its archetype. This would be so if no substance were explicitly heard mentioned here.
In that case, the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) would [be used] because its constituent material is husks. However, in this instance, the removal of husks is explicitly heard in the scripture;
therefore, there is no sacrificial cake. It is heard in the context of the Guest-offering (ātithya):
"The offering to Viṣṇu consists of nine potsherds.

"In the first [offering] connected with the Trika, there is an offering to Viṣṇu on three potsherds. Regarding this, there is an inquiry:

The word "pṛṣṭha" (back) should refer to the ritual action, because it is taught as being of such a nature.
The word *pṛṣṭha* would refer to the action (*karman*). Why? Because it is taught as such. This is the teaching:
wherein this word *pṛṣṭha* is understood as a name for an action.

This [word *pṛṣṭha*] here is also of such a nature. What is its "suchness" (*tathātva*)? It is the commonality of the word *pṛṣṭha*. In that context, the word *pṛṣṭha* was understood to denote a ritual action; this very same word is used here. Therefore, it must be understood here too as denoting that same thing, because there is no distinction. If another meaning were postulated, a single word would have multiple meanings. What is the fault in that? When the word is uttered, there would be doubt.

There would be no cognition of the meaning; in that case, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) would not be established. And the employment of words is for the sake of linguistic usage. Furthermore, other factors such as context (*prakaraṇa*) would have to be depended upon. But if there were a single meaning, the cognition of the meaning would be independent [of such factors]. Therefore, it is improper for there to be multiple meanings. Consequently, the word *pṛṣṭha* is the name of the ritual action (*karman*). When it is the name of the ritual action, [the subsequent application of the term follows].

In that case, if those very rites are being taught here, then their origin [in the original context] would be rendered purposeless. If, on the other hand, this fault is to be avoided and this *upasthāna* (ritual attendance) is understood as occurring there [in the original context], then this present section would be contradicted. Therefore, this is an injunction based on similarity:
"They attend with the *pṛṣṭha* hymns."
"They stand by means of actions similar to the back," it is said; and that similarity occurs through specific qualities (*dharmas*). Therefore, those qualities must be performed.
The word "back" (*pṛṣṭha*) is a designation for action;
it is as it truly is;
that [is it].
*{7/240: Regarding this and what follows, see ad MS 1.4.3}* *{7/241: E2: If here [the word] has another meaning}* *{7/242: E2:
it stands near [or attends to]}*
*{7/243: E2: upatiṣṭhata}* Or rather, because of the instruction regarding the designation and because of the prohibition, the word "pṛṣṭha" should apply to the substances.

But this is not so; the word "pṛṣṭha" does not refer to the ritual action (*karman*). What then? The word "pṛṣṭha" would apply to substances (*dravya*). It is a designation for the *ṛg*-substances, namely the verses such as "abhitvā śūra nonumaḥ" and so forth. Why? Because of the instruction regarding the designation. There is an instruction regarding the designation...

Regarding the statement, "They attend with the *pṛṣṭha*-stotras," the meaning is that they place [the fire] over [it] by means of the *pṛṣṭha*-stotras. But how can this word for "attending" (*upasthāna*) be understood as having the sense of "placing over"? It is said:

Due to a specific restriction (*upagraha-viśeṣa*), the *ātmanepada* ending occurs for the root *upatiṣṭhati* when it has a mantra as its instrument (*karaṇa*). However, the mantra is the instrument of the act of recitation (*abhidhāna*), not of the act of standing near (*upasthāna*). Standing near is performed by means of the body.

Or [it may be] by means of the mind (*manas*). Therefore, it is for the purpose of denotation. This is the contradiction: if the word *pṛṣṭha* is assumed to refer to ritual actions, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is contradicted;

for in that case, the mantra does not function as an instrument (*karaṇa*). If, on the other hand, the middle voice is followed, there is a contradiction regarding the act of standing near (*upasthāna*).

In that case, it would follow that the word has the meaning of denotation (*abhidhāna*). There, compliance with the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is logical. For the word *pṛṣṭha*, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), becomes meaningful when it denotes the mantra that is the instrument for the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra]. The middle voice, however, is justified precisely by the mantra being the instrument. Therefore, the word *pṛṣṭha* refers to the mantras that are the instruments for the *pṛṣṭha*. He says: This is not correct. For the meaning of "standing near" (*upasthāna*) is established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) through the root *upatiṣṭhati*. The meaning of "denotation" follows from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the middle voice. And a direct scriptural statement should not be set aside by an indicative mark. It is replied:
In this case, the Vedic text is not sublated. The verb *tiṣṭhati* expresses its own primary meaning, namely, "standing near. However, that [meaning] is for the sake of denotation;
by means of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), the verb *tiṣṭhati* expresses "one should stand near the fire" in order to bring about the act of denotation. Therefore, there is no contradiction.

He said: Even so, the mantra is the instrument of the act of naming, not of the act of attending (*upatiṣṭhati*). In that case, there is simply no connection between the mantra and the act of attending. Likewise, [it is said]:
"They attend with the *pṛṣṭha* hymns."
Thus, the recitation would be purposeless. It is said in reply:

the mantra becomes the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the act of attendance (*upasthāna*) by bringing about its expression (*abhidhāna*), since it accomplishes its own specific purpose. For that which is devoid of purpose is not performed. Therefore, the word "back" (*pṛṣṭha*) refers only to the mantras. And if it refers to the mantras, [then...]
There is no attainment of dharmas. For the mantras do not possess dharmas; they are devoid of dharmas. [53] {7/249} NOTES:
E2: incapable of expressing the meaning}* *{7/247:
E2 omits "becomes"}*
The rule for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is that it follows the previous [model], as indicated by the term *upatiṣṭhate*. MS_7.4.1.
Without reference to anything else, it is heard [in scripture]:
"One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya."
Thus it is said. In this regard, the following meaning is established:
"This sacrifice is enjoined"; for the act of sacrificing (*yajati*) consists in the connection of these [factors]—the substance, the fruit, and the enjoyer.
Thus it has been said:
"In the relationship between action and its fruit, the action is subordinate and the fruit is primary."
"Because there is a connection with each respective object, there is indeed a relation through the action;

therefore, it must be an instruction regarding the action. This too has been stated: "The sacrifice (*yajati*) accomplishes the *apūrva* (the unseen potency). And from that *apūrva*, the fruit arises at a later time."

Regarding the statement "An injunction (*codanā*) is an instigation (*ārambha*)," when this is the case, in the passage "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya," it is understood thus: "One desiring spiritual luster should accomplish spiritual luster by performing the Sūrya sacrifice through the production of the *apūrva*.
He asks: where is there a sacrifice (*yajati*) joined with the instrumental case?
In that case, it is logical to accept the status of a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*), as in the injunction:
"One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. But here, since there is no instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*), how is the meaning of the instrumental understood? It is said in reply:

What is the purpose here of the sacrifice (yajati) being indicated by the third case ending, when the subordinate status of actions toward their fruit is established by its very nature? Even where that [subordinate status] is explicitly heard, it is entirely redundant there as well, because its meaning is already understood. Likewise,
Even where there is a second scriptural mention,
such as "one should offer the Agnihotra," there too it is either a case of a change in case-ending, or...

Either there would be no intention to speak, or it would be purposeless; however, in no way whatsoever can the subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) toward the ritual action (*karman*) be denied. Therefore, it is stated here that the *apūrva* is accomplished by means of the sacrifice (*yāga*).
In this regard, the sacrifice is understood;
it is a worldly thing (*laukika*). However, it is not understood how the *apūrva* is accomplished by means of that [sacrifice].

In this case, however, it is stated only that "one should accomplish the *apūrva* by means of sacrifice"; the manner of accomplishment (*itikartavyatā*) has not been stated. And for those matters where the manner of performance is already known, only the fact that they ought to be performed is taught.
For example:

"One should cook rice. However, for those [actions] which are not known, they are taught together with their *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance), such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). If this is so, then surely it is known.
Since the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is prescribed for the production of the *apūrva* through sacrifice, it must surely exist. He says:
"If it exists in the world,"
From that, it would indeed be known. But if it does not exist at all, how can it be known? It is said: certainly it exists.

It is both worldly and Vedic. The worldly [injunction] refers to such rites as the *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka* and others; the Vedic refers to such rites as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and others. If these injunctions are preceded by that [knowledge], they depend upon it [for their efficacy]; thus, one should accomplish the *apūrva* (the unseen transcendental result) through the *saurya* sacrifice.
Since the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is not known [from other sources], it follows that there is no injunction regarding the procedure;
nor is it enjoined. Therefore, because there is no injunction of the procedure, the sacrifice (*yajati*) possesses its prior state—that is, it is characterized by an unenjoined procedure.

Now, as for those who say that one "should sacrifice," meaning one should perform a *yajña*, or that one "should offer oblations," meaning one should perform a *homa*—do they not have a requirement for the nature of dharma? We reply: they do. Even though the act of sacrificing (*yajati*), whose procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is already known, consists in relinquishing a substance toward a deity, nevertheless, when it is performed for the sake of a fruit, [it requires a further connection with dharma].

At that time, one desires [the performance of] dharmas. For indeed, no fruit arises from adharma. How is this known? For the learned (śiṣṭas) record in their tradition that for one who—being impure, lying down, or with feet raised—discharges an unclean substance with his left hand, or with his foot, or in any such manner, there is no fruit. But for one who, being pure, in a clean place, self-restrained, facing east, and with a concentrated mind, [discharges] a clean substance with his right hand...

The traditional authorities (smaranti) maintain that when one offers [an oblation] to a deity with both mantras and observances (niyama), the fruit thereof accrues to him. Therefore, whatever sacrifice (*yajati*) is enjoined for the sake of a fruit, all of it requires ritual details (*dharma*). Consequently, those [sacrifices] also possess a requirement for ritual details. When such a requirement exists, there is a connection with the proximate ritual details in the archetype (*prakṛti*), provided there is no contradiction; and this applies likewise in the ectype (*vikṛti*).
But [it is known] by means of inferential cognitions.

Now this is considered:
is the procedure (itikartavyatā) unrestricted— whether worldly or Vedic— or is it exclusively worldly?
Or is it Vedic?

Since there is no distinction here, a state of non-restriction might be assumed. To this it is said: it must be worldly (*laukika*). Indeed, that means for accomplishing what is to be done must be worldly. Why? Because its application is observed [in the world]. For its application is seen in various instances therein.
Just as in the case of the *pārvaṇasthālīpāka*,
the *aṣṭakācaru*,
and so forth— wherever an *apūrva* is accomplished by means of a sacrifice—

In each such case, its operation is observed. Therefore, by positive concomitance (*anvaya*), it is understood that this [sacrifice] is the means for accomplishing the *apūrva* of the sacrifice. And this [sacrifice] is also a sacrifice; therefore, for this too, that very same [means] is the means.
"Because of the statement that it is indeed Vedic [in the case of the *āgrahāyaṇa* ritual], it is therefore different from that. (MS 7.4.3)
He asks:
Is this the general rule—that everywhere there is the worldly procedure (*itikartavyatā*)? Indeed, that is how it appears to be obtained. That being the case, we reply:
"But because of a direct scriptural statement (*vacana*), it is different from that. Where there is a direct Vedic statement, [the Vedic procedure applies].
In that case, it would not be worldly;
by the force of the statement, it must be Vedic alone, as in the case of the Upasads and the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice.

Or it may be restricted by the indicative mark (liṅga), because the indicative mark possesses that quality. MS 7.4.4.
Or rather, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) would be determined by the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Which one? That which has the indicative mark;

and the Vedic [procedure] has the indicative mark. Therefore, it is the Vedic one. But what, then, is the indicative mark? First, regarding the *saurya* oblation of rice, it is heard: "At the *prayāja* offering, he offers a *kṛṣṇala* weight of gold."

"Thus [it is said]: 'In the same way, one chooses a Hotṛ priest for the Pitṛyajña who is not an Ārṣeya. By these indicative marks (liṅga), it is known that there is a Vedic *itikartavyatā* (procedure). How so? Because they are its qualities (*tadguṇatvāt*).
For these—namely the *prayāja*s and so forth—are the qualities of the Vedic *apūrva*. And if this procedure belonging to that [Vedic *apūrva*] were applied [here],..."

Therefore, these [subsidiary acts] exist within these primary rites; thus, statements such as "At each *prayāja* offering, one offers a *kṛṣṇala* weight of gold" become applicable. Consequently, the Vedic procedure (*itikartavyatā*) should be restricted [to the Vedic context].
