because the gender possesses a positive quality}, or rather, because it is preceded by what is not logical, wherever there may be statements that are constant restatements (nityānuvāda). // MS_7,4.5 //
Or rather, it should not be so—that [the procedure] is Vedic. For what reason? Because by these indicative marks (*liṅga*), the Vedic [procedure] cannot be restricted.
Why? Because they are preceded by what is illogical (*anyāya*). For a statement that is preceded by logic is what establishes [a conclusion]; and these [marks] are not preceded by logic.

For the application of a Vedic injunction is not logical, since it is already restricted to the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices by means of context and other such factors. How then are these indicative marks (liṅga) to be understood? It is said:

they apply where there are statements that are constant restatements (nityānuvāda). In this case, for instance, [the text says]: "He cuts half of the sacrificial grass (barhis), but not the other half."
Wherever the sacrificial grass (barhis) shall be; for what reason? Because it is said [in the scripture] regarding the sacrificial grass that exists.
And in this case, there is no sacrificial grass (*barhis*). "He does not choose a *hotṛ*, nor an *ārṣeya*" will be a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*).

[57] But surely, being a permanent restatement, it would be purposeless. What can be done with that which has no meaning? The statement "at each *prayāja* he offers a *kṛṣṇala* grain" will pertain to the *prayājas*. But how, in this instance, can both the *prayājas* and the *kṛṣṇala*-offering be spoken of?
For in that case, the sentence would be split. If that is so, then [the text] will not mention the *prayāja* offerings; rather, it will enjoin the offering of *kṛṣṇala* grains during the *prayāja*.

Since the offering of *kṛṣṇala* grains cannot be performed when the *prayāja* offerings do not exist, one will perform the *prayāja* offerings by implication. Therefore, there is no restriction by the Vedic indicative power (*liṅga*); according to the stated reasoning, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is worldly.

And it cannot be said that they exist simultaneously;
furthermore, because the qualities are mutually contradictory, there would have to be a conceptualization of them according to their respective objects.

To this he says: "Now, why do both procedures not operate simultaneously? What would follow from this? In this way, the equal requirement for the ritual acts (*karman*) would not be sublated on either side. If they were to operate simultaneously, and the act were performed independently by one [procedure], the operation of the second would be contradicted. Therefore, because their simultaneous operation is mutually contradictory, the determination of the meaning follows as it has been stated.

It may be so; the meaning is that there would be the activity of a single [moment]. How does the conceptualization of phenomena according to their actual state arise from the activity of a single [moment]?

Those phenomena which have arisen during the activity toward specific effects, those very same ones occur here as well toward those same effects. Otherwise, the phenomena of the second [moment] would be inconsistent with the previous phenomena.
Because those tasks have been accomplished, such is the conceptualization of reality (*yathārtha-kalpanā*) that arises from a single activity (*pravṛtti*).

Therefore, by the statement "there should be a conceptualization of reality," it is meant that there is a single activity; and within that single activity, there is what is called "worldly activity" (*laukikī pravṛtti*), according to the very principle already explained. [58] {7/279}

But it should be restricted because of its being a constituent part, since qualities are denotative;
because of the connection, it is like the denotation itself, just as "dhenu" [is connected] with "kiśora."

The word "tu" (but) serves to set aside the previous position. It should not be the case that the worldly procedure (*itikartavyatā*) applies; rather, the Vedic procedure should be prescribed. Why? Because of its participation (*bhāgitvāt*). The Vedic procedure also participates in the performance, for it too is the procedure for the *apūrva*. And since both participate equally, the Vedic [procedure] [is to be adopted].

It must be so. Because these are denoters (*abhidhāna*). These elements, such as the *prayāja* offerings and others, when seen in the *saurya* and other rites, become denoters of this matter; that is to say, they serve as indicators of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) belonging to the Vedic archetype.

Why? Because of their connection. For these are connected with that very procedure; therefore, by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), they cause it to be understood, just like a denoter. As, for example, in the *kauṇḍapāyināmayana*, the term "agnihotra" [denotes the borrowed procedure].
Thus, a designation (*abhidhāna*) is the denoter of an action;
it brings along those properties (*dharma*) that accompany that action.

Since this designation would not be appropriate here if those properties were absent, the existence of those properties in that [action] is understood. In the same way, here too, the perception of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth is non-existent in the Vedic [text].

Regarding the statement "it is appropriate," its existence here too will be understood. [Objection: But surely, in the absence of a logical principle (*nyāya*), an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not a cause. [Response: That is true;
however, the logical principle has already been stated [in the rule] by means of the term "participation" (*bhāgitvāt*).
As for the argument that "worldly practice proceeds from what is observed," we reply:
even if it were to proceed from what is observed, nevertheless, only the Vedic [practice] should be regulated. How so? Just as a cow [is milked] by means of its calf.
For example,
the expression "a black calf-cow" (*kṛṣṇakiśorā dhenuḥ*). Although the word *dhenu* is observed to be applied to a cow that gives milk, [it is here used for a female calf].

Nevertheless, because of the commonality of the designation, since the term "horse-cow" (aśvadhenu) also applies to a mare, it is recognized as referring to a mare by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the colt. Likewise here, although the worldly application is observed, nevertheless, because it shares a commonality of procedure (*itikartavyatā*), it is to be understood as Vedic by means of that indicative mark. Or, because of the equality of their origins, there may be existence according to one's respective capacity.

Alternatively, there is no restriction based on indicative mark (*liṅga*). Why? Because the origins (*utpatti*) are equal. The origins of the ritual elements (*dharma*), such as the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, are equal for all [principal rites] like the *āgneya* sacrifice insofar as they function as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) to those principals;

they do not function as subsidiaries to one another. What follows from this? If the *anuyāja* offerings and so forth were to be subsidiaries of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, then wherever the principal [rite] is located...
In that case, by the observation of the *prayājas*, the *anuyājas* and so forth would be inferred as being subordinate members (*aṅga*);
however, when these are equal in their status as primary elements (*samapradhāna*),
then by the observation of the *prayājas*, it is permissible for the *prayājas* themselves to be inferred [as primary].

Or rather, the properties belong to the *prayāja*s, but not to the *anuyāja*s and so forth. Therefore, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not determinative. As for the argument that it is "like the name" (*abhidhānavat*), we reply:
that is appropriate in that case, for there, a word belonging to one thing is applied to another and thereby [conveys] its properties.

It has been stated that [the text] extends [the application]. Furthermore, that is an injunction (*vidhi*), such as "it should be offered like the Agnihotra. This one, however, is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Therefore, in this case, there is no application even of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth;
how much less of the *anuyāja* offerings and so forth? Consequently, the comparison is unequal.

"Like the designation. Therefore, the application (bhāva) should be according to the respective context (*adhikāra*). Those ritual elements (*dharma*) which are prescribed for the sake of a specific new undertaking (*apūrva-adhikāra*) should belong to that very undertaking alone.
If this is so, then by the verbal suffix in the statement "one should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya," there is the origination of the injunction of the primary act.

And let there be a statement regarding the remaining [auxiliaries]. How so? Because an auxiliary that is being described as not an auxiliary cannot serve any purpose. Therefore, for the auxiliaries established by that [statement], there will be a determination of their specific distinctions based on these indicative marks (*liṅga*). Regarding this, it is said:

And a statement regarding both the origin and the supplementary details is contradictory in the case of a single [act]. (MS 7.4.9) *{7/285: Cf. Maitr.S. 2.2.2; Tait.S. 2.3.2}
In a single word, the origination of the primary act and the prescription of its subsidiaries cannot both occur.

Why? Because the primary act, once originated, requires the subsidiaries; and it is through that requirement that they are grasped. Therefore, this too is not tenable. Furthermore, if the subsidiaries were also prescribed by the word "nirvapet" (he should offer), [it would be impossible].

Consequently, there would also be a connection with the fruit for those [subsidiaries], and thus their status as subsidiaries (*aṅgatva*) itself would be contradicted. Therefore, this argument also does not hold. For this reason, the means is precisely that which is worldly, as previously stated.
[Note: Or rather, the remainder of the injunction (*vidhyanta*) should proceed according to the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*) when there is a scriptural injunction (*codanā*).
For there is indeed the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga). MS 7.4.10.

Or rather, it is the *vidhyanta* (the end of the injunction) that operates in an injunction such as that concerning the *saurya* sacrifice, not worldly customs (*dharma*). But what is this so-called *vidhyanta*? The end of an injunction is the *vidhyanta*. Now, what is an injunction (*vidhi*)? It is that sentence, upon perceiving which a person engages in some purpose or desists from something.

That is the *vidhi* (injunction). For by means of it, a matter is enjoined. Just as in common worldly usage one says, "Devadatta, drive the white cow hither," where "drive hither" (*abhyāja*) and so forth constitute the beginning of the injunction;

the rest is the end. Likewise in the Veda, in the statement "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]," the phrase "should sacrifice" is the beginning of the injunction, and the subsequent portion is the end of the injunction.

The entire *Pauroḍāśika* Brāhmaṇa is devoid of its own primary injunction (*pradhānavidhi*). Therefore, this opening of the injunction (*vidhyādi*), joined with that [Brāhmaṇa], impels a person toward the accomplishment of a specific transcendental result (*apūrva*). Consequently, that [Brāhmaṇa] constitutes its conclusion (*anta*). Similarly, in the case of "One should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), there is the opening of the injunction; the *Saumika* Brāhmaṇa is its conclusion (*vidhyanta*). This is what is called an "injunctional conclusion" (*vidhyanta*).

And in these [rites] such as the Saurya and others, there is the beginning of the injunction (vidhyādi), but there is no end of the injunction (vidhyanta). In these cases too, that end of the injunction would have to be supplied. How so? A sentence that is incomplete must be completed either by supplying an ellipsis (adhyāhāra) or...

Or [the connection may be established] by means of the assumption of an interrupted sequence (*vyavahita-kalpanā*). In that regard, the assumption of an interrupted sequence is superior to *adhyāhāra* (supplying an ellipsis). For in the case of *adhyāhāra*, something not heard in the text would have to be imagined;

whereas in the other case, there is a connection with what is actually heard. Therefore, a portion of a *brāhmaṇa* passage, though separated [in the text], is assumed to complete this [sentence]. Just as: "For spring, he sacrifices *kapiñjala* birds; for summer, he sacrifices *kalaviṅka* birds. [And so on.]
Thus [it is said]. By that, the Vedic procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is obtained.
If that *brāhmaṇa* passage is imagined to be within it, then it does not exist there. This results in what is called "the peacock's dance. For example:
When a peacock dances, one part is revealed while another is concealed; so too here, this is concealed and that is revealed.
This is not a fault, for its existence there is perceptible, whereas here it is inferential. And the inferential does not subvert the perceptible. [Objection: In that case, it would not apply here.
Because it contradicts direct perception. It might be so, if there were a contradiction; however, there is no contradiction. That will apply there as well, and this has already been stated here.

"Or rather, the end of the injunction (*vidhyanta*) should proceed according to the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*) when there is a scriptural injunction (*codanā*). It is said: "What does 'according to the model' mean? He replies: "In the eighth [book], he will establish the rule regarding the model sacrifice, stating 'this is its model. To that, it is said:

Or rather, the end of the injunction (*vidhyanta*) should proceed just as it does from the archetype (*prakṛti*). Whichever is the archetype of that rite— whether for one whose archetype is the Āgneya,
or for one whose [archetype] is the Agnīṣomīya— from that very archetype [the details should be taken].
"In every case, [the procedure] is from that of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice.

Now, why is a worldly (laukika) ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) not postulated? It is said: because there is no worldly injunction (*vidhi*), the ritual procedure itself does not exist. How then could it be postulated? He replied:
"Let worldly *itikartavyatā* (procedural requirements) be obtained; what is the use of postulating a Vedic injunction? It is replied:
"For here the *itikartavyatā* is indeed Vedic, not worldly. Why? Because in this way, the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*), such as the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, becomes supported."
"tasyābhyāja" is the beginning of the rule}*
an unmentioned word would have to be supplied}* *{7/291:
he who [is the performer] of a particular action}*
Because it has the characteristic of being a reason, that which lacks the characteristic [of inference] would be worldly [inference]. (MS 7.4.11)

If the Vedic means is accepted because of an indicative mark (*liṅga*), then, by that same principle, the worldly means would apply where there is no such mark. In a ritual action where no indicative mark whatsoever exists, the worldly procedure should be the rule. For example:
"One whose kinsmen have departed should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni. [62] {7/295} NOTES:

Because the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is as before and because of the commonality of the injunctive word (*codanā-śabda*), [the rite] may be determined even by a single [mark], just as by the "pot-full" (*sthālīpulāka*) method.

To this it is replied: it would be so if the Vedic means were based on indicative marks (*liṅga*). But that is not based on indicative marks. What, then, is its basis? It is based on the end of the injunction (*vidhyanta*). The end of the injunction is also preceded by logic (*nyāya*), and that logic is the same for all modified rites (*vaikṛta*) that possess indicative marks.

And why? Because of the commonality of the word *codanā*. In the injunction for ritual action (*karmacodanā*), the verbal form is identical. In every case, there is the beginning of the injunction (*vidhyādi*), but not the end of the injunction (*vidhyanta*). Furthermore, the connection with the end of the injunction heard elsewhere is equal in terms of its requirement. Thus, this logical mark (*liṅga*), when observed even in a single instance, makes known that all [other instances] possessing the same logic are likewise endowed with *dharma*. Just as one knows the ripeness of other grains in a cooking pot by crushing a single *pulāka* grain among those being cooked equally.
The reason for this is equal to that for others, namely, its established status. Therefore, in all cases, the Vedic procedure (*itikartavyatā*) applies.
Now, as for what was said—that the worldly procedure is one whose activity is observed—we reply:

This is taught as an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*). And that which is an inference based on general observation is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only when it is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*). But this [inference] is deviant. For we observe that sacrifices such as the *gaṇayāga* do not have such a procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Therefore, "because they proceed from what is observed" is not a valid reason.
As for the argument that because they share the character of Vedic [acts], their indicative marks (*liṅga*) must be preceded by [Vedic authority], to this we reply:

It is said that [the *codanā*] is the cause. And its existence is preceded by the word (*śabda*). Moreover, this [existence] is understood through the word in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, but not everywhere. Therefore, there is no [independent] status as a constituent part (*bhāgitva*). Consequently, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is obtained only through the final injunction (*vidhyanta*), and not otherwise. Now, why are these modified (*vaikṛta*) sentences not accepted as being incomplete?

"What is the use of filling these? Those that are deficient would be meaningless. Let them be; what is the harm? It is not fitting for the learned to accept them. [The opponent says: 'It must have arisen from negligence. [The author replies: There is no negligence regarding even a single syllable or a single vowel-measure (*mātrā*). How could it occur in such an extensive treatise? Why? Because the oral tradition (*sāṃpradāyika*) is the same."

Thus it has been said. Even the delusion of the learned would not persist for many thousands of ages. And their completion is appropriate when considered in relation to those [who possess the marks]. Therefore, they do not accept [the texts] as deficient. Consequently, this is the Vedic procedure (*itikartavyatā*). *NOTES: {7/296: For those who possess the marks and those who do not possess the marks}*

*{7/297: The fact that [the procedure] is a previously unknown *itikartavyatā* (manner of performance) regarding the status of being a participant}* *{7/298: This is known as "this"*} *{7/300: And the traditional transmission is equal [in both cases] (MS 1.2.8)*.

In a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*), that which pertains to the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāhika*) [should be performed] because it is its archetype; however, due to the addition of further elements, it should be designated by the name of the one-day rite (*aikāhika*), just like the one-day rite itself.
Having prescribed the sacrificial session (*sattra*) with the rule, "Those desiring offspring should undertake the Gavāmayana," it is further recorded:
"Jyotis, Gauḥ, Āyuḥ..."

Thus [it is said]; he will state that in the Gavāmayana, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) is that of the Dvādaśāha, as in the rule "of the Dvādaśāha among groups. In that case, the properties (*dharma*) of the Dvādaśāha are obtained through the extended application (*codaka*). The individual properties of the one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*) are also obtained by their respective names. Among those, the Dvādaśāha properties which are not in conflict with the one-day sacrifice properties [are to be adopted].

These are performed according to what has been previously established. When there is a conflict, a doubt arises: should the ritual procedure (*dharma*) of the *dvādaśāha* (twelve-day sacrifice) be performed, or that of the *ekāha* (one-day sacrifice)? What is the prima facie view? On this point, the Sūtra itself provides the starting point: "In a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), the [procedure] of the *dvādaśāha* applies, because it is its archetype (*prakṛti*). Since the *jyotiṣṭoma* is the archetype of the *dvādaśāha*, the details are obtained through the extended application (*vidhyanta*) of that very archetype.

[Objection: But in that case, the name [of the sacrifice] would be contradicted. [Reply: The name, such as *Jyotis* and so forth, will not be contradicted. It will be accounted for by the addition of further elements. Those modifications of the hymns (*stotra*) and recitations (*śastra*) which are additional to those of the *jyotiṣṭoma*—[these additions will justify the specific names].

Because of the addition of that [element], as in the case of the *ekāha*. Just as in that very *jyotiṣṭoma* which is an *ekāha*, the word "jyotis" occurs due to the addition of something extra; for while the elements belonging to the *jyotiṣṭoma* exist [in the *ekāha*], they are absent in the [simple] *jyotiṣṭoma*. This word is intended to signify the additional properties (*dharma*). [64] {7}

Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the twelve-day (*dvādaśāha*) rites regarding those [elements] that are additional. Therefore, the set of ritual properties (*dharma-jāta*) belonging to the twelve-day sacrifice that are not contradictory should be performed. This is another interpretation of the rule: "From the arrival of the additional [elements], it should bear that name, just like the one-day (*ekāha*) sacrifices. Those certain ritual properties which are mentioned as being additional to those of the one-day sacrifices in the context of the twelve-day sacrifice—such as "the *abhiplava* occurs every day," "it occurs every day"—from the arrival of those additional ones, it should bear that name. Thus, this day of the twelve-day sacrifice is called "Jyotis" or "Āyus."

How so? Like the case of a single-day sacrifice (*ekāha*). Just as in that very single-day sacrifice, the term "Jyotis" and so forth is used when specific additional properties (*vaiśeṣika-dharma*) belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma have been introduced, so too here, due to the commonality of the introduction of additional [elements], the term will be used figuratively (*gauṇa*). For example, because of the presence of the *pṛṣṭha* chants belonging to the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*), the single-day sacrifice Viśvajit is called a "six-day rite. They call that single-day sacrifice a "six-day rite."

Thus it is here as well: if [the name] is figurative, it does not bring about [the acquisition of] [the rite]; therefore, there is no acquisition of the ritual property (*dharma*) from a mere name. *Notes: {7/301: Tāṇḍya Brāhmaṇa 4.1.4, 7}*
the Gaurīvita}* *{7/308: Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 18.15}*
And because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*). (MS 7.4.14)

This is known from an indicative mark (*liṅga*), namely that it should be performed according to the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāhika*). What is the indicative mark? It is: "With two [hair-cuts] he cuts the hair; with two, the skin; with two, the blood; with two, the flesh.
Having thus enumerated six pairs, it says:

"In that there are twelve *upasads*, [the text] shows the twelve-fold *upasat* as a characteristic of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), saying, 'one thereby perfects the self. This is appropriate if a set of twelve-day characteristics that are contradictory [to the one-day sacrifice] must be performed; otherwise, the six-fold *upasat* belonging to the one-day sacrifice [would apply]."

Therefore, we see that what belongs to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) must be performed. Likewise, there is this further indicative mark (*liṅga*): "If they were to slaughter an additional animal at the *ekādaśinī*, one's dear enemy would not be left behind [unovercome]. But if they were to combine two animals together..."
They should not shorten their lifespan.
If these cattle, which possess the Brahman, are sacrificed, no unpleasantness exceeds one's enemy;
therefore, one should not shorten one's lifespan.

In the *ekādaśinī*, [the text] demonstrates the practice (*dharma*) pertaining to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāhika*). How so? When there is a distribution (*vihāra*), an excess of animals occurs. And because of the fear of such excess, there is a grouping of two by two. If the practice of a single-day sacrifice were to apply, there would be no distribution. In that case, this demonstrated rule would not be tenable. Therefore, the procedure of the twelve-day sacrifice must be performed.

*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 6.2.5;

Or rather, because [the word] denotes the ritual act (*kratu*), those [additional elements] are not non-verbal (*aśabdattva*). (MS 7.4.15)

Nor is the procedure of the twelve-day sacrifice to be performed. What then? That of the one-day sacrifice. For what reason? Because the procedure of the twelve-day sacrifice is obtained through the general rule (*codaka*), whereas that of the one-day sacrifice is obtained through the name. And the name is more powerful than the general rule. Why? Because it is directly perceived. The name is directly perceived, while the general rule is inferential.
But is not the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) also directly perceived? True; the ritual procedure is directly perceived in the archetype (*prakṛti*), but in the ectype (*vikṛti*) it is inferred.
However, the name, on the other hand, is directly perceived even in the ectype.
Direct perception is more authoritative than inference;
therefore, the rite should be performed on a single day.
Now, it was argued that the name [of the sacrifice] refers to the qualified person (adhikārin). To this, it is replied:

There is no word for the additional [verses]. There is no verbal designation for the additional [verses]. It has been stated that these words, *jyotis* and so forth, are names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*), according to the principle: "Or rather, it should be a name, because it is something new at its origin" (JS 1.4.2).

As for the argument that "it should bear that name because of the arrival of the additional [verses]," we reply: the arrival of the additional [verses] is due to a direct scriptural statement (*vacana*), not by virtue of the name. As for what was said...

"Because in their absence, the word [denoting them] does not exist. These [elements], such as longevity (*āyus*) and so forth, are never absent from the *jyotiṣṭoma*. How, then, is the non-existence of the word observed in their absence? As for the claim that "in the *jyotiṣṭoma* there is no word such as 'light' (*jyotis*) and so forth," this is because it is a different ritual action (*karmāntara*). The word "longevity" and so forth does not exist in the *jyotiṣṭoma*, not because of the absence of the properties (*dharma*), but because it is a one-day rite (*aikāhika*) with a conflicting set of properties that must be performed. Due to the addition of further elements, it would bear that name. This is the second explanation and resolution of the point regarding "like the one-day rite" (*ekāhavat*).

If it were secondary, it would be a mere restatement and thus meaningless. Therefore, by the reasoning previously stated, it is a name that brings about the application of the ritual details (*dharma*).
The gender [of a compound] would be a property of the aggregate, because it serves that purpose, just like a substance. (MS 1.4.2) MS 7.4.16.

Now, as for the indicative mark (liṅga) that was taught—the observation of the twelve-fold attendance (*upasat*)—its refutation is stated: "The indicative mark would be a property of the aggregate. This indicative mark would be a property of the aggregate.

The *dvādaśāha* is a collection of days; it is enjoined for the sake of a result, as in the injunction: "Those desiring prosperity should undertake the *dvādaśāha*. The *gavāmayana* is also another collection of days, and it is prescribed for that very same purpose—the accomplishment of the result. Through the substitution of that function (*tatkāryāpatti*), it adopts the ritual details (*dharmas*) of the *dvādaśāha*.
Nor [is it extended] by *codaka*,

as in the case of a substance. Just as the properties (*dharma*) that are prescribed for rice as a substance are obtained for its substitutes which take over its function, so it is not [extended] by *codaka*.

in the case of wild rice (nīvāra) which has taken on the function of that [sacrificial grain] as a substitute}—it is not so, because the meaning pertains to the substance; for the aggregate is subordinate.* MS_7.4.17.

This is not correct. Why? Because it is a property of the *artha* (the purpose/meaning). The meaning is that it is a property of the *apūrva* (the transcendental result). The property of the *apūrva* is the state of having twelve *upasads*, not a property of the collection (*saṃghāta*). Why? Because the collection is subordinate (*guṇa*). In this context, the days (*ahāni*) are the primary elements; thus, by the expression "by the twelve-day [rite]," the number twelve [is predicated of the days].

Their quality (*guṇa*) means the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). It is precisely the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) that is understood as the object of action, not the qualifier. Just as when it is said, "Let the king's man be brought," it is the man who is brought, not the king. And likewise, [as in the following example:]...

When it is said, "Devadatta eats delicacies," neither vegetables nor soup are understood; rather, that which is the primary thing is what is understood. What follows from this? From this it follows that the days possess the fruit, not the aggregate. And the ritual properties (dharmas) belong to that which possesses the fruit. Therefore, the state of having twelve *upasads* is not a property of the aggregate. Thus [67].

If, however, the ritual properties (*dharma*) are not obtained in the Gavāmayana because they have been superseded by the requirements of the task at hand, then this [objection] is not a valid refutation.

*{7/321: E2: the state of being a twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāhatva*)}
Through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), there would be the acquisition of properties (dharma) in the case of substances. 6.4.18.

As for what was stated, "like a substance" (*dravyavat*): that is appropriate in the case of substances. For in those cases, wild rice (*nīvāra*) which has undergone the functional transformation (*kāryāpatti*) of rice acquires the properties of that [rice] by virtue of having undergone that functional transformation. Here, however, the reason adduced—that the state of having twelve *upasads* is not at all a property of the aggregate—is not established. Therefore, "like a substance" is not a valid example.
He asks: "In that case, how is this observation of a logical mark (liṅgadarśana) [to be understood]? To this it is replied: [as stated in the notes].
The observation of a mark (liṅga) belongs to one who is already engaged in activity. (MS 7.4.19)

In the Gavāmayana sacrifice, the first day is the twelve-day [rite], the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra. Its characteristic feature is the performance of twelve Upasad rites. In adopting that [number], there is favor shown to the primary [element]. In adopting six Upasad rites, however, there would be favor shown to the secondary elements such as the Jyotis and others;
for what purpose would one wish to bypass the favor due to the primary element at its proper time?

It does not exist. Therefore, for the sake of favoring that [sacrifice], there is the presence of twelve *upasads*. Thus, this observation applies to that which is fixed by the primary application (*mukhyayā pravṛttyā*), and not by extension through the rule of transfer (*codaka*). For the rule of transfer is weaker than the name. And it will be stated:
"When there is a conflict between contradictory properties, the property of the majority shall prevail;
or rather, that of the principal [element] prevails because it is enjoined as something not previously established, as in common worldly practice.
Now, as for the second observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that was mentioned:
The vision of the monastery on the eleventh day. Regarding this, it is said: [68] {7/328} NOTES:
*{7/324: E2: kāraṇaṃ}*
Therefore, [it is] by way of the primary [meaning].
The observation regarding the monastery is that the specific [injunctions] which are not introduced as general rules (anārabhyavāda) serve the purpose of the archetype (prakṛti). MS_7.4.20.

The performance of the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice is prescribed without reference to a specific context. The animals should originate from that [set] as their starting point. Thus, they should be offered day after day in successive order.
On the first day they should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni; on the second, a ewe dedicated to Sarasvatī; on the third, a brown animal dedicated to Soma.
The offering to Varuṇa is at the end. Then again, during the turnings back,
they should sacrifice a goat to Agni on the first day,
and a ewe to Sarasvatī on the second day.

"A brown one for Soma on the third day, and one belonging to Varuṇa at the end. Since these are isolated injunctions (*anārabhyavāda*), they apply to the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*) and thus enter into the Jyotiṣṭoma.
However, because there is no plurality of days in that [Jyotiṣṭoma], they cannot apply there; consequently, they move to another archetype, the Dvādaśāha. There too—
Furthermore, [the objection] that "it is not logical for there to be a rotation of the Jyotis and other sacrifices" refers to the third *prakṛti* (archetype) entered into the Gavām Ayana;
such is the view regarding what has arrived in this manner.
For just as cattle are the source [of their products], if those cattle were indeed the source; [F2 (fn.): if those cattle were the source];
likewise [E2 omits "tathā"].
Furthermore, [in the case] of the Jyotis and other [sacrifices], when they undergo their cyclic rotations,
they arrive at the Gavāmayana.
